p4-82.q: 500 is an unhandled error in this server; 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from upstream; 503 Service Unavailable means overloaded or down for maintenance (often with Retry-After); 504 means the gateway timed out waiting for upstream.
i: ALB 502 often means the target closed the connection or returned malformed responses (keep-alive timeout mismatches).
ALB 504 means the target didn't respond within the idle timeout.
429 Too Many Requests for rate limiting.
503 should include Retry-After when planned maintenance or overload.
f: Why might ALB return 502 intermittently?
Target keep-alive timeout shorter than ALB idle timeout, so connections close unexpectedly.
What does 503 from ALB mean?
No healthy targets registered.
p4-82.y: 500 means something broke inside our service. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer got an invalid response from the service behind it, for example the container crashed. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily overloaded or in maintenance, ideally with a Retry-After header. When I troubleshoot, these tell me which layer to look at first.
x: These are server-side errors, and each one points to a different layer, which is very useful when troubleshooting.

500 Internal Server Error means something failed inside our own service, usually an unhandled exception. The fix is in our code or data, so I go to the logs with the correlation id. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer, like our ALB or API gateway, got an invalid response from the service behind it. Often the container crashed, closed the connection, or isn't listening on the right port. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily unable to handle requests, for example overloaded, in maintenance, or the load balancer has no healthy targets. Ideally it includes a Retry-After header. And 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream took too long.
So when I see these, I know where to look. 500, our application logs. 502 or 503, the ALB target health and ECS task events. 504, slow queries or downstream calls.
During a deployment issue, a spike of 503s told us that new tasks were failing health checks, not that the code was throwing. I can walk through how I'd debug each.

p4-83.q: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) are simple classes or records that shape exactly what an API accepts or returns. They decouple the API contract from the database schema, prevent over-posting and data leaks, allow versioning, and let each endpoint carry only what it needs.
i: Records are ideal: immutable, value equality, concise.
Map with explicit code, Mapperly (source generated) or AutoMapper (now commercial for new versions).
Separate request and response DTOs.
c:
public sealed record CreateShipmentRequest(int SiteId, int KitCount, DateOnly ShipDate);
public sealed record ShipmentResponse(int Id, string Status, DateTimeOffset? DeliveredAt);
f: AutoMapper or manual mapping?
Manual or source-generated mapping is explicit and fast; AutoMapper hides errors until runtime.
Should DTOs have logic?
No, only data and validation attributes.
p4-83.y: A DTO, or data transfer object, is a simple class that defines exactly what the API sends or receives. It keeps the API contract separate from the database entities. So I can change the database without breaking clients, avoid exposing sensitive fields, and prevent over-posting. I use C# records for DTOs.
p4-83.k: dto, data transfer object, api contract, records
x: A DTO, or Data Transfer Object, is a simple class or record that defines exactly what data crosses a boundary, like what an API accepts in a request or returns in a response. It holds data only, with no business behaviour.

The main reason to use DTOs is to separate the API contract from the internal model. Database entities change for internal reasons, and if they were the contract, every schema change could break clients. DTOs also let us hide internal or sensitive fields, prevent over-posting, because input DTOs only contain fields the client may set, put validation attributes on inputs, and shape data per use case, like a short list item versus a full detail view.

In our services, DTOs are C# records, which are concise and immutable. For reads, we project directly into DTOs with a Select in EF Core, so SQL only fetches the needed columns. For writes, we map request DTOs to entities in the service layer.
In a clinical system this separation is important, because we must never accidentally expose something like treatment assignment data. I can explain mapping options like Mapster or manual mapping.

p4-84.q: Exposing EF entities directly leaks the schema and sensitive fields, couples clients to database changes, enables over-posting, and causes serialization cycles and lazy-loading surprises. DTOs give a stable, safe contract.
i: Navigation properties create cycles (JSON ReferenceHandler is a band-aid).
Lazy loading during serialization creates N+1 queries.
Projection with Select into DTOs also generates efficient SQL.
Security example: an entity with IsUnblinded or audit fields accidentally serialized to the client.
f: How do you return data efficiently?
Project to DTOs in the query so only needed columns are selected.
What is over-posting?
Clients setting fields they shouldn't by sending extra properties.
p4-84.y: Returning EF entities directly ties the API to the database design, so a schema change breaks clients. It can also leak sensitive or internal fields, create circular references when serializing, trigger lazy loading, and allow over-posting on input. In a clinical system, accidentally exposing an unblinding field would be serious, so we always map to DTOs.
p4-84.k: ef entities, dto, security, over-posting, api design
x: Exposing EF entities directly from an API looks quick, but it causes several real problems.

First, coupling. The database schema becomes the public contract, so renaming a column or splitting a table breaks clients. Second, data leakage. Entities often have internal or sensitive fields, and adding a new column could silently expose it. Third, over-posting. If you bind input directly to an entity, a client can set fields it shouldn't, like a status or an approval flag. Fourth, serialization problems. Navigation properties cause circular references, and with lazy loading, serializing can trigger many extra queries. And fifth, performance: you usually load full entities, and their relationships, instead of only the columns needed.
In a clinical trial system, the leakage risk is serious. Accidentally exposing a blinding-related field would be a major compliance issue, not just a bug.

So in our services, every endpoint uses DTOs. Reads use Select projections into DTOs, and writes map request DTOs to entities in the service layer, with tests that check responses contain only expected fields. I can explain how we keep the mapping code manageable.

p4-85.q: A DTO is the transport shape between layers or services (API contracts); a ViewModel is shaped for one UI view and may include display-only data like dropdown options. In APIs we mostly use DTOs; ViewModels belong to MVC or front-end code.
i: BFF responses are close to view models for a specific screen.
Keep both free of business logic.
In our APIs, request DTOs (commands) and response DTOs (views) are separate records.
ViewModels belong to Razor/MVC; in React the client shapes its own view state.
f: Can a DTO be a ViewModel?
Sometimes, if the API is designed for one screen.
What is a command object?
An input DTO that represents an intent, as in CQRS.
p4-85.y: A DTO carries data across a boundary, like an API request or response, and has no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for a specific screen in server-rendered MVC or Razor pages, and can include display-specific data. With a React front end, our APIs return DTOs, and the client shapes its own view state.
x: A DTO and a ViewModel are both simple data classes, but they serve different purposes.

A DTO, Data Transfer Object, carries data across a boundary, like between an API and its clients, or between services. It's a transport contract, shaped for the use case and kept stable, with no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for one specific screen, usually in server-rendered MVC or Razor Pages. It contains exactly what that view needs, and can include display-only data, like formatted dates, dropdown lists or flags that control what's shown.
In an API-first architecture with a separate front end, like React, the server mostly deals with DTOs. The front end builds its own view state from them, so the ViewModel concept moves to the client.

In our system, the APIs return DTOs, for example a ShipmentSummaryDto for lists and a ShipmentDetailDto for one shipment. The React front end then combines them into what each screen needs. In older MVC parts of the system, we had ViewModels with select lists for forms. I can talk about how we design DTOs for list versus detail endpoints.

p4-86.q: [ApiController] turns on API behaviours: attribute routing is required, invalid model state returns 400 ProblemDetails automatically, binding sources are inferred ([FromBody] for complex types, [FromRoute]/[FromQuery] for simple ones), multipart/form-data is inferred for IFormFile, and error status codes get ProblemDetails.
i: Can be applied at assembly level.
Customise the automatic 400 with InvalidModelStateResponseFactory or disable with SuppressModelStateInvalidFilter.
Services are inferred for parameters registered in DI (.NET 7+).
Since .NET 7, parameters registered in DI are inferred as services in [ApiController] actions without [FromServices].
f: Why do some actions not hit my breakpoint with bad input?
The automatic 400 filter returns before the action runs.
How do you customise the 400 response?
Configure ApiBehaviorOptions.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory.
p4-86.y: The ApiController attribute turns on API-friendly behaviours: it automatically returns a 400 with validation errors when the model is invalid, infers where parameters come from, like body or route, requires attribute routing, and returns errors as ProblemDetails. It removes a lot of repetitive code from every action.
x: ApiController is an attribute I put on API controllers, and it switches on a set of behaviours that make building Web APIs simpler and more consistent.

First, automatic validation responses. If the model is invalid, it returns a 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body before the action runs, so I don't need "if not ModelState IsValid" in every action. Second, binding source inference. Complex types come from the body, route values from the route, and simple types from the query string, so fewer FromBody attributes. Third, attribute routing is required, so routes are explicit. Fourth, error status codes are returned as ProblemDetails, the standard error format.
It's usually applied on a base controller, or at assembly level, so every API controller gets it.

In our services, we put it on a shared base controller and customised InvalidModelStateResponseFactory, so validation errors also include our correlation id. That way, every 400 from every service has the same shape, and support can trace it in the logs. I can explain how it compares with minimal APIs, which handle this differently.

p4-87.q: Routing maps URLs to endpoints. Attribute routing puts templates on controllers and actions ([Route("api/studies/{id}")]) and is the standard for APIs; conventional routing uses one template in Program.cs such as {controller}/{action}/{id?}, typical for MVC sites.
i: Route constraints ({id:int}, {date:datetime}) and tokens ([controller]).
Minimal APIs use MapGet/MapPost with the same routing engine.
Avoid ambiguous routes; route order and specificity resolve matches.
Route templates support optional parameters ({id?}), defaults and catch-all ({*path}).
f: What's a route constraint for?
Matching only valid formats; not for input validation.
Can you mix both?
Yes, but APIs usually stick to attribute routing.
p4-87.y: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it. Attribute routing puts the route on the controller or action, like Route api slash shipments, which is clear and flexible, and it's the standard for APIs. Conventional routing uses one central pattern, like controller slash action slash id, which is common in older MVC apps.
p4-87.k: routing, attribute routing, conventional routing, endpoints
x: Routing is how ASP.NET Core maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it, like a controller action or a minimal API handler.

There are two styles. Attribute routing puts the route template directly on the controller and actions, for example Route "api/studies/{studyId}/shipments" on the controller, and HttpGet "{id}" on an action. It's explicit, supports route constraints like int, and matches REST resource design well, so it's the standard for APIs and is required with ApiController. Conventional routing defines one central pattern in Program.cs, like "controller/action/id", and all controllers follow it. It's common in traditional MVC websites, where URLs follow a predictable pattern.
Minimal APIs use their own MapGet and MapPost calls, which are essentially attribute routing in code, and route groups help share prefixes and policies.

In our services, we use attribute routing with versioned, resource-based routes, like api/v1/studies/{studyId}/shipments. That makes the URL design visible right in the code and in the OpenAPI document. I can explain route constraints or versioning next.

p4-88.q: I accept query parameters such as ?status=Shipped&siteId=12&sortBy=shipDate&desc=true, apply them to IQueryable before paging so SQL does the work, and allow-list sortable and filterable fields to prevent injection and slow queries.
i: Build queries conditionally; never concatenate SQL.
Indexes to support common filters and sorts.
Stable sort with a tie-breaker (Id) for consistent paging.
f: Offset vs keyset paging?
Keyset (WHERE Id > last) is faster for deep pages; offset is simpler.
How do you stop huge page sizes?
Cap page size on the server.
p4-88.y: I accept filter and sort parameters in the query string, but only for a known list of fields, never raw SQL or any column name. I build the query step by step on IQueryable, adding Where clauses for each filter and an OrderBy for the sort, then apply paging. Everything runs in the database, and the most used filters have indexes.
p4-88.k: filtering, sorting, paging, iqueryable, query parameters
x: Filtering and sorting in an API is about giving clients flexibility while keeping the queries safe and fast.

I accept parameters in the query string, like status equals Shipped, siteId equals 12, sortBy equals shipDate and descending equals true, usually bound to a query object. Then I build the query step by step on IQueryable. For each filter that's present, I add a Where clause. For sorting, I map the sortBy value to a known expression from an allow-list, never to a raw column name or SQL string, which prevents injection and stops clients from sorting by unindexed columns. Then I apply paging with Skip and Take, or keyset paging for large tables, and return the total count or a next link.
Because everything stays on IQueryable until the end, EF Core translates it all into one SQL query, so the database does the work.

On our shipment search, I made sure the most common filter combinations, study, status and ship date, were covered by an index, and checked the execution plans. That kept the search fast as the data grew. I can explain keyset versus offset paging.

p4-89.q: OpenAPI is the standard JSON/YAML description of an API; Swagger UI renders it interactively. In .NET 9+ the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi generates documents (Swashbuckle is no longer in templates), with XML comments, examples and auth settings; Scalar or Swagger UI can render it.
i: .NET 10 supports OpenAPI 3.1 and XML doc comments in generated docs.
Generate clients (NSwag, Kiota) from the spec.
Contract-first or code-first; version documents per API version.
f: Why did templates drop Swashbuckle?
Microsoft moved to a built-in, maintained OpenAPI generator.
How do you keep docs accurate?
Generate from code and test the spec in CI.
p4-89.y: OpenAPI is a standard way to describe an API: endpoints, parameters, request and response models and status codes. Swagger is the tooling around it, like the interactive Swagger UI. In .NET, I generate the document from the code, and since .NET 9 it's built in. We share it with front-end and vendor teams and generate clients from it.
p4-89.k: swagger, openapi, api documentation, swagger ui
x: OpenAPI is a standard, machine-readable way to describe a REST API, in JSON or YAML. It lists every endpoint, its parameters, request and response models, status codes and security requirements. Swagger is the original name and now the name of the tooling around it, like Swagger UI, which renders the document as an interactive page where you can try the calls.

In .NET, the document is generated from the code. Historically we used Swashbuckle, and since .NET 9, there's built-in support with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi. To make it genuinely useful, I add XML comments, ProducesResponseType for every status code, examples, and the authentication scheme so you can test with a token.

The real value is that the contract is shared. Front-end and vendor teams read it, and they can generate typed clients from it, so they don't hand-code requests. We also publish it per version, and in our pipeline, a check compares the new document with the previous one to catch breaking changes.
For security, Swagger UI is enabled only in non-production environments. I can explain how we handle breaking changes with versioning.

p4-90.q: HTTPS only; authentication with JWTs from OIDC/SSO; authorization policies and resource-level checks; input validation; rate limiting; restricted CORS; security headers; no secrets or PHI in logs; dependency scanning; and least-privilege access to data and cloud resources.
i: OWASP API Top 10 as the checklist (Part 2 Q51).
Secrets in Secrets Manager; managed identities/roles.
WAF at the edge, request size limits.
Audit logs for sensitive actions.
f: Most common API security bug?
Broken object level authorization (missing per-resource checks).
How do you test API security?
Automated authz tests, DAST scans and penetration tests.
p4-90.y: I secure an API in layers: HTTPS everywhere, authentication with JWT from our identity provider, authorization with policies and per-record checks, input validation, and DTOs so we don't leak data. Then rate limiting, secure headers, secrets in Secrets Manager, logging without sensitive data, and regular dependency and security scans.
p4-90.k: api security, authentication, authorization, jwt, owasp
x: I secure an API in layers, so that if one control fails, the others still protect it.

First, transport: HTTPS only, with HSTS. Second, authentication: every request needs a valid JWT from Keycloak, our identity provider, and we validate the issuer, audience, signature and expiry. Third, authorization: role and policy checks, plus resource-level checks, like "does this user have access to this specific study", which is critical in multi-tenant clinical data. Fourth, input: DTOs, validation, parameterised queries through EF Core, and size limits. Fifth, abuse protection: rate limiting and restricted CORS. And sixth, operations: secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, no sensitive data in logs, least-privilege IAM and database roles, dependency scanning in the pipeline, and audit logs for every change.
Security also covers logout and token lifetime. We use short [15-minute] access tokens, and for immediate logout, we added a token-id denylist in Redis that the API checks in about [1 ms].
Every new endpoint goes through a security checklist in code review. I can go deeper into any of these layers.

p4-91.q: The access token is short-lived (e.g. [15 minutes]) and sent on every API call; the refresh token is long-lived, stored securely and sent only to the identity provider to get new access tokens, and it can be revoked. This limits exposure if an access token leaks.
i: Refresh token rotation: each use returns a new one; reuse of an old one signals theft.
Store refresh tokens server-side (BFF) or in secure HttpOnly cookies.
Our logout fix revokes refresh tokens and denylists access token jti.
Access tokens are validated locally by APIs; refresh tokens are validated only by the identity provider.
f: Why not long-lived access tokens?
They can't easily be revoked and increase damage if stolen.
Where should refresh tokens never be stored?
localStorage or anywhere JavaScript can read.
p4-91.y: An access token is short-lived, maybe [15 minutes], and is sent with every API call to prove who you are. A refresh token lives longer and is used only to get a new access token from the identity provider, without logging in again. If an access token leaks, it expires soon, and refresh tokens can be revoked. That's how we fixed our logout issue.
p4-91.k: access token, refresh token, jwt, oauth, token lifetime
x: An access token and a refresh token work together, but they have very different jobs and lifetimes.

The access token is short-lived, in our case [15 minutes]. It's sent with every API call, usually as a bearer JWT, and the API validates it to know who the user is and what they can do. Because it's short-lived, if it leaks, the damage window is small. The refresh token lives much longer, hours or days. It's never sent to the APIs, only to the identity provider's token endpoint, to get a new access token when the old one expires, so the user doesn't have to log in again. It must be stored securely, and it can be revoked on the server, and with rotation, each use issues a new one.

We used this in a real fix. Users reported that after logging out, their old token still worked until it expired. We revoked the refresh token on logout, and added a denylist of token ids in Redis, which every API checks in about [1 ms]. So logout became immediate.
I can explain how token rotation detects stolen refresh tokens.

p4-92.q: Role-based authorization ([Authorize(Roles = "StudyManager")]) is simple but coarse; policy-based uses named policies with requirements and handlers registered in AddAuthorization, plus resource-based checks via IAuthorizationService for rules like "this user can access this study".
i: Requirements + handlers keep rules testable.
RequireAssertion for quick inline rules.
Resource-based: pass the resource to AuthorizeAsync.
f: How do you apply a policy?
[Authorize(Policy = "CanUnblind")] or RequireAuthorization("CanUnblind").
Fallback policy?
A default policy applied to endpoints without attributes, e.g. require authenticated users.
p4-92.y: Role-based authorization checks if the user is in a role, like Admin. Policy-based authorization is more flexible: a policy is a set of requirements, like a claim, a role, or custom logic, written in a handler. I register policies with AddAuthorization, then use them on endpoints. We use policies for things like checking the user has access to a specific study.
p4-92.k: role-based authorization, policy-based authorization, policies, authorization handler
x: Both control what an authenticated user can do, but policies are more flexible.

Role-based authorization checks whether the user is in a role, like Authorize with Roles equals StudyManager. It's simple, but coarse. You end up with many roles and checks scattered across code. Policy-based authorization defines a named policy, made of one or more requirements. A requirement can check a claim, a role, or run custom logic in an authorization handler. I register policies in AddAuthorization in Program.cs, then use Authorize with Policy, or RequireAuthorization on minimal API endpoints. Roles are really just one kind of policy underneath.
For checks that depend on the actual data, there's resource-based authorization. I inject IAuthorizationService, and call AuthorizeAsync with the user, the resource and a requirement.

That's essential in our clinical system. Being a study manager isn't enough, you must be assigned to that specific study. So we have a StudyAccess requirement and handler that checks the user's study assignments, and returns 403 if they're not on the study. I can show that handler.

p4-93.q: Over-posting is when clients send extra fields that bind to properties they shouldn't set (IsAdmin, Status). I prevent it with input DTOs containing only allowed fields and never binding entities directly; [Bind] or [BindNever] are weaker alternatives.
i: Mass assignment is the same issue (OWASP API3: broken object property level authorization).
Response DTOs prevent the reverse: excessive data exposure.
Integration test sending {"status":"Delivered","isAdmin":true} to verify extra fields are ignored.
System.Text.Json UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow (.NET 8) can reject unknown fields entirely.
f: Is [Bind] enough?
It works but is easy to forget; DTOs are clearer.
How do you test for it?
Send extra fields and assert they're ignored.
p4-93.y: Over-posting is when a client sends extra fields, like isAdmin, and the server saves them because it binds directly to the entity. I prevent it by binding only to request DTOs that contain just the allowed fields, then mapping them to entities myself. I also have tests that send extra fields and check they're ignored.
x: Over-posting, also called mass assignment, is when a client sends extra fields that the server didn't intend to accept, and they get saved because the API binds directly to an entity.

For example, a user updates their profile, but adds "isAdmin: true" or "status: Approved" to the JSON. If the action takes the EF entity as its parameter and saves it, those fields are written to the database. It's a well-known security issue in the OWASP API Top 10.

The main prevention is input DTOs. Each endpoint has a request DTO containing only the fields that the client is allowed to set. Then the service layer loads the entity and maps only those fields onto it. Server-controlled values, like status, created-by and approval flags, are set by the server logic, never by the client. The Bind attribute is an older alternative, but DTOs are cleaner.

We also have tests that send extra fields, like a different study id or an approval flag, and assert they're ignored. In a GxP system, an unauthorised status change would be an audit finding, so we take it seriously. I can talk about how this relates to authorization checks.

p4-94.q: I limit size (Kestrel MaxRequestBodySize, [RequestSizeLimit]), stream instead of buffering, compress, paginate responses, and send big files through presigned S3 uploads or chunked uploads rather than JSON bodies.
i: Defaults: Kestrel about 30 MB request body; IIS has its own limit.
Form limits: FormOptions.MultipartBodyLengthLimit.
Response compression with Brotli/Gzip (careful with secrets and BREACH).
Streaming request bodies: read Request.Body directly or use MultipartReader instead of buffering IFormFile.
f: What happens over the limit?
Kestrel returns 413 Payload Too Large.
How do you stream JSON responses?
Return IAsyncEnumerable<T>, which System.Text.Json serializes as it goes.
p4-94.y: First I set sensible size limits, in Kestrel and per endpoint, so huge requests are rejected early. For large data, I don't buffer everything in memory, I stream the request body. For really large files, the client uploads directly to S3 with a presigned URL, and the API only receives a reference. For big imports, I process them in the background.
p4-94.k: large payloads, request size limit, streaming, s3, upload
x: Large payloads can exhaust memory and threads, so I handle them in several ways.

First, limits. Kestrel has a default maximum body size of about 30 MB, and I set tighter limits per endpoint with the RequestSizeLimit attribute, so oversized requests are rejected early, before we read them. Second, streaming. Instead of buffering the whole body into memory, or into a big model object, I read the request stream directly and process it incrementally. Third, for really large files, I don't send them through the API at all. The client uploads directly to S3 using a presigned URL, and the API only gets the object key. Fourth, for heavy processing, the API accepts the request, returns 202 Accepted, and a background worker does the work. And on the response side, pagination and response compression.

Our CSV import follows this. Files are limited to [5 MB, roughly 10,000 rows], the parser streams rows instead of loading everything, and processing runs in the background with a status endpoint. Each user can have at most [2] imports running at once.
I can explain the presigned URL flow in more detail.

p4-95.q: I use IFormFile for small files and streaming (MultipartReader) for large ones; validate size, extension and content (magic bytes), scan for malware, store outside the web root (S3) with random names, and process asynchronously. Our CSV import used a [5 MB] limit, streamed parsing and a file hash for duplicate detection.
i: Never trust the client's file name or content type.
IFormFile buffers to disk above 64 KB, so huge files still cost disk.
Antiforgery is required for form uploads in minimal APIs (.NET 8+) unless disabled.
Large files: disable form value model binding and stream sections with MultipartReader to avoid buffering.
f: How do you check file type?
Read the first bytes (magic numbers) and validate parsing, not just extension.
Why random names?
To prevent path traversal and overwriting.
p4-95.y: For small files, I accept IFormFile with a size limit, check the extension and the actual content, and never trust the file name. I store files outside the web root, like S3, and scan them if needed. For large files, I use presigned S3 uploads or stream the multipart body. Our CSV import checks size, format and content before processing.
p4-95.k: file upload, iformfile, multipart, s3, validation
x: For file uploads, I think about three things: size, safety and where the file ends up.

For small files, I accept an IFormFile with a request size limit. For larger ones, I stream the multipart body with MultipartReader, so the file isn't buffered in memory, or I use presigned S3 uploads, where the client uploads straight to S3. Then validation. I check the size, the extension against an allow-list, and the actual content, like magic bytes, because the extension and content type can be faked. I never trust the original file name, I generate a random one. Files are stored outside the web root, usually in S3 with encryption, and scanned for malware when required. Processing happens asynchronously.

Our CSV import is a good example. The upload is limited to [5 MB]. We check it's really a CSV, then a streaming parser validates the header and each row, collecting all row errors with their line numbers, before anything is saved. Users get a clear error report instead of a partial import.
I can explain how we avoided importing the same file twice.

p4-96.q: Contract: OpenAPI, versioning, DTOs, validation and ProblemDetails errors. Security: authentication, authorization, rate limits and HTTPS. Resilience: timeouts, retries, idempotency keys and health checks. Observability: structured logs, correlation ids, metrics and alerts. Operations: config validation at startup, graceful shutdown, CI/CD and documentation.
i: Performance: pagination, caching, async I/O, efficient queries.
Backward compatibility: additive changes, deprecation policy.
Tests: unit, integration, contract and load tests.
Startup checks: ValidateOnStart for options, health checks for dependencies, and fail fast on misconfiguration.
f: What's often forgotten?
Timeouts on outbound calls and config validation at startup.
How do you version?
URL segment or header via Asp.Versioning, keeping old versions for a deprecation period.
p4-96.y: A production-ready API needs clear contracts with DTOs and OpenAPI, validation and consistent ProblemDetails errors, and security with authentication, authorization and rate limits. It needs logging with correlation ids, metrics and health checks, resilience with timeouts and retries, and paging for lists. Plus startup checks for configuration, versioning, and automated tests in the pipeline.
p4-96.k: production ready api, api design, best practices, checklist
x: For me, production-ready means the API is not only correct, but also safe, observable and easy to operate at 2 a.m.

I think in six areas. Contract: DTOs, OpenAPI documentation, versioning, which matters for us because our APIs serve the legacy portal, the new React modules and integrations, validation, and consistent ProblemDetails errors. Security: HTTPS, JWT authentication, policy and resource-level authorization, rate limiting, restricted CORS, and secrets in a secret store. Resilience: timeouts and retries with Polly for downstream calls, idempotency keys for creates, health checks and graceful shutdown. Observability: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics, tracing and CloudWatch alarms. Performance: async all the way, paging, caching and efficient queries. And quality: automated tests, and a CI/CD pipeline with quality gates and security scans.
A detail people often skip is validating configuration at startup, with ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting fails the deployment instead of the first request.
When I joined new work, I turned this into a checklist that every new service in our team follows. That's how our correlation-id middleware ended up in [4] services. I can go deeper into any area.

p4-97.q: At every boundary for its purpose: shape and format at the API (model validation, FluentValidation or .NET 10 built-in minimal API validation), business rules in the service/domain layer, and constraints in the database (keys, unique, check constraints) as the last defence. UI validation is only for user experience.
i: Validate early, fail fast with clear messages.
Domain invariants enforced in entities (encapsulation).
Database constraints catch race conditions that app checks miss.
Example: API checks the CSV format, the service checks "site belongs to an active country/depot", and the database's unique index stops duplicate site numbers.
f: Why also in the database?
Concurrent requests can pass app checks simultaneously; unique constraints stop duplicates.
FluentValidation vs data annotations?
FluentValidation handles complex, conditional rules better and is easier to test.
p4-97.y: Validation happens at several layers, each with its own job. The API checks the shape and format of the request. The service layer checks business rules, like a site must belong to an active depot. The database enforces constraints, like unique site numbers, as the final safety net. That way bad data is stopped as early as possible, but nothing slips through.
x: Validation should happen at every boundary, but each layer validates for a different purpose.

At the API layer, I validate the shape and format of the request: required fields, lengths, ranges, formats, using data annotations or FluentValidation. ApiController returns a 400 automatically when that fails, so bad input is stopped as early and cheaply as possible. In the service or domain layer, I validate business rules, which need context or data, like "a site must belong to an active depot", or "you can't ship more kits than are available". Those return a 422 with a clear message. And in the database, constraints are the final safety net: primary and foreign keys, unique indexes and check constraints. They catch anything that slips through, including race conditions between two concurrent requests.
UI validation is useful for user experience, but it's never trusted, because anyone can call the API directly.

In our system, for example, the unique site number is checked in the service for a friendly message, and enforced by a unique index for correctness. I can explain how we report multiple validation errors at once.

p4-98.q: Clients send an idempotency key header; the server stores the key with the result and on a repeat returns the stored result instead of executing again. I back it with natural keys and unique constraints, optimistic concurrency, and disabling double-submit in the UI.
i: Store key, request hash and response; reject same key with different payload (422).
Expire keys after a window (24 hours).
Race: insert the key first with a unique constraint to claim it.
f: What if two identical requests arrive together?
The unique constraint lets one win; the other waits or gets 409.
Is this needed for GET?
No, GET is already safe and idempotent.
p4-98.y: For requests that create something, I use an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores it with the result, so a repeated request returns the same result instead of creating a duplicate. I also add unique constraints in the database. Our CSV import uses a file hash to block importing the same file twice.
p4-98.k: duplicate requests, idempotency key, idempotency, unique constraint
x: Duplicate requests happen all the time: users double-click, clients retry after a timeout, and message brokers redeliver. So I design for it on purpose.

The main technique for creates is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique key, often in an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. If the same key comes again, it returns the stored result instead of executing again. I back that with database protection: natural keys with unique constraints, so even a race between two requests can't create two rows, and optimistic concurrency for updates. On the client side, disabling the button after submit helps, but it's never enough.
For messaging, consumers are idempotent too. We store processed message ids, so redelivered messages are skipped.

A real example is our CSV import. We store a hash of each uploaded file per study. If the same file is uploaded again, we reject it with a clear message instead of importing the rows twice. I can explain how idempotency keys expire.

p5-1.q: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM for .NET: it maps classes to tables, translates LINQ to SQL, tracks changes to entities and writes them back in SaveChanges, and manages schema through migrations. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Cosmos DB and more through providers.
i: Core pieces: DbContext (unit of work), DbSet (tables), change tracker, model built from conventions, attributes and Fluent API.
EF Core 8: complex types, raw SQL for unmapped types, JSON columns; EF Core 9/10: better LINQ translation, named query filters (10), LeftJoin operator (10), vector search for SQL Server.
Performance tools: AsNoTracking, compiled models, compiled queries, ExecuteUpdate/Delete, DbContext pooling.
In IRT: EF Core for most CRUD and domain writes, Dapper or raw SQL for heavy reporting.
f: Is EF Core slow?
Not inherently; most problems come from query shape (N+1, over-fetching, tracking).
What's new in EF Core 10?
LeftJoin/RightJoin LINQ operators, named query filters, JSON and vector improvements.
p5-1.y: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's ORM for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, and it translates my queries into SQL, tracks changes to objects, and saves them back. It also handles migrations for schema changes. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL and others. Most of our IRT services use EF Core with SQL Server.
p5-1.k: ef core, entity framework, orm, database
x: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM, an object-relational mapper, for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, instead of writing SQL and mapping rows by hand.

It maps entity classes to tables and properties to columns, using conventions plus configuration in OnModelCreating. When I write a LINQ query over a DbSet, EF Core translates it into SQL, runs it, and turns the rows back into objects. When I change objects and call SaveChanges, its change tracker works out the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements and runs them in one transaction. Migrations keep the database schema in step with the model. It supports many databases through providers, like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite and Cosmos DB.
The trade-off is a little overhead and the risk of inefficient queries if you don't watch the generated SQL. So I always check the SQL for important queries.

In our IRT services, EF Core with SQL Server is the main data access layer. We use AsNoTracking and projections for reads, ExecuteUpdate for bulk changes, and reviewed idempotent migration scripts for releases. I can go into any of those.

p5-2.q: ADO.NET gives raw connections, commands and data readers: fastest and full control, but manual SQL and mapping. EF Core adds LINQ, change tracking, migrations and relationships for productivity, with some overhead. Dapper sits between: you write SQL, it maps results fast.
i: EF Core itself uses ADO.NET underneath.
Choose EF Core for domain writes and typical queries; Dapper/raw SQL for complex reports or bulk paths.
SqlBulkCopy for very large inserts.
Both must use parameters to avoid SQL injection.
f: Can you mix EF Core and Dapper?
Yes, even sharing the same connection and transaction.
When is raw ADO.NET justified?
Extreme performance paths, streaming large results, or special features like table-valued parameters.
p5-2.y: ADO.NET is the low-level way: I open connections, write SQL, and read rows manually, which gives full control and top speed but more code. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET and does the mapping, change tracking and SQL generation for me, so I'm much more productive. I use EF Core by default, and Dapper or raw SQL for a few performance-critical or reporting queries.
p5-2.k: ef core, ado.net, dapper, orm, comparison
x: ADO.NET and EF Core both talk to the database, but at very different levels of abstraction.

ADO.NET is the low-level foundation: you open a connection, create a command with SQL text and parameters, execute it, and read rows with a data reader, mapping each column to your objects by hand. It's the fastest option and gives full control, but it's a lot of repetitive code and easy to get wrong. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET. You write LINQ, and it generates the SQL, maps the results, tracks changes, handles relationships, and manages migrations. That's much more productive and safer for everyday work, with a small performance overhead that rarely matters.
There's also a middle ground, Dapper, a micro-ORM: you write the SQL yourself, and it maps the results to objects very quickly.

My rule: EF Core for most CRUD and business operations, and Dapper or raw ADO.NET for hot paths or complex reporting SQL that's been tuned by hand. In our services, almost everything is EF Core, with a few heavy reports using Dapper. I can explain when EF Core's overhead actually matters.

p5-3.q: DbContext is a session with the database combining unit of work, change tracker and connection management; the model is configured in OnModelCreating. DbSet<T> represents a table you query with LINQ and add or remove entities from.
i: DbContext is not thread-safe and is registered as scoped; one per request or unit of work.
AddDbContextPool reuses instances for performance; IDbContextFactory for background or Blazor.
Configurations split into IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> classes and ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly.
f: What happens if two threads use one DbContext?
EF throws "A second operation was started on this context"; use separate contexts.
Context pooling caveat?
State must be reset; don't store per-request data in context fields.
p5-3.y: DbContext is the main EF Core class. It represents a session with the database: it manages the connection, tracks changes, and saves them in a transaction. A DbSet is a property on the DbContext for one entity type, like Shipments, which I query with LINQ and add or remove from. DbContext is short-lived, one per request.
x: DbContext and DbSet are the two central types in EF Core.

DbContext represents a session with the database. It combines several responsibilities: it's a unit of work, because it collects changes and saves them together in one transaction; it holds the change tracker, which knows the state of every loaded entity; and it manages the database connection, opening it only when needed. The model, meaning table names, keys, relationships and indexes, is configured in OnModelCreating, usually with separate configuration classes per entity. In ASP.NET Core, a DbContext is registered as scoped, one per request, and it's not thread-safe.

A DbSet of T represents a table, or more precisely the collection of entities of that type. I use it to query, with LINQ, which starts as an IQueryable that's translated into SQL, and to add or remove entities, which are saved on SaveChanges.

In our IRT services, each bounded context has its own DbContext, for example inventory and shipments, with only the DbSets it needs, rather than one giant context for the whole database. That keeps the models smaller and clearer. I can explain how we configure entities.

p5-4.q: Include loads a navigation of the root entity; ThenInclude loads the next level from that navigation, e.g. Studies.Include(s => s.Sites).ThenInclude(site => site.Shipments). Filtered includes (EF Core 5+) restrict loaded children with Where, OrderBy and Take.
i: Multiple collection includes can cause a cartesian explosion; AsSplitQuery runs separate queries.
Projection with Select is often better than Include for read-only views.
Include is ignored if you project to a non-entity type.
f: What is a cartesian explosion?
Joining several collections multiplies rows, sending huge duplicate data.
Split query downside?
Multiple round-trips and possible inconsistency without a transaction.
p5-4.y: Include loads a related entity together with the main one, like shipments with their site. ThenInclude goes one level deeper from that related entity, like the site's country. Both turn into joins in a single query. I use them carefully, because including too much can load a lot of data. For read screens, I often use a Select projection instead.
p5-4.k: include, theninclude, eager loading, ef core
x: Both are used for eager loading related data, but at different levels of the object graph.

Include loads a navigation property of the root entity you're querying. ThenInclude continues from that navigation to load the next level down. For example, querying studies, Include sites, then ThenInclude shipments, loads each study with its sites, and each site with its shipments, all in one query. You can chain multiple Includes for different branches, and since EF Core 5 you can filter inside Include too, like only active sites.

The thing to watch is that deep or multiple collection includes can create a huge result set, because SQL joins multiply the rows, which is called cartesian explosion. If a study has 300 sites and each has 50 shipments, the parent data is repeated for every row. AsSplitQuery fixes this by running a separate query for each collection. Often the better option is a Select projection into a DTO with just the fields needed.
In our IRT services, I prefer projections for read endpoints and use Include mainly when loading an aggregate to update it. I can show an example of split queries.

p5-5.q: dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentIndex generates Up and Down code from model changes, which I review like any code; then I generate an idempotent SQL script (dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent) or a migration bundle for the pipeline, so DBAs and the regulated release process can review and run it.
i: Don't call Database.Migrate() at app startup in production with multiple instances (race conditions); run migrations as a pipeline step.
Migration bundles (efbundle) are self-contained executables.
Data migrations and expand/contract for zero-downtime.
Model snapshot file must be committed and merged carefully.
f: Why idempotent scripts?
They can run against any environment state safely, checking applied migrations.
How do you resolve migration conflicts between branches?
Remove and re-create the later migration after merging, or merge snapshots carefully.
p5-5.y: I change my entity classes or configuration, then run dotnet ef migrations add with a clear name. EF Core compares the model with the last snapshot and generates a migration with Up and Down methods. I review the generated code. For deployment, we generate an idempotent SQL script, review it, and apply it as a controlled step in the release, not automatically at startup.
p5-5.k: ef core migrations, dotnet ef, schema changes, database
x: EF Core migrations are how the database schema evolves in step with the C# model.

When I change the model, for example adding a property or an index, I run dotnet ef migrations add with a descriptive name, like AddShipmentStatusIndex. EF Core compares the current model with the last snapshot and generates a migration class with an Up method, to apply the change, and a Down method, to reverse it. I review that code like any other code, because generated migrations can do surprising things, like dropping and recreating a column on a rename, which loses data. If needed, I edit it, for example to add a data migration step.

For deployment, I don't run migrations automatically at application startup. I generate an idempotent SQL script with dotnet ef migrations script with the idempotent option. That script checks the migrations history table, so it can safely run against any environment. It's reviewed and applied by the release pipeline.
In our regulated environment, that script is part of the release evidence for FV, UAT and production. I can explain how we keep migrations backward-compatible during rolling deployments.

p5-6.q: In Code First the C# model is the source of truth and migrations create and evolve the schema; in Database First you scaffold entities from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold) and the database stays the source of truth. IRT uses [Code First for newer services and scaffolding for legacy schemas].
i: Code First suits greenfield services owning their data.
Database First suits shared or DBA-owned databases.
EF Core Power Tools helps with reverse engineering.
Hybrid: scaffold once from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold), then continue Code First with migrations.
f: Can you switch later?
Yes, by creating a baseline migration from the existing schema.
How do you keep scaffolded code customisable?
Partial classes and templates (T4) so re-scaffolding doesn't overwrite custom code.
p5-6.y: Code First means I write the C# entity classes first and EF Core creates and updates the database with migrations. Database First means the database already exists and I generate the classes from it with scaffolding. For new services I use Code First, and for an existing database I scaffold once and can then continue with Code First.
p5-6.k: code first, database first, scaffolding, ef core
x: These are two approaches to deciding what's the source of truth: the C# model or the database.

In Code First, the C# entity classes and their configuration are the source of truth. You design the model in code, and migrations create and evolve the database schema. It works well when the development team owns the database, because the schema is versioned with the code, reviewed in pull requests, and reproducible in every environment. In Database First, the database already exists, often designed and owned by DBAs, or it's a legacy schema. You use dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold to generate the entity classes and DbContext from the existing tables, and you re-scaffold when the schema changes. It's the practical choice when you can't control the schema.
EF Core removed the old EDMX designer, so both approaches now produce plain code. You can also mix them: scaffold once from an existing database, then continue with migrations.

In our IRT services, newer services are Code First with migrations, while some older shared databases were scaffolded Database First, because other systems depend on that schema. I can explain how we handle schema changes there.

p5-7.q: LINQ-to-Entities is LINQ over DbSet/IQueryable that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; only translatable methods are allowed in filters (Where, Select, OrderBy, string Contains/StartsWith, EF.Functions). The query is an expression tree until enumerated.
i: ToQueryString() shows the SQL without running it.
EF.Functions.Like, DateDiffDay and others map to SQL functions.
Final Select projections can call client code (top-level only).
The provider translates expression trees to SQL; ToQueryString() shows the SQL without executing it.
f: What triggers execution?
Enumeration: ToList, First, Count, foreach, await ToListAsync.
How do you see generated SQL quickly?
query.ToQueryString() or logging.
p5-7.y: LINQ to Entities is LINQ used against EF Core. Instead of running in memory, my LINQ query becomes an expression tree that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database. So Where, Select and OrderBy happen in SQL Server. I can see the generated SQL with ToQueryString, which helps when tuning.
p5-7.k: linq to entities, ef core, iqueryable, sql translation
x: LINQ-to-Entities means writing LINQ queries against EF Core's DbSet, which is an IQueryable, and having EF Core translate them into SQL that runs in the database.

When I write something like Shipments where status is Pending, order by date, take 20, nothing runs yet. EF Core builds an expression tree describing the query. When I enumerate it, for example with ToListAsync, the provider translates the whole expression tree into one SQL statement, sends it to SQL Server, and maps the rows back into objects. So filtering, sorting, paging and aggregates all happen in the database, which is efficient.

The key restriction is that only translatable operations can be used. Standard operators, comparisons, many string and date functions, work fine. But a custom C# method inside a Where can't be translated, and EF Core will throw an exception rather than silently loading everything.

That's different from LINQ-to-Objects, which runs on in-memory collections using delegates. Knowing which one you're in, IQueryable or IEnumerable, is one of the most important things in EF Core performance. I can explain how to check the generated SQL.

p5-8.q: Client-side evaluation happens when you use methods EF can't translate (custom C# functions, some string or date operations) inside a filter. Since EF Core 3, it throws instead of silently loading everything into memory; only the final projection may run client code.
i: Fixes: rewrite with translatable methods, EF.Functions, computed columns, or map a database function with HasDbFunction.
AsEnumerable() explicitly switches to in-memory after filtering in SQL.
Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions in Where throw instead of silently evaluating on the client; only the final Select projection may run client-side.
Common causes: calling your own C# methods in Where, string.Format, or unsupported overloads; fix with translatable expressions or a mapped DB function.
f: Why did EF Core 3 change this?
Silent client evaluation loaded whole tables and caused serious performance issues.
Is AsEnumerable dangerous?
Only if used before filtering, which loads too much data.
p5-8.y: Client-side evaluation happens when part of a query can't be translated into SQL, like calling my own C# method inside a Where. Since EF Core 3, that throws an error instead of quietly loading all rows into memory, which was a big performance trap. Only the final Select can run in C#. I fix it by rewriting the query with translatable expressions.
p5-8.k: client-side evaluation, ef core, query translation, performance
x: Client-side evaluation is when part of a query runs in .NET memory instead of in the database, which can mean loading far more data than needed.

It happens when the query uses something EF Core can't translate into SQL, like calling a custom C# method inside a Where clause, or certain complex string operations. In old EF Core 2, it silently switched to client evaluation: it pulled every row into memory and then filtered, which was a hidden performance disaster. Since EF Core 3, it throws an exception instead, except in the final Select projection, where running C# on the results is harmless.
The other cause is our own code: calling AsEnumerable, ToList or ToArray too early in the chain. Everything after that point runs in memory. So filtering after ToList loads the whole table first.

To avoid it, I keep the query on IQueryable until the end, rewrite custom logic into translatable expressions, and check the generated SQL with ToQueryString or logging. In a code review on our team, I once caught a ToList before a Where on a large shipment table. Moving it to the end cut the data loaded from the whole table to a few rows. I can show the difference.

p5-9.q: I use AsNoTracking for reads, project to DTOs with Select, filter and page in SQL, avoid N+1 with Include or projections, use AsSplitQuery for multiple collections, add the right indexes, batch writes, use ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete for set-based changes, and measure with logged SQL and execution plans.
i: DbContext pooling and compiled models reduce startup and per-request overhead.
Avoid lazy loading in APIs.
Check for implicit conversions and non-SARGable predicates in generated SQL.
The shipment-list fix: index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE plus projection took [9 s to under 300 ms].
f: How do you detect N+1?
Log SQL and look for repeated similar queries per row, or use MiniProfiler.
AsNoTracking vs AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution?
The latter de-duplicates entity instances without tracking.
p5-9.y: First I look at the generated SQL and the execution plan. Then the usual fixes: use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, project only the columns I need with Select, avoid N+1 queries, add paging, and make sure the right indexes exist. For big updates I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. That's how our shipment list went from [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds].
p5-9.k: ef core performance, optimization, asnotracking, projection, n+1
x: For EF Core performance, I start by looking at the generated SQL and the execution plan, because most problems are in the query, not in EF itself.

Then I apply a set of habits. For read-only queries, AsNoTracking, so no change-tracking overhead. Project with Select into DTOs, so SQL fetches only the needed columns. Filter and page in the database, keeping everything on IQueryable. Avoid N+1 queries by using projections or Include, and use AsSplitQuery when several collections are included. Make sure the right indexes exist for the filters and sort order. For bulk changes, use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities. For very hot paths, compiled queries and DbContext pooling reduce overhead. And always pass cancellation tokens, so abandoned requests stop querying.
I log the generated SQL in development, and in production, Query Store and our Grafana latency dashboards show which queries need attention.
A concrete example: our shipment list screen went from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms] mainly through a SARGable rewrite, a covering index, and server-side paging. I can walk through that.

p5-10.q: SaveChanges detects changes in tracked entities and writes all pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements in one transaction, batching them where possible. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking a thread during I/O, which is what I use in ASP.NET Core.
i: Returns the number of affected rows; throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException or DbUpdateException.
Interceptors (SaveChangesInterceptor) for auditing and soft delete.
ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled can be turned off for bulk adds.
SaveChanges wraps all changes in one transaction by default and batches statements (SQL Server batching).
f: Is SaveChanges transactional?
Yes, each call is one transaction unless you've started an explicit one.
Why call SaveChanges once per unit of work?
Fewer round-trips and all-or-nothing behaviour.
p5-10.y: SaveChanges looks at all the tracked changes and writes them to the database as inserts, updates and deletes, inside one transaction by default. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking the thread while waiting for the database. In ASP.NET Core I always use SaveChangesAsync, so the server can handle other requests meanwhile.
x: SaveChanges is the method that writes all pending changes tracked by the DbContext to the database.

When I call it, EF Core first runs change detection, comparing tracked entities with their original snapshots to find what's added, modified and deleted. Then it generates the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, batching them where possible, and runs them all inside one transaction. So either all of the changes are saved, or none are. After success, it updates the entities, for example with generated identity values and new concurrency tokens, and marks them as unchanged. It returns the number of rows affected.

SaveChangesAsync does exactly the same, but asynchronously. While the database is doing the work, the thread is released back to the thread pool, instead of sitting idle. In ASP.NET Core, that's what you want, because it lets the server handle more requests under load. So in web APIs and services, I always use SaveChangesAsync, passing the cancellation token.

One more point: I call it once per unit of work, at the end of the operation, not after every small change. That keeps the operation atomic and reduces round trips. I can explain how concurrency tokens work with it.

p5-11.q: EF Core 7+ ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete run set-based SQL without loading entities; AddRange with batching handles moderate inserts. For very large loads I use SqlBulkCopy (or a library like EFCore.BulkExtensions) into a staging table, then MERGE set-based.
i: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker and interceptors; handle auditing separately.
Batch size (MaxBatchSize) affects round-trips.
Wrap staging plus merge in a transaction.
c:
await db.Shipments.Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.Pending && s.CreatedAt < cutoff)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(u => u.SetProperty(s => s.Status, ShipmentStatus.Expired), ct);
f: Downside of ExecuteUpdate?
Tracked entities in memory aren't updated, and SaveChanges interceptors don't run.
How fast is SqlBulkCopy?
Hundreds of thousands of rows per second, depending on table and indexes.
p5-11.y: For large updates or deletes, I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities into memory. For large inserts, I batch them, or use SqlBulkCopy or a bulk extension library, which is much faster than adding thousands of entities one by one. Our CSV import saves rows in batches inside one transaction.
p5-11.k: bulk operations, executeupdate, executedelete, sqlbulkcopy, ef core
x: Bulk operations are where the default EF Core approach, loading entities, changing them, and saving, becomes too slow.

For updates and deletes, EF Core 7 added ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. They translate directly into a single set-based UPDATE or DELETE statement, without loading any rows into memory or using the change tracker. For example, marking all expired kits at a depot as unusable becomes one SQL statement instead of thousands of tracked updates. For inserts, AddRange plus SaveChanges already batches statements, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand rows. For very large loads, like tens or hundreds of thousands of rows, I use SqlBulkCopy, or a bulk extensions library, which uses SQL Server's bulk insert path and is much faster. I usually process in chunks, so transactions and memory stay manageable.
One caution: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker, so audit logic in SaveChanges interceptors doesn't run. In a GxP system, we make sure auditing still happens for those operations.
Our CSV import of [about 10,000] rows uses batched inserts in chunks inside a transaction, after validation. I can explain why we chose that over SqlBulkCopy.

p5-12.q: EF.CompileAsyncQuery caches the LINQ-to-SQL translation of a query shape so very hot paths skip translation cost. EF already caches translations internally, so compiled queries give only small gains; compiled models (dotnet ef dbcontext optimize) help startup for large models.
i: EF Core 9+ supports precompiled queries for native AOT (experimental).
Use only after profiling shows translation cost matters.
EF Core already caches query plans; compiled queries mainly save the expression-tree compare and translation cost on very hot paths.
c:
static readonly Func<IrtDbContext, int, Task<Shipment?>> ById =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((IrtDbContext db, int id) => db.Shipments.FirstOrDefault(s => s.Id == id));
f: When are compiled queries worth it?
Extremely hot, simple queries in high-throughput services.
What is a compiled model?
A generated model that avoids building the model at startup.
p5-12.y: A compiled query is a LINQ query that EF Core translates once and then reuses, using EF.CompileAsyncQuery. EF Core already caches query plans, so this only saves the small cost of processing the query each time. I'd use it only for very hot queries that run thousands of times per second, after measuring.
x: Compiled queries are a way to skip the cost of translating a LINQ query into SQL every time it runs.

Normally, when EF Core executes a LINQ query, it has to process the expression tree and produce SQL. It caches that work internally, keyed by the shape of the query, so repeated queries are already fairly cheap. But there's still some overhead in computing the cache key from the expression tree on every call. With EF.CompileAsyncQuery, or EF.CompileQuery, I define the query once, as a static delegate with parameters. EF Core translates it once, and every call reuses it directly, so the overhead disappears.

The gain is real but small, usually noticeable only on very hot paths with simple queries, executed thousands of times per second. Compiled queries are also less flexible, because the query shape is fixed.

So my rule is to use them only after measuring shows translation overhead matters. In our services, I've used a compiled query for a frequently called lookup, getting a kit by its number, which sits on a hot path during dispensing. For most queries, indexes and projections matter far more. I can explain other EF hot-path optimisations.

p5-13.q: Use LogTo(Console.WriteLine) on the options builder, or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command log category at Information, which logs SQL and timing. EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows parameter values, for development only.
i: ToQueryString() for one query.
Interceptors (DbCommandInterceptor) can log slow queries or add query tags.
TagWith("ShipmentList") adds comments to SQL to find it in Query Store.
In tests or dev: optionsBuilder.LogTo(Console.WriteLine, LogLevel.Information); never EnableSensitiveDataLogging in production.
f: Why not enable sensitive data logging in production?
It logs parameter values that may contain personal data.
How do you find which code issued a slow query?
TagWith or TagWithCallSite to add identifying comments.
p5-13.y: I set the log level for the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command category to Information, and EF Core logs every SQL command it runs, with timings. For a single query, ToQueryString shows the SQL without running it. I never turn on sensitive data logging in production, because it would log parameter values.
p5-13.k: log sql, ef core logging, toquerystring, debugging
x: Seeing the SQL that EF Core generates is essential, because that's where most performance problems show up.

There are a few ways. The simplest in development is LogTo on the DbContext options, for example LogTo Console.WriteLine, filtered to Information level. In an ASP.NET Core app, I can enable the log category Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command at Information level in configuration, and the SQL appears in the normal logs, with execution times. For a single query, ToQueryString returns the SQL without executing it, which is handy in tests and debugging. And for parameter values, EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows them, but only in development, because in production it could log personal or clinical data.
Outside the application, SQL Server tools help too: Query Store shows the heaviest queries over time, and Extended Events can capture specific ones.

In our team, during code reviews of data-heavy changes, we look at the generated SQL for new queries. That's how we've caught N+1 queries and accidental client-side evaluation before they reached production. I can explain how to read the execution plan next.

p5-14.q: Relationships are configured with navigations and foreign keys by convention or Fluent API (HasOne/WithMany, HasMany/WithMany). One-to-one: Subject and Consent; one-to-many: Study and Sites; many-to-many: Users and Studies, with EF Core 5+ creating the join table automatically or using an explicit join entity with extra data.
i: Delete behaviour: Cascade, Restrict, SetNull, configured per relationship.
Required vs optional by FK nullability.
Explicit join entities when the join has data (role, assigned date).
c:
b.Entity<Site>().HasOne(s => s.Study).WithMany(st => st.Sites).HasForeignKey(s => s.StudyId).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
b.Entity<User>().HasMany(u => u.Studies).WithMany(s => s.Users).UsingEntity<StudyAssignment>();
f: Why Restrict on delete?
To avoid accidental cascades deleting regulated data.
What are multiple cascade paths?
SQL Server rejects schemas where deletes can cascade by more than one path.
p5-14.y: In EF Core, I define relationships with navigation properties and configure them with the Fluent API. One-to-many is the most common, like a site with many shipments, using a foreign key on the shipment. One-to-one uses a foreign key with a unique constraint. Many-to-many can be automatic with a hidden join table, or an explicit join entity if it needs extra columns.
p5-14.k: relationships, one-to-many, many-to-many, one-to-one, ef core, fluent api
x: EF Core supports all three relationship types, configured by convention or with the Fluent API.

One-to-many is the most common. A principal has a collection navigation, and the dependent has a reference navigation and a foreign key. For example, a Site has many Shipments, and each Shipment has a SiteId. In Fluent API, that's HasMany Shipments WithOne Site HasForeignKey SiteId, and I choose the delete behaviour explicitly. One-to-one uses reference navigations on both sides, and the dependent holds the foreign key, for example a Subject and their ConsentRecord, configured with HasOne WithOne. Many-to-many, since EF Core 5, can be configured with collections on both sides, and EF creates the join table automatically.
But when the link itself has data, like a role or an assigned date, I model an explicit join entity instead.

That's our case for users and studies. A user can be on many studies, and a study has many users, but each assignment has a role and an assigned date, which our authorization checks use. So we have an explicit StudyAssignment entity. I can explain how we configure cascade deletes safely.

p5-15.q: Shadow properties exist in the EF model and table but not in the C# class, such as LastModifiedBy or a foreign key; they're accessed with EF.Property<T>(entity, "Name") in queries and through the change tracker. They keep infrastructure concerns like audit columns out of domain classes.
i: Set them in a SaveChanges interceptor.
Query filters can use them (soft delete IsDeleted).
Common use: audit columns (CreatedAt, UpdatedBy) set in SaveChanges via ChangeTracker without polluting the domain model.
f: When would EF create a shadow FK?
When a navigation exists without an FK property in the class.
Downside?
Less discoverable in code.
p5-15.y: A shadow property is a column that EF Core knows about but that isn't a property on my C# class. I access it through the change tracker or EF.Property. It's handy for things like audit columns, such as created date or updated by, which I set in SaveChanges without cluttering my domain classes.
p5-15.k: shadow properties, ef core, audit columns
x: Shadow properties are properties that exist in the EF Core model and in the database table, but not in the C# entity class.

You configure them in OnModelCreating with Property of type and a name, and EF Core tracks them like normal properties. To read or filter by them in queries, you use EF.Property with the entity and the property name. To set them, you go through the change tracker, for example entry.Property of "LastModifiedBy" CurrentValue. EF Core also creates shadow properties automatically, for example a foreign key column when the class only has a navigation property.

They're useful when a column matters to the database but shouldn't clutter the domain model. The classic use is audit columns, like CreatedBy, CreatedAt, LastModifiedBy and LastModifiedAt. Instead of adding these to every entity class, I define them as shadow properties on all entities, and set them centrally in a SaveChanges interceptor, using the current user and TimeProvider.
In our services, that's how audit columns are populated consistently, so no developer can forget to set them, which matters for GxP audit trails. I can show the interceptor code.

p5-16.q: Owned entities map value objects as part of their owner with OwnsOne/OwnsMany, e.g. an Address inside Site stored in the Site table's columns; they have no identity of their own. EF Core 8 complex types (ComplexProperty) are a newer option for value objects with value semantics, and owned types can be mapped to JSON columns.
i: Value objects: immutable, compared by value (Money, Address, TemperatureRange).
OwnsMany can map to a separate table or JSON.
Owned types can map to the same table (columns prefixed) or a separate table; in EF Core 8, complex types are an alternative for value objects.
c:
b.Entity<Site>().OwnsOne(s => s.Address);   // Address_City, Address_Country columns
b.Entity<Site>().ComplexProperty(s => s.StorageRange);  // EF Core 8 complex type
f: Owned type vs complex type?
Owned types are entity types with hidden keys; complex types are true value types without identity.
Why JSON columns?
Flexible nested data queried with JSON functions without extra tables.
p5-16.y: An owned entity is a type that has no identity of its own and belongs to its owner, like an Address inside a Site. By default its columns are stored in the owner's table, with prefixed names. It's a nice way to model value objects. In EF Core 8 there are also complex types for the same idea.
p5-16.k: owned entity, value object, ef core, complex types
x: Owned entities are how EF Core maps value objects, types that don't have their own identity and only exist as part of another entity.

You configure them with OwnsOne for a single value object, or OwnsMany for a collection. For example, a Site has an Address, with street, city, postcode and country. Address isn't an entity on its own, it has no id, and it only makes sense as part of a site. With OwnsOne, EF Core stores the address fields as columns in the Site table, like Address_City, and loads them automatically whenever the site is loaded. OwnsMany stores the collection in a separate table, but it's still owned and loaded with its owner. Since EF Core 8, complex types offer a similar option for value objects.

The benefit is a richer domain model. Instead of loose string properties on Site, I have a proper Address type, with its own validation, which can be reused in other entities like Depot, while the database stays simple.
In our IRT model, addresses and some quantity-with-unit values are owned types. That made validation consistent across sites and depots. I can explain how this relates to domain-driven design.

p5-17.q: Fluent API HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status }) with IsUnique, HasFilter or IncludeProperties (SQL Server), or the [Index] attribute on the class; migrations then create the index. I base indexes on real query patterns and verify with execution plans.
i: Unique indexes enforce business rules (one kit number per study).
Filtered indexes for hot subsets.
Name indexes explicitly for stable migrations.
c:
b.Entity<Shipment>().HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status, s.ShipmentDate })
 .IncludeProperties(s => new { s.SiteId, s.KitCount }).HasDatabaseName("IX_Shipments_Study_Status_Date");
f: What does IncludeProperties do?
Adds INCLUDE columns so the index covers the query.
Unique index vs unique constraint?
Functionally similar in SQL Server; a constraint expresses intent and is backed by an index.
p5-17.y: I configure indexes in OnModelCreating with HasIndex, or with the Index attribute on the class. I can make them unique, combine several columns, add a filter, and include extra columns for SQL Server. Then a migration creates them. For example, a unique index on study and site number stops duplicate sites.
p5-17.k: indexes, hasindex, ef core, unique index
x: In EF Core, indexes are part of the model, so they're defined in code and created through migrations, which keeps them versioned and reviewed.

With the Fluent API, in the entity configuration, I call HasIndex with the columns. For example, HasIndex of StudyId and Status creates a composite index, and column order matters. I can add IsUnique for a unique index, like a kit number. HasFilter creates a filtered index, for example only active rows. And with SQL Server, IncludeProperties adds included columns, to make a covering index. HasDatabaseName gives it a clear name. Alternatively, the Index attribute on the entity class works for simple cases. Then I add a migration, and the index is created through our normal release scripts.
The important part is choosing indexes from real query patterns, using the execution plan, rather than adding them everywhere, because every index slows down writes.

The covering index from our shipment list fix, on StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate including the displayed columns, was added exactly this way, through a reviewed migration script. I can show the configuration code.

p5-18.q: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, can't be null, and there's one per table (clustered by default in SQL Server). A foreign key is a column referencing another table's primary or unique key, enforcing referential integrity so you can't have orphan rows.
i: Surrogate keys (identity, sequence, GUID) vs natural keys (kit number).
GUID PKs: use sequential GUIDs (NEWSEQUENTIALID, or Guid.CreateVersion7 in .NET 9) to avoid fragmentation.
Index foreign key columns; SQL Server doesn't do it automatically.
Choose surrogate keys (int/bigint identity or sequential GUID) for stability; natural keys can change.
f: Should every FK be indexed?
Usually, for joins and to avoid locking scans on deletes of the parent.
What is Guid.CreateVersion7?
A .NET 9 API creating time-ordered UUIDv7 values, better for index locality.
p5-18.y: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, it can't be null, and there's only one per table. A foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table, which keeps the relationship valid, so a shipment can't point to a site that doesn't exist.
p5-18.k: primary key, foreign key, relational database, constraints
