p6-62.k: flaky test, test reliability, intermittent failure
x: A flaky test is a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails, without any change to the code. It's harmful because it destroys trust in the test suite. When tests fail randomly, people start rerunning builds and ignoring failures, and then they miss real bugs.

The usual causes are: timing issues in asynchronous code, like fixed sleeps, or not waiting for something to finish; shared state between tests, where the order they run in matters; dependence on the real time, time zones or random values; reliance on external services or the network; and in UI tests, not waiting for elements properly.

To handle them, first, I identify them: CI test history shows which tests fail intermittently. Then I don't ignore them. If I can't fix one immediately, I quarantine it, so it doesn't block the build, but I create a ticket to fix it quickly, so it doesn't stay hidden forever. Then I fix the root cause: replace sleeps with proper waiting, like awaiting the task or polling for a condition with a timeout; make each test create and clean up its own data; inject TimeProvider instead of using the real clock; use fixed seeds for random values; and replace external calls with fakes or containers. Automatic retries can hide flakiness, so I use them very carefully.
I once fixed a test that failed only around midnight, because it used the real clock. That was part of our time-zone bug in [2023].

p6-63.q: Coverage is the percentage of lines or branches executed by tests. 100 percent is rarely worth it: coverage shows what ran, not whether it was verified. I aim for high coverage on business logic with meaningful assertions, and use thresholds on new code as a guard.
i: Mutation testing (Stryker.NET) measures test quality by injecting bugs.
Branch coverage is more informative than line coverage.
Coverage shows untested code, not tested behaviour; assertions matter.
100 percent is costly; aim for high coverage on business rules and risky paths, plus mutation testing (Stryker.NET) to check test quality.
f: What does mutation testing tell you?
Whether tests fail when code is changed, i.e. if assertions are meaningful.
What to exclude from coverage?
Generated code, simple DTOs and startup wiring.
p6-63.y: Test coverage shows the percentage of code run by tests. It's useful to find untested code, but high coverage doesn't mean good tests, because tests without proper assertions also count. 100 percent is usually not worth the cost. I aim for high coverage on business rules and risky code, like our 80 percent gate on new code.
p6-63.k: test coverage, code coverage, 100 percent coverage
x: Test coverage measures how much of the code is executed when the tests run, usually as the percentage of lines or branches. Branch coverage is more useful, because it shows whether both sides of each if statement were tested.

Coverage is useful for one thing in particular: finding code that has no tests at all. If an important class has zero coverage, that's a clear risk. Teams often set a minimum for new code, for example [80 percent] in a SonarQube quality gate, so coverage doesn't drop over time.

But high coverage doesn't mean good tests. A test can execute every line and check nothing, with no meaningful assertions, and still count as 100 percent. Coverage shows what code ran, not whether the behaviour was verified.

So is 100 percent desirable? Usually not as a goal. Getting from about 80 to 100 percent often means testing trivial code, like simple properties, generated code or framework configuration, which costs time and produces fragile tests that break on every refactoring. That effort is better spent on testing important business logic and edge cases well, and on integration tests. For critical logic, like calculations or security rules, I do aim for very thorough coverage.
When our quality gate failed at [68 percent] against [80 percent], we didn't just add tests to hit the number. We added meaningful tests for the real missing paths, and fixed it in [half a day].

p6-64.q: Good tests are fast, isolated, repeatable, readable and test one behaviour, with clear names (Method_Scenario_Expected). Arrange-Act-Assert: set up inputs and doubles, call the method once, then assert outcomes.
i: One logical assertion per test; use theory data for variations ([Theory], [InlineData]).
Avoid logic in tests.
Builders or object mothers for test data.
f: Why one behaviour per test?
Failures point to exactly what broke.
FIRST principles?
Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.
p6-64.y: A good unit test checks one behaviour, has a clear name that says what's expected, and is fast, independent and repeatable. Arrange-Act-Assert is the structure: arrange the data and dependencies, act by calling the method once, and assert the result. I test behaviour, not internal details, so refactoring doesn't break tests.
p6-64.k: unit test design, arrange act assert, aaa, best practices
x: A good unit test is fast, independent, repeatable, and tests one behaviour, so that when it fails, you immediately know what broke.

I structure every test with Arrange, Act, Assert. Arrange sets up the situation: create the object under test, its test doubles, and the input data. Act performs the one action being tested, usually a single method call. Assert checks the outcome: the return value, the changed state, or an important interaction, like a message being published. Keeping these three parts clearly separated makes tests easy to read.

Some principles I follow. Name tests by behaviour, for example CalculateDeliveryDate_WhenSiteIsClosedOnWeekend_ReturnsNextMonday, so the name explains what broke. Test one behaviour per test. Test behaviour, not implementation, so refactoring doesn't break tests needlessly. Don't share state between tests, so they can run in any order. Avoid logic like loops and if statements inside tests. Use realistic, meaningful test data. Cover the edge cases and error paths, not only the happy path. And make tests deterministic: control time with TimeProvider and avoid real network calls.
For similar cases with different inputs, I use parameterised tests, like xUnit's Theory with InlineData, instead of copying the same test.
In my team, I review test quality as carefully as production code, because tests are what let us change code with confidence.

p6-65.q: For async, make test methods async Task and await the call; never use .Result; control time with FakeTimeProvider; test cancellation. For exceptions, use Assert.ThrowsAsync<T> (xUnit) or FluentAssertions-style checks, and assert the message or properties that matter.
i: FakeTimeProvider.Advance to trigger timers and delays deterministically.
Test that OperationCanceledException is thrown when the token is cancelled.
Use await Assert.ThrowsAsync<T>() and never async void tests; FakeTimeProvider makes timeouts deterministic.
f: Why avoid .Result in tests?
It can deadlock in some contexts and wraps exceptions in AggregateException.
How do you test retries with delays quickly?
Inject TimeProvider and advance fake time.
p6-65.y: I write the test method as async Task and await the code, never use async void or .Result. For exceptions, I use await Assert.ThrowsAsync with the expected exception type and check the message if it matters. For timeouts and delays, I use a fake time provider, so tests don't actually wait.
p6-65.k: async testing, exception testing, throwsasync, xunit
x: For asynchronous code, the main rule is to make the test itself async and await the code under test. In xUnit or NUnit, the test method returns Task, and I await the call. I never use .Result or .Wait, because they can deadlock and hide the real exception inside an AggregateException. To set up async dependencies with Moq, I use ReturnsAsync, or ThrowsAsync to simulate failures.

For exceptions, I assert both that the right exception is thrown and that it has the right details. In xUnit, that's await Assert.ThrowsAsync of the exception type, passing the call, and then I check the message or properties. With FluentAssertions, it's await act.Should().ThrowAsync, with the type and message. I also test what happens around the exception: for example, that a failed save doesn't publish a message, or that a retry policy tries the right number of times before giving up.

Some async-specific cases are worth testing. Cancellation: pass a cancelled CancellationToken and check that the method stops with OperationCanceledException. Timeouts and delays: use the injected TimeProvider, with FakeTimeProvider in tests, so I can move time forward instantly instead of waiting. And background work: instead of sleeping, wait for a condition with a timeout.
These keep async tests fast, reliable and free of flakiness.

p6-66.q: Unit-test handlers with the message as input and dependencies mocked. Integration tests start a real broker in Testcontainers, publish a message, and assert the consumer's effect (database row, outgoing message) with polling and timeouts; contract tests check message schemas between producers and consumers.
i: Test idempotency by publishing the same message twice.
Test failure paths: DLQ routing, retries.
Keep handler logic separate from broker plumbing for testability.
f: How do you wait for async effects?
Poll with a timeout instead of fixed sleeps.
What's a message contract test?
Verifying the producer's schema matches what the consumer expects.
p6-66.y: For unit tests, I test the message handler logic separately from the broker. For integration tests, I run real Kafka or RabbitMQ in Docker with Testcontainers, publish a test message, and check the consumer processed it, including retries, dead-lettering and duplicate handling. I also use contract tests for message formats.
p6-66.k: kafka testing, rabbitmq testing, testcontainers, messaging tests
x: I test Kafka and RabbitMQ integrations at three levels, because each one catches different problems.

First, unit tests of the message handling logic. I keep the business logic separate from the messaging library, so a handler receives a deserialised message and does its work. I can test it with test doubles, including edge cases like duplicate messages, which should be idempotent, and invalid messages, which should go to the dead-letter path. I also test serialisation, so the message format matches the contract.

Second, integration tests with a real broker. With Testcontainers, the tests start real RabbitMQ or Kafka containers. Then I publish a message, and check that the consumer processes it and that the expected result happens, for example a row in the database or a message published to the next queue. For waiting, I poll for the result with a timeout, never a fixed sleep. These tests catch real problems: wrong exchange or queue names, bindings, acknowledgements, retries, dead-lettering, and serialisation settings.
Third, contract tests between producers and consumers, using a schema registry or a tool like Pact, so a producer can't change a message in a way that breaks consumers.
After the kit-assignment notification problem caused by autoAck, I added an integration test that makes processing fail once, and checks that the message is retried, not lost.

p7-1.q: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React reconciles changes efficiently (virtual DOM diffing) to update only what changed in the real DOM.
i: React 18 introduced concurrent rendering, automatic batching and transitions.
React 19 (Dec 2024): Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic, the use() hook, ref as a prop, and Server Components support.
React Compiler (stable 2025) auto-memoises components, reducing manual useMemo/useCallback.
One-way data flow: props down, events up.
f: What is reconciliation?
React compares the new element tree with the previous one and applies minimal DOM changes.
Why keys in lists?
Stable keys let React match items between renders and keep state correct.
p7-1.y: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. I describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React updates the page efficiently when the state changes. It's maintained by Meta and has a huge ecosystem. I build reusable React components with TypeScript for our IRT screens.
x: React is a JavaScript library, created by Meta, for building user interfaces out of components. It focuses only on the view layer, and leaves things like routing and data fetching to other libraries you choose.

There are a few core ideas. First, components: the UI is split into small, reusable pieces, like a button, a form or a shipment table, and each component is a function that returns what should be shown, written in JSX, which looks like HTML inside JavaScript. Second, it's declarative: I describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and React takes care of updating the page when that data changes. I don't manipulate the DOM by hand. Third, state and props: props are inputs passed from a parent, and state is data a component owns and can change. When state changes, React re-renders the component. Fourth, efficient updates: React compares the new output with the previous one, a process called reconciliation, and only changes the parts of the real DOM that actually changed. And data flows one way, from parent to child, which makes behaviour easier to follow.
Hooks, like useState and useEffect, let function components manage state and side effects.
In our applications, we use React with TypeScript for newer screens, like the CSV import screen I built, where users upload a file and see a clear row-by-row error report.

p7-2.q: A component is a function (or class) that returns UI; an element is the plain object it returns describing what to render. <Button /> creates an element of type Button; React calls the component to get more elements until it reaches DOM elements.
i: Elements are immutable descriptions; cheap to create.
JSX compiles to jsx() calls (new JSX transform).
An element is a plain object describing UI ({type, props}); a component is a function that returns elements.
JSX <Button/> compiles to a jsx() call that creates an element.
f: Is JSX required?
No, but it's the standard and compiles to function calls.
What is a fragment?
<>...</> groups elements without adding a DOM node.
p7-2.y: A component is a function that takes props and returns what should be shown. An element is the plain object that a component returns, describing one piece of UI, which is what JSX creates. So a component is like a blueprint, and elements are what it produces each time it renders.
x: A component and an element are related, but they're different things.

A component is a function, or in older code a class, that describes a piece of UI. It accepts inputs, called props, and returns what should be displayed. For example, a ShipmentRow component that takes a shipment and returns a table row. It's like a blueprint, or a template, that can be reused many times.

An element is the result of using a component. It's a plain, lightweight JavaScript object that describes what should appear on the screen: its type, like a div, or the ShipmentRow component, and its props. When I write JSX, like angle bracket ShipmentRow with a shipment, that creates an element. Elements are immutable; once created, you don't change them. When data changes, React creates new elements, compares them with the previous ones, and updates the real DOM only where something changed.

So a simple way to say it: a component is the recipe, and an element is a description of one dish made from that recipe, at one moment in time. Elements are not the actual DOM nodes either; they're descriptions that React uses to create and update the DOM.
This distinction also explains why we never call components directly as functions in JSX code; we create elements, and React decides when to call the component.

p7-3.q: Functional components are plain functions using hooks for state and effects: less code, easier reuse through custom hooks, and the modern standard. Class components extend React.Component with this.state and lifecycle methods; they're still supported but only needed for error boundaries today.
i: Hooks rules: call at top level, only in components or custom hooks.
Lifecycle mapping: componentDidMount/Update/WillUnmount ≈ useEffect with cleanup.
Hooks replaced most class lifecycle methods; error boundaries are the main case still needing a class.
Function components are simpler, easier to test and work with concurrent features.
f: Why are error boundaries still classes?
They rely on componentDidCatch/getDerivedStateFromError, which have no hook equivalent.
Can you mix both?
Yes, in the same app.
p7-3.y: Class components are the older way, with this.state and lifecycle methods like componentDidMount. Functional components are just functions, and with hooks like useState and useEffect, they can do everything classes did, with less code and easier reuse. Today I write only functional components. Error boundaries are the main thing that still needs a class.
p7-3.k: functional components, class components, hooks, react
x: In React, components can be written as classes or as functions, and today functional components with hooks are the standard.

Class components extend React.Component. They have a render method that returns the UI, state stored in this.state and updated with this.setState, and lifecycle methods for side effects, like componentDidMount when the component first appears, componentDidUpdate after updates, and componentWillUnmount for cleanup. The downsides were more boilerplate, confusion around the this keyword and binding, and related logic being split across different lifecycle methods.

Functional components are plain functions that take props and return JSX. Since hooks were introduced in React 16.8, they can do everything classes can. useState manages state, useEffect handles side effects, with the cleanup function replacing componentWillUnmount, and other hooks like useContext, useMemo and useRef cover the rest. They're shorter and easier to read and test. Most importantly, custom hooks let you reuse stateful logic between components, like a useShipments hook that fetches data with loading and error states, which was hard to do with classes.
The only thing that still needs a class is an error boundary, though libraries provide function-friendly wrappers.
In our code, all new components are functional with hooks, and we convert older class components when we work on them.

p7-4.q: Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child; state is data owned by a component that changes over time (useState) and triggers a re-render. Props flow down and are controlled by the parent; state is local and changed by the component itself, often passed down as props.
i: Lift state up to the nearest common parent when siblings need it.
State updates are asynchronous and batched; use functional updates (setCount(c => c + 1)).
Never mutate state directly; create new objects or arrays.
State updates are asynchronous and batched (automatic batching in React 18+).
f: Why functional updates?
They use the latest state when updates are batched.
Derived state?
Compute it during render instead of storing it.
p7-4.y: Props are inputs passed into a component from its parent, and the component can't change them. State is data the component owns and can change, using useState, which causes it to re-render. So props flow down from the parent, and state lives inside the component. When two components need the same state, I lift it up to their common parent.
p7-4.k: props, state, props vs state, react
x: Props and state are the two kinds of data that control what a React component shows.

Props, short for properties, are inputs passed into a component from its parent, like arguments to a function. For example, a ShipmentRow receives a shipment object as a prop. Props are read-only inside the component: the component must never change them. If the parent passes new props, the component re-renders with them.

State is data that a component owns and manages itself, and which can change over time, usually because of user actions or data loading. For example, whether a dropdown is open, the text in a search box, or the list of shipments after an API call. In a functional component, I create state with useState, which gives me the current value and a setter function. Calling the setter tells React the state changed, and React re-renders the component.

So the difference is: props come from outside and are read-only; state lives inside and is changed by the component itself. Props flow down from parent to child. When a child needs to change something, the parent passes down a callback function as a prop, and the child calls it. That's how data flows one way, which keeps behaviour predictable.
A practical rule is to keep state in the closest common parent of the components that need it, which is called lifting state up.

p7-5.q: The dependency array is the second argument of useEffect, useMemo and useCallback: the hook re-runs when any listed value changes (compared with Object.is). An empty array runs the effect once after the first render (and cleanup on unmount); no array runs it after every render.
i: In development StrictMode, effects run twice on mount to reveal missing cleanups.
The ESLint react-hooks/exhaustive-deps rule catches missing dependencies.
Objects created during render change every time, causing repeated effects.
f: Why does my effect run twice in development?
StrictMode intentionally double-invokes to find bugs.
What's a stale closure?
An effect using old values because dependencies were omitted.
p7-5.y: The dependency array in useEffect tells React when to run the effect again. With values in it, the effect runs whenever one of them changes. If it's empty, the effect runs only once, after the first render, which is good for initial data loading. If there's no array at all, it runs after every render. Missing a dependency causes stale-data bugs.
x: The dependency array is the second argument to hooks like useEffect, useMemo and useCallback. It tells React when to rerun the effect, or recalculate the value: only when one of the listed values has changed since the last render.

For useEffect, there are three cases. With no array at all, the effect runs after every render, which is rarely what you want. With an array of values, like userId, the effect runs after the first render and then again whenever userId changes. That's the normal case, for example fetching a user's data whenever the selected user changes. With an empty array, the effect runs only once, after the component first mounts, because there's nothing that can change. That's used for one-time setup, like subscribing to an event. If the effect returns a cleanup function, React runs it before the effect runs again, and when the component unmounts. That's where you unsubscribe, or cancel a request.

The important rule is that the array must include every value from the component that the effect uses, like props, state, and functions. If you leave one out, the effect keeps using an old value, which is called a stale closure, and causes subtle bugs. The ESLint rule for exhaustive dependencies catches this, and we keep it switched on.
Also, in development with Strict Mode, React runs effects twice on purpose, to help find missing cleanups.

p7-6.q: useMemo caches a computed value between renders until dependencies change; useCallback caches a function reference so memoised children (React.memo) don't re-render because of a new function prop. useCallback(fn, deps) equals useMemo(() => fn, deps).
i: Only use them when profiling shows a benefit or for referential stability in dependencies.
React Compiler can make most manual memoisation unnecessary.
useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function identity (useCallback(fn) is useMemo(() => fn)).
React Compiler (stable 2025) can memoize automatically, reducing manual use.
f: Does useMemo guarantee caching?
No, React may discard cached values; treat it as an optimisation.
When does useCallback help?
When passing callbacks to memoised children or as effect dependencies.
p7-6.y: useMemo remembers the result of a calculation and recalculates it only when its dependencies change. useCallback remembers a function itself, so the same function object is passed on each render, which matters when passing it to memoized child components. So useMemo is for values, useCallback is for functions. I use them only where profiling shows a benefit.
x: useMemo and useCallback are both React hooks for avoiding unnecessary work between renders, by remembering something until its dependencies change.

useMemo remembers the result of a calculation. You give it a function and a dependency array, and it only recalculates when a dependency changes. For example, filtering and sorting a large list of shipments: useMemo makes sure that work only happens when the list or the filter changes, not on every render.

useCallback remembers a function itself. Normally, every render creates a new function object, even if the code is the same. That matters when the function is passed as a prop to a child component wrapped in React.memo, or used in another hook's dependency array: a new function each time would make the child re-render, or the effect rerun, every time. useCallback returns the same function instance until its dependencies change.
So the difference is: useMemo caches a value, useCallback caches a function. In fact, useCallback of a function is the same as useMemo returning that function.

I don't use them everywhere, because they have their own cost and make code harder to read. I use them when there's a real reason: an expensive calculation, a memoised child component, or a value used as a dependency. And the new React Compiler can apply this memoisation automatically, which reduces the need to write them by hand.

p7-7.q: useRef returns a mutable object whose .current persists across renders without causing a re-render. It's used for DOM references (focusing an input) and for values like timers, previous values or abort controllers.
i: React 19 allows ref as a regular prop for function components (forwardRef no longer needed).
Don't read or write ref.current during render for values that affect output.
Changing ref.current doesn't re-render; useful for DOM nodes, timers and previous values.
f: useRef vs useState?
Changing a ref doesn't re-render; changing state does.
What is forwardRef for?
Passing refs to child components (unnecessary in React 19).
p7-7.y: useRef gives me a box that keeps a value across renders without causing a re-render when it changes. I use it mainly to access a DOM element directly, like focusing an input, and to store things like a timer id or the previous value of a prop.
x: useRef is a React hook that gives you a mutable object with a current property, which stays the same for the whole life of the component. The key difference from state is that changing ref.current does not cause a re-render.

It has two main uses. The first is accessing a DOM element directly. You create a ref, attach it to an element with the ref attribute, and then ref.current points to that DOM node. That's useful for things React doesn't handle declaratively, like focusing an input when a dialog opens, scrolling to an element, measuring its size, or integrating with a non-React library, like a chart.

The second is keeping a value between renders without displaying it. For example, storing a timer id so you can clear it later, an AbortController for cancelling a request, the previous value of a prop for comparison, or a flag saying whether a request is still current. If that value were in state, every change would re-render the component unnecessarily.
So my rule is: if changing a value should update what's on screen, use state; if it's just something the component needs to remember behind the scenes, use a ref.
One caution: you shouldn't read or write ref.current during rendering, only in effects and event handlers, because rendering should stay predictable.

p7-8.q: Context passes values (theme, current user, locale) down the tree without prop drilling. It's fine for low-frequency global values; Redux Toolkit adds a predictable store, devtools and middleware for complex shared state, and libraries like Zustand are lighter alternatives. Server data is best handled by React Query.
i: Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes; split contexts and memoise values.
Redux Toolkit with RTK Query reduces boilerplate.
Context passes values without prop drilling; every consumer re-renders when the value changes.
Redux Toolkit adds a store with selectors, devtools and middleware; use it for complex shared state.
f: Is Context a state manager?
It's a transport mechanism; state still lives in useState/useReducer.
When choose Redux?
Large apps with complex shared client state and many updates.
p7-8.y: The Context API shares values, like the logged-in user or theme, with any component in the tree without passing props through every level. Redux, with Redux Toolkit, is a full state management library with a central store, actions, devtools and middleware. Context is fine for simple, rarely changing data, and Redux suits large, frequently updated shared state.
p7-8.k: context api, redux, state management, prop drilling
x: The Context API is React's built-in way to share data with many components without passing props down through every level, which is called prop drilling.

You create a context, wrap part of the component tree in its Provider with a value, and any component inside can read that value with the useContext hook. It's ideal for data that many components need and that changes rarely: the current user, the theme, the language, or feature flags. One thing to know is that when the provider's value changes, every component that uses that context re-renders, so it's not great for data that changes very often.

Redux is a separate library for managing global application state. All the shared state lives in one store, and it's changed only by dispatching actions, which reducers handle in a predictable way. Modern Redux Toolkit removes most of the old boilerplate, and RTK Query handles API data and caching. Redux gives you very good dev tools, like seeing every action and the state at each step, middleware for side effects, and fine-grained subscriptions, so components only re-render when the part they use changes.

So I'd use Context for simple, low-frequency shared values, and Redux, or a lighter library like Zustand, for complex, frequently changing shared state. And for server data, like API results, I prefer a dedicated tool like React Query or RTK Query rather than putting it in global state myself.

p7-9.q: I use a typed API client (fetch or axios) with interceptors for tokens and errors, and React Query (TanStack Query) or a custom hook to fetch, cache and retry. The UI shows a loading indicator, an error message with retry, and an empty state, and maps ProblemDetails errors to user-friendly messages.
i: React Query handles caching, background refetch, deduplication and invalidation after mutations.
Abort requests on unmount or parameter change.
Suspense and error boundaries for declarative loading/error UI.
f: Why React Query over useEffect fetching?
It handles caching, races, retries and refetching for you.
How do you refresh after a mutation?
Invalidate the related query keys.
p7-9.y: I use a library like React Query, or RTK Query, which handles fetching, caching, loading and error states, retries and refetching for me. Each screen shows a loading indicator, a clear error message with a retry, and an empty state. All API calls go through one client that adds the auth token and handles common errors.
p7-9.k: api calls, loading state, error handling, react query
x: For API calls in React, I want three things handled consistently: loading, errors, and avoiding race conditions or outdated data.

My preferred approach is a server-state library like TanStack Query, also called React Query, or RTK Query. You give it a key and a fetch function, and it returns the data along with isLoading and error states. It also handles caching, so the same data isn't fetched twice, retries, refreshing stale data, and cancelling outdated requests. For changes, it has mutations, which can refresh related data afterwards.

Without a library, I'd write a custom hook, like useShipments, using useEffect and useState for data, loading and error. It's important to cancel the request with an AbortController in the effect's cleanup, so if the user changes the filter quickly, an old response doesn't overwrite a newer one.

The API calls themselves go through one shared API client, using fetch or axios, which adds the auth token, handles common errors like 401 by redirecting to login, and reads our problem details responses.
On screen, I show a loading skeleton or spinner, a clear error message with a retry button, and an empty state when there's no data. An error boundary catches unexpected rendering errors.
In our CSV import screen, that meant clear progress while the file was being validated, and a helpful row-by-row error report when it failed.

p7-10.q: In a controlled component React state holds the input value (value + onChange), giving validation and formatting on every keystroke. In an uncontrolled component the DOM holds the value, read with a ref or form submission, which is simpler and faster for big forms; React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.
i: File inputs are always uncontrolled.
React 19 form actions work naturally with uncontrolled forms.
Controlled: value lives in React state; uncontrolled: DOM holds it and you read via refs.
React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.
f: Which is better?
Controlled for dynamic validation; uncontrolled for performance and simplicity.
Warning "changing an uncontrolled input to controlled"?
The value went from undefined to defined; initialise state properly.
p7-10.y: In a controlled component, React state holds the input's value and updates it on every change, so React is the single source of truth. In an uncontrolled component, the browser keeps the value and I read it when needed with a ref. Controlled is simpler for validation, and libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs for better performance.
p7-10.k: controlled components, uncontrolled components, forms, react
x: Controlled and uncontrolled components are two ways to handle form inputs in React.

In a controlled component, React state is the single source of truth for the input's value. The input's value attribute is set from state, and an onChange handler updates the state on every keystroke. So React always knows the current value. That makes it easy to validate as the user types, disable a submit button until the form is valid, format input automatically, or change the value from code, like resetting the form. The downside is more code, and re-rendering on every keystroke, which can matter in very large forms.

In an uncontrolled component, the DOM itself keeps the value, like in a plain HTML form. React doesn't track each change. When I need the value, usually on submit, I read it, either through a ref, or from the form data. You can set a starting value with defaultValue. It's simpler and faster for basic forms, and it's required for file inputs, because their value can only be set by the user.

In practice, for most real forms, I use React Hook Form. It uses uncontrolled inputs internally for performance, but still gives full validation, often with a Zod schema, error messages and form state. So I get the convenience of controlled behaviour without the re-render cost.

p7-11.q: Causes are a parent re-rendering (children re-render by default), new object, array or function props each render, context values that change often, and state kept too high in the tree. Fixes: move state down, React.memo with stable props (useMemo/useCallback), split contexts, virtualise long lists, and measure with React DevTools Profiler.
i: Re-renders aren't always bad; only fix measured problems.
Keys: changing keys remount components.
Parent re-renders, new object/function props each render, and context value changes.
Profile with React DevTools before optimizing with memo.
f: How do you find unnecessary renders?
React DevTools Profiler "why did this render".
What does React.memo do?
Skips re-rendering if props are shallowly equal.
p7-11.y: Unnecessary re-renders happen when a parent re-renders and all its children follow, when new objects or functions are created on every render and passed as props, or when a context value changes. I first profile with React DevTools, then fix it by moving state closer to where it's used, and using memo, useMemo and useCallback where it actually helps.
x: Unnecessary re-rendering happens when components render again even though what they show hasn't changed. A little is normal and fine, but in large screens it can make the UI slow.

The common causes are these. First, a parent re-renders, and by default, all its children re-render too, even if their props are the same. Second, new object, array or function props created on every render, like an inline style object, or an inline arrow function as onClick. Even with React.memo on the child, those are new references each time, so the child still re-renders. Third, Context: when a provider's value changes, every consumer re-renders, and if the value is a new object on every render, they re-render every time. Fourth, state kept too high in the tree, so a small change, like typing in a search box, re-renders a whole page. Fifth, derived data stored in state and synced with effects, causing extra render cycles. And sixth, unstable list keys, like using the array index, which can make React recreate items.

To fix them: measure first with the React DevTools Profiler. Then move state down to where it's used, memoise expensive children with React.memo, use useMemo and useCallback for stable props, split contexts, use stable ids as keys, and virtualise long lists, so only visible rows render.
The new React Compiler handles much of the memoisation automatically.

p7-12.q: Login through the SSO/OIDC provider (Authorization Code with PKCE), keep tokens in memory or HttpOnly cookies (BFF), not localStorage; an auth context exposes the user and roles; protected route components redirect unauthenticated users and hide unauthorised UI, while the API always enforces authorization.
i: Silent token renewal; handle 401 by re-authenticating.
MSAL or oidc-client-ts libraries.
Route guards only hide UI; real protection is on the API with token validation.
f: Is hiding UI enough?
No, the backend must enforce every permission.
Why not localStorage?
Any XSS can read it.
p7-12.y: The user logs in through our SSO identity provider, and the app keeps the session, ideally in secure cookies. Protected routes check if the user is logged in and has the right role, and redirect to login otherwise. But that only hides screens. The real protection is on the API, which validates the token and permissions on every request.
p7-12.k: react authentication, protected routes, route guards, sso
x: In React, authentication is mostly handled by the identity provider and the backend; the React app's job is to sign the user in, call APIs with the token, and show only the right screens.

For sign-in, I use OpenID Connect with the authorization code flow and PKCE, through a library like MSAL or oidc-client, with our corporate single sign-on. Even better, for security, is the backend-for-frontend pattern: the server handles the tokens and the browser only gets a secure, HttpOnly session cookie, so no tokens are exposed to JavaScript. If tokens are in the browser, I keep them in memory rather than local storage, to reduce the risk from cross-site scripting.
The auth state, like the current user and their roles, is provided through a context, so any component can check it.

To protect routes, I wrap private routes with a component, often called ProtectedRoute or RequireAuth. With React Router, it checks the auth state: if the user isn't signed in, it redirects to login and remembers where they were going; if they don't have the required role, it shows a forbidden page. Menus and buttons are also hidden based on permissions.

But the most important point: hiding things in the UI is only for user experience. Real security is enforced on the server, where every API validates the token and checks permissions. A user can always bypass front-end checks.

p7-13.q: React Hook Form (or Formik) for state and performance, with a schema validator (Zod or Yup) whose types are shared with TypeScript; show field errors, disable submit while saving, and map server validation errors (ProblemDetails) back to fields.
i: zodResolver connects schema validation.
Server is still the source of truth for validation.
React Hook Form with Zod schemas for validation shared with types.
c:
const schema = z.object({ siteNumber: z.string().min(3), kitCount: z.number().int().positive() });
const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });
f: Why Zod?
One schema gives runtime validation and TypeScript types.
How do you show server errors?
setError on fields from the ProblemDetails errors dictionary.
p7-13.y: I use React Hook Form with a schema library like Zod for validation, which keeps forms fast and the rules in one place, and the same schema gives the TypeScript types. I show errors next to each field, disable submit while saving, and show server-side validation errors too, since the API validates again.
p7-13.k: forms, react hook form, zod, validation
x: For forms in React, I want three things: good performance, clear validation, and simple code. For anything beyond a couple of fields, I use React Hook Form.

React Hook Form registers inputs and keeps their values mostly uncontrolled, so typing doesn't re-render the whole form, which keeps large forms fast. It tracks the form state, like which fields are touched, dirty or invalid, and whether it's submitting. On submit, it gives me all the values, already validated.

For validation, I define a schema with Zod, and connect it with a resolver. The schema describes each field, like required, a maximum length, a valid date, or a rule across fields, like the end date being after the start date. With TypeScript, the same schema also gives me the form's type, so there's one source of truth. Error messages appear next to each field, and the first invalid field is focused, which helps accessibility.

On submit, I disable the button while the request is in progress, to avoid double submissions. If the API returns validation errors, as a problem details response, I map them back onto the matching fields, because the server always validates too.
For very simple forms, controlled inputs with useState are fine.
In the CSV import screen I built, the upload form used this approach, with clear client-side checks for file type and size, and server-side validation for the content.

p7-14.q: Feature-based folders (shipments/, sites/) with components, hooks, API calls and tests together; a shared library of reusable UI components; a typed API layer (generated from OpenAPI); routing with lazy-loaded routes; global state kept minimal; and lint, format and test standards.
i: Code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense.
Storybook for component documentation.
Absolute imports and barrel files used carefully.
Feature-based folders (shipments/, imports/) with components, hooks and API clients together.
f: Why feature folders?
Related code changes together, making features easier to find and own.
How do you share components across apps?
An internal package or monorepo library.
p7-14.y: I organise by feature rather than by file type, so each feature, like shipments or imports, has its components, hooks and API calls together. Shared UI components and utilities live in a common folder. I use TypeScript everywhere, a clear routing structure, lazy loading for big screens, and consistent patterns for data fetching and state.
p7-14.k: react project structure, feature folders, architecture
x: For a large React application, I structure it by feature rather than by type of file, so the code for one business area lives together.

At the top, there's an app folder for application setup: routing, providers, like the auth and query client providers, and the main layout. Then a features folder, with one folder per business area, like shipments, studies or imports. Each feature contains its own components, hooks, API calls, types and tests, and exposes a small public interface through an index file. Other features use only that interface. Then shared folders for things used across features: UI components like buttons and tables, often from a design system, utility functions, and the shared API client.

A few principles go with it. Keep components small and focused, with logic in custom hooks. Keep server data in a library like React Query, and only truly global client state in Context or a store. Use TypeScript in strict mode. Use lazy loading for routes, so users only download the code for the pages they open. Enforce rules with ESLint, Prettier and import restrictions. And test with Vitest or Jest and React Testing Library, plus Playwright for end-to-end tests.
When an app becomes very large, with separate teams, it can be split further into packages in a monorepo, or micro-frontends, but I'd only do that when the team structure really needs it.

p7-15.q: React is a focused UI library: flexible, large ecosystem, easy to adopt piece by piece and a simpler learning curve. Angular is a full framework with DI, routing, forms and RxJS built in, offering strong conventions for large teams. IRT uses both: Angular modules for older areas and React components for newer work.
i: Angular's recent signals and standalone components simplify it.
Choice depends on team skills and existing code.
React: flexible library, huge ecosystem, team experience; Angular: batteries-included framework with strong conventions.
Both are fine; choose on team skills and project needs.
f: Which would you choose for a new project?
Usually React with TypeScript, unless the team is strongly Angular.
What are Angular signals?
Reactive primitives for fine-grained change detection.
p7-15.y: React is a flexible library focused on the UI, with a huge ecosystem, and you choose your own tools for routing and state. Angular is a complete framework with strong conventions built in. Both are good choices. We use React for new screens because of the team's experience, flexibility and the ecosystem.
p7-15.k: react vs angular, frontend framework, comparison
x: React and Angular are both excellent choices, so it depends on the team and the project. Here are the trade-offs, and why we use React.

Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google. It includes routing, forms, an HTTP client, dependency injection and testing tools, and it uses TypeScript by default. Everything has an official way to do it, which gives consistency across large teams. It has a steeper learning curve, though, with concepts like modules, decorators and RxJS.

React is a library focused on the UI. You choose your own libraries for routing, state and data fetching, which gives a lot of flexibility. It's mostly just JavaScript or TypeScript with JSX, so it's quick to learn, and it has a huge ecosystem and community, with plenty of developers available.

For our team, we chose React for new screens for a few reasons: the team's experience, IQVIA's in-house React design system, the modularity of building each feature as its own npm package, the ecosystem, and how easy it is to build small, reusable components. We didn't rewrite everything at once, because it's a GxP-regulated product. Our legacy portal is ASP.NET MVC with Angular sub-applications, and new modules are built in React with TypeScript, module by module, calling our newer .NET APIs, so I work with both. For example, when I fixed the reverse-tabnabbing issue, I fixed [about 40] links across both React and Angular code.
If I joined a team that uses Angular, I'd be happy with it. The fundamentals, components, state, and calling APIs safely, are the same.

p7-16.q: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialised as undefined, and can be redeclared; let is block-scoped and reassignable; const is block-scoped and can't be reassigned (but objects it points to can be mutated). Use const by default, let when reassigning, never var.
i: let/const are in the temporal dead zone before declaration.
Classic bug: var in loops with closures shares one variable.
var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let/const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone.
const prevents reassignment, not mutation of objects.
f: Is a const array immutable?
No, you can push to it; use Object.freeze for shallow immutability.
Why avoid var?
Function scoping and hoisting cause subtle bugs.
p7-16.y: var is function-scoped and can be used before it's declared, which leads to bugs. let and const are block-scoped, so they only exist inside their curly braces. const means the variable can't be reassigned, though an object it points to can still be changed. I use const by default, let when I need to reassign, and never var.
x: var, let and const are the three ways to declare variables in JavaScript, and they differ in scope, hoisting and reassignment.

var is the old way. It's function-scoped, meaning it's visible throughout the whole function, ignoring blocks like if statements and loops. It's hoisted and initialised as undefined, so you can use it before its declaration line without an error, which hides bugs. And it can be declared again in the same scope. A classic problem is var in a loop with callbacks: all the callbacks share one variable and see the final value.

let and const were introduced in ES2015 and are block-scoped: they only exist inside the nearest curly braces. They're also hoisted, but not initialised, so using them before the declaration throws an error. That period is called the temporal dead zone. They can't be redeclared in the same scope.

The difference between let and const is reassignment. let can be reassigned. const can't be reassigned after it's created. But const doesn't make the value immutable. A const object or array can still have its contents changed; you just can't point the variable to a different object.
My rule is: use const by default, let only when the value must change, like a counter, and never var. ESLint rules enforce this in our projects.

p7-17.q: Declarations are processed before code runs: function declarations are fully hoisted, var is hoisted as undefined, and let/const/class are hoisted but in the temporal dead zone, so accessing them early throws ReferenceError.
i: Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to variables follow variable rules.
Declarations are registered during the creation phase before code runs.
Function declarations are fully hoisted; function expressions assigned to var are hoisted as undefined.
let/const/class are hoisted but in the TDZ: access before declaration throws ReferenceError.
f: What prints console.log(x); var x = 5?
undefined.
And with let?
ReferenceError.
p7-17.y: Hoisting means JavaScript processes declarations before running the code, so they're known at the top of their scope. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so I can call them before they appear. var is hoisted but set to undefined. let and const are hoisted too, but using them before the declaration throws an error, which is called the temporal dead zone.
p7-17.k: hoisting, javascript, temporal dead zone, var
x: Hoisting is JavaScript's behaviour of processing declarations before running the code in a scope. It feels as if declarations are moved to the top of their scope, though really the engine registers them during a setup phase.

How it behaves depends on what's declared. Function declarations are hoisted completely, both the name and the body, so you can call a function before the line where it's written. var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined. So if you use a var variable before its declaration, you don't get an error, you get undefined, which can hide bugs. let and const are hoisted too, but not initialised. Using them before the declaration throws a ReferenceError. The time between the start of the scope and the declaration is called the temporal dead zone. Classes behave like let. And function expressions or arrow functions assigned to a variable follow the variable's rules. So with var, the variable exists but is undefined, and calling it fails with "is not a function"; with const, you get a ReferenceError.

In practice, hoisting is mostly something to understand, not rely on. I declare variables before using them, use const and let instead of var, and let ESLint flag anything used before it's defined. That avoids the confusing bugs hoisting can cause.

p7-18.q: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope finished, for example a counter factory or a debounce function keeping its timer. React hooks rely heavily on closures.
i: Stale closures in React effects come from capturing old state.
A function keeps access to variables from its outer scope even after the outer function returns.
Uses: private state, factories, React hooks capturing state (stale closures are a common bug).
f: Memory risk?
Closures keep captured objects alive as long as the function exists.
Same concept in C#?
Yes, lambdas capturing variables.
p7-18.y: A closure is when a function remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. It's used for private data and factory functions. In React, every render's functions capture that render's state, which is why you can get a stale value in a timer if you're not careful.
x: A closure in JavaScript is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, and can keep using them even after that outer function has finished running.

Every function in JavaScript keeps a reference to its surrounding scope. So if an outer function creates a local variable and returns an inner function that uses it, the inner function keeps access to that variable, and the variable stays alive as long as the inner function exists.

A simple example: a function makeCounter creates a variable count set to zero, and returns a function that adds one to count and returns it. Each time I call makeCounter, I get a new counter with its own private count. Nothing outside can change count directly, so closures are also a way to create private state.

Closures are everywhere in real code: event handlers and callbacks that use variables from the component, functions like debounce and memoise, and React hooks, where every render's functions capture that render's props and state. That's also where a common bug comes from: a stale closure, when a callback or effect keeps using an old value of state. That's why the dependency array in useEffect matters.
The classic loop issue is a closure issue too: callbacks created in a loop with var all share one variable, while let creates a new variable for each iteration.

p7-19.q: A Promise represents a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected, handled with then/catch. async/await is syntax over Promises that reads like synchronous code with try/catch. Promise.all runs in parallel and fails fast; Promise.allSettled waits for all; Promise.race and Promise.any return the first to settle or succeed.
i: Unhandled rejections crash Node by default (since Node 15).
Sequential awaits in loops can be slow; use Promise.all for independent calls.
A Promise is pending, fulfilled or rejected; async/await is syntax over promises.
Promise.all for parallel work; Promise.allSettled when partial failures are fine.
f: Promise.all vs allSettled?
all rejects on the first failure; allSettled reports every result.
Is await blocking?
No, it yields to the event loop until the promise settles.
p7-19.y: A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, and it can be pending, fulfilled or rejected. I can chain then and catch on it. async and await are just a cleaner way to write the same thing, so asynchronous code reads like normal step-by-step code with try-catch. For parallel calls, I use Promise.all.
x: A Promise is an object that represents the future result of an asynchronous operation, like an API call. It's in one of three states: pending, while waiting; fulfilled, with a value; or rejected, with an error. Once it's settled, it doesn't change.

With Promises directly, you handle the result by chaining then for success, catch for errors, and finally for cleanup. Each then returns a new Promise, so steps can be chained one after another. There are also helpers for running several at once: Promise.all waits for all of them and fails if any fails, Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each result, Promise.race takes the first to settle, and Promise.any takes the first success.

async and await is newer syntax built on top of Promises. It doesn't replace them; it makes them easier to read. An async function always returns a Promise, and inside it, await pauses that function until the Promise settles, without blocking the main thread. Errors are handled with a normal try, catch and finally. So the code reads top to bottom like synchronous code.

I use async and await almost everywhere for clarity. But I still use Promise.all to run independent calls in parallel, because awaiting them one after another would make them run in sequence and be slower.

p7-20.q: Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks for sequential async steps, hard to read and to handle errors in; it's solved with Promises and async/await, or by splitting into named functions.
i: util.promisify converts Node callback APIs to Promises.
Error-first callbacks were the old Node convention.
Deeply nested callbacks make error handling and flow hard to follow.
Fix with promises/async-await and small named functions.
f: Why is error handling hard with callbacks?
Every level must check and pass errors manually.
Modern Node APIs?
Promise-based versions like fs/promises.
p7-20.y: Callback hell is when asynchronous steps are nested inside each other's callbacks, again and again, so the code moves to the right like a pyramid and becomes hard to read and handle errors. The fix is using Promises and async-await, and breaking logic into small named functions.
x: Callback hell is what happens when asynchronous code is written with nested callbacks, where each step is passed a function to call when it finishes, and the next step goes inside that function. With several steps in a row, the code keeps moving to the right, forming a pyramid shape, which is why it's also called the pyramid of doom.

For example: read a file, and in its callback, parse it, and in that callback, call an API, and in that callback, save the result. Each level also needs its own error check, usually the "if error, return" pattern in Node.js. The problems are that it's hard to read, hard to follow the flow, easy to forget error handling at one level, and difficult to do things like run steps in parallel or retry.

The solutions came in stages. First, naming the functions and keeping them flat helps a little. Then Promises allowed chaining with then, and one catch for all errors. And today, async and await lets you write the same sequence as straight, top-to-bottom code, with normal try and catch. In Node.js, most built-in modules now have Promise versions, like fs/promises, and util.promisify converts older callback functions.
So in modern code, callback hell is mostly avoided simply by using async and await consistently.

p7-21.q: Optional chaining user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of throwing if something is null or undefined. Nullish coalescing count ?? 0 uses the default only for null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0, '' and false.
i: ??= assigns only if null/undefined.
Same operators exist in C# (?. and ??).
a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if a is null/undefined.
x ?? y uses y only for null/undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and "".
f: Why ?? instead of ||?
So valid falsy values like 0 aren't replaced.
Does ?. work with function calls?
Yes, fn?.() calls only if fn exists.
p7-21.y: Optional chaining, the question mark dot, safely reads a nested property and returns undefined instead of throwing if something in the chain is null. Nullish coalescing, the double question mark, gives a default value only when the left side is null or undefined. Unlike the OR operator, it keeps valid values like zero or an empty string.
p7-21.k: optional chaining, nullish coalescing, javascript, typescript
x: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing are two JavaScript and TypeScript operators that make it much safer and cleaner to work with values that might be null or undefined.

Optional chaining, the question mark dot operator, lets you access a property deeply without checking each level. For example, user question-mark-dot address question-mark-dot city. If user or address is null or undefined, the whole expression simply returns undefined, instead of throwing a "cannot read property of undefined" error. It also works for calling functions that might not exist, and for array access.
Nullish coalescing, the double question mark operator, provides a default value, but only when the left side is null or undefined. For example, settings dot pageSize double question mark 20.

The important difference is from the older OR operator. OR returns the right side for any falsy value: zero, an empty string, false, and NaN, as well as null and undefined. So if pageSize was deliberately set to zero, OR would wrongly replace it with 20. Double question mark keeps zero, empty strings and false, and only replaces null or undefined.

They're often used together, like user question-mark-dot name double question mark "Guest". There's also the nullish assignment operator, which sets a value only if it's currently null or undefined. I use these all the time, especially with API data that may have missing fields.

p7-22.q: any turns off type checking entirely; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it (typeof, instanceof, type guards or schema validation) before use. Prefer unknown for untrusted data like API responses or caught errors.
i: catch (e) is unknown with useUnknownInCatchVariables (part of strict).
never represents impossible values (exhaustiveness checks).
any disables type checking; unknown forces you to narrow before use.
Use unknown for parsed JSON and catch variables (useUnknownInCatchVariables in strict).
f: How do you narrow unknown API data?
Validate with Zod and get typed results.
What is never used for?
Exhaustive switch checks and functions that never return.
p7-22.y: any turns off type checking completely, so TypeScript lets you do anything with it, and bugs slip through. unknown also accepts any value, but forces me to check its type before using it. So unknown is the safe choice for things like parsed JSON or caught errors, and I avoid any.
x: any and unknown are both TypeScript types that can hold any value, but they're opposites in terms of safety.

any switches off type checking. You can assign anything to it, and you can do anything with it: call methods, access properties, pass it anywhere, and TypeScript won't complain. So errors only appear at runtime. It's also contagious: values derived from an any are any too, so type safety silently disappears from parts of the code.

unknown is the safe version. You can assign anything to it, but you can't use it until you prove what it is. Before calling a method or reading a property, you must narrow the type, using checks like typeof, instanceof, the in operator, or a type guard function, or validate it with a schema library like Zod. So TypeScript forces you to handle the uncertainty.

In practice, I use unknown for values whose type I genuinely don't know: JSON from an API, data parsed from storage, or the error in a catch block, which TypeScript now types as unknown by default in strict mode. Then I validate it, for example with Zod, which also gives me the correct type.

I avoid any, and our ESLint rules flag explicit any. The only acceptable uses are temporary migrations from JavaScript, or rare cases with badly typed libraries, and even then, I keep it as small and isolated as possible.

p7-23.q: Generics are type parameters that make code reusable while keeping types, for example function first<T>(items: T[]): T or ApiResponse<Shipment>, with constraints using extends.
i: Utility types: Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, Record<K, V>.
keyof and conditional types for advanced typing.
Example: function apiGet<T>(url: string): Promise<T> gives typed API responses.
c:
async function get<T>(url: string): Promise<T> { const r = await fetch(url); return r.json() as Promise<T>; }
const shipment = await get<Shipment>('/api/shipments/42');
f: Generic constraint example?
<T extends { id: number }> ensures T has an id.
Difference from C# generics?
TypeScript generics are erased at runtime; C# generics exist at runtime.
p7-23.y: Generics let me write a function or type that works with many types while keeping type safety. For example, an apiGet function that takes a type parameter T and returns a Promise of T, so each call gets the right response type. It's the same idea as generics in C#.
x: Generics in TypeScript let you write functions, classes and types that work with many types, while still keeping full type safety. Instead of fixing a type, you use a type parameter, usually called T, which is filled in when the code is used.

A simple example is a function that returns the first item of an array. Without generics, you'd either write it for each type, or use any and lose type information. With a generic, function first of T, taking an array of T and returning T, if you pass an array of shipments, TypeScript knows the result is a shipment.

Generics are used everywhere in real code. For example, a generic API helper, like get of T taking a URL, which returns a Promise of T, so each call is typed. Or a generic ApiResponse of T type that wraps any data. React's useState is generic, so useState of Shipment array gives you typed state. Generic components, like a Table of T that receives rows of T and column definitions for T.

You can also constrain generics with extends, for example T extends an object with an id property, so the function can safely use id. You can give defaults for type parameters, and the built-in utility types, like Partial, Pick, Omit and Record, are all generics.
The benefit is reusable code without losing type checking. It's the same idea as generics in C#, which I use every day.

p7-24.q: A union A | B means a value is one of several types, such as 'Pending' | 'Shipped'; an intersection A & B means a value has all members of both; narrowing is TypeScript refining a union inside checks (typeof, in, instanceof, discriminant properties).
i: Discriminated unions with a kind field give exhaustive switches.
Union: A | B (either); intersection: A & B (both).
Narrowing via typeof, in, instanceof, and discriminated unions with a kind field.
c:
type Result = { ok: true; data: Shipment } | { ok: false; error: string };
function show(r: Result) { if (r.ok) console.log(r.data.id); else console.error(r.error); }
f: What is a discriminated union?
A union whose members share a literal property used to tell them apart.
Custom type guard?
A function returning `x is Type`.
p7-24.y: A union type means a value can be one of several types, like string or number, or a fixed set of values like the shipment status. An intersection type combines several types into one with all their properties. Type narrowing is when TypeScript figures out the exact type after a check, like typeof, or a status field in a discriminated union.
p7-24.k: union types, intersection types, type narrowing, typescript
x: Union types, intersection types and narrowing are how TypeScript models values that can take different shapes.

A union type, written with a vertical bar, means a value can be one of several types. For example, string or number, or a status that's one of the literal strings Pending, Shipped or Delivered. That's a very common way to model fixed sets of values.

An intersection type, written with an ampersand, combines several types into one that has all their properties. For example, a Shipment type and an Auditable type combined give an object with the shipment fields and the audit fields.

Type narrowing is how TypeScript works out the more specific type inside a union, based on checks in your code. If a value is string or number and I check typeof value equals string, inside that if block TypeScript knows it's a string. Other ways to narrow are instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and custom type guard functions that return "value is Type".

The most useful pattern is a discriminated union. Each type in the union has a common literal property, like kind or status. For example, an API result that's either success with data, or error with a message. A switch on that property narrows it fully. And with a never check in the default case, TypeScript gives an error if I add a new case and forget to handle it.

p7-25.q: In TypeScript, strict: true enables strict checks such as strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and strictFunctionTypes, catching null and type bugs at compile time. In JavaScript, 'use strict' (and ES modules automatically) turns silent errors into exceptions and forbids some unsafe features.
i: Turn on strict for new projects; migrate old ones gradually.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds safety for arrays and records.
JS "use strict" disallows silent errors (undeclared variables); ES modules are strict by default.
TypeScript "strict": true enables strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and more.
f: What does strictNullChecks do?
Makes null and undefined separate types you must handle.
Are ES modules strict?
Yes, always.
p7-25.y: In JavaScript, use strict turns on stricter rules, like throwing errors for undeclared variables, and ES modules are strict automatically. In TypeScript, the strict setting turns on all the strict checks, like strict null checks and no implicit any. I always turn on strict mode in TypeScript projects, because it catches many bugs early.
p7-25.k: strict mode, use strict, typescript strict
x: Strict mode can mean two things, and both are worth knowing.

In TypeScript, strict mode is the strict option in tsconfig. It turns on a group of stronger type checks. The most important is strictNullChecks, where null and undefined are no longer allowed everywhere, so TypeScript forces you to handle missing values, which prevents the most common runtime errors. Others include noImplicitAny, which reports values whose types TypeScript can't infer instead of quietly using any; strict function types; strictPropertyInitialization, which checks class properties are initialised; and treating catch errors as unknown. For new projects, I always turn strict mode on, and many teams add extra options too, like noUncheckedIndexedAccess. For older code, it can be enabled gradually.

In JavaScript, strict mode is enabled with the "use strict" directive at the top of a file or function. It makes JavaScript less forgiving. For example, assigning to an undeclared variable throws an error instead of creating a global variable by accident, this is undefined in plain function calls instead of the global object, and some unsafe features, like the with statement, aren't allowed. ES modules and classes are in strict mode automatically.
And in React, there's also StrictMode, a component that runs extra checks in development, like rendering components twice to find side effects.
All three exist to catch mistakes early, which is why I keep them on.

p7-26.q: Node runs JavaScript on one thread with an event loop; asynchronous I/O (via libuv) lets it serve many requests while waiting. Synchronous calls (fs.readFileSync, heavy CPU loops) block the event loop and stall every request, so CPU-heavy work goes to worker threads or other services.
i: Event loop phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close; microtasks (Promises) run between.
libuv thread pool handles fs, DNS and crypto.
Node runs JS on a single thread with an event loop; I/O is async through libuv.
CPU-heavy sync work blocks every request; use worker threads.
f: How do you detect event loop blocking?
Event loop lag metrics (perf_hooks monitorEventLoopDelay).
Worker threads vs cluster?
Worker threads share a process for CPU tasks; cluster runs multiple processes for scaling.
p7-26.y: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread. Synchronous code blocks that thread until it finishes, so a slow synchronous operation blocks every other request. Asynchronous code, like file or network calls with callbacks, Promises or async-await, lets Node handle other work while waiting. So in Node, I keep all input and output asynchronous.
p7-26.k: node.js, synchronous, asynchronous, event loop, blocking
x: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread, using an event loop. Understanding synchronous versus asynchronous code is critical because of that.

Synchronous code runs line by line and blocks the thread until it finishes. In Node, that's dangerous, because while the main thread is busy, nothing else can happen: no other request is handled, no timer fires, and no response is sent. For example, using readFileSync on a large file inside a request handler, or doing a heavy calculation like hashing a big file, freezes the whole server for every user.

Asynchronous code starts an operation, like reading a file, querying a database or calling an API, and lets the main thread continue with other work. Node hands the I/O to the operating system, or to its internal thread pool from libuv, and when the result is ready, a callback is queued, and the event loop runs it. With Promises and async and await, the code still reads top to bottom, but the thread is free while waiting. That's why Node can handle thousands of concurrent connections with one thread, as long as the work is mostly I/O.

So my rules in Node are: always use the asynchronous versions of I/O functions, never synchronous ones in request handling. For CPU-heavy work, use worker threads, or move it to a separate service or queue. And monitor event loop delay, because it shows when something is blocking.
It's the same principle as async and await in ASP.NET Core: don't block threads while waiting for I/O.

p7-27.q: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js providing routing, request/response helpers and middleware. Middleware are functions (req, res, next) that run in order for logging, auth, parsing and error handling; error middleware has four arguments (err, req, res, next).
i: Express 5 (2024) handles rejected promises in async handlers automatically.
Same concept as ASP.NET Core middleware.
Express middleware is (req, res, next); error middleware has four args (err, req, res, next), similar to ASP.NET Core's pipeline.
c:
app.use((req, res, next) => { req.headers['x-correlation-id'] ??= randomUUID(); next(); });
app.use((err: Error, req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => res.status(500).json({ title: 'Server error' }));
f: What happens if middleware doesn't call next?
The request hangs unless it sends a response.
Express vs Fastify?
Fastify is faster with schema-based validation; Express is simpler and more widespread.
p7-27.y: Express is the most popular minimal web framework for Node, for building APIs and web apps. Middleware in Express are functions that receive the request, the response and a next function. They run in order, can change the request or response, end it, or call next. Error middleware has an extra error parameter. It's the same idea as ASP.NET Core middleware.
x: Express is the most popular web framework for Node.js. It's minimal and flexible: it gives you routing, middleware and helpers for requests and responses, and you add whatever else you need through packages.

Middleware is the core concept of Express. A middleware is a function that receives three things: the request, the response, and a next function. Middleware functions run in the order they're registered, forming a pipeline that every request passes through. Each one can do something with the request, like reading headers or adding data, modify the response, end the request by sending a response, or call next to pass control to the next middleware. If it neither responds nor calls next, the request just hangs.

Typical middleware includes parsing JSON bodies with express.json, logging, CORS, security headers with Helmet, authentication that validates a token and attaches the user to the request, and rate limiting. Middleware can be applied globally with app.use, to a path, or to a single route, and routers group related routes with their own middleware.

Error-handling middleware is special: it has four parameters, starting with the error. When any middleware or route calls next with an error, or, in Express 5, an async handler throws, Express skips to the error middleware, which can log it and send a consistent error response.
It's the same idea as the middleware pipeline in ASP.NET Core, which I use every day.

p7-28.q: Use try/catch around awaited calls, a central error-handling middleware returning consistent JSON (problem details), never swallow rejections, add process-level handlers for unhandledRejection and uncaughtException that log and exit so the orchestrator restarts cleanly, and log with correlation ids.
i: Operational errors (expected) vs programmer errors (bugs).
Don't keep running after uncaughtException; state may be corrupt.
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers to error middleware automatically.
Handle process-level unhandledRejection to log and exit cleanly.
f: Why exit on uncaughtException?
The process may be in an unknown state; restart is safer.
How do you return errors consistently?
One error middleware mapping error types to status codes.
p7-28.y: I use try-catch around awaited code, and send all errors to one central error middleware that logs them and returns a clean response. Express 5 passes errors from async handlers to that middleware automatically. I also handle unhandled rejections at the process level, log them, and restart cleanly instead of running in a broken state.
p7-28.k: node.js error handling, express, try catch, unhandled rejection
x: In Node.js, I handle errors at three levels: where they happen, in one central place, and as a last safety net for the whole process.

Where they happen: for asynchronous code with async and await, I use try and catch around operations that can fail and that I can do something about, like retrying a call or returning a specific message. For Promises without await, every chain needs a catch. I never leave a Promise rejection unhandled.

Central handling: in Express, I add error-handling middleware with four parameters at the end of the pipeline. All errors are passed there, either by calling next with the error, or automatically in Express 5 when an async handler throws.
