p17-2.q: I define microservice boundaries around business capabilities, not around technical layers or database tables. The main tool is domain-driven design: I find the bounded contexts, the places where a word like "shipment" or "subject" has one clear meaning and one team owns the rules.
p17-2.k: microservice boundaries, service boundaries, how to split microservices, decompose monolith, bounded context, how do you decide services
x: I define microservice boundaries around business capabilities, not around technical layers or database tables. The main tool is domain-driven design: I find the bounded contexts, the places where a word like "shipment" or "subject" has one clear meaning and one team owns the rules.

Then I check a few signals. First, data ownership: each service should own its data, and no other service should write to its tables. Second, change together, live together: if two things always change in the same release, they probably belong in one service. Third, communication: if two services need many chatty synchronous calls to finish one request, the boundary is probably wrong. Fourth, team ownership: one team should be able to own and deploy a service on its own.
I also avoid going too small. Nano-services that each hold one table create network calls, distributed transactions and operational cost with no real benefit.

In our IRT, for example, randomisation, supply and shipments, drug accountability and notifications are natural boundaries, because each has its own rules, data and users. When in doubt, I start with a well-structured modular monolith and split a module out only when there's a clear reason, like independent scaling or a separate team.

p17-3.q: When a chain like A to B to C gets slow, my first job is to prove where the time is going, and my second job is to stop the slowness from spreading.
p17-3.k: a calls b calls c, service c slow, downstream service slow, chain of services slow, cascading latency, service a b c
x: When a chain like A to B to C gets slow, my first job is to prove where the time is going, and my second job is to stop the slowness from spreading.

To find it, I use distributed tracing with a correlation id. A trace shows each hop with its duration, so I can see that A waits on B, and B waits on C. Then I look at C's own metrics: latency percentiles, error rate, CPU, memory, thread pool, database time and any of its own downstream calls. Usually the cause is in C's dependency, like a slow query, a lock, a missing index, or an external API, or it's resource saturation after a traffic jump or a recent release.

While fixing C, I protect A and B. Every call has a timeout, so B doesn't wait forever. Retries are limited, with backoff and jitter, so we don't hammer C even harder. A circuit breaker on B's calls to C fails fast when C is unhealthy, and B returns a fallback or a clear error. Bulkheads keep C's slowness from using up all of B's threads or connections.
Long term, I ask whether the chain needs to be synchronous at all. If B only needs to inform C, a message on a queue removes the dependency completely.

p17-4.q: A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly failing, so we fail fast instead of piling up slow requests. It has three states. Closed is normal: calls go through, and failures are counted. When failures cross a threshold, for example more than half of calls failing within 30 seconds with at least 20 calls, the breaker opens. While open, calls fail immediately without touching the dependency. After a break duration, it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through. If they succeed, it closes again; if not, it opens again.

In .NET I implement it with Polly, which is now built into Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. On a typed HttpClient, I add a resilience pipeline with a timeout, a retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker, in that order, so retries happen inside the breaker's view. The key is to only count real failures, like timeouts and 5xx, not 404s or validation errors.

p17-5.q: I secure microservices in layers, and for authentication I use OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with JWT access tokens from a central identity provider, never home-grown logins in each service.
p17-5.k: secure microservices, microservices security, authentication for microservices, which authentication microservices, oauth microservices, service to service auth
x: I secure microservices in layers, and for authentication I use OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with JWT access tokens from a central identity provider, never home-grown logins in each service.

For users, the front end signs in through the identity provider with the authorization code flow with PKCE. The provider issues a short-lived access token, a JWT, and each API validates it: the signature against the provider's public keys, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. Then authorization is done with roles, scopes or policies in each service, because only the service knows its own rules.

For service-to-service calls, I use the client credentials flow, so each service has its own identity and only the scopes it needs. On top of that, mutual TLS or a service mesh can encrypt and authenticate traffic inside the network.

Around authentication, there's the rest: an API gateway for rate limiting and a single entry point, HTTPS everywhere, secrets in a vault, least privilege on databases, input validation, and audit logging.
In our IRT, Keycloak is the identity provider. The React app uses OIDC, our newer .NET APIs validate Keycloak JWTs with the bearer handler, and permissions come from role, module and action rules.

So the layers work like this. An API gateway can also validate tokens early and reject bad traffic, but each service still validates the token itself, because of defence in depth.
In our IRT, the React app uses Keycloak OIDC, and every new .NET API validates the JWT in middleware, with role and module checks in policies.

p17-7.q: An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, but POST is not, and POST is where retries and double clicks cause duplicate orders or payments.
p17-7.k: idempotency rest api, idempotent api, idempotency key, prevent duplicate requests, retry safe api, double submit api
x: An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, but POST is not, and POST is where retries and double clicks cause duplicate orders or payments.

The standard way is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique key, like a GUID, and sends it in a header, for example Idempotency-Key. On the server, before doing the work, I check a store for that key. If it's new, I record it as in progress, do the work, and save the response with the key. If the same key comes again, I return the saved response instead of doing the work again. If it's still in progress, I return 409. Keys expire after a sensible period, like 24 hours.

The store must be atomic: a unique constraint in the database, or a Redis SET with NX, so two parallel requests can't both pass the check. Ideally the key is saved in the same transaction as the business change.

I add database constraints too, as a last safety net. In our IRT, I used exactly this for re-randomisation: an idempotency key from the UI, plus a unique constraint of one assignment per subject per stage, so a retry can never randomise twice.

p17-8.q: That's called a captive dependency. A singleton lives for the whole application, so if it takes a scoped service in its constructor, that scoped instance gets captured and lives forever too, instead of living for one request.
p17-8.k: singleton depends on scoped, captive dependency, scoped inside singleton, singleton scoped problem, inject scoped into singleton, cannot consume scoped service from singleton
x: That's called a captive dependency. A singleton lives for the whole application, so if it takes a scoped service in its constructor, that scoped instance gets captured and lives forever too, instead of living for one request.

The drawbacks are serious. A DbContext is scoped, so a captured DbContext is shared across all requests and threads. DbContext is not thread-safe, so you get random concurrency exceptions, stale cached entities, growing memory from change tracking, and data from one user's request leaking into another. Anything request-specific, like the current user, would also be wrong for everyone after the first request.

ASP.NET Core protects you in development: scope validation is on, and you get an error like "Cannot consume scoped service from singleton". In production that check is off by default, so the bug can slip through if you don't test properly.

The fixes: make the consumer scoped too, if it doesn't need to be a singleton. Or, if it must be a singleton, like a background service, inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope for each unit of work, resolve the scoped service inside it, and dispose the scope afterwards. For DbContext specifically, IDbContextFactory is a clean option.
I always enable ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild, so these mistakes fail at startup.

For state in a large React app, the first step is to separate the types of state, because they need different tools. Server state, meaning data from APIs, is best handled by a data-fetching library like React Query, or RTK Query, which gives caching, loading states, refetching and invalidation. Global client state, like the logged-in user, selected study or UI preferences, goes into Redux Toolkit or a small store like Zustand. Local UI state, like whether a dialog is open, stays in useState inside the component. Form state goes into a form library like React Hook Form. And URL state, like filters and paging, goes into the query string, so links are shareable.
The mistakes I avoid are putting everything into Redux, and putting fast-changing values into one big Context, which re-renders every consumer.
In our React shell, we use Redux Toolkit for shared state, with slices per feature module, and axios with interceptors for API calls, so each npm feature package stays independent.

p17-10.q: They solve different problems. useState stores state: a value that belongs to the component and, when you change it with the setter, makes React re-render. useMemo doesn't store state at all; it caches the result of a calculation between renders and only recalculates when its dependencies change.
p17-10.k: usestate vs usememo, use state vs use memo, usememo usestate difference, react usememo, react usestate
x: They solve different problems. useState stores state: a value that belongs to the component and, when you change it with the setter, makes React re-render. useMemo doesn't store state at all; it caches the result of a calculation between renders and only recalculates when its dependencies change.

So with useState, I destructure count and setCount from useState(0), and calling setCount triggers a re-render with the new value. With useMemo, I write const total = useMemo(() => items.reduce(...)) with items in the dependency array, and React reuses the previous total until items changes.

The typical uses of useMemo are two. First, expensive calculations, like filtering or sorting thousands of rows. Second, keeping the same object or array reference between renders, so a child wrapped in React.memo, or a useEffect dependency, doesn't see a "new" value every time.

A common mistake is using useMemo everywhere. It has its own cost and makes code harder to read, so I use it only when the profiler shows a slow calculation or unnecessary re-renders. Another mistake is storing derived values in useState and syncing them with useEffect; it's simpler and safer to calculate them during render, with useMemo if needed.

p17-11.q: First I measure, with the React DevTools Profiler and the "highlight updates" option, to see which components re-render and why. Optimising without measuring usually adds complexity with no benefit.

Then I apply the right fix. Keep state as close as possible to where it's used, so a change in one input doesn't re-render the whole page. Wrap pure, expensive child components in React.memo, so they skip rendering when their props haven't changed. Make props stable: use useCallback for functions and useMemo for objects and arrays passed to memoised children, because a new function or object on every render breaks memo. Split big Contexts, or put fast-changing values in a store with selectors, like Redux Toolkit or Zustand, so components subscribe only to the slice they need. Use stable keys in lists, never array indexes when items can move. For very long lists, use virtualisation, so only visible rows render.
Avoid creating components inside other components, because that remounts them every time.

In our React shell, a drug accountability grid was slow because every keystroke in a filter re-rendered all rows. [Moving the filter state down, memoising the row component and virtualising the grid made typing smooth again.]

p17-12.q: Code splitting means breaking one big JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks, and lazy loading means downloading a chunk only when it's needed. Together they make the first page load much faster.

In React, I use React.lazy with a dynamic import, like const Reports = lazy(() => import('./Reports')), and wrap it in Suspense with a fallback spinner. The most useful place is route-level splitting: each page is its own chunk, so the login page doesn't download the reporting module. I also lazy load heavy components that aren't visible at first, like charts, rich editors or big dialogs. Vite and webpack create the chunks automatically from dynamic imports. I add an error boundary around lazy parts, because a chunk download can fail after a deployment, and I can prefetch likely next pages on hover.
In Angular, it's built into the router: loadChildren for a feature module, or loadComponent for a standalone component, and the new @defer blocks in templates.
Then I check the result with the bundle analyser and Lighthouse.
In our React shell, each feature module is a separate npm package, and the shell lazy loads each one by route, so a site user who never opens drug accountability never downloads that code.

p17-13.q: In production, I can't attach a debugger to the user's browser, so I rely on good telemetry and a clear process.

First, collect evidence. Error monitoring, like Sentry or Datadog RUM, captures JavaScript errors with stack traces mapped back to the TypeScript source through uploaded source maps, plus the browser, the release version and the user's steps. An error boundary in React catches render errors, shows a friendly message, and reports the error. Second, reproduce. I check the browser's DevTools, the network tab for failing or slow calls, the console for errors, and the performance tab for long tasks. I try the same browser, role and data as the user.
Third, check performance. Lighthouse, Web Vitals data from real users, like LCP, INP and CLS, and tools like GTmetrix or WebPageTest show slow loading, big bundles or layout shifts.
Common causes are a new release with a chunk loading error, a browser-specific API, an unhandled null from the API, or a slow endpoint.
Finally, I fix forward or roll back, and add a test so it doesn't come back.

The report is built on Google Lighthouse. It shows Web Vitals, like Largest Contentful Paint, which is when the main content appears, Total Blocking Time, and Cumulative Layout Shift, which measures things jumping around. It also has a waterfall chart, showing every request the page makes, in order, with its size and timing, so you can spot a huge image, a slow API call, render-blocking scripts or too many requests. And it gives specific recommendations, like compressing images, enabling caching, or reducing unused JavaScript. You can also track a page over time and get alerts if it gets slower.

It's similar to Google PageSpeed Insights and WebPageTest. The limitation is that it tests public URLs from its own servers, so for an internal app behind login, I'd use Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools or in the CI pipeline instead, plus real-user monitoring.
I use these tools after a release to check that bundle sizes and load times haven't got worse.

p17-16.q: I always start by measuring, because the slow part is rarely where you guess.

First, find the bottleneck. For a quick view, I use cProfile or py-spy, which can attach to a running process without changing code and shows a flame graph. For a web service, I check traces and logs to see whether time goes into the database, external calls or Python code itself.

Then I fix based on what I find. If it's I/O, like database or HTTP calls, I reduce the number of calls, batch them, add indexes, cache results, or use async with asyncio and httpx so calls run concurrently. If it's CPU in pure Python loops, I use better algorithms and data structures, like sets and dicts for lookups instead of lists, vectorise with NumPy or pandas, use built-in functions, or move the hot path to a compiled library. Because of the GIL, threads don't speed up CPU work, so for that I use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor. For memory, I use generators to stream large data instead of loading everything.
For web services, I also check the server setup: enough uvicorn or gunicorn workers, connection pooling, and no blocking calls inside async code, which freezes the event loop.
Then I measure again, to prove the improvement.

p17-17.q: All three run your code on AWS, but they differ in how much you manage.
p17-17.k: ecs vs eks vs lambda, ecs eks lambda difference, aws container options, when to use eks, aws compute choices, eks vs ecs
x: All three run your code on AWS, but they differ in how much you manage.

ECS, Elastic Container Service, is AWS's own container orchestrator. You define a task definition with your Docker image, CPU, memory and environment, and an ECS service keeps the desired number of tasks running behind a load balancer. With Fargate, there are no servers to manage. It's simple and deeply integrated with IAM, CloudWatch and load balancers.

EKS, Elastic Kubernetes Service, is managed Kubernetes. AWS runs the control plane, and you use standard Kubernetes objects like Deployments, Services and Ingress. It's more powerful and portable across clouds, with a huge ecosystem like Helm and service meshes, but it needs more Kubernetes skill and operational effort.

Lambda is serverless functions. You upload code, it runs in response to events, like an API Gateway request, an S3 upload or an SQS message, it scales automatically, even to zero, and you pay per invocation. The limits are a 15-minute maximum, cold starts and less control.

So my rule is: Lambda for event-driven glue and spiky, short tasks; ECS for most containerised APIs and workers when you're on AWS; and EKS when you already have Kubernetes skills or need its ecosystem or portability.

If traffic is normal but CPU jumped, something changed, so I check for a recent deployment, a configuration change, or a new type of request.

To protect users quickly, I scale out by increasing the desired task count, and check that auto scaling is working and that its CPU target isn't too high. If a release caused it, I roll back to the previous task definition revision.

Then I find the root cause. Container Insights shows CPU per task: if one task is hot, it may be stuck in a loop or retry storm. Traces and logs show which endpoints got slower. For .NET, I use dotnet-counters for CPU, garbage collection and thread pool queue length, and dotnet-trace for a CPU profile, which points to the hot method. Common causes are a new inefficient code path, heavy JSON serialisation, too much logging, regex backtracking, garbage collection pressure from big allocations, or thread pool starvation from sync-over-async code.
Finally, I fix the cause, load test the fix, and tune auto scaling and alarms, so we scale before latency suffers.

p17-19.q: A task that keeps starting and stopping is ECS replacing tasks that exit or fail health checks, so I need the reason it stops.
p17-19.k: ecs task restarting, ecs task keeps stopping, ecs task crash loop, ecs stopped task reason, container keeps restarting ecs, task stops and starts
x: A task that keeps starting and stopping is ECS replacing tasks that exit or fail health checks, so I need the reason it stops.

First, the stopped task's details. In the ECS console or with describe-tasks, every stopped task has a stopped reason and an exit code. "Essential container exited" with exit code 1 usually means the app crashed at startup. Exit code 137 means it was killed, often out of memory, which shows as OutOfMemoryError. "Task failed ELB health checks" means it started but the load balancer marked it unhealthy. "CannotPullContainerError" means an image or permission problem.

Second, the logs, in CloudWatch Logs for that task, just before it stopped. Startup crashes are often a missing environment variable, a secret the task role can't read, a wrong connection string, or a port mismatch.

Third, health checks. If the app is slow to start, the health check grace period may be too short, so ECS kills it before it's ready. I check the health check path, the expected status code, timeouts, and that the container listens on the right port.
Fourth, resources: memory limits too low, or CPU too small for startup.
The deployment circuit breaker can also roll back automatically. Once fixed, I add a startup configuration check, so failures are clear in logs.

p17-20.q: Yes. In IQVIA's newer services on AWS I've worked with RDS for SQL Server, for relational data with transactions and joins, and DynamoDB for simpler, high-volume lookups like status and event data. Our main CIRT platform itself uses on-premise SQL Server.
p17-20.k: rds and dynamodb, partition key dynamodb, dynamo db partition key, dynamic db partition key, hash key dynamodb, what is partition key
x: Yes. In IQVIA's newer services on AWS I've worked with RDS for SQL Server, for relational data with transactions and joins, and DynamoDB for simpler, high-volume lookups like status and event data. Our main CIRT platform itself uses on-premise SQL Server.

In DynamoDB, the partition key is the attribute DynamoDB uses to decide where an item is stored. It hashes the partition key value and places the item in one of many physical partitions. Every item must have it, and if the table has only a partition key, it must be unique, like an order id.

A table can also have a sort key. Then the primary key is the combination of both, and many items can share the same partition key, stored together and sorted by the sort key. For example, partition key is shipmentId and sort key is the event timestamp, so I can query all events for one shipment in time order.

The partition key matters for performance. Each partition has throughput limits, so the key should have many distinct values with evenly spread traffic. A key like "status" with only a few values creates hot partitions and throttling. And queries need the partition key; without it you're doing a slow, expensive scan.

p17-21.q: In DynamoDB, you design keys from your access patterns, not from entities, because you can only query efficiently by key.
p17-21.k: dynamodb key design, design partition keys large scale, dynamo db key design, single table design, hot partition dynamodb, dynamodb access patterns
x: In DynamoDB, you design keys from your access patterns, not from entities, because you can only query efficiently by key.

So first I list every access pattern: get shipment by id, list events for a shipment in time order, list shipments for a site by status, and so on. Then I design the partition key and sort key to answer them.

The partition key needs high cardinality and even traffic, like a shipment id or customer id, so load spreads across partitions. I avoid low-cardinality keys like status or date, which create hot partitions. If one key is naturally very busy, I use write sharding: add a suffix, like a random number from 1 to 10, and query all shards in parallel.
The sort key gives ordering and range queries, and I often use composite values, like "EVENT#2026-11-24T10:00", so begins_with and between work.

For other access patterns, I add global secondary indexes, with their own partition and sort keys, keeping in mind they're eventually consistent. Many teams use single-table design, storing related entities in one table with generic keys like PK and SK, so one query fetches a whole aggregate.
I also use TTL to expire old items, and on-demand capacity for unpredictable traffic.

p17-22.q: It depends on what I'm caching, and there are usually several layers.
p17-22.k: caching in aws, aws caching service, elasticache, which cache aws, redis aws, cloudfront caching
x: It depends on what I'm caching, and there are usually several layers.

For application data, like reference data, configuration, sessions or expensive query results, I use ElastiCache, normally the Redis or Valkey engine, because it supports rich data types, expiry, persistence and replication. The common pattern is cache-aside: the service checks Redis first, and on a miss it reads the database, stores the value with a TTL, and returns it. On writes, I update the database and then delete the cache key, so the next read refreshes it. I add random jitter to TTLs, so many keys don't expire at once, and use a lock or single-flight to prevent a stampede on hot keys.

For static content and cacheable API responses at the edge, I use CloudFront, which caches close to users. API Gateway also has its own response cache. For DynamoDB, DAX is a microsecond read cache. And inside each service, a small in-memory cache, like IMemoryCache in .NET, is the fastest layer, for data that rarely changes.

I'm careful with what not to cache: anything that must be strongly consistent, or user-specific data without a proper key. In our CIRT platform, which runs on-premise, Redis caches study configuration, refreshed by RabbitMQ events.

Parameters are organised in a hierarchy, like /myapp/prod/Database/Timeout, so I can load all settings for one service and environment with one call, by path. There are three types: String, StringList, and SecureString, which is encrypted with a KMS key, so it can hold sensitive values too. Access is controlled with IAM, so each service's role can read only its own path. Every change is versioned, so you can see history and roll back, and changes can trigger events through EventBridge.
There's a standard tier, which is free, with values up to 4 KB, and an advanced tier with larger values and parameter policies, like expiry.

In .NET, I use the Amazon.Extensions.Configuration.SystemsManager package, so Parameter Store becomes a normal configuration source, bound to the options pattern, with optional reload. In ECS, I can also inject parameters as environment variables in the task definition.
In IQVIA's newer services on AWS that I've worked on, settings live in Parameter Store, much like Azure DevOps variable groups hold settings for our on-premise CIRT releases.

p17-24.q: Both store values outside your code, and both can encrypt with KMS, but they're designed for different jobs.
p17-24.k: parameter store vs secrets manager, secrets manager vs parameter store, ssm vs secrets manager, where to store secrets aws, secret rotation aws
x: Both store values outside your code, and both can encrypt with KMS, but they're designed for different jobs.

Parameter Store is mainly for configuration. It stores plain strings and SecureStrings in a hierarchy, with versioning and IAM access. The standard tier is free, which makes it great for lots of settings, like URLs, timeouts and feature flags. It can store secrets as SecureString, but it has no built-in rotation.

Secrets Manager is purpose-built for secrets, like database passwords, API keys and SFTP credentials. Its main advantage is automatic rotation: for RDS and other databases, it can rotate the password on a schedule with a Lambda function, updating both the database and the secret, so nobody needs to touch the password. It also supports cross-region replication, resource policies for cross-account access, and generating random passwords. It costs per secret per month, plus API calls.

So my rule is: configuration in Parameter Store, real secrets in Secrets Manager, especially anything that should rotate. Applications read both at runtime with their IAM role, and cache the values, to avoid throttling and cost.
In our AWS services, database credentials live in Secrets Manager with rotation, and normal settings live in Parameter Store.

p17-25.q: A 2 GB image is slow to push, pull and start, and has a bigger attack surface, so I'd shrink it step by step.
p17-25.k: reduce docker image size, docker image 2gb, docker image too big, smaller docker image, optimize docker image, slim docker image
x: A 2 GB image is slow to push, pull and start, and has a bigger attack surface, so I'd shrink it step by step.
First, I look at what's inside, with docker history and a tool like dive, which shows the size of each layer. Usually the culprits are a full SDK base image, build tools, caches and unneeded files.

Then the main fixes. Use a multi-stage build: compile in a stage based on the SDK image, then copy only the published output into a small runtime image. For .NET, that means building with the sdk image and running on the aspnet runtime image, or an Alpine or chiselled Ubuntu variant, which can be around 100 MB or less. Add a .dockerignore, so bin, obj, node_modules, .git and test data never enter the build context. Combine package installs into one RUN, with --no-install-recommends, and clean the package cache in the same layer, because deleting files in a later layer doesn't reduce size. Don't copy large data files or models into the image; mount or download them at runtime.
For .NET, trimming or a self-contained single file, or even Native AOT for suitable apps, can go further.
I then scan the smaller image and check that startup and tests still pass.

p17-26.q: Blue-green deployment means running two identical production environments. Blue is the current live version, and green is the new version. You deploy and test the new version on green while blue keeps serving users. When green is verified, you switch traffic from blue to green in one step, usually at the load balancer or DNS. If something goes wrong, you switch back to blue immediately, because it's still running.
p17-26.k: blue green deployment, blue-green, blue green release, zero downtime deployment, blue and green environment, switch traffic deployment
x: Blue-green deployment means running two identical production environments. Blue is the current live version, and green is the new version. You deploy and test the new version on green while blue keeps serving users. When green is verified, you switch traffic from blue to green in one step, usually at the load balancer or DNS. If something goes wrong, you switch back to blue immediately, because it's still running.
The benefits are near-zero downtime, instant rollback, and the ability to test the real production setup before users see it.

The costs: you need double capacity during the switch, and the database is the hard part. Both versions usually share one database, so schema changes must be backward compatible, using the expand-and-contract approach: add new columns first, deploy code that works with both, and remove old columns only later.

On AWS, ECS supports blue-green through CodeDeploy, with two target groups behind the load balancer, a test listener, and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms. Kubernetes can do it by switching a Service's selector between two deployments.
It's different from canary, where you shift traffic gradually, like 10 percent first, and from rolling deployment, where instances are replaced one by one.

p17-27.q: Automatic rollback needs two things: a reliable signal that the deployment is bad, and a fast, safe way to go back to the last good version.
p17-27.k: automatic rollback, auto rollback pipeline, rollback cicd, rollback production deployment, deployment rollback strategy, rollback on failure
x: Automatic rollback needs two things: a reliable signal that the deployment is bad, and a fast, safe way to go back to the last good version.

For the way back, I build once and keep every versioned artifact or image, so rollback is redeploying the previous version, never rebuilding. Database changes are backward compatible, so the old code still works with the new schema.

For the signal, I use several checks. Readiness and health checks fail the deployment if new instances don't start. Smoke tests run right after deployment against key endpoints. And during a bake period, monitoring alarms watch error rate and latency compared with the baseline.

Then the tools act. In ECS, the deployment circuit breaker with rollback enabled returns to the last stable task definition if tasks fail to become healthy, and CodeDeploy blue-green can roll back on CloudWatch alarms. In Kubernetes, a failed rollout can be undone with rollout undo, and tools like Argo Rollouts automate canary analysis. In Azure DevOps, a post-deployment gate can query monitoring, and a failure stage redeploys the previous release.

I also use feature flags, so a risky feature can be turned off without a deployment. In our releases, we keep the previous tagged release ready, and [rolled back a UAT release within 15 minutes] once when a setting was missing.

p17-28.q: I follow the test pyramid, adjusted for microservices: many fast unit tests, a good layer of integration and contract tests, and a few end-to-end tests.
p17-28.k: microservices testing strategy, testing microservices, unit tests microservices, test pyramid microservices, contract testing, integration tests microservices
x: I follow the test pyramid, adjusted for microservices: many fast unit tests, a good layer of integration and contract tests, and a few end-to-end tests.

Unit tests cover business logic in isolation, like validators, domain rules and handlers, with xUnit or NUnit, and Moq or fakes for dependencies. They run in seconds on every build. I focus on behaviour and edge cases, not on mocking every line.

Integration tests check a service with its real dependencies. In .NET, WebApplicationFactory hosts the API in memory, and Testcontainers starts a real SQL Server, PostgreSQL or RabbitMQ in Docker, so I test real queries, migrations and message handling, not mocks.

Contract tests protect the boundaries between services. With Pact, the consumer defines what it expects from an API, and the provider's pipeline verifies it, so a breaking change is caught before deployment, without running all services together.
End-to-end tests, with Playwright, cover a few critical user journeys in a deployed environment, because they're slow and fragile.
Around that: performance tests for key endpoints, security scans, and quality gates in SonarQube on coverage of new code.
In our regulated IRT, we add formal verification on top, and every rule in a feature like the CSV import has a unit test matching it.

p17-29.q: I follow a fixed order: scope, find the slow step, restore service, then fix the root cause.
p17-29.k: api 200ms to 5 seconds, api suddenly slow, response time increased, api latency increased production, slow api production, api slow troubleshoot
x: I follow a fixed order: scope, find the slow step, restore service, then fix the root cause.

Scope first. Is it every endpoint or one? All users or some? Since when exactly? And what changed at that time: a deployment, a configuration change, a data growth, a traffic spike, or a change in a dependency?

Then find where the 5 seconds go. Distributed traces break the request into spans, so I can see if it's the database, a downstream API, a queue or the code itself. If it's the database, I check Query Store or the slow query log for the query whose duration jumped, and its execution plan. Common causes are a plan change from parameter sniffing, a missing index after a new filter, lock blocking, or a table that grew. If it's the application, I check thread pool starvation from sync-over-async, connection pool exhaustion, garbage collection pauses, or a new N+1 query. If it's a downstream call, I check its latency and whether timeouts and retries are making it worse.
To restore service, I roll back a bad release, scale out, or force the last good query plan.
Then I fix it properly. [In March 2025, our shipments API went from about 200 milliseconds to 3 seconds because of parameter sniffing; I forced the good plan, then fixed the index.]

p17-30.q: If there are 500s but nothing in the application logs, the error is probably happening before or outside our code, or our logging is losing it. So I work from the outside in.
p17-30.k: 500 errors no logs, http 500 not in logs, errors not logged, 500 but logs empty, missing logs 500 error, server error no log
x: If there are 500s but nothing in the application logs, the error is probably happening before or outside our code, or our logging is losing it. So I work from the outside in.

First, confirm where the 500 comes from. I check the response headers and body, and the load balancer or gateway logs and metrics. An ALB returning 502 or 503, or an API Gateway integration error, is different from a 500 generated by our app. On IIS, a 500.30 or 502.5 means the ASP.NET Core app failed to start, which is in the Windows event log, not our app logs.
Second, check the hops between: the reverse proxy, the ingress, a WAF, or the gateway timing out. Their access logs show which upstream answered.

Third, check whether our logging works at all. A crash at startup happens before logging is configured. An unhandled exception middleware might return 500 without logging. Logs might be dropped because the logging sink is down, buffered and lost when the container dies, or filtered by a wrong log level. A process killed for memory leaves no log.
Fourth, check the container or host: restarts, exit codes and out-of-memory kills.
Then I fix the cause and the visibility: global exception logging, startup logging to console, and correlation ids returned to users.

p17-31.q: When it only happens in production, I stop trying to guess and focus on what's different between production and my machine.
p17-31.k: cannot reproduce locally, issue not reproducible, works on my machine, production only bug, reproduce production issue, hard to reproduce bug
x: When it only happens in production, I stop trying to guess and focus on what's different between production and my machine.

First, gather evidence from production itself: logs and traces filtered by correlation id for the failing requests, the exact time, the user, the data involved, the version deployed and the environment. Patterns matter: does it happen for one site, one study, one browser, or only under load?

Then compare the differences. Data: production has volumes and edge cases, like special characters, nulls or old records, that test data doesn't. Configuration: a setting, feature flag or secret differs. Infrastructure: several instances instead of one, a load balancer, time zones, culture settings, Linux instead of Windows. Concurrency: race conditions only appear under real parallel load. And dependencies: real third-party systems behave differently from mocks.

To reproduce, I copy the exact request, use masked production data in a lower environment, match the configuration, and use load tests for concurrency issues. If it still won't reproduce, I add targeted logging or metrics around the suspected code, release them, and wait for the next occurrence. For memory or CPU issues, I take a dump from production.
[Once, a date filter bug appeared only for US sites, because I'd tested only in Indian time; I fixed it by storing everything in UTC.]

p17-32.q: Centralised logging means every service sends its logs to one searchable place, so I can follow a request across all of them.
p17-32.k: centralized logging microservices, centralised logging, log aggregation microservices, central logging, logs across services, aggregate logs
x: Centralised logging means every service sends its logs to one searchable place, so I can follow a request across all of them.

There are four parts. First, structured logs. Each service writes JSON with consistent fields: timestamp, level, service name, environment, version, message, exception, and, most importantly, a correlation or trace id. In .NET I use Serilog or the built-in logger with message templates.

Second, correlation. The first service generates a trace id, or reads it from the incoming request, and every outgoing HTTP call and every message carries it in a header. With OpenTelemetry and W3C trace context, this is automatic, and the same id links logs and traces.

Third, collection and shipping. Services either write to stdout and an agent collects them, like Fluent Bit, the CloudWatch agent or the Datadog agent, or they ship directly through a sink. Agents are better, because the app doesn't block on the log platform.
Fourth, the central store and tools: Elasticsearch with Kibana, Splunk, Datadog, CloudWatch Logs or Azure Log Analytics, with search, dashboards, alerts and retention rules.
I also mask personal data and secrets before logging. In our CIRT platform, Serilog sends logs to Splunk, and the correlation id in each message lets support trace one request across services.

p17-33.q: With different stacks, I don't standardise the logging library; I standardise the format, the correlation and the pipeline.
p17-33.k: centralized logging different languages, polyglot logging, logging across java and dotnet, logging standard multiple teams, opentelemetry logging, common log format
x: With different stacks, I don't standardise the logging library; I standardise the format, the correlation and the pipeline.

First, a shared logging standard that every team follows: JSON output, a common set of field names, like timestamp, level, service.name, environment, version, trace_id, span_id and message, and agreed log levels. Using a known schema, like OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions or the Elastic Common Schema, avoids arguing about names.

Second, OpenTelemetry as the common layer. It has SDKs for .NET, Java, Node, Python and Go, and uses W3C trace context headers, so a trace started in a .NET service continues in a Java service, and every log line carries the same trace id. Each team keeps its own library: Serilog or ILogger in .NET, Logback or Log4j2 with a JSON encoder in Java, pino in Node.

Third, collection outside the apps. Services write to stdout, and the OpenTelemetry Collector or Fluent Bit collects, enriches, masks and forwards everything to one backend, like Elastic, Splunk, Datadog or CloudWatch. Changing backends later doesn't touch any service.

Fourth, governance: a shared starter package or template per stack, and a check in the pipeline or dashboards that flag services missing trace ids. That keeps five teams consistent without forcing one language.

p17-34.q: Both clouds have managed services for this, and they map quite closely.
p17-34.k: managed logging services aws azure, cloudwatch logs vs log analytics, azure monitor logging, aws logging services, centralized logging cloud services, cloud logging options
x: Both clouds have managed services for this, and they map quite closely.

On AWS, the core is CloudWatch Logs. Services in ECS, Lambda and EKS send logs there through the awslogs driver, the Lambda runtime, or Fluent Bit. Logs are grouped into log groups, searched with CloudWatch Logs Insights, and turned into metrics and alarms. X-Ray, or the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry, adds distributed tracing. For heavy search and dashboards, Amazon OpenSearch Service gives a managed Elasticsearch-style stack, often fed by subscription filters or Kinesis Data Firehose. S3 is used for cheap long-term archive, queried with Athena. CloudTrail is the audit log of AWS API calls.

On Azure, the core is Azure Monitor with a Log Analytics workspace. Application Insights collects application logs, requests, dependencies and traces, and can use OpenTelemetry. Everything is queried with KQL, the Kusto query language, with workbooks for dashboards and alert rules. Diagnostic settings send platform logs from resources like App Service and AKS to the workspace, and Container Insights covers AKS.
Many teams also use third-party platforms that work across clouds, like Datadog, Splunk, Elastic Cloud or Grafana Loki.
In our on-premise CIRT platform, we use Splunk, and our newest services also use OpenTelemetry with Datadog.

p17-35.q: I choose based on how many services there are, how much control we need, and the team's operational skills.
p17-35.k: azure web app vs aks, app service vs kubernetes, web app or aks, when to use aks, azure app service vs aks, paas vs kubernetes
x: I choose based on how many services there are, how much control we need, and the team's operational skills.

Azure App Service, often called Web App, is a fully managed platform for web apps and APIs. You deploy code or a container, and Azure handles the servers, patching, scaling, TLS certificates and deployment slots for zero-downtime swaps. It integrates easily with Azure AD, Key Vault and Application Insights. It's ideal for a handful of web apps or APIs, a small team, or when you want to go live quickly with little operations work.

AKS, Azure Kubernetes Service, is managed Kubernetes. It gives much more control and flexibility: many microservices with complex networking, sidecars and service meshes, custom scaling with KEDA based on queue length, background workers, stateful workloads, GPU nodes, and portability across clouds. But you need Kubernetes skills to manage cluster upgrades, node pools, ingress, security policies and monitoring.
There's also a middle option, Azure Container Apps, which runs containers with Kubernetes-style features like KEDA scaling and Dapr, without managing a cluster.
So my rule: a few web apps or APIs, use App Service; many containerised services with a platform team, use AKS; containers without cluster management, consider Container Apps.

p17-36.q: Both are ways to coordinate a business process that spans several services.
p17-36.k: orchestration vs choreography, saga orchestration, saga choreography, event choreography, workflow orchestration microservices
x: Both are ways to coordinate a business process that spans several services.

In orchestration, one central component, the orchestrator, tells each service what to do and in what order. For example, an order orchestrator calls payment, then inventory, then shipping, and handles failures. The flow is easy to see and change in one place, and easy to monitor. The downside is that the orchestrator can become a bottleneck or a "god service" that knows too much.

In choreography, there is no central controller. Each service listens for events and reacts. Payment publishes "PaymentCompleted", inventory listens and reserves stock, then publishes "StockReserved", and so on. Services are loosely coupled and independent, but the overall flow is spread across many services, so it's harder to understand, debug and change, and you can get hidden cyclic dependencies.

My rule is: choreography for simple flows with few steps, where services just react to facts; orchestration for long, complex processes with many steps, compensation and timeouts, often using a workflow engine like Step Functions, Durable Functions or a saga orchestrator.
In our IRT, notifications work by choreography: services publish events to RabbitMQ and the notification consumers react, while the study transfer is a clearly orchestrated sequence of steps.

p17-37.q: A saga is a way to keep data consistent across several microservices without a distributed transaction. Each service has its own database, so you can't wrap all the changes in one ACID transaction. Instead, the saga is a sequence of local transactions, and each step publishes an event or message that triggers the next step.
p17-37.k: saga pattern, distributed transaction microservices, compensating transaction, saga failure, saga rollback, long running transaction
x: A saga is a way to keep data consistent across several microservices without a distributed transaction. Each service has its own database, so you can't wrap all the changes in one ACID transaction. Instead, the saga is a sequence of local transactions, and each step publishes an event or message that triggers the next step.

The key part is failure handling. If a step fails in the middle, the saga runs compensating transactions for the steps that already succeeded, in reverse order. For example, if the order was created and payment was taken, but stock reservation fails, the saga refunds the payment and cancels the order. A compensation is a business undo, not a database rollback, so it must be designed explicitly, and it must be idempotent, because it might run more than once.
Sagas can be coordinated by choreography, with services reacting to events, or by an orchestrator that tracks the state and decides the next step.

I also design for the in-between states, because users can see them, like "payment pending". Steps use retries for temporary errors, timeouts for stuck steps, and an outbox, so the local change and its event are always saved together. And every saga has a correlation id, so I can trace it end to end.

p17-38.q: The outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem. When a service saves data to its database and then publishes an event to a message broker, those are two separate systems. If the save succeeds but the publish fails, or the service crashes between them, other services never hear about the change. If you publish first and the save fails, you've announced something that never happened.
p17-38.k: outbox pattern, transactional outbox, dual write problem, reliable event publishing, outbox table, publish event after save
x: The outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem. When a service saves data to its database and then publishes an event to a message broker, those are two separate systems. If the save succeeds but the publish fails, or the service crashes between them, other services never hear about the change. If you publish first and the save fails, you've announced something that never happened.

With the outbox, the service writes the business change and the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction. So either both are saved or neither is. Then a separate background publisher, or a change-data-capture tool like Debezium, reads unsent rows from the outbox, publishes them to the broker, and marks them as sent.

This gives at-least-once delivery. The publisher might send the same event twice, for example if it crashes after publishing but before marking it, so consumers must be idempotent, usually by storing processed message ids.

In .NET, libraries like MassTransit and NServiceBus have a built-in outbox, or you can build a simple one with EF Core and a BackgroundService. I also add publisher confirms on RabbitMQ, so the publisher knows the broker really accepted the message before marking it sent.

p17-39.q: An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of your microservices. Clients call the gateway, and it routes each request to the right service, so clients don't need to know how many services there are or where they run.
p17-39.k: api gateway pattern, what does api gateway do, gateway microservices, ocelot yarp, edge service, single entry point
x: An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of your microservices. Clients call the gateway, and it routes each request to the right service, so clients don't need to know how many services there are or where they run.

Besides routing, it handles cross-cutting concerns in one place. Authentication: validate tokens before requests reach services. Rate limiting and throttling, per client or API key. TLS termination. Request and response transformation. Caching of common responses. CORS. And logging and metrics for all traffic, often adding a correlation id.
It can also do aggregation: one client call fans out to several services and combines the results, which reduces chatty calls from mobile apps.

The risks are that it becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck, so it must be highly available and scaled, and that business logic creeps into it. I keep the gateway thin: routing and cross-cutting concerns only.
Examples are AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, Kong, and in .NET, YARP or Ocelot. Each service still validates tokens itself, for defence in depth.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, partner-facing APIs go through API Gateway with per-partner keys and throttling.

p17-40.q: Backend for Frontend means building a separate, thin backend for each type of client, like one for the web app and one for the mobile app, instead of one general-purpose API for everyone.
p17-40.k: backend for frontend, bff pattern, bff, separate backend per client, mobile backend web backend, bff authentication
x: Backend for Frontend means building a separate, thin backend for each type of client, like one for the web app and one for the mobile app, instead of one general-purpose API for everyone.

The reason is that different clients need different things. A mobile screen wants a small, combined response in one call, because the network is slow. The web dashboard wants richer data. A single generic API either over-fetches for mobile or forces many calls. With a BFF, each frontend team owns a backend shaped exactly for its screens: it calls the downstream microservices, aggregates and trims the data, and returns what the screen needs.

BFFs are also popular for security in single-page apps. The BFF handles the OpenID Connect login, keeps the tokens on the server, and gives the browser only a secure, HttpOnly cookie. So no access token is stored in browser JavaScript, which reduces the risk from cross-site scripting.
The downsides are more services to maintain and some duplicated logic between BFFs. So I keep business rules in the core services, and the BFF only does composition and client-specific shaping.
In .NET, a BFF is often an ASP.NET Core app with YARP for proxying, plus the Duende BFF library for the security part.

p17-41.q: In microservices, instances start, stop and move all the time, especially with autoscaling and containers, so services can't call each other with fixed IP addresses. Service discovery is how a service finds the current, healthy instances of another service.
p17-41.k: service discovery, client side discovery, server side discovery, consul eureka, dns service discovery, how services find each other
x: In microservices, instances start, stop and move all the time, especially with autoscaling and containers, so services can't call each other with fixed IP addresses. Service discovery is how a service finds the current, healthy instances of another service.

There are two styles. In client-side discovery, the calling service asks a service registry, like Consul or Eureka, for the healthy instances, and does the load balancing itself. In server-side discovery, the caller just calls a stable name or load balancer, and the platform routes to a healthy instance.
The registry is kept up to date by registration: instances register when they start and are removed when health checks fail.

Today, most platforms make this mostly invisible. In Kubernetes, each Service gets a stable DNS name, like orders.default.svc.cluster.local, and kube-proxy routes to healthy pods. In AWS ECS, Cloud Map and Service Connect give DNS names, or you use an internal load balancer. In .NET, Aspire's service discovery lets HttpClient use logical names, resolved from configuration or the platform.

Health checks are essential, so traffic never goes to a dead instance. In our on-premise CIRT platform, services use stable DNS names behind internal load balancers, with health checks removing unhealthy nodes.

p17-42.q: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different parts of the system may show different data for a short time, but if no new changes happen, they all become consistent eventually. It's the normal result of microservices that own separate databases and communicate through events.
p17-42.k: eventual consistency, strong vs eventual consistency, consistency microservices, read your own writes, stale data, cap theorem consistency
x: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different parts of the system may show different data for a short time, but if no new changes happen, they all become consistent eventually. It's the normal result of microservices that own separate databases and communicate through events.

For example, when a shipment is marked as dispatched, the shipment service updates its own database immediately and publishes an event. The inventory and reporting services update a few hundred milliseconds later, when they process that event. In between, a report might still show the old status.

To make this acceptable, I do a few things. Show honest states in the UI, like "Requested" or "Processing", instead of pretending something finished instantly. Support read-your-own-writes where it matters, so the user who made the change sees it straight away, for example by returning the updated data from the command or reading from the owning service. Keep the delay small and monitored, with alerts on queue lag. And design idempotent consumers and replay, so nothing is lost.

Where strong consistency is truly required, like assigning a unique randomisation slot, I keep that inside one service and one database transaction. In our IRT, the randomisation assignment and the kit allocation are written together in one transaction.

p17-43.q: The strangler fig pattern is a way to replace a legacy system gradually instead of rewriting it all at once. The name comes from a fig tree that grows around an old tree until it can stand on its own.
p17-43.k: strangler fig, strangler pattern, migrate monolith to microservices, incremental migration, legacy modernization pattern, strangle the monolith
x: The strangler fig pattern is a way to replace a legacy system gradually instead of rewriting it all at once. The name comes from a fig tree that grows around an old tree until it can stand on its own.

You put a routing layer, like a proxy, a gateway or simply links in the UI, in front of the old system. Then you build new functionality, one piece at a time, in the new system, and route just that piece to it. Over time, more and more routes move to the new system, and the legacy parts are switched off when nothing uses them anymore.
The benefits are lower risk, because each step is small and can be rolled back, continuous delivery of value, and no long feature freeze.
The challenges are running two systems side by side, keeping data in sync, and avoiding duplicated business rules. I make sure each rule has one owner at any time.

This is exactly how our IRT is being modernised. It started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on a .NET Framework 4.8 core with an ASP.NET MVC and Angular portal. New .NET APIs wrap the legacy transaction engine through an API, and the UI moves to a React shell one module at a time, with drug accountability being migrated now.

p17-44.q: I prefer database per service, where each microservice owns its data and nobody else reads or writes its tables directly. Others get data through its API or its events.
p17-44.k: database per service, shared database microservices, separate database per microservice, data ownership, shared db anti pattern
x: I prefer database per service, where each microservice owns its data and nobody else reads or writes its tables directly. Others get data through its API or its events.

The reasons are independence and safety. A service can change its schema without breaking other teams. It can choose the right database type, like SQL Server for transactions and DynamoDB for simple high-volume lookups. It can scale on its own. And there's one clear owner of each piece of data and its rules.
A shared database looks easier at first, but it couples everyone. One team's schema change breaks another service, deployments must be coordinated, and nobody really owns the data.
Database per service has costs. Queries across services need API composition or a read model built from events. Transactions across services need sagas. And you have more databases to run.
So it's a trade-off. During a migration, I accept a shared database for a while, with clear ownership of each table, and separate it step by step.

Our IRT has an interesting variation: database per study, meaning per tenant, where each clinical trial has its own SQL Server database from a common model schema of [about 560] tables, which gives strong isolation between sponsors' trials.

p17-45.q: Because each service owns its own database, I can't just write a SQL join across services. There are two main approaches.
p17-45.k: query across microservices, join data across services, api composition, cqrs read model, data aggregation microservices, reporting across microservices
x: Because each service owns its own database, I can't just write a SQL join across services. There are two main approaches.

The first is API composition. A composer, which could be an API gateway, a BFF, or one of the services, calls each service's API, often in parallel, and combines the results in memory. It's simple and the data is fresh, but it's slower, it fails if one service is down, and it's bad for large result sets or complex filtering and sorting across services.

The second is a read model, using CQRS. A dedicated query service listens to events from all the relevant services and maintains its own denormalised view, shaped exactly for the query, like a table or a search index. Queries are then fast and simple. The cost is eventual consistency, since the view is slightly behind, and more infrastructure.
For reporting and analytics, a third option is to stream data into a data warehouse or lake, and run reports there.
My choice depends on the need: API composition for small, on-screen lookups; a read model for frequent, complex queries or search; a warehouse for heavy reporting.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment status events feed a reporting view, so reports don't call the shipment service live.

p17-46.q: CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It means separating the model that changes data, the commands, from the model that reads data, the queries.
p17-46.k: cqrs, command query responsibility segregation, separate read and write, read model write model, cqrs mediatr, when to use cqrs
x: CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It means separating the model that changes data, the commands, from the model that reads data, the queries.

At a simple level, it's just code organisation: commands like CreateShipment go through handlers with validation and business rules, and queries like GetShipments use simple, optimised reads, often projections straight to DTOs. In .NET, MediatR makes this clean, with a handler per command and per query, and pipeline behaviours for validation and logging. That level is useful in most services.

At an advanced level, the read side has its own separate data store, updated from events published by the write side. That allows independent scaling, and read models shaped exactly for each screen or search, like a denormalised table or Elasticsearch index. But it brings eventual consistency, more infrastructure and more complexity.
So I use the simple form often, and the separate-store form only where reads and writes have very different needs, like heavy reporting or search on top of a transactional system.
It's often paired with event sourcing, but it doesn't require it.
Our newer IRT APIs follow clean architecture with MediatR commands and queries, and FluentValidation running as a pipeline behaviour before every command.

p17-47.q: In event sourcing, instead of storing only the current state of an entity, you store every change as an immutable event, like ShipmentCreated, ShipmentDispatched and ShipmentDelivered. The current state is rebuilt by replaying the events in order, often with snapshots so you don't replay thousands of events every time.
p17-47.k: event sourcing, event store, events as source of truth, event sourcing pros cons, replay events, audit with events
x: In event sourcing, instead of storing only the current state of an entity, you store every change as an immutable event, like ShipmentCreated, ShipmentDispatched and ShipmentDelivered. The current state is rebuilt by replaying the events in order, often with snapshots so you don't replay thousands of events every time.

The advantages are strong. You get a complete, built-in audit trail of what happened and when, which is very attractive in regulated domains. You can rebuild state at any point in time, which helps debugging. You can create new read models later by replaying history. And events naturally feed other services.

The disadvantages are real too. It's a different way of thinking, and the learning curve is steep. Querying current state needs separate read models, so it usually goes with CQRS and eventual consistency. Event schemas must evolve carefully, because old events stay forever. And mistakes in events can't be simply edited; you fix them with new correcting events.
So I'd use it where history and audit are core to the business and the team is ready for it, not as a default.
In our IRT, we get audit through history tables and an audit trail for every change, without full event sourcing, which keeps the model simpler.

p17-48.q: gRPC is a high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google. You define services and messages in a .proto file with Protocol Buffers, and tools generate strongly typed client and server code for many languages, including C#.
p17-48.k: grpc vs rest, what is grpc, grpc dotnet, protobuf, when to use grpc, grpc streaming
x: gRPC is a high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google. You define services and messages in a .proto file with Protocol Buffers, and tools generate strongly typed client and server code for many languages, including C#.

Compared with REST and JSON, it's faster and smaller, because Protocol Buffers is a compact binary format and it runs over HTTP/2, with multiplexing on one connection. It has a strict contract, so breaking changes are obvious. And it supports streaming in both directions, which is great for real-time feeds.

The downsides: browsers can't call gRPC directly without gRPC-Web, the binary messages aren't human-readable, so debugging with curl or Postman is harder, and HTTP/2 can be tricky through some proxies and load balancers. Public APIs and partners usually expect REST.

So I use gRPC for internal, service-to-service calls where performance and strong contracts matter, like high-volume internal lookups or streaming, and REST for public APIs, browser clients and partner integrations.

In ASP.NET Core, gRPC is built in: AddGrpc, map the service, and use the generated client with the HttpClient factory, so it gets the same resilience policies. You can even expose both from one service with JSON transcoding.

p17-49.q: A distributed monolith is a system that's split into many services, but they're still so tightly coupled that you have all the problems of a monolith plus all the problems of distributed systems. You can't deploy one service without deploying several others, a change touches many repos, services share a database, and one user request needs a long chain of synchronous calls.
p17-49.k: distributed monolith, microservices anti pattern, tightly coupled microservices, avoid distributed monolith, microservices mistakes
x: A distributed monolith is a system that's split into many services, but they're still so tightly coupled that you have all the problems of a monolith plus all the problems of distributed systems. You can't deploy one service without deploying several others, a change touches many repos, services share a database, and one user request needs a long chain of synchronous calls.

The signs are: releases that must be coordinated across teams, shared libraries with business logic that every service depends on, services that break whenever another changes its API, and an outage in one service taking everything down.

To avoid it, I start with good boundaries around business capabilities, so most changes stay inside one service. Each service owns its data, with no shared database. Communication is mostly asynchronous for side effects, so services don't depend on each other being up. APIs are versioned and backward compatible, with contract tests, so services deploy independently. Shared libraries contain only technical concerns, like logging or messaging helpers, never business rules. And each service has its own pipeline.
Sometimes the honest answer is that a modular monolith is the better design, until there's a real reason, like independent scaling or separate teams, to split.

p17-50.q: A modular monolith is one deployable application that's internally split into well-defined modules, each with its own domain logic, its own data tables or schema, and a clear public interface. Modules don't reach into each other's internals; they talk through interfaces or in-process events.
p17-50.k: modular monolith, monolith vs microservices, when not to use microservices, modular architecture, monolith first
x: A modular monolith is one deployable application that's internally split into well-defined modules, each with its own domain logic, its own data tables or schema, and a clear public interface. Modules don't reach into each other's internals; they talk through interfaces or in-process events.

It gives many of the design benefits of microservices, like clear boundaries and ownership, without the operational cost: one deployment, one process, in-process calls instead of network calls, real ACID transactions, simple debugging and much simpler infrastructure.

It's better than microservices when the team is small, the domain is still being understood and boundaries are likely to change, the load doesn't need independent scaling, or the organisation doesn't have strong DevOps and observability yet. Splitting too early often produces a distributed monolith.

The trick is to enforce the boundaries, otherwise it becomes a big ball of mud. I use separate projects per module, internal classes, architecture tests with a library like NetArchTest to block forbidden references, and separate database schemas.
Later, when a module needs independent scaling, a different technology or its own team, it can be extracted into a microservice with much less pain, because its boundary is already clean.

p17-51.q: A dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed successfully, so one bad message doesn't block the queue or get retried forever.
p17-51.k: dead letter queue, dlq strategy, poison message, failed messages queue, rabbitmq dead letter, sqs dlq
x: A dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed successfully, so one bad message doesn't block the queue or get retried forever.

First I separate failure types. Transient failures, like a database timeout, get a few retries with backoff, ideally using delayed redelivery so the consumer isn't hammering a struggling dependency. Permanent failures, like a message with invalid data, called a poison message, go straight to the dead-letter queue, because retrying won't help.

In RabbitMQ, I configure a dead-letter exchange on the queue, so rejected or expired messages are routed there. In SQS, a redrive policy moves a message to the DLQ after a maximum receive count, like five.

The DLQ is useless if nobody looks at it, so I add an alarm when its depth is above zero, and I keep the original headers, the error reason and the number of attempts with each message. Then there's a clear process: inspect, fix the bug or the data, and replay the messages back to the main queue with a tool or a script. Since consumers are idempotent, replaying is safe.
In our CIRT platform, failed vendor messages land in a dead-letter queue with an alert, and the support team can replay them after the fix.

p17-52.q: Ordering is hard to guarantee globally, so I first ask: ordering of what? Usually we only need ordering per entity, like all events for one shipment in order, not every event in the whole system.
p17-52.k: message ordering, ordered messages, kafka ordering partition key, fifo queue, out of order events, sequence number
x: Ordering is hard to guarantee globally, so I first ask: ordering of what? Usually we only need ordering per entity, like all events for one shipment in order, not every event in the whole system.

The standard approach is partitioning by key. In Kafka, messages with the same key, like the shipment id, go to the same partition, and a partition is read in order by one consumer in the group. In SQS FIFO queues, the message group id does the same thing. In RabbitMQ, ordering holds within one queue with one consumer, but multiple consumers or redeliveries can reorder messages.

But ordering can still break, through retries, redeliveries or producers sending from different instances. So I also make consumers tolerant. Each event carries a version number or sequence number for its entity, and the consumer ignores anything older than what it has already applied. Or the consumer re-reads the current state from the source instead of trusting the event payload.
I also avoid designs that need ordering across different entities, because they limit parallelism a lot.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment events on Kafka are keyed by shipment id, and consumers store the last version applied, so a late, older event can't overwrite newer data.

p17-53.q: For a long outage, retries and circuit breakers alone aren't enough, so I plan how the system behaves while the dependency is down.
p17-53.k: dependency down for an hour, downstream outage, service unavailable long time, graceful degradation, fallback when service down
x: For a long outage, retries and circuit breakers alone aren't enough, so I plan how the system behaves while the dependency is down.
First, fail fast. The circuit breaker opens, so requests aren't waiting on timeouts and threads aren't piling up. Health and alerts tell the team quickly which dependency is down.

Then graceful degradation, depending on how important the dependency is. If it's only for enrichment, like showing recommendations or a non-critical widget, I hide that part or return cached or default data, and the main feature keeps working. If the work can wait, I make it asynchronous: accept the request, put it on a queue, show the user "accepted, processing", and process it when the dependency returns. The queue buffers the backlog.
If the dependency is truly critical, like a payment or a safety check, I fail clearly with a helpful message, rather than doing something unsafe or inconsistent.
When it comes back, I control the recovery: the backlog drains at a limited rate, so we don't overwhelm the recovering service, and I check the DLQ and replay anything that failed.
In our IRT, if a depot's system is down, shipment requests queue up, and site users see "pending", which we clear when the depot recovers.

p17-54.q: A sidecar is a helper container that runs next to the main application container, in the same pod, sharing its network and lifecycle. It adds capabilities without changing the application code, like a logging agent, a proxy or a secrets fetcher.
p17-54.k: sidecar pattern, service mesh, istio linkerd, envoy sidecar, what is service mesh, mtls service mesh
x: A sidecar is a helper container that runs next to the main application container, in the same pod, sharing its network and lifecycle. It adds capabilities without changing the application code, like a logging agent, a proxy or a secrets fetcher.

A service mesh uses sidecar proxies, usually Envoy, next to every service, plus a control plane, to manage all service-to-service traffic. Tools are Istio, Linkerd, or AWS App Mesh historically. All calls go through the proxies, so the mesh can provide, in one consistent way: mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts and circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canary releases, and detailed metrics and tracing for every call, all configured centrally, without code in each service.

The benefits are consistency across languages and teams, and strong security with zero-trust mTLS. The costs are complexity, extra latency and memory for each proxy, and a steep learning curve. Newer approaches, like Istio's ambient mode, reduce the per-pod sidecar overhead.

I'd consider a mesh when there are many services in different languages, and strict security or traffic-control needs. For a smaller number of .NET services, libraries like Polly, OpenTelemetry and a gateway usually give enough, with much less to operate.

p17-55.q: I don't measure size in lines of code. A service is the right size when it maps to one business capability, can be owned by one team, and can be changed and deployed independently most of the time.
p17-55.k: how big should microservice be, microservice size, too small microservices, nano services, granularity microservices
x: I don't measure size in lines of code. A service is the right size when it maps to one business capability, can be owned by one team, and can be changed and deployed independently most of the time.
Signs that services are too big: several teams keep changing the same service, deployments are risky because unrelated features ship together, or parts of it have very different scaling needs.

Signs they're too small, sometimes called nano-services: almost every feature needs changes in several services, services call each other constantly in long chains, transactions need sagas for things that should be simple, and the operational overhead, like pipelines, monitoring and on-call, outweighs the benefits.

So I start from the domain, using domain-driven design and bounded contexts, and group things that change together and need strong consistency together. Data that must be updated in one transaction is a strong hint that it belongs in one service.

It's also fine to start a bit bigger and split later when there's a real reason, like independent scaling, a different release cadence, or a separate team, because merging services back is harder than splitting a clean module.
In our IRT, inventory and shipments stay together, because kit allocation and the shipment request must be consistent.

p17-56.q: An anti-corruption layer is a translation layer between your domain and an external or legacy system whose model you don't want leaking into your code.
p17-56.k: anti corruption layer, acl ddd, translate legacy model, adapter for legacy system, protect domain model
x: An anti-corruption layer is a translation layer between your domain and an external or legacy system whose model you don't want leaking into your code.

Legacy systems and third-party APIs often have confusing names, odd data formats, magic codes and different concepts. If your new service uses those directly, its model gets "corrupted" by them, and every change in the external system ripples through your code.
