So I put an adapter in between. My domain code talks only to an interface in my own language, like IShipmentGateway with CreateShipment taking my own Shipment type. The implementation of that interface calls the external system, maps my types to theirs and back, converts codes, handles their error formats and retries. If the external system changes, or is replaced, only the adapter changes.
It's especially useful during a strangler migration, where new services must work with an old system for a long time.

In our IRT modernisation, the new .NET APIs talk to the legacy transaction engine through a translation layer, so the new code uses clean names and DTOs, while the old procedures and formats stay hidden behind it. When parts of the legacy side are replaced, the new code doesn't change.

p17-57.q: I share code carefully, because shared libraries can couple services as badly as a shared database.
p17-57.k: shared library microservices, nuget package shared code, code sharing microservices, common library, shared contracts
x: I share code carefully, because shared libraries can couple services as badly as a shared database.

What I'm happy to share is technical, cross-cutting code: logging and OpenTelemetry setup, a messaging wrapper, standard health checks, authentication setup, error-handling middleware, and maybe a result type. I publish these as versioned NuGet packages in a private feed, like Azure Artifacts or GitHub Packages, with semantic versioning, so each service upgrades when it's ready, not forced all at once.

What I avoid sharing is business logic and domain models. If two services share a domain library, a change for one forces a change and redeployment of the other, which brings back the monolith's coupling. A little duplication is better than the wrong coupling.

For contracts, like message and event schemas or API clients, I prefer generating them from a single source, such as an OpenAPI spec, a protobuf file or a schema registry, rather than hand-sharing DTO classes. That keeps each side independent and catches breaking changes.
I also keep shared libraries small, well tested, backward compatible, with few dependencies of their own.
In our CIRT platform, common logging and messaging helpers ship as internal NuGet packages from Azure DevOps Artifacts, while domain models stay inside each service.

p17-58.q: They're both messages, but they mean different things, and that affects how I design them.
p17-58.k: command vs event, events vs commands messaging, integration event, domain event, message types
x: They're both messages, but they mean different things, and that affects how I design them.

A command is a request to do something, addressed to one specific receiver that owns the action. It's named in the imperative, like CreateShipment or SendEmail. The sender expects it to be handled, and the receiver can accept or reject it. It's usually sent to a queue with one consumer.

An event is a statement that something has already happened. It's named in the past tense, like ShipmentCreated or SubjectRandomised. The publisher doesn't know or care who listens; zero, one or many subscribers can react. It can't be rejected, because it's a fact. Events are published to a topic or exchange.

This distinction matters for coupling. With commands, the sender depends on the receiver. With events, the publisher is independent of its subscribers, so you can add new consumers without changing the publisher.

There's also domain events versus integration events. Domain events are raised inside a service, between parts of its own domain. Integration events are published outside, to other services, and are part of the public contract, so they're versioned and kept stable.
In our IRT, SubjectRandomised is an integration event that the notification and reporting consumers both listen to.

p17-59.q: There are two main styles, and both are valid.
p17-59.k: event payload design, fat event vs thin event, event carried state transfer, notification event, event schema design
x: There are two main styles, and both are valid.

A thin event, or notification event, contains just the id and type, like "Shipment 123 changed". Consumers then call the owning service to get the current data. It's small and always gives fresh data. But every consumer makes a call back, which adds load and coupling, and if the owner is down, consumers can't proceed.

A fat event, or event-carried state transfer, contains the relevant data, like the shipment's status, site, kit count and timestamps. Consumers have everything they need without calling back, so they're more independent and resilient, and the owner gets less load. The downsides are bigger messages, more care about schema changes, and the risk of including sensitive data that not every consumer should see.

I usually go in the middle: include the data consumers commonly need, plus the id and a version number, so they can ignore stale events. I don't include sensitive personal data unless every subscriber genuinely needs it, especially in clinical systems where patient data must be minimised.
And I version event schemas, adding fields in a backward-compatible way.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment events carry status, location and a version, so most consumers never call back.

p17-60.q: I don't keep the HTTP request open for minutes, because it ties up resources and will hit gateway and load balancer timeouts, usually 30 to 120 seconds.
p17-60.k: long running request api, async request reply, 202 accepted, background job api, polling status endpoint, long running task web api
x: I don't keep the HTTP request open for minutes, because it ties up resources and will hit gateway and load balancer timeouts, usually 30 to 120 seconds.

Instead, I use the asynchronous request-reply pattern. The client sends the request, the API validates it, saves a job record, puts the work on a queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status endpoint, like /jobs/123. A background worker processes the job and updates its status and progress. The client polls the status endpoint, which returns pending, running, completed with a link to the result, or failed with an error. Instead of polling, the client can get a push notification with SignalR or a webhook when it's done.
The worker should be idempotent and able to resume, because it might crash in the middle. For very large jobs, I split the work into chunks and track progress per chunk.
I also use an idempotency key on the submit request, so a double click doesn't start two jobs.

This is how our study data transfer works. A transfer is submitted, a worker moves the data in steps, and the UI shows progress. [It took a transfer from around 40 minutes of manual steps to under 10 minutes, with clear status for the user.]

p17-61.q: Backpressure is what happens, and what you do, when a producer sends work faster than a consumer can process it. If nothing controls it, queues grow without limit, memory runs out, latency gets huge and the system can fall over.
p17-61.k: backpressure, consumer slower than producer, queue growing, flow control, load shedding, bounded queue
x: Backpressure is what happens, and what you do, when a producer sends work faster than a consumer can process it. If nothing controls it, queues grow without limit, memory runs out, latency gets huge and the system can fall over.

There are a few ways to handle it. Buffering: a durable queue absorbs spikes, which is fine if the consumer catches up later. But the queue must be monitored, with alerts on depth and age of the oldest message. Scaling consumers: autoscale workers on queue depth, for example KEDA on Kubernetes or ECS scaling on SQS backlog. Limiting the producer: bounded queues or channels, rate limits, or the consumer signalling to slow down; for example, a bounded System.Threading.Channels channel makes the writer wait when it's full. And load shedding: when overloaded, reject low-priority work quickly with 429 or 503, rather than slowing everything down.
In RabbitMQ, I set a prefetch count, so each consumer only takes a limited number of unacknowledged messages, which spreads load and stops one consumer hoarding work.
The key is to choose deliberately what happens under overload, rather than discovering it in production.
In our CIRT notification consumers, prefetch limits and a separate queue for bulk jobs keep urgent emails flowing during large imports.

p17-62.q: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means giving one machine more resources: more CPU, memory or faster disks. It's simple and needs no code changes, but there's a ceiling, it gets expensive, it often needs downtime to resize, and one machine is still a single point of failure.
p17-62.k: horizontal vs vertical scaling, scale out vs scale up, stateless services scaling, autoscaling, scale microservices
x: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means giving one machine more resources: more CPU, memory or faster disks. It's simple and needs no code changes, but there's a ceiling, it gets expensive, it often needs downtime to resize, and one machine is still a single point of failure.

Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, means adding more instances of the service behind a load balancer. It has almost no ceiling, gives redundancy, and fits cloud autoscaling well, adding instances when load rises and removing them when it falls, which saves cost.

But horizontal scaling needs the service to be stateless. No in-memory session or cache that other instances need, no local files that must be shared, and no assumptions that one instance handles all requests for a user. State goes to a shared store, like Redis or a database, files go to blob storage, and background jobs need locking or a queue so they don't run twice.
Databases are the hard part. Relational databases usually scale up first, then add read replicas, caching and sometimes sharding.
In our on-premise CIRT, the web tier scales out across load-balanced IIS servers with Redis for shared cache, while each study's SQL Server database scales up.

p17-63.q: When a service scales to several instances, each one runs the same scheduled jobs, so a nightly job could run three times. There are a few ways to avoid that.
p17-63.k: distributed lock, run job once multiple instances, scheduled job multiple servers, leader election, quartz clustering, hangfire
x: When a service scales to several instances, each one runs the same scheduled jobs, so a nightly job could run three times. There are a few ways to avoid that.

A distributed lock: before running, each instance tries to take a lock in a shared store, like a Redis key with SET NX and an expiry, a SQL Server application lock, or a DynamoDB conditional write. Only the one that gets it runs the job. The expiry matters, so a crashed instance doesn't hold the lock forever.
A clustered scheduler: Quartz.NET in clustered mode or Hangfire store job state in a shared database, and guarantee that each trigger fires on only one node.

A separate worker: move scheduled jobs out of the web service into one dedicated worker with a single instance, or use the platform scheduler, like EventBridge Scheduler or a Kubernetes CronJob, to start one task.
Also, I make the job itself idempotent, so even if it accidentally runs twice, it doesn't send duplicate emails or double-process data, for example by recording what it already handled.
In our CIRT platform, the AlertWatchDog runs on Quartz, and jobs are designed to be safe if a run overlaps or repeats.

p17-64.q: When I call several services in parallel, for example with Task.WhenAll, some may succeed and some fail, so I decide up front what partial success means for that feature.
p17-64.k: partial failure, parallel calls failure, task whenall error handling, fan out fan in, aggregate results partial
x: When I call several services in parallel, for example with Task.WhenAll, some may succeed and some fail, so I decide up front what partial success means for that feature.

First, I classify each dependency as required or optional. If a required call fails, the whole operation fails with a clear error. If an optional one fails, like recommendations or a secondary widget, I return the rest with that section empty, and include a flag or warning, so the UI can show "some information is unavailable".

Technically, each call has its own timeout and resilience policy, so one slow service doesn't hold the whole response. With Task.WhenAll, if any task throws, awaiting it rethrows only the first exception, so I handle each task's result individually, or wrap each call in a method that returns a result object with success or error, instead of throwing.
I also set an overall deadline for the aggregate request, and cancel the outstanding calls with a CancellationToken when it's reached.
For writes, parallel partial failure is more serious, because it leaves inconsistent data. There I prefer a saga or a queue, rather than parallel calls.
On our IRT dashboard, if the shipment summary call fails, the page still loads subject and inventory data and shows a small warning for that panel.

p17-65.q: The twelve-factor app is a set of principles for building cloud-friendly services that are easy to deploy and scale. The main ones I use every day are these.
p17-65.k: twelve factor app, 12 factor app, cloud native principles, 12 factor, stateless processes config in environment
x: The twelve-factor app is a set of principles for building cloud-friendly services that are easy to deploy and scale. The main ones I use every day are these.

One codebase per app, tracked in version control, deployed to many environments. Dependencies declared explicitly, like NuGet or npm packages, not assumed on the server. Config in the environment, not in code, so the same build runs everywhere. Backing services, like databases, caches and brokers, are attached resources, swapped by changing a connection setting. Build, release and run are separate stages: build once, combine with config to make a release, then run it. Processes are stateless; any state goes to a backing service. Port binding: the app is self-contained and exposes itself on a port, like Kestrel does. Concurrency by scaling out processes. Disposability: fast startup and graceful shutdown, handling SIGTERM. Dev and prod parity, using containers to keep environments similar. Logs as event streams, written to standard output, and collected by the platform. And admin tasks, like migrations, run as one-off processes.
ASP.NET Core on containers fits these principles naturally.
Our older on-premise CIRT predates some of these, with config transforms and IIS, but our newer services follow them.

p17-66.q: Adding a new optional field to a response is normally safe, but only if clients are tolerant readers, meaning they ignore fields they don't recognise. Most JSON clients do this by default, though some strict deserialisers or generated clients can fail on unknown properties, so I check how the important clients are built.
p17-66.k: backward compatibility api, tolerant reader, adding fields to api, breaking change detection, openapi diff
x: Adding a new optional field to a response is normally safe, but only if clients are tolerant readers, meaning they ignore fields they don't recognise. Most JSON clients do this by default, though some strict deserialisers or generated clients can fail on unknown properties, so I check how the important clients are built.
On the request side, a new field must be optional, with a sensible default, so old clients that don't send it still work exactly as before. Making a new field required is a breaking change.

Other things that look small but break clients: renaming a field, changing its type, like from number to string, changing an enum by removing values, changing date formats, changing default sorting or pagination, or changing the meaning of an existing value. Even adding a new enum value can break a client with a strict switch statement, so I document that enums may grow.

To catch these automatically, I generate the OpenAPI spec in the build and compare it with the previous version using a diff tool, like oasdiff, failing the build on breaking changes. Contract tests with Pact add the consumer's point of view.
For events, the same rules apply, and I treat the event schema as a published contract.

p17-67.q: A stateless service doesn't keep any client-specific data in its own memory between requests. Every request carries what it needs, like a token, and any lasting state is stored in a shared backing service, like a database, Redis or blob storage. So any instance can handle any request, instances can be added or removed freely, and a crash loses nothing important. That's what makes horizontal scaling, rolling deployments and autoscaling easy.
p17-67.k: stateful vs stateless, stateless service, sticky sessions, session state microservices, why stateless
x: A stateless service doesn't keep any client-specific data in its own memory between requests. Every request carries what it needs, like a token, and any lasting state is stored in a shared backing service, like a database, Redis or blob storage. So any instance can handle any request, instances can be added or removed freely, and a crash loses nothing important. That's what makes horizontal scaling, rolling deployments and autoscaling easy.

A stateful service keeps state locally, like in-memory sessions, a local cache that must be consistent, uploaded files on local disk, or WebSocket connections. Then a user must keep hitting the same instance, which needs sticky sessions, and restarting or scaling an instance loses or moves that state. Load is also harder to balance.

Some things are naturally stateful, like databases, brokers, or SignalR connections, and need special handling: StatefulSets in Kubernetes, managed services, or a backplane, like Redis for SignalR, so messages reach users on any instance.
So I keep application services stateless and push state into managed, purpose-built stores.
In our CIRT web tier, session data and cache moved to Redis, so the load balancer can send any request to any IIS server without sticky sessions.

p17-68.q: Chaos engineering is deliberately injecting failures into a system, in a controlled way, to find weaknesses before they cause real outages. The idea is that systems will fail anyway, so it's better to learn how they fail on our own schedule.
p17-68.k: chaos engineering, chaos monkey, fault injection, resilience testing, aws fault injection service, game day
x: Chaos engineering is deliberately injecting failures into a system, in a controlled way, to find weaknesses before they cause real outages. The idea is that systems will fail anyway, so it's better to learn how they fail on our own schedule.

The process is like a scientific experiment. Define the steady state, meaning what normal looks like in metrics, like error rate and latency. Form a hypothesis, like "if one instance of the shipment service dies, users won't notice". Inject a failure: kill instances, add network latency, make a dependency return errors, fill a disk, or take down an availability zone. Then observe whether the steady state holds. Keep the blast radius small at first, with a clear way to stop the experiment, and expand gradually.

Tools include AWS Fault Injection Service, Azure Chaos Studio, Chaos Mesh for Kubernetes, and Polly's chaos strategies in .NET, which can inject faults and latency into HttpClient calls in test environments.
Teams often run game days, where they practise an incident scenario together, testing both the system and the people and runbooks.
It's valuable only after the basics are in place: monitoring, alerts and resilience patterns. Otherwise you'll just break things without learning much.

p17-69.q: During a rolling or blue-green deployment, old and new versions of the service run at the same time against the same database. So every schema change must work with both versions. I use the expand and contract pattern, also called parallel change.
p17-69.k: zero downtime database migration, expand contract pattern, backward compatible schema change, rolling deployment database, parallel change
x: During a rolling or blue-green deployment, old and new versions of the service run at the same time against the same database. So every schema change must work with both versions. I use the expand and contract pattern, also called parallel change.

Expand: first, add new things without removing old ones. Add a new column as nullable, or a new table. Deploy code that writes to both old and new, and reads from the old. Backfill existing data in batches, so we don't lock large tables.
Migrate: deploy code that reads from the new column. Verify everything works in production.
Contract: only when no running version uses the old column, stop writing to it, and then drop it in a later release.
So renaming a column becomes add, copy, switch, remove, across several deployments, instead of one risky rename.

Other rules: never make a column required in the same release that starts populating it; create indexes online on large tables, where the edition supports it; and keep migrations small and reversible.

With EF Core, I generate SQL migration scripts, review them, and apply them in the pipeline before the new code. In our CIRT platform, the SSDT database projects follow the same idea, since hundreds of study databases must be updated.

p17-70.q: Multi-tenancy means one application serves many customers, or tenants, while keeping each tenant's data separate and secure.
p17-70.k: multi tenancy, multi tenant architecture, tenant isolation, database per tenant, shared schema tenant id, row level security
x: Multi-tenancy means one application serves many customers, or tenants, while keeping each tenant's data separate and secure.

There are three main data isolation models. Database per tenant: each tenant gets its own database. It gives the strongest isolation, easy per-tenant backup, restore and deletion, and per-tenant performance tuning, but it's more expensive and schema changes must be rolled out to many databases. Schema per tenant: one database, separate schemas, which is a middle ground. And shared database with a tenant id column on every table: cheapest and simplest to operate at scale, but every query must filter by tenant, and one mistake can leak data.

For the shared model, I enforce isolation in the platform, not by trusting every developer: EF Core global query filters on tenant id, SQL Server row-level security as a second layer, and tests that try to read across tenants.
The tenant is resolved from the token or the host name, early in the request, and stored in a scoped tenant context that the data layer uses.
Noisy neighbours are another concern: one big tenant shouldn't slow others, so I use per-tenant rate limits and monitoring.
Our IRT uses database per study, because sponsor data separation and audit requirements in clinical trials make strong isolation worth the cost.

p17-71.q: Time zones cause many subtle bugs, so I keep one simple rule: store and transfer instants in UTC, and convert to local time only at the edges, for display or for business rules that genuinely depend on local time.
p17-71.k: time zones microservices, utc dates, datetimeoffset, date handling distributed systems, store dates in utc
x: Time zones cause many subtle bugs, so I keep one simple rule: store and transfer instants in UTC, and convert to local time only at the edges, for display or for business rules that genuinely depend on local time.

In .NET, I use DateTimeOffset or UTC DateTime for timestamps, never DateTime.Now in server code, and I inject a TimeProvider, which arrived in .NET 8, so code and tests can control the clock. APIs use ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, like 2026-03-10T09:30:00Z, so there's no ambiguity.

Some values aren't instants. A date of birth or a visit date is a calendar date, so I use DateOnly, not midnight UTC, otherwise it can shift by a day when converted. A recurring local time, like "send at 9 AM site time", needs the IANA time zone id stored, like Asia/Kolkata, and conversion with daylight saving rules. Daylight saving transitions mean some local times happen twice or not at all, so scheduling code must handle that.
Servers and containers should run in UTC too.

In our IRT, sites in many countries see dates in their own time zone, while everything is stored in UTC. [A visit window bug at US sites came from a midnight conversion, and we fixed it by storing the date as a date.]

p17-72.q: I do it step by step, so each step is small and reversible.
p17-72.k: extract service from monolith, migrate feature without downtime, monolith decomposition steps, carve out microservice
x: I do it step by step, so each step is small and reversible.

First, inside the monolith, I make the feature's boundary clean: its code depends on the rest only through an interface, and its tables are accessed only by its own code. This refactoring alone reduces risk.
Second, I build the new service with the same behaviour, with its own API and database. To start, it can read data that's replicated or synced from the monolith.

Third, I run them in parallel. Often I use shadow traffic or parallel runs: requests go to the old code, and the new service is called in the background, and I compare results and log differences, without affecting users. This catches logic differences safely.

Fourth, I switch traffic gradually, behind a feature flag or at the routing layer, starting with a small group of users or tenants, while monitoring errors, latency and data consistency. Rollback is just flipping the flag back.
Fifth, I move the data ownership: the new service becomes the source of truth, and the monolith reads from it, through its API or events.
Finally, I remove the old code and tables.
This is the pattern we follow when moving modules from the old MVC and Angular portal to the React shell, one module at a time, with drug accountability now in progress.

p17-73.q: Both describe something that happened, but they have different scope and purpose.
p17-73.k: domain event vs integration event, domain events ddd, mediatr notifications, internal vs external events
x: Both describe something that happened, but they have different scope and purpose.

A domain event is raised inside a service, inside its domain model, to let other parts of the same service react. For example, when a kit's status changes to damaged, the Kit aggregate raises KitDamaged, and a handler in the same service updates the inventory count or writes an audit entry. They're in-process, often dispatched with MediatR notifications, usually in the same transaction or right after saving, and they can use rich internal types, because nobody outside sees them.

An integration event is published outside the service, through a broker, so other services can react. For example, KitDamaged might become an integration event that the reporting or notification service consumes. Because it's a public contract between services, it uses simple, stable, versioned DTOs, includes only the data others need, and is published reliably, ideally through the outbox pattern, so it isn't lost if the broker is down.
A common flow is: the domain event is raised, a handler converts it to an integration event, writes it to the outbox in the same transaction, and a publisher sends it later.
Keeping them separate means internal refactoring doesn't break other services.

p17-74.q: I'd push updates to the browser instead of having it poll every few seconds.
p17-74.k: real time dashboard design, live updates, signalr dashboard, websockets dashboard, push updates to browser
x: I'd push updates to the browser instead of having it poll every few seconds.

The data flow: when something changes, the owning service publishes an event. A dashboard service consumes these events, updates a small read model or aggregate counters, like shipments by status, in Redis or a database, and pushes a change notification to the connected browsers.

For the push, in .NET I'd use SignalR, which uses WebSockets and falls back to other transports automatically. Clients join groups, like a study or a site, so they only receive relevant updates, and authorisation is checked when joining a group. With several server instances, I'd use a Redis backplane, or a managed service like Azure SignalR Service, so a message reaches clients connected to any instance. On AWS, API Gateway WebSocket APIs are an option.

On the client, when the page loads, it gets the full current state through a normal API call, then applies live updates. If the connection drops, it reconnects and reloads the state, so it never misses changes.
To avoid flooding the browser, I'd batch or throttle updates, like at most once a second per widget.
For a dashboard that's fine with slight delays, polling every 30 seconds is honestly simpler, and that's a valid choice too.

p17-75.q: Access tokens are short-lived, like 5 to 15 minutes, so a stolen one isn't useful for long. A refresh token is a longer-lived credential that the client uses to get a new access token from the identity provider without asking the user to log in again.
p17-75.k: refresh token, refresh token rotation, where to store tokens, token storage spa, access token expiry, silent refresh
x: Access tokens are short-lived, like 5 to 15 minutes, so a stolen one isn't useful for long. A refresh token is a longer-lived credential that the client uses to get a new access token from the identity provider without asking the user to log in again.

Because refresh tokens are powerful, I protect them carefully. Refresh token rotation: each time it's used, the provider issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is ever used again, that suggests theft, and the provider revokes the whole token family. They have an absolute lifetime and an idle timeout, and they're revoked on logout or password change.

Storage is the tricky part for single-page apps. Local storage is readable by any JavaScript, so an XSS bug could steal tokens. Options, from most to least secure: a BFF that keeps tokens on the server and gives the browser an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; or keeping tokens only in memory, with rotation, and silent re-authentication when the page reloads.
Mobile apps use the platform's secure storage, like Keychain or Keystore.
In our React shell, the Keycloak adapter keeps tokens in memory and refreshes them before expiry, and an idle timer logs the user out after inactivity, which is a Part 11 requirement.

p17-76.q: Role-based checks answer "is this user a site user?". But they can't answer "is this user allowed to see this particular subject?", because that depends on the resource itself, like which site or study it belongs to.
p17-76.k: resource based authorization, object level authorization, idor, bola, check ownership, iauthorizationservice
x: Role-based checks answer "is this user a site user?". But they can't answer "is this user allowed to see this particular subject?", because that depends on the resource itself, like which site or study it belongs to.

If an API only checks roles, a user at site A can change the id in the URL, from /subjects/101 to /subjects/202, and see site B's subject. That's called IDOR, insecure direct object reference, or BOLA, broken object level authorization, and it's the number one risk in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

Resource-based authorization fixes it. After loading the resource, I check the relationship between the user and that resource: does the subject's site belong to the user's assigned sites? In ASP.NET Core, I inject IAuthorizationService and call AuthorizeAsync with the user, the subject and a requirement, handled by a handler that compares the subject's site with the user's sites. If it fails, return 403, or 404 if I don't want to reveal the resource exists.
Even better, I filter at the query level, so a site user's queries only ever return their own sites' data, using a global filter.
I also write tests that try to access another user's resources, because this bug is easy to miss.
In our IRT, site users only see their own site's subjects and kits, enforced in queries and checks.

p17-77.q: Cross-site request forgery is an attack where a malicious website makes the user's browser send a request to our application, and the browser automatically attaches our cookies, so the request runs as the logged-in user. For example, a hidden form on a bad site posts to our "change email" endpoint.
p17-77.k: csrf, cross site request forgery, xsrf, antiforgery token, samesite cookie, prevent csrf
x: Cross-site request forgery is an attack where a malicious website makes the user's browser send a request to our application, and the browser automatically attaches our cookies, so the request runs as the logged-in user. For example, a hidden form on a bad site posts to our "change email" endpoint.

It's a risk mainly when authentication uses cookies, because browsers send cookies automatically. APIs that use bearer tokens in the Authorization header aren't vulnerable in the same way, because the attacker's page can't add that header.

Defences. SameSite cookies: Lax or Strict means the browser won't send the cookie on most cross-site requests; Lax is the default in modern browsers, and it's a strong first layer. Anti-forgery tokens: the server issues a secret token, included in forms or a header, and validates it on every state-changing request; the attacker's site can't read it. In ASP.NET Core MVC and Razor Pages, this is built in with ValidateAntiForgeryToken and the form tag helper. Also, never change state with GET requests, and check the Origin header for sensitive actions.
Our legacy MVC portal uses anti-forgery tokens on its forms, and the React shell calls APIs with bearer tokens.

p17-78.q: Cross-site scripting happens when an attacker manages to get their JavaScript running in another user's browser, inside our site. It can steal tokens, read data on the page, or perform actions as the user. It usually comes from displaying user-supplied data without escaping it, like a comment containing a script tag.
p17-78.k: xss, cross site scripting, prevent xss, dangerouslysetinnerhtml, angular sanitization, content security policy
x: Cross-site scripting happens when an attacker manages to get their JavaScript running in another user's browser, inside our site. It can steal tokens, read data on the page, or perform actions as the user. It usually comes from displaying user-supplied data without escaping it, like a comment containing a script tag.

Modern frameworks help a lot by default. React escapes all values in JSX, so text is shown as text, not HTML. Angular sanitises values bound into the template, and strips dangerous content from innerHTML bindings.

The risks come from bypassing these protections: dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React, bypassSecurityTrustHtml in Angular, direct DOM manipulation, building URLs from user input, like a javascript: link, or third-party libraries that insert HTML. If I really must render HTML, I sanitise it first with a library like DOMPurify.

Other layers. A Content Security Policy header that only allows scripts from our own origin, and blocks inline scripts, so even injected markup can't run. HttpOnly cookies, so scripts can't read session cookies. Output encoding on the server for any HTML it generates. And validation of input.
In our React screens, we never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML for user data, and email templates are encoded on the server.

p17-79.q: SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, so an attacker can change the query itself, like adding OR 1 equals 1, or even dropping tables.
p17-79.k: sql injection, prevent sql injection, parameterized queries, ef core sql injection, fromsqlraw injection, dapper parameters
x: SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, so an attacker can change the query itself, like adding OR 1 equals 1, or even dropping tables.
The main defence is parameterised queries, always. The SQL text is fixed, and user values are sent separately as parameters, so the database treats them as data, never as code.

In EF Core, LINQ queries are parameterised automatically. For raw SQL, FromSql and ExecuteSql with interpolated strings are safe, because EF converts the interpolated values into parameters. The dangerous one is FromSqlRaw with string concatenation; with FromSqlRaw, I always pass parameters separately. In Dapper, I pass an anonymous object of parameters, never concatenated values. In ADO.NET, I use SqlParameter.
Parameters can't be used for identifiers, like table or column names or sort direction. For dynamic sorting, I map the user's choice to a whitelist of known column names, never insert it directly.
Stored procedures are safe too, unless they build dynamic SQL inside with concatenation; then they must use sp_executesql with parameters.
Defence in depth: the application's database login has least privilege, and static analysis flags string-built SQL.
In our IRT, data access uses parameterised queries and stored procedures, and code review checks for raw SQL.

p17-80.q: Passwords must never be stored in plain text or with reversible encryption, and not with fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second with GPUs.
p17-80.k: password hashing, store passwords, bcrypt argon2, pbkdf2, salt and hash, aspnet identity password hasher
x: Passwords must never be stored in plain text or with reversible encryption, and not with fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second with GPUs.

The right way is a slow, salted, adaptive password hashing algorithm: Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count. The salt is a unique random value per password, stored with the hash, so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables don't work. The work factor makes each guess expensive, and it can be increased over time as hardware gets faster.

In .NET, ASP.NET Core Identity's PasswordHasher uses PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 and a high iteration count, and it supports upgrading hashes when the user next logs in. Libraries are available for Argon2 and bcrypt.
Better still is not handling passwords at all: delegate login to an identity provider, like Keycloak, Azure AD or Cognito, which handles hashing, lockout, MFA and password policies properly.
Plus related controls: account lockout or throttling after failed attempts, checking new passwords against known breached lists, and MFA.
In our IRT, Keycloak handles passwords, with password policy and lockout configured, which are also Part 11 requirements.

p17-81.q: The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years from real-world data. The latest 2025 edition is very similar to 2021, and the ones I keep in mind are these.
p17-81.k: owasp top 10, owasp, web security risks, broken access control, security misconfiguration, owasp api top 10
x: The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years from real-world data. The latest 2025 edition is very similar to 2021, and the ones I keep in mind are these.

Broken access control is number one: users acting outside their permissions, like IDOR, where changing an id shows someone else's data. Security misconfiguration: default settings, verbose errors, open storage, missing headers. Software supply chain failures: vulnerable or compromised dependencies, packages and build tools. Cryptographic failures: weak or missing encryption, like plain-text passwords or no TLS. Injection: SQL injection, command injection, and XSS. Insecure design: missing security thinking in the architecture, like no rate limiting on password reset. Authentication failures: weak passwords, no MFA, poor session handling. Software or data integrity failures: unsigned updates or insecure deserialisation. Logging and alerting failures: attacks not noticed. And mishandling of exceptional conditions, like failing open or leaking errors.
There's also a separate OWASP API Security Top 10, where broken object level authorization is number one.

In practice, I map these to concrete habits: authorization checks per resource, parameterised queries, dependency scanning in pipelines, security headers, central logging with alerts, and threat modelling for new features.

p17-82.q: Security headers tell the browser to apply extra protections. The ones I add are these.
p17-82.k: security headers, content security policy, hsts, x content type options, x frame options, secure headers asp.net core
x: Security headers tell the browser to apply extra protections. The ones I add are these.
Strict-Transport-Security, or HSTS, which tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the site, preventing downgrade attacks. In ASP.NET Core, UseHsts adds it outside development.

Content-Security-Policy, which controls where scripts, styles, images and frames can load from. It's the strongest defence against XSS, for example script-src 'self' blocks inline and third-party scripts. I start in report-only mode to find what breaks, then enforce.
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so browsers don't guess content types, which can turn an upload into a script.
Frame protection, with frame-ancestors in the CSP, or X-Frame-Options: DENY, to prevent clickjacking.
Referrer-Policy, like strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so full URLs with ids aren't leaked to other sites.
Permissions-Policy, to disable browser features we don't use, like camera or geolocation.
And I remove headers that reveal technology versions, like Server and X-Powered-By.
For APIs, I also set Cache-Control: no-store on responses with sensitive data.
I add these with middleware, or a library like NetEscapades.AspNetCore.SecurityHeaders, or at the gateway or reverse proxy, and check them with a scanner as part of testing.

p17-83.q: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more different kinds of evidence: something you know, like a password; something you have, like a phone or security key; and something you are, like a fingerprint. Even if the password is stolen, the attacker can't log in without the second factor. It blocks the vast majority of account takeover attacks.
p17-83.k: mfa, multi factor authentication, two factor authentication, totp, add 2fa, webauthn passkeys
x: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more different kinds of evidence: something you know, like a password; something you have, like a phone or security key; and something you are, like a fingerprint. Even if the password is stolen, the attacker can't log in without the second factor. It blocks the vast majority of account takeover attacks.

Common second factors are: TOTP authenticator apps, which generate a 6-digit code every 30 seconds from a shared secret; push notifications to an app; SMS codes, which are better than nothing but vulnerable to SIM swapping; and the strongest, FIDO2 security keys or passkeys using WebAuthn, which are phishing-resistant, because they're tied to the real website's domain.

The best way to add it is through the identity provider, not custom code. Keycloak, Azure AD, Cognito and Okta all support MFA, conditional policies and passkeys with configuration. If I'm using ASP.NET Core Identity directly, it has built-in TOTP support with recovery codes.

Important details: recovery codes for lost devices, rate limiting on code entry, requiring MFA again for sensitive actions, which is step-up authentication, and remembering trusted devices for a limited time.
For our users, these policies are configured centrally in Keycloak.

p17-84.q: Least privilege means every user, service and process gets only the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more, for only as long as it needs them. If something is compromised, the damage is limited.
p17-84.k: least privilege, principle of least privilege, minimum permissions, iam least privilege, database least privilege
x: Least privilege means every user, service and process gets only the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more, for only as long as it needs them. If something is compromised, the damage is limited.
I apply it at every layer.
Application users: role-based permissions that match real job functions, and resource-level checks, so a site user only sees their own site.

Services: each service has its own identity, like an IAM role or a managed identity, with a policy that allows only specific actions on specific resources, like s3:GetObject on one bucket, not s3:* on everything. I avoid wildcards, and use tools like IAM Access Analyzer to find unused permissions.

Databases: the application connects with a login that can read and write its own tables or run its procedures, but not change schema or drop tables. Migrations use a separate, more privileged identity in the pipeline.
Pipelines: deployment credentials scoped to one environment, with production deployments needing approval.
Developers: no standing production access; temporary, audited access when needed.
Network: services can only reach what they need, through security groups and network policies.
And regular access reviews, removing permissions that are no longer used. In regulated work, those reviews are also an audit requirement.

p17-85.q: They're often confused, but they serve different purposes.
p17-85.k: encryption vs hashing vs encoding, hashing vs encryption, base64 is not encryption, symmetric vs asymmetric encryption
x: They're often confused, but they serve different purposes.

Encoding transforms data into another format for compatibility, like Base64 for binary data in JSON, or URL encoding. It's not security at all: anyone can decode it, no key needed. A common mistake is thinking Base64 protects a secret.

Hashing is a one-way function that turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint, like SHA-256. You can't reverse it. The same input always gives the same hash, and a tiny change gives a completely different hash. It's used for integrity checks, like verifying a file wasn't changed, and with slow, salted algorithms, for storing passwords.

Encryption is two-way: data is scrambled with a key, and can be decrypted with the right key. It protects confidentiality. Symmetric encryption, like AES, uses one shared key, and it's fast, used for data at rest. Asymmetric encryption, like RSA or elliptic curve, uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, or a private key to sign and a public key to verify, which is how TLS and JWT signatures work.
In .NET, I use the built-in System.Security.Cryptography classes, never my own algorithms, and for app-level protection of data like cookies, the Data Protection API.

p17-86.q: Logs are copied to many places and kept for a long time, so sensitive data in logs is a real breach risk. I treat logs as if many people can read them.
p17-86.k: pii in logs, mask sensitive data logs, phi logging, log redaction, gdpr logging, data masking serilog
x: Logs are copied to many places and kept for a long time, so sensitive data in logs is a real breach risk. I treat logs as if many people can read them.

First, don't log it at all. I log ids and outcomes, not personal data. For example, log the subject id and the action, not the subject's date of birth or initials. Request and response bodies aren't logged by default, especially for endpoints that handle personal data.

Second, structured logging makes it controllable. With Serilog, I can use destructuring policies that mask or exclude specific properties, and .NET's Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance redaction lets me classify data as sensitive and automatically redact it in logs.
Third, scrub at the pipeline: the log shipper or the logging platform can mask patterns like email addresses or card numbers, as a safety net.
Fourth, protect logs themselves: access control, encryption, and retention limits.
Also be careful with exception messages, which sometimes contain data values, and with tokens in URLs or headers, which should never be logged.

In clinical systems, this matters doubly, with patient privacy rules and audit requirements. In our CIRT services, we log subject and kit identifiers, never names or contact details, and Splunk access is restricted.

p17-87.q: With session cookies, the server creates a session after login, stores the session data on the server or in a shared store, and gives the browser a cookie with a session id. The browser sends the cookie automatically on each request. It's simple and secure for traditional web apps, especially with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags, and sessions can be revoked instantly by deleting them. But it needs shared session storage when scaling out, it's tied to one domain, and needs CSRF protection.
p17-87.k: cookies vs tokens, session vs jwt, cookie authentication vs jwt, stateful vs stateless auth, which is better cookie or token
x: With session cookies, the server creates a session after login, stores the session data on the server or in a shared store, and gives the browser a cookie with a session id. The browser sends the cookie automatically on each request. It's simple and secure for traditional web apps, especially with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags, and sessions can be revoked instantly by deleting them. But it needs shared session storage when scaling out, it's tied to one domain, and needs CSRF protection.

With token-based authentication, the client gets a signed token, usually a JWT, and sends it in the Authorization header. The server validates it without storing anything, so it scales easily and works across domains, for mobile apps and service-to-service calls. The downsides are that revocation is harder, and in browsers, storing the token safely is tricky, because JavaScript-readable storage is exposed to XSS.

Modern best practice for browser apps often combines them: a BFF does the OAuth login on the server, keeps tokens server-side, and uses a secure cookie with the browser. APIs called by other services or mobile apps use bearer tokens.
So it's not that one is always better; it depends on the client type.

p17-88.q: File uploads are a common attack route, so I apply several checks.
p17-88.k: secure file upload, file upload security, validate uploaded files, malware scan upload, upload vulnerabilities
x: File uploads are a common attack route, so I apply several checks.
Size limits: set a maximum request size and file size, so nobody can fill the disk or memory. In ASP.NET Core, through RequestSizeLimit and Kestrel or form options.

Type validation: allow only the types the feature needs, with an allow-list. Don't trust the file extension or the Content-Type header, because both are set by the client. Check the file's actual signature, its magic bytes, and for documents, parse them safely.
Names: never use the user's file name for storage, because of path traversal tricks like dot-dot-slash. Generate a random name, and keep the original name only as metadata, sanitised.

Storage: store outside the web root, ideally in object storage like S3 or blob storage, in a private bucket, so uploaded files can never be executed by the web server. Serve downloads through the API with authorization checks, or short-lived signed URLs, and with Content-Disposition: attachment.
Scanning: run antivirus or malware scanning before marking the file as available.
Content risks: CSV files can contain formula injection, so exports escape leading equals signs, and images can carry metadata with personal data, so strip it.
And log uploads for audit.

p17-89.q: JWTs can be signed in two ways.
p17-89.k: hs256 vs rs256, symmetric vs asymmetric signing, jwt signing algorithm, rs256 jwks, which jwt algorithm
x: JWTs can be signed in two ways.

Symmetric signing, like HS256, uses one shared secret key both to sign and to verify. It's simple and fast. The problem is that every service that verifies tokens must have the same secret, and anyone with the secret can also create valid tokens. So if any one service leaks it, an attacker can forge tokens for the whole system. It's only reasonable when the issuer and the verifier are the same application.

Asymmetric signing, like RS256 with RSA or ES256 with elliptic curves, uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Only the identity provider holds the private key. APIs just need the public key, which isn't secret, so a compromised API can't create tokens. Public keys are published at the JWKS endpoint, with a key id, which makes key rotation easy: the provider adds a new key, starts signing with it, and APIs pick it up automatically.
So for distributed systems and microservices, asymmetric signing is the right choice.

One classic attack is algorithm confusion, where an attacker changes the header's algorithm to "none" or to HS256 using the public key as a secret. Validation must only accept the expected algorithms; ASP.NET Core's JWT handler does this properly when configured with the authority.

p17-90.q: A threat model is a structured way to think about what could go wrong with a feature's security before building it, so security is designed in, not patched on later.
p17-90.k: threat modeling, stride, threat model feature, security design review, attack surface
x: A threat model is a structured way to think about what could go wrong with a feature's security before building it, so security is designed in, not patched on later.

I keep it lightweight, often a one-hour session with the team. First, draw a simple data-flow diagram: users, services, data stores, external systems, and the trust boundaries between them, like the internet to our API, or our service to a vendor.

Then go through each element with STRIDE as a checklist. Spoofing: can someone pretend to be another user or service? Tampering: can data be changed in transit or at rest? Repudiation: can someone deny an action because there's no audit trail? Information disclosure: can data leak through APIs, logs or errors? Denial of service: can someone overload it? Elevation of privilege: can a user do more than they should?

For each real threat, we agree a mitigation, like adding resource-level authorization, signing a webhook, or rate limiting, and track it as a work item with an owner. Risks we accept are written down.
The model is revisited when the design changes.
[When we threat-modelled the drug accountability return screens, it showed that the return quantity API needed a site ownership check, which we added before release.]

p17-91.q: Webhooks are HTTP calls between systems, so both sides need to trust each other.
p17-91.k: webhook security, verify webhook signature, hmac webhook, secure webhook endpoint, webhook replay attack
x: Webhooks are HTTP calls between systems, so both sides need to trust each other.

When receiving webhooks, the biggest risk is someone calling the endpoint pretending to be the provider. So I verify a signature: the provider signs the request body with a shared secret using HMAC-SHA256 and sends it in a header. I recompute the HMAC over the raw body and compare with a constant-time comparison. I also check a timestamp header and reject old requests, like older than five minutes, to prevent replay attacks, and store the event id to ignore duplicates, since providers retry. The endpoint responds quickly with 2xx and queues the work, so the provider doesn't time out and resend.

When sending webhooks, I do the same in reverse: sign each payload, include a timestamp and a unique id, use HTTPS only, retry with backoff on failure, and let customers rotate their secrets. I also protect against SSRF, because customers provide the URLs: block internal addresses, like localhost and private IP ranges, and metadata endpoints.
Payloads contain minimal data, often just an id, so the receiver fetches details through the authenticated API.
[Our vendor status callbacks in the newer data transfer API verify an HMAC signature and timestamp before queuing the message.]

p17-92.q: Server-side request forgery happens when an attacker makes our server send a request to a URL they choose. It's a risk whenever the server fetches a URL provided by a user, like importing an image from a link, previewing a URL, or calling a customer-provided webhook.
p17-92.k: ssrf, server side request forgery, prevent ssrf, metadata endpoint attack, url fetch vulnerability
x: Server-side request forgery happens when an attacker makes our server send a request to a URL they choose. It's a risk whenever the server fetches a URL provided by a user, like importing an image from a link, previewing a URL, or calling a customer-provided webhook.

The danger is that our server sits inside the network, so the attacker can reach things they normally can't: internal admin APIs, databases with HTTP interfaces, or the cloud metadata endpoint, like 169.254.169.254 on AWS, which can expose temporary credentials. That's how some well-known cloud breaches happened.

To prevent it, I avoid fetching user-supplied URLs where possible. If needed, I validate against an allow-list of domains, and resolve the host name and block private, loopback, link-local and metadata IP ranges. I check again after redirects, or disable redirects, because an allowed URL can redirect to an internal one. DNS rebinding is another trick, so I connect to the IP I validated.
At the infrastructure level, on AWS, I require IMDSv2, which uses session tokens and blocks simple SSRF access to metadata, and restrict outbound traffic with security groups or an egress proxy.
Least-privilege roles limit the damage if something still gets through.

p17-93.q: First, I assess it. Is the vulnerable package actually used by us, and is the vulnerable code path reachable? What's the severity, and is there a known exploit? Which applications and environments use it? Transitive dependencies matter too, because often the vulnerable package is pulled in by another one.
p17-93.k: vulnerable dependency, nuget vulnerability, npm audit, dependency scanning, cve in package, dependabot
x: First, I assess it. Is the vulnerable package actually used by us, and is the vulnerable code path reachable? What's the severity, and is there a known exploit? Which applications and environments use it? Transitive dependencies matter too, because often the vulnerable package is pulled in by another one.

Tools help: dotnet list package --vulnerable, NuGet audit warnings during restore, npm audit, and automated scanners like Dependabot, Snyk or GitHub's dependency graph, which open pull requests with the fixed version.

Then I fix it. Normally, upgrade to the patched version, run the full test suite, and deploy through the normal pipeline, quickly for critical issues. If the direct package has no fix yet, I can pin the transitive dependency to a fixed version, with a direct reference or npm overrides. If there's no fix at all, I mitigate: disable the affected feature, add input validation or a WAF rule, and track it.
Afterwards, I check for signs of exploitation in logs if the risk was high, and document it.
To prevent surprises, the pipeline runs dependency scanning on every build and fails on high or critical findings, and we keep dependencies reasonably up to date, so upgrades are small.
In a validated environment, even a security patch goes through change control, but we fast-track critical ones.

p17-94.q: The Data Protection API is ASP.NET Core's built-in system for encrypting and signing data that the app itself needs to read back later. The framework uses it for authentication cookies, anti-forgery tokens and TempData, and I can use it for things like protecting a token in a URL.
p17-94.k: data protection api, asp.net core data protection, key ring, data protection keys, protect unprotect, cookie encryption keys
x: The Data Protection API is ASP.NET Core's built-in system for encrypting and signing data that the app itself needs to read back later. The framework uses it for authentication cookies, anti-forgery tokens and TempData, and I can use it for things like protecting a token in a URL.

I get an IDataProtector from IDataProtectionProvider with a purpose string, then call Protect and Unprotect. The purpose string isolates uses, so data protected for "password reset" can't be unprotected as something else. ToTimeLimitedDataProtector adds expiry.

The important production detail is the key ring. Keys are generated and rotated automatically, every 90 days by default. By default they're stored locally, which is fine on one machine. But with several instances behind a load balancer, or containers that restart, each instance would have different keys, so a cookie issued by one instance can't be read by another, and users get logged out or see anti-forgery errors.

So in production, I persist the keys to a shared location, like Redis, a database, blob storage or S3, set the same application name for all instances, and protect the keys at rest, with Azure Key Vault, a certificate, or AWS KMS.
This is a classic issue when moving an app from one server to a load-balanced or containerised setup.

p17-95.q: A Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which sources are allowed for scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames and API calls. If an attacker injects a script, the browser refuses to run it because it doesn't match the policy. It's one of the strongest defences against XSS.
p17-95.k: content security policy, csp, csp rollout, csp report only, nonce csp, csp angular react
x: A Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which sources are allowed for scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames and API calls. If an attacker injects a script, the browser refuses to run it because it doesn't match the policy. It's one of the strongest defences against XSS.

A strict policy looks like: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; connect-src for our API and identity provider. Inline scripts are blocked unless they have a nonce, a random value per response, or a hash.
Rolling it out on an existing site needs care, because it can break things: inline scripts, inline event handlers, third-party analytics, fonts from CDNs, or older libraries that use eval.

So I start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, which doesn't block anything but reports violations to an endpoint. I collect reports for a couple of weeks, fix or allow the legitimate sources, remove inline code where possible, and only then switch to enforcing mode. I keep reporting on, to catch new issues.
Modern React and Angular builds with Vite or the Angular CLI work well with a strict CSP, because scripts are external files; Angular also supports nonces for its inline styles.

p17-96.q: The honest answer is that you can't hide a secret in a browser app. Everything in the JavaScript bundle, including environment variables injected at build time, like Vite's VITE_ variables or Angular's environment files, is visible to anyone who opens the developer tools.
p17-96.k: api keys in frontend, hide api key react, environment variables frontend secret, secrets in spa, vite env secret
x: The honest answer is that you can't hide a secret in a browser app. Everything in the JavaScript bundle, including environment variables injected at build time, like Vite's VITE_ variables or Angular's environment files, is visible to anyone who opens the developer tools.

So the rule is: never put real secrets in front-end code. Only public values belong there, like the API base URL, the identity provider's URL, a public client id, or a publishable key that's designed to be public and restricted, like a maps key locked to our domain.

When the front end needs to call a service that requires a secret key, the call goes through our own backend. The browser calls our API with the user's token; our API adds the secret, which it reads from a vault, and calls the third-party service. That's also where rate limits and authorization are applied.
For our own APIs, the front end doesn't use API keys at all. Users log in with OpenID Connect, and the app sends a short-lived access token.
I also check build output and the repo with secret scanning, because developers sometimes put a key in a .env file that ends up in the bundle.
Our React shell's Vite variables contain only URLs and the public Keycloak client id.

p17-97.q: A traditional network firewall works at the network and transport layers. It allows or blocks traffic based on IP addresses, ports and protocols, like "allow HTTPS on port 443 from anywhere, block everything else", or "only the app servers can reach the database on port 1433". In the cloud, security groups, network ACLs and Azure network security groups play this role.
p17-97.k: waf vs firewall, web application firewall, aws waf, network firewall, what is waf
x: A traditional network firewall works at the network and transport layers. It allows or blocks traffic based on IP addresses, ports and protocols, like "allow HTTPS on port 443 from anywhere, block everything else", or "only the app servers can reach the database on port 1433". In the cloud, security groups, network ACLs and Azure network security groups play this role.

A web application firewall works at the application layer, layer 7. It understands HTTP and inspects the content of requests: URLs, headers, query strings and bodies. It can block common attack patterns, like SQL injection strings, cross-site scripting payloads, known bad bots, requests from certain countries, or too many requests from one IP. Examples are AWS WAF on CloudFront, an ALB or API Gateway, Azure Web Application Firewall on Front Door or Application Gateway, and Cloudflare.
They complement each other: the network firewall limits who can talk to what, and the WAF filters malicious content in allowed traffic.

But a WAF is a safety net, not a replacement for secure code. It can be bypassed with clever encoding and can produce false positives, so I start rules in count mode, review what would be blocked, then enable blocking. The application must still validate input and use parameterised queries.

p17-98.q: The trick is to have two valid credentials for an overlap period, so nothing breaks during the switch.
p17-98.k: secret rotation, rotate database password, certificate rotation, zero downtime rotation, key rotation
x: The trick is to have two valid credentials for an overlap period, so nothing breaks during the switch.

For database passwords or API keys, the common approach is dual credentials. Create a new secret while the old one still works. Update the secret store. Applications pick up the new value, either by reloading configuration periodically, or by fetching a fresh secret when authentication fails, then retrying. After all instances use the new one, revoke the old one. AWS Secrets Manager automates this with rotation Lambdas, using alternating users, so one is always valid.

For signing keys, like JWT keys, the identity provider publishes both the old and new public keys in its JWKS. It starts signing with the new key, and once old tokens have expired, removes the old key.

For TLS certificates, I automate renewal well before expiry, using AWS Certificate Manager, Key Vault auto-renewal, or Let's Encrypt with cert-manager, and alert at 30 days before expiry for anything manual. Expired certificates are a surprisingly common cause of outages.
Better still, remove secrets entirely where possible: IAM roles and managed identities rotate credentials automatically.
The application side matters: don't cache secrets forever, and don't require a restart to pick up a new one.

p17-99.q: Sometimes the question isn't whether a user can see a record, but which fields of it they can see. In clinical trials, this is critical: blinded users must never see which treatment a subject received, while unblinded roles, like pharmacists or the safety team, can.
p17-99.k: field level security, data level authorization, hide fields by role, blinded unblinded access, column level security, mask fields by permission
x: Sometimes the question isn't whether a user can see a record, but which fields of it they can see. In clinical trials, this is critical: blinded users must never see which treatment a subject received, while unblinded roles, like pharmacists or the safety team, can.
I enforce it on the server, never just by hiding fields in the UI, because anyone can call the API directly or look at the network response.

The approach: the user's permissions, from their role, determine a data access level. The API builds different DTOs, or projections, for different access levels, so sensitive fields are simply not selected from the database for blinded users. A blinded user's response doesn't contain the treatment arm at all, not even as null with a hint. Reports and exports follow the same rules, and so do logs and error messages.
For extra protection, the database can enforce it too, with views or column permissions, so a reporting tool can't bypass the application.
Testing is essential: automated tests call each endpoint as a blinded user and assert that unblinded fields never appear.
In our IRT, role and field-level blinding is a core feature, and things like kit numbers that could reveal the treatment are handled carefully.

p17-100.q: All three are identity providers that support OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, so applications integrate with them in a similar way. The differences are about hosting, features and ecosystem.
p17-100.k: keycloak vs azure ad vs cognito, identity provider comparison, entra id vs keycloak, which identity provider, cognito user pool
x: All three are identity providers that support OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, so applications integrate with them in a similar way. The differences are about hosting, features and ecosystem.

Keycloak is open source and self-hosted. You run it yourself, on-premise or in the cloud, which gives full control, deep customisation of login flows and themes, user federation with LDAP and Active Directory, and no per-user licence cost. The trade-off is that you operate it: upgrades, high availability, database backups and security patching.

Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure AD, is a managed service, ideal when the organisation already uses Microsoft 365, with corporate single sign-on, conditional access, MFA and B2B guest users built in. Entra External ID handles customer-facing identity.

Amazon Cognito is AWS's managed service, with user pools for app users, integration with API Gateway and ALB, and identity pools for temporary AWS credentials. It's cost-effective for customer apps on AWS, though less flexible for complex enterprise scenarios.
For the .NET API, it barely matters: AddJwtBearer with the authority and audience works with all of them.
We use Keycloak for our on-premise IRT, because it runs inside our network and supports our compliance needs, like password policies and lockout.

p17-101.q: With TLS termination, or SSL offloading, the load balancer or gateway handles the HTTPS connection with the client, decrypts the traffic, and forwards it to the backend, often as plain HTTP inside the private network. It's simple and efficient: certificates are managed in one place, like AWS Certificate Manager on an ALB, backends don't spend CPU on encryption, and the load balancer can inspect and route by HTTP content, and apply a WAF.
p17-101.k: tls termination, ssl offloading, end to end encryption, https load balancer, tls passthrough, re encryption
x: With TLS termination, or SSL offloading, the load balancer or gateway handles the HTTPS connection with the client, decrypts the traffic, and forwards it to the backend, often as plain HTTP inside the private network. It's simple and efficient: certificates are managed in one place, like AWS Certificate Manager on an ALB, backends don't spend CPU on encryption, and the load balancer can inspect and route by HTTP content, and apply a WAF.

The risk is that traffic between the load balancer and the backend is unencrypted. Inside a well-isolated private network, many teams accept that. But for sensitive data, compliance requirements, or a zero-trust approach, it's not enough.

End-to-end TLS means traffic is encrypted all the way. There are two styles. Re-encryption: the load balancer terminates TLS, inspects the request, then opens a new TLS connection to the backend. TLS passthrough: the load balancer just forwards the encrypted bytes, using a layer 4 balancer, and the backend terminates TLS, but then the load balancer can't route by path.
In ASP.NET Core behind a terminating proxy, I configure the forwarded headers middleware, so the app knows the original request was HTTPS and uses the right client IP and scheme.
For healthcare data, I prefer re-encryption to the backend.

p17-102.q: For reference types, the == operator by default compares references, meaning whether two variables point to the same object in memory. Equals is a virtual method, and by default it also compares references, but classes can override it to compare values.
p17-102.k: double equals vs equals, == vs equals, reference equality vs value equality, operator equality c#, referenceequals
x: For reference types, the == operator by default compares references, meaning whether two variables point to the same object in memory. Equals is a virtual method, and by default it also compares references, but classes can override it to compare values.

The difference shows up when a type overrides them. String is the classic example: both == and Equals are overridden to compare the characters, so two different string objects with the same text are equal either way.

But == is resolved at compile time, based on the variable's declared type, while Equals is resolved at runtime, based on the actual object. So if two strings are stored in variables of type object, == compares references and can return false, while Equals still compares the text and returns true. That's a classic interview trick.
For value types, like int or a struct, Equals compares the values. A struct's default Equals uses reflection, which is slow, so for performance-sensitive structs, I implement IEquatable of T.
Records generate value-based Equals and == for you.
If I override Equals, I must also override GetHashCode, and usually the == and != operators, so they behave consistently. And for a guaranteed reference check, I use ReferenceEquals.

p17-103.q: The rule is: if two objects are equal according to Equals, they must return the same hash code. The reverse isn't required; different objects can share a hash code, which is a collision.
p17-103.k: gethashcode, equals and gethashcode, override gethashcode, hash code contract, dictionary key custom class, hashcode.combine
x: The rule is: if two objects are equal according to Equals, they must return the same hash code. The reverse isn't required; different objects can share a hash code, which is a collision.

This matters because hash-based collections, like Dictionary and HashSet, first use the hash code to find the bucket, and only then call Equals within that bucket. If I override Equals to compare by value but leave the default GetHashCode, which is based on the object reference, two "equal" objects will usually land in different buckets. Then a dictionary lookup with an equal key fails to find the entry, and a HashSet happily stores duplicates. Those bugs are very confusing.
So whenever I override Equals, I override GetHashCode using the same fields. In modern .NET, HashCode.Combine of the fields does it neatly.

Another important rule: the hash code shouldn't change while the object is used as a key. If I mutate a field that's part of the hash after adding the object to a dictionary, it's effectively lost in the wrong bucket. That's why keys should be immutable.
Records and value tuples generate correct Equals and GetHashCode automatically, so for value-like keys, like a composite key of study id and site id, I use a record struct.

p17-104.q: In C#, a string can't be changed after it's created. Any operation that looks like it modifies a string, like concatenation, Replace or ToUpper, actually creates a new string and leaves the original as it was.
p17-104.k: string immutability, stringbuilder, string concatenation in loop, string vs stringbuilder, immutable string c#
x: In C#, a string can't be changed after it's created. Any operation that looks like it modifies a string, like concatenation, Replace or ToUpper, actually creates a new string and leaves the original as it was.

There are good reasons. It's thread-safe, because nobody can change a string another thread is reading. It's safe to use as a dictionary key, since its hash never changes. It allows string interning, where identical literals share one instance. And it's secure, because a validated value, like a file path, can't be changed afterwards.

The cost is that repeated concatenation in a loop creates many temporary strings. Building a string from 10,000 pieces with plus-equals copies the growing string every time, which is roughly quadratic, and creates a lot of garbage for the GC.
StringBuilder fixes this. It keeps a growable internal buffer and appends into it, and only creates the final string when you call ToString.

My rule: for a few concatenations, or one expression, plain concatenation or interpolation is fine and more readable; the compiler optimises it. In loops or when building large text, like a CSV export or an email body, I use StringBuilder, or string.Join for joining collections.
For very hot paths, there's also Span-based formatting and string.Create.

p17-105.q: Both are about creating objects safely with object initialiser syntax.
p17-105.k: required keyword, init only setter, init accessor, required members c# 11, object initializer immutability
x: Both are about creating objects safely with object initialiser syntax.

An init-only setter, written with init instead of set, lets a property be assigned during object initialisation, but not afterwards. So I can write new Shipment with Id equals 5 and Status equals Pending, and after that the object is effectively read-only. It gives immutability without needing a long constructor. Records use init properties by default.

The required modifier, from C# 11, goes further: the compiler forces the caller to set that property in the object initialiser. If someone writes new Shipment without setting a required property, it's a compile error, not a runtime null reference later. It works well with nullable reference types, because a required non-nullable string won't produce a "might be null" warning.
If a constructor sets all the required members itself, I mark it with SetsRequiredMembers, so callers using that constructor aren't forced to set them again.
I use these a lot for DTOs, options classes and commands: required plus init gives objects that are always complete and can't be changed by accident.
One caution: System.Text.Json respects required since .NET 7, so a missing JSON property causes a deserialisation error, which is usually what I want for incoming requests.

p17-106.q: Primary constructors let me declare constructor parameters directly on the class or struct declaration, like public class ShipmentService(IShipmentRepository repo, ILogger of ShipmentService logger). Those parameters are in scope throughout the class body, so I can use them in methods without declaring private fields and writing a constructor to assign them.
