p17-106.k: primary constructor, c# 12 primary constructors, class primary constructor, primary constructor dependency injection
x: Primary constructors let me declare constructor parameters directly on the class or struct declaration, like public class ShipmentService(IShipmentRepository repo, ILogger of ShipmentService logger). Those parameters are in scope throughout the class body, so I can use them in methods without declaring private fields and writing a constructor to assign them.
Records already had this, but in C# 12 it came to normal classes and structs. It removes a lot of boilerplate, especially for dependency injection in services and controllers.

There are some differences from records that are worth knowing. In a class, primary constructor parameters don't become public properties; they're just captured parameters. They're not readonly, so the class could accidentally reassign one; if I care about that, I assign it to a readonly field explicitly. And if the class has other constructors, they must call the primary constructor using this.
One subtle trap: if I both capture a parameter and also use it to initialise a property, the class ends up with two copies of the state, and the compiler warns about it.
I find them great for small services and handlers with a few injected dependencies. For classes with complex validation in the constructor, I still use a regular constructor, because it's clearer.

p17-107.q: yield return lets me write a method that produces a sequence one item at a time, lazily, without building the whole collection in memory.
p17-107.k: yield return, iterator c#, yield break, lazy sequence, custom ienumerable, state machine iterator
x: yield return lets me write a method that produces a sequence one item at a time, lazily, without building the whole collection in memory.

When a method returns IEnumerable of T and uses yield return, the compiler turns it into a state machine class. Nothing runs when the method is called. Code runs only when someone enumerates the result, for example with foreach. Each time the consumer asks for the next item, the method runs until the next yield return, hands back that value, and pauses, remembering where it was. yield break ends the sequence early.

This is useful for reading large files line by line, paging through an API, or generating sequences on demand, because only one item is in memory at a time, and if the consumer stops early, for example with Take of 10, the rest is never produced.

There are some gotchas. Because execution is deferred, argument validation inside an iterator doesn't run until enumeration starts, so I put validation in a non-iterator wrapper method, or a local function. Enumerating twice runs the whole method twice. And a using block inside an iterator stays open until enumeration finishes or the enumerator is disposed.
For asynchronous sources, like paging through an API, I use async iterators: IAsyncEnumerable with yield return and await foreach.

p17-108.q: An IEnumerable is often not a collection, but a recipe that's executed every time it's enumerated. That's deferred execution. So if I enumerate the same IEnumerable twice, the work runs twice.
p17-108.k: multiple enumeration, possible multiple enumeration warning, enumerate twice, ienumerable evaluated twice, tolist materialize
x: An IEnumerable is often not a collection, but a recipe that's executed every time it's enumerated. That's deferred execution. So if I enumerate the same IEnumerable twice, the work runs twice.

For example, if a method receives an IEnumerable from a LINQ query over a database or an iterator that reads a file, and the code calls Count, then later does a foreach, that's two database queries or two file reads. If the source is expensive, it's slow. If the source changes between enumerations, the two passes can see different data, giving inconsistent results. And some sources can't be enumerated twice at all, like a stream reader or a network response.
Tools like ReSharper and Rider warn about "possible multiple enumeration" for this reason.

The fix depends on the situation. If I need to go over it several times, I materialise it once with ToList or ToArray and use that. If I only need one pass, I write the logic in one loop. And in method signatures, if the method needs to enumerate several times or needs the count, I accept IReadOnlyCollection or IReadOnlyList instead of IEnumerable, which tells callers I expect a materialised collection.
[I once found a report that ran the same query three times because of this, and ToList fixed it.]

p17-109.q: A Dictionary is a hash table. When I add a key, it calls GetHashCode on the key, maps the hash to a bucket index, and stores the entry there. Entries that land in the same bucket, collisions, are chained together.
p17-109.k: dictionary internals, hash table c#, dictionary lookup o(1), dictionary vs list lookup, hash collision, dictionary capacity
x: A Dictionary is a hash table. When I add a key, it calls GetHashCode on the key, maps the hash to a bucket index, and stores the entry there. Entries that land in the same bucket, collisions, are chained together.

When I look up a key, it computes the hash, goes straight to the bucket, and then compares the keys in that bucket using Equals. With a good hash function, buckets contain very few entries, so lookup, insert and remove are O(1) on average. Compare that with searching a List, which is O(n), because it may check every element.

As the dictionary grows past its capacity, it resizes: allocates a bigger array, roughly doubling, and re-inserts every entry, which is an O(n) operation. So if I know the approximate size, I pass the capacity to the constructor and avoid repeated resizing.
Performance depends on the key's hash. A bad GetHashCode, like one that returns the same value for everything, turns the dictionary into a slow linked list, O(n) per lookup.

Also, Dictionary isn't thread-safe for writes; for concurrent use I'd use ConcurrentDictionary. It doesn't keep insertion order guaranteed, and for string keys, I often pass StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase to make lookups case-insensitive.

p17-110.q: I use a HashSet when I need fast membership checks or uniqueness, and I don't care about order or duplicates.
p17-110.k: hashset vs list, hashset c#, contains performance, unique values collection, set operations c#
x: I use a HashSet when I need fast membership checks or uniqueness, and I don't care about order or duplicates.

A List keeps items in order and allows duplicates, and Contains has to scan the list, which is O(n). A HashSet stores unique items using hashing, so Contains, Add and Remove are O(1) on average. Add returns false if the item already exists, which is handy for de-duplication.

The difference is huge in loops. If I check, for each of 10,000 incoming records, whether its id is in a list of 10,000 existing ids, that's around 100 million comparisons with a List, but only about 10,000 hash lookups with a HashSet.
HashSet also has efficient set operations: UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith and IsSubsetOf, which are perfect for things like "which kit ids in the file are not in the database".
The trade-offs: a HashSet uses more memory than a List, there's no index access, and the order isn't guaranteed. And it relies on good Equals and GetHashCode for the element type.
In LINQ, Distinct, Except and Intersect use a set internally, but if I do repeated lookups, I build the HashSet once myself.
In our CSV import, I load the existing kit numbers into a HashSet once, so validating each row is a fast lookup.

p17-111.q: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe for individual operations, but there are a few traps.
p17-111.k: concurrentdictionary, getoradd pitfall, concurrentdictionary thread safe, lazy getoradd, addorupdate
x: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe for individual operations, but there are a few traps.

The biggest is that the value factory in GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate isn't guaranteed to run only once. If two threads ask for the same missing key at the same time, both may run the factory, and only one result is stored. If the factory is expensive, like a database call, or has side effects, like creating a connection, that's a problem. The common fix is to store Lazy of T values, so the dictionary only stores the Lazy wrapper, and the expensive work runs once when Value is accessed, with thread-safe Lazy mode.

Second, compound operations aren't atomic. Checking ContainsKey and then adding, or reading a value and then updating it, can race with other threads. I use the atomic methods instead: GetOrAdd, AddOrUpdate, TryUpdate with a comparison value, or TryRemove.
Third, the values themselves aren't protected. If the value is a mutable List, two threads can still modify it at the same time.
Fourth, some operations, like Count, Keys or ToArray, lock all internal locks, so calling them often under load hurts performance.
And finally, a ConcurrentDictionary used as a cache grows forever unless something evicts entries. For caching, I'd usually use IMemoryCache or HybridCache instead, which have expiry and size limits.

p17-112.q: All three limit concurrent access to something, but they fit different situations.
p17-112.k: lock vs semaphoreslim, monitor c#, async lock, semaphoreslim waitasync, mutex vs semaphore, thread synchronization
x: All three limit concurrent access to something, but they fit different situations.

lock is the simplest: it ensures only one thread at a time runs a block of code, using an object as the lock. Under the hood, it's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit in a try-finally. It's fast and right for protecting small, synchronous critical sections, like updating a shared counter or list. But you can't await inside a lock; the compiler stops you, because the continuation might run on a different thread, which would break the lock's ownership. In .NET 9, there's also a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type that's a bit faster.
Monitor is what lock uses, with extra features like TryEnter with a timeout, and Wait and Pulse for signalling. I rarely use it directly.

SemaphoreSlim allows a set number of threads in at once, not just one, and it supports async with WaitAsync. So it's my choice when I need mutual exclusion around async code, like "only one refresh of this cache at a time", using a semaphore with a count of one, or for throttling, like "at most five concurrent calls to the vendor API". Always release it in a finally block.
Mutex and Semaphore, without Slim, work across processes, but they're heavier, so I only use them when coordinating separate processes on one machine.

p17-113.q: Interlocked provides atomic operations on shared variables, without taking a lock.
p17-113.k: interlocked, interlocked increment, atomic operations c#, compareexchange, lock free counter
x: Interlocked provides atomic operations on shared variables, without taking a lock.

A simple counter++ looks like one step, but it's actually three: read the value, add one, write it back. If two threads do it at the same time, both can read the same value, and one increment is lost. With Interlocked.Increment, the whole read-modify-write happens as one atomic CPU instruction, so no update is lost, and it's much cheaper than a lock.

The main methods are Increment, Decrement and Add, for counters; Exchange, which sets a value and returns the old one atomically; and CompareExchange, which sets a value only if it currently equals an expected value. CompareExchange is the building block for lock-free algorithms. For example, to update a shared reference safely, I read the current value, compute a new one, and call CompareExchange; if another thread changed it in between, the call fails, and I retry.

Typical uses: counting requests or processed messages, generating sequence numbers inside a process, making sure something runs only once with a flag set from 0 to 1, or swapping in a new configuration object.
It only works for single variables, though. If several values must change together consistently, I still need a lock.

p17-114.q: An async void method can't be awaited, and that causes two main problems.
p17-114.k: async void, async void exception, async void event handler, fire and forget async, avoid async void
x: An async void method can't be awaited, and that causes two main problems.

First, exceptions. In an async Task method, an exception is captured in the returned Task, and the caller sees it when it awaits. In async void, there's no Task to hold the exception, so it's raised directly on the synchronisation context or the thread pool. In ASP.NET Core or a console app, an unhandled exception there can crash the whole process. And no try-catch around the call can catch it, because the caller has already moved on.

Second, the caller can't know when it finished. It can't await it, can't wait for it in tests, and can't sequence work after it. So you get race conditions, like a DbContext being disposed at the end of a request while the async void method is still using it, which gives ObjectDisposedException at random.
The only legitimate use is event handlers, like a button click in WinForms or WPF, because the event signature requires void. Even then, I wrap the body in try-catch.

Everywhere else, I return Task or ValueTask. If I truly want fire-and-forget, I don't hide it in async void; I put the work on a background queue processed by a hosted service, with proper error handling and logging, and a fresh DI scope.

p17-115.q: Task.WhenAll takes several tasks and returns a task that completes when all of them are finished. It's how I run independent async operations concurrently, like calling three services at once, so the total time is roughly the slowest call instead of the sum. With tasks of T, it returns an array of results.
p17-115.k: task whenall, task whenany, whenall exceptions, run tasks in parallel, aggregateexception, parallel async calls
x: Task.WhenAll takes several tasks and returns a task that completes when all of them are finished. It's how I run independent async operations concurrently, like calling three services at once, so the total time is roughly the slowest call instead of the sum. With tasks of T, it returns an array of results.

For exceptions: if any task fails, the WhenAll task faults. When I await it, only the first exception is thrown, which surprises people. All the exceptions are still available in the WhenAll task's Exception property, an AggregateException, and each individual task has its own status and exception. So if I need to know about every failure, I keep a reference to the WhenAll task and inspect it, or check each task.
Also, WhenAll doesn't cancel the other tasks when one fails; they keep running. If I want that, I pass a shared CancellationTokenSource and cancel it on the first failure.

Task.WhenAny completes as soon as any one task completes, and returns that task. It's useful for timeouts, racing a task against Task.Delay, or processing results as they arrive. It doesn't throw if the winning task failed; I await the returned task to observe its result or exception. Since .NET 6, WaitAsync with a timeout is a cleaner way to add a timeout.

p17-116.q: If I have, say, 5,000 items and each needs an API call, starting them all at once with Task.WhenAll would open thousands of connections, overload the downstream service, hit rate limits, and maybe run out of sockets. So I limit how many run at the same time.
p17-116.k: throttle async calls, parallel foreachasync, limit concurrent tasks, semaphoreslim throttling, max degree of parallelism async
x: If I have, say, 5,000 items and each needs an API call, starting them all at once with Task.WhenAll would open thousands of connections, overload the downstream service, hit rate limits, and maybe run out of sockets. So I limit how many run at the same time.

The cleanest option in modern .NET is Parallel.ForEachAsync, available since .NET 6. I pass the items, ParallelOptions with MaxDegreeOfParallelism, like 10, and a CancellationToken, and an async lambda for each item. It processes at most 10 at once and starts the next as soon as one finishes.

Before that, the common pattern was a SemaphoreSlim with a count of 10: each task awaits WaitAsync before the call and releases in a finally block, and then Task.WhenAll over all the tasks. It works well, but all tasks are created up front.
For producer-consumer pipelines, I use System.Threading.Channels with a fixed number of consumer tasks reading from a bounded channel, or TPL Dataflow blocks with a bounded capacity.
The right limit depends on the downstream: its rate limits, the connection pool size, and database capacity. I make it configurable and measure.
Combined with retries and backoff, this keeps batch jobs fast without hurting the services they call.

p17-117.q: IAsyncDisposable is the asynchronous version of IDisposable. It has one method, DisposeAsync, which returns a ValueTask. It exists because some cleanup naturally involves I/O, like flushing a buffered stream to disk, closing a network connection gracefully, or committing and closing a database connection. With the synchronous Dispose, that I/O would block a thread, which hurts scalability and can even cause deadlocks.
p17-117.k: iasyncdisposable, await using, disposeasync, async dispose, async cleanup c#
x: IAsyncDisposable is the asynchronous version of IDisposable. It has one method, DisposeAsync, which returns a ValueTask. It exists because some cleanup naturally involves I/O, like flushing a buffered stream to disk, closing a network connection gracefully, or committing and closing a database connection. With the synchronous Dispose, that I/O would block a thread, which hurts scalability and can even cause deadlocks.

To use it, I write await using, either as a block or as a declaration, like await using var connection equals new SqlConnection. The object is disposed asynchronously at the end of the scope, even if an exception is thrown.

Many framework types implement it: streams, SqlConnection, DbContext, Utf8JsonWriter, and the DI container's scopes. ASP.NET Core's DI disposes scoped services asynchronously at the end of the request if they implement it.

When I write my own class that holds async resources, I implement IAsyncDisposable, and usually IDisposable too, so it works for callers who can't use async. The recommended pattern has a protected virtual DisposeAsyncCore method, so derived classes can add their own cleanup.
One gotcha: if a service only implements IAsyncDisposable and someone disposes the DI scope synchronously, .NET throws an exception, so I use CreateAsyncScope in background workers.

p17-118.q: A finalizer, written with the tilde syntax like a destructor, is a method the garbage collector calls before reclaiming an object's memory. Dispose is a method that my code calls explicitly, usually through using, to release resources at a known time.
p17-118.k: finalizer, destructor c#, dispose pattern, gc.suppressfinalize, safehandle, unmanaged resources
x: A finalizer, written with the tilde syntax like a destructor, is a method the garbage collector calls before reclaiming an object's memory. Dispose is a method that my code calls explicitly, usually through using, to release resources at a known time.

The key difference is timing and reliability. Dispose runs immediately and deterministically. A finalizer runs at some unknown later time, on the finalizer thread, after the GC notices the object is unreachable, and may not run at all if the process exits abruptly.

Finalizers are also costly. Objects with finalizers survive at least one extra GC, because they go to the finalization queue first, which promotes them to an older generation and increases memory pressure.

So the classic dispose pattern was: Dispose releases resources and calls GC.SuppressFinalize, so the finalizer doesn't run; the finalizer is only a safety net for unmanaged resources if someone forgot to dispose.

In modern .NET, I almost never write a finalizer. Unmanaged handles should be wrapped in a SafeHandle, which has its own reliable finalization, and my class just implements IDisposable and disposes the SafeHandle. For classes that only hold managed disposables, like a DbContext or HttpClient, I implement Dispose without any finalizer.

p17-119.q: The Large Object Heap is a separate area of the managed heap for objects of 85,000 bytes or more, like big arrays, large strings or big byte buffers. It's treated differently because copying large objects is expensive. LOH objects are collected only with generation 2, the most expensive collection, and by default they aren't compacted, so the heap can become fragmented, with free gaps that are too small for new large objects.
p17-119.k: large object heap, loh, arraypool, memory pooling, loh fragmentation, recyclablememorystream
x: The Large Object Heap is a separate area of the managed heap for objects of 85,000 bytes or more, like big arrays, large strings or big byte buffers. It's treated differently because copying large objects is expensive. LOH objects are collected only with generation 2, the most expensive collection, and by default they aren't compacted, so the heap can become fragmented, with free gaps that are too small for new large objects.

So if a service allocates big buffers frequently, for example reading every uploaded file into a new byte array, or building large JSON strings, it triggers frequent gen 2 collections, longer pauses, and growing memory.

Pooling reuses large buffers instead of allocating new ones. ArrayPool of T, usually ArrayPool of byte dot Shared, lets me rent an array of at least the size I need and return it when I'm done, in a finally block. The same buffers are used again and again, so garbage is greatly reduced. I must remember the rented array can be larger than requested, and I mustn't use it after returning it.
Related tools: RecyclableMemoryStream from Microsoft for pooled memory streams, ObjectPool for expensive objects, and streaming APIs, so I never need the whole payload in memory in the first place.
I confirm the problem first with dotnet-counters, watching gen 2 collections and LOH size.

p17-120.q: Both are special kinds of structs aimed at correctness and performance.
p17-120.k: readonly struct, ref struct, span ref struct, stackonly struct, defensive copy, struct performance
x: Both are special kinds of structs aimed at correctness and performance.

A readonly struct declares that all its fields are readonly, so the struct is immutable. Besides making the intent clear, it helps performance. When you call a method on a struct through a readonly reference, like an in parameter or a readonly field, the compiler normally makes a defensive copy, because it can't be sure the method won't modify the struct. With a readonly struct, it knows nothing can change, so it skips those copies. I use readonly structs for small value types, like a Money or Coordinates type.

A ref struct is a struct that must live only on the stack. It can't be boxed, can't be a field of a class or a normal struct, couldn't traditionally be used as a generic type argument, can't be captured in lambdas, and historically couldn't be used across await in async methods. Span of T is the famous example. These rules make it safe for Span to point at stack memory or slices of arrays, because it can never outlive the memory it points to.

C# 13 relaxed some rules: ref structs can implement interfaces and be used as generic arguments with the allows ref struct constraint, and can be used in async methods and iterators, as long as they don't cross an await or yield.

p17-121.q: Variance describes whether a generic type can be used with more specific or more general type arguments than declared.
p17-121.k: covariance contravariance, in and out generic, variance c#, ienumerable covariance, func contravariance
x: Variance describes whether a generic type can be used with more specific or more general type arguments than declared.

Covariance, marked with the out keyword, lets me use a more derived type where a base type is expected, for types that only produce values. IEnumerable of T is covariant, so an IEnumerable of string can be assigned to an IEnumerable of object. That's safe, because I can only read from it, and every string is an object.

Contravariance, marked with the in keyword, goes the other way, for types that only consume values. Action of T and IComparer of T are contravariant, so an Action of object can be used where an Action of string is needed. That's safe, because a method that accepts any object can certainly accept a string.
Func of T result is both: contravariant in its input parameters and covariant in its return type.
List of T is invariant, so a List of string can't be assigned to a List of object. If that were allowed, I could add an integer through the object list into what is really a list of strings.
Arrays are covariant for historical reasons, which isn't type-safe: putting the wrong type into a covariant array compiles but throws ArrayTypeMismatchException at runtime.
Variance only applies to interfaces and delegates, and only to reference types.

p17-122.q: Source generators are compiler plug-ins that run during the build. They inspect my code, like classes marked with a certain attribute, and generate additional C# code that's compiled together with it.
p17-122.k: source generators, roslyn source generator, reflection vs source generator, compile time code generation, aot friendly
x: Source generators are compiler plug-ins that run during the build. They inspect my code, like classes marked with a certain attribute, and generate additional C# code that's compiled together with it.

The main reason to use them instead of reflection is that the work moves from runtime to compile time. Reflection discovers types and members while the app is running, which costs startup time and CPU, allocates memory, and is a problem for Native AOT and trimming, because the trimmer can't see which members are used through reflection and may remove them. Generated code is just normal code: fast, visible, debuggable, and trimming-safe.

.NET itself uses them a lot. System.Text.Json source generation creates serialisation code for my types, which speeds up startup and supports AOT. GeneratedRegex compiles regular expressions at build time. LoggerMessage generates high-performance logging methods. And the Configuration binder and minimal API request delegates have generators for AOT.
Popular libraries use them too, like Mapperly for object mapping, which generates mapping code instead of reflection-based AutoMapper.
Writing my own generator is more advanced. Today, I'd use the incremental generator API for performance, and I'd only do it for real repetitive boilerplate across a codebase.
In our newer services, I use LoggerMessage and GeneratedRegex.

p17-123.q: An expression tree represents code as data. When a lambda is assigned to an Expression of Func type, instead of compiling it to executable code, the compiler builds an object tree describing it: a parameter, a member access, a comparison, a constant, and so on. Other code can then inspect that tree and translate it into something else.
p17-123.k: expression trees, expression of func, linq expression, iqueryable expression tree, build dynamic query
x: An expression tree represents code as data. When a lambda is assigned to an Expression of Func type, instead of compiling it to executable code, the compiler builds an object tree describing it: a parameter, a member access, a comparison, a constant, and so on. Other code can then inspect that tree and translate it into something else.

That's exactly how LINQ providers work. When I write a Where clause on an EF Core IQueryable, the lambda becomes an expression tree, and EF Core walks the tree and translates it into SQL. With a plain IEnumerable, the same lambda is a compiled delegate and runs in memory. That's why some C# methods can't be used inside EF queries: the provider doesn't know how to translate them.

Other uses: building dynamic queries at runtime, like combining filters chosen by the user on a search screen, using Expression.AndAlso or a library like LinqKit's PredicateBuilder. Strongly typed property selectors, like in FluentValidation's RuleFor, or Moq's Setup, which read the property name from the expression. And generating fast code at runtime by compiling an expression into a delegate, which was a common way to avoid slow reflection.
Compiling expressions is relatively expensive, so compiled delegates should be cached.

p17-124.q: A static class can't be instantiated; all its members are static. It's fine for stateless helpers, like extension methods, simple calculations or constants.
p17-124.k: static class vs singleton, singleton pattern c#, thread safe singleton, static vs singleton di, lazy singleton
x: A static class can't be instantiated; all its members are static. It's fine for stateless helpers, like extension methods, simple calculations or constants.

A singleton is a normal class with exactly one instance. The classic implementation has a private constructor and a static Instance property, made thread-safe with Lazy of T or a static readonly field.

The singleton has real advantages over a static class. It can implement interfaces and be passed around as a dependency, so it can be mocked in tests. It can hold state that's initialised lazily. And it can inherit from a base class.

But in modern .NET, I almost never write the classic singleton pattern. Instead, I register a normal class in the DI container with AddSingleton. The container ensures there's one instance, while my class stays a plain, testable class with constructor injection, and consumers depend on an interface, not on a static Instance property.
Static classes and classic singletons both share a problem: they're global state, hidden dependencies that make testing and reasoning harder.

My rule: static for pure, stateless functions; DI singletons for shared services, like a cache, a configuration provider or an HttpClient wrapper. And any singleton must be thread-safe, because many requests use it at once.

p17-125.q: float and double are binary floating-point types: float is 32-bit with about 7 significant digits, and double is 64-bit with about 15 to 17. They're very fast, because CPUs support them in hardware, and they have a huge range. But they store numbers in base 2, so many decimal fractions, like 0.1, can't be represented exactly. That's why 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 in double, and small errors build up in repeated calculations.
p17-125.k: decimal vs double, money in c#, floating point precision, double rounding error, float vs double vs decimal
x: float and double are binary floating-point types: float is 32-bit with about 7 significant digits, and double is 64-bit with about 15 to 17. They're very fast, because CPUs support them in hardware, and they have a huge range. But they store numbers in base 2, so many decimal fractions, like 0.1, can't be represented exactly. That's why 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 in double, and small errors build up in repeated calculations.

decimal is a 128-bit decimal floating-point type, with 28 to 29 significant digits, which stores numbers in base 10. So 0.1 is exact. It's slower and has a smaller range, but it's precise for decimal values.

So for money, prices, quantities with fixed decimal places, and anything where exact decimal results and rounding matter, I use decimal. For scientific calculations, measurements, graphics or statistics, where tiny errors are acceptable and speed matters, double.

A few related points. Never compare doubles with double-equals; use a tolerance. Use Math.Round with an explicit MidpointRounding mode, because the default is banker's rounding. And in SQL Server, use decimal with a fixed precision and scale, not float, for money columns, and make sure EF Core maps the precision explicitly.

p17-126.q: DateTime stores a date and time, with a Kind property that says whether it's UTC, local or unspecified. The problem is that Kind is easily lost, for example when reading from a database or JSON, so you get an unspecified value and nobody knows which time zone it was in. DateTime.Now on a server is especially risky, because it depends on the server's time zone.

DateTimeOffset stores a date and time plus an offset from UTC, like plus 5:30. So it represents an exact instant unambiguously, and it's what I use for timestamps: when something happened, created and modified dates, and API values. SQL Server has a matching datetimeoffset type.

DateOnly and TimeOnly, added in .NET 6, represent just a calendar date or just a time of day. They're right for things like a date of birth, a visit date or a store opening time, where a time or time zone makes no sense. Storing a birth date as a midnight DateTime can shift it by a day when time zones are converted.

Note that an offset isn't a time zone. Plus 5:30 doesn't tell you about daylight saving rules. For future local times, like "every day at 9 AM in New York", I store the IANA time zone id and convert with TimeZoneInfo.
And I use TimeProvider instead of calling the clock directly, so tests can control time.

p17-127.q: They all prevent changes, but in different ways.
p17-127.k: immutable collections, readonly collection vs immutable, frozendictionary, frozenset, ireadonlylist, collections c# 8
x: They all prevent changes, but in different ways.

A read-only collection, like ReadOnlyCollection or IReadOnlyList, is a read-only view over another collection. My code can't modify it through that view, but whoever owns the underlying List can still change it, and I'll see the changes. It's about API design: exposing a collection without letting callers modify it.

Immutable collections, from System.Collections.Immutable, like ImmutableList and ImmutableDictionary, can never change. Methods like Add return a new collection, sharing most of the structure with the old one, so it's efficient. They're great for thread-safety, because readers never need locks, and for snapshot semantics, like a configuration state that's swapped atomically. Lookups are slower than in a normal List or Dictionary, though, because they're tree-based.

Frozen collections, FrozenDictionary and FrozenSet, came in .NET 8. They're also immutable, but they're optimised for read speed instead of updates. Creating one is relatively expensive, because it analyses the data to build the fastest possible lookup, but after that, lookups are faster than a normal Dictionary.

So I use IReadOnlyList for exposing data from methods, immutable collections for shared state that changes occasionally, and frozen collections for data built once at startup and read constantly, like lookup tables or permission maps.

p17-128.q: Since C# 8, interfaces can provide a default implementation for a member. Classes that implement the interface get that behaviour automatically, unless they provide their own.
p17-128.k: default interface methods, default implementation interface, interface with method body, c# 8 interface
x: Since C# 8, interfaces can provide a default implementation for a member. Classes that implement the interface get that behaviour automatically, unless they provide their own.

The main reason this was added is evolving an interface without breaking existing implementations. Before, adding a new method to a published interface broke every class that implemented it, which is a real problem for libraries with many consumers. Now the library can add the method with a default body, and old implementations keep compiling.

It also allows some trait-like reuse, where small bits of shared behaviour are defined in terms of other interface members. For example, an ILogger-like interface could have a default LogError method that calls the core Log method with an error level.

There are some rules worth knowing. The default member is only accessible through the interface type, not through the class variable, unless the class implements it. Interfaces still can't have instance fields, so they can't hold state. And it can lead to diamond-inheritance ambiguities if two interfaces provide the same default, which must be resolved in the class.
I use them sparingly: mostly for API evolution in shared libraries. For sharing actual behaviour and state, an abstract base class or composition is usually clearer.

It's also a nice example of how C# keeps adding features that remove the need for reflection or code duplication.

p17-130.q: Native AOT, ahead-of-time compilation, compiles a .NET application directly to native machine code at publish time, instead of shipping IL that the JIT compiles at runtime. The result is a self-contained executable that doesn't need the .NET runtime installed.
p17-130.k: native aot, ahead of time compilation, trimming, publish aot, startup time .net, aot limitations
x: Native AOT, ahead-of-time compilation, compiles a .NET application directly to native machine code at publish time, instead of shipping IL that the JIT compiles at runtime. The result is a self-contained executable that doesn't need the .NET runtime installed.

The benefits are very fast startup, often a few tens of milliseconds, lower memory use, and smaller deployments. That's valuable for serverless functions like AWS Lambda, where cold starts matter, for containers that scale quickly, and for command-line tools.
Trimming is part of it: the publish process analyses the app and removes unused code from the framework and libraries, to reduce size.

The limitations come from the fact that everything must be known at compile time. No runtime code generation, so no Reflection.Emit, and dynamic assembly loading isn't supported. Reflection over types that the trimmer can't see may break, so libraries must be AOT-compatible. Serialisation needs source-generated System.Text.Json contexts. And not everything supports it; for example, EF Core's AOT support is still limited, and some popular libraries rely on reflection.
ASP.NET Core supports AOT for minimal APIs with the slim builder, and the compiler shows warnings for anything incompatible.
I'd use it for Lambdas and small, focused services, and stay on the normal JIT for large apps with heavy reflection-based libraries.

p17-131.q: These are about how .NET turns IL into machine code, balancing startup speed and peak performance.
p17-131.k: tiered compilation, readytorun, jit compilation, dynamic pgo, startup performance .net, r2r
x: These are about how .NET turns IL into machine code, balancing startup speed and peak performance.

The JIT compiles methods the first time they're called. Tiered compilation means it first compiles quickly with few optimisations, tier 0, so the app starts fast. Methods that are called often get recompiled in the background with full optimisations, tier 1. Long-running loops can switch to optimised code mid-execution, which is on-stack replacement.

Dynamic PGO, profile-guided optimisation, is on by default since .NET 8. While running tier 0 code, the runtime collects data about how the code is actually used, like which types are passed to an interface call, and the tier 1 compile uses that to optimise, for example devirtualising and inlining the common case. This gave many apps a noticeable free speed-up.

ReadyToRun is a publish option that pre-compiles IL to native code ahead of time, while keeping the IL. The app starts faster, because less JIT work is needed at startup, and the JIT can still re-optimise hot methods later. The files are bigger.

So for a service where startup matters, like containers that scale often or Lambdas, I'd enable ReadyToRun, or consider Native AOT. For long-running services, the defaults with tiered compilation and dynamic PGO work very well.

p17-132.q: Thread pool starvation happens when all thread pool threads are busy, usually blocked waiting, so new work, like incoming requests or async continuations, has to wait for a free thread. The thread pool adds new threads slowly, roughly one or two per second once it's above the minimum, so under load, response times explode while CPU stays low.
p17-132.k: thread pool starvation, threadpool starvation, sync over async, blocking calls async, slow requests low cpu
x: Thread pool starvation happens when all thread pool threads are busy, usually blocked waiting, so new work, like incoming requests or async continuations, has to wait for a free thread. The thread pool adds new threads slowly, roughly one or two per second once it's above the minimum, so under load, response times explode while CPU stays low.

The most common cause is sync over async: calling .Result or .Wait or GetAwaiter().GetResult on async code. The thread blocks waiting for an operation whose continuation also needs a thread pool thread, so under load, threads are all blocked waiting for each other. Other causes are long synchronous I/O, like a synchronous database or file call, Thread.Sleep, or long locks in hot paths.
The symptoms: requests get very slow or time out, the thread count keeps climbing, and CPU isn't high. Health checks may time out too, causing restarts.

To detect it, I use dotnet-counters and watch the thread pool queue length and thread count; a growing queue is the signal. A memory dump or dotnet-stack shows many threads blocked in the same place, like waiting on a Task.
The fix is to make the call chain async all the way, remove blocking calls, and use async APIs for I/O. Raising the minimum threads is only a temporary relief.

x: The best answer is to avoid it, by making the calling code async as well, all the way up. In ASP.NET Core, controllers, middleware, hosted services and even Main can be async, so there's almost always a way.
When I truly can't, for example in a legacy interface that I can't change, or a constructor, there are some options and risks.

Blocking with .Result, .Wait or GetAwaiter().GetResult works, but it blocks a thread. In apps with a synchronisation context, like classic ASP.NET on .NET Framework, WinForms or WPF, it can deadlock: the async method tries to resume on the context that's blocked waiting for it. ASP.NET Core has no synchronisation context, so it doesn't deadlock there, but blocking still wastes threads and can cause thread pool starvation under load. If I must block, GetAwaiter().GetResult is preferable to .Result, because it throws the original exception instead of an AggregateException, and in libraries, ConfigureAwait of false reduces deadlock risk.
For constructors, I avoid async work entirely. Instead I use an async factory method, like CreateAsync, or lazy async initialisation, or do the work in a hosted service at startup.
For event handlers in desktop apps, async void with try-catch is acceptable.
Our legacy .NET Framework code had a few of these deadlocks, so this is a real concern in our migration.

p17-134.q: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more operations that run concurrently, so it works most of the time and fails occasionally, which makes it hard to reproduce.
p17-134.k: race condition, race condition example, check then act, thread safety bug, concurrency bug
x: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more operations that run concurrently, so it works most of the time and fails occasionally, which makes it hard to reproduce.

A classic example is check-then-act. Two requests try to reserve the last kit at a site. Both read the stock and see one available. Both pass the check. Both reserve it. Now we've allocated two kits when only one existed. Each request was correct on its own; the problem is the interleaving.
Another example is a shared counter incremented by many threads without synchronisation, where updates are lost, or a lazy cache initialised twice.
Race conditions happen both in memory and in databases, and with multiple server instances, an in-memory lock doesn't help at all.

Fixes depend on where the shared state lives. In memory: locks, Interlocked, or concurrent collections. In the database: make the check and update one atomic operation, like UPDATE with a WHERE condition on the available quantity and checking the rows affected, use optimistic concurrency with a row version, or a unique constraint so the second insert fails. Across instances: a distributed lock, or a single queue consumer per key.
In our IRT, kit allocation uses database transactions and concurrency checks for exactly this reason.

p17-135.q: Lazy of T defers creating an object until it's first needed, and then caches it. I give it a factory function, and the first time I read its Value property, it runs the factory and stores the result. Later reads return the same instance without running the factory again.
p17-135.k: lazy of t, lazy initialization, lazy thread safety mode, lazy loading object c#, deferred initialization
x: Lazy of T defers creating an object until it's first needed, and then caches it. I give it a factory function, and the first time I read its Value property, it runs the factory and stores the result. Later reads return the same instance without running the factory again.

It's useful when an object is expensive to create, like loading a large lookup table or building a complex client, and it may not be needed in every code path, so I don't pay the cost at startup or at all if unused.

It's also thread-safe by default. With the default mode, ExecutionAndPublication, if many threads read Value at the same time, only one runs the factory, and the others wait and get the same result. That makes it a simple way to implement a thread-safe singleton or a one-time initialisation, and it's the standard trick to make ConcurrentDictionary's GetOrAdd run the factory only once.

One gotcha: if the factory throws, Lazy caches the exception by default, and every later access rethrows it. That's bad for transient failures, like a network error at startup. In that case, I use the PublicationOnly mode, or a custom approach that retries.
For async initialisation, Lazy of Task of T works, though libraries like AsyncLazy handle retry and cancellation better.

p17-136.q: Both rethrow an exception from a catch block, but they treat the stack trace differently.
p17-136.k: throw vs throw ex, rethrow exception, preserve stack trace, exceptiondispatchinfo, wrap exception
x: Both rethrow an exception from a catch block, but they treat the stack trace differently.
throw, on its own, rethrows the current exception and preserves its original stack trace, so I can still see where the error really happened, deep in the call chain.

throw ex resets the stack trace to the current location, the catch block. All information about where the exception actually originated is lost, which makes debugging production issues much harder. Code analysis tools flag it as a warning.
So inside a catch block, if I want to log something and let the exception continue, I use plain throw.

If I want to add context, I wrap it: throw new ShipmentProcessingException with a useful message and the original exception as the inner exception. Then both the new context and the original stack trace are preserved.

If I need to rethrow an exception later, outside the catch block, for example after capturing it in one thread and rethrowing on another, ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture and Throw preserve the original stack trace. That's what await does internally.
And often the best choice is not to catch at all. I only catch when I can handle the exception, add useful context, or translate it, and let global exception handling deal with the rest.

p17-137.q: Exception filters let me add a condition to a catch block using the when keyword, like catch HttpRequestException when ex.StatusCode equals NotFound. The catch block only runs if the condition is true; otherwise the exception keeps propagating as if that catch block didn't exist.
p17-137.k: exception filters, catch when, when keyword catch, filter exceptions c#, catch specific condition
x: Exception filters let me add a condition to a catch block using the when keyword, like catch HttpRequestException when ex.StatusCode equals NotFound. The catch block only runs if the condition is true; otherwise the exception keeps propagating as if that catch block didn't exist.
There are a few advantages over catching and then rethrowing inside an if statement.
The stack isn't unwound when the filter is evaluated. If the filter returns false, the exception continues with its original state intact, which makes debugging and crash dumps more useful.

The code is cleaner, especially with several catch blocks for the same exception type but different conditions, like handling a SqlException differently for a deadlock, error number 1205, versus a unique constraint violation, 2627 or 2601.

A neat trick is logging in a filter: catch Exception when LogAndReturnFalse of ex. The filter logs the exception at the point where it happened, with the full stack, and returns false, so the exception isn't actually caught and continues upwards.
Polly-style transient error checks also benefit, for example catching only specific HTTP status codes for a retry.
Filters should be quick and must not throw, because an exception inside a filter is swallowed and treated as false.

p17-138.q: Exceptions are for exceptional, unexpected situations, like a database being down, a bug, or a broken invariant. They're expensive to throw, they're invisible in method signatures, and using them for normal business outcomes, like "validation failed" or "stock not available", turns control flow into hidden jumps.
p17-138.k: result pattern, exceptions vs result, error handling without exceptions, oneof, either type, railway oriented
x: Exceptions are for exceptional, unexpected situations, like a database being down, a bug, or a broken invariant. They're expensive to throw, they're invisible in method signatures, and using them for normal business outcomes, like "validation failed" or "stock not available", turns control flow into hidden jumps.

The Result pattern makes the expected outcome explicit. A method returns a Result object that is either success with a value or failure with an error, like a code and message. The caller must handle both cases, and the signature tells you the operation can fail. It's also faster, because no exception is thrown.

In practice, I use both. Expected business failures, like a validation error, a not-found entity, a rule violation such as "site not active", or a conflict, return a Result. The API layer maps it to the right HTTP response: 400, 404, 409 or 422 with ProblemDetails. Unexpected technical failures throw exceptions, which go to the global exception handler, are logged, and become a 500.
Libraries like FluentResults, ErrorOr or OneOf help, or a small custom Result type.
The main downside is more verbose code, and teams must apply it consistently.
In our newer IRT APIs, MediatR handlers return results for business rules, and FluentValidation errors become 400 responses automatically.

p17-139.q: System.Text.Json is the built-in serialiser in modern .NET, and ASP.NET Core's default. Newtonsoft.Json, or Json.NET, is the older, very popular third-party library.
p17-139.k: system.text.json vs newtonsoft, json.net vs system text json, json serialization c#, migrate newtonsoft, jsonserializeroptions
x: System.Text.Json is the built-in serialiser in modern .NET, and ASP.NET Core's default. Newtonsoft.Json, or Json.NET, is the older, very popular third-party library.

System.Text.Json is faster and allocates less, because it works on UTF-8 bytes and spans, and it supports source generation for even better performance and Native AOT. It's secure by default and strict: case-sensitive property matching by default outside ASP.NET Core, no comments or trailing commas unless enabled, and no automatic loosely typed conversions, like a number in a string.

Newtonsoft is more feature-rich and flexible: very lenient parsing, JObject and LINQ to JSON for dynamic JSON, rich converters, reference loop handling, and many settings. A lot of older code and libraries depend on it.

System.Text.Json has caught up a lot: polymorphic serialisation with JsonDerivedType, JsonNode for dynamic documents, required properties, ReferenceHandler for cycles, and naming policies including snake case.
When migrating, the differences that bite are case sensitivity, how enums, dates and nulls are handled, private setters, and custom converters, which must be rewritten.
My approach: System.Text.Json for new code, with web defaults; Newtonsoft only where a legacy behaviour or library needs it. In our legacy .NET Framework code, Newtonsoft is still used.

p17-140.q: String comparisons can be ordinal, comparing the raw character codes, or culture-sensitive, following the linguistic rules of a culture, like how accented letters sort.
p17-140.k: string comparison ordinal, stringcomparison, culture sensitive comparison, turkish i problem, case insensitive compare c#
x: String comparisons can be ordinal, comparing the raw character codes, or culture-sensitive, following the linguistic rules of a culture, like how accented letters sort.

The problem is that some methods are culture-sensitive by default, like string.Compare, StartsWith with a string argument, and ToUpper and ToLower, so the result can change depending on the server's culture settings. The famous example is the Turkish I problem: in Turkish culture, the uppercase of "i" isn't "I", so a case-insensitive check like "file".ToUpper() equals "FILE" fails on a Turkish machine. Bugs like this appear only for certain users or servers.
Culture-sensitive comparison is also slower than ordinal.

So my rule is: for identifiers, codes, keys, file paths, URLs, HTTP headers, configuration keys and anything machine-readable, use ordinal comparison, StringComparison.Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase. For dictionary keys that should be case-insensitive, pass StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase. Only use culture-sensitive comparison for text shown to and sorted for users, with the user's culture explicitly.
I always pass the StringComparison argument explicitly, and the code analysers, CA1307 and CA1309, help enforce it.
For normalising case, I use ToUpperInvariant, not ToUpper.
In a global product with sites in many countries, like ours, this matters.

p17-141.q: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the calling code can pick one at runtime without knowing the details. It replaces big if-else or switch blocks that choose behaviour based on a type or setting.
p17-141.k: strategy pattern, strategy design pattern c#, replace switch with strategy, pluggable algorithm, strategy with dependency injection
x: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the calling code can pick one at runtime without knowing the details. It replaces big if-else or switch blocks that choose behaviour based on a type or setting.

For example, imagine calculating resupply quantities for sites, where studies use different methods: a simple min and max level, or a predictive method based on upcoming visits. Instead of one method with a growing switch statement, I define an interface, IResupplyStrategy, with a method like CalculateQuantity. Then I write MinMaxResupplyStrategy and PredictiveResupplyStrategy, each with its own logic and its own unit tests. The calling service gets the right strategy, based on the study's configuration, and just calls CalculateQuantity.
With dependency injection, I register all strategies, inject an IEnumerable of them, and pick by a key property, or use .NET 8 keyed services, resolving by the strategy name.
The benefits: each algorithm is isolated and testable, adding a new one doesn't touch existing code, which is the open-closed principle, and the choice can come from configuration.
The pluggable SFTP providers I built are also a Strategy: one interface, three provider implementations, selected by configuration.
I don't use it for two simple cases; an if statement is fine there.

p17-142.q: The Decorator pattern wraps an object with another object that implements the same interface, adding behaviour before or after delegating to the wrapped one. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a decorator. Decorators can be stacked.
p17-142.k: decorator pattern, decorator design pattern c#, scrutor decorate, add caching with decorator, cross cutting decorator
x: The Decorator pattern wraps an object with another object that implements the same interface, adding behaviour before or after delegating to the wrapped one. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a decorator. Decorators can be stacked.
It's perfect for cross-cutting concerns that I don't want inside the business class: caching, logging, retries, timing metrics or authorization checks.

For example, I have an IStudyConfigProvider that reads study configuration from the database. I write a CachedStudyConfigProvider that also implements IStudyConfigProvider, takes the real provider in its constructor, and checks the cache first, only calling the inner provider on a miss. The database class stays simple, and caching can be added, removed or tested separately.

In ASP.NET Core's built-in DI, registering decorators is a bit manual: I register the inner class, then register the interface with a factory that creates the decorator around it. The Scrutor library makes it one line with services.Decorate.

The framework uses the pattern a lot too: DelegatingHandler for HttpClient is a decorator chain, where each handler adds behaviour like logging or auth headers. MediatR pipeline behaviours work the same way around handlers. And Stream wrappers, like BufferedStream or GZipStream, are decorators.

p17-143.q: A factory is an object or method whose job is creating other objects, so the calling code doesn't need to know which concrete class to create or how to build it.
p17-143.k: factory pattern, factory method, abstract factory, factory with dependency injection, func factory c#
x: A factory is an object or method whose job is creating other objects, so the calling code doesn't need to know which concrete class to create or how to build it.

The Factory Method lets a method decide which class to instantiate, often based on input, like a NotificationSenderFactory that returns an EmailSender or SmsSender based on the channel. The Abstract Factory creates families of related objects that belong together.

With dependency injection, most object creation is handled by the container, so I need fewer factories. But I still use them when: the concrete type depends on runtime data, like the study's configuration or a user's choice, which the container can't know at startup; the object needs both injected services and runtime parameters, like a file processor that needs a logger and a file path; or creation is complex and needs validation.

In .NET, the factory itself is registered in DI and gets its dependencies injected. It can use IServiceProvider internally, carefully, or ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance, which builds an object using DI for services plus the runtime parameters I pass. Keyed services in .NET 8 often replace simple factories that choose by name. IHttpClientFactory and IDbContextFactory are framework examples.
I avoid factories that just wrap new for no reason.

p17-144.q: The Builder pattern constructs a complex object step by step, usually with a fluent interface, and produces the final object at the end with a Build method. It's useful when an object has many optional parts, or when the construction steps need validation, so a constructor with ten parameters would be confusing and error-prone.
p17-144.k: builder pattern, builder design pattern c#, fluent builder, test data builder, step by step object creation
x: The Builder pattern constructs a complex object step by step, usually with a fluent interface, and produces the final object at the end with a Build method. It's useful when an object has many optional parts, or when the construction steps need validation, so a constructor with ten parameters would be confusing and error-prone.

ASP.NET Core itself is full of builders: WebApplication.CreateBuilder configures services, configuration and logging, and then Build gives the app. The configuration builder, the host builder, and EF Core's ModelBuilder are builders too. StringBuilder is a simple builder for strings.

In my own code, I use builders a lot for test data. A ShipmentBuilder has sensible defaults for every field, and methods like WithStatus, WithSite or WithKits. So a test only states what matters to it: new ShipmentBuilder().WithStatus(Delivered).Build(). Tests become shorter and clearer, and when the Shipment class gets a new required field, I only update the builder, not hundreds of tests.
Another use is building complex queries or requests, like a report filter or an email message with optional attachments and recipients, where Build validates that required parts are present.
For simple objects, object initialisers with required and init properties are enough, and I don't add a builder.

p17-145.q: The Observer pattern lets one object, the subject, notify many other objects, the observers, when something changes, without knowing who they are. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe, and the subject just raises a notification. It keeps them loosely coupled.
p17-145.k: observer pattern, observer design pattern c#, events c#, publish subscribe in process, iobservable
x: The Observer pattern lets one object, the subject, notify many other objects, the observers, when something changes, without knowing who they are. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe, and the subject just raises a notification. It keeps them loosely coupled.

In C#, events are the built-in implementation. A class declares an event, like ShipmentStatusChanged; other objects subscribe with plus-equals and a handler; and the class raises the event, which calls every subscriber. IObservable and IObserver are the more formal interfaces, and Rx.NET builds a powerful reactive library on them, and RxJS in Angular follows the same idea.

A big gotcha with events is memory leaks: the subject holds references to the subscribers' handlers, so a long-lived subject, like a singleton, keeps short-lived subscribers alive if they never unsubscribe. So I always unsubscribe, typically in Dispose.
Exceptions are another issue: if one handler throws, the following handlers aren't called.

In modern web back ends, I rarely use C# events for business logic. Inside a service, I use domain events with MediatR notifications, which work well with DI and scoped services. Across services, the same idea becomes publish-subscribe messaging through RabbitMQ or Kafka.

p17-146.q: The Adapter pattern makes a class with an incompatible interface usable where a different interface is expected, by wrapping it in an adapter that translates the calls. It's like a travel plug adapter.
p17-146.k: adapter pattern, adapter design pattern, wrapper class, wrap third party library, interface adapter c#
x: The Adapter pattern makes a class with an incompatible interface usable where a different interface is expected, by wrapping it in an adapter that translates the calls. It's like a travel plug adapter.

I use it mostly to isolate third-party libraries and external systems. For example, our SFTP integration needed to support three different SFTP libraries, and each has its own classes, method names, exceptions and connection handling. I defined our own simple interface, ISftpClient, with the operations we need, like Connect, Upload, Download and List. Then I wrote one adapter per library, each implementing ISftpClient and translating calls and exceptions to our own types. The rest of the code only knows ISftpClient.

The benefits: business code is independent of the library, so switching or upgrading the library touches only the adapter; it's easy to mock our own small interface in unit tests; and library-specific exceptions are translated into our own, so callers handle errors consistently.
The same idea applies to the anti-corruption layer for legacy systems, which is basically an adapter at the service boundary.
The Adapter differs from the Decorator, which keeps the same interface and adds behaviour, and from the Facade, which simplifies a complex subsystem behind one easier interface.

p17-147.q: In the Chain of Responsibility pattern, a request passes through a chain of handlers. Each handler decides whether to process it, pass it on to the next, or stop the chain. The sender doesn't know which handler will deal with it.
p17-147.k: chain of responsibility, chain of responsibility pattern, pipeline pattern, middleware chain, handler chain c#
x: In the Chain of Responsibility pattern, a request passes through a chain of handlers. Each handler decides whether to process it, pass it on to the next, or stop the chain. The sender doesn't know which handler will deal with it.

ASP.NET Core's middleware pipeline is the best-known example. Each middleware gets the HttpContext and a next delegate; it can do work before calling next, after it, or short-circuit, like the authentication middleware returning 401 without calling the rest. HttpClient's DelegatingHandlers and MediatR pipeline behaviours are the same idea.

I've used it for validation and rule checks. For example, before allowing a subject to be randomised, a series of checks must pass: is the site active, is consent recorded, is the subject eligible, is there drug stock. Each check is a small class implementing a common interface. The chain runs them in order, and stops with a clear message at the first failure. Adding a new rule means adding a class and registering it, without touching the others, and each rule is unit-tested alone.
The risks are that the order of handlers matters and must be explicit, and that it can be hard to see which handler did what, so I log the outcome of each step.

p17-148.q: The Specification pattern puts a business rule or query criteria into its own small, named, reusable object. Instead of repeating the same Where conditions in many places, I create a class like ActiveSitesInCountrySpecification, which encapsulates the condition, and use it wherever I need that filter.
p17-148.k: specification pattern, specification pattern ef core, reusable query filters, ardalis specification, business rule objects
x: The Specification pattern puts a business rule or query criteria into its own small, named, reusable object. Instead of repeating the same Where conditions in many places, I create a class like ActiveSitesInCountrySpecification, which encapsulates the condition, and use it wherever I need that filter.

A specification usually exposes an expression, like Expression of Func of Site, bool, so it can be used both with EF Core, which translates it to SQL, and in memory, to check a single object. Specifications can be combined with And, Or and Not, building complex rules from simple named ones.

With repositories, it keeps the repository small. Instead of a method for every query combination, like GetActiveSitesByCountryWithDepots, the repository has one method that takes a specification. The Ardalis.Specification library also lets specifications include related data, ordering and paging.
The benefits: business rules have names that the business understands, the logic lives in one place, and each specification is easy to unit test.

The downside is more classes and abstraction. With EF Core, many teams simply use extension methods on IQueryable, like query.ActiveOnly().InCountry(code), which give most of the benefit with less ceremony. That's often what I do, and I use full specifications when the rules are complex and reused heavily.

p17-149.q: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, with a fixed sequence of steps, and lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall flow.
p17-149.k: template method pattern, template method design pattern, abstract base class steps, hook methods, skeleton algorithm
x: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, with a fixed sequence of steps, and lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall flow.

For example, every file import follows the same process: open the file, validate the header, read each row, validate the row, transform it, save in batches, and write a summary. A base class, ImportJobBase, implements the Run method with that sequence, and declares abstract or virtual methods for the parts that differ, like ValidateRow and MapRow. A KitImportJob and a SiteImportJob only implement those parts. The common logic, like batching, error collection, logging and progress reporting, is written once, so every import behaves consistently.
Hook methods are optional steps with a default empty implementation, like OnCompleted, which subclasses can override if they need to.

The downside is that it relies on inheritance, which creates tight coupling between the base and derived classes, and deep hierarchies get hard to follow. So in modern code, I often prefer composition: one ImportRunner class that takes an IRowHandler strategy for the varying parts. It gives the same consistent flow, but the parts are swappable and easier to test.
BackgroundService in .NET is a small template method example: StartAsync is fixed, and you override ExecuteAsync.

p17-150.q: Clean architecture organises code in layers, with the business rules at the centre and technical details on the outside. The core idea is the dependency rule: source code dependencies only point inward. The inner layers know nothing about the outer ones.
p17-150.k: clean architecture, onion architecture, dependency rule, domain application infrastructure layers, hexagonal architecture
x: Clean architecture organises code in layers, with the business rules at the centre and technical details on the outside. The core idea is the dependency rule: source code dependencies only point inward. The inner layers know nothing about the outer ones.

In a typical .NET solution there are four projects. Domain is at the centre: entities, value objects, domain events and business rules, with no dependencies on frameworks or databases. Application contains use cases, like commands and queries with their handlers, and defines interfaces it needs, like IShipmentRepository or IEmailSender. It depends only on Domain. Infrastructure implements those interfaces with real technology: EF Core, SQL Server, RabbitMQ, SMTP, external APIs. And the API layer, the presentation, contains controllers or minimal API endpoints, and wires everything together with dependency injection.

Because Application defines the interfaces and Infrastructure implements them, the business logic doesn't depend on the database or frameworks. That's dependency inversion. So business rules are easy to unit test, and technical details can be changed with less impact.
The costs are more projects, more mapping and some ceremony, which is overkill for simple CRUD services.
Our newer IRT APIs follow this structure, with MediatR handlers in the Application layer and EF Core in Infrastructure.

p17-151.q: Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature instead of by technical layer. Each feature, or use case, like CreateShipment or GetSiteInventory, gets its own folder or file containing everything it needs: the request, the validation, the handler with its data access, and the response. Slices are independent of each other.
p17-151.k: vertical slice architecture, feature folders, vertical slices vs layers, organize by feature, minimal api vertical slice
x: Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature instead of by technical layer. Each feature, or use case, like CreateShipment or GetSiteInventory, gets its own folder or file containing everything it needs: the request, the validation, the handler with its data access, and the response. Slices are independent of each other.

In a layered structure, adding one feature means touching a controller, a service, a repository, DTOs and mappings across several projects. With vertical slices, a change is usually contained in one place, so it's easier to find, understand and delete code. Each slice can also choose the simplest approach it needs: one might use EF Core with projections, another raw SQL with Dapper, without forcing every feature through the same abstraction layers.

Compared with clean architecture, which focuses on the direction of dependencies between layers, vertical slices focus on cohesion around features. They aren't really opposites: many teams combine them, keeping a shared domain model and infrastructure, but organising the application layer by feature, often with MediatR handlers.
The risk with vertical slices is duplication between slices, and shared logic leaking in random ways, so I extract shared domain rules into the domain model when I notice repetition.
For CRUD-heavy services with many independent features, I like slices. For complex domains, I add a richer domain layer.

p17-152.q: DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself, means each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code, so a change doesn't need to be made in many places. KISS, Keep It Simple, means choosing the simplest solution that works, because simple code is easier to understand, test and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, means not building features or abstractions for imagined future needs.
p17-152.k: dry kiss yagni, dont repeat yourself, keep it simple, you aint gonna need it, wrong abstraction, design principles
x: DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself, means each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code, so a change doesn't need to be made in many places. KISS, Keep It Simple, means choosing the simplest solution that works, because simple code is easier to understand, test and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, means not building features or abstractions for imagined future needs.

DRY can go wrong when it's applied to code that only looks similar, but represents different business concepts. If I merge them into one shared method or base class, they're now coupled. When one changes for its own reasons, the shared code gets parameters and flags for each caller, and becomes harder to understand than the duplication was. That's the wrong abstraction. A common rule of thumb is the rule of three: tolerate duplication twice, and abstract when the third case shows the real pattern.
Across microservices, DRY is even riskier: sharing business code between services couples their deployments, so a little duplication is often better.

YAGNI and KISS work together: no generic plugin framework for one use case, no repository over a repository. I'd rather keep code simple and refactor when a real need appears, supported by good tests.

p17-153.q: I use BenchmarkDotNet, because accurate micro-benchmarking is surprisingly hard to do by hand with a Stopwatch. The JIT needs warm-up, tiered compilation changes the code over time, the GC can pause in the middle, and the compiler can optimise away code whose result isn't used. BenchmarkDotNet handles all of that: it runs warm-up iterations, many measured iterations, separate processes, and gives statistics like the mean, error and standard deviation.
p17-153.k: benchmarkdotnet, benchmark c#, micro benchmark, measure performance c#, memorydiagnoser
x: I use BenchmarkDotNet, because accurate micro-benchmarking is surprisingly hard to do by hand with a Stopwatch. The JIT needs warm-up, tiered compilation changes the code over time, the GC can pause in the middle, and the compiler can optimise away code whose result isn't used. BenchmarkDotNet handles all of that: it runs warm-up iterations, many measured iterations, separate processes, and gives statistics like the mean, error and standard deviation.

I write a class with methods marked Benchmark, for example comparing two ways of parsing a file line, set one as the Baseline, add MemoryDiagnoser to see allocations per operation, and use Params to test different input sizes. Then I run it in Release mode, never Debug, with BenchmarkRunner.
The results show time and allocated bytes per operation, and the ratio to the baseline. Allocations matter as much as time in a server app, because they drive GC pressure.

Some good practices: benchmark realistic data, return or consume results so code isn't eliminated, and remember that a micro-benchmark only tells you about that small piece. Before optimising, I first profile the real application, with dotnet-trace or a profiler, to find the actual hot spot, then use benchmarks to compare fixes.
I also keep important benchmarks in the repo to catch regressions.

p17-154.q: These are the .NET diagnostic command-line tools, and they work on Windows, Linux and in containers.
p17-154.k: dotnet counters, dotnet trace, dotnet dump, dotnet gcdump, diagnose production dotnet, diagnostic tools
