dotnet-counters is my first step. It shows live performance counters for a running process: CPU, working set, GC heap size and collection counts per generation, allocation rate, thread pool thread count and queue length, exception count, and ASP.NET Core request rates. It quickly tells me what kind of problem I have, like a memory leak, GC pressure or thread pool starvation, without stopping the app.

dotnet-trace collects a detailed trace, like CPU sampling, over a period of time. I open it in Visual Studio, PerfView or speedscope to see which methods use the most CPU. It's for "the service is slow and CPU is high".

dotnet-dump captures a full memory dump of the process, and can analyse it with commands like dumpheap stat, to see which object types use the most memory, and gcroot, to see what keeps an object alive. It's for memory leaks and hangs, and clrstack shows what every thread is doing, which helps with deadlocks and blocked threads.
dotnet-gcdump is a lighter heap snapshot, good for comparing two snapshots to find growth.
In containers, I either include the tools in a debug image, or attach a sidecar, sharing the diagnostics socket. Dumps contain data, so they're handled securely.

p17-155.q: In modern .NET, AssemblyLoadContext is the way to load plugin assemblies at runtime, replacing AppDomains from .NET Framework.
p17-155.k: plugin architecture, assemblyloadcontext, load assembly dynamically, plugin loading .net, isolated plugin dependencies
x: In modern .NET, AssemblyLoadContext is the way to load plugin assemblies at runtime, replacing AppDomains from .NET Framework.

The structure is: a shared contracts assembly defines the plugin interface, like IDataTransferJob, referenced by both the host and the plugins. Each plugin is built as a separate assembly with its own dependencies. At startup, the host scans a plugins folder, creates a custom AssemblyLoadContext for each plugin, loads its main assembly, finds types that implement the interface, and creates them, often with ActivatorUtilities so they get DI services.

The custom load context uses AssemblyDependencyResolver, which reads the plugin's deps.json, so each plugin can use its own versions of dependencies without conflicting with the host or other plugins. The shared contracts assembly must be loaded from the host's context, otherwise the types won't match and casting to the interface fails, which is the most common plugin bug.
Load contexts can be collectible, so a plugin can be unloaded, but only if no references to it remain.
A simpler alternative, when plugins are known at build time, is to reference them as packages and register them with DI, selected by configuration. That's often enough.
Our newer data transfer APIs run integration jobs as plugins, so new vendor integrations can be added without changing the host.

p17-156.q: .NET Aspire is a set of tools and libraries for building and running distributed, cloud-ready applications, especially for the local development experience.
p17-156.k: dotnet aspire, aspire app host, aspire dashboard, aspire service defaults, local orchestration .net
x: .NET Aspire is a set of tools and libraries for building and running distributed, cloud-ready applications, especially for the local development experience.

The App Host is a small C# project where I describe the application's parts in code: the API projects, a front end, and resources like SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ or PostgreSQL. When I run it, Aspire starts everything, runs the infrastructure in containers, and wires up connection strings and service discovery automatically. So a new developer can clone the repo and press F5, instead of following a long setup document.
The Aspire dashboard shows all services, their logs, traces and metrics in one place, using OpenTelemetry, so I can follow a request across services locally.
Service defaults is a shared project that adds OpenTelemetry, health checks, service discovery and HTTP resilience to every service with one call, so they're consistent.
Integrations are NuGet packages for common services, like Redis or Azure Service Bus, which register clients with health checks and telemetry built in.
For deployment, Aspire can generate manifests and deploy to Azure Container Apps or Kubernetes, though teams often keep their own pipelines.
I see it as very useful for local development and consistency, even if production deployment uses Terraform or existing pipelines.

p17-157.q: Knowing this helps me pick the right collection.
p17-157.k: big o collections, collection complexity, list vs dictionary vs linkedlist, sorteddictionary complexity, choose collection c#
x: Knowing this helps me pick the right collection.

List of T is a dynamic array. Index access is O(1). Add at the end is O(1) on average, with occasional resizing. Insert or remove in the middle is O(n), because elements shift. Contains or IndexOf is O(n), because it scans. Sort is O(n log n).
Dictionary and HashSet are hash tables, with O(1) average for add, remove and lookup by key, and no ordering.

SortedDictionary is a balanced tree, with O(log n) for add, remove and lookup, keeping keys sorted. SortedList is an array-backed sorted collection with O(log n) lookup by binary search, but O(n) inserts; it uses less memory.
LinkedList has O(1) insert and remove when you already have the node, but O(n) to find anything, and poor cache locality, so it's rarely the best choice in practice.
Queue and Stack are O(1) for enqueue, dequeue, push and pop.
PriorityQueue, added in .NET 6, is a heap: O(log n) to enqueue and dequeue the item with the smallest priority, and O(1) to peek.
In practice, the biggest real-world win is usually replacing repeated List.Contains or First lookups inside loops with a Dictionary or HashSet built once, turning O(n squared) into O(n).

p17-158.q: An async method that awaits I/O, like a database query or an HTTP call, doesn't use a thread while waiting. The thread goes back to the pool, and when the I/O completes, a thread picks up the continuation. That's what makes servers scalable.
p17-158.k: task.run vs async, when to use task.run, task.run in asp.net core, cpu bound vs io bound, offload work thread pool
x: An async method that awaits I/O, like a database query or an HTTP call, doesn't use a thread while waiting. The thread goes back to the pool, and when the I/O completes, a thread picks up the continuation. That's what makes servers scalable.

Task.Run queues a delegate to run on a thread pool thread. It's for CPU-bound work: it moves the work off the current thread. In a desktop app, that's useful to keep the UI thread responsive while doing a heavy calculation.

In ASP.NET Core, the request is already running on a thread pool thread. So wrapping work in Task.Run and immediately awaiting it just swaps one pool thread for another, adding overhead and no benefit. And wrapping a synchronous I/O call in Task.Run, called fake async, still blocks a thread; it just hides it. The right fix there is a truly async API.

Task.Run in ASP.NET Core is useful only in specific cases: running several CPU-bound pieces of work in parallel, or starting fire-and-forget background work, though for that I prefer a hosted service with a queue, because it handles errors, scopes and shutdown properly.
So: async and await for I/O; Task.Run only for CPU-bound work that genuinely benefits from running elsewhere.

p17-159.q: Tuples group a few values together without defining a class. Modern C# uses ValueTuple, which is a struct, with nice syntax: a method can return (int Count, decimal Total), and the caller reads result.Count and result.Total. The element names are a compile-time feature, so they make the code readable without creating a type.
p17-159.k: tuples c#, value tuple, deconstruction, return multiple values, named tuple, tuple vs class
x: Tuples group a few values together without defining a class. Modern C# uses ValueTuple, which is a struct, with nice syntax: a method can return (int Count, decimal Total), and the caller reads result.Count and result.Total. The element names are a compile-time feature, so they make the code readable without creating a type.

Deconstruction splits a tuple, or any type with a Deconstruct method, into separate variables: var (count, total) equals GetSummary(). Records support it automatically through their positional parameters, and I can use underscore as a discard for values I don't need. Deconstruction also enables neat tricks, like swapping two variables with (a, b) equals (b, a).
Tuples also work well in pattern matching, like switching on a tuple of two values, for example (status, isUrgent) switch, which is much clearer than nested if statements.

I use tuples for private and internal helper methods that return two or three related values, and for local grouping in LINQ. I avoid them in public APIs, DTOs and anything serialised, because element names don't survive serialisation and they don't carry meaning or validation. If a tuple is passed around a lot, it's a sign it should become a record.
The older System.Tuple class, with Item1 and Item2, is a reference type, and I don't use it in new code.

p17-160.q: A local function is a method declared inside another method. It's only visible inside that method, so it keeps helper logic close to where it's used without cluttering the class.
p17-160.k: local functions, local function vs lambda, static local function, nested method c#
x: A local function is a method declared inside another method. It's only visible inside that method, so it keeps helper logic close to where it's used without cluttering the class.

They differ from lambdas in a few useful ways. Local functions can be declared after they're used, are named, and can be recursive easily. They support generics, ref and out parameters, params and iterators with yield return. And performance: a lambda that captures variables allocates a closure object and a delegate on the heap. A local function that's only called directly can capture variables into a struct on the stack, so no allocation, which matters in hot paths.
Marking a local function as static prevents it from capturing any variables of the enclosing method, which makes dependencies explicit and avoids accidental captures.

Two common uses. First, argument validation for iterators and async methods. Because an iterator's body runs lazily, I validate arguments in the outer method, which runs immediately, and put the yield return logic in a local function. Same for async methods, when I want validation exceptions thrown immediately rather than inside the task. Second, splitting a long method into readable steps that don't make sense as class-level methods.
I use lambdas when I need a delegate to pass somewhere, like to LINQ or an event.

p17-161.q: I always paginate list endpoints, because returning everything works in testing and fails in production when a table grows.
p17-161.k: api pagination design, paged response, page size limit, next page link, continuation token, cursor pagination api
x: I always paginate list endpoints, because returning everything works in testing and fails in production when a table grows.

The request takes either a page number and page size, or a cursor. Page size has a sensible default, like 25, and a hard maximum, like 100, enforced on the server, so nobody can request a million rows.

The response wraps the items with metadata: for page-based paging, the page number, page size and total count; for cursor-based paging, a next cursor or continuation token, and whether there are more items. Some APIs also return links to the next and previous pages, or use the Link header, so clients don't build URLs themselves.

Which style I choose depends on the data. Offset paging, with skip and take, is simple and lets users jump to page 10, which suits admin screens. But it gets slow on deep pages, because the database still reads all the skipped rows, and results shift if rows are added while paging. Cursor or keyset paging uses the last item's sort key, like "created after this date and id", which is fast at any depth and stable, so it's better for large tables, infinite scrolling and API consumers syncing data.
Ordering must be deterministic, so I always add a unique tie-breaker, like the id, to the sort.
Total counts can be expensive on big tables, so I make them optional.

p17-162.q: An ETag is a version identifier for a resource, returned in a response header. It can be a hash of the content, or a version number like SQL Server's rowversion. Clients use it in conditional requests, for two purposes.
p17-162.k: etag, if none match, if match, conditional request, 304 not modified, 412 precondition failed, optimistic concurrency http
x: An ETag is a version identifier for a resource, returned in a response header. It can be a hash of the content, or a version number like SQL Server's rowversion. Clients use it in conditional requests, for two purposes.

Caching: the client sends If-None-Match with the ETag it has. If the resource hasn't changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body. That saves bandwidth and processing, which helps for large resources that are fetched often, like study configuration.

Concurrency control: when updating, the client sends If-Match with the ETag it got when it read the resource. The server checks it against the current version. If someone else changed the resource in the meantime, the versions don't match, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting the other person's change, which is the lost update problem. The client then reloads and lets the user merge or retry. Some APIs also return 428 Precondition Required if If-Match is missing on updates, to force clients to use it.

In ASP.NET Core, I implement this myself: map the entity's row version to the ETag header, read If-Match in the update endpoint, and pass the version into EF Core's concurrency token check, so the database enforces it.
It's the HTTP version of optimistic concurrency.

p17-163.q: HTTP caching headers tell browsers, CDNs and proxies whether and how long they can reuse a response, which can massively reduce load.
p17-163.k: cache control header, http caching api, no store, max age, private public cache, vary header
x: HTTP caching headers tell browsers, CDNs and proxies whether and how long they can reuse a response, which can massively reduce load.

Cache-Control is the main header. max-age equals 300 means the response can be reused for 300 seconds. public allows shared caches, like a CDN, to store it, while private means only the user's own browser may cache it, which is right for user-specific data. no-cache means the client may store it but must revalidate with the server before using it, often with an ETag. no-store means don't store it anywhere, which I use for sensitive data, like patient information or tokens.
Vary tells caches which request headers change the response, like Accept-Language or Authorization, so different versions are cached separately.

For APIs, my defaults are: sensitive or user-specific data gets no-store or private, no-cache; truly public, rarely changing data, like a list of countries or static reference data, gets public with a max-age, maybe through a CDN; and responses with ETags support cheap revalidation.

In ASP.NET Core, I set headers directly, use the ResponseCache attribute, or use output caching middleware for server-side caching of whole responses, which is different: it's the server reusing its own response, regardless of what clients do.
Getting caching wrong with user data can leak information between users, so I'm conservative.

p17-164.q: Content negotiation is how the server picks the response format based on what the client asks for. The client sends an Accept header, like application/json or application/xml, and the server chooses a matching output formatter. If several are acceptable, it uses the client's preference order.
p17-164.k: content negotiation, accept header, output formatters, return xml or json, produces attribute, 406 not acceptable
x: Content negotiation is how the server picks the response format based on what the client asks for. The client sends an Accept header, like application/json or application/xml, and the server chooses a matching output formatter. If several are acceptable, it uses the client's preference order.

In ASP.NET Core controllers, JSON is the default formatter, using System.Text.Json. I can add others, like XML with AddXmlSerializerFormatters, or a custom formatter for CSV. By default, if the client asks for a format the server doesn't support, ASP.NET Core falls back to JSON; setting ReturnHttpNotAcceptable to true makes it return 406 Not Acceptable instead, which is stricter.

The Produces attribute restricts or documents which content types an action returns, and Consumes does the same for request bodies, checked against the Content-Type header, which returns 415 Unsupported Media Type if it doesn't match.
Minimal APIs are simpler: they return JSON by default and don't do full content negotiation, so for other formats, I return a specific result, like Results.Text or a file.

In practice, most modern APIs are JSON only, and that's fine. I've used negotiation mainly for exports, where the same report endpoint returns JSON for the UI and CSV for download, based on the Accept header or a format parameter.
Accept-Language for localisation is a related kind of negotiation.

p17-165.q: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the highest level of the Richardson maturity model for REST. The idea is that responses include links telling the client what it can do next, like a shipment response containing links to "cancel" or "track", only when those actions are allowed. So the client discovers actions from the response, instead of hard-coding URLs and business rules.
p17-165.k: hateoas, hypermedia, rest maturity model, richardson maturity model, links in api response
x: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the highest level of the Richardson maturity model for REST. The idea is that responses include links telling the client what it can do next, like a shipment response containing links to "cancel" or "track", only when those actions are allowed. So the client discovers actions from the response, instead of hard-coding URLs and business rules.
The benefits in theory: clients are less coupled to URL structures, and the server controls which actions are available based on the current state and the user's permissions.

In practice, I rarely see full HATEOAS in real projects, including ours. Most front ends are built together with the API, so they know the URLs. Client developers find it more work to parse links than to call documented endpoints, and the tooling, like OpenAPI clients, is built around fixed endpoints.

What I do use are the practical parts. Pagination links in list responses, like next and previous. A Location header on 201 Created pointing to the new resource. And flags in responses indicating allowed actions, like canCancel or canReturn, computed on the server from the state and the user's permissions, so the UI shows the right buttons without duplicating business rules. That gives most of the benefit with less complexity.

p17-166.q: Data annotations are attributes on model properties, like Required, StringLength, Range or EmailAddress. They're built in, simple, and ASP.NET Core with ApiController checks them automatically before the action runs, returning a 400 with validation problem details. They're fine for simple rules on simple DTOs.
p17-166.k: fluentvalidation vs data annotations, validation library, complex validation rules, validator classes, abstractvalidator
x: Data annotations are attributes on model properties, like Required, StringLength, Range or EmailAddress. They're built in, simple, and ASP.NET Core with ApiController checks them automatically before the action runs, returning a 400 with validation problem details. They're fine for simple rules on simple DTOs.

FluentValidation is a library where rules live in a separate validator class, like CreateShipmentValidator inheriting AbstractValidator, written as fluent code: RuleFor Quantity GreaterThan zero, RuleFor SiteId NotEmpty, and so on.

I prefer FluentValidation for real applications, for a few reasons. Complex rules are much easier: conditional rules with When, rules that compare properties, collection rules with RuleForEach, and async rules that check the database, like "site must exist and be active". Validators are classes, so they can use dependency injection. Messages are easy to customise and localise. Rules are kept out of the DTO, which stays clean. And validators are very easy to unit test.

The FluentValidation team no longer recommends the automatic ASP.NET Core integration, so I run validators explicitly, typically in a MediatR pipeline behaviour, or in an endpoint filter for minimal APIs.
That's how our newer IRT APIs work: FluentValidation in a MediatR behaviour, so every command is validated before its handler runs.

p17-167.q: Model binding maps data from the HTTP request, like route values, query strings, headers, form fields and the body, to the action's parameters. The built-in binders handle common types and JSON bodies well. A custom model binder lets me control how a specific type is created from the request when the defaults don't fit.
p17-167.k: custom model binder, imodelbinder, model binder provider, bind custom type, typeconverter binding, tryparse binding
x: Model binding maps data from the HTTP request, like route values, query strings, headers, form fields and the body, to the action's parameters. The built-in binders handle common types and JSON bodies well. A custom model binder lets me control how a specific type is created from the request when the defaults don't fit.

Typical reasons: binding a strongly typed id, like StudyId, from a route string; parsing a comma-separated list in the query string, like ids equals 1,2,3, into a list; or combining values from several sources, like a header and a route value, into one object.

To write one, I implement IModelBinder, read the value with the ValueProvider, convert it, and either set the result as success or add a model state error. Then I register it with a ModelBinder attribute on the type or parameter, or globally through an IModelBinderProvider.

But often there's a simpler option. For simple types, if the type has a static TryParse method, both controllers and minimal APIs can bind it from route and query values automatically. Minimal APIs also support a static BindAsync method for custom binding from the whole HttpContext.
So I first try TryParse or BindAsync, and only write a full model binder for complex cases in controllers.

p17-168.q: Route constraints restrict which values a route parameter accepts, so the route only matches when the value fits. They're written inside the route template after a colon, like api/shipments/{id:int}, {id:guid}, {code:alpha}, {name:minlength(3)}, {page:range(1,1000)}, or {date:datetime}. Several can be combined, and there's regex for patterns.
p17-168.k: route constraints, int route constraint, guid route constraint, custom route constraint, route parameter constraint
x: Route constraints restrict which values a route parameter accepts, so the route only matches when the value fits. They're written inside the route template after a colon, like api/shipments/{id:int}, {id:guid}, {code:alpha}, {name:minlength(3)}, {page:range(1,1000)}, or {date:datetime}. Several can be combined, and there's regex for patterns.

They're mainly for disambiguating routes. For example, I might have shipments/{id:int} and shipments/{reference} for lookups by a text reference. The int constraint ensures a numeric value goes to the first, and anything else goes to the second. Without constraints, they'd conflict.

An important point is that constraints aren't validation. If a constraint fails, the route simply doesn't match, so the client gets a 404 Not Found, not a 400 Bad Request explaining the problem. That's confusing for an API consumer who passed an invalid value. So I use constraints for routing decisions, and do input validation separately, returning proper 400 errors with clear messages.
I can also write custom constraints by implementing IRouteConstraint, and register them with a name, for example a constraint that only matches valid study codes.
Also, the datetime and decimal constraints use the invariant culture, which is good, because routes shouldn't depend on the server's culture.

p17-169.q: Endpoint filters are the minimal API version of MVC action filters. They run before and after the endpoint handler, can inspect and change the arguments, short-circuit with a different result, or modify the result after the handler runs.
p17-169.k: endpoint filters, minimal api filters, iendpointfilter, addendpointfilter, validation filter minimal api
x: Endpoint filters are the minimal API version of MVC action filters. They run before and after the endpoint handler, can inspect and change the arguments, short-circuit with a different result, or modify the result after the handler runs.

I add one with AddEndpointFilter on an endpoint or on a route group, either as a lambda or a class implementing IEndpointFilter. The filter receives an EndpointFilterInvocationContext, which gives access to the HttpContext and the handler's arguments, and a next delegate to call the rest of the pipeline.

Common uses: validation, where a generic filter finds the argument of a type, runs its FluentValidation validator, and returns a 400 validation problem if it fails, so the handler only runs with valid input; logging or timing for specific endpoints; checking a tenant or feature flag; and wrapping or transforming results consistently.
Filters on a route group apply to every endpoint in that group, which keeps cross-cutting logic in one place. Multiple filters run in the order they're added, like middleware, first in, first to run.

Compared with middleware, endpoint filters run after routing, so they know which endpoint is executing and can access its typed arguments. Middleware runs for every request and only sees the raw HttpContext. So I use middleware for global concerns and endpoint filters for endpoint-specific ones.

p17-170.q: MapGroup, added in .NET 7, creates a group of minimal API endpoints that share a common route prefix and common configuration. For example, var shipments equals app.MapGroup("/api/shipments"), and then shipments.MapGet("/{id}"), shipments.MapPost("/") and so on.
p17-170.k: mapgroup, route groups, minimal api organization, group endpoints, minimal api structure large project
x: MapGroup, added in .NET 7, creates a group of minimal API endpoints that share a common route prefix and common configuration. For example, var shipments equals app.MapGroup("/api/shipments"), and then shipments.MapGet("/{id}"), shipments.MapPost("/") and so on.

The real benefit is applying configuration once to all endpoints in the group: RequireAuthorization with a policy, endpoint filters like validation, rate limiting, tags for OpenAPI documentation, CORS policies and versioning. Groups can be nested, so an api group requires authentication, and an admin group inside it adds an admin policy.

It's also the key to organising minimal APIs in a larger project. A common pattern is one static class per feature with an extension method, like MapShipmentEndpoints, that takes the route builder, creates the group and maps its endpoints. Program.cs then just calls app.MapShipmentEndpoints() and similar for each feature. So Program.cs stays small, and each feature's endpoints live together, which fits vertical slice architecture nicely. Some teams use libraries like Carter or FastEndpoints for even more structure.
The handlers themselves are best kept small: they bind input, call a service or MediatR, and return a typed result, while the business logic lives elsewhere.

p17-171.q: In minimal APIs, a handler can return results from the Results class, like Results.Ok or Results.NotFound, which return the IResult interface, or from TypedResults, which return concrete types, like Ok of ShipmentDto or NotFound.
p17-171.k: typedresults, results union type, minimal api return types, openapi minimal api responses, results vs typedresults
x: In minimal APIs, a handler can return results from the Results class, like Results.Ok or Results.NotFound, which return the IResult interface, or from TypedResults, which return concrete types, like Ok of ShipmentDto or NotFound.
TypedResults have two advantages.

First, OpenAPI documentation. Because the return type is concrete, the framework knows exactly what the endpoint returns, and generates the response schema and status codes automatically, without needing Produces attributes or metadata calls.
Second, testing. In a unit test, I can call the handler directly and check that the result is of type Ok of ShipmentDto and inspect its Value, without casting or running an HTTP server.

When a handler can return different results, like Ok or NotFound or ValidationProblem, I declare the return type as a union: Results of Ok of ShipmentDto, NotFound, ValidationProblem. The compiler then checks that the handler only returns those types, and OpenAPI documents all three responses. This is clearer than returning IResult, where anything can come back.
There's no big performance difference; it's mainly about correctness, documentation and testability.
So in new minimal APIs, I use TypedResults with union return types by default, and Results only for quick prototypes.

p17-172.q: Response compression reduces the size of responses sent to the client, using algorithms like Brotli or Gzip, which can shrink JSON and HTML by 70 to 90 percent. That reduces bandwidth and speeds up responses over slower networks.
p17-172.k: response compression, gzip brotli, compress api responses, usresponsecompression, breach attack compression
x: Response compression reduces the size of responses sent to the client, using algorithms like Brotli or Gzip, which can shrink JSON and HTML by 70 to 90 percent. That reduces bandwidth and speeds up responses over slower networks.
The client says what it supports in the Accept-Encoding header, and the server compresses the response and sets the Content-Encoding header.

In ASP.NET Core, I add AddResponseCompression and UseResponseCompression, configure Brotli and Gzip providers, choose the compression level, and the MIME types to compress. For HTTPS, I have to opt in with EnableForHttps, because of security concerns.

But the first question is where compression should happen. If the app runs behind IIS, NGINX, a load balancer or a CDN that already compresses responses, I let them do it, because they're usually more efficient, and the app shouldn't compress twice. The middleware is useful when the app is exposed directly through Kestrel or the proxy can't compress.
Compression costs CPU, so the "fastest" level is often a better trade-off for dynamic responses. It's not useful for already compressed content, like images or zip files, or for very small responses.

The security issue is attacks like BREACH, which can extract secrets from compressed HTTPS responses that mix secrets with attacker-controlled input. So I avoid compressing responses that contain tokens alongside user input.

p17-173.q: Since .NET 8, ASP.NET Core has request timeout middleware. I register it with AddRequestTimeouts, add UseRequestTimeouts to the pipeline, and set a default timeout, plus named policies for specific endpoints, using the RequestTimeout attribute or WithRequestTimeout on minimal API endpoints. A long export endpoint might get two minutes, while normal endpoints get ten seconds.
p17-173.k: request timeout middleware, addrequesttimeouts, request timeout .net 8, cancel slow requests, timeout policy endpoint
x: Since .NET 8, ASP.NET Core has request timeout middleware. I register it with AddRequestTimeouts, add UseRequestTimeouts to the pipeline, and set a default timeout, plus named policies for specific endpoints, using the RequestTimeout attribute or WithRequestTimeout on minimal API endpoints. A long export endpoint might get two minutes, while normal endpoints get ten seconds.

The important thing to understand is how it works. When the timeout expires, it doesn't kill the request. It triggers HttpContext.RequestAborted, the request's cancellation token. So it only helps if my code passes that cancellation token all the way down, to EF Core queries, HttpClient calls and other async operations, so they stop when the token is cancelled. If the code ignores the token, the work continues anyway.
When the timeout fires and the response hasn't started, the middleware returns 504 Gateway Timeout by default, which I can customise.
Timeouts are also disabled while debugging, so they don't interfere.

Why bother? Without timeouts, slow requests keep holding resources, like database connections and threads, long after the client has given up, because the load balancer usually times out first. Under load, that makes everything slower. A server-side timeout, slightly shorter than the load balancer's, frees those resources and keeps the service healthy.

p17-174.q: ASP.NET Core apps on IIS use the ASP.NET Core Module, ANCM, which is installed with the .NET Hosting Bundle. There are two hosting models.
p17-174.k: iis hosting asp.net core, in process vs out of process, aspnetcore module, ancm, host asp.net core on iis, web.config asp.net core
x: ASP.NET Core apps on IIS use the ASP.NET Core Module, ANCM, which is installed with the .NET Hosting Bundle. There are two hosting models.

In-process hosting, the default since ASP.NET Core 3.0, runs the app inside the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, using the IIS HTTP server instead of Kestrel. Requests don't travel through an extra hop, so it's faster, with higher throughput.

In out-of-process hosting, IIS acts as a reverse proxy. ANCM starts the app as a separate process running Kestrel, and forwards requests to it over a local port. It's a bit slower, but the app process is separate from IIS, which can help in some isolation scenarios.
The setting is the hostingModel attribute in web.config, or AspNetCoreHostingModel in the project file.

Some practical points. Each app needs its own application pool when using in-process hosting, with "No Managed Code" selected. Startup errors often show as a 500.30 error, and enabling stdout logging in web.config temporarily helps diagnose them. The app_offline.htm file takes the app offline during deployment, so files aren't locked. And IIS handles Windows authentication, TLS and process recycling.
Our CIRT platform runs on IIS on-premise, so I've dealt with these settings, especially app pools and 500.30 startup errors during deployments.

So HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress shows the proxy's IP, and Request.Scheme shows http if the proxy terminated TLS, even though the user connected with https.

x: When an ASP.NET Core app runs behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, like NGINX, an AWS ALB or Azure Front Door, the app sees the proxy as the client. So HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress shows the proxy's IP, and Request.Scheme shows http if the proxy terminated TLS, even though the user connected with https.

That breaks several things: redirect URLs and generated links use http instead of https, the OpenID Connect redirect URI is wrong, so login fails, HTTPS redirection loops, rate limiting by IP limits everyone together, and logs show the wrong client IP.

The proxy adds headers with the original values: X-Forwarded-For for the client IP, X-Forwarded-Proto for the original scheme, and X-Forwarded-Host. The forwarded headers middleware, UseForwardedHeaders, reads them and updates the request, so the rest of the app sees the real values. It should run early in the pipeline.

Security matters here, because clients can send fake X-Forwarded-For headers. So I configure KnownProxies or KnownNetworks, so the middleware only trusts headers from our real proxies, and ForwardLimit for chains of proxies.
On IIS with in-process hosting, and in some container setups, this is handled automatically, but behind a cloud load balancer, I configure it explicitly.

p17-176.q: Localization lets the app show text, dates and numbers in the user's language and format.
p17-176.k: localization asp.net core, globalization, resource files, request localization, accept language, multi language api
x: Localization lets the app show text, dates and numbers in the user's language and format.

ASP.NET Core has built-in support. I call AddLocalization, store translated strings in resource files per culture, like Messages.fr.resx, and inject IStringLocalizer of T to get the translated text by key. UseRequestLocalization decides each request's culture, with providers that check, in order, a query string, a cookie, and the Accept-Language header, falling back to a default culture. I list the supported cultures explicitly.
Once the culture is set, formatting of dates, numbers and currencies follows it automatically when using culture-aware formatting.

For APIs, I think carefully about what to localise. Data values, like dates and amounts in JSON, should stay culture-neutral, using ISO 8601 and plain numbers, and the front end formats them for display. What the API might localise are user-facing messages, like validation errors, and generated documents, like emails and PDF reports.
For front ends, React and Angular have their own i18n libraries, like react-i18next or Angular's built-in i18n.
In our IRT, sites are in many countries, so emails are generated from templates per language, and dates are shown in each site's format, while the stored data stays in UTC and neutral formats.

p17-177.q: Sometimes clients need to create or update many items at once, like 500 kit status changes, and calling a single-item endpoint 500 times is slow and chatty. So I design a bulk endpoint, carefully.
p17-177.k: bulk api, batch endpoint, bulk create api, partial success response, 207 multi status, batch operations api
x: Sometimes clients need to create or update many items at once, like 500 kit status changes, and calling a single-item endpoint 500 times is slow and chatty. So I design a bulk endpoint, carefully.
First, limits: a maximum number of items per request, like 1,000, to protect the server, and for larger volumes, an asynchronous job with a file upload instead.

Second, the transaction semantics, which must be explicit. All-or-nothing: if any item fails validation, nothing is saved, and the response lists all the errors. That's simpler for clients and right when items depend on each other. Or partial success: valid items are saved, and the response contains a result per item, with its index or client-provided reference, status and any error. For partial success, I return 200 with a detailed body, or 207 Multi-Status, and never just a 201, which would hide failures.
Third, idempotency: an idempotency key for the whole request, or a client reference per item, so a retried request doesn't create duplicates.
Fourth, efficient processing: validate everything first, load needed data in a few queries, not one per item, and write in batches.
And for long-running bulk work, return 202 Accepted with a status URL.
I document clearly which mode the endpoint uses, because clients handle them very differently.

p17-178.q: A good error response helps two audiences: the developer debugging the integration, and the program that needs to react automatically.
p17-178.k: api error design, error codes api, problem details errors, error response format, machine readable errors
x: A good error response helps two audiences: the developer debugging the integration, and the program that needs to react automatically.

I use the standard ProblemDetails format, RFC 9457, with type, title, status, detail and instance. Then I add extensions: a stable, machine-readable error code, like SITE_NOT_ACTIVE or KIT_ALREADY_DISPENSED, that clients can switch on, because messages change but codes don't; a trace id, so support can find the logs; and for validation errors, an errors dictionary with field names and messages, so the UI can show them next to each field.

The HTTP status code must be correct: 400 for invalid input, 401 and 403 for auth, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts like duplicate or concurrency errors, 422 for valid input that breaks a business rule, 429 for rate limits, and 5xx only for server-side problems. Clients often decide whether to retry based on the status.
What I never include: stack traces, SQL errors, internal server names or anything that reveals the system's internals, especially in production. Those go to the logs, linked by the trace id.
I document the error codes in the OpenAPI spec, and keep them consistent across services, using shared middleware.
In our newer IRT APIs, a global exception handler returns ProblemDetails with a trace id for every error.

p17-179.q: Normally, searching or filtering is a read, so GET with query parameters is the REST-correct choice. It's cacheable, bookmarkable, idempotent, and easy to call and log. For simple filters, like status, date range, site and page, I always use GET.
p17-179.k: post vs get for search, complex search api, search endpoint design, query string length limit, get with body
x: Normally, searching or filtering is a read, so GET with query parameters is the REST-correct choice. It's cacheable, bookmarkable, idempotent, and easy to call and log. For simple filters, like status, date range, site and page, I always use GET.

But some searches don't fit well in a query string. Complex filters with nested conditions, like "status in these five values and site in these 200 sites, or created before this date". Long lists of ids can exceed URL length limits, which are around 2,000 characters in some browsers and proxies, and servers have limits too. And sensitive values in a URL get logged by proxies, load balancers and browser history, which matters for personal data.

In those cases, I use POST to a dedicated search resource, like POST /api/subjects/search, with the criteria as a JSON body. It's a common, accepted pattern. I document that it's a safe, read-only operation, even though it uses POST. GET with a body isn't a good option, because many clients, proxies and frameworks ignore or reject it.
An alternative is to create a saved search: POST the criteria, get back a search id, and GET the results with that id, which also allows sharing and paging.
HTTP also now has a draft QUERY method for exactly this, but support isn't widespread yet.

p17-180.q: ASP.NET Core supports several authentication schemes side by side. A scheme is a named handler, like the JWT bearer handler, a cookie handler, or a custom one.
p17-180.k: multiple authentication schemes, api key authentication, jwt and api key, authentication handler custom, policy scheme
x: ASP.NET Core supports several authentication schemes side by side. A scheme is a named handler, like the JWT bearer handler, a cookie handler, or a custom one.

For API keys, which partners or older systems might use, I write a custom authentication handler by inheriting AuthenticationHandler. It reads the key from a header, like X-API-Key, looks it up, comparing a hash of the key, not plain text, and with a constant-time comparison, and if it's valid, creates a ClaimsPrincipal with claims like the client id and its permissions. If the header is missing, it returns NoResult, so other schemes can try.
Then I register both: AddAuthentication with JWT as the default, AddJwtBearer, and AddScheme for the API key handler.

To choose per request, there are two approaches. On endpoints, Authorize with AuthenticationSchemes listing which schemes are accepted, or a policy that specifies them. Or a policy scheme, with AddPolicyScheme and ForwardDefaultSelector, which looks at the request, like whether it has an Authorization bearer header or an API key header, and forwards to the right handler.
Authorization policies then work on claims, regardless of how the user was authenticated.
API keys are long random values, stored hashed, scoped, rotatable, rate-limited, and only sent over HTTPS.

p17-181.q: IClaimsTransformation lets me modify or add claims to the user's ClaimsPrincipal after authentication, before authorization runs. I implement its TransformAsync method and register it in DI, and ASP.NET Core calls it during authentication.
p17-181.k: iclaimstransformation, claims transformation, add claims after authentication, enrich claims, permissions from database
x: IClaimsTransformation lets me modify or add claims to the user's ClaimsPrincipal after authentication, before authorization runs. I implement its TransformAsync method and register it in DI, and ASP.NET Core calls it during authentication.

The typical use is enriching the identity with application-specific data that isn't in the token. Identity providers usually issue tokens with generic claims, like the user id, email and maybe some roles. But my application's permissions, like which studies and sites a user can access and which actions they can perform, live in the application database. So the transformation looks up the user's permissions and adds them as claims, and authorization policies can then simply check for those claims.

Other uses: mapping claim names from different identity providers to one standard set, or flattening nested role claims, like Keycloak's realm_access roles in a JSON structure, into standard role claims that the Authorize attribute understands.

There are some gotchas. It can be called more than once per request, so it must be idempotent: check whether the claims were already added. It runs on every request, so database lookups must be cached, like in memory or Redis with a short expiry, otherwise every request pays for extra queries. And I don't put too many claims in, especially if they end up in a cookie.

p17-182.q: For years, ASP.NET Core templates used Swashbuckle to generate the OpenAPI document and show the Swagger UI. In .NET 9, Microsoft removed Swashbuckle from the templates and added built-in OpenAPI document generation in the Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi package. In .NET 10, it supports OpenAPI 3.1.
p17-182.k: openapi .net 9, microsoft.aspnetcore.openapi, swashbuckle removed, scalar api reference, swagger ui .net 9
x: For years, ASP.NET Core templates used Swashbuckle to generate the OpenAPI document and show the Swagger UI. In .NET 9, Microsoft removed Swashbuckle from the templates and added built-in OpenAPI document generation in the Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi package. In .NET 10, it supports OpenAPI 3.1.

With the built-in support, I call AddOpenApi and MapOpenApi, and the document is served at openapi/v1.json. It works with both controllers and minimal APIs, and supports document and operation transformers, which are hooks to customise the output, like adding a security scheme for JWT bearer tokens, or adding descriptions and examples. It also works with Native AOT, and the document can be generated at build time, which is useful for checking breaking changes in the pipeline.

The built-in package doesn't include a UI. For interactive documentation, I add one separately: Swagger UI from Swashbuckle's UI package pointed at the new document, or Scalar, which many teams now use.
Swashbuckle still works and has been actively maintained again, so existing projects don't need to migrate urgently, especially if they use its filters heavily.
For new .NET 9 or 10 services, I use the built-in generator, add a bearer security scheme with a transformer, and expose the UI only in non-production environments.

p17-183.q: The key is never loading the whole file into memory. If I read a 2 GB file into a byte array and return it, the server needs 2 GB of memory per concurrent download, it lands on the Large Object Heap, and the server can run out of memory quickly.
p17-183.k: stream file download, filestreamresult, large file download api, range requests, download without loading memory
x: The key is never loading the whole file into memory. If I read a 2 GB file into a byte array and return it, the server needs 2 GB of memory per concurrent download, it lands on the Large Object Heap, and the server can run out of memory quickly.

Instead, I stream it. In ASP.NET Core, I return a file result with a Stream, like Results.File or File in a controller with a FileStream opened with async and sequential-scan options, or a stream from blob storage. The framework copies the stream to the response in small chunks, so memory use stays small, regardless of file size.

Setting enableRangeProcessing to true supports HTTP range requests, so clients can resume interrupted downloads, and video players can seek. I set the content type and a Content-Disposition header with a safe file name, and ETag and Last-Modified headers for caching.

For generated content, like a large CSV export, I write directly to the response body as I go, or return an IAsyncEnumerable for JSON, so rows stream from the database to the client without being collected first.

When files are in cloud storage, the best option is often not to stream through the API at all: the API checks permissions and returns a short-lived pre-signed URL, and the client downloads directly from S3 or Blob Storage.

p17-184.q: ASP.NET Core has built-in HTTP logging middleware. I enable it with AddHttpLogging and UseHttpLogging, and choose which fields to log: request method, path, query, headers, status code, duration, and optionally request and response bodies, with a size limit. Since .NET 8, it supports combining everything into one log entry per request, and an IHttpLoggingInterceptor to customise or redact per request.
p17-184.k: http logging middleware, log request body, addhttplogging, request response logging, log api requests
x: ASP.NET Core has built-in HTTP logging middleware. I enable it with AddHttpLogging and UseHttpLogging, and choose which fields to log: request method, path, query, headers, status code, duration, and optionally request and response bodies, with a size limit. Since .NET 8, it supports combining everything into one log entry per request, and an IHttpLoggingInterceptor to customise or redact per request.

But I'm careful with what gets logged, because logs are widely accessible and kept for a long time. By default, headers are redacted unless explicitly allowed, and I keep it that way for Authorization, cookies and API keys. Request and response bodies can contain personal data or credentials, so I don't log them in production, except for specific, non-sensitive endpoints, during a limited investigation, with masking.

What I always want per request is: method, route template rather than the full URL, status code, duration, user or client id, and the trace id, in one structured log entry. Serilog's request logging middleware, UseSerilogRequestLogging, does this neatly, with enrichment from the HttpContext.
Health check and metrics endpoints are excluded, otherwise they flood the logs.
For debugging production issues, distributed traces with OpenTelemetry often give better insight than logging bodies, without the privacy risk.

p17-185.q: IHttpContextAccessor gives access to the current HttpContext from places that don't receive it directly, like a service class. I register it with AddHttpContextAccessor, inject it, and read HttpContext from it. A common use is a CurrentUser service that reads the user's claims, or getting the correlation id for logging.
p17-185.k: ihttpcontextaccessor, httpcontext in service, access httpcontext outside controller, httpcontext null background thread
x: IHttpContextAccessor gives access to the current HttpContext from places that don't receive it directly, like a service class. I register it with AddHttpContextAccessor, inject it, and read HttpContext from it. A common use is a CurrentUser service that reads the user's claims, or getting the correlation id for logging.
It works using AsyncLocal, so the context flows with the async execution of the request.

There are several pitfalls. Outside a request, like in a background service, a hosted service or a message consumer, HttpContext is null, so code that depends on it fails there. If code captures the HttpContext and uses it after the request ends, for example in fire-and-forget work, it may be reading a recycled or disposed context, which causes strange bugs. HttpContext isn't thread-safe, so it mustn't be used from parallel tasks. And it couples business logic to the web layer, making it harder to test and reuse.

So my approach: in the business layer, I depend on a small abstraction, like ICurrentUser with UserId and Permissions. The web implementation reads from IHttpContextAccessor; a background job or message consumer provides its own implementation, using the user from the message. Tests just use a fake.
And I copy the values I need while the request is active, never the HttpContext itself.

p17-186.q: For a large MVC application, I'd avoid a big-bang rewrite and migrate incrementally.
p17-186.k: migrate asp.net mvc to core, .net framework to .net core migration, system.web adapters, yarp incremental migration, upgrade assistant
x: For a large MVC application, I'd avoid a big-bang rewrite and migrate incrementally.

Microsoft's recommended approach is the strangler fig with YARP. I create a new ASP.NET Core app that sits in front of the old one as a reverse proxy. Requests for migrated routes are handled by the new app, and everything else is forwarded to the legacy app. I then move controllers and views one area at a time. The System.Web adapters help share code, and can share session and authentication between the two apps, so users don't notice which app served the page.

Before moving code, I prepare it: move business logic into class libraries targeting .NET Standard 2.0, so both old and new apps can use them; remove System.Web dependencies like HttpContext.Current from business code; and update packages to versions that support modern .NET. The .NET Upgrade Assistant helps analyse and convert projects.

The main differences to handle: Global.asax and web.config become Program.cs, middleware and appsettings.json; HTTP modules and handlers become middleware; built-in DI replaces third-party containers; authentication changes; and bundling, Razor and some HTML helpers differ.
Our approach is similar in spirit: rather than converting the legacy MVC portal, we're moving modules to the React shell with new .NET APIs, while shared Keycloak SSO keeps the experience seamless.

p17-187.q: SignalR is ASP.NET Core's library for real-time communication between server and clients. It lets the server push messages to browsers instantly, like notifications, live dashboards or progress updates, without the client polling.
p17-187.k: signalr, signalr scale out, redis backplane, azure signalr service, websockets asp.net core, real time asp.net core
x: SignalR is ASP.NET Core's library for real-time communication between server and clients. It lets the server push messages to browsers instantly, like notifications, live dashboards or progress updates, without the client polling.

It uses WebSockets when available, and falls back automatically to Server-Sent Events or long polling. I define a Hub class on the server with methods clients can call, and the server can call methods on clients: all clients, a specific user, or a group, like everyone viewing a particular study. The JavaScript and .NET clients handle connection and automatic reconnection.
Authentication works with the same JWT or cookie, though for WebSockets in browsers, the token is passed as a query string parameter, so I make sure it's not logged.

Scaling out is the tricky part. Each connection lives on one server. If server A wants to send a message to a user connected to server B, it can't, by itself. Solutions: a Redis backplane, where every server publishes messages through Redis pub-sub so all servers receive them; or a managed service, like Azure SignalR Service, which holds all the connections itself, so app servers don't. Sticky sessions are also needed for the fallback transports, unless WebSockets-only mode is used.
For AWS, API Gateway WebSocket APIs are an alternative, especially for serverless.

p17-188.q: Server-Sent Events is a simple standard for the server to push a stream of text events to the browser over a normal HTTP connection. The browser uses the EventSource API, which reconnects automatically and can resume from the last event id. The response has the text/event-stream content type, and the server writes events as they happen.
p17-188.k: server sent events, sse, sse vs websockets, eventsource, streaming updates http, typedresults serversentevents
x: Server-Sent Events is a simple standard for the server to push a stream of text events to the browser over a normal HTTP connection. The browser uses the EventSource API, which reconnects automatically and can resume from the last event id. The response has the text/event-stream content type, and the server writes events as they happen.

Compared with WebSockets: SSE is one-way, server to client only, while WebSockets are two-way. SSE runs over plain HTTP, so it works through most proxies, load balancers and firewalls without special configuration, and benefits from HTTP/2 multiplexing. It's text-only, and reconnection is built in.

So SSE fits well when the client mostly listens: live notifications, progress of a long-running job, a dashboard feed, or streaming an AI model's response token by token, which is exactly how many LLM APIs stream output. WebSockets are better for genuinely interactive two-way communication, like chat or collaborative editing, or binary data.

In ASP.NET Core, I can write SSE manually by setting the content type and flushing writes to the response, and .NET 10 adds TypedResults.ServerSentEvents, which takes an IAsyncEnumerable and streams it as events. SignalR can also use SSE as one of its transports.
One caution: the browser's EventSource can't set an Authorization header, so I use cookies or a fetch-based client.

p17-189.q: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections and requests queue behind each other.
p17-189.k: http2, http3, quic, kestrel http2, multiplexing, head of line blocking
x: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections and requests queue behind each other.

HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests and responses over a single TCP connection at the same time, as independent streams. It also compresses headers with HPACK, which saves a lot for APIs with large headers like tokens, and supports stream prioritisation. Fewer connections means less TLS handshaking. gRPC requires HTTP/2.

But HTTP/2 still runs over TCP, so if one packet is lost, all streams on that connection wait for the retransmission. That's TCP head-of-line blocking, and it hurts on unreliable networks, like mobile.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP. Each stream is independent, so a lost packet only delays its own stream. QUIC also has faster connection setup, combining the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes, and connection migration, so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data keeps its connection.

Kestrel supports both. HTTP/2 is enabled by default with TLS. HTTP/3 is supported since .NET 7, requiring TLS and the platform's QUIC library, and I configure the endpoint with HttpProtocols.Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3, and clients discover it through the Alt-Svc header.
In practice, the load balancer or CDN in front often handles HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with clients, and talks to the app over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.

p17-190.q: ASP.NET Core supports session state as an opt-in feature. I call AddSession with a distributed cache, and UseSession. The browser gets a cookie with a session id, and on the server, ISession stores small values, like strings or byte arrays, keyed by that id. Unlike classic ASP.NET, it doesn't store objects directly; I serialise them, often as JSON.
p17-190.k: session state asp.net core, addsession, distributed session, session vs cookie, isession
x: ASP.NET Core supports session state as an opt-in feature. I call AddSession with a distributed cache, and UseSession. The browser gets a cookie with a session id, and on the server, ISession stores small values, like strings or byte arrays, keyed by that id. Unlike classic ASP.NET, it doesn't store objects directly; I serialise them, often as JSON.
The storage is an IDistributedCache. The in-memory one only works on a single server. With multiple instances, I use Redis or SQL Server, so any instance can read the session.

Some important behaviours. The session is loaded on first access, and since session access in ASP.NET Core can be synchronous, I call LoadAsync first to avoid blocking. Session data isn't locked, so concurrent requests from the same user can overwrite each other's changes, which differs from the old ASP.NET behaviour. Sessions expire after an idle timeout. And the session cookie is marked essential, or it won't be set when the user hasn't consented to non-essential cookies under privacy settings.

Should I use it? For APIs, no; APIs should be stateless, with state in the client or the database. For server-rendered web apps, it's fine for small, temporary data, like a multi-step wizard, but not for authentication or anything important.
Our legacy MVC portal uses session state, which is one reason Redis was introduced for the load-balanced IIS servers.

p17-191.q: All three are ways to build web UIs with .NET.
p17-191.k: razor pages vs mvc, blazor vs mvc, blazor server vs webassembly, server side rendering .net, which ui framework .net
x: All three are ways to build web UIs with .NET.

MVC uses controllers and views. Controllers handle requests and choose views, with models in between. It's well suited to large applications with many related actions, and to teams familiar with the pattern. It's also the basis of Web API controllers.

Razor Pages is page-focused: each page has a .cshtml file and a PageModel class with handlers like OnGet and OnPost. For page-based apps, like forms and admin screens, it's simpler and more cohesive than MVC, because everything for a page is in one place. Microsoft recommends it for new server-rendered page apps.

Blazor lets you build interactive UIs with C# components instead of JavaScript. Since .NET 8, Blazor Web Apps support several render modes per component: static server rendering, interactive server, where the UI runs on the server and updates the browser over a SignalR connection, interactive WebAssembly, where .NET runs in the browser, and auto, which starts on the server and switches to WebAssembly once it's downloaded.

My choice: for APIs consumed by React or Angular, which is our main setup, controllers or minimal APIs. For a simple internal tool built by .NET developers, Razor Pages or Blazor, which avoids a separate JavaScript stack. For rich public-facing apps with a large front-end team, React or Angular.

p17-192.q: By default, the request body is a forward-only stream. Once something reads it, like model binding or a middleware, it's consumed, and anything after that sees an empty body. That's a common problem when a middleware wants to log the body, or verify a webhook signature, and the controller also needs to bind it.
p17-192.k: read request body twice, enablebuffering, request body stream, body already read, middleware read body
x: By default, the request body is a forward-only stream. Once something reads it, like model binding or a middleware, it's consumed, and anything after that sees an empty body. That's a common problem when a middleware wants to log the body, or verify a webhook signature, and the controller also needs to bind it.

The solution is Request.EnableBuffering(). It makes the body seekable by buffering it, in memory for small bodies and in a temporary file for larger ones. After reading it, I reset the position to zero with Request.Body.Position equals 0, so the next reader starts from the beginning.

The typical middleware code is: call EnableBuffering, read the body asynchronously with a StreamReader with leaveOpen set to true, do what I need, like computing the HMAC signature, then reset the position, and call the next middleware.

A few cautions. Buffering large bodies uses memory or disk, so I only do it where needed, like specific webhook routes, and with a size limit. I read asynchronously, because synchronous I/O is disabled by default in Kestrel. And for very high throughput, the newer System.IO.Pipelines-based Request.BodyReader is more efficient.
For webhook signature checks, an alternative is binding the body as a raw string or byte array in the endpoint itself, verifying it, then deserialising manually.

p17-193.q: Open generic registration means registering a generic interface with a generic implementation once, without specifying the type argument, like services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>)). When something asks for IRepository of Shipment, the container automatically creates EfRepository of Shipment. One registration covers every entity type.
p17-193.k: open generics di, register generic repository, typeof irepository<>, generic service registration, decorate open generic
x: Open generic registration means registering a generic interface with a generic implementation once, without specifying the type argument, like services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>)). When something asks for IRepository of Shipment, the container automatically creates EfRepository of Shipment. One registration covers every entity type.
The framework uses this itself. ILogger of T is registered as an open generic, which is why any class can ask for ILogger of its own type. IOptions of T works the same way.
Other common uses: generic handlers or validators, like IValidator of T; MediatR pipeline behaviours, which are open generics applied to every request type; and generic caching decorators.
Constraints work too: if the implementation has generic constraints, like where T is an entity, the container only uses it for types that satisfy them, since .NET 5 or so.

A few limitations of the built-in container. It can't do convention-based scanning, like "register all classes ending in Service", so I use the Scrutor library for assembly scanning and for decorating open generics. And when there are several registrations for the same closed type, the last one wins for a single resolve, while IEnumerable gives all of them.
I use this for cross-cutting behaviours, but I don't create generic repositories over EF Core by default.

p17-194.q: Named options let me have several configured instances of the same options class, each with a name. For example, I have a VendorApiOptions class with BaseUrl, timeout and credentials, and three vendors, each needing its own settings. Instead of three nearly identical classes, I register one class three times with names: services.Configure of VendorApiOptions with "DepotA" bound to one configuration section, "DepotB" bound to another, and so on.

x: Named options let me have several configured instances of the same options class, each with a name. For example, I have a VendorApiOptions class with BaseUrl, timeout and credentials, and three vendors, each needing its own settings. Instead of three nearly identical classes, I register one class three times with names: services.Configure of VendorApiOptions with "DepotA" bound to one configuration section, "DepotB" bound to another, and so on.

To read them, I use IOptionsMonitor or IOptionsSnapshot, and call Get with the name, like optionsMonitor.Get("DepotA"). IOptions of T doesn't support names; it only gives the default, unnamed instance.

The framework uses named options a lot. Each authentication scheme has its own named options, which is how you can configure two JWT bearer schemes differently. HttpClient factory's named clients also use named options under the hood.
Validation works per name too, with ValidateDataAnnotations or a custom IValidateOptions, which receives the name, so I can validate each vendor's settings at startup with ValidateOnStart.
Post-configure and ConfigureAll let me apply common defaults to all named instances, like a default timeout, and then override per name.
I used this pattern for integration settings, where each partner has its own endpoint and credentials, and a new partner is just a new configuration section.

p17-195.q: The Generic Host is the .NET foundation for running any long-lived app: it provides dependency injection, configuration, logging, and the lifetime management for hosted services, with graceful startup and shutdown. It's used for console apps, worker services, and as the base of web apps. Historically, you created it with Host.CreateDefaultBuilder and a chain of callbacks, like ConfigureServices and ConfigureWebHostDefaults.
p17-195.k: generic host, webapplication builder, host createdefaultbuilder, hostapplicationbuilder, worker service host
x: The Generic Host is the .NET foundation for running any long-lived app: it provides dependency injection, configuration, logging, and the lifetime management for hosted services, with graceful startup and shutdown. It's used for console apps, worker services, and as the base of web apps. Historically, you created it with Host.CreateDefaultBuilder and a chain of callbacks, like ConfigureServices and ConfigureWebHostDefaults.

WebApplication, introduced in .NET 6 with minimal hosting, is a simpler, more direct API built on top of the Generic Host, specifically for web apps. WebApplication.CreateBuilder gives a builder with Services, Configuration, Logging and Environment as properties; I register services, call Build, then configure middleware and endpoints on the app, and Run. No Startup class, no nested callbacks. It still uses the Generic Host under the hood, so hosted services and everything else work.
For non-web apps, .NET 7 introduced Host.CreateApplicationBuilder, which gives the same simple linear style as WebApplication, but without the web server. The Worker Service template uses it.

So today: WebApplication.CreateBuilder for APIs and web apps, Host.CreateApplicationBuilder for workers and consumers, and the older callback style only in existing code. The concepts, like DI, configuration and hosted services, are identical across all of them.

p17-196.q: A Worker Service is a .NET app built on the Generic Host with one or more BackgroundService classes. To run it as an operating system service, I add one line and the matching package.
p17-196.k: windows service .net, systemd service .net, usewindowsservice, addwindowsservice, worker service deployment, run background service on server
x: A Worker Service is a .NET app built on the Generic Host with one or more BackgroundService classes. To run it as an operating system service, I add one line and the matching package.

For Windows, the Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.WindowsServices package and builder.Services.AddWindowsService with a service name. This makes the host respond to the Windows Service Control Manager: start, stop and shutdown signals map to the host's lifetime, so StopAsync runs on service stop. Then I install it with sc.exe create, or with PowerShell New-Service, pointing to the published exe, and set the recovery options, like restart on failure, and the account it runs under, ideally a managed service account with least privilege.

For Linux, the Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Systemd package and AddSystemd. It integrates with systemd's notifications and logging format. Then I create a unit file in /etc/systemd/system with the ExecStart path, the user, Restart equals always, and environment variables, and enable it with systemctl.

A few things to watch. The working directory is different for services, for example System32 on Windows, so I use AppContext.BaseDirectory for file paths. Logging should go to a central sink or the event log, not just the console. And configuration and secrets per environment.
In our CIRT environment, some RabbitMQ consumers run as Windows services on the application servers.

p17-197.q: I follow a few simple conventions so the API is predictable.
p17-197.k: rest naming conventions, api url design, plural nouns api, nested resources url, resource naming, api endpoint naming
x: I follow a few simple conventions so the API is predictable.
Use nouns for resources, not verbs, because the HTTP method is the verb. So GET /shipments, POST /shipments, GET /shipments/{id}, not /getShipments or /createShipment.
Use plural nouns for collections, consistently: /sites, /kits, /subjects.

Use nesting for clear parent-child relationships, but only one level deep, like /sites/{siteId}/subjects. Deep nesting, like /studies/1/sites/2/subjects/3/visits/4, gets fragile; once a resource has its own id, it can be addressed directly, like /visits/4.
Use lowercase with hyphens for multi-word names, like /return-shipments, and keep JSON property names in camelCase.
Use query parameters for filtering, sorting and paging: /shipments?status=pending&sort=-createdAt&page=2.

For actions that don't map neatly to CRUD, like cancel or dispatch, there are two reasonable choices: model it as a state change, PATCH the status, or a sub-resource action, like POST /shipments/{id}/cancel. I prefer the second when the action has its own rules and side effects, because it's clearer and easier to authorise.
Version at the start of the path if using URL versioning, like /api/v1.
And above all, be consistent across the whole API, documented in the team's API guidelines.

p17-198.q: PATCH applies a partial update, changing only some fields of a resource. There are two common formats.
p17-198.k: json patch, json merge patch, patch partial update, jsonpatchdocument, partial update api
x: PATCH applies a partial update, changing only some fields of a resource. There are two common formats.

JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7396, sends a JSON object with just the fields to change, like status equals Cancelled. Fields that aren't included stay the same, and a field set to null is removed or cleared. It's simple and intuitive for clients. The limitation is that you can't distinguish "set to null" from some other intentions, and you can't update individual array elements; arrays are replaced entirely.

JSON Patch, RFC 6902, sends a list of operations: add, remove, replace, move, copy and test, each with a path, like op replace, path /status, value Cancelled. It's more powerful, it can modify array items and include test operations that act like preconditions, but it's more complex for clients.

In ASP.NET Core, JsonPatchDocument of T supports JSON Patch. Historically it needed Newtonsoft.Json, and .NET 10 added a System.Text.Json-based implementation. I apply the patch to a DTO, not directly to the EF entity, then validate the DTO, and map the allowed fields to the entity, to prevent over-posting through patch paths.
For merge patch, I deserialise into a DTO with nullable or optional wrapper properties, so I know which fields were actually sent.
In practice, for simple partial updates, I often prefer specific endpoints, like PUT status, which are easier to validate and authorise.

p17-199.q: For data annotations, I can create my own attribute by inheriting ValidationAttribute and overriding IsValid. The method gets the value and a ValidationContext, and returns ValidationResult.Success or a ValidationResult with an error message and the member name. For example, a FutureDate attribute that checks a date is after today, or a ValidCountryCode attribute that checks against a list.
p17-199.k: custom validation attribute, validationattribute, data annotation custom, ivalidatableobject, cross field validation
x: For data annotations, I can create my own attribute by inheriting ValidationAttribute and overriding IsValid. The method gets the value and a ValidationContext, and returns ValidationResult.Success or a ValidationResult with an error message and the member name. For example, a FutureDate attribute that checks a date is after today, or a ValidCountryCode attribute that checks against a list.
The ValidationContext gives access to the whole object being validated, so I can compare with other properties, and to the service provider, though I avoid heavy dependency use inside attributes.

For rules that involve several properties, like "end date must be after start date", there are two options: a class-level attribute, or implementing IValidatableObject on the model, whose Validate method returns any number of results. ASP.NET Core runs it after the property-level attributes pass.

Once created, the attribute works anywhere data annotations work: ApiController's automatic 400 responses, Validator.TryValidateObject, options validation with ValidateDataAnnotations, and Blazor forms.

That said, for complex rules, especially ones that need the database or services, I prefer FluentValidation, because attributes can't easily do async work or use injected services cleanly, and they get hard to test once they need dependencies. Custom attributes are best for small, reusable, self-contained rules.

p17-200.q: Both let me share data between different parts of the pipeline during a single request, like a tenant id resolved in middleware and used in a controller and repository.
p17-200.k: httpcontext items, share data per request, scoped service per request, request context data, per request state
x: Both let me share data between different parts of the pipeline during a single request, like a tenant id resolved in middleware and used in a controller and repository.

HttpContext.Items is a dictionary on the HttpContext, with object keys and object values, that lives only for the current request. It's built in and quick to use. But it's untyped, so values need casting, keys can clash between components unless I use private object keys, and it ties consumers to HttpContext, which isn't available in background work or easy to set up in unit tests.

A scoped service is a class registered with AddScoped, so DI creates one instance per request. A middleware gets it injected, through InvokeAsync parameters, and sets properties, like TenantContext.TenantId. Controllers, handlers and repositories inject the same instance and read it. It's strongly typed, discoverable, easy to fake in tests, and doesn't depend on HTTP, so the same TenantContext can be filled by a message consumer for background processing.

So I use a scoped service for anything important that business code depends on, like the current user, tenant or study context, and correlation data. HttpContext.Items is fine for small, internal, web-layer-only details, like passing something between two middlewares.
One reminder: scoped services must not be captured by singletons, or they'll leak across requests.

p17-201.k: host spa with asp.net core, serve react from asp.net core, static files spa fallback, mapfallbacktofile, spa deployment
x: There are two main approaches.

Serving the SPA from the ASP.NET Core app: the front-end build output, the index.html and bundled JavaScript and CSS, is copied into wwwroot. The app uses UseStaticFiles to serve the files, and MapFallbackToFile("index.html") so that deep links, like /shipments/123, return index.html and the client-side router handles them, while /api routes go to the controllers.
