It's one deployment, one origin, so no CORS, and cookies work simply. For caching, the hashed bundle files get a long max-age, while index.html is not cached, so users get new versions after a deployment.

Serving the SPA separately: the front end is deployed to static hosting, like S3 with CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps or a CDN, and calls the API on its own domain. It's cheaper and faster to serve globally, front end and back end deploy independently, and the API stays focused on data. The costs are CORS configuration, or putting both behind one domain with path routing on the CDN.
During development, Vite or the Angular CLI dev server runs the front end with hot reload, and proxies API calls to the ASP.NET Core app, to avoid CORS.
In our IRT, the React shell is built with Vite and deployed separately, and the MVC portal links into it, sharing the Keycloak SSO session.

p17-202.q: The environment name comes from the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable, with standard values Development, Staging and Production, defaulting to Production if it's not set. IWebHostEnvironment, or IHostEnvironment for workers, exposes it, along with paths like the content root and web root.
p17-202.k: iwebhostenvironment, aspnetcore environment, development vs production, environment specific config, isdevelopment
x: The environment name comes from the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable, with standard values Development, Staging and Production, defaulting to Production if it's not set. IWebHostEnvironment, or IHostEnvironment for workers, exposes it, along with paths like the content root and web root.
Configuration uses it automatically: appsettings.json is loaded first, then appsettings.{Environment}.json overrides it, then environment variables and other sources override those.
In code, app.Environment.IsDevelopment() is typically used to enable the developer exception page, Swagger UI or detailed errors only in development.

To use it safely, I follow a few rules. The default being Production is a good thing: if someone forgets the variable, the app runs with the safest settings. I keep environment checks few and at the edges, mostly in Program.cs, and drive behaviour differences through configuration values, like a feature flag for Swagger, rather than scattering IsDevelopment checks in business code. Business logic should behave identically in every environment, otherwise testing in UAT doesn't prove production behaviour. And no secrets in appsettings.Development.json committed to the repo; local secrets go in user secrets.
I can also add custom environments, like UAT, matched with IsEnvironment("UAT"), and an appsettings.UAT.json, which fits validated release flows like ours, with separate UAT and production settings.

p17-203.q: This is a very common issue, and I check things in a fixed order.
p17-203.k: null request body, model binding null, frombody null, 415 unsupported media type, json not binding asp.net core
x: This is a very common issue, and I check things in a fixed order.

First, the Content-Type header. If the client doesn't send application/json, ASP.NET Core can't use the JSON input formatter. With ApiController, that usually gives a 415 Unsupported Media Type, but in some setups, the parameter is just null.

Second, the JSON shape versus the DTO. If the JSON doesn't match, like a wrapping object the DTO doesn't expect, a string where a number is expected, or an invalid date format, deserialisation fails. With ApiController, that returns a 400 with details in the problem details response, so I look at that response body carefully. Without ApiController, the parameter becomes null and ModelState has the error.

Third, property naming and casing. ASP.NET Core uses camelCase and case-insensitive matching by default, but custom JsonSerializerOptions may have changed that. Properties also need public setters or a matching constructor, and fields aren't bound by default.

Fourth, the binding source. A complex type in a controller with ApiController is inferred as FromBody, but without it, or for simple types, I may need FromBody explicitly. And only one parameter can be bound from the body.
Fifth, something read the body earlier, like a logging middleware without EnableBuffering.
To see what's happening, I log ModelState errors, test with a known-good request in an HTTP file or Postman, and enable debug logging for model binding.

p17-204.q: By default, System.Text.Json serialises enums as their underlying numbers, so a ShipmentStatus of Delivered becomes 3 in JSON. That's fragile and unreadable: clients must know what 3 means, and if someone reorders or inserts enum members, the numbers change and break clients silently.
p17-204.k: enum as string json, jsonstringenumconverter, enum serialization api, enum names in json, stringenumconverter
x: By default, System.Text.Json serialises enums as their underlying numbers, so a ShipmentStatus of Delivered becomes 3 in JSON. That's fragile and unreadable: clients must know what 3 means, and if someone reorders or inserts enum members, the numbers change and break clients silently.

So I usually serialise them as strings. In ASP.NET Core, I add a JsonStringEnumConverter to the JSON options: for controllers through AddJsonOptions, and for minimal APIs by configuring JsonOptions with ConfigureHttpJsonOptions. Then the JSON contains "Delivered", or "delivered" if I pass a camelCase naming policy. Incoming requests accept the string names too.

In .NET 8 and later, there's also a generic JsonStringEnumConverter of TEnum, which works with source generation and Native AOT, and I can put JsonConverter attributes on specific enums. .NET 9 added JsonStringEnumMemberName to customise individual member names.

A few related practices. Assign explicit numeric values to enum members anyway, especially if they're stored in the database, so reordering doesn't corrupt data. Document in the API that new values may be added, so clients handle unknown values gracefully. And make sure OpenAPI shows the string values, which the built-in generator does when the converter is configured.
For EF Core, storing enums as strings is a separate choice, done with HasConversion of string.

p17-205.q: Kestrel has sensible defaults, but for production I review a few limits, depending on whether Kestrel faces the internet directly or sits behind a reverse proxy.
p17-205.k: kestrel limits, max request body size, kestrel configuration, connection limits, request header limits
x: Kestrel has sensible defaults, but for production I review a few limits, depending on whether Kestrel faces the internet directly or sits behind a reverse proxy.

MaxRequestBodySize defaults to about 30 MB. I lower it for normal APIs, so nobody can send huge bodies, and raise it only for specific upload endpoints with the RequestSizeLimit attribute, or DisableRequestSizeLimit for streaming uploads to storage. Form and multipart limits are separate, in FormOptions.

Request header limits, like MaxRequestHeadersTotalSize and MaxRequestLineSize, protect against oversized headers. Sometimes I need to raise them, for example when SSO cookies or large tokens make headers bigger, which is a known cause of 400 or 431 errors.

Timeouts: KeepAliveTimeout and RequestHeadersTimeout limit slow clients holding connections open, which helps against slowloris-style attacks. MinRequestBodyDataRate and MinResponseDataRate drop connections that send or read data too slowly.
Connection limits: MaxConcurrentConnections and MaxConcurrentUpgradedConnections, for WebSockets, can cap resource use per instance.
HTTP/2 settings, like max streams per connection, exist too.

I configure these in appsettings under the Kestrel section, or in code with ConfigureKestrel, and keep them consistent with the limits on the proxy or load balancer in front, otherwise the first one to reject a request gives a confusing error.

p17-206.q: A covering index is a non-clustered index that contains every column a query needs, so SQL Server can answer the query from the index alone, without going back to the table.
p17-206.k: covering index, include columns, index include, avoid key lookup, nonclustered index include
x: A covering index is a non-clustered index that contains every column a query needs, so SQL Server can answer the query from the index alone, without going back to the table.

Normally, a non-clustered index stores the indexed key columns plus a pointer to the row. If the query needs other columns, SQL Server does a key lookup for each matching row, jumping to the clustered index to fetch them. For a few rows that's fine, but for thousands of rows, those lookups get very expensive, and the optimiser may give up on the index and scan the whole table instead.

INCLUDE columns solve this. I create an index with key columns for filtering and sorting, and add other columns with INCLUDE. For example, an index on SiteId and Status, including ShipmentDate and KitCount. The included columns are stored only at the leaf level, not in the key, so they don't affect sorting and keep the index key small, but the query is fully covered.

There are trade-offs. Every included column makes the index bigger and makes inserts and updates slower, because the index must be maintained. So I don't include everything; I cover the important, frequent queries, and check the execution plan to confirm the key lookup is gone.
[Adding one covering index to the shipment search query removed a key lookup on about 40,000 rows and cut its time from several seconds to under 200 milliseconds.]

p17-207.q: A key lookup appears in an execution plan when SQL Server uses a non-clustered index to find the matching rows, but the index doesn't contain all the columns the query needs. For each row found, it goes back to the clustered index, using the clustering key, to fetch the missing columns. On a heap, a table without a clustered index, the same thing is called a RID lookup.
p17-207.k: key lookup, rid lookup, bookmark lookup, execution plan key lookup, fix key lookup
x: A key lookup appears in an execution plan when SQL Server uses a non-clustered index to find the matching rows, but the index doesn't contain all the columns the query needs. For each row found, it goes back to the clustered index, using the clustering key, to fetch the missing columns. On a heap, a table without a clustered index, the same thing is called a RID lookup.

In the plan, it shows as an Index Seek joined with a Nested Loops to a Key Lookup. The cost is per row: one extra random read for every row. If the seek returns 10 rows, it doesn't matter. If it returns 50,000 rows, it can dominate the query's cost.

To fix it, I look at the key lookup operator's Output List, which shows exactly which columns it fetched. Then I have a few options. Add those columns to the index as INCLUDE columns, making it covering. Remove columns from the query that aren't really needed, like a SELECT star where the screen only uses four columns; in EF Core, that means projecting to a DTO with Select instead of loading whole entities. Or, if the predicate also uses columns that aren't in the key, rethink the index key order.
I also watch for the opposite problem: when the estimate is wrong, SQL Server may pick a seek plus lookup for many more rows than expected, which is often a statistics or parameter sniffing issue.

p17-208.q: Fragmentation happens as data is inserted, updated and deleted. When a page is full and a new row must go in the middle, SQL Server splits the page, moving half the rows to a new page somewhere else. Over time, the logical order of pages doesn't match their physical order, which is external fragmentation, and pages are left partly empty, which is internal fragmentation, or low page density.
p17-208.k: index fragmentation, rebuild vs reorganize, index maintenance, fill factor, page splits
x: Fragmentation happens as data is inserted, updated and deleted. When a page is full and a new row must go in the middle, SQL Server splits the page, moving half the rows to a new page somewhere else. Over time, the logical order of pages doesn't match their physical order, which is external fragmentation, and pages are left partly empty, which is internal fragmentation, or low page density.

On spinning disks, logical order really mattered for range scans. On modern SSDs and SANs, external fragmentation matters much less; low page density matters more, because more pages means more I/O and more memory used in the buffer pool.

There are two maintenance options. Reorganize is a lightweight, always-online operation that reorders leaf pages and compacts them, suitable for moderate fragmentation. Rebuild drops and recreates the index, fully defragmenting it and updating its statistics with a full scan; it can be online in Enterprise edition and Azure SQL, but it's heavier.

The old rule of thumb was reorganize between 5 and 30 percent fragmentation, and rebuild above 30. Today, many experts recommend focusing on updating statistics regularly, which often gives most of the benefit, and maintaining indexes less often, based on measured impact. Tools like Ola Hallengren's maintenance scripts handle this well.
A suitable fill factor can reduce page splits on indexes with random inserts, like GUID keys.

p17-209.q: By default, SQL Server uses read committed with locking: readers take shared locks, so a reader can be blocked by a writer holding an exclusive lock, and a writer can be blocked by readers. Under heavy mixed load, that causes blocking and sometimes deadlocks.
p17-209.k: snapshot isolation, read committed snapshot, rcsi, row versioning, readers block writers, tempdb version store
x: By default, SQL Server uses read committed with locking: readers take shared locks, so a reader can be blocked by a writer holding an exclusive lock, and a writer can be blocked by readers. Under heavy mixed load, that causes blocking and sometimes deadlocks.

Row versioning offers an alternative. When it's on, SQL Server keeps previous versions of modified rows in the version store, in tempdb, or in the database itself with Accelerated Database Recovery. Readers read the last committed version instead of waiting for locks.

Read committed snapshot isolation, RCSI, is a database setting that makes the default read committed level use versioning. Each statement sees data as it was when the statement started. Readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers. It's usually a big reduction in blocking with no code changes, and it's the default in Azure SQL Database.

Snapshot isolation is a separate level that a transaction must request explicitly. The whole transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start. If it tries to update a row that another transaction changed after the snapshot, it gets an update conflict error, so the code must handle and retry it.

The costs: more tempdb usage and a bit more overhead for updates, and some code that relied on blocking behaviour, like a read-then-update pattern, may need explicit locking hints or a different approach.

p17-210.q: WITH NOLOCK, which is the same as the READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level, tells SQL Server to read without taking shared locks and to ignore other transactions' locks. People add it to stop queries being blocked, and it does make blocking go away, but it can return wrong data.
p17-210.k: nolock, with nolock, read uncommitted, dirty reads, nolock problems, nolock hint
x: WITH NOLOCK, which is the same as the READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level, tells SQL Server to read without taking shared locks and to ignore other transactions' locks. People add it to stop queries being blocked, and it does make blocking go away, but it can return wrong data.
The obvious problem is dirty reads: reading changes from a transaction that hasn't committed and might roll back, so you see data that never officially existed.

The less obvious problems are worse. Because the scan isn't protected while pages split and rows move, a NOLOCK query can miss rows entirely, or read the same row twice. So a count or a sum can simply be wrong, even for data that wasn't being changed logically. Queries can even fail with an error about data movement.

For reports that are just approximate, like a dashboard estimate, this may be acceptable. But for anything where correctness matters, like stock levels, financial data, or clinical supply quantities, it's not acceptable.

The better fix for blocking is read committed snapshot isolation, which gives readers a consistent, committed version of the data without blocking, plus good indexes and short transactions, so locks are held briefly.
When I see NOLOCK sprinkled across old stored procedures, I treat it as a sign of a past blocking problem, and look for the real cause.

p17-211.q: SQL Server normally takes fine-grained locks, like row or page locks, so different transactions can work on different rows of the same table at the same time. But each lock uses memory. When a single statement acquires a lot of locks on one table, around 5,000, or when lock memory gets high, SQL Server converts them into a single table lock. That's lock escalation.
p17-211.k: lock escalation, row lock to table lock, escalation threshold, lock_escalation, large update blocking
x: SQL Server normally takes fine-grained locks, like row or page locks, so different transactions can work on different rows of the same table at the same time. But each lock uses memory. When a single statement acquires a lot of locks on one table, around 5,000, or when lock memory gets high, SQL Server converts them into a single table lock. That's lock escalation.

It saves memory, but a table-level exclusive lock blocks everyone else using that table until the transaction ends. So a large update or delete, like updating 100,000 rows in one statement, can suddenly block all other users, even those working on unrelated rows.

To avoid problems, I process large changes in batches, like 2,000 to 4,000 rows per transaction in a loop, so each batch stays below the escalation threshold and locks are released frequently. That's my standard approach for purges, backfills and large data fixes. Good indexes also help, because without them, a statement may scan and lock far more rows than it changes.

For partitioned tables, the LOCK_ESCALATION table option can be set to AUTO, so escalation goes to the partition level instead of the whole table. It can also be disabled for a table, but that risks high lock memory, so I rarely do that.
Monitoring tools and extended events can show when escalation happens.

p17-212.q: When users say the system is hanging, blocking is one of the first things I check.
p17-212.k: find blocking sql server, sp_whoisactive, blocking chain, head blocker, sys.dm_exec_requests, blocked process report
x: When users say the system is hanging, blocking is one of the first things I check.

For a live problem, I query sys.dm_exec_requests, which shows each running request, its wait type, how long it's been waiting, and the blocking_session_id. Following the blocking session ids leads to the head blocker, the session at the top of the chain, which is blocking others but isn't blocked itself. Then I look at what it's doing with sys.dm_exec_sql_text, and its open transactions.

The community procedure sp_WhoIsActive makes this much easier: it shows all active sessions with their SQL text, waits, blocking info, and optionally the plans and locks, in one result. Older tools like sp_who2 work too, with less detail.

Common findings: a transaction left open by application code, for example a transaction started and an exception swallowed without rollback, or a session that's "sleeping" with an open transaction; a long-running update or report without good indexes; or a query waiting for user input inside a transaction.
For recurring or past blocking, I enable the blocked process report with a threshold, like 10 seconds, and capture it with Extended Events, or use a monitoring tool.
Killing the head blocker is a last resort, because its transaction rolls back, which can take time. The real fix is shorter transactions, better indexes, or RCSI.

p17-213.q: Query Store is a SQL Server feature, on by default for new databases since SQL Server 2022 and in Azure SQL, that records the history of queries, their execution plans, and their runtime statistics, like duration, CPU, reads and executions, over time. It's like a flight recorder for query performance.
p17-213.k: query store, sql server query store, force plan, regressed queries, plan regression, query performance history
x: Query Store is a SQL Server feature, on by default for new databases since SQL Server 2022 and in Azure SQL, that records the history of queries, their execution plans, and their runtime statistics, like duration, CPU, reads and executions, over time. It's like a flight recorder for query performance.

It's very useful in a few situations. Plan regression: when a query suddenly becomes slow, Query Store shows whether its plan changed, and lets me compare the old good plan with the new bad one. I can then force the good plan as an immediate fix, while working on the root cause. Finding top resource consumers: which queries use the most CPU or I/O over a period. Comparing before and after a release or an index change. And on SQL Server 2022, automatic features like parameter-sensitive plan optimisation and query store hints build on it.
To use it, I look at the Regressed Queries and Top Resource Consuming Queries reports in SSMS, or query the catalog views directly.

[That's how we diagnosed a query that went from 200 milliseconds to 5 seconds in March 2025: Query Store showed a new plan compiled for an unusual parameter value, a classic parameter sniffing case. Forcing the previous plan fixed it within minutes, and then we fixed the query properly.]

p17-214.q: Both store intermediate results in tempdb, but they behave differently.
p17-214.k: temp table vs table variable, #temp vs @table, table variable performance, temp table statistics, tempdb objects
x: Both store intermediate results in tempdb, but they behave differently.

A temporary table, with a hash prefix like #Kits, is a real table in tempdb. It has statistics, so the optimiser can estimate row counts accurately. It can have indexes added after creation. It's visible to nested stored procedures called from the creating session. It's affected by transactions and rollbacks. And it can cause statement recompilations when its data changes significantly.

A table variable, like @Kits, is declared like a variable, scoped to the batch or procedure. It historically had no statistics, and the optimiser assumed it held one row, which led to terrible plans when it actually held thousands. Since SQL Server 2019, deferred compilation improves this by using the actual row count at first execution, but there are still no column statistics. Its data isn't rolled back by a transaction rollback, which is occasionally useful for logging. And it causes fewer recompilations.

My rule: table variables for small sets, a few hundred rows or fewer, and for passing data around simply. Temporary tables for larger intermediate results, especially when they're joined or filtered further, because good statistics matter there.
Also, table-valued parameters, which pass a set of rows from .NET to a procedure, are table variables, so the same considerations apply.

p17-215.q: A table-valued parameter lets me pass a whole set of rows from the application to a stored procedure or query in one parameter, instead of sending many separate calls or building a long IN list.
p17-215.k: table valued parameters, tvp, pass list to stored procedure, sql where in list, user defined table type
x: A table-valued parameter lets me pass a whole set of rows from the application to a stored procedure or query in one parameter, instead of sending many separate calls or building a long IN list.

First, I create a user-defined table type in SQL Server, like dbo.KitIdList with a KitId column, and a primary key if useful. The procedure declares a parameter of that type, which must be READONLY. Inside, I can join to it like any table.

From .NET with ADO.NET or Dapper, I build a DataTable, or a list of SqlDataRecord, or use Dapper's AsTableValuedParameter, and pass it as a SqlParameter with SqlDbType.Structured and the type name. EF Core can use it through raw SQL with a SqlParameter too.

The benefits are big. One round trip instead of thousands. Set-based processing in SQL, like inserting or updating many rows in one statement. Fully parameterised, so no SQL injection, and the query plan can be reused, unlike dynamic IN lists of varying lengths, which create a new plan for every different count.
For very large data, like hundreds of thousands of rows, SqlBulkCopy into a staging table is faster.
Since EF Core 8, a list Contains in LINQ is translated using OPENJSON with a single JSON parameter, which solves the varying plan problem for simple cases.

p17-216.q: A scalar user-defined function returns a single value, and is often used in a SELECT list or a WHERE clause, like dbo.GetKitStatus of KitId. It looks clean, but traditionally it has serious performance problems.
p17-216.k: scalar udf performance, scalar function slow, inline table valued function, udf inlining, function in where clause
x: A scalar user-defined function returns a single value, and is often used in a SELECT list or a WHERE clause, like dbo.GetKitStatus of KitId. It looks clean, but traditionally it has serious performance problems.

The function is executed once per row, like a hidden loop, with its own overhead for each call. If the function itself queries tables, it runs a query for every row, which is an N+1 problem inside the database. The optimiser couldn't see inside the function, so it estimated its cost poorly. And queries that use scalar functions couldn't run in parallel; the whole query was forced into a serial plan.

SQL Server 2019 introduced scalar UDF inlining, which automatically converts many simple scalar functions into inline expressions, removing much of the cost. But not every function qualifies, for example ones with certain constructs or that depend on the time, so I don't rely on it blindly.

Better alternatives: an inline table-valued function, which is a single SELECT statement returning a table. The optimiser expands it into the calling query like a view with parameters, so it's set-based and fully optimised, used with CROSS APPLY. Or put the logic directly in the query with a join or a CASE expression. Or a computed column, persisted and indexed if needed.
Multi-statement table-valued functions have similar problems to scalar ones, so I avoid them in hot paths too.

p17-217.q: A view is a stored SELECT query that acts like a virtual table. It doesn't store data itself; when I query it, SQL Server expands its definition into my query. Views are useful to simplify complex joins, to provide a stable interface to consumers, like a reporting tool, while the underlying tables change, and for security, giving users access to a view with selected columns and rows instead of the base tables.
p17-217.k: sql views, indexed view, materialized view sql server, view vs table, schemabinding view
x: A view is a stored SELECT query that acts like a virtual table. It doesn't store data itself; when I query it, SQL Server expands its definition into my query. Views are useful to simplify complex joins, to provide a stable interface to consumers, like a reporting tool, while the underlying tables change, and for security, giving users access to a view with selected columns and rows instead of the base tables.
Performance-wise, a normal view is just a query; it's as fast as the query it expands to. Views stacked on views can get hard for the optimiser, and can hide expensive joins, so I avoid deep nesting.

An indexed view, which other databases call a materialised view, has a unique clustered index, so its result is actually stored and kept up to date automatically when the base tables change. It's great for expensive aggregations that are read often, like totals of kits by site and status: the query reads pre-computed results instead of aggregating millions of rows.

But it has requirements and costs. The view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, use two-part names, and follow many restrictions, like no outer joins or certain aggregates. Every insert, update and delete on the base tables must also update the indexed view, so it slows writes, and can increase blocking.
So I use indexed views for read-heavy aggregates on tables that aren't written heavily.

p17-218.q: A trigger is code that runs automatically in the database when data changes, like AFTER INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, or INSTEAD OF a change, often used on views. Inside, the special inserted and deleted tables contain the new and old versions of the affected rows.
p17-218.k: triggers sql server, after trigger, instead of trigger, trigger pros cons, audit trigger, inserted deleted tables
x: A trigger is code that runs automatically in the database when data changes, like AFTER INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, or INSTEAD OF a change, often used on views. Inside, the special inserted and deleted tables contain the new and old versions of the affected rows.

The advantages: a trigger runs no matter how the data is changed, whether by the application, a script, a data fix or another system. That makes triggers useful for audit trails and history tables, enforcing complex integrity rules that constraints can't express, and keeping denormalised data in sync.

The disadvantages are significant. Triggers are hidden: developers reading the application code don't see them, so behaviour seems magical and debugging is harder. They run inside the same transaction, so they make every write slower and hold locks longer. A common bug is writing triggers that assume one row, when a statement can affect many rows at once, so they must be set-based. Triggers can call other triggers, creating chains that are hard to follow. And business logic in triggers is hard to test and version.
So I use triggers sparingly, mainly for audit or history capture where guaranteed coverage matters, and keep them simple and set-based. For business rules, I prefer the application layer.
For history, temporal tables are now often a cleaner alternative.

p17-219.q: System-versioned temporal tables keep a full history of every change to a table automatically. When I enable them, SQL Server adds two period columns, valid from and valid to, and creates a linked history table. Whenever a row is updated or deleted, the old version is moved to the history table with the time range it was valid for. The application doesn't need any code for this.
p17-219.k: temporal tables, system versioned tables, history table, for system_time, point in time query, audit history sql
x: System-versioned temporal tables keep a full history of every change to a table automatically. When I enable them, SQL Server adds two period columns, valid from and valid to, and creates a linked history table. Whenever a row is updated or deleted, the old version is moved to the history table with the time range it was valid for. The application doesn't need any code for this.

I can then query the data as it was at any point in time using FOR SYSTEM_TIME, like AS OF a specific date and time, or BETWEEN two times, or ALL, to see every version of a row. That's great for audits, investigating "who changed this and what was it before", recovering from accidental updates, and reports that must show data as of a past date.
EF Core supports temporal tables too: I configure IsTemporal in the model, and LINQ has TemporalAsOf, TemporalAll and similar methods.

Some limitations. The period times are in UTC, based on when the transaction started. It records what changed and when, but not who changed it or why, so for a regulated audit trail, I still need the user and the reason, usually stored in columns on the row itself. History tables can grow large, so a retention policy is needed. And schema changes need care.
In regulated systems, I see temporal tables as a solid foundation for history, combined with application-level audit information.

p17-220.q: Partitioning splits one large table into multiple partitions based on a column, usually a date, like one partition per month. To queries, it's still one table. Underneath, each partition is stored separately and can be on different filegroups.
p17-220.k: table partitioning, partition function, partition scheme, partition switching, partition elimination, large table management
x: Partitioning splits one large table into multiple partitions based on a column, usually a date, like one partition per month. To queries, it's still one table. Underneath, each partition is stored separately and can be on different filegroups.

It's mainly a data management feature, rather than a magic performance feature. The big wins are these. Partition switching: I can move a whole partition in or out of the table almost instantly, as a metadata operation. So archiving or deleting a month of old data becomes switching that partition out to an archive table, instead of a huge, slow, log-heavy DELETE. Loading data can work the same way. Maintenance per partition: index rebuilds and statistics updates can target only the recent, active partitions. And lock escalation can be set to the partition level.

For queries, partition elimination helps when the query filters on the partition column, because SQL Server only reads the relevant partitions. But if queries don't filter on it, partitioning can even make them slower, because they must check every partition. Good indexes usually matter more for query speed.

So I'd consider partitioning for very large tables, hundreds of millions of rows, with a natural time-based access pattern and data lifecycle needs, like logs, events or audit records. For normal-sized tables, it adds complexity without benefit.

p17-221.q: Sharding splits data across multiple separate databases, often on separate servers, where each shard holds a subset of the rows, based on a shard key, like tenant id or customer id. It's horizontal scaling for the database, when one server can't handle the data volume or the write load, even after scaling up, indexing and adding read replicas.
p17-221.k: sharding, database sharding, shard key, horizontal partitioning across servers, resharding, tenant sharding
x: Sharding splits data across multiple separate databases, often on separate servers, where each shard holds a subset of the rows, based on a shard key, like tenant id or customer id. It's horizontal scaling for the database, when one server can't handle the data volume or the write load, even after scaling up, indexing and adding read replicas.

Choosing the shard key is the most important decision. A good key spreads data and load evenly, and keeps related data together, so most queries hit only one shard. Tenant id is a natural choice for multi-tenant systems. A bad key creates hotspots, where one shard gets most of the traffic.

The challenges are significant. Queries across shards, like global reports, must fan out to every shard and combine results, which is slow and complex. Transactions across shards aren't available, so you need sagas or careful design. Unique constraints and joins only work within a shard. Resharding, when a shard gets too big, means moving data while the system is live. And operations, like backups, schema changes and monitoring, multiply with the number of shards.
So sharding is a last resort. Before it, I'd use caching, read replicas, archiving old data, and splitting data by service.
Database per tenant, like our database per study in IRT, is a simple form of sharding by tenant, with each study fully isolated.

p17-222.q: A read replica is a copy of the primary database that's kept up to date by replication and accepts read-only queries. Sending reporting and read-heavy queries to replicas takes load off the primary, which handles all the writes. In SQL Server, this is done with Always On availability groups and readable secondaries; in AWS, RDS and Aurora read replicas; and in Azure SQL, read scale-out.
p17-222.k: read replicas, read scale out, always on availability groups readable secondary, replica lag, read write splitting
x: A read replica is a copy of the primary database that's kept up to date by replication and accepts read-only queries. Sending reporting and read-heavy queries to replicas takes load off the primary, which handles all the writes. In SQL Server, this is done with Always On availability groups and readable secondaries; in AWS, RDS and Aurora read replicas; and in Azure SQL, read scale-out.

In the application, I use separate connection strings: one for the primary, and one with ApplicationIntent equals ReadOnly for the replica, and route queries accordingly, for example a separate read-only DbContext for reports and search.

The main pitfall is replication lag. Asynchronous replicas can be seconds behind, or more under heavy load. So if a user saves something and the next screen reads from a replica, they might not see their change, which looks like a bug. For that, I read from the primary right after a write, or route all of that user's reads to the primary for a short time.

Other pitfalls: long-running queries on a replica can be affected by or interfere with replication, depending on the database. Replicas need the same indexes, and possibly extra ones for reporting. And failover changes which server is primary, so the connection should use the listener or cluster endpoint, not a server name.
So replicas suit reports, exports and search, where slight staleness is fine.

p17-223.q: The recovery model controls how the transaction log is managed, and therefore which restore options you have.
p17-223.k: recovery model, full recovery model, simple recovery, transaction log backup, point in time restore, rpo rto database
x: The recovery model controls how the transaction log is managed, and therefore which restore options you have.

In the simple recovery model, the log is truncated automatically after checkpoints, so it doesn't grow much, but there are no log backups. You can only restore to the time of your last full or differential backup. Anything after that is lost. It's fine for development databases or data that can be easily rebuilt.

In the full recovery model, every change is kept in the log until a log backup is taken. With a chain of full, differential and regular log backups, say every 15 minutes, I can restore the database to any point in time, like just before someone ran a bad update at 10:42. That's essential for production databases with important data. The log must be backed up regularly, otherwise it grows until the disk fills, which is a classic production incident.
Bulk-logged is a variation that minimally logs bulk operations, used temporarily during large loads.
These choices connect to RPO, how much data we can afford to lose, which drives the log backup frequency, and RTO, how fast we must recover, which depends on database size and restore speed.

And backups are only real if restores are tested. I'd regularly restore to a test server to prove the backups work and measure the time it takes. In managed services like RDS or Azure SQL, point-in-time restore is built in.

p17-224.q: An implicit conversion happens when SQL Server compares two values of different data types, and silently converts one to match the other, following data type precedence rules.
p17-224.k: implicit conversion, convert_implicit, nvarchar vs varchar index, data type mismatch query, ef core varchar parameter
x: An implicit conversion happens when SQL Server compares two values of different data types, and silently converts one to match the other, following data type precedence rules.

The problem is when the conversion is applied to the column instead of the parameter. A classic example: a column is varchar, but the application sends the parameter as nvarchar, which is .NET's default for strings. nvarchar has higher precedence, so SQL Server converts every value in the varchar column to nvarchar to compare. Depending on the collation, that can turn an index seek into an index scan of the entire table, because the index is on the original varchar values. The query still returns the right result, just much slower, and CPU goes up.
In the execution plan, it shows as CONVERT_IMPLICIT, and a warning icon on the SELECT operator mentions that the conversion may affect the cardinality estimate or seek plan.

The fix is to make the types match. In EF Core, I configure the column as non-Unicode, with IsUnicode false or the column type varchar, so EF sends varchar parameters. In Dapper or ADO.NET, I specify DbType.AnsiString for varchar columns. In stored procedures, parameters should be declared with the same type and length as the columns.
Other common mismatches are numbers stored in string columns, and dates compared to strings.

p17-225.q: GUIDs are attractive as keys: they're globally unique, can be generated by the application before saving, don't reveal record counts, and make merging data from different databases easy.
p17-225.k: guid primary key, uniqueidentifier clustered index, newsequentialid, guid fragmentation, uuid v7, int vs guid key
x: GUIDs are attractive as keys: they're globally unique, can be generated by the application before saving, don't reveal record counts, and make merging data from different databases easy.

The problem is using a random GUID, from NEWID or Guid.NewGuid, as the clustered index key in SQL Server. The clustered index orders the table by its key. Random values mean each new row goes to a random place in the index, not at the end. That causes constant page splits, heavy fragmentation, lower page density, more I/O, and more memory needed to keep the active part of the index cached. It's also 16 bytes, four times an int, and the clustered key is copied into every non-clustered index, so all indexes get bigger.

Alternatives. Sequential GUIDs: NEWSEQUENTIALID in SQL Server, or sequential GUID generation in the app, like EF Core's default value generator for SQL Server, or the new UUID version 7 with Guid.CreateVersion7 in .NET 9, which is time-ordered. Inserts then go to the end, like an identity.
Or use an int or bigint identity as the clustered primary key, and add a GUID as a separate public identifier with a unique non-clustered index, so external APIs don't expose sequential ids.
For DynamoDB or distributed stores, random keys are actually good, because they spread load, so the right choice depends on the database.

p17-226.q: An identity column generates incrementing values automatically for one table when a row is inserted. It's simple and the most common choice. The application only knows the new id after the insert, which EF Core retrieves with OUTPUT. Identity values can have gaps, after rollbacks or server restarts, so they shouldn't be used where gaps matter, like invoice numbers that must be continuous.
p17-226.k: identity vs sequence, sql sequence, hilo ef core, key generation, identity gaps, sequence cache
x: An identity column generates incrementing values automatically for one table when a row is inserted. It's simple and the most common choice. The application only knows the new id after the insert, which EF Core retrieves with OUTPUT. Identity values can have gaps, after rollbacks or server restarts, so they shouldn't be used where gaps matter, like invoice numbers that must be continuous.

A sequence is an independent database object that generates numbers on request with NEXT VALUE FOR. It isn't tied to a table, so one sequence can provide ids for several tables, or for a business number like a shipment reference. I can get a value before inserting, control start, increment, cycling and caching. It also has gaps after restarts when caching is used.

HiLo is an EF Core strategy that uses a sequence efficiently. EF reserves a block of ids at once, say 10, with one round trip, and assigns them to new entities in memory. The application knows ids before saving, which helps when building object graphs, and batching inserts is more efficient, because EF doesn't need to read back generated ids one by one. The trade-off is larger gaps and ids that aren't strictly in insert order.
For business-facing numbers, like a kit or shipment number with a format and no gaps allowed, I use a separate, dedicated mechanism with proper locking, rather than relying on identity values.

p17-227.q: Soft delete means marking a record as deleted, with an IsDeleted flag and usually DeletedAt and DeletedBy columns, instead of physically removing it. It's common when data must be kept for audit, regulatory reasons or undo, which is the norm in clinical systems.
p17-227.k: soft delete ef core, isdeleted flag, global query filter soft delete, hasqueryfilter, logical delete
x: Soft delete means marking a record as deleted, with an IsDeleted flag and usually DeletedAt and DeletedBy columns, instead of physically removing it. It's common when data must be kept for audit, regulatory reasons or undo, which is the norm in clinical systems.
In EF Core, I implement it in two parts.

First, intercepting deletes. In a SaveChanges interceptor, or an override of SaveChanges, I look in the ChangeTracker for entities in the Deleted state that implement an ISoftDeletable interface, change their state to Modified, and set IsDeleted, DeletedAt and DeletedBy. So the application code just calls Remove as usual.

Second, hiding deleted rows. A global query filter, configured with HasQueryFilter of e such that not e.IsDeleted, is automatically added to every query on that entity, including Includes, so deleted records disappear without every developer remembering a Where clause. For admin or audit screens, IgnoreQueryFilters shows them. EF Core 10 adds named filters, so soft delete and tenant filters can be turned off separately.

Some gotchas. Unique constraints must allow a deleted duplicate, using a filtered unique index with WHERE IsDeleted equals 0. Related entities aren't deleted automatically, so I decide how cascades work. Performance needs indexes that include IsDeleted. And soft-deleted personal data may still need real deletion for privacy laws.

p17-228.q: When I load an entity with several collection navigations using Include, like a Shipment with its Kits and its StatusHistory, EF Core by default generates one SQL query with JOINs. The problem is that joining two independent collections multiplies the rows: a shipment with 100 kits and 20 history entries returns 100 times 20, which is 2,000 rows, each repeating all the shipment's columns. With more collections or more parent rows, the data transferred grows enormously. That's the cartesian explosion, and EF Core logs a warning about it.
p17-228.k: cartesian explosion, assplitquery, split query ef core, multiple include performance, single query vs split query
x: When I load an entity with several collection navigations using Include, like a Shipment with its Kits and its StatusHistory, EF Core by default generates one SQL query with JOINs. The problem is that joining two independent collections multiplies the rows: a shipment with 100 kits and 20 history entries returns 100 times 20, which is 2,000 rows, each repeating all the shipment's columns. With more collections or more parent rows, the data transferred grows enormously. That's the cartesian explosion, and EF Core logs a warning about it.

AsSplitQuery tells EF Core to load each collection with a separate SQL query: one for the shipments, one for the kits, one for the history, joined in memory. Total rows are 1 plus 100 plus 20, instead of 2,000. It can be enabled per query, or as the default with UseQuerySplittingBehavior.

But split queries have trade-offs. More round trips to the database. And consistency: the separate queries aren't run as one snapshot, so if data changes between them, the results can be inconsistent, unless I use a transaction with snapshot or serialisable isolation. Ordering with Skip and Take needs a unique, stable sort.

So I use single queries for one collection or small data, split queries for multiple large collections, and often the best option is projecting with Select into exactly the DTO shape the screen needs.

p17-229.q: Interceptors let me hook into EF Core's operations and inspect, change or suppress them. They're registered with AddInterceptors when configuring the DbContext, and can use dependency injection.
p17-229.k: ef core interceptors, savechangesinterceptor, dbcommandinterceptor, audit with interceptor, connection interceptor
x: Interceptors let me hook into EF Core's operations and inspect, change or suppress them. They're registered with AddInterceptors when configuring the DbContext, and can use dependency injection.

There are several types. SaveChanges interceptors run before and after SaveChanges, with access to the ChangeTracker. Command interceptors run around every SQL command, seeing the command text and parameters, and can modify them or the results. Connection interceptors run when connections open and close. Transaction interceptors run around transactions. And materialisation interceptors run when entities are created from query results.

What I've used them for. Audit fields: a SaveChanges interceptor sets CreatedBy, CreatedAt, ModifiedBy and ModifiedAt on any entity implementing IAuditable, using the current user service, so no developer has to remember. Audit trail: capturing old and new values of changed properties into audit records in the same SaveChanges. Soft delete: converting deletes into updates of an IsDeleted flag. Outbox: converting domain events raised by entities into outbox rows in the same transaction. Slow query logging: a command interceptor that logs commands taking longer than a threshold, with their duration. And connection setup: setting session context, like the tenant id, with sp_set_session_context, for row-level security.
They keep these cross-cutting concerns in one place, out of business code.

p17-230.q: Value converters transform a property's value when it's written to the database and when it's read back. I configure them with HasConversion in the model configuration.
p17-230.k: value converters, ef core hasconversion, store enum as string, strongly typed id ef core, encrypt column ef core
x: Value converters transform a property's value when it's written to the database and when it's read back. I configure them with HasConversion in the model configuration.

Common uses. Enums as strings: HasConversion of string stores "Delivered" instead of 3, which is readable in the database and safe if enum members are reordered. Strongly typed ids: a ShipmentId record struct wrapping a Guid or int, converted to the primitive for storage, so the domain model can't mix up a ShipmentId with a SiteId. Value objects: like a Money or EmailAddress type stored as a simple column. Collections or simple objects stored as a delimited string or JSON, though JSON columns are now better for that. Date handling, like storing DateTime always as UTC with the Kind restored on read. And encryption: encrypting a sensitive column on write and decrypting on read, though database-level features like Always Encrypted are often stronger.
EF Core has many built-in converters, and since EF Core 6, pre-convention model configuration can apply a converter to all properties of a type at once.

The main caveat is querying. EF translates queries using the stored values, so some operations on converted properties can't be translated to SQL, like calling methods on a value object. Comparisons for equality usually work fine, but anything more complex may fail or force client evaluation, so I test the queries I need.

p17-231.q: EF Core 7 and later can map an owned type, or a collection of owned types, to a single JSON column, using ToJson in the configuration. For example, a Study entity could store its flexible settings, or a shipment its list of temperature readings, as JSON, while the rest of the entity stays in normal columns.
p17-231.k: json columns ef core, tojson, store json in sql server, openjson, json_value, owned types json
x: EF Core 7 and later can map an owned type, or a collection of owned types, to a single JSON column, using ToJson in the configuration. For example, a Study entity could store its flexible settings, or a shipment its list of temperature readings, as JSON, while the rest of the entity stays in normal columns.

The nice part is that queries still work in LINQ. EF translates filters on JSON properties into SQL Server's JSON functions, like JSON_VALUE and OPENJSON, so I can write Where s.Settings.MaxKits greater than 10, and it becomes SQL. Updates can modify just part of the JSON. EF Core 8 added primitive collections, like a List of int stored as JSON, and SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL now have a native json data type, which is more efficient than nvarchar.

When is it a good fit? For data that's naturally a document, owned by one entity and usually read together with it: flexible attributes that vary by study or customer, configuration blobs, or small nested lists. It avoids lots of small tables and joins.

When is it a bad fit? For data that needs relational integrity, foreign keys, frequent filtering and sorting, or joins with other tables. Filtering on JSON properties can't use normal indexes unless I add computed columns with indexes on the extracted values.
So I use it selectively, not as a way to avoid designing a schema.

p17-232.q: Normally, ASP.NET Core creates a new DbContext instance for each request and disposes it at the end. Creating a DbContext is fairly cheap, but in very high-throughput services, the setup work, like initialising internal services and the change tracker, adds up.
p17-232.k: dbcontext pooling, adddbcontextpool, context pooling performance, pooled dbcontext factory
x: Normally, ASP.NET Core creates a new DbContext instance for each request and disposes it at the end. Creating a DbContext is fairly cheap, but in very high-throughput services, the setup work, like initialising internal services and the change tracker, adds up.

With AddDbContextPool instead of AddDbContext, EF Core keeps a pool of DbContext instances. When a request needs one, it takes one from the pool; at the end, the context is reset, clearing tracked entities and state, and returned to the pool for the next request. That reduces allocation and setup overhead. AddPooledDbContextFactory does the same for code that creates contexts through a factory, like background services or Blazor.

Benchmarks show measurable gains only for very high request rates with simple queries, so for many apps it's a minor optimisation. It's worth turning on when profiling shows context creation in the hot path.

The important limitation: because instances are reused, the DbContext must not hold per-request state in its own fields, like a tenant id or current user injected through the constructor, since a pooled instance could carry one request's state into another. Constructor injection of scoped services into a pooled DbContext doesn't work as usual. For multi-tenant scenarios, I set the per-request state after getting the context from the pool, using a factory or a custom approach that resets it.
Note this is different from database connection pooling, which ADO.NET does anyway.

p17-233.q: ADO.NET keeps a pool of open database connections per connection string, 100 by default. When code opens a connection, it gets one from the pool, and closing or disposing it returns it to the pool. If all connections are in use, the next request waits, and after the timeout, it fails with an error like "Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool. This may have occurred because all pooled connections were in use and max pool size was reached."
p17-233.k: connection pool exhaustion, timeout expired max pool size, connection leak, sqlconnection pool, max pool size reached
x: ADO.NET keeps a pool of open database connections per connection string, 100 by default. When code opens a connection, it gets one from the pool, and closing or disposing it returns it to the pool. If all connections are in use, the next request waits, and after the timeout, it fails with an error like "Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool. This may have occurred because all pooled connections were in use and max pool size was reached."

The common causes. Connection leaks: code that opens connections or data readers without disposing them, especially when an exception skips the close, so connections are never returned. Long-running queries or transactions holding connections for a long time. Sync-over-async or thread pool starvation, where connections are held while threads wait. A traffic spike with slow database responses, so more requests hold connections at once. And slightly different connection strings creating separate pools.

To diagnose, I check the number of connections from the app's host in sys.dm_exec_sessions, look at what those sessions are doing, and review code for missing using statements or DbContexts not disposed. EF Core and DI handle disposal correctly if contexts are scoped properly.
The fixes are disposing connections with using, shorter transactions, faster queries, and async code all the way. Increasing Max Pool Size only hides the problem, and can overload the database.

p17-234.q: Dapper is a micro-ORM: I write the SQL myself, and Dapper maps results to objects and handles parameters. It's very fast, with almost no overhead over raw ADO.NET, and gives complete control over the SQL.
p17-234.k: dapper vs ef core, micro orm, dapper performance, use both dapper and ef, raw sql vs orm
x: Dapper is a micro-ORM: I write the SQL myself, and Dapper maps results to objects and handles parameters. It's very fast, with almost no overhead over raw ADO.NET, and gives complete control over the SQL.

EF Core is a full ORM: LINQ queries translated to SQL, change tracking, relationships, migrations, concurrency handling, interceptors and much more. Developers are productive, and the code is strongly typed and refactor-friendly.
The performance gap has narrowed a lot in recent versions. EF Core with AsNoTracking and projections to DTOs is close to Dapper for most queries, so performance alone rarely decides it.

I use EF Core for most application code, especially writes, where change tracking, validation of relationships, concurrency tokens and transactions save a lot of code and mistakes, and for typical queries.

I use Dapper, or EF Core's raw SQL features like SqlQuery, when I need hand-tuned SQL: complex reporting queries with window functions or CTEs, queries against legacy stored procedures, bulk reads where every millisecond counts, or databases that EF doesn't model well.
Using both in the same service is completely fine, even sharing the same connection and transaction.
In our CIRT platform, the newer APIs use EF Core, while the legacy parts rely heavily on stored procedures with ADO.NET-style data access.

p17-235.q: EnableRetryOnFailure turns on EF Core's retrying execution strategy for SQL Server. When a command fails with a transient error, like a brief network drop, a failover, or Azure SQL throttling, EF Core waits and retries automatically, with an increasing delay, up to a maximum number of attempts. That makes the app much more resilient in cloud environments, where short blips are normal.
p17-235.k: execution strategy ef core, enableretryonfailure, retry transient sql errors, user initiated transactions not supported, sql azure transient
x: EnableRetryOnFailure turns on EF Core's retrying execution strategy for SQL Server. When a command fails with a transient error, like a brief network drop, a failover, or Azure SQL throttling, EF Core waits and retries automatically, with an increasing delay, up to a maximum number of attempts. That makes the app much more resilient in cloud environments, where short blips are normal.

The catch is transactions. If I start a transaction myself, with BeginTransaction, and a command fails in the middle, EF can't just retry that one command, because the earlier work in the transaction was rolled back. So EF Core throws an error saying user-initiated transactions aren't supported with the retrying strategy.

The fix is to wrap the whole unit of work in the strategy: get it with context.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy, and call ExecuteAsync with a delegate that begins the transaction, does all the work, saves and commits. If a transient failure happens, the strategy re-runs the entire delegate from the start, including beginning a new transaction.

That means the delegate must be safe to repeat. It should reload any data it depends on, rather than reusing state from the failed attempt, and avoid side effects outside the database, like sending an email, inside the retried block.
There's also a subtle case where the commit succeeded but the connection failed before confirming it. Making operations idempotent, or using verifySucceeded, protects against applying it twice.

p17-236.q: char is fixed-length: char(10) always uses 10 bytes, padding shorter values with spaces. It's good for values that are always the same length, like a two-letter country code or a fixed-format code.
p17-236.k: char vs varchar, varchar vs nvarchar, unicode columns, utf8 collation, column data type choice, nvarchar max
x: char is fixed-length: char(10) always uses 10 bytes, padding shorter values with spaces. It's good for values that are always the same length, like a two-letter country code or a fixed-format code.
varchar is variable-length, using only the bytes needed plus two bytes of overhead, so it's better for values of varying length, like names or descriptions.

nvarchar and nchar store Unicode, traditionally UTF-16, using two bytes per character for most text. They can store any language: Japanese, Arabic, Hindi, accented names. varchar uses a code page, so characters outside it get lost or become question marks, unless the column uses a UTF-8 collation, available since SQL Server 2019, which lets varchar store Unicode as UTF-8.

So for any text that users type, like names, addresses or comments, especially in a global system, I use nvarchar, or varchar with a UTF-8 collation. For internal codes and identifiers that are guaranteed ASCII, varchar saves space.

Other practices. Size columns realistically, not nvarchar(max) everywhere. Max types are stored differently, can't be index keys, and the declared size affects the memory grants the optimiser requests. And match the parameter types from the application to the column types, because a mismatch, like nvarchar parameters against a varchar column, can cause implicit conversions and index scans.

p17-237.q: NULL means unknown or missing, not zero and not empty string, and it follows three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL return unknown, not true or false.
p17-237.k: null in sql, count star vs count column, null comparison, is null, ansi nulls, coalesce isnull
x: NULL means unknown or missing, not zero and not empty string, and it follows three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL return unknown, not true or false.

That leads to classic surprises. WHERE Column equals NULL returns nothing; I must use IS NULL. WHERE Status not equals 'Shipped' excludes rows where Status is NULL, because NULL not equals 'Shipped' is unknown. NOT IN with a subquery that returns any NULL returns no rows at all, which is a nasty bug; NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem.

COUNT of star counts all rows. COUNT of a column counts only rows where that column isn't NULL. COUNT DISTINCT also ignores NULLs. Aggregates like SUM and AVG ignore NULLs, so AVG of a column with NULLs isn't the same as SUM divided by COUNT star. And SUM of all NULLs returns NULL, not zero, so I wrap it in COALESCE.
For defaults, COALESCE is standard SQL and accepts many arguments, while ISNULL is SQL Server-specific, takes two, and uses the first argument's data type, which can truncate values.
NULLs in unique constraints: SQL Server allows only one NULL in a unique column, unlike some databases, so a filtered unique index is used to allow many.
In design, I make columns NOT NULL unless missing values are genuinely meaningful.

p17-238.q: WHERE filters individual rows before they're grouped. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. So conditions on raw columns go in WHERE, and conditions on aggregates, like COUNT, SUM or AVG, go in HAVING.
p17-238.k: where vs having, having clause, filter aggregates, group by having, logical query processing order
x: WHERE filters individual rows before they're grouped. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. So conditions on raw columns go in WHERE, and conditions on aggregates, like COUNT, SUM or AVG, go in HAVING.

For example, to find sites with more than 50 dispensed kits this year: WHERE DispenseDate is in this year and Status equals Dispensed limits the rows first, then GROUP BY SiteId, then HAVING COUNT of star greater than 50 keeps only the groups with enough kits.

This follows the logical processing order of a query: FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, and finally TOP or OFFSET. That order also explains why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE, because SELECT hasn't happened yet, but you can use it in ORDER BY.

For performance, I put row conditions in WHERE whenever possible, not in HAVING, so fewer rows are grouped. The optimiser can often move simple HAVING conditions on grouping columns into WHERE, but writing it correctly makes intent clear and doesn't depend on that.
It's a basic question, but I've seen real bugs where a condition was put in HAVING on a non-aggregated column, or a filter on an outer-joined table in WHERE turned a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

p17-239.q: An upsert updates a row if it exists, or inserts it if it doesn't. It's very common when syncing data from external systems, like vendor shipment statuses.
p17-239.k: upsert sql server, merge statement, insert or update, merge race condition, update then insert pattern
x: An upsert updates a row if it exists, or inserts it if it doesn't. It's very common when syncing data from external systems, like vendor shipment statuses.

SQL Server's MERGE statement can do it in one statement: MERGE into the target, USING the source, ON the key, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, and optionally WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE. It's powerful for syncing a whole set of rows from a staging table.

But MERGE has a reputation for problems. It isn't safe under concurrency by default: two sessions can both see that a row doesn't exist and both try to insert, causing primary key violations, unless I add a HOLDLOCK or SERIALIZABLE hint. It has had a number of bugs over the years, especially with filtered indexes, triggers and certain features. And it's easy to write in a way that does something unexpected.

For single-row upserts, many SQL Server developers prefer an explicit pattern inside a transaction: UPDATE with UPDLOCK and SERIALIZABLE hints, and if no rows were affected, INSERT. The lock hints prevent the race. For sets of rows, an UPDATE joined to the staging table followed by an INSERT of rows that don't exist, in one transaction.
In EF Core, there's no built-in upsert yet, so for high volumes I use SQL directly or a library.

p17-240.q: SQL Server is designed for set-based operations: describing what result you want for a whole set of rows in one statement, and letting the optimiser decide how to do it efficiently, using indexes, joins, parallelism and batching.
p17-240.k: cursor vs set based, sql cursor performance, row by row processing, rbar, while loop sql
x: SQL Server is designed for set-based operations: describing what result you want for a whole set of rows in one statement, and letting the optimiser decide how to do it efficiently, using indexes, joins, parallelism and batching.

A cursor processes rows one at a time, like a loop in procedural code. Each iteration fetches a row and runs separate statements for it. People call this RBAR, "row by agonising row". For a large table, it's typically orders of magnitude slower than an equivalent set-based UPDATE or INSERT ... SELECT, because each row has its own overhead, locks are held longer, and the optimiser can't optimise the whole operation. WHILE loops that process one row at a time have the same problem.
So when I see a cursor, I try to rewrite it as one or a few set-based statements, using joins, CASE expressions, window functions like ROW_NUMBER or running totals with SUM OVER, and CTEs.

There are legitimate uses for cursors or loops. Administrative tasks that must run something per database or per object, like maintenance across many study databases. Calling a stored procedure that only works one row at a time and can't be changed. And deliberately processing in batches, which is a loop over chunks of thousands of rows, not single rows, to control locking and log growth.
If I must use a cursor, I declare it LOCAL FAST_FORWARD for lower overhead.

p17-241.q: Dynamic SQL is building a SQL statement as a string and executing it, which is sometimes necessary, like search screens with many optional filters, dynamic sorting, or administrative scripts that work across tables or databases.
p17-241.k: dynamic sql, sp_executesql, exec vs sp_executesql, dynamic search query, quotename, dynamic sql injection
x: Dynamic SQL is building a SQL statement as a string and executing it, which is sometimes necessary, like search screens with many optional filters, dynamic sorting, or administrative scripts that work across tables or databases.

The rules I follow. Use sp_executesql, not EXEC of a concatenated string. sp_executesql takes parameters separately, so user values are never part of the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection. It also allows plan reuse, because the SQL text is the same for different parameter values.

Never concatenate user input as values. Only the structure of the query is built dynamically, like adding "AND SiteId equals @SiteId" when that filter is present, and the values are always passed as parameters.

For identifiers, like table names, column names or sort direction, which can't be parameters, I validate them against a whitelist of allowed names, and wrap them with QUOTENAME to handle special characters safely.

For catch-all search queries with optional filters, building the WHERE clause dynamically with only the filters actually used often gives much better plans than one static query with "OR @Param IS NULL" conditions, which tends to produce poor, generic plans. OPTION RECOMPILE is the other alternative for those.
Dynamic SQL runs with the caller's permissions, and it's harder to read and review, so I keep it small, well commented, and print it in debug mode.

p17-242.q: In stored procedures that change data, I use a standard pattern so errors never leave a transaction half-done or open.
p17-242.k: try catch sql server, xact_abort, t sql error handling, rollback in catch, throw vs raiserror, xact_state
x: In stored procedures that change data, I use a standard pattern so errors never leave a transaction half-done or open.

At the top, SET XACT_ABORT ON, and SET NOCOUNT ON. With XACT_ABORT on, most runtime errors automatically roll back the whole transaction and abort the batch. Without it, some errors only fail the current statement, and the transaction continues, which can leave partial changes. It also matters when the client times out: the transaction is rolled back instead of staying open, holding locks.

Then BEGIN TRY, BEGIN TRANSACTION, the statements, COMMIT TRANSACTION, END TRY. And BEGIN CATCH: if there's an open transaction, checked with @@TRANCOUNT greater than zero or XACT_STATE, ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; then log the error if needed, and rethrow it with THROW, so the application knows it failed. THROW, available since SQL Server 2012, preserves the original error number and message, and is simpler than RAISERROR.
Logging inside the CATCH should happen after the rollback, otherwise the log row is rolled back too.

Nested transactions in SQL Server aren't real nested transactions: an inner COMMIT only decrements the counter, and any ROLLBACK rolls back everything. So procedures called from other procedures should be careful about starting their own transactions, or use save points.
On the .NET side, I still handle SqlException and use transactions consistently.

p17-243.q: Whenever a SQL Server task can't proceed, it waits, and SQL Server records why and for how long. Wait statistics answer the question "what is the server spending its time waiting for?", which points you to the type of bottleneck before you tune anything.
p17-243.k: wait stats, sys.dm_os_wait_stats, pageiolatch, cxpacket, lck_m waits, sql server waits tuning
x: Whenever a SQL Server task can't proceed, it waits, and SQL Server records why and for how long. Wait statistics answer the question "what is the server spending its time waiting for?", which points you to the type of bottleneck before you tune anything.

I look at sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the server overall, filtered to exclude benign background waits, and sys.dm_exec_session_wait_stats or Query Store's wait categories for specific sessions or queries.

The common ones and what they suggest. PAGEIOLATCH: waiting to read data pages from disk, which suggests not enough memory for the working set, or queries reading too much data due to missing indexes. WRITELOG: waiting for transaction log writes, so slow log storage or too many tiny commits. LCK_M waits: blocking, waiting on locks held by others. CXPACKET and CXCONSUMER: parallelism, often normal, but heavy amounts may mean large scans or a cost threshold for parallelism that's too low. SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD: CPU pressure. RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE: queries waiting for memory grants, often due to big sorts or hashes from poor estimates. ASYNC_NETWORK_IO: the client isn't consuming results fast enough, often the application reading row by row or fetching huge result sets.
Wait stats are cumulative since restart, so I compare snapshots over a time window, during the problem period, rather than reading the totals.

p17-244.q: tempdb is a shared system database used by every database on the instance for temporary tables, table variables, sorts and hashes that spill out of memory, the row version store for snapshot isolation, and some internal work. Because everything shares it, it can become a bottleneck.
p17-244.k: tempdb contention, tempdb allocation contention, pagelatch tempdb, tempdb files, tempdb spills
x: tempdb is a shared system database used by every database on the instance for temporary tables, table variables, sorts and hashes that spill out of memory, the row version store for snapshot isolation, and some internal work. Because everything shares it, it can become a bottleneck.

Allocation contention is the classic problem. When many sessions create and drop temporary objects at a high rate, they all compete for the same allocation pages, which show up as PAGELATCH waits on tempdb pages. Mitigations: multiple tempdb data files of equal size, usually one per CPU core up to eight, which modern SQL Server setup does by default; newer versions also reduced this contention a lot, and SQL Server 2019 added memory-optimised tempdb metadata.

Other tempdb problems. Spills: a sort or hash join that doesn't get enough memory writes to tempdb, which is slow, and shows as a warning in the execution plan. Fixing estimates, indexes, or the query usually helps. Version store growth: with RCSI or snapshot isolation, a long-running transaction prevents old row versions from being cleaned up, so tempdb grows. And running out of space, which can affect every database on the server.
So I monitor tempdb size and usage, keep it on fast storage, size it properly up front so it doesn't keep auto-growing, and look for queries with spills or excessive temporary object use.

p17-245.q: SQL Server records missing index suggestions when the optimiser thinks an index would have helped a query. They appear in execution plans as a green hint, and in the missing index DMVs, along with an estimated improvement. They're a useful starting point, but I never create them blindly.
p17-245.k: missing index dmv, missing index suggestion, sys.dm_db_missing_index_details, index recommendations, database tuning advisor
x: SQL Server records missing index suggestions when the optimiser thinks an index would have helped a query. They appear in execution plans as a green hint, and in the missing index DMVs, along with an estimated improvement. They're a useful starting point, but I never create them blindly.

The limitations. Suggestions are made per query, without considering other indexes, so you often get several overlapping suggestions that should be combined into one. They don't consider the cost of maintaining the index on inserts and updates. The key column order isn't always ideal; equality columns are listed before inequality columns, but not ordered by selectivity. They often include many INCLUDE columns, sometimes nearly the whole table. They ignore filtered indexes and columnstore options. And the DMVs reset when the server restarts.

My approach: look at the suggestion together with the actual query and its execution plan, check existing indexes on the table to see if one can be extended instead of adding a new one, consider the write load on that table, design the index with the right key order and only the needed included columns, test it on a copy with realistic data, and then deploy it through the normal database change process.
After deploying, I verify that the query uses it and check index usage stats later, removing indexes that are never used.

p17-246.q: A query with LIKE '%term%' can't use a normal index, because of the leading wildcard, so it scans the whole table, and it can't handle word forms, relevance ranking or multiple terms well.
p17-246.k: full text search sql server, contains freetext, like wildcard performance, elasticsearch vs sql, search engine
x: A query with LIKE '%term%' can't use a normal index, because of the leading wildcard, so it scans the whole table, and it can't handle word forms, relevance ranking or multiple terms well.

SQL Server full-text search builds a special full-text index of words in text columns. Queries use CONTAINS for precise word and phrase searches, including prefix searches like "ship*", word forms through inflection, and proximity; and FREETEXT for meaning-based searching. CONTAINSTABLE and FREETEXTTABLE return relevance ranks. It handles stop words and language-specific word breaking, and the index is updated automatically in the background as data changes. Azure SQL supports it too.
It's a good choice when the search is part of a transactional application, the data is already in SQL Server, and requirements are moderate, like searching notes, descriptions or document text.

A dedicated search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, is better when search is a core feature: typo tolerance and fuzzy matching, faceted navigation, rich relevance tuning, autocomplete, searching across data from many services, very large volumes, or semantic and vector search.
