The cost is another system to run and keep in sync, usually through events or change data capture, with eventual consistency.
So I start with what the database offers, and move to a search engine when the requirements clearly need it.

p17-247.q: SSDT, SQL Server Data Tools, uses a declarative, state-based approach. The database project contains the desired definition of every object: tables, views, procedures, indexes, as CREATE scripts in source control. Building the project validates all the references and produces a dacpac, a package describing the target schema.
p17-247.k: ssdt, dacpac, sql database project, sqlpackage, state based migrations, database ci cd
x: SSDT, SQL Server Data Tools, uses a declarative, state-based approach. The database project contains the desired definition of every object: tables, views, procedures, indexes, as CREATE scripts in source control. Building the project validates all the references and produces a dacpac, a package describing the target schema.

At deployment, SqlPackage compares the dacpac with the actual database and generates a script to make the database match: adding columns, altering procedures, creating indexes. Pre-deployment and post-deployment scripts handle data changes, like populating a new column or seeding reference data, and they must be written to be safely re-runnable.

In the pipeline, the build creates the dacpac as an artifact. The release first generates the deployment script, or a deploy report, for review, which is important in regulated environments, and then publishes it to each environment, with publish profiles setting options like BlockOnPossibleDataLoss, which stops the deployment if a change would drop data.

The advantages: the full schema is always visible in source control, drift is detected, and the same package can be deployed to many databases. The risks: automatically generated scripts can do expensive things, like rebuilding a large table to change column order, so reviewing the generated script matters.
Our CIRT platform uses SSDT database projects, and the same model schema is deployed to every study database.

p17-248.q: A single DELETE of millions of rows is risky. It runs as one huge transaction, so the transaction log grows enormously, it can escalate to a table lock and block all users, it can take a very long time, and if it's cancelled, the rollback takes just as long.
p17-248.k: delete millions of rows, purge old data, archive data sql, batch delete, data retention job
x: A single DELETE of millions of rows is risky. It runs as one huge transaction, so the transaction log grows enormously, it can escalate to a table lock and block all users, it can take a very long time, and if it's cancelled, the rollback takes just as long.

So I do it in batches. A loop deletes, for example, 5,000 rows at a time, using DELETE TOP of 5,000 with a condition on an indexed column, like a date, and continues until no rows are affected. Each batch is its own short transaction, so locks are released quickly, below the escalation threshold, and log space can be reused between log backups. Sometimes I add a short delay between batches to reduce the impact on other users, and run it during quiet hours.

For archiving, each batch first copies rows to the archive table and then deletes them, in the same transaction, often using DELETE with an OUTPUT clause into the archive table, which does both in one statement.
For tables that are partitioned by date, switching out an old partition is almost instant, which is much better for regular retention.

Other points: make sure the delete condition uses an index, check for foreign keys and cascades, which can multiply the work, and consider regulatory retention rules. In clinical systems, data often must be kept for many years, so archiving is more common than deleting.

p17-249.q: Both are mature, powerful relational databases, and EF Core supports both well, with Npgsql as the PostgreSQL provider.
p17-249.k: sql server vs postgresql, postgres vs mssql, npgsql, postgresql for dotnet, switch to postgres
x: Both are mature, powerful relational databases, and EF Core supports both well, with Npgsql as the PostgreSQL provider.

Licensing and cost: PostgreSQL is open source and free, which makes it very attractive in the cloud, like RDS, Aurora PostgreSQL or Azure Database for PostgreSQL. SQL Server has licence costs, especially Enterprise edition.

Features where they differ. PostgreSQL has excellent JSON support with jsonb and GIN indexes, arrays as a column type, rich extensions like PostGIS and pgvector for vector search, and partial and expression indexes. SQL Server has strong tooling, like SSMS, Query Store, and SQL Server Agent for jobs, built-in columnstore, in-memory OLTP, and deep integration with Windows and Microsoft tools.

Behaviour differences that bite during migration. Identifiers: PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lowercase, so naming conventions matter. Case-sensitive string comparison by default in PostgreSQL. Different concurrency internals: PostgreSQL uses MVCC by default, similar to SQL Server's snapshot isolation, and needs VACUUM to clean up old row versions. Stored procedure language, T-SQL versus PL/pgSQL, so procedures must be rewritten. Data types like datetime2 versus timestamp with time zone, and identity versus serial or identity columns.
Our CIRT core runs on SQL Server, while the developer RAG index uses PostgreSQL with pgvector.

p17-250.q: SELECT star returns every column of a table, and in application code, it causes several problems.
p17-250.k: select star, avoid select *, select all columns problem, select specific columns, projection performance
x: SELECT star returns every column of a table, and in application code, it causes several problems.

Performance: it reads and sends more data than needed, over the network and into memory. Wide columns, like large text or binary columns, make this much worse. It also prevents covering indexes from being used, because no non-clustered index includes every column, so SQL Server must do key lookups or scan the clustered index.

Fragility: if someone adds a column to the table later, the query returns it automatically. Code that relies on column order breaks, views defined with SELECT star don't pick up changes consistently until refreshed, and an INSERT ... SELECT star can fail or put data in the wrong columns.
Security: new sensitive columns can leak into results, logs and APIs without anyone deciding they should.
Readability: it's not clear which columns the code actually uses.

In EF Core, loading entire entities is the same thing. For read-only screens, I project with Select into a DTO with only the needed columns, which EF translates into a SELECT of just those columns, often making a big difference.
SELECT star is fine for ad hoc queries while exploring data, and EXISTS of SELECT star in a subquery is fine, because the columns aren't actually returned.

p17-251.q: A transaction holds its locks until it commits or rolls back. The longer it runs, the more damage it can do.
p17-251.k: long running transaction, open transaction problems, transaction log growth, blocking long transaction, keep transactions short
x: A transaction holds its locks until it commits or rolls back. The longer it runs, the more damage it can do.
Blocking: other sessions that need the locked rows, pages or tables wait, so the application slows down for many users, and deadlocks become more likely.
Transaction log growth: the log can't be truncated past the oldest active transaction, so a transaction left open for hours makes the log grow until the disk fills, even with regular log backups.
Version store growth: with snapshot isolation or RCSI, old row versions in tempdb can't be cleaned up while an old transaction might need them, so tempdb grows.
Recovery and rollback time: if it fails or the server restarts, rolling it back takes a long time, and the database may take longer to recover.
Replication and availability group lag can also increase.

Common causes in applications: doing slow work inside a transaction, like calling an external API, sending an email or waiting for user input; processing a huge batch in one transaction; or a bug where an exception skips the commit and the connection stays open with the transaction.

So I keep transactions as short as possible: prepare and validate data before starting, only include the database writes that must be atomic, do external calls outside, process large changes in batches, and monitor for old open transactions with DBCC OPENTRAN or DMVs.

p17-252.q: A normal, rowstore index stores data row by row. A columnstore index stores data column by column, in compressed segments of around a million rows.
p17-252.k: columnstore index, clustered columnstore, analytics sql server, batch mode, reporting performance, olap vs oltp
x: A normal, rowstore index stores data row by row. A columnstore index stores data column by column, in compressed segments of around a million rows.

That's ideal for analytics: queries that scan many rows but only a few columns, like summing quantities by site and month over millions of shipments. The query reads only the needed columns, the data is highly compressed, often 10 times smaller, and SQL Server processes it in batch mode, handling many rows per operation, which makes aggregations dramatically faster. Segment elimination also skips segments that can't match the filter.

There are two main uses. A clustered columnstore index makes the whole table columnar, which is right for data warehouse fact tables and large history or log tables that are mostly appended and aggregated. A non-clustered columnstore index on a transactional table enables real-time operational analytics: the OLTP workload uses the normal rowstore indexes, while reports use the columnstore, without a separate warehouse.
The trade-offs: they're poor for single-row lookups and frequent small updates, because updates are handled through a delta store and deleted bitmaps, and need maintenance to stay efficient.

So I'd consider a non-clustered columnstore for heavy reporting on a big transactional table, and clustered columnstore for warehouse or history tables. For example, aggregating supply and dispensing history for forecasting reports is a typical fit.

p17-253.q: Both are SQL Server features for finding out what changed in tables, so other systems can sync or react, without adding timestamp columns or triggers everywhere.
p17-253.k: change data capture, cdc sql server, change tracking, debezium, stream database changes, sync data changes
x: Both are SQL Server features for finding out what changed in tables, so other systems can sync or react, without adding timestamp columns or triggers everywhere.

Change Tracking is lightweight. It records that a row changed, the primary key and the type of change, plus a version number, but not the old or new values. A consumer asks "what changed since version X?", then reads the current values from the table. It's synchronous with the transaction, has low overhead, and is great for syncing caches, mobile clients or search indexes, where only the latest state matters.

Change Data Capture is richer. It reads the transaction log asynchronously and records the full history of changes in change tables: inserts, deletes, and the before and after values of updates, with the order of operations. It's suited to auditing, data warehouse loading, and streaming changes to other systems. Tools like Debezium read CDC and publish each change as an event to Kafka, which is a common way to implement the outbox pattern or feed other services without changing application code.

The trade-offs: CDC uses more storage, needs SQL Server Agent jobs for capture and cleanup on-premise, and adds some latency and operational work. Change Tracking is simpler but loses intermediate values.
So: Change Tracking for "give me what's changed so I can sync", CDC for "give me every change, with history".

p17-254.q: There are a few ways, and the right one depends on the kind of data.
p17-254.k: ef core seed data, hasdata, seeding reference data, useseeding, migration data seeding, lookup tables seed
x: There are a few ways, and the right one depends on the kind of data.

HasData, in the model configuration, defines seed rows for an entity, with explicit primary key values. EF Core includes inserts, updates and deletes for that data in migrations, comparing with the previous model. It works well for small, stable reference data, like statuses, country codes or types, that should be identical in every environment. Its limitations: keys must be hard-coded, it can't depend on data already in the database, and changes to large seed sets create noisy migrations.

EF Core 9 added UseSeeding and UseAsyncSeeding, configured on the DbContext options, which run custom seeding code when EnsureCreated or Migrate runs. That's more flexible: it can check whether data exists first and use any logic.

Custom migration code with migrationBuilder.Sql, or a post-deployment script in a database project, is another option, especially when the data change must happen at a precise point in the schema evolution.
For test data and local development, I keep it separate from reference data, in a seeding tool or test fixtures, never in production migrations.

In regulated systems, reference data changes are part of the validated release, reviewed like code. Configuration that differs per study or customer isn't seed data at all; it belongs in configuration tooling, like our Admin console.

p17-255.q: Row-level security lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who is running the query, without changing the queries.
p17-255.k: row level security, rls sql server, security policy predicate, tenant isolation database, session_context
x: Row-level security lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who is running the query, without changing the queries.

I create an inline table-valued function, the predicate, that returns a row when access is allowed, like when the row's TenantId equals the tenant id stored in the session context. Then I create a security policy that applies the function as a filter predicate on the table, so SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE silently only see allowed rows, and optionally a block predicate, which prevents inserting or updating rows into another tenant.

For applications that connect with one shared database login, the user or tenant identity is set per connection with sp_set_session_context, for example through an EF Core connection interceptor right after the connection opens, and the predicate reads it with SESSION_CONTEXT.
It's a strong defence in depth for multi-tenant databases: even if a developer forgets a WHERE clause, or a reporting tool queries the table directly, data from other tenants isn't exposed.

The cautions. The predicate runs for every query, so it must be simple and backed by indexes, otherwise performance suffers. Session context must be reset correctly on pooled connections. Admin and maintenance processes need a way to bypass it safely. And it isn't a replacement for authorization in the application, which still decides what each user may do.

After any of these, Angular runs change detection to update the view. That's why, in classic Angular, changing a component property inside a click handler or an HTTP callback just works, without calling anything.

These remove a lot of boilerplate for the common "reload data when a filter changes" pattern, and avoid race conditions from slower responses arriving after faster ones.
They're still evolving, so I check their stability status for the Angular version in use.

My general approach: signals for synchronous state and templates, RxJS for complex async event streams, and these functions at the boundary.

The Angular team now recommends inject, and there's a migration schematic to convert constructor injection. For unit tests, both work the same way with TestBed.

p17-264.q: Angular has a tree of injectors, and where a service is provided decides how many instances exist and who shares them.

At the top is the environment injector hierarchy. providedIn root in the Injectable decorator registers a singleton for the whole app, and it's tree-shakable: if nothing injects it, it's removed from the bundle. Services provided in an application's providers, or in a lazy-loaded route's providers, live in environment injectors. A lazy route with its own providers gets its own child injector, so a service provided there is a separate instance for that feature.

Then there's the element injector hierarchy, following the component tree. If a component lists a service in its providers array, each instance of that component gets its own instance of the service, shared with its children, and destroyed with the component. That's useful for state that belongs to one part of the screen, like a form wizard's state service or one editor instance per tab. viewProviders limits visibility to the component's own view, not projected content.

When a component injects something, Angular searches up the element injectors first, then the environment injectors, until it finds a provider. Modifiers change the search: Optional, Self, SkipSelf and Host, which are options on the inject function.
A common bug is accidentally providing a "global" service in a component's providers, creating separate instances and making shared state look broken.

p17-267.q: An auth interceptor adds the access token to outgoing requests, and handles expired tokens transparently.
p17-267.k: token refresh interceptor, 401 retry angular, refresh token interceptor, queue requests during refresh, httpinterceptorfn auth

The flow: the interceptor attaches the bearer token to requests going to our API, and only to our API's URLs, never to third-party domains. If a response comes back 401, it tries to refresh the token, and on success, retries the original request with the new token. If the refresh fails, it logs the user out and redirects to the login page.

The tricky part is concurrency. A screen often fires several requests at once, and they might all get 401 at the same time. Without care, each one triggers its own refresh, and with refresh token rotation, the second refresh uses an already-used refresh token and fails, logging the user out. So the interceptor keeps a single in-flight refresh: a flag plus a BehaviorSubject, or a shared Observable with shareReplay. The first 401 starts the refresh; other requests wait for it with filter and take of one, then retry with the new token.

Other details: don't intercept the refresh call itself, to avoid loops; retry each request only once; and refresh proactively before expiry when possible, which avoids most 401s. Libraries like angular-auth-oidc-client or keycloak-angular handle much of this.
In our apps, the Keycloak adapter refreshes tokens before expiry, and the interceptor attaches the current token.

It's needed when the output depends on something other than the input reference, like a mutable array that changes internally, or external state. The async pipe is the famous impure pipe. Impure pipes must be very cheap, otherwise they slow the whole page.
Often a better alternative to an impure pipe is immutable data, or a computed signal.

Automatic subscription management: it subscribes when the component is rendered and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so there are no memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions. It works well with OnPush change detection, because it marks the component for check whenever a new value arrives, so the view updates even though no input changed. And it leads to a declarative style: the component exposes streams, and the template consumes them, without manual subscribe calls that copy values into component fields.

A few things to watch. Each async pipe on the same Observable creates a separate subscription, so for an HTTP Observable used in several places, I'd cause several HTTP calls. The fix is to subscribe once with @if, using the as syntax to alias the value, or to share the stream with shareReplay. Errors in the stream need handling with catchError in the component, otherwise the subscription ends.

With signals, toSignal plays a similar role: it converts the Observable to a signal once, and the template reads it without a pipe. In newer code, I often use that, but the async pipe remains a perfectly good pattern, especially in existing RxJS-heavy apps like our older Angular sub-apps.

It's useful when I need to apply logic to several elements without adding a wrapper div that would break the layout or CSS, like inside a table row or a flex container. It's the key to customisable components. For example, a reusable data table component can accept an ng-template for how to display a cell, through a content child query or an input. The table renders that template for each row with ngTemplateOutlet, passing the row as context. The consumer controls the cell markup, and the table controls the layout, sorting and paging.

p17-276.q: Angular scopes component styles so a component's CSS doesn't leak out and affect other components. The ViewEncapsulation setting controls how.

Emulated is the default. Angular adds unique attributes to the component's elements and rewrites its CSS selectors to include those attributes, so styles only apply inside that component's template. ShadowDom uses the browser's real Shadow DOM, giving true isolation, but global styles, like a design system's base styles, don't reach inside. None makes the component's styles global, which is occasionally used for theme files, but it risks conflicts.

Special selectors: :host styles the component's own host element, like making it display block, and :host with a class lets the component react to a class on itself. :host-context applies styles based on an ancestor, like a dark theme class higher up.

To style inside a child component, especially third-party ones like Angular Material, people use ::ng-deep, which disables encapsulation for that rule. It's deprecated, though still widely used, because there's no full replacement. Better options are the child component's inputs, CSS custom properties, which pass through encapsulation, or the library's theming APIs.

In a large app, I keep component styles small, use a shared design system for consistency, and rely on CSS variables for theming. We keep the Angular sub-apps visually consistent with the React shell through shared design tokens.

p17-277.q: Server-side rendering means the Angular app runs on the server, in Node.js, and returns fully rendered HTML for the requested page. It used to be called Angular Universal. Since Angular 17, SSR is built into the CLI: ng new with the ssr option, or ng add @angular/ssr. Prerendering, or static site generation, renders pages at build time for content that doesn't change per request.

Hydration is what happens next in the browser. Instead of throwing away the server HTML and re-rendering everything, which caused flicker, Angular reuses the existing DOM and attaches event listeners and state to it. Full hydration has been stable since Angular 16. Event replay captures clicks that happen before hydration finishes and replays them. Incremental hydration, in Angular 19 and later, hydrates @defer blocks only when triggered, reducing JavaScript work further.

The challenges: code must not touch browser-only objects, like window or localStorage, during server rendering, so I guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender, and HTTP data fetched on the server is transferred to avoid fetching it twice.
For internal, login-only business apps like ours, SSR adds little, so we don't use it; it matters most for public, content-heavy sites.

p17-279.q: Angular officially supports upgrading one major version at a time, so going from 8 to 17 is nine steps, not one jump. I'd plan it as a project.

First, preparation. Make sure there's a good test suite and an end-to-end smoke test, because each step needs verifying. Check the third-party libraries, since they're usually the real blocker: each library needs a version compatible with each Angular version, and some are abandoned, so they must be replaced. Also check the Node.js and TypeScript versions each Angular version needs.

Then, step by step, using the Angular Update Guide at angular.dev/update, which lists the changes for each version pair. For each version, run ng update for @angular/core and @angular/cli, which applies automatic migrations to the code, then update other Angular packages like Material, fix compile errors, run tests, and commit. Keeping each step in its own commit or branch makes problems easy to isolate.

The big milestones along the way: Ivy becoming the only engine in version 12 and 13, which removed View Engine and broke old libraries; the removal of IE11 support; strict typed forms in 14; standalone components in 14 and 15; and the builder change to esbuild and the new control flow in 17. Those later features are optional migrations, which I'd do after the upgrade itself.
Our older sub-apps are on Angular 8 and 12, and the plan has been to move modules to React rather than upgrade them all.

p17-280.q: This is a common pattern in modernisation: the legacy MVC application keeps its layout, menu and authentication, while specific pages host a modern Angular sub-application.
p17-280.k: angular in mvc, embed angular in razor page, angular sub app, angular hybrid mvc, angular inside legacy app
x: This is a common pattern in modernisation: the legacy MVC application keeps its layout, menu and authentication, while specific pages host a modern Angular sub-application.

The Angular app is built separately with the Angular CLI, producing JavaScript and CSS bundles. The MVC view for that page includes the bundles with script and link tags, and contains the root element, like a custom app-root tag, where Angular bootstraps. Settings that the Angular app needs, like the API URL, the current study, the user's culture or an anti-forgery token, can be passed from the server into the page, for example as a JSON block or data attributes that the app reads at startup.

Routing needs care. Either the Angular app uses hash-based routing, so it doesn't conflict with MVC routes, or MVC routes all sub-paths of that page to the same view, and Angular's base href is set to that page's path.
Authentication is shared: if the MVC site uses cookies, the Angular app calls the same site's APIs and the cookie is sent automatically, with anti-forgery protection; or both use SSO and tokens.
Styles must not clash with the MVC site's global CSS, so encapsulation and prefixed classes help.
Deploying means copying the Angular build output into the MVC site, ideally with hashed file names for cache busting.
Our legacy portal hosts Angular 8 and 12 sub-apps in this way, for screens like the advanced subject view and the material forecasting dashboard.

p17-281.q: NgRx is a Redux-style state management library for Angular, built on RxJS.
p17-281.k: ngrx, ngrx store, ngrx effects, ngrx selectors, redux in angular, ngrx actions reducers
x: NgRx is a Redux-style state management library for Angular, built on RxJS.

The store holds the application state as one immutable object tree. Components never change it directly. Instead, they dispatch actions, which are plain objects describing events, like "Shipments Page Opened" or "Shipment Cancelled", created with createAction or grouped with createActionGroup.

Reducers are pure functions that take the current state and an action and return a new state, created with createReducer and on handlers. They contain no side effects, so state changes are predictable and easy to test.

Selectors read and derive data from the store, created with createSelector. They're memoised, so derived values, like "pending shipments for the selected site", are recalculated only when their inputs change. Components use store.select, or selectSignal to get a signal.

Effects handle side effects, like API calls. An effect listens for specific actions, calls a service, and dispatches a success or failure action with the result, typically using switchMap or exhaustMap and catchError. The reducers then update the state from those actions.
Redux DevTools show every action and state change, with time-travel debugging, which is very helpful.

The downside is boilerplate and indirection. For simple apps or local component state, it's overkill, and services with signals are enough. It pays off in large apps with lots of shared state and complex async flows, and with several developers needing consistent patterns.

p17-282.q: NgRx SignalStore is a newer, lighter state management approach from the NgRx team, built on Angular signals instead of RxJS and the Redux pattern.
p17-282.k: ngrx signalstore, signal store, signalstate, withstate withmethods, ngrx signals, lightweight state angular
x: NgRx SignalStore is a newer, lighter state management approach from the NgRx team, built on Angular signals instead of RxJS and the Redux pattern.

I create a store with signalStore and compose it from features: withState defines the initial state, which becomes signals for each property; withComputed adds derived signals; withMethods adds methods that update the state with patchState, or perform async work, using rxMethod for RxJS-based flows or plain async functions; and withHooks runs logic on init and destroy. There are also reusable features, like withEntities for collections with ids, and community features for things like devtools and request status.
The store is an injectable service, provided at the root for global state or at a component level for local, feature-specific state, which is a nice flexibility.

Compared with the classic NgRx store: there are no actions, reducers and effects as separate files, so there's far less boilerplate; components call methods directly; it's signal-based, so it works naturally with OnPush, zoneless change detection and signal inputs; and it's more modular, with stores per feature rather than one global tree. The trade-off is less of the strict event-driven traceability that actions give, though NgRx has added an events plugin for those who want it.
For new Angular apps, I'd start with SignalStore or simple signal-based services, and use the classic store only where the Redux pattern adds clear value.

p17-283.q: In RxJS, when an Observable errors, the stream terminates. No more values come through, and in a long-lived stream, like a search box or a polling feed, a single error stops it working until the page is reloaded. That's the most common RxJS bug.
p17-283.k: rxjs error handling, catcherror, retry rxjs, error kills observable, retry with delay, finalize rxjs
x: In RxJS, when an Observable errors, the stream terminates. No more values come through, and in a long-lived stream, like a search box or a polling feed, a single error stops it working until the page is reloaded. That's the most common RxJS bug.

catchError intercepts the error and returns a replacement Observable: a fallback value, like an empty array, with of; or EMPTY to complete silently; or a rethrow of a friendlier error with throwError. The key trick for long-lived streams is to put catchError inside the inner Observable, within switchMap, not at the end of the outer stream. Then only that one request fails, and the outer stream keeps listening for the next search term.

retry resubscribes to the source after an error, a number of times. Since RxJS 7, retry accepts a config with count and a delay function, which allows exponential backoff, like retry with count 3 and delay of a timer based on the retry count. I only retry for transient errors, like network failures or 503, not 400 or 404.
finalize runs when the stream completes, errors or is unsubscribed, which is useful for turning off a loading spinner.
In Angular, HTTP errors can also be handled centrally in an interceptor, for logging, notifications or redirects on 401, while components handle errors specific to their screens.

p17-284.q: These all combine multiple Observables, but they emit at different times.

forkJoin waits until all source Observables complete, then emits once with the last value from each. It's like Promise.all, and it's the right choice for running several HTTP calls in parallel and using all the results together, like loading a site, its inventory and its users before showing a page. If any source errors, the whole thing errors, and if any source never completes, forkJoin never emits, so it's not for long-lived streams.

combineLatest emits whenever any source emits, after each source has emitted at least once, giving the latest value from each. It's for combining ongoing streams, like filters: when the status filter, the date range or the search term changes, recalculate the results with the latest of all three. A common surprise is that nothing emits until every source has emitted once, so startWith helps.

withLatestFrom is driven by one primary stream: when the primary emits, it combines that value with the latest value of the others, but the others emitting doesn't trigger anything. It's ideal for "when the user clicks save, take the current form value and selected site".
zip pairs values by index: the first from each, then the second from each, and so on. It's rarely needed, mostly when values correspond one to one.
With signals, computed covers many of combineLatest's use cases more simply.

p17-285.q: A typeahead calls an API as the user types, so it needs to avoid flooding the server and handle responses arriving out of order.

I start with a stream of the input's values, from a reactive form control's valueChanges, or a signal converted with toObservable. Then a pipeline of operators.
debounceTime of about 300 milliseconds waits until the user pauses typing, so we don't call the API for every keystroke.
map to trim the text, and filter out terms that are too short, like fewer than two characters, perhaps returning an empty result for those.
distinctUntilChanged skips the call if the term is the same as last time, like when the user types a letter and deletes it.

switchMap calls the search API. Its key feature is that when a new term arrives, it unsubscribes from the previous request, and Angular's HttpClient cancels it. So a slow response for an old term can never overwrite the results for the newer term. That's the race condition people get with mergeMap or plain promises.
Inside switchMap, catchError returns an empty result on failure, so one failed request doesn't kill the stream, and I can track loading state with a signal or startWith.
The template shows the results with the async pipe, or a signal from toSignal.
On the server side, the search endpoint should be fast, limited and indexed, because even with debouncing, it gets called a lot.

p17-286.q: A cold Observable starts producing values separately for each subscriber. Angular's HttpClient calls are cold: each subscription sends a new HTTP request. So if a template has two async pipes on the same HTTP Observable, or two components subscribe to the same service method's result, the request is sent twice.
p17-286.k: hot vs cold observable, shareReplay, share rxjs, multicast, duplicate http calls angular, cache http observable
x: A cold Observable starts producing values separately for each subscriber. Angular's HttpClient calls are cold: each subscription sends a new HTTP request. So if a template has two async pipes on the same HTTP Observable, or two components subscribe to the same service method's result, the request is sent twice.

A hot Observable produces values regardless of subscribers, and all subscribers share the same source, like DOM events, a WebSocket stream, or a Subject. Late subscribers miss earlier values, unless the stream replays them.

share and shareReplay turn a cold Observable into a shared, hot one. share multicasts to all current subscribers through one subscription to the source. shareReplay also replays the last N values to new subscribers, so shareReplay with bufferSize 1 is the common way to cache an HTTP result: the first subscriber triggers the request, and everyone after gets the cached value without a new call.

The pitfalls. With the old shareReplay of 1 signature, the source subscription stays alive even when all subscribers leave, which can leak for long-lived sources; using the config with refCount true unsubscribes when there are no subscribers left. A cached error or stale value stays cached, so I need a way to refresh, like a Subject that triggers reloading. And caching in a root service means data persists across the whole session.
For simple shared state, a signal or BehaviorSubject in a service is often clearer.

p17-287.q: Rendering thousands of rows with a simple loop creates thousands of DOM elements and component instances, which makes initial rendering slow, scrolling janky, and change detection expensive.
p17-287.k: virtual scroll angular, cdk virtual scroll, large list performance angular, render thousands of rows, infinite scroll angular

The main techniques. Virtual scrolling: the Angular CDK's cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport, with the cdkVirtualFor directive, only renders the rows visible in the viewport plus a small buffer, and recycles them as the user scrolls. The list can have 50,000 items, but only about 30 are in the DOM. It works best with a fixed row height, set with itemSize; variable heights are harder. Data grids like AG Grid have virtualisation built in, including columns.

Server-side paging or infinite scrolling: often the user doesn't need all items at once, so loading pages on demand, with filters and search on the server, is better than sending everything to the browser.

Reducing the work per row: OnPush change detection on row components, a proper track expression in @for so rows are reused when data refreshes, pure pipes instead of method calls in templates, and avoiding heavy components inside each row, like rendering a dropdown only when a row is edited.
Using @defer for parts of each row that aren't immediately needed.
I'd measure with Angular DevTools' profiler and the browser's performance panel to see whether the time goes to change detection or DOM rendering.
[Our material forecasting dashboard was the kind of screen where server-side paging and OnPush made the difference.]

p17-288.q: Angular has a built-in i18n system. I mark text in templates with the i18n attribute, and in code with the $localize tagged template. Locale data also drives the built-in date, number, currency and percent pipes, and plural and select expressions handle grammar rules.

Then the build produces a separate compiled version of the app per locale, with translations baked in. Locale data also drives the built-in date, number, currency and percent pipes, and plural and select expressions handle grammar rules.

The advantage of the built-in approach is performance: translations are compiled in, so there's no runtime lookup cost. The disadvantages: a separate build and deployment per language, usually served under a path like /fr/, and switching language means loading a different version of the app, a full page reload.

Runtime libraries, like Transloco or the older ngx-translate, load translation files at runtime and translate with a pipe or directive. One build serves all languages, and users can switch language instantly. The cost is a small runtime overhead and less compile-time checking. Many business apps choose this for its flexibility.

Either way, I keep dates and numbers in neutral formats in the data, format them in the UI with the user's locale, think about right-to-left languages for layouts if needed, and avoid concatenating translated fragments, because word order differs between languages.

p17-289.q: Angular's router gives a component access to the current route's information through ActivatedRoute: route parameters, like the id in /shipments/:id; query parameters, like ?status=pending; the fragment; resolved data; and static data defined on the route.

There are two ways to read them. The snapshot, like route.snapshot.paramMap.get of id, gives the value at the moment the component was created. That's fine if the component is always recreated when the parameter changes. But Angular reuses the component when navigating from /shipments/1 to /shipments/2 within the same route, so the snapshot becomes stale. Route parameters, query parameters and resolver data are then bound directly to component inputs with the same name. p17-290.q: With lazy-loaded routes, each feature's code is downloaded only when the user navigates to it. That keeps the initial bundle small, but the first navigation to a feature waits for its chunk to download, which feels slow on poor networks.
p17-290.k: preloading strategy, preloadallmodules, custom preloading strategy, lazy loading preloading, quicklink angular
x: With lazy-loaded routes, each feature's code is downloaded only when the user navigates to it. That keeps the initial bundle small, but the first navigation to a feature waits for its chunk to download, which feels slow on poor networks.
Preloading downloads lazy-loaded route chunks in the background after the app has loaded and become interactive, so later navigation is instant, while initial load stays fast.

Angular has built-in strategies. NoPreloading, the default, only loads on demand. PreloadAllModules preloads every lazy route once the app is stable. That's simple and works for small to medium apps, but in large apps it downloads a lot of code that many users never need, wasting bandwidth.

A custom preloading strategy gives more control. I implement PreloadingStrategy, and decide per route, for example preloading only routes marked with data preload true, the ones most users visit, or only routes the current user's role can access, or skipping preloading on slow connections using the Network Information API. Libraries like ngx-quicklink preload routes whose links are currently visible on the screen, which is a smart middle ground.
It's configured with withPreloading in provideRouter for standalone apps.
Route-level @defer and canMatch guards complement this: canMatch prevents users from downloading features they're not allowed to use.

p17-291.q: This error appears in development mode when a value bound in a template changes after Angular has already checked it during the same change detection cycle. Typical causes. A child component, or a lifecycle hook like ngAfterViewInit, changes a property on the parent that the parent's template already rendered. For example, a child emits an event in ngOnInit that sets the parent's title. A getter or method in the template that returns a new value each time, like new Date or a new object or array, so the second check sees a different value. Or a service shared between parent and child that's updated during rendering.

The fix is to correct the data flow rather than hide the error. Move the logic earlier, like into ngOnInit or the constructor, so the value is set before the view is checked. Avoid updating parent state from a child's lifecycle hooks; instead let the parent compute it, or restructure into a shared service or signal that's set before rendering. Make template expressions stable, using computed signals or pure pipes instead of methods that create new objects.
Workarounds like setTimeout or calling detectChanges again make the error go away, but they hide a design problem and cause an extra render, so I use them only as a last resort.

p17-292.q: When an Angular screen feels sluggish, I want to know whether the time goes to change detection, rendering, or our own code.

Angular DevTools, the browser extension, is the first tool. The component explorer shows the component tree with inputs, outputs and state. The profiler records change detection cycles while I interact with the app: it shows how many cycles ran, what triggered them, and how much time each component took. Common findings: a mousemove or scroll listener, or a setInterval, triggering change detection constantly; one expensive component, often with a method call in the template that does heavy work; or the whole tree being checked because nothing uses OnPush. The browser's Performance panel adds the full picture: scripting versus rendering versus layout, long tasks, and memory.

The fixes follow from what I find. OnPush on components, so they're only checked when inputs change or events happen inside them. Signals, which allow more targeted updates. Running noisy events outside the Angular zone with NgZone.runOutsideAngular, or moving to zoneless. Pure pipes or computed signals instead of template methods. Proper tracking in @for loops. And @defer or virtual scrolling for heavy parts.
I always measure before and after, because guesses about performance are often wrong.

Smaller bundles matter for users on slow hospital or clinic networks, which is a real consideration for site users.

p17-295.q: Both are methods on ChangeDetectorRef, used when Angular doesn't automatically notice a change, typically with OnPush components.
