x: Both are methods on ChangeDetectorRef, used when Angular doesn't automatically notice a change, typically with OnPush components.

markForCheck marks the current component and all its ancestors up to the root as dirty, so they'll be checked in the next change detection cycle. It doesn't run change detection immediately. It's the right tool when an OnPush component's state changed because of something Angular didn't see, like a value pushed from a service subscription, or a callback from a third-party library. The async pipe calls markForCheck internally, which is why it works with OnPush.

detectChanges runs change detection immediately and synchronously, but only for this component and its children. It's useful when I need the view updated right now, for example before measuring the DOM, or for a component that I've detached from the change detection tree with detach, which I then update manually for performance, like a component that redraws only on a timer. Calling it at the wrong time, like during another change detection cycle, can cause errors.
There's also checkNoChanges, used in dev mode for verification.

In modern Angular with signals, these are needed much less: when a signal read in a template changes, Angular marks the component for check automatically. When I find myself calling them often, it usually means state should be in signals or Observables used with the async pipe.

p17-296.q: I split components into two kinds, which makes features easier to test, reuse and change.
p17-296.k: smart vs dumb components, container presentational, angular component design, feature structure angular, reusable components angular
x: I split components into two kinds, which makes features easier to test, reuse and change.

Smart components, or containers, know about the application. They inject services or stores, load data, handle routing parameters, call APIs and decide what happens on user actions. They usually correspond to a page or a major section, like ShipmentListPage. Their templates mostly compose presentational components and pass data down.

Presentational components, or dumb components, only know about their inputs and outputs. They receive data through inputs, render it, and emit events through outputs when the user does something, like ShipmentTable emitting a cancelClicked event with the shipment id. No services, no HTTP, no store access. That makes them easy to reuse in different contexts, easy to test with simple inputs, and ideal for OnPush change detection, since they only change when inputs change.

A feature folder typically contains the routes, the page-level smart components, the presentational components, the feature's data service or store, and its models. Shared, generic UI components, like buttons, dialogs and form fields, live in a shared library or the design system.

I don't follow it dogmatically: a small component with one simple service call doesn't need splitting. But for anything substantial, keeping data logic separate from display pays off, especially when the same table or form appears in several places.

p17-297.q: By default, when the user navigates away from a route, Angular destroys its component, and when they come back, it creates a new one. Any state in the component, like the scroll position, filters, an expanded row, or data already loaded, is lost, and data is fetched again.
p17-297.k: route reuse strategy, routereusestrategy, keep component state on navigation, cache route component, tabs keep state angular
x: By default, when the user navigates away from a route, Angular destroys its component, and when they come back, it creates a new one. Any state in the component, like the scroll position, filters, an expanded row, or data already loaded, is lost, and data is fetched again.

A RouteReuseStrategy lets me customise this. It's a class with methods that the router calls during navigation: shouldDetach decides whether to keep a route's component when leaving it; store saves the detached component tree; shouldAttach and retrieve decide whether to restore a stored component when navigating back; and shouldReuseRoute decides whether to reuse the current component when navigating between two URLs that match the same route config.

A common use is a list-detail flow: the user filters a long list, opens a detail page, and comes back, expecting the list exactly as it was. By detaching and storing the list route, it reappears instantly with its state. Another is a tabbed interface where each tab is a route.

There are pitfalls. Stored components stay in memory, with their subscriptions active, so I need to limit what's stored and clear it, for example on logout. Lifecycle hooks like ngOnInit don't run again on reattach, so components may need to refresh data explicitly.
Often a simpler solution is keeping filter state in the URL's query parameters, or in a service or store, so a new component can restore it.

p17-298.q: An attribute directive changes the appearance or behaviour of an existing element, without adding or removing elements. I create a class with the Directive decorator and a selector in square brackets, like appAutofocus or appHighlightOverdue, and apply it as an attribute.
p17-298.k: custom attribute directive, hostlistener, hostbinding, host property directive, autofocus directive, directive example angular
x: An attribute directive changes the appearance or behaviour of an existing element, without adding or removing elements. I create a class with the Directive decorator and a selector in square brackets, like appAutofocus or appHighlightOverdue, and apply it as an attribute.
Inside, I can inject ElementRef to access the host element, and Renderer2 to change it in a platform-safe way, which also works with server-side rendering.

HostListener subscribes to events on the host element or globally on the window or document. For example, a directive that listens for paste events on an input and strips spaces from pasted kit numbers, or one that closes a dropdown on a document click outside it.
HostBinding binds a property of the host element to a directive property, like adding a CSS class, class.overdue, when an input date is in the past, or setting attr.aria-label.

In modern Angular, the recommended approach is the host property in the Directive decorator, like host colon with class.overdue mapped to isOverdue(), and click mapped to onClick of $event, instead of the decorators, which keeps all host bindings in one place and works well with signal inputs.
Directive composition, with hostDirectives, lets a component include existing directives in its own host, so behaviours like focus handling or tooltips can be reused.
Directives are a great way to package small behaviours, like autofocus, input masks, permission checks or click-outside detection, once and use them everywhere.

p17-299.q: A classic bug: a component fetches data in useEffect based on a prop, like the selected site id. The user switches from site A to site B quickly. Both requests are in flight, and if A's response arrives after B's, the component shows site A's data while site B is selected.
p17-299.k: useeffect race condition, abortcontroller react, useeffect cleanup fetch, stale response react, ignore flag useeffect
x: A classic bug: a component fetches data in useEffect based on a prop, like the selected site id. The user switches from site A to site B quickly. Both requests are in flight, and if A's response arrives after B's, the component shows site A's data while site B is selected.
The fix is the effect's cleanup function. React runs the cleanup before running the effect again, and when the component unmounts. There are two common patterns.

An ignore flag: inside the effect, declare let ignore equals false, and in the cleanup, set ignore to true. When the response arrives, only update state if ignore is still false. The stale response is simply discarded.

AbortController, which is better: create a controller in the effect, pass controller.signal to fetch, or to axios through its signal option, and call controller.abort in the cleanup. The outdated request is actually cancelled, saving bandwidth, and the aborted promise rejects with an AbortError, which I ignore rather than showing as an error.
The cleanup also prevents setting state after unmount.

Honestly, though, in real apps I avoid hand-written fetching in effects. Libraries like TanStack Query or RTK Query handle caching, deduplication, race conditions, retries and loading states for me, keyed by the query parameters. Effects are better kept for synchronising with external systems.

p17-300.q: In React 18 and later, when a component is wrapped in StrictMode, React deliberately mounts it, unmounts it, and mounts it again in development. So every effect runs, its cleanup runs, and it runs again. Render functions are also called twice. This only happens in development; production builds run effects once.
p17-300.k: strictmode double render, useeffect runs twice, react 18 strict mode effects, double api call development, strict mode react
x: In React 18 and later, when a component is wrapped in StrictMode, React deliberately mounts it, unmounts it, and mounts it again in development. So every effect runs, its cleanup runs, and it runs again. Render functions are also called twice. This only happens in development; production builds run effects once.

The purpose is to surface bugs early. React is moving towards features, like preserving state when components are hidden and shown again, where components may be mounted and unmounted multiple times. If an effect doesn't clean up properly, like a subscription that isn't removed, a timer that isn't cleared, or an event listener that's added twice, the double invocation exposes it as duplicate behaviour. Double rendering exposes impure render functions that have side effects.

So the right response is not to disable StrictMode, but to make effects resilient: every effect that sets something up should return a cleanup that tears it down, and the effect should work correctly when run twice. For data fetching, the abort or ignore pattern handles it, and the second request is the one that counts. For things that truly must happen once per app, like initialising analytics, I do them outside components, at module level, or guard with a ref.
The duplicate API call in development looks alarming in the network tab, but it's expected, and libraries like TanStack Query deduplicate it anyway.

p17-301.q: Both run after React has updated the DOM, but at different moments.
p17-301.k: uselayouteffect vs useeffect, layout effect, measure dom react, flicker react, useinsertioneffect
x: Both run after React has updated the DOM, but at different moments.

useEffect runs after the browser has painted the screen. It doesn't block painting, so the user sees the update quickly. It's the right default for most side effects: data fetching, subscriptions, logging, timers and syncing with external systems.

useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints. The browser waits for it to finish. It's for cases where I need to read the layout and change something before the user sees it, otherwise there would be a visible flicker. The typical example is positioning a tooltip or popover: measure the target element's position and size with getBoundingClientRect, then set the tooltip's position. With useEffect, the tooltip would first render in the wrong place and then jump.
Because it blocks painting, heavy work in useLayoutEffect makes the UI feel slow, so I keep it small and only use it when there's a real flicker problem.
On the server, during server-side rendering, layout effects don't run, and React used to warn about it, so components using it need care in SSR apps.
There's also useInsertionEffect, which runs even earlier, before layout effects, and is meant only for CSS-in-JS libraries to inject styles.
In practice, I use useEffect almost always, and useLayoutEffect a few times a year.

p17-302.q: React.memo makes a component skip re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props. It's useful for expensive components that re-render often with the same props, like rows in a large list or a heavy chart.
p17-302.k: react memo not working, react.memo pitfalls, memo with object props, unnecessary memo, when to use react memo
x: React.memo makes a component skip re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props. It's useful for expensive components that re-render often with the same props, like rows in a large list or a heavy chart.
But it often doesn't help, for a few reasons.

New object, array or function props on every render. If the parent passes style equals an object literal, items equals data.filter of something, or onClick equals an arrow function, those are new references every time, so the shallow comparison always fails, and memo does nothing except add comparison cost. The fix is useMemo for derived objects and arrays, and useCallback for functions, or moving constants outside the component.
Children as props. JSX children are new elements on every render, so a memoised component that receives children re-renders anyway.
Context. If the component uses a context that changes, it re-renders regardless of memo.
Its own state or hooks changing triggers re-renders too; memo only affects re-renders caused by the parent.
And sometimes it's simply not needed: if the component is cheap, re-rendering costs less than the memo bookkeeping. React's rendering is fast, and re-rendering isn't the same as DOM updates.
So I measure first with the React DevTools Profiler, and memoise where it shows a real cost. The React Compiler, now stable, does much of this memoisation automatically.

p17-303.q: Batching means React groups several state updates into a single re-render, instead of re-rendering after each one. If a click handler calls setLoading, setData and setError, React renders once with all three changes, which is faster and avoids showing intermediate, inconsistent states.
p17-303.k: automatic batching, react 18 batching, setstate batching, multiple setstate one render, flushsync
x: Batching means React groups several state updates into a single re-render, instead of re-rendering after each one. If a click handler calls setLoading, setData and setError, React renders once with all three changes, which is faster and avoids showing intermediate, inconsistent states.

Before React 18, batching only happened inside React event handlers. Updates inside promises, setTimeout, native event listeners or other async callbacks weren't batched, so after an API call, setting three state values caused three separate renders.

React 18 introduced automatic batching: with the new createRoot API, all updates are batched, regardless of where they come from, including async callbacks, timeouts and promises. Apps get fewer renders without any code change. Note that apps still using the old ReactDOM.render, like React 17 apps upgraded without switching to createRoot, keep the old behaviour.

In rare cases, I need an update to be applied immediately, for example to read the updated DOM right after setting state, like scrolling to a newly added item. flushSync forces React to apply the updates inside it synchronously. It hurts performance, so it's used sparingly.

A related point: because of batching, state isn't updated immediately after calling the setter; the new value is available on the next render. For updates based on the previous value, I use the functional form, setCount of c such that c plus one.

p17-304.q: These are concurrent features from React 18 that keep the UI responsive when an update triggers expensive rendering.
p17-304.k: usetransition, usedeferredvalue, concurrent rendering react, starttransition, non urgent updates, keep ui responsive
x: These are concurrent features from React 18 that keep the UI responsive when an update triggers expensive rendering.

The idea is to separate urgent updates, like typing in an input, which must feel instant, from non-urgent ones, like filtering a large list based on that input, which can lag slightly. React can interrupt rendering of a non-urgent update if something urgent happens, and work on it in the background.

useTransition gives me a startTransition function and an isPending flag. I wrap the expensive state update in startTransition: the input's own state updates immediately, while the filtered list update is a transition. If the user keeps typing, React abandons the outdated render. isPending lets me show a subtle loading indicator. In React 19, transitions can also wrap async functions, called Actions, which track pending state across the whole async operation.

useDeferredValue gives a deferred version of a value: it lags behind the real value during heavy rendering. I pass the deferred value to the expensive child, ideally memoised, so the input stays responsive while the child catches up. It's useful when I don't control where the state is set, for example the value comes from props.
Neither makes the work itself faster; they just prioritise it. If filtering 50,000 items is slow, virtualisation or server-side filtering is still the real fix.

p17-305.q: Suspense lets a component "wait" for something before rendering, and shows a fallback UI, like a spinner or skeleton, from the nearest Suspense boundary above it, until the content is ready.
p17-305.k: react suspense, suspense data fetching, suspense fallback, suspense boundaries, use hook react 19, suspense query
x: Suspense lets a component "wait" for something before rendering, and shows a fallback UI, like a spinner or skeleton, from the nearest Suspense boundary above it, until the content is ready.
It started with React.lazy for code splitting: a lazily loaded component suspends while its JavaScript chunk downloads, and the Suspense boundary shows the fallback.

For data, a component suspends when it reads data that isn't ready yet. Under the hood, the data source throws a promise; React catches it, shows the fallback, and retries rendering when the promise resolves. Application code doesn't do this manually. Suspense-enabled data libraries do: TanStack Query's useSuspenseQuery, RTK Query with suspense patterns, Relay, and frameworks like Next.js. React 19's use hook can read a promise passed in, typically created by a framework or a parent, and suspend until it resolves.

The benefits: components can assume data is available, without loading checks everywhere; loading states are coordinated declaratively by where boundaries are placed, so one skeleton can cover a whole section, or separate ones per widget; and with server rendering, content can stream in as it becomes ready.
Errors aren't handled by Suspense; they go to the nearest error boundary, so I pair them.
A pitfall is creating promises during render without caching, which causes infinite suspending, which is why libraries manage this.

p17-306.q: React 19, released in December 2024, focused on making async data mutations and forms simpler.
p17-306.k: react 19 features, useactionstate, useoptimistic, use hook, react actions, ref as prop react 19
x: React 19, released in December 2024, focused on making async data mutations and forms simpler.

Actions: functions that run inside a transition, including async functions. React tracks the pending state, errors and optimistic updates for them automatically. A form element can take a function as its action prop, so submitting the form calls the function with the FormData, and React handles the pending state and resets the form after success.

useActionState wraps an action and gives back the current state, like the result or an error message from the last submission, a wrapped action to pass to the form, and an isPending flag. It removes a lot of boilerplate around loading and error state for submissions.
useFormStatus lets a child component, like a submit button, read whether its parent form is pending, without prop drilling.
useOptimistic shows an optimistic value immediately while an async action runs, like showing a new comment instantly, and automatically reverts to the real state when the action finishes or fails.
use reads a resource during render: a promise, suspending until it resolves, or a context, and unlike other hooks, it can be called conditionally.

Other changes: ref is now a normal prop for function components, so forwardRef is no longer needed; Context can be used directly as a provider; document metadata, like title tags, can be rendered in components; and better error reporting.
Our shell is on React 17, so using these would follow an upgrade.

p17-307.q: React Server Components are components that run only on the server. They render to a special serialised format that's streamed to the browser, and their own code is never sent to the client. They can be async functions that directly access databases, the file system or internal APIs, and secrets stay on the server.
p17-307.k: react server components, rsc, server components vs client components, use client directive, next.js app router
x: React Server Components are components that run only on the server. They render to a special serialised format that's streamed to the browser, and their own code is never sent to the client. They can be async functions that directly access databases, the file system or internal APIs, and secrets stay on the server.

Client components are the familiar kind, marked with the "use client" directive at the top of the file. They're sent to the browser, hydrated, and can use state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs.

The two are combined in one tree: server components fetch data and render the static parts, and pass data as props into client components for the interactive parts. Server Functions, marked "use server", let client components call server-side functions, like for form submissions, without writing an API endpoint.

The benefits: smaller JavaScript bundles, because server-only code and heavy libraries used for rendering stay on the server; faster initial loads, since data fetching happens close to the data; no client-server request waterfalls; and simpler data access.

The trade-offs: they need a framework with a server, most commonly the Next.js App Router, plus a new mental model about which code runs where, and props passed to client components must be serialisable.

For a single-page app like our React shell, built with Vite and served as static files with .NET APIs, Server Components don't apply directly. They make most sense for content-heavy, public-facing apps.

p17-308.q: The React Compiler is a build-time tool, a Babel plugin, that automatically memoises components and hooks. It analyses the code, understands which values depend on which props and state, and inserts memoisation so that components, calculations and callbacks are only recomputed when their inputs actually change. It reached its stable 1.0 release in October 2025, after being used in production at Meta.
p17-308.k: react compiler, auto memoization react, react forget, babel plugin react compiler, do we still need usememo
x: The React Compiler is a build-time tool, a Babel plugin, that automatically memoises components and hooks. It analyses the code, understands which values depend on which props and state, and inserts memoisation so that components, calculations and callbacks are only recomputed when their inputs actually change. It reached its stable 1.0 release in October 2025, after being used in production at Meta.
The result is similar to wrapping things in React.memo, useMemo and useCallback everywhere it matters, but done correctly and automatically, without cluttering the code or missing dependencies.

So in projects using the compiler, most manual useMemo and useCallback calls become unnecessary, and new code can be written more simply. They still work and can remain, for example where a memoised value is used as an effect dependency and the exact identity must be guaranteed, or for precise control.

The compiler relies on the code following the Rules of React: components and hooks must be pure during render, props and state must not be mutated, and hooks must be called unconditionally. Code that breaks these rules is skipped, so the compiler's ESLint plugin is useful to find violations. Adopting it in an existing codebase is usually done gradually, directory by directory, with testing.
It works with React 19 natively, and with React 17 and 18 through a runtime package, so even our React 17 shell could adopt it later.

p17-309.q: Create React App used to be the standard way to start a React project, but it's been deprecated since early 2025, and it was slow for large projects because it bundled everything with webpack, even in development.
p17-309.k: vite vs webpack, vite vs create react app, why vite, vite dev server, esbuild rollup vite, cra deprecated
x: Create React App used to be the standard way to start a React project, but it's been deprecated since early 2025, and it was slow for large projects because it bundled everything with webpack, even in development.

Vite works differently in development. It serves source files as native ES modules directly to the browser, and only transforms the files the browser requests, using esbuild, which is written in Go and extremely fast. So the dev server starts almost instantly, regardless of project size, and hot module replacement updates the browser in milliseconds after a change. Dependencies are pre-bundled once.

For production, Vite builds optimised bundles with Rollup, or Rolldown in newer versions, with code splitting, tree shaking, hashed file names and CSS handling. Configuration is much simpler than webpack's, and there's a large plugin ecosystem. It supports TypeScript, JSX, CSS modules and environment variables out of the box, and has library mode for building packages.
webpack is still powerful and very flexible, and is used in many existing projects and tools, like Module Federation's original implementation, but it's more complex to configure and slower.
Vitest, a test runner built on Vite, shares the same configuration and is very fast.
Our React shell and feature packages use Vite, and developer experience improved a lot compared with older webpack-based setups.

p17-310.q: Vite loads environment variables from .env files: .env for all modes, .env.development and .env.production for specific modes, and .local variants that aren't committed to Git. Only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to the client code, as import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL. There are also built-ins like import.meta.env.MODE, DEV and PROD. For TypeScript, I declare the variables in a vite-env.d.ts file, so they're typed.
p17-310.k: vite env variables, import.meta.env, vite_ prefix, env files vite, runtime config react, mode vite
x: Vite loads environment variables from .env files: .env for all modes, .env.development and .env.production for specific modes, and .local variants that aren't committed to Git. Only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to the client code, as import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL. There are also built-ins like import.meta.env.MODE, DEV and PROD. For TypeScript, I declare the variables in a vite-env.d.ts file, so they're typed.
The important thing to understand is that these values are replaced at build time. They're baked into the JavaScript bundle as plain strings. That leads to two pitfalls.

Secrets: anything with the VITE_ prefix is visible to anyone who opens the browser's developer tools. So only public values belong there, like API URLs and public client ids, never API keys or secrets.

Build once, deploy many: if the API URL is baked in, I need a different build for each environment, which means production doesn't run the exact artifact tested in UAT. In regulated environments, that's a real concern. The workaround is runtime configuration: the app fetches a config.json at startup, or the server injects a small script that sets window variables, and the deployment pipeline writes the correct values per environment.
Our React shell uses Vite environment variables for things like the API and Keycloak URLs.

p17-311.q: A portal renders a component's children into a different DOM node, outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy, using createPortal of the JSX and a target element, often document.body or a dedicated modal-root element.
p17-311.k: react portals, createportal, modal portal, render outside root, tooltip overflow hidden
x: A portal renders a component's children into a different DOM node, outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy, using createPortal of the JSX and a target element, often document.body or a dedicated modal-root element.

The main use is overlays: modals, dialogs, tooltips, dropdown menus and toasts. If a modal is rendered inside a deeply nested component, CSS can break it. A parent with overflow hidden can clip it, a parent with a transform or a lower z-index stacking context can make it appear behind other content, and positioning becomes complicated. Rendering it directly under body avoids all of that.

The nice part is that a portal still behaves like a normal child in React's tree. It receives props and context from its React parent, like the theme or the current user, and events bubble up through the React tree, not the DOM tree. So a click inside the modal still reaches onClick handlers on the React ancestors, which is sometimes surprising and needs stopPropagation.

Accessibility needs care with portals: focus should move into the modal when it opens, be trapped inside while it's open, and return to the triggering element when it closes; the rest of the page should be hidden from screen readers; and Escape should close it.
In practice, component libraries like MUI handle this: MUI's Dialog, Popover and Menu use portals and manage focus internally.

p17-312.q: A ref gives direct access to a DOM element or a component instance, for things like focusing an input, scrolling, measuring, or integrating with non-React libraries.
p17-312.k: forwardref, ref as prop react 19, useimperativehandle, expose methods from child component, focus input from parent
x: A ref gives direct access to a DOM element or a component instance, for things like focusing an input, scrolling, measuring, or integrating with non-React libraries.

Before React 19, a function component couldn't receive a ref as a normal prop. If a parent wanted to focus an input inside my custom TextField component, I had to wrap the component in forwardRef, which passed the ref as a second argument, and attach it to the inner input. Reusable component libraries used forwardRef everywhere.

In React 19, ref is just a regular prop for function components. The component accepts ref in its props and passes it to the inner element, and forwardRef is no longer needed, and will be deprecated in a future version.

useImperativeHandle customises what the parent gets through the ref. Instead of exposing the whole DOM node, the component exposes a small, controlled API, like an object with focus, clear or scrollToRow methods. For example, a data grid component might expose scrollToRow and resetFilters, while keeping its internal DOM private.

But it's an escape hatch. React's normal data flow is props down and events up, and most things that look like "call a method on the child", like opening or closing a dialog, are better expressed as props, like an open prop. I use imperative handles for genuinely imperative actions, like focus, scrolling, playing media or triggering animations.

p17-313.q: All three are ways to reuse logic across components, and they reflect React's history.
p17-313.k: higher order component, hoc vs hooks, render props, reuse logic react, withauth hoc, custom hooks vs hoc
x: All three are ways to reuse logic across components, and they reflect React's history.

A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra props or behaviour, like withAuth of Dashboard, which checks authentication, or Redux's old connect. They work, but they have problems: wrapper hell with many nested wrappers in DevTools, unclear where a prop comes from, prop name collisions between HOCs, and awkward TypeScript types.

Render props pass a function as a prop, or as children, and the component calls it with its data, like a MouseTracker with a render prop receiving the mouse position. They're more explicit than HOCs, but create deeply nested JSX, sometimes called callback pyramids.

Custom hooks, since React 16.8, replaced most uses of both. A hook like useAuth, useDebounce or useShipments encapsulates stateful logic, and any component calls it directly and gets the values. There's no extra component in the tree, it's clear where values come from, they compose easily, and TypeScript types are simple.

So today, I use custom hooks by default. HOCs still have a place for wrapping components with cross-cutting behaviour at the route level, like requiring a permission to render a page, and render props or children-as-a-function are still useful for flexible UI components where the consumer controls rendering, like a virtualised list's row renderer.

p17-314.q: Compound components are a set of components that work together to form one UI element, sharing state implicitly, while letting the consumer arrange them freely. The classic HTML example is select and option. In React, think of Tabs with Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel, or an Accordion with Accordion.Item, Accordion.Header and Accordion.Content.
p17-314.k: compound components, compound component pattern react, tabs component pattern, context compound component, flexible component api
x: Compound components are a set of components that work together to form one UI element, sharing state implicitly, while letting the consumer arrange them freely. The classic HTML example is select and option. In React, think of Tabs with Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel, or an Accordion with Accordion.Item, Accordion.Header and Accordion.Content.

The parent component holds the shared state, like which tab is active, and provides it through a React context. The child components read the context to know whether they're active and to change the state, like a Tab calling setActive on click. The consumer writes clean, declarative JSX, putting the pieces where they want, adding custom elements between them, without passing state or callbacks manually.
The benefits: a flexible API without dozens of configuration props, like tabsConfig arrays with render functions; clear structure in the JSX; and the component's internal state stays hidden.

Some details. The children should give a helpful error if used outside their parent, by checking for a missing context. The parent can support both uncontrolled use, with internal state, and controlled use, with value and onChange props. And accessibility is handled inside, like ARIA roles and keyboard navigation for tabs.
MUI and headless libraries like Radix use this pattern widely, and it's how I build reusable UI pieces in a design system.

p17-315.q: Prop drilling is passing data through several layers of components that don't use it themselves, just so a deeply nested child can receive it. For example, the current user passed from App to Layout to Sidebar to Menu to MenuItem. It makes intermediate components noisy, tightly coupled, and harder to refactor.
p17-315.k: prop drilling, avoid prop drilling, pass props many levels, context vs composition, component composition react
x: Prop drilling is passing data through several layers of components that don't use it themselves, just so a deeply nested child can receive it. For example, the current user passed from App to Layout to Sidebar to Menu to MenuItem. It makes intermediate components noisy, tightly coupled, and harder to refactor.
There are several solutions, and I choose based on the situation.

Composition first. Often the intermediate components can accept children or element props, so the parent renders the deep component directly and passes it down as a ready-made element. The data then only goes where it's used. This is underused and very effective.

Context, for data that many components at different levels need, which changes infrequently: the current user, theme, locale, permissions, or the selected study. It's built in and simple, but every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so I keep contexts small and focused, and memoise the value.
A state management library, like Redux Toolkit or Zustand, for application state that's shared widely and updated often, because components subscribe to just the slice they need through selectors.
A server-state library, like TanStack Query or RTK Query, for API data. Any component can call the same query hook, and it gets cached data, so there's no need to pass fetched data down at all.
Passing props one or two levels is fine and explicit; I don't treat every prop as drilling.

p17-316.q: When a context's value changes, every component that consumes that context re-renders, even if it only uses a small part of the value. React.memo doesn't stop it.
p17-316.k: context performance, context re render, split context, usememo context value, context selector, context vs redux performance
x: When a context's value changes, every component that consumes that context re-renders, even if it only uses a small part of the value. React.memo doesn't stop it.

Common pitfalls. Passing an object literal as the value, like value equals user and setUser in braces. That's a new object on every render of the provider, so all consumers re-render whenever the provider re-renders, even if nothing changed. The fix is to memoise the value with useMemo.

Putting too much in one context, like the user, theme, notifications and filters together. A change to notifications re-renders every component using the theme. The fix is splitting into separate, focused contexts, one per concern.

Mixing frequently changing state with stable functions. A common trick is splitting state and dispatch into two contexts: components that only trigger updates consume the dispatch context, which never changes, so they don't re-render when the state changes.
Using context for high-frequency updates, like form input values or real-time data. Context isn't designed for that.

If a part of the app needs fine-grained subscriptions, a store library like Redux Toolkit or Zustand is better, because components subscribe through selectors and only re-render when their selected value changes. There's also use-context-selector as a library.
So I use context for low-frequency, app-wide values, and a store or a server-state library for the rest.

p17-317.q: Both are popular state management libraries for React, with different philosophies.
p17-317.k: zustand vs redux, zustand, state management comparison react, lightweight state management, redux alternatives
x: Both are popular state management libraries for React, with different philosophies.

Redux Toolkit is the official, modern way to use Redux. It has a single store, slices with reducers and actions created by createSlice, Immer for simple immutable updates, createAsyncThunk for async logic, and RTK Query for API caching. It gives a strict, predictable structure, excellent DevTools with time travel and action history, middleware, and patterns that scale well across large teams. The cost is more concepts and some ceremony, though far less than old Redux.

Zustand is minimal. I create a store with a function that defines state and actions together, and components use a hook with a selector, like useStore of s such that s.selectedSite, re-rendering only when that selection changes. No providers needed, very little boilerplate, small bundle size, and it works outside React too. It can use the Redux DevTools and middleware like persist and immer. The trade-off is less enforced structure, so large teams need their own conventions.

My choice: for large applications with many developers, complex shared state, and a need for strict patterns and auditability of state changes, Redux Toolkit. For small to medium apps, or local feature state, Zustand. In both cases, server data belongs in a server-state library, like RTK Query or TanStack Query, which removes most of the state that used to go into Redux.
Our React shell uses Redux Toolkit.

p17-318.q: Normalised state means storing each type of data like tables in a database: each entity type in its own collection, keyed by id, with references by id instead of nested copies. Instead of an array of shipments where each shipment contains a full site object and an array of kit objects, I store shipments, sites and kits separately, as objects mapping id to entity, plus an array of ids for ordering.
p17-318.k: normalized state redux, createentityadapter, entity adapter, ids and entities, normalize nested data redux
x: Normalised state means storing each type of data like tables in a database: each entity type in its own collection, keyed by id, with references by id instead of nested copies. Instead of an array of shipments where each shipment contains a full site object and an array of kit objects, I store shipments, sites and kits separately, as objects mapping id to entity, plus an array of ids for ordering.

The benefits: each item exists in exactly one place, so updating a site updates it everywhere it's referenced, with no inconsistent copies. Lookups by id are O(1) instead of searching arrays. And updates are simpler and cheaper, which reduces unnecessary re-renders, because components can select single items.

Redux Toolkit's createEntityAdapter makes this easy. It creates the standard shape, ids and entities, and provides reducer helpers like addOne, addMany, setAll, updateOne, upsertMany and removeOne, which I use inside a slice's reducers. It also generates memoised selectors: selectAll, selectById, selectIds and selectTotal. I can configure a sortComparer to keep ids sorted, and a custom selectId if the id field isn't called id.
When API responses are nested, I flatten them when storing, either manually or with a library like normalizr.
With RTK Query, much of the server data is cached per query instead, so I normalise mainly for client-side state with many cross-references or frequent individual updates.

p17-319.q: A selector is a function that reads data from the Redux store, like state.shipments.items. With useSelector, a component re-renders whenever the selector's result changes, compared by reference.
p17-319.k: reselect, createselector, memoized selectors, selector re render, derived data redux
x: A selector is a function that reads data from the Redux store, like state.shipments.items. With useSelector, a component re-renders whenever the selector's result changes, compared by reference.

The problem comes with derived data. A selector like "pending shipments", which filters the array, returns a new array every time it runs, even if the shipments haven't changed. useSelector runs selectors after every dispatched action, sees a new reference, and re-renders the component on every action in the whole app. The filtering also re-runs every time, which is wasteful for large lists.

createSelector, from Reselect and re-exported by Redux Toolkit, creates memoised selectors. I give it input selectors, like selectShipments and selectStatusFilter, and a result function that combines them. It only recomputes when an input's result changes by reference; otherwise it returns the cached previous result, the same reference, so the component doesn't re-render.

There are some subtleties. By default, the cache size was one, so a selector used with different arguments in several components, like a selectShipmentsBySite with a site id, kept recalculating; newer Reselect versions use weakMapMemoize by default, which handles multiple arguments better, or I create a selector instance per component with useMemo. And input selectors themselves must be simple and not create new objects.
Redux Toolkit's development checks warn when a selector returns a new reference for the same inputs, which catches many of these issues.

p17-320.q: React Hook Form is a form library that manages form state with uncontrolled inputs and refs by default, so typing in one field doesn't re-render the whole form. That makes it fast, even for large forms, with very little code.
p17-320.k: react hook form, zod validation, zodresolver, form validation react typescript, schema validation forms
x: React Hook Form is a form library that manages form state with uncontrolled inputs and refs by default, so typing in one field doesn't re-render the whole form. That makes it fast, even for large forms, with very little code.

I call useForm, which gives me register to connect native inputs, handleSubmit to validate and submit, and formState with errors, isSubmitting and isDirty. For controlled components, like MUI inputs or date pickers, I use the Controller component or useController. useFieldArray handles dynamic lists of fields, like adding multiple kit lines to a return.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema library. I define the form's schema once: for example, quantity is a number, at least 1, at most the dispensed quantity; reason is a string with a minimum length, required when the status is Damaged, using refine or superRefine for cross-field rules. Then z.infer gives me the TypeScript type from the schema, so the type and the validation rules can never drift apart.

The zodResolver connects them: useForm with resolver equals zodResolver of the schema. Validation runs on submit, or on blur or change if configured, and errors appear in formState.errors, with messages from the schema.
When the server returns validation errors, I map them back to fields with setError.
The same Zod schema can even be shared with a Node backend, though with a .NET backend, the server has its own FluentValidation rules.

p17-321.q: TypeScript types only exist at compile time. When I write const data equals await response.json() as Shipment, TypeScript simply trusts me. If the API returns something different, like a renamed field, a null where I expected a string, a date as a number, or an error object instead of data, nothing catches it at runtime. The app then fails somewhere far from the cause, like "cannot read property of undefined" deep in a component, which is hard to debug.
p17-321.k: runtime validation api response, zod parse api, typescript types not runtime, validate json react, safeparse
x: TypeScript types only exist at compile time. When I write const data equals await response.json() as Shipment, TypeScript simply trusts me. If the API returns something different, like a renamed field, a null where I expected a string, a date as a number, or an error object instead of data, nothing catches it at runtime. The app then fails somewhere far from the cause, like "cannot read property of undefined" deep in a component, which is hard to debug.

Runtime validation closes that gap. I define a Zod schema for the response, and parse the JSON with it. If the data matches, I get a correctly typed object. If not, I get a clear error saying exactly which field is wrong, right at the API boundary. safeParse returns a success flag instead of throwing, so I can log the problem and show a friendly error.
Zod can also transform data while parsing, like converting ISO date strings to Date objects, or applying defaults.

It's most valuable for data from external or less trusted sources: third-party APIs, data from local storage, URL parameters, and messages from other windows. For our own APIs, where types are generated from the backend's OpenAPI spec, the contract is already strong, so I use runtime validation selectively, for critical screens and during API changes.
The cost is a little bundle size and CPU, which is usually negligible.

p17-322.q: Utility types transform existing types, so I don't have to repeat definitions. The ones I use most:
p17-322.k: typescript utility types, partial pick omit record, readonly typescript, returntype parameters, required typescript
x: Utility types transform existing types, so I don't have to repeat definitions. The ones I use most:
Partial of T makes all properties optional, which is perfect for update payloads or patch functions, like updateShipment taking a Partial of Shipment. Required of T does the opposite.

Pick of T and keys creates a type with only some properties, like Pick of Shipment, id and status, for a summary component. Omit of T and keys removes properties, like Omit of Shipment and id for a create form, where the server generates the id.

Record of K and V describes an object with keys of type K and values of type V, like Record of ShipmentStatus to string for status labels. With a union of string literals as K, TypeScript ensures every status has a label, so adding a new status shows errors wherever a mapping is missing.
Readonly of T makes properties read-only, useful for state and props that mustn't be mutated.

ReturnType of a function type and Parameters of a function type extract types from functions, like getting the type of what a hook returns without exporting it separately. Awaited unwraps promise types.
NonNullable removes null and undefined, and Extract and Exclude filter union types.
These keep types derived from a single source, so when the base type changes, everything derived from it updates automatically.

p17-323.q: A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common literal property, the discriminant, which TypeScript uses to narrow the type.
p17-323.k: discriminated unions typescript, tagged union, loading success error state, exhaustive switch never, union types state
x: A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common literal property, the discriminant, which TypeScript uses to narrow the type.

The classic UI use is request state. Instead of separate isLoading, error and data fields, which allow impossible combinations, like loading true with data and an error at the same time, I define one type: either status 'idle', or status 'loading', or status 'success' with data of type Shipment array, or status 'error' with an error message. Each state carries exactly the data it needs.

When I check state.status equals 'success', TypeScript narrows the type, so state.data is available and typed, and in the 'error' branch, state.error is available. In other branches, accessing data is a compile error. Impossible states become unrepresentable.

For exhaustiveness, in a switch over the status, the default case assigns the value to a variable of type never. If someone adds a new status, like 'cancelled', without handling it, the compiler errors in every switch that misses it.
The same pattern fits many domain concepts: Redux actions with a type property, form steps, permission results, or events like KitDispensed versus KitReturned, each with different fields.
It's one of the most valuable TypeScript features for making front-end code correct, because it moves bugs from runtime to compile time.

p17-324.q: as const is a const assertion. It tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, most specific type, and make everything read-only. Without it, an object like status: 'pending' is inferred as status: string. With as const, it's the literal 'pending', and arrays become read-only tuples. A common use is defining a list of values once, like const statuses equals pending, shipped, delivered as const, and deriving a union type from it with typeof statuses of number, so the runtime array and the type stay in sync.
p17-324.k: satisfies typescript, as const, const assertion, literal types typescript, satisfies vs type annotation
x: as const is a const assertion. It tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, most specific type, and make everything read-only. Without it, an object like status: 'pending' is inferred as status: string. With as const, it's the literal 'pending', and arrays become read-only tuples. A common use is defining a list of values once, like const statuses equals pending, shipped, delivered as const, and deriving a union type from it with typeof statuses of number, so the runtime array and the type stay in sync.

satisfies, added in TypeScript 4.9, checks that a value matches a type without changing the inferred type of the value. With a normal type annotation, like const config: Record of string, Route equals something, TypeScript checks the value but then forgets the specific keys; config.shipments isn't known, and any string key is allowed. With satisfies Record of string, Route instead, TypeScript validates every entry against Route, catching typos and missing properties, but still remembers the exact keys and literal values, so autocomplete and narrowing work.
They combine nicely: as const satisfies some type gives an immutable, precisely typed object that's also validated against a contract, like a route table, a permission map or a configuration object.
I use satisfies a lot for configuration objects, and as const for lists of literal values and lookup tables.

p17-325.q: These are the building blocks of TypeScript's type-level programming, and the built-in utility types are made from them.
p17-325.k: keyof typeof, mapped types, conditional types, infer keyword, advanced typescript types, indexed access types
x: These are the building blocks of TypeScript's type-level programming, and the built-in utility types are made from them.

keyof T gives a union of T's property names. For Shipment, keyof Shipment is 'id' or 'status' or 'site'. It's useful for type-safe functions, like a sortBy function whose key parameter must be a real property of the item type.

typeof in a type position gets the type of a value, like typeof defaultConfig, so I can derive types from constants instead of writing them twice. Combined, keyof typeof obj gives the keys of an object value.
Indexed access types, like Shipment of 'status', give the type of one property.

Mapped types create a new type by transforming each property of another: for each K in keyof T, map to some new type. That's how Partial and Readonly are built. I can also remap keys, like turning status into onStatusChange handlers.

Conditional types choose a type based on a condition: T extends string ? A : B. With infer, they can extract parts of types, like the element type of an array, or the resolved type of a promise, which is how Awaited and ReturnType work.

In everyday application code, I mostly use keyof, typeof and indexed access. Mapped and conditional types matter more when writing shared libraries, generic hooks, or typed API clients, where they let one generic definition give precise types for many cases.

p17-326.q: Type narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broad type to a more specific one inside a code block. Built-in checks narrow automatically: typeof x equals 'string', instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and checking a discriminant property.
p17-326.k: type guards, user defined type guard, is keyword typescript, assertion functions, asserts keyword, narrowing typescript
x: Type narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broad type to a more specific one inside a code block. Built-in checks narrow automatically: typeof x equals 'string', instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and checking a discriminant property.

A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate, like value is Shipment. Inside, I write the runtime check, for example that it's an object with an id number and a status string. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the variable to Shipment in that branch. It's useful for unknown data, like JSON from local storage, errors in catch blocks, which are unknown, or filtering arrays: items.filter of isShipment gives a Shipment array, and newer TypeScript versions can infer simple predicates automatically.

An assertion function has a return type like asserts value is Shipment, or asserts condition. Instead of returning a boolean, it throws if the check fails, and after the call, TypeScript treats the value as narrowed for the rest of the scope. It's handy for invariants, like assertDefined of the current user at the start of a function.

The important caution: TypeScript trusts these functions completely. If the runtime check is wrong or incomplete, the types lie, and bugs appear later. So for complex shapes, I prefer a schema library like Zod, which generates both the check and the type from one definition.

p17-327.q: TypeScript enums, like enum ShipmentStatus with Pending and Shipped, look familiar to C# developers, but they have some quirks.
p17-327.k: enums vs union types typescript, string literal union, const enum, typescript enum pitfalls, enum alternative
x: TypeScript enums, like enum ShipmentStatus with Pending and Shipped, look familiar to C# developers, but they have some quirks.

Numeric enums allow any number to be assigned, and have reverse mappings, so they're less type-safe than they look. Regular enums generate runtime JavaScript objects, adding code. const enums are inlined, but they cause problems with isolated module compilation, which tools like Vite, esbuild and Babel use. And enums are a TypeScript-only construct: Node's native TypeScript type stripping, and the erasableSyntaxOnly option, don't support them, because they aren't just types.

A union of string literals, like type ShipmentStatus equals 'Pending' or 'Shipped' or 'Delivered', has no runtime cost, works directly with JSON from APIs, which are plain strings, gives autocomplete and exhaustiveness checks, and is just JavaScript with types erased.
When I also need the values at runtime, for a dropdown list or validation, I define a const array or object with as const, and derive the union type from it, so one definition serves both purposes.
So for new code, I prefer string literal unions, or as const objects. Enums are fine where a codebase already uses them consistently, and string enums are much safer than numeric ones.
For API contracts generated from a .NET backend, I configure the generator to produce string unions, matching enums serialised as strings.

p17-328.q: The tsconfig controls how strict TypeScript is and how it understands the project. The options I care about most:
p17-328.k: tsconfig options, strict mode typescript, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, tsconfig react vite, moduleResolution bundler, typescript configuration
x: The tsconfig controls how strict TypeScript is and how it understands the project. The options I care about most:

strict set to true, which turns on a group of checks, especially strictNullChecks, so null and undefined must be handled explicitly, and noImplicitAny. It catches a huge class of bugs. For an existing JavaScript-heavy codebase, I'd enable it gradually, but new projects start strict.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess, which makes array and record lookups include undefined in their type, because the item might not exist. It's stricter, but it catches real bugs with lookups by id or index.
exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which distinguishes between a missing property and one explicitly set to undefined, useful for patch-style objects.
noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch, for clean code, though linting can cover some of this.

For a Vite React project: jsx set to react-jsx, the modern transform without importing React; module ESNext with moduleResolution set to bundler, which matches how Vite resolves imports; isolatedModules true, since Vite transpiles each file separately; noEmit true, because Vite does the building and TypeScript only type-checks; and types for vite/client, to type import.meta.env.
paths for import aliases, like @ pointing to src, which must match the Vite config.
And I run tsc with noEmit in the pipeline, because Vite's dev server doesn't type-check.

p17-329.q: MUI, Material UI, is customised mainly through the theme. I create a theme with createTheme, defining the palette, like primary and secondary colours, error and warning colours; typography, like font family and sizes; spacing; breakpoints; shape, like border radius; and component defaults and style overrides, for example making all buttons non-uppercase, or giving every TextField a small size by default. The ThemeProvider at the root makes it available everywhere.

I create a theme with createTheme, defining the palette, like primary and secondary colours, error and warning colours; typography, like font family and sizes; spacing; breakpoints; shape, like border radius; and component defaults and style overrides, for example making all buttons non-uppercase, or giving every TextField a small size by default. The ThemeProvider at the root makes it available everywhere.

That's the foundation of a consistent design system: components use theme values, so changing a brand colour happens in one place. A company design system built on MUI usually ships as a theme package plus extra components.

For one-off styling, there are two main tools. The sx prop applies styles directly on a component, with access to theme values through shorthand, like p of 2 for padding using the spacing scale, or color 'primary.main', and responsive values by breakpoint. It's great for small layout adjustments. styled creates a reusable styled component, like a StatusBadge, with styles defined once, which is better for anything reused or complex.
Performance-wise, sx is fine for most cases, but in very large lists, a styled component or theme override avoids recalculating styles per item.
I avoid hard-coded colours and pixel values in components, and keep everything tied to the theme.
Our React shell uses MUI 5 together with IQVIA's React design system.

p17-330.q: Large grids are common in business apps, like lists of kits, shipments or subjects, and performance and usability both matter.
p17-330.k: mui datagrid, ag grid react, large table react, server side pagination grid, virtualized table, grid performance react
x: Large grids are common in business apps, like lists of kits, shipments or subjects, and performance and usability both matter.

The first decision is client-side or server-side data. For a few thousand rows, loading everything and letting the grid sort, filter and page in the browser is simple and fast. For tens of thousands or more, or data that changes often, I use server-side mode: the grid sends sort, filter and page parameters to the API, and the API returns one page with a total count. MUI's DataGrid supports this with paginationMode, sortingMode and filterMode set to server, and AG Grid has the server-side and infinite row models.
Virtualisation is essential: both MUI DataGrid and AG Grid render only the visible rows and columns, so the DOM stays small even with thousands of rows loaded.

For React performance: keep the columns definition stable with useMemo, or outside the component, because a new columns array on every render causes the grid to recalculate; memoise custom cell renderers; and avoid heavy components inside cells.
Usability features: column visibility and ordering saved per user, export to CSV or Excel, keyboard navigation, and accessible markup.

Feature-wise, MUI DataGrid's free version covers basic needs, while advanced features, like row grouping, tree data and Excel export, are in the paid tiers, similar to AG Grid's enterprise edition, so licence choice is part of the decision.

p17-331.q: Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification or other assistive technologies can use the app. It's also often a legal or contractual requirement, usually targeting WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA.
p17-331.k: accessibility react, a11y react, aria attributes, keyboard navigation, screen reader react, wcag
x: Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification or other assistive technologies can use the app. It's also often a legal or contractual requirement, usually targeting WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA.

The basics come first. Use semantic HTML elements, like button, nav, main, table and label, instead of clickable divs, because they have built-in keyboard support and meaning for screen readers. Every input has an associated label. Images have meaningful alt text, or empty alt if decorative. Headings follow a logical order.
Keyboard support: everything must work with the keyboard, with a visible focus indicator, a logical tab order, and no keyboard traps, except intentionally inside open modals.

Focus management in SPAs: when a modal opens, move focus into it and return it afterwards; after client-side navigation, move focus to the new page's heading, so screen reader users know the page changed.

ARIA, used carefully, for custom widgets: roles, states like aria-expanded or aria-selected, and aria-live regions to announce dynamic updates like "Shipment saved" or validation errors. The first rule of ARIA is to prefer native elements where possible.
Sufficient colour contrast, and never using colour alone to convey meaning, like statuses shown only as red or green.
Component libraries like MUI handle much of this. I add eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe checks in tests, and manual keyboard and screen reader testing.

p17-332.q: React Router lets me define routes as a tree, where parent routes render shared layout, and child routes render inside the parent through the Outlet component. For example, a parent route for /sites/:siteId renders the site header and tabs, and child routes render the inventory, shipments or users tab inside it. Index routes define what shows at the parent path itself, and layout routes without a path group routes that share a layout, like all authenticated pages.
p17-332.k: react router nested routes, outlet react router, react router loaders, createbrowserrouter, react router v6 v7, route layout
x: React Router lets me define routes as a tree, where parent routes render shared layout, and child routes render inside the parent through the Outlet component. For example, a parent route for /sites/:siteId renders the site header and tabs, and child routes render the inventory, shipments or users tab inside it. Index routes define what shows at the parent path itself, and layout routes without a path group routes that share a layout, like all authenticated pages.

Hooks give access to routing information: useParams for path parameters, useSearchParams for query strings, which is a good place to keep filter state so it's shareable and works with the back button, useNavigate for programmatic navigation, and useLocation.

Since version 6.4, with createBrowserRouter, routes can have loaders and actions. A loader fetches data before the route renders, and the component reads it with useLoaderData, so data loading starts in parallel with the code download, avoiding waterfalls. Actions handle form submissions and mutations, and loaders revalidate automatically afterwards. errorElement shows an error UI for failures in that branch, and lazy loads route code on demand. In version 7, these ideas merged with the Remix framework.
Many teams, including ours, still use simpler component-based routing, with data fetching through RTK Query or TanStack Query inside components, which also works well.
Route-level code splitting with lazy imports keeps the initial bundle small.

p17-333.q: Both let separate teams build features independently and combine them into one application, but they integrate at different times.
p17-333.k: module federation, micro frontends react, npm packages micro frontend, runtime vs build time integration, shell app feature modules
x: Both let separate teams build features independently and combine them into one application, but they integrate at different times.

With npm packages, each feature module is built and published as a versioned package to a registry, and the shell application installs specific versions and builds everything together. It's build-time integration. The benefits: simplicity, full type checking across packages, one optimised bundle with shared dependencies deduplicated, and a clear, tested combination of versions in each shell release, which is important for validated releases. The downside: releasing a feature change means publishing a new package version and then rebuilding and redeploying the shell.

With Module Federation, from webpack 5 and now available for Vite and Rspack, each feature is deployed separately as a remote, and the shell loads it at runtime from a URL. Teams can deploy their part independently without redeploying the shell, and shared libraries like React are loaded once and shared at runtime. The downsides: runtime failures if versions of shared dependencies are incompatible, more complex setup, type sharing needs extra tooling, and the exact combination in production changes whenever any team deploys, which makes testing and validation harder.

Our React shell uses the npm package approach: feature modules like drug accountability and material block are separate repos published to the Azure DevOps feed, which fits our regulated release process, where every production combination must be validated.

p17-334.q: A monorepo keeps several related projects, like a shell app, feature packages and a shared component library, in one repository, with tooling that understands the relationships between them.
p17-334.k: monorepo frontend, npm workspaces, nx turborepo, pnpm workspaces, monorepo vs polyrepo, shared packages monorepo
x: A monorepo keeps several related projects, like a shell app, feature packages and a shared component library, in one repository, with tooling that understands the relationships between them.

The basic building block is workspaces, from npm, pnpm or Yarn. The root package.json lists the workspace folders, dependencies are installed once at the root, and local packages are linked to each other automatically, so the shell can use the latest local version of a feature package without publishing it. pnpm is popular because it's fast and strict about dependencies.

On top of that, build orchestrators like Turborepo or Nx add: running tasks like build, test and lint across packages in the right dependency order; caching, so unchanged packages aren't rebuilt or retested, locally and in CI with remote caching; and affected detection, so the pipeline only builds and tests the packages changed by a commit and their dependants. Nx also adds generators, dependency graphs and boundary rules to stop forbidden imports.
The benefits: atomic changes across packages in one pull request, consistent tooling and versions, easier refactoring, and simpler code sharing.
The trade-offs: the repository grows, CI needs smart caching to stay fast, and access control is per repo, so if teams need strict separation, separate repos are easier.
Our feature modules are separate repositories published as npm packages, which is the polyrepo approach. A monorepo would be a reasonable alternative for tighter integration.

Then hooks fail with the "Invalid hook call" error, because the package's components use a different React instance than the app's renderer, and context providers from the app aren't visible inside the package.

In the build, using Vite's library mode or tsup, I mark these as external, so they're imported from the host app at runtime rather than bundled. The output is ES modules, with TypeScript declaration files generated, and the package.json exports field points to them. sideEffects false allows tree shaking.
For local testing with the shell, npm link can cause duplicate React copies too, so I prefer a workspace setup, or tools like yalc.
Versioning follows semantic versioning, with a changelog, because the shell pins versions. That's how our feature packages work with the React shell through the Azure DevOps feed.

p17-338.q: Core Web Vitals are Google's main user-experience metrics, measured from real users.

x: Core Web Vitals are Google's main user-experience metrics, measured from real users.

Largest Contentful Paint measures loading: when the largest visible element, like a main image or text block, is rendered. Good is under 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint, which replaced First Input Delay in 2024, measures responsiveness: how quickly the page visibly responds to clicks, taps and key presses throughout the visit. Good is under 200 milliseconds. Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability: how much content jumps around unexpectedly. Good is under 0.1.

For a React single-page app, improving LCP means a smaller initial bundle through code splitting and lazy routes, compressing and caching assets, serving from a CDN, preloading critical fonts and images, and showing meaningful content quickly instead of a blank page waiting on several API calls in sequence.

Improving INP means keeping the main thread free: avoiding long JavaScript tasks, memoising expensive renders, virtualising large lists, using transitions for non-urgent updates, debouncing expensive handlers, and moving heavy computation to web workers.

Improving CLS means reserving space for images, ads, and content that loads later, with width and height or skeleton placeholders of the right size, and avoiding inserting banners above existing content.
I measure with Lighthouse and tools like GTmetrix in the lab, and with the web-vitals library sending real-user data to monitoring.

A simple useDebounce hook debounces a value. It takes the value and a delay, keeps a debounced copy in state, and in a useEffect, sets a timeout to update the debounced copy after the delay. Sometimes I need a debounced callback instead of a debounced value, like for auto-save. For React 18: update react and react-dom, and replace ReactDOM.render with createRoot. That turns on concurrent features and automatic batching. Code that depended on synchronous, unbatched updates in async callbacks might behave differently, so I test flows with timeouts and promises. In StrictMode, effects now run twice in development, which exposes missing cleanups that need fixing. Types changed too: React.FC no longer includes children implicitly, so components that accept children must declare them.

The bigger effort is often the libraries: MUI, Redux, React Router, testing libraries and any design system packages must support the new version. In a shell with separate feature packages, every package's peerDependencies range must allow the new version, and they all need testing together, because everything must share one React instance.

For React 19: run the official codemods, which handle many changes. Removed APIs include propTypes and defaultProps on function components, string refs, legacy context and ReactDOM.render. ref becomes a normal prop, so forwardRef can be removed over time. Error handling changed slightly.
Testing is critical: run unit tests, the end-to-end suite, and manual checks of key screens. In a regulated product, the upgrade is a validated change with regression testing.
Our shell is on React 17, so this is a real roadmap item.

p17-343.q: useSyncExternalStore is a React 18 hook for subscribing to data that lives outside React, like a state management library's store, browser APIs, or any custom event source, in a way that's safe with concurrent rendering.

I give it a subscribe function, which registers a callback and returns an unsubscribe function, a getSnapshot function that returns the current value, and optionally a getServerSnapshot for server rendering. React re-renders the component when the snapshot changes.

The reason it exists is tearing. With concurrent rendering, React can pause rendering in the middle and continue later. If an external store changes during that pause, different components in the same render could read different versions of the data, showing an inconsistent UI. useSyncExternalStore guarantees a consistent snapshot for the whole render.

Library authors are the main users: Redux's useSelector, Zustand and others use it internally. In application code, I use it for browser state, like a useOnlineStatus hook that subscribes to the online and offline events and reads navigator.onLine, or a hook that reads from localStorage and listens for storage events from other tabs, or media queries.

One important rule: getSnapshot must return the same value, by reference, if nothing changed. Returning a new object each time causes an infinite re-render loop, so I return primitives or cached objects.
