p17-345.q: They all schedule code to run later, but in different queues.
p17-345.k: nexttick vs setimmediate, microtask vs macrotask, event loop phases node, settimeout 0, promise then order
x: They all schedule code to run later, but in different queues.

Microtasks run as soon as the current operation finishes, before the event loop moves on. In Node, process.nextTick callbacks run first, then promise callbacks, like then and the continuation after await. Both queues are drained completely before anything else happens.

Macrotasks run in the event loop's phases. setTimeout and setInterval callbacks run in the timers phase, once their delay has passed. setTimeout of zero actually means at least about one millisecond. setImmediate callbacks run in the check phase, right after the poll phase, where I/O callbacks are processed.

So within the same synchronous block: nextTick runs first, then promises, then the timers and immediates. Between setTimeout of zero and setImmediate, the order from the main module isn't guaranteed, because it depends on how fast the loop starts. But inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout of zero, because the check phase comes right after the poll phase.
In browsers there's no nextTick or setImmediate; promise microtasks run before the next macrotask, like a timer or a rendering step.
The practical lesson: recursively scheduling nextTick or promise callbacks can starve the event loop, because I/O never gets a turn. When I need to yield to let I/O run, I use setImmediate.

p17-346.q: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, so CPU-heavy work blocks everything else, and one process only uses one CPU core for JavaScript. These three features address that in different ways.
p17-346.k: worker threads, child process node, cluster module, cpu intensive node, multi core node, pm2 cluster
x: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, so CPU-heavy work blocks everything else, and one process only uses one CPU core for JavaScript. These three features address that in different ways.

Worker threads run JavaScript in separate threads inside the same process, each with its own event loop and memory, communicating by message passing, and able to share memory with SharedArrayBuffer. They're for CPU-intensive tasks, like parsing a large file, image processing, encryption or complex calculations, so the main thread stays responsive. A pool of workers, using a library like Piscina, avoids the cost of starting threads repeatedly.

Child processes start separate operating system processes with spawn, exec or fork. They're for running external programs, like a command-line tool or a Python script, or isolating risky work, since a crash doesn't affect the parent. They have more overhead than threads.

The cluster module starts several copies of the whole Node server, typically one per CPU core, sharing the same port, with the primary process distributing connections. It's for using all cores to handle more HTTP requests. PM2 does this for you.

In containers, though, I usually prefer running one Node process per container and scaling the number of containers with the orchestrator, like ECS or Kubernetes, which is simpler and gives better health checks and restarts. Workers are then used only for specific CPU-heavy tasks.

p17-347.q: Streams process data piece by piece, in chunks, instead of loading it all into memory. There are four types: Readable, like reading a file or an HTTP request; Writable, like writing a file or an HTTP response; Duplex, both, like a TCP socket; and Transform, a duplex that modifies data passing through, like gzip compression or CSV parsing.

x: Streams process data piece by piece, in chunks, instead of loading it all into memory. There are four types: Readable, like reading a file or an HTTP request; Writable, like writing a file or an HTTP response; Duplex, both, like a TCP socket; and Transform, a duplex that modifies data passing through, like gzip compression or CSV parsing.
With streams, I can process a 5 GB file with a few megabytes of memory, and start sending output before the input is fully read.

Backpressure is what keeps memory under control when the writer is slower than the reader. A writable stream's write method returns false when its internal buffer is full. A well-behaved producer then pauses until the drain event says it can continue. If code ignores this and keeps writing, data piles up in memory, and the process can crash.

The pipe method handles backpressure automatically, but it didn't handle errors well: an error in one stream didn't destroy the others, causing leaks. So the recommended way is stream.pipeline, or the promise version from stream/promises, which connects the streams, handles backpressure, forwards errors, and cleans up all streams when any of them fails or finishes.
Readable streams are also async iterable, so for await over a stream is a clean way to process chunks one by one, with backpressure handled naturally.
[I used a pipeline of a file read stream, a CSV parser and a batching transform to load large extract files without memory spikes.]

Today, Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array, so it works with standard typed array APIs too.

I create buffers with Buffer.from, from a string with an encoding, an array, or another buffer, and Buffer.alloc for a zero-filled buffer of a given size. Some important points. Encoding matters: reading UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 garbles text, and cutting a buffer in the middle of a multi-byte character breaks it, which is why streams use a StringDecoder when converting chunks to text. Buffer.allocUnsafe is faster because it doesn't zero the memory, but it may contain old data, which can leak sensitive information if not fully overwritten, so I only use it when I immediately fill it. Comparing buffers containing secrets, like HMAC signatures, should use crypto.timingSafeEqual, not equality checks. And large buffers held in memory count against the process's memory, so for big data, streams are better than reading whole files into buffers.

ES modules are the JavaScript standard: import and export statements, used in browsers and modern tooling. Imports are static and analysed before the code runs, which enables tree shaking in bundlers and top-level await. Loading is asynchronous.
In Node, a file is treated as ES module if it has the .mjs extension, or if the nearest package.json has "type": "module" and the file is .js. Otherwise .js is CommonJS, and .cjs is always CommonJS.

The differences that matter in practice. In ESM, file imports need the extension, like import from './utils.js'. __dirname and __filename don't exist; I use import.meta.dirname or import.meta.url. npm ci is for continuous integration and production builds. It deletes node_modules, installs exactly the versions recorded in package-lock.json, and fails if package.json and the lockfile don't match. It never modifies the lockfile. So builds are reproducible, and usually faster. In pipelines, I always use npm ci, often with caching of the npm cache directory.

Version ranges in package.json follow semantic versioning: major.minor.patch. A caret, like ^4.2.1, allows any version below the next major: 4.3.0 is fine, 5.0.0 isn't. It assumes minor and patch releases are backward compatible. For 0.x versions, caret is stricter, because 0.x minors can break. A tilde, like ~4.2.1, allows only patch updates: 4.2.9 but not 4.3.0. An exact version pins precisely.
The lockfile is what really decides what's installed; the ranges decide what updates are allowed when someone runs npm update or regenerates the lockfile.

In practice, I commit the lockfile, let Dependabot or Renovate propose updates as pull requests with the test suite running, and use exact versions for packages known to break in minor releases. pnpm and Yarn have equivalents, like pnpm install with frozen-lockfile.

x: Express is the classic, minimal web framework for Node. It's simple, extremely well known, and has a huge ecosystem of middleware. But it's unopinionated, so large projects need their own structure, and historically it had weak async error handling and limited TypeScript support. Express 5, released in late 2024, finally handles rejected promises in route handlers properly.

Fastify is a performance-focused framework with a similar feel. It's significantly faster than Express, thanks to optimised routing and JSON serialisation using schemas. It has built-in JSON Schema validation for requests and responses, a structured plugin system with encapsulation, first-class async support, built-in logging with Pino, and good TypeScript support.

NestJS is a full application framework built on top of Express or Fastify. It brings structure inspired by Angular and ASP.NET Core: modules, controllers, providers, dependency injection with decorators, guards, interceptors, pipes for validation, and integrations for GraphQL, microservices, queues and OpenAPI. For developers coming from .NET or Angular, it feels very familiar.

My choice: a small, focused service or a simple BFF: Fastify, or Express if the team knows it well. A larger application with many developers and complex domains: NestJS, because the enforced structure and DI keep it maintainable. Performance-critical endpoints: Fastify, possibly as NestJS's underlying adapter.

A class marked with the Injectable decorator is a provider. I register providers in a module's providers array, and inject them through constructor parameters; Nest resolves them using TypeScript metadata about the parameter types. Controllers, guards, interceptors and pipes all get their dependencies this way.

Modules organise the app into features. Each module declares its providers and controllers, exports the providers that other modules may use, and imports other modules it depends on. A provider is private to its module unless exported, which helps keep features encapsulated. Global modules, or dynamic modules with forRoot and forFeature, are used for shared infrastructure, like configuration or database connections.

Custom providers handle more cases: useValue for constants or mocks, useClass to swap implementations, useFactory for values that need logic or async setup, like creating a database client, and injection tokens, strings or symbols, for things that aren't classes, since TypeScript interfaces don't exist at runtime.

Scopes are like .NET lifetimes: the default is singleton, shared across the app; REQUEST scope creates a new instance per request; and TRANSIENT gives each consumer its own instance. Request scope bubbles up the dependency chain and costs performance, so I use it only when needed.
Testing is easy: the testing module lets me override providers with mocks.

As a safety net, I register process.on for unhandledRejection and uncaughtException to log the error with full details. But after an uncaught exception, the process state is unknown, so I log and exit with a non-zero code, and let the orchestrator, like ECS, Kubernetes or PM2, restart a fresh instance. I don't try to keep running.

Graceful shutdown is about handling planned stops, like deployments or scale-in. The orchestrator sends SIGTERM, and after a grace period, SIGKILL. On SIGTERM, the app should stop accepting new connections, with server.close; fail its readiness check, so the load balancer stops sending traffic; let in-flight requests finish; stop consuming new messages from queues, and finish or release the current ones; close database pools and other connections; and then exit. A timeout forces exit if something hangs.

In Docker, the Node process must receive the signals. If it's started through npm start or a shell script, signals may not reach it, so I run node directly as the main process, or use an init like tini, or the --init flag.

p17-355.q: The symptom is memory that grows steadily over time, until the process crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory", or the container is killed for exceeding its memory limit.
p17-355.k: node memory leak, heap snapshot node, inspect node memory, heap out of memory, chrome devtools node memory
x: The symptom is memory that grows steadily over time, until the process crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory", or the container is killed for exceeding its memory limit.

First, I confirm it's a leak and not just a high but stable working set. Monitoring process.memoryUsage, especially heapUsed, over hours shows whether memory returns to a baseline after garbage collection or keeps climbing.

To find the cause, I take heap snapshots. I run Node with --inspect and connect Chrome DevTools, or use the inspector API, or start with --heapsnapshot-signal, so sending a signal writes a snapshot, which is handy in a container. I take one snapshot after warm-up, run some load, take another, and compare them. The comparison view shows which object types grew, and the retainers path shows what's keeping them alive.

Common causes in Node. Global or module-level caches, like a plain object or Map used as a cache without any size limit or expiry. Event listeners added repeatedly and never removed, often with the MaxListenersExceededWarning as a hint. Closures that capture large objects, held by long-lived timers or callbacks. Unbounded arrays, like collecting metrics or logs in memory. And unresolved promises that pile up.

Fixes are usually bounded caches, like lru-cache, removing listeners, and clearing timers. The --max-old-space-size flag only delays the crash, though it's important to set it to suit the container's memory.

p17-356.q: High CPU in Node often shows up as slow responses for everyone, because one busy main thread delays every request. So first I measure event loop lag, how long callbacks wait to run, using perf_hooks' monitorEventLoopDelay or metrics from APM tools. High lag means something is blocking the loop.
p17-356.k: node cpu profiling, node --prof, clinic.js, flame graph node, event loop lag, blocked event loop
x: High CPU in Node often shows up as slow responses for everyone, because one busy main thread delays every request. So first I measure event loop lag, how long callbacks wait to run, using perf_hooks' monitorEventLoopDelay or metrics from APM tools. High lag means something is blocking the loop.

To find what, I take a CPU profile. Options: run with --inspect and record a profile in Chrome DevTools' Performance or Profiler tab; use --cpu-prof, which writes a profile file when the process exits; or use Clinic.js, which runs the app under load and produces a flame graph and a diagnosis of whether the issue is CPU, I/O or the event loop. Linux perf with --perf-basic-prof works for system-level profiling, and APM tools like Datadog or New Relic offer continuous profiling in production.

In a flame graph, wide bars are functions that use a lot of CPU time. Typical findings: synchronous functions like readFileSync or crypto's sync methods in request paths; JSON.parse and JSON.stringify of very large payloads; expensive regular expressions, sometimes vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking; heavy loops over large arrays; and logging too much, synchronously.
Fixes include switching to async APIs, streaming large payloads, caching results, moving CPU-heavy work to worker threads or another service, and simplifying regexes.

p17-357.q: Configuration comes from environment variables, following the twelve-factor approach: the same build runs everywhere, with different environment variables set by the platform, like ECS task definitions or Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets.
p17-357.k: node configuration, dotenv, validate env variables, zod env, process.env, config management node
x: Configuration comes from environment variables, following the twelve-factor approach: the same build runs everywhere, with different environment variables set by the platform, like ECS task definitions or Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets.

For local development, a .env file loaded with dotenv, or Node's built-in --env-file flag since Node 20, provides values. The .env file is in .gitignore, and a .env.example with dummy values documents what's needed.

The important part is validating configuration at startup. process.env values are all strings or undefined, so a typo or a missing variable otherwise causes a confusing failure much later. I define a schema, with Zod or envalid, for example PORT as a number with a default, DATABASE_URL as a required URL, LOG_LEVEL as one of a few values, and FEATURE_X as a boolean parsed from the string. At startup, the app parses process.env with the schema; if anything is missing or invalid, it logs a clear message listing the problems and exits immediately. The result is a typed config object that the rest of the app imports, instead of reading process.env all over the code.

Secrets, like database passwords and API keys, come from a secret store, injected as environment variables by the platform or fetched at startup from AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and are never logged.
In NestJS, the ConfigModule supports the same validation approach.

p17-358.q: I use structured logging: each log entry is a JSON object with fields, not just a text line, so logs can be searched and filtered in a central system, like by request id, user id or error type.
p17-358.k: node logging, pino, winston, structured logging node, json logs node, log correlation id node
x: I use structured logging: each log entry is a JSON object with fields, not just a text line, so logs can be searched and filtered in a central system, like by request id, user id or error type.

Pino is my preferred library, because it's very fast and produces JSON by default. Logging is a hot path, and slow logging blocks the event loop. Winston is another popular option, more flexible but slower. I create one logger configured with the level from configuration, and child loggers that add context, like logger.child with the module name, or per request with the request id.

For HTTP services, pino-http or the framework's integration logs each request with method, route, status code and duration, and attaches a request-scoped logger. To carry the request id or trace id into every log line, including deep in service code, I use AsyncLocalStorage, which keeps per-request context across async calls, or the OpenTelemetry integration, which adds trace and span ids automatically, so logs and traces link up.

Good practices: log at appropriate levels, info for significant events and error with the full error object, so the stack is captured; redact sensitive fields, which Pino supports with paths like headers.authorization; avoid logging whole request bodies; and write to standard output, letting the platform collect logs, rather than writing files inside containers.
In development, pino-pretty makes the JSON human-readable.

p17-359.q: Every request body, query string and path parameter is untrusted input, so I validate it at the edge, before it reaches business logic.
p17-359.k: node request validation, zod express, joi validation, class-validator nestjs, json schema validation fastify, validate body node
x: Every request body, query string and path parameter is untrusted input, so I validate it at the edge, before it reaches business logic.

The approach depends on the framework. With Express, I use a schema library like Zod or Joi, and a small middleware that validates req.body, req.query and req.params against the route's schema. If validation fails, it responds with 400 and a structured list of errors; if it passes, it replaces the raw input with the parsed, typed values, so defaults and type coercion are applied. With Zod, the TypeScript type is inferred from the schema, so the handler is typed without separate interfaces.

Fastify has validation built in using JSON Schema on each route, compiled for speed with Ajv. Response schemas also speed up serialisation and prevent leaking extra fields. TypeBox or Zod type providers give TypeScript types from those schemas.

NestJS uses DTO classes with class-validator decorators, like IsString and IsInt, and a global ValidationPipe with whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted options, which strip or reject unknown properties, protecting against mass assignment. Zod-based pipes are an alternative.

Whatever the tool, I validate types, required fields, lengths, ranges, formats and allowed values, limit body size, and reject unknown fields for sensitive endpoints. Business-rule validation, like whether a site is active, happens later, in the service layer.

p17-360.q: These are the main options for database access in Node with TypeScript, at different levels of abstraction.
p17-360.k: prisma vs typeorm, knex query builder, drizzle orm, node orm comparison, database access node typescript
x: These are the main options for database access in Node with TypeScript, at different levels of abstraction.

Prisma defines the data model in its own schema file, generates a fully typed client, and handles migrations. Queries are very type-safe, and autocomplete is excellent. It's productive and popular. The trade-offs are its own schema language, less control over generated SQL, and some complex queries needing raw SQL.

TypeORM is a classic ORM with decorators on entity classes, similar to Entity Framework or Hibernate, supporting Active Record and Data Mapper patterns, relations and migrations. It's familiar for developers from .NET or Java, but its type safety for queries is weaker, and it has had a reputation for bugs and slower maintenance.
Knex is a query builder, not a full ORM. I write queries in JavaScript that map closely to SQL, with migrations and seeds. It gives control and flexibility, but little type safety by itself.
Drizzle is a newer, lightweight, TypeScript-first ORM. The schema is defined in TypeScript, queries look like SQL but are fully typed, it's fast, and it works well in serverless environments.
My choice: Prisma or Drizzle for new TypeScript services, Drizzle when I want SQL-like control and small footprint, plain SQL with a driver like pg for very simple services or heavy reporting.
In all cases, I use parameterised queries, connection pooling, and migrations run in the pipeline.

p17-361.q: There are a few practices I always follow for Node containers.
p17-361.k: node docker best practices, node dockerfile, node user docker, npm ci docker, multi stage node docker, node pid 1
x: There are a few practices I always follow for Node containers.
Use an official, slim base image with a specific Node LTS version, like node:22-slim or Alpine, pinned, never latest.

Use a multi-stage build. The build stage installs all dependencies with npm ci and compiles TypeScript. The final stage copies only the compiled output and production dependencies, installed with npm ci --omit=dev, so dev tools and source files aren't in the image.
Order the Dockerfile for caching: copy package.json and package-lock.json first, install dependencies, then copy the source. Then code changes don't reinstall dependencies.
Use a .dockerignore to exclude node_modules, .git, .env files and test files.
Don't run as root: the official images have a node user, and I switch to it with USER node.
Set NODE_ENV to production, which many libraries use to enable optimisations.

Handle signals properly: start with CMD node dist/server.js directly, not npm start, so the Node process receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown. Or use tini, or docker run with --init, to handle PID 1 duties like reaping zombie processes.
Set memory limits consistently: Node's heap limit should fit within the container's memory limit, using --max-old-space-size if needed.
Add a health check endpoint for the orchestrator, and log to standard output.
Finally, scan the image for vulnerabilities in the pipeline.

p17-362.q: There are now several ways, and they fit different stages.
p17-362.k: run typescript node, ts-node vs tsx, node type stripping, tsc build node, typescript node 22 23
x: There are now several ways, and they fit different stages.

Compile with tsc: TypeScript compiles .ts files to JavaScript in a dist folder, and Node runs the JavaScript. It's the traditional, reliable production approach. tsc also does full type checking, which runtime tools skip.

Run directly in development with a loader. ts-node was the original tool, but it's slower and had ES module issues. tsx, which uses esbuild, is now popular: tsx watch src/server.ts runs TypeScript directly, very fast, with reload on changes. It strips types without checking them, so I run tsc --noEmit separately in the editor or pipeline.

Native type stripping: since Node 22.6 behind a flag, and enabled by default from Node 23.6 and later 22.x versions, Node can run .ts files directly by removing type annotations. It only supports erasable syntax, meaning types that can simply be deleted. Features that generate code, like enums, namespaces and parameter properties in constructors, aren't supported unless using the transform option, and TypeScript added the erasableSyntaxOnly setting to flag them. It doesn't read tsconfig paths and doesn't type-check.
Bundlers like esbuild or tsup can also produce a single optimised JavaScript file, which is great for Lambda functions.
My setup: tsx or native stripping for development, tsc type checking in CI, and compiled JavaScript or a bundle in production images.

p17-363.q: AsyncLocalStorage, from the async_hooks module, lets me store data that's available throughout an asynchronous call chain, without passing it explicitly through every function. It's similar to AsyncLocal in .NET, or thread-local storage, but follows async operations instead of threads.
p17-363.k: asynclocalstorage, async context node, request context node, correlation id node, cls hooked
x: AsyncLocalStorage, from the async_hooks module, lets me store data that's available throughout an asynchronous call chain, without passing it explicitly through every function. It's similar to AsyncLocal in .NET, or thread-local storage, but follows async operations instead of threads.

I create one AsyncLocalStorage instance. At the start of each request, a middleware calls run with a context object, like the request id, the user id and a request-scoped logger, and the rest of the request handling runs inside that callback. Anywhere deeper in the code, in services, repositories, or the logger, getStore returns the context for the current request, even after many awaits, timers and promise chains, and different concurrent requests each see their own context.

Common uses: adding the correlation or trace id to every log line automatically; tracking the current user or tenant for auditing or multi-tenant data access; and request-scoped caching. OpenTelemetry's Node SDK uses it to keep track of the active span, which is how traces propagate automatically.

Some cautions. Context can be lost with some older callback-based libraries or custom thenables, though that's rare now. It adds a small performance cost. And it's easy to overuse; explicit parameters are clearer for core business data, so I keep it for cross-cutting concerns like logging and tracing.
Node 24 improved its implementation and performance.

p17-364.q: EventEmitter is Node's built-in publish-subscribe mechanism. Many core objects, like streams, servers and sockets, are emitters, and code subscribes with on and unsubscribes with off or removeListener.
p17-364.k: eventemitter memory leak, maxlistenersexceededwarning, remove event listener node, eventemitter node, once listener
x: EventEmitter is Node's built-in publish-subscribe mechanism. Many core objects, like streams, servers and sockets, are emitters, and code subscribes with on and unsubscribes with off or removeListener.

By default, an emitter warns when more than 10 listeners are added for the same event: "MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected". It's a heuristic, not an error, but it usually points to a real bug: code that adds a listener repeatedly, like on every request or every retry, without removing it. Each listener stays referenced by the emitter, along with everything its closure captures, so memory grows, and the handler runs many times for each event, causing duplicate work.

Typical examples: adding an error or close listener to a long-lived shared connection inside a request handler; subscribing to process events in a function that's called repeatedly; or a reconnection loop that re-registers handlers.

Fixes: register listeners once, at setup time, rather than per operation; use once for listeners that should only fire one time; always remove listeners when the work is done, in a finally block or cleanup function; and use AbortSignal with events.on or the signal option, which removes listeners automatically when aborted. events.once also returns a promise for waiting on a single event.
Raising the limit with setMaxListeners is only appropriate when many listeners are genuinely expected, not to silence the warning.

p17-365.q: In Express 4, if an async route handler threw an error or a promise rejected, Express didn't catch it. The rejection was unhandled, the request hung until it timed out, and in modern Node, the unhandled rejection could crash the process. So everyone wrapped handlers with try-catch and called next with the error, or used a helper like express-async-handler, or the express-async-errors package, which patches Express.
p17-365.k: express async error handling, express 5 promises, express error middleware, async handler express, unhandled rejection express
x: In Express 4, if an async route handler threw an error or a promise rejected, Express didn't catch it. The rejection was unhandled, the request hung until it timed out, and in modern Node, the unhandled rejection could crash the process. So everyone wrapped handlers with try-catch and called next with the error, or used a helper like express-async-handler, or the express-async-errors package, which patches Express.

Express 5, which became the stable release in late 2024, fixed this. When a handler or middleware returns a rejected promise, Express automatically passes the error to the error-handling middleware. So async handlers can simply throw.

Either way, I have one central error-handling middleware, the special four-argument function, registered after all routes. It maps known error types to responses, like a ValidationError to 400 with details, NotFoundError to 404, and a custom AppError with its own status code and error code, and for anything unexpected, logs the full error with the request id and returns a generic 500 without internal details. Responses use a consistent format, like Problem Details.
I also add a 404 handler for unknown routes, and make sure errors in streams or background callbacks are handled where they occur, since they aren't part of the request's promise.

p17-366.q: Node handles all JavaScript for all requests on one thread. If one operation takes 200 milliseconds of CPU, every other request waits 200 milliseconds. So keeping each piece of work short is critical.
p17-366.k: blocking event loop, sync functions node, json parse large, redos, cpu work node, event loop blocked
x: Node handles all JavaScript for all requests on one thread. If one operation takes 200 milliseconds of CPU, every other request waits 200 milliseconds. So keeping each piece of work short is critical.
Common ways the loop gets blocked, and the fixes.
Synchronous APIs in request paths: readFileSync, existsSync, execSync, and crypto's sync functions, like pbkdf2Sync. I use the async versions. Sync APIs are fine during startup only.
Large JSON: JSON.parse and JSON.stringify are synchronous and can take a long time for very large payloads. I limit payload sizes, paginate, or stream JSON.
Heavy computation: big loops, sorting huge arrays, image processing, compression, PDF generation. I move these to worker threads, a separate service, or a job queue.

Catastrophic regular expressions: certain regex patterns with nested quantifiers take exponential time on crafted input, which is the ReDoS attack. I keep regexes simple, limit input length, and use linting tools that detect unsafe patterns.
Processing large collections in one go: I split work into chunks and yield between them with setImmediate, so other requests get a turn.
To detect blocking, I monitor event loop delay with perf_hooks and alert when it's high, and use CPU profiles to find the culprit.

p17-367.q: Prototype pollution is a JavaScript-specific vulnerability. Every object inherits from Object.prototype. If an attacker can make the application set a property on Object.prototype itself, that property suddenly appears on every object in the process. This can change application logic, like an isAdmin property becoming true everywhere, bypass security checks, crash the app, or in some cases lead to remote code execution through template engines or child process options.
p17-367.k: prototype pollution, __proto__ attack, object merge vulnerability, javascript security, json parse proto
x: Prototype pollution is a JavaScript-specific vulnerability. Every object inherits from Object.prototype. If an attacker can make the application set a property on Object.prototype itself, that property suddenly appears on every object in the process. This can change application logic, like an isAdmin property becoming true everywhere, bypass security checks, crash the app, or in some cases lead to remote code execution through template engines or child process options.

It usually happens through unsafe recursive merge, deep clone or set-by-path functions that copy user-controlled JSON into objects. If the input contains a key like __proto__ or constructor.prototype, a naive merge walks into the prototype and writes there. Many popular libraries had such bugs over the years.

Protections. Validate input with a schema that only allows expected properties, like Zod or JSON Schema, which also strips unknown keys. Avoid writing your own deep merge of untrusted data, and keep libraries like lodash updated. Block dangerous keys, __proto__, constructor and prototype, in any code that sets properties by dynamic key. Use Map instead of plain objects for user-keyed data, or objects created with Object.create of null, which have no prototype. Object.freeze of Object.prototype at startup is a strong but blunt option, which can break some libraries. Node also has a flag to disable __proto__.
And dependency scanning catches known vulnerable package versions.

p17-368.q: The npm ecosystem has had many supply chain attacks: typosquatted package names, maintainer accounts compromised and malicious versions published, and in 2025, self-spreading worms that stole tokens through install scripts. A typical project has hundreds of transitive dependencies, so the risk is real.
p17-368.k: npm supply chain attack, malicious npm package, typosquatting, npm audit, lockfile security, install scripts risk
x: The npm ecosystem has had many supply chain attacks: typosquatted package names, maintainer accounts compromised and malicious versions published, and in 2025, self-spreading worms that stole tokens through install scripts. A typical project has hundreds of transitive dependencies, so the risk is real.

The protections I use. Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, so builds use exactly the reviewed versions, and a newly published malicious version doesn't slip in automatically. Review new dependencies before adding them: is it necessary, is it maintained, how popular is it, and is the name spelled correctly? Fewer dependencies is better. Disable or restrict install scripts, which run arbitrary code at install time, using ignore-scripts, or pnpm's approach of only allowing scripts for approved packages. Run dependency scanning, like npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk or Socket, in the pipeline, failing on high-severity issues. Delay adopting brand-new versions for a few days, since malicious releases are usually caught quickly; tools like Renovate support a minimum release age. Use a private registry or proxy, like Azure Artifacts or AWS CodeArtifact, so packages come through a controlled source. Protect our own publishing with 2FA and short-lived tokens, and publish with provenance from CI.
And CI build agents shouldn't have more secrets than they need, because a malicious package runs with the agent's permissions.

p17-369.q: Since Node 18, fetch is available globally, stable since Node 21, implemented by the undici library. So for HTTP calls, I no longer need axios or node-fetch, and the same API works in browsers and Node.
p17-369.k: fetch in node, undici, node 18 fetch, http client node, axios vs fetch, fetch timeout abortsignal
x: Since Node 18, fetch is available globally, stable since Node 21, implemented by the undici library. So for HTTP calls, I no longer need axios or node-fetch, and the same API works in browsers and Node.
Using it well in a server requires a few things that fetch doesn't do by default.

Timeouts: fetch has no default timeout, so a hanging server can hold the request forever. I pass signal equals AbortSignal.timeout of, say, 5,000 milliseconds, or combine signals with AbortSignal.any to support cancellation as well.
Error handling: fetch only rejects on network errors. A 404 or 500 response resolves successfully, so I always check response.ok or the status, and throw or handle errors explicitly.
Consuming the body: if I don't read or cancel the response body, the connection may not be released back to the pool, so I always read it, even on errors.
Connection pooling and keep-alive are handled by undici's global agent, and for heavy use, I can configure an undici Agent or Pool with connection limits.
Retries, backoff and circuit breaking aren't built in, so I add them with a small wrapper or a library, only retrying safe requests.
Axios is still a fine choice in existing code, especially for its interceptors, which our React apps use for adding tokens; in Node services, I prefer native fetch with a thin wrapper.

p17-370.q: These all take several promises and combine them, but they resolve or reject differently.
p17-370.k: promise.all vs allsettled, promise race, promise any, parallel promises javascript, promise combinators
x: These all take several promises and combine them, but they resolve or reject differently.

Promise.all resolves with an array of all results once every promise resolves, and rejects immediately if any one rejects, with that first error. The other operations keep running, but their results are ignored. I use it when every result is required, like loading a page's essential data in parallel.

Promise.allSettled waits for all of them, regardless of success, and resolves with an array of objects, each with a status, fulfilled or rejected, and a value or reason. It never rejects. I use it when operations are independent and I want to know the outcome of each, like sending notifications to several recipients, or loading optional dashboard widgets, where one failure shouldn't hide the others.

Promise.race settles as soon as the first promise settles, whether it resolves or rejects. The classic use was implementing a timeout, racing the operation against a timer, though AbortSignal.timeout is cleaner today, because it also cancels the operation.

Promise.any resolves with the first promise that fulfils, ignoring rejections, and only rejects, with an AggregateError, if all of them reject. It's useful for redundancy, like trying several mirrors or replicas and taking the fastest successful response.
Important: none of them limit concurrency. For hundreds of operations, I use a concurrency limiter, like p-limit, rather than starting them all at once.

p17-371.q: The Global Interpreter Lock is a lock in CPython, the standard Python interpreter, that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It simplifies memory management, since reference counting doesn't need fine-grained locks, and makes C extensions easier to write.
p17-371.k: gil, global interpreter lock, python threading cpu, free threaded python, python 3.13 no gil, python multicore
x: The Global Interpreter Lock is a lock in CPython, the standard Python interpreter, that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It simplifies memory management, since reference counting doesn't need fine-grained locks, and makes C extensions easier to write.
The effect is that Python threads can't run CPU-bound Python code in parallel on multiple cores. Ten threads doing heavy calculations take about as long as one thread, or longer.

But for I/O-bound work, like HTTP calls, database queries and file reads, the GIL is released while waiting for I/O, so threads, or asyncio, work well for concurrency. Many C-based libraries, like NumPy, also release the GIL during heavy computations, so they can use multiple cores.

For CPU-bound Python code, the usual options are multiprocessing or concurrent.futures' ProcessPoolExecutor, which use separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL; moving the hot code into a compiled library; or running multiple worker processes, which web servers like Gunicorn do anyway.

Things are changing. Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build without the GIL, and in Python 3.14 the free-threaded build became officially supported, though not the default. Many libraries are still adapting, and single-threaded code can be slightly slower in that build.
For our RAG service, the work is mostly I/O, calling embedding APIs and the database, so async FastAPI suits it well, and the GIL isn't a bottleneck.

p17-372.q: I choose based on whether the work is I/O-bound or CPU-bound, and how many concurrent operations there are.
p17-372.k: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio, python concurrency, concurrent futures, io bound vs cpu bound python, threadpoolexecutor
x: I choose based on whether the work is I/O-bound or CPU-bound, and how many concurrent operations there are.

asyncio is for lots of concurrent I/O-bound work: thousands of HTTP calls, database queries or WebSocket connections, handled on a single thread with an event loop, using async and await. It's very efficient, because waiting tasks don't use threads. The catch is that every library in the chain must be async-aware, like httpx or aiohttp instead of requests, and asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy, and a single blocking call stalls everything.

threading is for I/O-bound work with libraries that are synchronous, or a moderate number of concurrent operations. The GIL is released during I/O, so threads overlap their waits. ThreadPoolExecutor from concurrent.futures makes it simple: submit tasks, get futures, collect results. It's also how async code runs blocking functions, with asyncio.to_thread.

multiprocessing is for CPU-bound work: data processing, parsing large files, heavy calculations. Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so it uses multiple cores. ProcessPoolExecutor is the convenient interface. The costs are higher memory, slower start-up, and data passed between processes must be pickled, which is slow for large objects.
In web services, FastAPI with async endpoints handles I/O concurrency, while CPU-heavy tasks go to a process pool or a separate worker, like Celery.

p17-373.q: The syntax looks almost the same, but the runtime model differs.
p17-373.k: python asyncio vs c# async, python async await, event loop python, coroutine python, asyncio gather
x: The syntax looks almost the same, but the runtime model differs.

In Python, async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it doesn't run anything; it returns a coroutine object, which only runs when awaited or scheduled on the event loop as a task, with asyncio.create_task. In C#, calling an async method starts running it immediately, synchronously, until the first incomplete await, and returns a Task that's already in progress.

Python's asyncio runs on a single-threaded event loop. All coroutines share that thread, and concurrency comes from switching at await points. There's no thread pool involved unless you explicitly use one. C# continuations run on thread pool threads, so async code can also run in parallel on multiple cores.

Because Python's loop is single-threaded, any blocking call, like time.sleep, requests.get or a heavy computation, freezes every coroutine. In C#, blocking is wasteful too, but it blocks one thread, not everything.

The equivalents: asyncio.gather is like Task.WhenAll, asyncio.wait_for or asyncio.timeout is like a timeout with a CancellationToken, and asyncio.TaskGroup, since 3.11, gives structured concurrency, where if one task fails, the others are cancelled. Cancellation in Python is delivered as a CancelledError raised at an await point, rather than a token passed explicitly.
Coming from .NET, the biggest adjustment is never mixing blocking libraries into async code.

p17-374.q: A generator is a function that uses yield to produce values one at a time, lazily. Calling it returns a generator object; each call to next runs the function until the next yield, returns that value, and pauses, keeping its local state. When the function ends, it raises StopIteration, which for loops handle automatically. It's very similar to yield return in C#.

Calling it returns a generator object; each call to next runs the function until the next yield, returns that value, and pauses, keeping its local state. When the function ends, it raises StopIteration, which for loops handle automatically. It's very similar to yield return in C#.

The main benefit is memory efficiency. Reading a 10 GB log file with a generator that yields one parsed line at a time uses almost no memory, whereas building a list of all lines would load everything. Generators also allow infinite sequences and pipelines, where each stage is a generator consuming the previous one, like read lines, filter errors, parse fields, and only the items actually consumed are processed.
Generator expressions are the lazy version of list comprehensions, written with parentheses: sum of x squared for x in numbers doesn't create an intermediate list.
yield from delegates to another generator, which is useful for recursion, like walking a directory tree.

Some cautions. A generator can only be iterated once; after it's exhausted, it yields nothing. Errors appear when iterating, not when calling the function. And it's lazy, so code that looks like it ran may not have run.
Async generators, with async def and yield, work with async for, for streaming data from APIs or databases.

To write one, I define an outer function that takes the original function, and inside, a wrapper function that accepts star args and double-star kwargs, does something before, calls the original, does something after, and returns the result. The outer function returns the wrapper. I always apply functools.wraps to the wrapper, so the decorated function keeps its original name, docstring and signature, which matters for debugging, logging and frameworks that inspect functions, like FastAPI.
A decorator with arguments, like retry with attempts equals 3, needs one more level: a function that takes the arguments and returns the actual decorator.
For async functions, the wrapper must be async and await the original.

Common uses: timing and logging, caching with functools.lru_cache or cache, retries with backoff, which the tenacity library provides, access checks, and registering functions. Frameworks rely on them heavily: FastAPI's app.get, pytest's fixture and parametrize, and dataclass and property are all decorators.

They're like attributes plus middleware in .NET: a clean way to add cross-cutting behaviour without changing the function's body. I avoid stacking too many, because it makes control flow hard to follow.

A class becomes a context manager by implementing two methods. __enter__ runs at the start and returns the resource, which is bound by as. __exit__ runs at the end; it receives the exception type, value and traceback if an error occurred, and can do cleanup, like closing, releasing or rolling back. If __exit__ returns True, the exception is suppressed, which is rarely what I want.
The easier way is contextlib.contextmanager: a generator function where the code before yield is setup, the yielded value is the resource, and the code after yield, in a finally block, is cleanup.

Common uses: files and network connections; database transactions, committing on success and rolling back on exceptions; acquiring and releasing locks; temporarily changing settings, like a working directory; and timing a block of code.

Async context managers, with __aenter__ and __aexit__, or contextlib.asynccontextmanager, are used with async with, for things like database sessions and HTTP clients. FastAPI's lifespan function, which sets up and tears down resources at application startup and shutdown, is an async context manager.
contextlib.ExitStack manages a dynamic number of context managers.

p17-377.q: In Python, default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called. So if the default is a mutable object, like a list or dictionary, the same object is shared across all calls that use the default.

x: In Python, default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called. So if the default is a mutable object, like a list or dictionary, the same object is shared across all calls that use the default.

For example, def add_item of item, and items equals an empty list, appends the item and returns items. The first call returns a list with one item. The second call, which I'd expect to return a new list with one item, returns a list with two, because it's the same list object as before. The data leaks between calls, which causes confusing bugs, especially in long-running services, where state accumulates across requests.
The standard fix is to use None as the default, and create a new object inside the function: items equals None, then if items is None, items equals an empty list.

The same principle applies in other places. Class attributes defined with mutable values are shared by all instances, so per-instance lists should be created in __init__. Dataclasses protect against this: they raise an error for a mutable default, and I use field with default_factory equals list instead. Pydantic models handle mutable defaults safely by copying them.
Linters like Ruff flag mutable default arguments automatically, which is one reason I always run a linter.

p17-378.q: == checks equality of values, by calling the __eq__ method. is checks identity: whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory. Using is with numbers or strings sometimes seems to work, because Python caches small integers and some strings, but that's an implementation detail and a common bug.

Using is with numbers or strings sometimes seems to work, because Python caches small integers and some strings, but that's an implementation detail and a common bug.
Copying relates to the same idea. Assigning b equals a doesn't copy anything; both names refer to the same object, so changing one changes the other.

A shallow copy, with list of a, a slice, dict.copy or copy.copy, creates a new outer container, but the items inside are the same objects. So with a list of lists, changing an inner list through the copy also changes it in the original.

A deep copy, with copy.deepcopy, recursively copies everything, so the copy is completely independent. It's slower and uses more memory, and can be surprising for objects holding resources, but it's what I need when duplicating nested, mutable data, like a configuration template that each job modifies.
Immutable objects, like tuples of immutable items and frozen dataclasses, avoid many of these issues, which is one reason I prefer immutable data where possible.

p17-379.q: They all define structured data with typed fields, but they serve different purposes.

x: They all define structured data with typed fields, but they serve different purposes.

A NamedTuple is an immutable tuple with named fields. It's lightweight, works anywhere tuples work, and is good for small, simple return values or records. But it can't easily have defaults computed per instance, and being a tuple, it can be compared and unpacked by position, which is sometimes surprising.

A dataclass, from the standard library, generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from type-annotated fields. It's a plain Python class, mutable by default, or immutable with frozen equals True, with slots for memory efficiency, and default_factory for mutable defaults. Type hints aren't enforced at runtime; passing a string where an int is declared just works. It's my choice for internal domain objects and data passed between functions in trusted code.

A Pydantic model validates and converts data at runtime. Passing the string "5" to an int field converts it, and passing "abc" raises a clear validation error. It parses nested structures, serialises to and from JSON, and generates JSON Schema. Pydantic v2's core is written in Rust, so it's fast. It's the right choice at system boundaries: API requests and responses, which is why FastAPI uses it, configuration with pydantic-settings, and data from files, queues or external APIs.
So: Pydantic at the edges where data is untrusted, dataclasses inside, and NamedTuple for tiny records.

p17-381.q: Type hints annotate variables, function parameters and return values with types, like def get_kit of kit_id int returning Kit or None. Python itself doesn't enforce them at runtime; they're for tools and humans.

Static type checkers, like mypy or Pyright, analyse the code using the hints and find errors before running it: passing the wrong type, forgetting that a function can return None, calling methods that don't exist, or missing cases. Editors use the same information for accurate autocomplete and safe refactoring.

For someone coming from C# and TypeScript, it brings back a lot of the safety I'm used to. In practice, I add hints to all function signatures, run mypy in strict mode, or at least with disallow-untyped-defs, in the pipeline, and fix issues as they come. For existing untyped code, I enable checking gradually, module by module.
Pydantic and FastAPI use the same type hints at runtime for validation and documentation, so good hints pay off twice. Our RAG service runs mypy in CI.

Poetry manages dependencies through pyproject.toml, resolves versions, creates a lockfile, manages the virtual environment, and builds packages. It's mature and widely used.

uv, from the makers of Ruff, is the newer tool, written in Rust and extremely fast. It can replace pip, pip-tools, venv, and even manage Python versions themselves. uv add adds a dependency, uv lock creates a cross-platform lockfile, uv sync installs exactly what's locked, and uv run runs commands in the environment. It has become very popular because installs take seconds instead of minutes, which matters a lot in CI and Docker builds.

Whatever the tool, the principles are the same as with npm and NuGet: declare direct dependencies, commit a lockfile, install exactly from the lockfile in CI and Docker, and keep dependencies updated with automated pull requests and vulnerability scanning.

Common dependencies: get_db, which yields a database session, and because it uses yield, the code after yield runs when the request finishes, closing the session, like a scoped service with disposal in .NET; get_current_user, which reads the bearer token, validates it, and returns the user, or raises an HTTP 401; get_settings; pagination parameters; and permission checks, like a require_role factory that returns a dependency.

p17-384.q: FastAPI's BackgroundTasks lets an endpoint schedule a function to run after the response is sent, in the same process. It's simple and great for small, quick follow-up work, like sending a notification email or writing an audit entry, where the user shouldn't wait.
p17-384.k: fastapi background tasks, celery, task queue python, arq, background job python, redis queue python
x: FastAPI's BackgroundTasks lets an endpoint schedule a function to run after the response is sent, in the same process. It's simple and great for small, quick follow-up work, like sending a notification email or writing an audit entry, where the user shouldn't wait.

But it has clear limits. The work runs in the web server's process, so heavy tasks compete with request handling. There's no persistence: if the process restarts or crashes, pending tasks are lost. There are no retries, scheduling, or visibility into what's running. And it doesn't distribute work across machines.

A task queue, like Celery, or lighter options like RQ, Dramatiq or arq for async code, solves this. The API puts a task message on a broker, like Redis or RabbitMQ, and returns immediately, often with a job id. Separate worker processes, which can scale independently, pick up tasks and run them. Tasks get retries with backoff, time limits, result storage, scheduled and periodic jobs, monitoring with tools like Flower, and they survive web server restarts.

So I use BackgroundTasks for small, best-effort work, and a task queue for anything that's long-running, CPU-heavy, must not be lost, or needs retries, like re-indexing documents, generating large reports, or calling slow external APIs.
On AWS, SQS with a worker container or a Lambda is a managed alternative. In our developer RAG system, re-indexing runs from the pipeline, outside the API process.

For async, I create an async engine with create_async_engine and an async driver, like asyncpg for PostgreSQL, configure the connection pool size, and create an async_sessionmaker. In FastAPI, a get_db dependency opens an AsyncSession per request with async with, yields it to the endpoint, and closes it afterwards. Queries use await session.execute of a select statement, then scalars to get model objects. Writes add objects to the session and await session.commit, with rollback on errors.

A few things I've learned to watch. Lazy loading doesn't work in async code: accessing a relationship that isn't loaded triggers I/O implicitly, which raises an error. So I load relationships explicitly with selectinload or joinedload in the query, which also avoids N+1 problems. expire_on_commit set to False in the sessionmaker avoids attributes being expired and reloaded after commit. One session per request, never shared across concurrent tasks. And the engine is created once at startup, in the lifespan, and disposed on shutdown.
It's quite similar to EF Core: the session is like the DbContext, with a unit of work and identity map, and Alembic is like EF migrations.

p17-386.q: Alembic is the migration tool for SQLAlchemy, similar to EF Core migrations.

After initialising it, I configure env.py to use the application's database URL and SQLAlchemy metadata, so it knows the models. When I change a model, alembic revision --autogenerate compares the models with the current database schema and generates a migration script with upgrade and downgrade functions, using operations like add_column, create_table and create_index. Each migration has a revision id and points to its parent, forming a chain. alembic upgrade head applies all pending migrations, and the current version is stored in an alembic_version table.

Autogenerate is a starting point, not the final answer, so I always review the generated script. It doesn't detect everything, like some renames, which it sees as drop and add, losing data; changes to certain constraints or server defaults; or custom types. Data migrations, like backfilling a new column, are written by hand with op.execute or batch updates.

In production, I follow the same practices as with any database: migrations are backward compatible with the currently running code, following expand and contract; they run as a separate step in the deployment pipeline, not automatically on every app start, especially with several instances; large table changes are done carefully, like creating indexes concurrently in PostgreSQL; and I test migrations against a copy of production-sized data.

p17-390.q: WSGI is the original standard interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by Flask and Django traditionally. It's synchronous: each request occupies a worker, a process or thread, until it finishes. So concurrency is limited by the number of workers, and long-lived connections like WebSockets don't fit.

x: WSGI is the original standard interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by Flask and Django traditionally. It's synchronous: each request occupies a worker, a process or thread, until it finishes. So concurrency is limited by the number of workers, and long-lived connections like WebSockets don't fit.

ASGI is the asynchronous successor. It supports async request handling, so one worker can handle many concurrent requests while they wait on I/O, and it supports WebSockets, HTTP/2 and lifespan events for startup and shutdown. FastAPI and Starlette are ASGI frameworks, and Django supports ASGI too.
Uvicorn is a fast ASGI server, built on uvloop and httptools. It runs the FastAPI app. On its own, it can run several worker processes with the workers option.

Gunicorn is a mature process manager and WSGI server. For ASGI apps, it's used as a process manager with Uvicorn's worker class: Gunicorn starts several Uvicorn worker processes, monitors them, restarts any that crash, and handles graceful restarts and timeouts. This combination was the classic production setup, because one Python process only uses one core for Python code.

In containers, there's another common approach: run a single Uvicorn process per container, and let ECS or Kubernetes run multiple containers and restart them. That's simpler and gives the orchestrator better visibility.
Either way, the number of workers is roughly tuned to CPU cores and memory.

p17-391.q: I start by working out where the time goes, rather than guessing.
p17-391.k: python profiling, cprofile, py-spy, line profiler, python performance, slow python code

At the service level, tracing with OpenTelemetry shows whether a slow request is spending time in our code, the database, or external calls like an embedding API. Often it's I/O: an N+1 query, a missing index, or calls made one after another that could run concurrently with asyncio.gather.

If the time is in Python code itself, I use a profiler. cProfile, built in, records every function call with call counts and cumulative time; I view the output with snakeviz as a graph, or sort by cumulative time. It has overhead and needs the code to run under it.

py-spy is a sampling profiler that attaches to a running process without restarting it or changing code, so it's safe in production. py-spy top shows live hot functions, and py-spy record produces a flame graph. py-spy dump shows what every thread is doing right now, which is great for hangs. Newer options include Scalene, which also profiles memory and separates Python from native time, and Pyinstrument.
For a specific hot function, line_profiler shows time per line.

Typical fixes: better algorithms or data structures, like a set for membership checks instead of a list; vectorising with NumPy or pandas instead of Python loops; caching with functools.cache; batching database or API calls; and moving CPU-heavy work to a process pool.

p17-392.q: LBYL, look before you leap, means checking conditions before acting: if key in dictionary, then read it. EAFP, easier to ask forgiveness than permission, means trying the operation and handling the exception: try reading the key, except KeyError.

Python culture generally favours EAFP. It avoids race conditions where the condition changes between the check and the action, like a file deleted after checking it exists. It's often cleaner, and exceptions in Python are relatively cheap. LBYL is still fine for simple, expected cases, and things like dict.get with a default avoid both.

Good practices for exceptions. Catch specific exceptions, never a bare except, which also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, and avoid catching Exception broadly except at the top level of a request or job, where I log it and return an error. Keep the try block small, so I only catch errors from the line I expect. Use raise from to chain exceptions when translating them, like raising a custom EmbeddingServiceError from the original httpx error, which keeps the original traceback. Create a small hierarchy of custom exceptions for the application, like a base AppError with NotFoundError and ValidationError, which FastAPI exception handlers map to HTTP responses. Use finally or context managers for cleanup.
Python 3.11 added exception groups and except star for handling multiple errors from concurrent tasks, like those in a TaskGroup.

p17-393.q: For HTTP calls in Python, I use httpx, which supports both sync and async with the same API, or requests for simple synchronous scripts.

Several things make it robust.

Reuse the client. Creating a new client per request loses connection pooling and keep-alive, so I create one httpx.AsyncClient at application startup, in the FastAPI lifespan, with a base URL, default headers and limits, and close it on shutdown. It's the same lesson as HttpClient in .NET.
Timeouts. requests has no default timeout at all, so a hung server blocks forever; httpx has a default of five seconds. I set explicit connect and read timeouts suited to the API.

Retries with backoff. The tenacity library provides a retry decorator with stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential with jitter, and retry_if_exception_type, so I retry only transient failures, like connection errors, timeouts, 429 and 503, and respect Retry-After. For non-idempotent POST requests, I retry only with an idempotency key.

And logging with the request id, plus OpenTelemetry instrumentation for httpx, so external calls appear in traces.
For the embedding API calls in our RAG service, batching and rate-limit-aware retries were essential.

pickle: unpickling data can execute arbitrary code, so I never unpickle data from untrusted sources, like uploads, network messages or shared caches. JSON is the safe choice for data exchange. The same applies to tools built on pickle, like some model file formats; for ML models, safer formats like safetensors exist.
eval and exec: running strings as code is dangerous with any user input. For parsing simple literals, ast.literal_eval is safe.
YAML: yaml.load with the default or full loader can create arbitrary Python objects; I always use yaml.safe_load.
subprocess: passing a command string with shell equals True and user input allows shell injection. I pass arguments as a list without the shell.
SQL: always parameterised queries, through SQLAlchemy or the driver's parameters, never f-strings in SQL.
Path traversal: building file paths from user input needs resolving the path and checking it stays inside the allowed directory.
Insecure randomness: random is predictable; for tokens and passwords, I use the secrets module.
Dependencies: typosquatted packages on PyPI exist, so I pin dependencies with a lockfile, scan them with pip-audit, and review new packages.
Tools help: Bandit, or Ruff's security rules, flag many of these patterns automatically in the pipeline.

p17-395.q: The key is not loading the whole file into memory at once, unless it comfortably fits.
p17-395.k: large csv python, pandas chunksize, csv module python, polars, process big file python, memory efficient python
x: The key is not loading the whole file into memory at once, unless it comfortably fits.

For row-by-row processing, the built-in csv module with DictReader reads one row at a time from a file object, which is a generator-like stream. Memory stays flat regardless of file size. I combine it with batching: collect rows into batches of, say, 5,000, validate them, and write each batch to the database with a bulk insert, like executemany or PostgreSQL's COPY, which is far faster than inserting rows one by one.

For analysis and transformation, pandas is convenient, but it loads data into memory, which can be several times the file size. read_csv with chunksize returns an iterator of DataFrames, so I can process a large file in chunks. Specifying dtypes and usecols, reading only the needed columns with the right types, reduces memory and speeds up parsing a lot. The pyarrow engine is also faster.

Polars is a newer DataFrame library written in Rust. It's much faster than pandas, uses all CPU cores, and its lazy API with scan_csv builds a query plan and processes data in a streaming way, even for files larger than memory. For heavy data work, it's my preferred choice now. DuckDB is another excellent option that can query CSV files with SQL directly.
Whatever the tool, I collect invalid rows with their line numbers into an error report instead of failing the whole file.

p17-396.q: Python 3.10 added the match statement, which compares a value against a series of patterns, and runs the first case that matches. It's much more than a switch statement on values; it can match on the structure of data.
p17-396.k: python match case, structural pattern matching, match statement python 3.10, pattern matching python, case guard python
x: Python 3.10 added the match statement, which compares a value against a series of patterns, and runs the first case that matches. It's much more than a switch statement on values; it can match on the structure of data.

Patterns include: literal values, like case "pending"; the wildcard underscore as a default; OR patterns, like case "shipped" or "delivered"; capture patterns, which bind parts of the value to names; sequence patterns, like case first, then star rest, for lists; mapping patterns, like case with a "type" key equal to "kit_dispensed" and a "kit_id" key captured into a variable, which is great for handling JSON events or messages; and class patterns, like case Shipment with status equal to "cancelled", which match on type and attributes, using dataclass fields. Guards add extra conditions with if after the pattern.

It's very useful for routing messages or events by type and shape, parsing command-line style inputs, and handling different variants of a result object, similar to discriminated unions in TypeScript or pattern matching with switch expressions in C#.

A gotcha: a bare name in a case is a capture pattern, not a comparison with a variable. case STATUS captures anything into a new variable named STATUS. To compare with constants, they must be dotted names, like Status.PENDING from an Enum, or literals.

p17-397.q: Python has two ways to describe an interface-like contract.
p17-397.k: python protocol, structural typing python, typing protocol, duck typing, abc abstract base class python, interface in python
x: Python has two ways to describe an interface-like contract.

Abstract base classes, from the abc module, are nominal: a class must explicitly inherit from the ABC and implement its abstract methods, otherwise it can't be instantiated. That's close to an abstract class or interface in C#, enforced at runtime.

Protocols, from typing, are structural, which is formalised duck typing. A Protocol defines the methods and attributes something must have, like an Embedder protocol with an embed method that takes a list of strings and returns a list of vectors. Any class that has a matching method is considered an Embedder by the type checker, without inheriting from it or even knowing the Protocol exists. That's like interfaces in TypeScript or Go.

Protocols are great for dependency injection and testing. My RAG code depends on the Embedder protocol, not on the Azure OpenAI client. Production passes the real client wrapper; tests pass a simple fake class with an embed method, and mypy verifies both fit the protocol. Third-party classes that I can't modify can also satisfy a protocol.

By default, protocols are only checked statically by mypy or Pyright. With the runtime_checkable decorator, isinstance checks work too, but they only check that the methods exist, not their signatures.
I use Protocols for boundaries between components, and ABCs when I want to share implementation in a base class.

p17-398.q: LEGB describes the order Python uses to look up a name: Local, the current function's scope; Enclosing, the scopes of any outer functions; Global, the module's scope; and Built-in, names like len and print. The first match wins.
p17-398.k: legb rule, python scope, closures python, nonlocal keyword, global keyword, late binding closures
x: LEGB describes the order Python uses to look up a name: Local, the current function's scope; Enclosing, the scopes of any outer functions; Global, the module's scope; and Built-in, names like len and print. The first match wins.

A closure is an inner function that remembers variables from its enclosing function's scope, even after the outer function has returned. For example, make_multiplier of n returns an inner function that multiplies its argument by n; each returned function keeps its own n. Decorators rely on closures: the wrapper remembers the original function.

Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local by default. So if an inner function tries to increment a counter from the outer function, Python raises an UnboundLocalError, because the assignment makes it local and it's read before being assigned. The nonlocal keyword says the name refers to the enclosing function's variable, and global refers to the module-level variable. I use nonlocal occasionally, but global almost never, because module-level mutable state is hard to reason about and test.

A classic gotcha is late binding: closures capture variables, not values. Creating lambdas in a loop, like functions that return i, gives functions that all return the last value of i, because they look up i when called. The fix is binding the current value as a default argument, or using functools.partial.
It's similar to the classic C# closure-in-a-loop problem from older versions.

p17-399.k: sqs standard vs fifo, fifo queue, message group id, deduplication id, sqs ordering, sqs throughput
x: SQS has two queue types.

Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, which means a message can occasionally be delivered more than once, and best-effort ordering, so messages can arrive out of order. They're the default choice for most workloads, as long as consumers are idempotent and don't depend on order.

FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing within a deduplication window and strict ordering within a message group. Their names must end in .fifo. Each message has a message group id, like a shipment id: messages in the same group are delivered in order, one at a time, while different groups are processed in parallel. A deduplication id, or content-based deduplication, makes SQS drop duplicates sent within five minutes, which protects against producer retries.

The trade-offs of FIFO: lower throughput, 300 messages per second per API action without batching, 3,000 with batching, and much higher with high-throughput mode, which partitions by message group. And if one message in a group fails repeatedly, it blocks that group until it's handled or moves to the dead-letter queue.

So I use FIFO when order per entity really matters, like applying status changes for the same shipment in sequence, and standard queues everywhere else, with idempotent consumers and version checks to handle duplicates and reordering.

p17-400.q: When a consumer receives a message from SQS, the message isn't deleted. It becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default. The consumer must process it and then explicitly delete it. If the consumer crashes or doesn't delete it in time, the message becomes visible again and another consumer receives it. That's how SQS guarantees messages aren't lost.
p17-400.k: sqs visibility timeout, message reappears sqs, changemessagevisibility, sqs receive delete, duplicate processing sqs
x: When a consumer receives a message from SQS, the message isn't deleted. It becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default. The consumer must process it and then explicitly delete it. If the consumer crashes or doesn't delete it in time, the message becomes visible again and another consumer receives it. That's how SQS guarantees messages aren't lost.

So the timeout must be longer than the processing time. If processing takes 50 seconds and the timeout is 30, the message reappears while it's still being processed, and a second consumer processes it too, causing duplicates and wasted work. If the timeout is far too long, a message from a crashed consumer waits a long time before being retried.

My approach: set the visibility timeout to comfortably more than the typical maximum processing time, like six times the Lambda timeout when Lambda consumes the queue, which AWS recommends. For work with variable duration, the consumer extends the timeout while working, with ChangeMessageVisibility, like a heartbeat. On a known transient failure, the consumer can set the visibility to a short value, so the message is retried sooner, or a longer one for backoff.
Combined with maxReceiveCount on a redrive policy, messages that keep failing go to the dead-letter queue instead of looping forever.
And consumers stay idempotent, because duplicates can still happen.

p17-401.q: Fan-out means one event is delivered to several independent consumers. On AWS, the classic way is to publish to an SNS topic, with several SQS queues subscribed to it. Each subscribed queue gets its own copy of every message, and each consumer service reads from its own queue.
p17-401.k: sns sqs fan out, fanout pattern aws, sns subscriptions, publish subscribe aws, sns filter policy
x: Fan-out means one event is delivered to several independent consumers. On AWS, the classic way is to publish to an SNS topic, with several SQS queues subscribed to it. Each subscribed queue gets its own copy of every message, and each consumer service reads from its own queue.

For example, when a shipment is delivered, the shipment service publishes one ShipmentDelivered message to an SNS topic. The notification service's queue, the reporting service's queue and the inventory service's queue each receive a copy. The publisher doesn't know who's listening, and new consumers can be added by subscribing a new queue, without changing the publisher.

Why put SQS queues between SNS and the consumers, rather than subscribing consumers directly? Because the queues buffer messages: if a consumer is down or slow, its messages wait in its own queue, with retries and its own dead-letter queue, and it doesn't affect other consumers. SNS alone would only retry delivery for a limited time.

Useful features: subscription filter policies, so a queue only receives messages with certain attributes or body content, like only "Damaged" status events; raw message delivery, so the queue gets the original payload without the SNS envelope; FIFO topics with FIFO queues when ordering matters; and encryption with KMS.
The queue policies must allow the topic to send to them.
EventBridge is the alternative when more advanced routing rules are needed.

p17-402.k: eventbridge vs sns vs sqs, event bus aws, eventbridge rules, choose aws messaging service, eventbridge pipes
x: They solve different messaging problems.
