SQS is a queue: messages wait until a consumer pulls and processes them, with one consumer group per queue. It's for buffering and distributing work, load levelling, and decoupling a producer from a single consumer that might be slow or temporarily down.

SNS is publish-subscribe: a message published to a topic is pushed immediately to all subscribers, like SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email or SMS. It's for simple, high-throughput fan-out, with basic filtering by attributes or payload.

EventBridge is an event bus with rule-based routing. Events are JSON, and rules match on any part of the event's content with rich patterns, then route to many targets, over 20 AWS services and API destinations for third-party HTTP APIs, with input transformation. It receives events from AWS services and SaaS partners automatically, has a schema registry, can archive and replay events, and supports cross-account buses. EventBridge Scheduler handles cron-like schedules, and Pipes connects sources like SQS or DynamoDB Streams to targets with filtering and enrichment.

My rule of thumb: SQS when work must be queued and processed reliably by one service; SNS for simple, very high-volume fan-out; EventBridge as the event backbone for event-driven architectures, with many event types and consumers and content-based routing. They're often combined: EventBridge routes events into SQS queues, which consumers process at their own pace.

p17-403.q: SQS is a message queue, not a stream. Once a message is processed and deleted, it's gone, and there's no replay or multiple independent readers. It's ideal for task processing.
p17-403.k: kinesis vs sqs, kinesis vs kafka, msk, data streams aws, streaming aws, kinesis shards
x: SQS is a message queue, not a stream. Once a message is processed and deleted, it's gone, and there's no replay or multiple independent readers. It's ideal for task processing.

Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's managed streaming service. Records are stored in shards for 24 hours by default, extendable up to a year. Multiple consumers can read the same stream independently, each tracking its position, and replay data. Ordering is guaranteed per partition key within a shard. Capacity is per shard, about 1 MB per second in and 2 MB per second out, with on-demand mode that scales automatically. It integrates closely with Lambda, Firehose for loading into S3 or Redshift, and analytics services. It's simpler to operate than Kafka, but less flexible.

Amazon MSK is managed Apache Kafka, with a serverless option. It's the choice when the team or ecosystem already uses Kafka: Kafka clients, Kafka Connect connectors, Kafka Streams, existing tooling and skills, or portability across clouds and on-premise. It offers longer retention, higher throughput per partition, compaction, and the full Kafka feature set, but needs more Kafka expertise.
So: SQS for job queues; Kinesis for AWS-native streaming, like clickstreams, logs, IoT telemetry and real-time analytics; MSK when Kafka compatibility matters.
IQVIA's newer AWS services use Kafka for shipment events, since several consumers need the same stream and replay.

p17-404.q: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows as state machines, defined in Amazon States Language: tasks that call Lambda or over 200 AWS services directly, choices, parallel branches, maps over items, waits, and built-in retries and catch blocks per step. It's visual, so the workflow and each execution's progress are easy to see.
p17-404.k: step functions standard vs express, step functions workflow, state machine aws, express workflow, orchestrate lambdas
x: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows as state machines, defined in Amazon States Language: tasks that call Lambda or over 200 AWS services directly, choices, parallel branches, maps over items, waits, and built-in retries and catch blocks per step. It's visual, so the workflow and each execution's progress are easy to see.
There are two workflow types.

Standard workflows can run for up to one year. They have exactly-once execution of each step, full execution history kept for 90 days and visible in the console, and support for long waits and human approval steps using task tokens, where the workflow pauses until something calls back. They're priced per state transition. They're for long-running, business-critical processes where auditability matters, like an order or onboarding workflow, or a data transfer with manual approval.

Express workflows run for up to five minutes, with very high throughput, over 100,000 executions per second. They have at-least-once execution for asynchronous express, or at-most-once for synchronous, so steps should be idempotent. Execution history goes to CloudWatch Logs rather than being kept by the service. They're priced by number of executions, duration and memory, which is much cheaper for high-volume, short workflows, like processing each incoming event or IoT message, or orchestrating a few calls behind an API request.
A common pattern combines them: a Standard workflow for the overall business process, calling Express workflows for high-volume inner steps.

p17-405.q: When Lambda is triggered by SQS, it receives a batch of messages, up to 10 by default, or more with a batching window. Without special handling, if the function throws an error, the whole batch is considered failed: all messages become visible again and are retried, including the ones that were processed successfully. That causes duplicate processing, and a single bad message can keep the whole batch failing until everything reaches the dead-letter queue.
p17-405.k: lambda sqs partial batch failure, reportbatchitemfailures, batchitemfailures, sqs lambda batch, poison message lambda
x: When Lambda is triggered by SQS, it receives a batch of messages, up to 10 by default, or more with a batching window. Without special handling, if the function throws an error, the whole batch is considered failed: all messages become visible again and are retried, including the ones that were processed successfully. That causes duplicate processing, and a single bad message can keep the whole batch failing until everything reaches the dead-letter queue.

The fix is partial batch responses. I enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping. The function processes each message individually, catching errors per message, and returns a response listing only the message ids that failed, in batchItemFailures. Lambda deletes the successful messages from the queue and only makes the failed ones visible again for retry.

A few details. If the function throws instead of returning the list, the whole batch still fails, so the handler catches per-message exceptions. For FIFO queues, once a message fails, I should stop processing and report it and all the following messages in that group as failed, to keep ordering. The redrive policy's maxReceiveCount sends repeatedly failing messages to the DLQ. And consumers remain idempotent, since retries and duplicates still happen.
Powertools for AWS Lambda, available for .NET, Python, TypeScript and Java, has a batch processing utility that implements this pattern cleanly.

p17-406.q: Lambda functions can be packaged in two ways.
p17-406.k: lambda layers, lambda container image, lambda deployment package, lambda zip vs container, lambda package size
x: Lambda functions can be packaged in two ways.
A zip archive contains the function code and its dependencies, up to 50 MB zipped when uploaded directly and 250 MB unzipped. It's the classic option, with the fastest cold starts for small packages.

Layers let me put shared code or dependencies, like a common library, a runtime extension or large packages, into a separate archive that several functions reference, up to five layers per function. They reduce duplication and deployment size for each function. But they have downsides: versioning layers across many functions is awkward, the code isn't visible in one place, which complicates local testing, and the total unzipped size limit still includes layers. For compiled languages like .NET, where dependencies are bundled at build time anyway, layers add little; they're more useful for Python or Node, and for Lambda extensions, like monitoring agents.

Container images package the function as an OCI image, up to 10 GB, built from AWS base images or any image that implements the runtime interface. They suit large dependencies, like machine learning libraries, teams that already standardise on Docker tooling and scanning, and custom runtimes. Images are stored in ECR. Cold starts are optimised with caching and lazy loading, though large images can still be slower.
My default: zip for small functions, bundled at build time, and container images for large or complex dependencies. For .NET, Native AOT zip packages give the fastest cold starts.

p17-407.q: When Lambda is invoked asynchronously, like by S3 events, SNS, EventBridge, or an InvokeAsync call, the caller doesn't wait for the result. Lambda queues the event internally and runs the function. If it fails, Lambda retries automatically, twice by default, with delays between attempts. Events can also expire if they wait too long, up to six hours by default.
p17-407.k: lambda destinations, lambda dlq, async invocation lambda, on failure destination, lambda retries async, event invoke config
x: When Lambda is invoked asynchronously, like by S3 events, SNS, EventBridge, or an InvokeAsync call, the caller doesn't wait for the result. Lambda queues the event internally and runs the function. If it fails, Lambda retries automatically, twice by default, with delays between attempts. Events can also expire if they wait too long, up to six hours by default.
What happens to events that still fail? There are two options.

A dead-letter queue, an SQS queue or SNS topic configured on the function, receives the original event after all retries fail. It only captures failures, and only the event payload, without details of the error.

Destinations are the newer, richer option. I can configure an on-failure destination and an on-success destination: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, another Lambda function, or S3 for failures. The record sent includes the original request, the response or error details, like the error message and type, and metadata like the number of attempts. That makes troubleshooting and automated handling much easier, and on-success destinations allow simple chaining without the function calling the next step itself.
I also tune the retry count and maximum event age to the use case: for time-sensitive events, fewer retries and a shorter age.

Note that these settings apply only to asynchronous invocation. For SQS triggers, the queue's own redrive policy and DLQ handle failures; for Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, the event source mapping has its own failure destinations.

p17-408.q: By default, Lambda runs in an AWS-managed network with internet access, but it can't reach resources in my private VPC, like an RDS database or ElastiCache. To reach them, I attach the function to the VPC, choosing private subnets and security groups. Lambda creates Hyperplane elastic network interfaces, shared across functions with the same subnet and security group combination, so the old problem of slow cold starts due to network interface creation is gone.
p17-408.k: lambda in vpc, lambda rds connection, lambda vpc eni, lambda internet access vpc, lambda database connections
x: By default, Lambda runs in an AWS-managed network with internet access, but it can't reach resources in my private VPC, like an RDS database or ElastiCache. To reach them, I attach the function to the VPC, choosing private subnets and security groups. Lambda creates Hyperplane elastic network interfaces, shared across functions with the same subnet and security group combination, so the old problem of slow cold starts due to network interface creation is gone.

Once in the VPC, the function no longer has internet access by default. If it needs to call external APIs or AWS services, it needs a NAT gateway in a public subnet for internet traffic, or VPC endpoints for AWS services, like S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager and SQS, which keep traffic private and avoid NAT costs.

Connecting to RDS has a classic problem: Lambda scales by creating many concurrent instances, each opening its own database connections. A burst of 500 concurrent invocations can exhaust the database's connection limit, causing errors for everything using that database. Solutions: RDS Proxy, which pools and shares connections between function instances; limiting the function's reserved concurrency; opening the connection outside the handler, so warm invocations reuse it; and IAM database authentication, which RDS Proxy supports, to avoid storing passwords.
Security groups must allow traffic from the Lambda's security group to the database's port.

p17-409.q: RDS Proxy is a fully managed database proxy for RDS and Aurora, supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Applications connect to the proxy's endpoint instead of directly to the database, and the proxy maintains a pool of database connections that it shares among clients.
p17-409.k: rds proxy, connection pooling rds, lambda database connections, rds proxy failover, too many connections rds
x: RDS Proxy is a fully managed database proxy for RDS and Aurora, supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Applications connect to the proxy's endpoint instead of directly to the database, and the proxy maintains a pool of database connections that it shares among clients.

The main problems it solves. Connection storms: serverless functions and highly scaled containers can open far more connections than the database can handle, especially during traffic spikes. The proxy multiplexes many client connections over fewer database connections, protecting the database's memory and CPU. Failover: during a Multi-AZ failover, the proxy keeps client connections open and routes them to the new primary, which can reduce failover time for applications significantly, and clients don't need to handle DNS changes. Security: the proxy can enforce IAM authentication and fetch database credentials from Secrets Manager, so applications don't store database passwords, and TLS can be required.

There are some limitations. Connection pinning: when a session uses features that depend on session state, like temporary tables, session variables or certain prepared statements, the proxy pins the client to one database connection, which reduces the pooling benefit. It adds a small amount of latency. And it costs extra, priced by the database's capacity.

So I use it for Lambda functions that access relational databases, for applications with spiky connection counts, and where faster failover matters. For a few long-running containers with their own connection pools, it's often unnecessary.

p17-410.q: Both are managed relational databases, but Aurora has a different, cloud-native architecture.
p17-410.k: aurora vs rds, amazon aurora, aurora serverless, aurora storage, aurora replicas, aurora global database
x: Both are managed relational databases, but Aurora has a different, cloud-native architecture.

Standard RDS runs a database engine, like PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or Oracle, on an instance with EBS storage. High availability uses Multi-AZ with a synchronous standby, and read replicas use asynchronous replication with their own copies of the data.

Aurora, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL only, separates compute from storage. The storage layer is distributed across three availability zones, with six copies of the data, automatically growing up to 256 TB, and self-healing. Replicas, up to 15, share the same storage volume, so replica lag is typically only milliseconds, and any replica can be promoted quickly in a failover, usually in under 30 seconds. Backups are continuous with point-in-time recovery, and database cloning is fast.

Extra features: Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity up and down in fine increments with load, good for variable workloads; Global Database, for cross-region replication with low lag and fast regional failover; and features like backtracking for MySQL. AWS also launched Aurora DSQL, a distributed, serverless option.

The trade-offs: Aurora costs more per instance and charges for I/O in the standard configuration, though the I/O-Optimized option helps for heavy workloads. And it doesn't support SQL Server, so SQL Server workloads use standard RDS.
I'd choose Aurora PostgreSQL for new, high-availability, read-heavy workloads, and standard RDS for smaller workloads or engines Aurora doesn't support.

p17-411.q: They're often confused, but they solve different problems.
p17-411.k: multi az vs read replica, rds high availability, rds failover, rds standby, multi az cluster
x: They're often confused, but they solve different problems.

Multi-AZ is for high availability and durability. RDS keeps a synchronous standby copy of the database in another availability zone. Every write is committed on both. The standby doesn't serve any traffic in the classic Multi-AZ instance deployment. If the primary fails, or its zone has a problem, or during certain maintenance, RDS automatically fails over to the standby, typically in one to two minutes, and the DNS endpoint points to the new primary. Applications just reconnect to the same endpoint. No data is lost, because replication is synchronous.

Read replicas are for read scaling. They use asynchronous replication, so they can lag behind the primary. They have their own endpoints and serve read-only queries, like reports and search, which takes load off the primary. They can be in other regions, for local reads or disaster recovery, and can be promoted to standalone databases manually, but promotion isn't automatic failover, and recent writes may be missing.
There's also a Multi-AZ DB cluster option for MySQL and PostgreSQL, with two readable standbys, which combines faster failover with some read capacity.
In production, I'd always use Multi-AZ for important databases, and add read replicas only if read load or reporting requires them, with the application aware of replica lag.

p17-412.q: DynamoDB has two capacity modes that affect cost and how it handles traffic.
p17-412.k: dynamodb on demand vs provisioned, dynamodb capacity mode, rcu wcu, dynamodb autoscaling, dynamodb throttling cost
x: DynamoDB has two capacity modes that affect cost and how it handles traffic.

On-demand mode charges per read and write request. There's no capacity planning: the table automatically accommodates traffic, scaling up instantly to previously seen peaks, and adapting to new peaks quickly. It's ideal for new tables with unknown traffic, spiky or unpredictable workloads, and development environments. In late 2024, AWS cut on-demand prices by half, which made it the sensible default for many more workloads.

Provisioned mode means I specify read capacity units and write capacity units per second. It's cheaper per request when traffic is steady and predictable and the capacity is well utilised, and reserved capacity reduces costs further. Auto scaling adjusts provisioned capacity based on utilisation targets, but it reacts over minutes, so sudden spikes beyond the provisioned level can be throttled, although burst capacity absorbs short spikes.

My approach: start with on-demand, observe the traffic pattern in CloudWatch, and switch to provisioned with auto scaling if the traffic is steady and the savings are significant. I can switch modes, with some limits on how often.
Either way, capacity is distributed across partitions, so a hot partition key can be throttled even if total capacity looks fine. Good key design matters more than the capacity mode.
On-demand tables can also have a maximum throughput set, to cap unexpected costs.

p17-413.q: DynamoDB throttles requests when they exceed available capacity, returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException or ThrottlingException. The SDKs retry automatically with backoff, so throttling first shows up as higher latency, then as errors.
p17-413.k: dynamodb throttling, hot partition, hot key dynamodb, provisionedthroughputexceeded, write sharding dynamodb, adaptive capacity
x: DynamoDB throttles requests when they exceed available capacity, returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException or ThrottlingException. The SDKs retry automatically with backoff, so throttling first shows up as higher latency, then as errors.

There are two kinds of causes. Table-level: total traffic exceeds the provisioned capacity, or exceeds on-demand's instant scaling for a sudden huge spike. Fixes are raising capacity, adjusting auto scaling, or switching to on-demand.

Partition-level, which is more common and subtle: each partition supports roughly 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes per second. If a large share of traffic targets one partition key, like a single popular item, a status value like "PENDING" used as a partition key, or today's date as the key for all writes, that partition is overwhelmed while the rest of the table is idle. That's a hot partition. Adaptive capacity helps by shifting capacity to busy partitions and isolating frequently accessed items, but it can't exceed the per-partition limit.

Fixes for hot keys: choose a partition key with high cardinality and evenly distributed access, like a shipment id rather than a status; write sharding, adding a random or calculated suffix to the key, like date plus a number from 1 to 10, and querying all shards in parallel when reading; caching hot reads with DAX or ElastiCache; and batching or smoothing write bursts through a queue.
CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB shows the most accessed keys, which pinpoints the hot partition quickly.

p17-414.q: DynamoDB Streams captures every change to items in a table, inserts, updates and deletes, as an ordered sequence of records, kept for 24 hours. Each record can include the keys only, the new image, the old image, or both, depending on the stream view type.
p17-414.k: dynamodb streams, change data capture dynamodb, dynamodb stream lambda, stream view type, react to dynamodb changes
x: DynamoDB Streams captures every change to items in a table, inserts, updates and deletes, as an ordered sequence of records, kept for 24 hours. Each record can include the keys only, the new image, the old image, or both, depending on the stream view type.
Records for the same item appear in the order the changes happened, and Lambda can process the stream through an event source mapping, receiving batches of changes.

Common uses. Event-driven reactions: when a new item is inserted, like a shipment, trigger a function that sends a notification or starts a workflow, without the writing service having to publish an event itself. It's like a built-in outbox. Maintaining derived data: updating aggregates, like counts per site, or denormalised copies of items in another table. Replicating data to other stores: pushing changes to OpenSearch for full-text search, to S3 for analytics, or to another system. Auditing: recording old and new values of every change. Global tables also use streams under the hood for cross-region replication.
There's also Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, an alternative with longer retention and more consumers.

Some considerations: processing is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent; a failing batch blocks the shard, so I configure bisect on error, maximum retries and an on-failure destination; and items expired by TTL appear as deletes, with a flag identifying them as system deletions.

p17-415.q: Conditional writes let a PutItem, UpdateItem or DeleteItem succeed only if a condition on the existing item is true, checked atomically by DynamoDB. If it's false, the write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, and nothing changes.
p17-415.k: dynamodb conditional write, condition expression, dynamodb transactions, transactwriteitems, optimistic locking dynamodb, prevent overwrite dynamodb
x: Conditional writes let a PutItem, UpdateItem or DeleteItem succeed only if a condition on the existing item is true, checked atomically by DynamoDB. If it's false, the write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, and nothing changes.

Common uses. Prevent overwriting: attribute_not_exists on the key makes a put create the item only if it doesn't already exist, which gives idempotent creation and unique constraints. Optimistic locking: items carry a version number; an update includes the condition that the version equals the value I read, and increments it. If someone else updated it first, my write fails, and I reload and retry. Business rules: decrement stock only if quantity is greater than zero, so two concurrent requests can't take the last item.

Transactions, with TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems, group up to 100 actions across multiple items and tables into an all-or-nothing operation, with ACID guarantees. For example, reserving a kit and creating the allocation record together, or maintaining a uniqueness record in a separate item alongside the main item. Each action can have its own condition, and if any condition fails, the whole transaction is cancelled, with the reasons returned per item. A client token makes transactions idempotent for retries.

The trade-offs: transactions cost twice the capacity of normal writes, and conflicts with concurrent transactions on the same items cause cancellations that need retries. So I use conditions widely and transactions only where multiple items truly must change together.

p17-416.q: Time to Live lets DynamoDB automatically delete items after a timestamp I specify. I enable TTL on the table and choose an attribute name, like expiresAt. Each item can store a Unix epoch time in seconds in that attribute. After that time, DynamoDB deletes the item in the background, without consuming write capacity, so it's free.
p17-416.k: dynamodb ttl, time to live dynamodb, expire items dynamodb, ttl attribute, automatic deletion dynamodb
x: Time to Live lets DynamoDB automatically delete items after a timestamp I specify. I enable TTL on the table and choose an attribute name, like expiresAt. Each item can store a Unix epoch time in seconds in that attribute. After that time, DynamoDB deletes the item in the background, without consuming write capacity, so it's free.

It's great for data that's only valuable for a limited time: sessions, temporary tokens, idempotency keys, cache entries, rate-limiting counters, and old events or logs that should be kept for, say, 90 days.

The gotchas. Deletion isn't immediate. Expired items are typically removed within a few days of expiry, not at the exact second. Until then, they still appear in reads, queries and scans. So the application must filter out expired items itself, for example with a filter expression comparing expiresAt with the current time, if correctness depends on expiry.
The value must be a number in epoch seconds. Milliseconds, or a date string, are silently ignored, and the item never expires, which is a common mistake.

TTL deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as deletes, marked as done by the service, so stream consumers can distinguish them from user deletions, for example to archive expired items to S3 before they disappear.
And for regulated data, automatic deletion must match the retention policy, which may require keeping data far longer than operational needs.

p17-417.q: DAX, DynamoDB Accelerator, is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. It's API-compatible: the application uses the DAX client, which has the same API as the DynamoDB client, and reads go through DAX. Cache hits return in microseconds instead of single-digit milliseconds. It caches individual items from GetItem and BatchGetItem in the item cache, and results of queries and scans in the query cache. Writes go through DAX to DynamoDB, updating the item cache.
p17-417.k: dax, dynamodb accelerator, dax vs elasticache, dynamodb caching, microsecond latency dynamodb
x: DAX, DynamoDB Accelerator, is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. It's API-compatible: the application uses the DAX client, which has the same API as the DynamoDB client, and reads go through DAX. Cache hits return in microseconds instead of single-digit milliseconds. It caches individual items from GetItem and BatchGetItem in the item cache, and results of queries and scans in the query cache. Writes go through DAX to DynamoDB, updating the item cache.

It's useful for read-heavy workloads with repeated reads of the same items, like hot product or configuration items, and for absorbing read spikes that would otherwise throttle hot partitions, without changing application logic much.

The limitations: it's eventually consistent; strongly consistent reads bypass the cache. The query cache isn't invalidated by writes, it just expires by TTL, so query results can be stale. It only caches DynamoDB, it runs in a VPC as a cluster with its own cost, and the SDK support varies by language.

ElastiCache, with Redis or Valkey, is a general-purpose cache. It's more work, since the application implements caching logic, like cache-aside with explicit keys and invalidation, but it's much more flexible: caching computed results, API responses, data from any source, plus data structures like sorted sets, counters, rate limiting, sessions and pub-sub.
So I'd use DAX for a quick, transparent speed-up of DynamoDB reads, and ElastiCache for broader caching needs.

p17-418.q: S3 offers storage classes with different costs and access characteristics.
p17-418.k: s3 storage classes, s3 lifecycle policy, glacier, intelligent tiering, s3 infrequent access, s3 cost optimization
x: S3 offers storage classes with different costs and access characteristics.

S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data, with low latency and high availability. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage, for a small monitoring fee, which is great when access patterns are unknown. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access and One Zone-IA are cheaper for data accessed rarely, but have retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration; One Zone stores data in a single availability zone, so it's for re-creatable data. Glacier Instant Retrieval is for archives that are rarely accessed but must be available in milliseconds. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive are the cheapest, for long-term archives, with retrieval times from minutes to hours, which fits compliance archives kept for years.

Lifecycle policies automate moving and deleting objects. A rule, which can be filtered by prefix or tags, defines transitions, like moving objects to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier after 180 days, and expiring them after seven years. Rules can also delete old versions in versioned buckets, and abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days, which otherwise silently cost money.

I design lifecycle rules around how data is actually used and the retention requirements. For regulated data, Object Lock can make objects immutable for the retention period, so they can't be deleted early, even by administrators.

p17-419.q: S3 can emit events when objects are created, deleted, restored or replicated. I configure notifications on the bucket, with filters by prefix and suffix, like uploads/ and .csv, and send them to a Lambda function, an SQS queue, an SNS topic, or to EventBridge, which can be enabled on the bucket to receive all events and route them with rules.
p17-419.k: s3 event notification, s3 trigger lambda, s3 to sqs, s3 eventbridge, process uploaded file aws, object created event
x: S3 can emit events when objects are created, deleted, restored or replicated. I configure notifications on the bucket, with filters by prefix and suffix, like uploads/ and .csv, and send them to a Lambda function, an SQS queue, an SNS topic, or to EventBridge, which can be enabled on the bucket to receive all events and route them with rules.

A typical file-processing flow: the client uploads a file directly to S3 using a pre-signed URL. The ObjectCreated event goes to an SQS queue. A worker, a Lambda function or an ECS service, reads the message, which contains the bucket and key, downloads or streams the file, validates and processes it, writes results to the database, and records the status. Putting SQS in the middle, rather than triggering Lambda directly, gives buffering, retries, a dead-letter queue and control over concurrency.

Some details. Events are delivered at least once, and rarely out of order, so processing must be idempotent, for example keyed by the object key and its version id or ETag. Keys in events are URL-encoded, so spaces and special characters need decoding. Avoid recursive loops, where a function triggered by uploads writes its output to the same prefix and triggers itself; I write outputs to a different prefix or bucket. And large files should be streamed rather than loaded into memory.
EventBridge is better when several consumers need the events, or more advanced filtering.

p17-420.q: S3 versioning keeps every version of an object in a bucket. When an object is overwritten, the old version is kept; when it's deleted, S3 adds a delete marker instead of removing the data, so the previous version can be restored. It protects against accidental overwrites and deletions, application bugs, and some ransomware scenarios. Once enabled, it can only be suspended, not removed. Old versions cost storage, so lifecycle rules expire noncurrent versions after a period. Versioning is also required for replication.
p17-420.k: s3 versioning, s3 object lock, worm storage, s3 compliance mode, protect from deletion s3, mfa delete
x: S3 versioning keeps every version of an object in a bucket. When an object is overwritten, the old version is kept; when it's deleted, S3 adds a delete marker instead of removing the data, so the previous version can be restored. It protects against accidental overwrites and deletions, application bugs, and some ransomware scenarios. Once enabled, it can only be suspended, not removed. Old versions cost storage, so lifecycle rules expire noncurrent versions after a period. Versioning is also required for replication.

Object Lock adds write-once-read-many protection on top of versioning. Locked object versions can't be deleted or overwritten until their retention period ends. There are two modes. Governance mode prevents deletion by most users, but users with special permission can bypass it, which is useful for testing or flexible policies. Compliance mode can't be bypassed by anyone, not even the root user, and the retention period can't be shortened; it's designed for regulatory requirements, like financial records or clinical data, that must be kept unchanged for a defined period. Legal holds lock objects indefinitely until the hold is removed, independent of retention periods.
For regulated audit data or validated documents, compliance mode Object Lock provides strong evidence that records weren't altered, which supports data integrity requirements.
MFA Delete is another protection, requiring MFA to permanently delete versions or change versioning.

p17-421.q: CloudFront is AWS's CDN. Serving a React or Angular build from S3 through CloudFront gives fast global delivery, HTTPS with a free ACM certificate, and caching at edge locations.
p17-421.k: cloudfront s3, origin access control, cloudfront spa routing, static website aws, cdn caching cloudfront, s3 private bucket cloudfront
x: CloudFront is AWS's CDN. Serving a React or Angular build from S3 through CloudFront gives fast global delivery, HTTPS with a free ACM certificate, and caching at edge locations.

Security: the S3 bucket stays private, with Block Public Access on, and is not configured as a public website. CloudFront uses Origin Access Control to sign its requests to S3, and the bucket policy only allows the CloudFront distribution to read objects. So users can't bypass CloudFront to access the bucket directly.

SPA routing: deep links, like /shipments/123, don't exist as files in S3, so S3 returns 403 or 404. I configure CloudFront custom error responses to return index.html with a 200 status for those errors, or use a CloudFront Function to rewrite paths without file extensions to index.html, which is cleaner because real API 404s aren't masked.

Caching: hashed asset files, like main.abc123.js, get long cache times, with Cache-Control max-age of a year and immutable, while index.html gets no-cache, so users pick up new releases immediately. After deployment, I invalidate index.html if needed.

Extra protection: response headers policies add security headers like HSTS and a Content Security Policy; AWS WAF can be attached; and API calls can go through the same distribution under /api to an ALB or API Gateway origin, so the app and API share one domain without CORS.

p17-422.q: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, and its routing policies decide which answer to return for a DNS query.
p17-422.k: route 53 routing policies, weighted routing, latency routing, failover routing, geolocation routing, dns aws
x: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, and its routing policies decide which answer to return for a DNS query.
Simple routing returns one record, or several values in random order, with no health checks per value.

Weighted routing splits traffic between records by weight, like 90 percent to the current version and 10 percent to a new one. It's useful for gradual migrations, canary releases at the DNS level, or A/B testing.
Latency-based routing sends users to the region with the lowest latency for them, for multi-region applications.

Failover routing has a primary and a secondary record. Route 53 health checks monitor the primary, and if it fails, DNS answers switch to the secondary, like a static maintenance site or a standby region. That's a building block of disaster recovery.

Geolocation routing answers based on the user's country or continent, for data residency, localised content or legal restrictions. Geoproximity routing is based on distance, with a bias to shift traffic between regions.
Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy records, a simple form of client-side load balancing with health checks.
IP-based routing uses the client's IP ranges.
Alias records are a Route 53 extension that point to AWS resources, like a load balancer, CloudFront or S3, at the zone apex, which a CNAME can't do, and they're free to query.
DNS changes are subject to caching by TTL, so for failover I keep TTLs short, like 60 seconds.

p17-423.q: VPC endpoints let resources in private subnets reach AWS services without going over the internet, and without needing a NAT gateway. Traffic stays on the AWS network, which improves security and can significantly reduce NAT data processing costs.
p17-423.k: vpc endpoints, gateway endpoint vs interface endpoint, privatelink, access s3 privately, nat gateway cost reduction
x: VPC endpoints let resources in private subnets reach AWS services without going over the internet, and without needing a NAT gateway. Traffic stays on the AWS network, which improves security and can significantly reduce NAT data processing costs.
There are two types.

Gateway endpoints are available only for S3 and DynamoDB. They're added as a target in the subnet route tables, so traffic to those services goes through the endpoint. They're free. Endpoint policies can restrict which buckets or tables can be accessed through them, and bucket policies can require access to come through a specific endpoint, which prevents data exfiltration to other accounts' buckets.

Interface endpoints, powered by PrivateLink, are available for most other AWS services, like Secrets Manager, SQS, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS, KMS and SSM, and for third-party and your own services. They create elastic network interfaces with private IP addresses in your subnets. With private DNS enabled, the normal service hostname resolves to these private IPs, so applications don't change anything. They're charged per hour per availability zone and per GB processed, and protected by security groups.

For example, ECS tasks in private subnets without internet access need interface endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager, plus the S3 gateway endpoint for image layers, to pull images and start.
I always add the free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, and interface endpoints where traffic is high or internet access isn't allowed.

p17-424.q: These are different ways to connect VPCs and services.
p17-424.k: vpc peering vs transit gateway, privatelink, connect vpcs, hub and spoke network aws, cross account networking
x: These are different ways to connect VPCs and services.

VPC peering creates a direct, private connection between two VPCs, in the same or different accounts and regions. It's simple, has no bandwidth bottleneck, and no hourly charge, only data transfer. But it isn't transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A can't reach C through B. With many VPCs, the number of peering connections grows quickly, becoming a mesh that's hard to manage. CIDR ranges can't overlap.

Transit Gateway is a regional hub that VPCs, VPN connections and Direct Connect gateways attach to. It routes between them, with route tables for segmentation, like keeping production and development apart while both reach shared services. It scales to thousands of VPCs and simplifies routing in a hub-and-spoke design, and can peer across regions. It costs per attachment per hour and per GB.

PrivateLink is different: instead of connecting whole networks, it exposes a specific service. A provider puts the service behind a Network Load Balancer and creates an endpoint service; consumers create interface endpoints in their VPCs. Traffic flows one way to that service only, and overlapping CIDRs don't matter. It's ideal for exposing a shared internal API to many teams or accounts, or consuming SaaS privately, with minimal network exposure.
In multi-account organisations, Transit Gateway for general connectivity plus PrivateLink for specific shared services is a common combination.

p17-425.q: Using several AWS accounts, organised with AWS Organizations, is the recommended way to structure an AWS environment. An account is the strongest isolation boundary in AWS.
p17-425.k: aws organizations, multi account strategy, service control policies, scp, control tower, landing zone
x: Using several AWS accounts, organised with AWS Organizations, is the recommended way to structure an AWS environment. An account is the strongest isolation boundary in AWS.

The benefits. Security isolation: a compromised credential or misconfiguration in a development account can't affect production. Blast radius: limits and quotas are per account, so one team's runaway process doesn't consume another's. Clear cost tracking per account, team or environment. Simpler permissions: instead of complex IAM conditions to separate environments in one account, each environment is its own account. And compliance: regulated workloads can live in tightly controlled accounts.

A typical structure has organisational units, like Security, with log archive and audit accounts; Infrastructure, with shared networking; Workloads, with separate dev, test and prod accounts per application; and Sandbox for experiments. AWS Control Tower sets up this landing zone with guardrails, account vending and centralised logging, and IAM Identity Center gives people single sign-on into accounts with role-based permission sets, instead of IAM users.

Service Control Policies are organisation-level guardrails. They define the maximum permissions available in an account or OU, applying even to administrators and the account's root user. They don't grant permissions; they limit them. Typical SCPs: deny leaving the organisation, deny disabling CloudTrail or GuardDuty, restrict which regions can be used, and deny creating resources without required tags.
Resource Control Policies, added in 2024, similarly limit permissions on resources.

p17-426.q: IAM evaluates every request against all policies that apply, and the logic is simple to remember: by default, everything is implicitly denied; an explicit allow grants access; and an explicit deny always wins over any allow.
p17-426.k: iam policy evaluation, explicit deny, implicit deny, permission boundary, resource policy vs identity policy, iam access denied why
x: IAM evaluates every request against all policies that apply, and the logic is simple to remember: by default, everything is implicitly denied; an explicit allow grants access; and an explicit deny always wins over any allow.

The policies involved within an account: identity-based policies attached to the user or role; resource-based policies, like an S3 bucket policy or KMS key policy; permission boundaries, which set the maximum permissions an identity can have; session policies, passed when assuming a role; and, from the organisation, Service Control Policies and Resource Control Policies.

The evaluation order, simplified: if any policy has an explicit deny matching the request, it's denied. Then the request must be allowed by SCPs, by the permission boundary if one is set, and by the session policy if there is one, because these are limits. Finally, it must be allowed by either the identity policy or the resource policy. For cross-account access, both sides must allow it: the caller's identity policy and the resource policy in the other account.

When I debug an AccessDenied error, I check, in order: the error message, which now often names the policy type that denied it; CloudTrail for the exact action, resource and principal; any explicit denies, including SCPs and bucket policies with conditions, like requiring encryption or a VPC endpoint; KMS key policies, which are commonly forgotten when accessing encrypted S3 objects or secrets; and the IAM policy simulator.

p17-427.q: ECS tasks use two different IAM roles, and confusing them is a common source of errors.
p17-427.k: ecs task role vs execution role, ecs iam role, task execution role permissions, container aws credentials, ecs secrets permission
x: ECS tasks use two different IAM roles, and confusing them is a common source of errors.

The task execution role is used by the ECS agent and Fargate infrastructure, not by my application code. It grants the permissions needed to start the task: pulling the container image from ECR, sending container logs to CloudWatch Logs, and fetching secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store that are injected as environment variables in the task definition. The managed policy AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy covers ECR and logs; secrets need extra permissions, including KMS decrypt if a customer key encrypts them.

The task role is used by my application inside the container. When the code uses the AWS SDK, the SDK automatically gets temporary credentials for this role from the container credentials endpoint. It grants whatever the application needs: reading from an S3 bucket, sending messages to SQS, reading and writing a DynamoDB table. Each service should have its own task role with least-privilege permissions.

Symptoms of mixing them up: if a task fails to start with errors pulling the image, or "unable to retrieve secret", the execution role is missing permissions. If the task runs but the application gets AccessDenied when calling S3 or SQS, the task role is missing permissions, or the task has no task role, so the SDK can't find credentials.
So the execution role gets the task running; the task role is what the running code uses.

p17-428.q: Pods running on EKS often need to call AWS services. The bad approach is giving the worker node's instance role all permissions, because then every pod on the node gets them, or storing access keys in Kubernetes secrets. The proper approaches give each workload its own IAM role.
p17-428.k: eks pod identity, irsa, iam roles for service accounts, eks aws credentials, pod iam role
x: Pods running on EKS often need to call AWS services. The bad approach is giving the worker node's instance role all permissions, because then every pod on the node gets them, or storing access keys in Kubernetes secrets. The proper approaches give each workload its own IAM role.

IRSA, IAM Roles for Service Accounts, was the original way. The cluster has an OIDC provider registered in IAM. A Kubernetes service account is annotated with an IAM role ARN, and the role's trust policy allows that specific service account in that namespace to assume it, using a web identity token that EKS projects into the pod. The AWS SDK picks this up automatically.

EKS Pod Identity is the newer, simpler option. An agent runs on the nodes, and I create a pod identity association, linking a namespace and service account to an IAM role, through the EKS API. The role's trust policy simply trusts the EKS Pod Identity service, so the same role can be reused across clusters without updating trust policies with each cluster's OIDC provider. It also supports session tags for attribute-based access control.

Either way, the pod gets temporary credentials scoped to its own role, following least privilege. I also block pods from reaching the node's instance metadata service, or set the hop limit to one, so pods can't fall back to the node's role.

p17-429.q: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, and its keys never leave KMS unencrypted. But KMS can only encrypt up to 4 KB directly, and calling KMS for every piece of data would be slow and costly. Envelope encryption solves this.
p17-429.k: kms envelope encryption, data key, aws kms, customer managed key, encrypt data aws, generate data key
x: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, and its keys never leave KMS unencrypted. But KMS can only encrypt up to 4 KB directly, and calling KMS for every piece of data would be slow and costly. Envelope encryption solves this.

The process: the application asks KMS to generate a data key, under a KMS key, often called the master key. KMS returns two copies of the data key: plaintext and encrypted under the KMS key. The application encrypts the data locally with the plaintext data key, using a fast algorithm like AES-GCM, then discards the plaintext key from memory, and stores the encrypted data key alongside the encrypted data. To decrypt, the application sends the encrypted data key to KMS, which decrypts it, if the caller has permission, and returns the plaintext data key, which then decrypts the data locally.

The benefits: large data can be encrypted efficiently; the KMS key itself never leaves KMS; access to data is controlled by KMS key policies and IAM, and every decrypt is logged in CloudTrail; and rotating the KMS key doesn't require re-encrypting all the data.

AWS services, like S3, EBS, RDS and Secrets Manager, use envelope encryption under the hood when you choose a KMS key. For application-level encryption, the AWS Encryption SDK implements it properly, including data key caching.
Customer managed keys give control over key policies, rotation and deletion, and allow cross-account access.

p17-430.k: cloudtrail vs cloudwatch vs config, aws audit, who changed resource aws, aws config rules, aws compliance monitoring
x: They answer different questions.

CloudWatch answers "how are my systems performing?" It collects metrics, like CPU, request counts and latency, and logs from applications and services, with alarms, dashboards, Logs Insights queries, and features like Container Insights, Application Signals and synthetic canaries. It's for operational monitoring.

CloudTrail answers "who did what, when, and from where?" It records API calls made in the account: the identity, the action, the time, the source IP and the request parameters, whether from the console, CLI, SDK or AWS services. Management events, like creating or deleting resources and changing IAM policies, are recorded by default; data events, like S3 object reads or Lambda invocations, can be enabled. Trails deliver logs to S3, ideally in a central, locked-down logging account, for security investigations and audits. CloudTrail Lake allows SQL queries over events.

AWS Config answers "what does my resource configuration look like, how has it changed, and is it compliant?" It records configuration snapshots of resources over time, with relationships between them, so I can see what a security group looked like last Tuesday. Config rules continuously evaluate resources against policies, like "S3 buckets must block public access" or "EBS volumes must be encrypted", flagging non-compliant resources, and can trigger automatic remediation. Conformance packs bundle rules for standards.
In an investigation, I'd use CloudWatch to notice a problem, Config to see what changed, and CloudTrail to find who changed it.

p17-431.q: CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query language for searching and analysing log groups. With structured JSON logs, fields are discovered automatically, which makes queries much more powerful.
p17-431.k: cloudwatch logs insights, query cloudwatch logs, logs insights query examples, find errors cloudwatch, parse logs aws
x: CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query language for searching and analysing log groups. With structured JSON logs, fields are discovered automatically, which makes queries much more powerful.
A typical investigation for a spike in errors:
First, filter errors and count them over time to see when it started: fields @timestamp, @message, then filter level = "Error", then stats count(*) by bin(5m).
Then group by error type or endpoint to see what's failing: stats count(*) by exceptionType, path, sorted by count descending.

Then follow one failing request: filter traceId = "the-id", sorted by @timestamp, across several log groups at once, since Insights can query multiple log groups, which shows the request's path through services.
For latency: stats avg(durationMs), pct(durationMs, 95), pct(durationMs, 99) by path, to find slow endpoints. And for unstructured lines, the parse command extracts fields using a pattern or regex.

Practical tips: choose a narrow time range, since queries are billed per GB scanned; save useful queries for the team; add query results to dashboards; and use metric filters or embedded metric format for things that need alarms, since Insights is for investigation, not continuous alerting. There's also a natural-language query generator, and support for SQL and OpenSearch PPL query languages now.
Good queries depend on good logs: consistent structured fields like correlation id, tenant, endpoint and duration.

p17-432.q: AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing: it records requests as they flow through services, with segments for each service and subsegments for calls to databases, HTTP APIs and AWS services, and shows a service map with latencies and error rates between components.
p17-432.k: aws x-ray, adot, aws distro for opentelemetry, tracing aws ecs lambda, cloudwatch application signals, service map aws
x: AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing: it records requests as they flow through services, with segments for each service and subsegments for calls to databases, HTTP APIs and AWS services, and shows a service map with latencies and error rates between components.

Today, the recommended way to instrument applications is OpenTelemetry, using the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry, ADOT. Applications use the standard OpenTelemetry SDK, like OpenTelemetry for .NET with ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SQL and AWS SDK instrumentation, and export spans over OTLP to a collector, which sends them to X-Ray, and metrics to CloudWatch. AWS has also announced that the older X-Ray SDKs and daemon are moving to maintenance, so OpenTelemetry is the path forward, and X-Ray now accepts OTLP directly.

How it fits each compute type. ECS: run the ADOT collector or CloudWatch agent as a sidecar container in the task definition, with the task role allowing X-Ray writes. Lambda: enable active tracing, and use the ADOT Lambda layer or Powertools for traces. EKS: run the collector as a DaemonSet or use the CloudWatch Observability add-on.
CloudWatch Application Signals builds on this, giving service-level dashboards with latency, errors and SLOs automatically.

Key practices: propagate trace context across HTTP calls and messages, including SQS and Kafka message attributes; sample sensibly, keeping all errors; and log the trace id with every log line to jump from a trace to its logs.

p17-433.q: ECS services support several deployment strategies.
p17-433.k: ecs rolling deployment, ecs blue green, ecs deployment circuit breaker, minimumhealthypercent, ecs rollback, codedeploy ecs
x: ECS services support several deployment strategies.

Rolling update is the default. ECS replaces tasks gradually, controlled by minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent. For example, 100 and 200 means ECS starts new tasks first, up to double the desired count, waits for them to pass health checks, then stops old tasks, so capacity never drops. 50 and 100 replaces half at a time without extra capacity.

The deployment circuit breaker watches a rolling deployment: if new tasks keep failing to start or fail health checks, it marks the deployment as failed, and with rollback enabled, automatically returns to the last successful deployment. CloudWatch alarms can also be attached to deployments, so if error rates or latency alarms fire during the deployment, it's rolled back too. Without this, a bad deployment could loop forever trying to start failing tasks.

Blue/green deployments create a full new set of tasks, the green environment, alongside the old blue one, then shift traffic at the load balancer. Since 2025, ECS supports blue/green natively, with lifecycle hooks to run tests, a test listener to check green before production traffic, and a bake time before old tasks are removed, allowing instant rollback by switching traffic back. Previously this required CodeDeploy, which also supports canary and linear traffic shifting. ECS now also has native linear and canary strategies.
I'd use rolling with circuit breaker and alarms as the baseline, and blue/green or canary for critical services.

p17-434.q: ECS service auto scaling adjusts the desired number of tasks in a service, using Application Auto Scaling.
p17-434.k: ecs service auto scaling, target tracking ecs, ecs scale on request count, step scaling, ecs scale on sqs queue depth
x: ECS service auto scaling adjusts the desired number of tasks in a service, using Application Auto Scaling.

Target tracking is the simplest and usually best. I pick a metric and a target, like average CPU at 60 percent, memory at 70 percent, or ALB request count per target at 500, and auto scaling adds or removes tasks to keep the metric near that target. Request count per target is often better than CPU for web APIs, because it reacts directly to load.
Step scaling uses CloudWatch alarms with steps, like add two tasks when CPU is above 70 percent and four when above 85 percent, which gives more control for unusual patterns.

Scheduled scaling changes the minimum and maximum capacity at specific times, like scaling up before business hours or a known batch window. Predictive scaling, now available for ECS, forecasts load from history and scales ahead of time.

For queue workers, I scale on queue backlog. The best metric is backlog per task: the approximate number of visible messages divided by running tasks, published as a custom metric or computed with metric math, with a target based on how many messages a task can process within acceptable latency.

Things to tune: minimum and maximum tasks, so there's always some capacity and costs are bounded; cooldowns, with scale-out fast and scale-in slower to avoid flapping; and enough cluster capacity, which Fargate handles automatically, while EC2 needs capacity providers.

p17-435.q: Capacity providers decide where ECS tasks run and manage the underlying capacity.
p17-435.k: ecs capacity providers, fargate spot, ecs managed scaling, ec2 capacity provider, spot interruption ecs
x: Capacity providers decide where ECS tasks run and manage the underlying capacity.

For Fargate, there are two built-in capacity providers: FARGATE and FARGATE_SPOT. Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare AWS capacity at up to about 70 percent discount, but tasks can be interrupted with a two-minute warning when AWS needs the capacity back. ECS sends SIGTERM, and the application should shut down gracefully, finishing or returning in-flight work.

For EC2-based clusters, a capacity provider links to an Auto Scaling group. With managed scaling, ECS scales the group based on the capacity tasks need, so instances are added when tasks can't be placed, and removed when they're empty. Managed termination protection prevents scale-in from terminating instances still running tasks. And ECS Managed Instances is a newer option where AWS manages the EC2 instances for you.

A capacity provider strategy on a service splits tasks between providers using base and weight. For example, base 2 on FARGATE means the first two tasks always run on regular Fargate, and weight 1 on FARGATE and 3 on FARGATE_SPOT puts three quarters of additional tasks on Spot. This keeps a guaranteed baseline while reducing cost.

Fargate Spot fits stateless, interruption-tolerant workloads: queue workers with idempotent processing, batch jobs, development and test environments, and extra capacity for web APIs above a stable baseline. I wouldn't use it for singletons or work that can't be retried.

p17-436.q: Amazon ECR is AWS's container registry, and a few practices keep it secure and tidy.
p17-436.k: ecr lifecycle policy, ecr image scanning, ecr immutable tags, container registry aws, ecr best practices
x: Amazon ECR is AWS's container registry, and a few practices keep it secure and tidy.

Tag immutability: I enable it, so a tag like 1.4.2 or a commit SHA can't be overwritten with a different image. Deployments reference immutable tags or digests, so what's tested is exactly what's deployed, and rollback means redeploying a previous tag. I avoid deploying "latest".

Scanning: basic scanning checks images for operating system vulnerabilities on push. Enhanced scanning, using Amazon Inspector, scans continuously, including programming language packages, like NuGet and npm dependencies, and rescans when new vulnerabilities are published, so already-deployed images get flagged too. Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub, so the pipeline can fail on critical vulnerabilities, and alerts can be raised.

Lifecycle policies automatically delete old images to control storage cost and clutter. For example: keep the last 30 images tagged with a release prefix, delete untagged images after seven days, and expire feature-branch images after 14 days. I'm careful never to delete images currently deployed or needed for rollback.

Access: repository policies and IAM control who can push and pull; CI pipelines push using OIDC-based roles, and ECS pulls with the task execution role. Cross-account pull is allowed through repository policies for multi-account setups, and replication copies images to other regions for disaster recovery.
Image signing with AWS Signer and verification at deployment add supply chain protection.

p17-437.q: Both settings matter a lot for zero-downtime deployments.
p17-437.k: alb health check, target group health check, deregistration delay, connection draining, 502 during deployment ecs, alb slow start
x: Both settings matter a lot for zero-downtime deployments.

Health checks: the target group periodically calls a path, like /health/ready, on each target. A target is healthy after a number of consecutive successes, and unhealthy after a number of failures. Only healthy targets receive traffic. During a deployment, new tasks only get traffic once they pass health checks, and ECS only stops old tasks once new ones are healthy. I tune the interval, timeout and thresholds, and make sure the health endpoint reflects true readiness: the app has started, warmed up and can reach its essential dependencies, without being so strict that a minor dependency issue takes down every task. ECS also has a health check grace period, so slow-starting apps aren't killed before they're ready.

Deregistration delay, or connection draining, is how long the ALB keeps an old target registered while it finishes in-flight requests, after it stops sending it new requests. The default is 300 seconds, which slows deployments; for APIs with short requests, 30 to 60 seconds is usually enough. Too short, and in-flight requests get cut off, causing 502 errors during deployments.
The application must cooperate: on SIGTERM, it should stop accepting new work but finish in-flight requests, within the ECS stop timeout.
Slow start mode gradually increases traffic to new targets, which helps apps with cold caches.

p17-438.q: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of design principles and questions for evaluating architectures, organised into six pillars.
p17-438.k: well architected framework, six pillars aws, well architected review, operational excellence, aws best practices pillars
x: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of design principles and questions for evaluating architectures, organised into six pillars.

Operational excellence: running and monitoring systems and continuously improving processes. Infrastructure as code, small reversible changes, runbooks, observability, and learning from failures through post-incident reviews.

Security: protecting data and systems. Strong identity with least privilege, traceability with logging and auditing, security at every layer, encryption in transit and at rest, and preparing for incidents.

Reliability: the workload performs correctly and recovers from failures. Automatic recovery, testing recovery procedures, scaling horizontally, managing service quotas, multi-AZ designs, and handling change through automation.

Performance efficiency: using resources efficiently as demand changes. Choosing the right services and instance types, using managed and serverless services, going global with CDNs, and experimenting.
Cost optimisation: avoiding unnecessary costs. Paying only for what you use, right-sizing, using Savings Plans and Spot, measuring efficiency, and attributing costs to teams with tags.
Sustainability: minimising environmental impact by maximising utilisation, using efficient hardware like Graviton, and reducing unnecessary data and processing.

The framework is used through Well-Architected reviews, often with the Well-Architected Tool, where teams answer questions per pillar, identify high-risk issues and plan improvements. There are also lenses for specific domains, like serverless, SaaS, machine learning and generative AI.
In interviews, I connect each pillar to a concrete decision I've made, like Multi-AZ for reliability or right-sizing for cost.

p17-439.q: These are AWS's main pricing models besides on-demand.
p17-439.k: savings plans vs reserved instances, spot instances, aws compute cost, compute savings plan, reduce ec2 cost
x: These are AWS's main pricing models besides on-demand.
On-demand pays by the second with no commitment. It's the most flexible and most expensive, good for unpredictable or short-term workloads.

Savings Plans give a discount, up to around 66 percent for Compute Savings Plans and up to 72 percent for EC2 Instance Savings Plans, in exchange for committing to a consistent amount of spend per hour, like 10 dollars per hour, for one or three years. Compute Savings Plans apply automatically across EC2 instance families, sizes, regions, Fargate and Lambda, which makes them flexible and the usual first choice. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to an instance family in a region, for bigger discounts.

Reserved Instances are the older model, committing to specific instance attributes. They're still used for services like RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Redshift, where Savings Plans don't apply, although AWS introduced Database Savings Plans recently.

Spot Instances use spare capacity at up to 90 percent discount, but can be interrupted with a two-minute notice. They fit fault-tolerant, flexible workloads: batch processing, CI runners, stateless web tiers above a baseline, and big data. Diversifying across instance types and zones reduces interruptions.

My approach: right-size first, using Compute Optimizer recommendations; turn off non-production environments at night; cover the steady baseline with Savings Plans; use Spot for interruptible work; and keep on-demand for the rest. Commit conservatively, based on actual historical usage.

p17-440.q: Traditionally, people used a bastion host: a public EC2 instance with SSH open, used as a jump box into private subnets. It's an attack surface, needs patching, and managing SSH keys is painful and hard to audit.
p17-440.k: session manager, ssm session manager, bastion host alternative, ec2 instance connect, no ssh access aws, port forwarding ssm
x: Traditionally, people used a bastion host: a public EC2 instance with SSH open, used as a jump box into private subnets. It's an attack surface, needs patching, and managing SSH keys is painful and hard to audit.

AWS Systems Manager Session Manager is the modern alternative. An SSM agent on the instance, installed by default on many AMIs, connects outbound to the Systems Manager service, so no inbound ports need to be open at all, not even SSH, and no bastion or public IP is required. Instances in private subnets need either a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for SSM.

Access is controlled by IAM policies, so I can allow specific people to start sessions only on specific instances, by tag, and require MFA through the identity provider. Every session is logged: who started it and when in CloudTrail, and the full session commands and output can be recorded to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, which is great for audits. It supports interactive shells on Linux and Windows, running commands, and port forwarding, including to remote hosts, so I can reach a private RDS database from my laptop through an instance, without exposing the database.
EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint is another option, allowing SSH or RDP to private instances through an endpoint, with IAM-controlled, short-lived access.
For ECS containers, ECS Exec uses the same Session Manager mechanism to open a shell into a running container for debugging.

p17-441.q: They're three different kinds of storage.
p17-441.k: ebs vs efs vs s3, block vs file vs object storage, efs ecs, shared file system aws, storage types aws
x: They're three different kinds of storage.

EBS is block storage: a virtual disk attached to one EC2 instance at a time, in a single availability zone, except Multi-Attach for special cases. It has low latency and is used for operating system disks, databases running on EC2, and applications needing a fast local file system. Volume types like gp3 let me set IOPS and throughput independently. Snapshots back it up to S3 incrementally. ECS on Fargate now supports attaching EBS volumes to tasks too.

EFS is a managed network file system using NFS, for Linux. Many instances, containers and Lambda functions can mount it at the same time, across availability zones. It grows and shrinks automatically, and has lifecycle tiers to reduce cost for rarely accessed files. It's for shared files: content management, shared configuration or uploads in legacy apps, home directories, and lifting and shifting apps that expect a shared file system. Latency is higher than EBS. For Windows file shares, there's FSx for Windows File Server.

S3 is object storage accessed over HTTP APIs, not mounted like a disk, although Mountpoint for S3 offers file-like access for reading. It's virtually unlimited, very durable, cheap, and the right default for files, uploads, backups, logs, data lakes and static assets.
My default for new cloud-native apps is S3 for files, with EFS only when software truly needs a shared POSIX file system, and EBS for instance-level storage.

p17-442.q: API Gateway offers two main types for RESTful APIs, plus WebSocket APIs.
p17-442.k: api gateway rest vs http api, http api cheaper, api gateway features, api gateway types, websocket api gateway
x: API Gateway offers two main types for RESTful APIs, plus WebSocket APIs.

HTTP APIs are the newer, simpler option. They're cheaper, up to around 70 percent less per request, and have lower latency. They support JWT authorizers natively, which work with Cognito or any OIDC provider, Lambda authorizers, IAM authorisation, CORS configuration, integrations with Lambda and HTTP backends, private integrations to ALB, NLB and Cloud Map through VPC links, and automatic deployments.

REST APIs have more features: API keys and usage plans with per-client throttling and quotas, which matters for partner APIs; request validation against models; request and response transformation with mapping templates; response caching; AWS WAF integration; private APIs reachable only from VPCs through interface endpoints; edge-optimised endpoints; canary release deployments; and direct integration with many AWS services, like putting a message on SQS or starting a Step Functions execution without a Lambda function in between.

My choice: HTTP API by default, for most Lambda or container backends with JWT authentication, because it's cheaper and simpler. REST API when I need usage plans and API keys, WAF, caching, private APIs, request validation, or service integrations. AWS has been adding features to REST APIs recently, like routing rules.
WebSocket APIs are for real-time, two-way communication, like live notifications or chat.
For ECS services, an ALB alone is often enough, and API Gateway adds value mainly for these features.

p17-443.q: Authorizers let API Gateway authenticate and authorise requests before they reach the backend, so invalid requests are rejected early.
p17-443.k: api gateway authorizer, lambda authorizer, jwt authorizer, cognito authorizer, iam authorization api gateway, authorizer caching
x: Authorizers let API Gateway authenticate and authorise requests before they reach the backend, so invalid requests are rejected early.

JWT authorizers, in HTTP APIs, validate JSON Web Tokens from any OIDC-compliant provider, like Cognito, Keycloak, Entra ID or Auth0. I configure the issuer and audience; API Gateway checks the signature using the provider's published keys, the expiry, issuer and audience, and can require specific scopes per route. Claims are passed to the backend. No code is needed.
Cognito user pool authorizers are the REST API equivalent for Cognito tokens.

Lambda authorizers run my own function to make the decision. A token-based authorizer receives the bearer token; a request-based one receives headers, query strings and context. The function validates the request, maybe checking a custom token, an API key in a database, or calling an external authorisation service, and returns an IAM policy allowing or denying the request, or a simple boolean for HTTP APIs, plus context values passed to the backend, like the user id and tenant. Results can be cached for a TTL, keyed by the token, to reduce latency and cost, but caching means revoked access may still work until the cache expires, and a cached policy must cover all the routes the token will be used for.
IAM authorisation requires requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4, which suits service-to-service calls within AWS.
Fine-grained authorisation, like whether this user can see this shipment, still belongs in the service.

p17-444.q: Cold starts happen when Lambda creates a new execution environment: downloading code, starting the runtime, and running initialisation code. For .NET, JIT compilation and loading dependencies, like dependency injection setup and SDK clients, can make cold starts take a second or more.
p17-444.k: lambda snapstart, snapstart dotnet, lambda cold start dotnet, native aot lambda, reduce cold start lambda
x: Cold starts happen when Lambda creates a new execution environment: downloading code, starting the runtime, and running initialisation code. For .NET, JIT compilation and loading dependencies, like dependency injection setup and SDK clients, can make cold starts take a second or more.

SnapStart, available for .NET 8 and later managed runtimes since late 2024, as well as Java and Python, addresses this. When I publish a function version, Lambda runs the initialisation phase once, takes a snapshot of the memory and disk state of the initialised environment, encrypts and caches it. New execution environments are resumed from the snapshot, rather than initialising from scratch, which can reduce cold start times dramatically.

Things to be careful about. Uniqueness: anything generated during initialisation, like random seeds, unique ids or cached credentials, is the same in every environment restored from the snapshot. There are runtime hooks, before snapshot and after restore, to refresh such state, and network connections opened during init may need re-establishing after restore. It works with published versions and aliases, not $LATEST. There's a cost for caching and restoring snapshots for .NET. And it can't be combined with provisioned concurrency.

The alternatives: Native AOT compilation, which removes JIT and gives very fast starts, but requires trimming-compatible code and libraries; provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments warm at a cost; and simply reducing initialisation work, lazy loading what isn't always needed, and choosing more memory, which also gives more CPU.

p17-445.q: There are a few ways to build .NET APIs on Lambda.
p17-445.k: aspnet core lambda, dotnet lambda api, lambda annotations framework, amazon lambda aspnetcoreserver, serverless dotnet
x: There are a few ways to build .NET APIs on Lambda.

Running a whole ASP.NET Core API in Lambda: the Amazon.Lambda.AspNetCoreServer.Hosting package lets an existing minimal API or controller-based app run in Lambda with one line, AddAWSLambdaHosting, specifying the event source, like an HTTP API or ALB. API Gateway sends every request to the same function, and the package translates Lambda events into ASP.NET Core requests, so routing, middleware, model binding and dependency injection all work. It's the easiest migration path, and the same code can still run locally or in a container. The downside is a larger function, with longer cold starts, since the whole app initialises, so SnapStart or Native AOT help.

The Lambda Annotations Framework is the more Lambda-native approach: I write normal C# methods with attributes, like LambdaFunction and HttpApi with a route, and dependency injection through a Startup class, and a source generator produces the Lambda handler code and the CloudFormation or SAM template. Each function is small and focused, with good cold start performance, and it supports Native AOT.
Plain handlers, implementing a function handler method directly, give full control for event-driven functions, like processing SQS messages or S3 events.

Tools: the .NET Lambda tools and test tool for local testing, SAM or CDK for deployment, and Powertools for AWS Lambda for .NET for structured logging, metrics, tracing, idempotency and batch processing.
For steady, high-traffic APIs, containers on ECS are often cheaper and simpler than Lambda.

p17-446.q: ElastiCache is AWS's managed in-memory cache, supporting several engines.
p17-446.k: elasticache redis vs memcached, valkey, elasticache serverless, redis cluster mode, elasticache options
