For apps requiring server-side rendering frameworks with full Node servers, App Service or Container Apps are better fits.

p17-487.q: Microsoft Entra External ID is Microsoft's customer and partner identity solution, also called CIAM: letting external users, like customers, patients or partners, sign up and sign in to your applications.
p17-487.k: entra external id, azure ad b2c, customer identity azure, ciam azure, external users sign in
x: Microsoft Entra External ID is Microsoft's customer and partner identity solution, also called CIAM: letting external users, like customers, patients or partners, sign up and sign in to your applications.

Azure AD B2C was the previous customer identity product. It's very flexible, with custom policies for complex identity journeys, but those XML policies were notoriously difficult. Microsoft stopped selling Azure AD B2C to new customers from May 2025, although existing customers remain supported for years, and External ID is the path forward.

External ID comes in two configurations. An external tenant is a separate tenant dedicated to consumer and business customers of your apps, with self-service sign-up, sign-in with email and password, one-time passcodes, social providers like Google and Facebook, branding of sign-in pages, custom user attributes collected at sign-up, custom authentication extensions to call your APIs during sign-in, and MFA. A workforce tenant configuration covers B2B collaboration: inviting partner users as guests into your organisation's tenant, so they sign in with their own organisation's identities, governed by conditional access and access reviews.
From the application's perspective, it's standard OpenID Connect and OAuth: the app uses MSAL or Microsoft.Identity.Web, validates tokens, and authorises with roles and claims.
For a new customer-facing portal on Azure, I'd choose External ID; for existing B2C deployments, I'd plan migration rather than rush it.

p17-488.q: Both are key Entra ID security features, part of a zero trust approach.
p17-488.k: conditional access, pim, privileged identity management, mfa policy entra, just in time admin access, zero trust azure
x: Both are key Entra ID security features, part of a zero trust approach.

Conditional Access is Entra's policy engine for sign-ins. Policies are if-then rules: if a sign-in matches certain conditions, then enforce controls. Conditions include which users or groups, which applications, the sign-in risk and user risk detected by Identity Protection, the device platform, whether the device is compliant or joined, the location, like trusted office networks or countries, and the client app. Controls include requiring MFA, requiring phishing-resistant MFA like passkeys for admins, requiring a compliant device, requiring a password change for risky users, limiting session lifetime, or blocking access. Common policies: MFA for everyone, block legacy authentication, stronger requirements for administrators, and block access from unexpected countries. Report-only mode tests policies before enforcing them.

Privileged Identity Management handles privileged roles, both Entra roles and Azure resource roles. Instead of permanent admin assignments, users are eligible for a role and activate it just in time, for a limited duration, like two hours, with MFA, a justification, a ticket number, and optionally approval from another person. Activations are audited and alerts can be raised. Access reviews regularly ask owners to confirm whether people still need their roles, removing stale access.
Together they reduce the risk of stolen credentials: even a compromised account has no standing admin rights, and risky sign-ins are challenged or blocked.

p17-489.q: Azure Container Registry is a private registry for container images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts.
p17-489.k: azure container registry, acr tasks, acr geo replication, acr private endpoint, acr content trust, container image azure
x: Azure Container Registry is a private registry for container images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts.

In a pipeline, CI builds the image, tags it with a version or commit SHA, and pushes it to ACR, authenticating with a workload identity federated service connection rather than admin credentials, which I keep disabled. ACR Tasks can also build images inside Azure, triggered by commits or by base image updates, so images are rebuilt automatically when a patched base image is published.

Security practices. Access through Entra ID and RBAC: AcrPush for pipelines, AcrPull for runtimes, like the AKS kubelet identity or a Container Apps managed identity. Network: private endpoints and disabling public access on the Premium tier, so images are pulled only over private networks. Scanning: Defender for Containers scans images in the registry for vulnerabilities, and continues scanning images that are running. Immutable tags, by locking images or repositories, so a released tag can't be overwritten. Premium features: geo-replication, keeping a single registry replicated across regions, so clusters in each region pull locally and quickly, with resilience if a region is down; and zone redundancy.

p17-490.q: Every container in a pod can declare requests and limits for CPU and memory, and they do different jobs.
p17-490.k: requests vs limits, kubernetes resources, qos class, guaranteed burstable besteffort, cpu request memory limit
x: Every container in a pod can declare requests and limits for CPU and memory, and they do different jobs.

Requests are what the container is guaranteed. The scheduler uses them to place pods: a node only accepts a pod if the sum of requests on it fits the node's allocatable capacity. So requests decide where pods go and how many fit on a node. If requests are too low, nodes get overpacked and pods fight for resources; too high, and you waste money on idle capacity.

Limits are the ceiling. For memory, if a container goes above its limit, the kernel kills it, and you see OOMKilled. For CPU, a container above its limit isn't killed, it's throttled, which shows up as latency.

Together they decide the pod's quality of service class. Guaranteed, when requests equal limits for every container: these pods are the last to be evicted under node pressure. Burstable, when requests are lower than limits. BestEffort, when nothing is set: first to be evicted.

My defaults for a .NET API: set memory request and limit to the same value, based on observed usage plus headroom, because memory isn't compressible; set a CPU request based on typical usage, and often no CPU limit, or a generous one, to avoid throttling. Then I check actual usage in metrics and adjust, since guesses are usually wrong.

p17-491.q: OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit, and the kernel killed it. kubectl describe pod shows the last state as OOMKilled with exit code 137, and the restart count climbing.
p17-491.k: oomkilled, exit code 137, pod out of memory, container memory limit exceeded, dotnet memory kubernetes
x: OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit, and the kernel killed it. kubectl describe pod shows the last state as OOMKilled with exit code 137, and the restart count climbing.

First I check whether it's a real leak or just a limit that's too low. I look at the container's memory graph over time, in Prometheus or Container Insights. A sawtooth that climbs steadily until the kill, after every restart, points to a leak. A sudden spike points to one big operation, like loading a large file or a huge query result into memory. A flat line just under the limit means the limit is simply too tight for normal work.

For .NET specifically, the runtime reads the container's memory limit and sizes the GC heap from it, but if the limit is very small, server GC with many heaps can still push close to it. Options are setting GCHeapHardLimitPercent, using workstation GC for small containers, or giving a realistic limit.

If it's a leak, I reproduce it, take a memory dump with dotnet-dump or dotnet-gcdump before the kill, and look for what's growing: caches without expiry, static collections, event handlers not removed, or undisposed objects.
For spikes, I stream instead of buffering, page large queries, and limit concurrency of heavy jobs.
Only after understanding the cause do I raise the limit, and I set an alert on memory near the limit so we hear about it before the kills.

p17-492.q: CPU limits in Kubernetes are enforced by the Linux CFS quota. The CPU limit is converted into a time budget per 100-millisecond period. A limit of 500m means the container may use 50 milliseconds of CPU time in each 100-millisecond window. If it uses that up early, for example because several threads run in parallel, it's paused until the next window. That's throttling.
p17-492.k: cpu throttling kubernetes, cfs quota, cpu limit latency, throttled container, remove cpu limits
x: CPU limits in Kubernetes are enforced by the Linux CFS quota. The CPU limit is converted into a time budget per 100-millisecond period. A limit of 500m means the container may use 50 milliseconds of CPU time in each 100-millisecond window. If it uses that up early, for example because several threads run in parallel, it's paused until the next window. That's throttling.

The symptom is confusing: average CPU looks fine, maybe 40 percent of the limit, but latency spikes, especially p99. Multi-threaded runtimes like .NET make it worse, because GC and the thread pool can burn the budget in a short burst. The metric to check is container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total compared with total periods. A high throttled ratio confirms it.

Fixes, depending on the situation: raise the CPU limit, or remove CPU limits for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests, which still guarantee a fair share, because CPU is compressible and unused CPU on the node is otherwise wasted. Many teams now keep memory limits but drop CPU limits. Also make sure the runtime sees a sensible CPU count. .NET uses the limit to size the thread pool and GC heaps, and DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT can be set if needed.
If CPU is genuinely saturated, the real fix is scaling out with the HPA or optimising the hot code path.

p17-493.q: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of replicas of a Deployment based on metrics. Every 15 seconds or so, it compares the current metric with the target and calculates the desired replicas: current replicas times current value divided by target, within the min and max I set.
p17-493.k: hpa, horizontal pod autoscaler, scale on custom metrics, hpa behavior, metrics server, autoscaling v2
x: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of replicas of a Deployment based on metrics. Every 15 seconds or so, it compares the current metric with the target and calculates the desired replicas: current replicas times current value divided by target, within the min and max I set.

CPU utilisation is the classic metric, measured as a percentage of the pod's CPU request, from the metrics server. So the HPA only works properly if requests are set realistically. Memory is usually a poor scaling signal for .NET, because the GC doesn't give memory back quickly, so pods don't scale back in.

Better signals are often application metrics: requests per second per pod, in-flight requests, or queue length for workers. With the autoscaling/v2 API, the HPA can use custom metrics through an adapter, like the Prometheus adapter, or external metrics, like the length of a RabbitMQ queue.

The behaviour section controls how fast it scales. I usually scale up quickly, say double the pods within a minute, and scale down slowly, with a stabilisation window of five minutes or more, to avoid flapping when traffic dips briefly.

Things that break it: missing requests, a minReplicas of one in production, which gives no redundancy, and pods with long startup times, where readiness probes and enough headroom matter, because new pods take time to help.

p17-494.q: KEDA, Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling, is a CNCF project that scales workloads based on event sources. It installs as an operator, and I describe scaling with a ScaledObject that points at a Deployment and lists triggers.
p17-494.k: keda, event driven autoscaling, scale to zero, scale on queue length, scaledobject, kafka lag scaling
x: KEDA, Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling, is a CNCF project that scales workloads based on event sources. It installs as an operator, and I describe scaling with a ScaledObject that points at a Deployment and lists triggers.

Under the hood, KEDA feeds external metrics into a normal HPA, so it doesn't replace the HPA, it makes it smarter. It has scalers for dozens of sources: RabbitMQ queue length, Kafka consumer lag, Azure Service Bus, AWS SQS, Redis lists, Prometheus queries, cron schedules, databases and more.

Two things it adds that the plain HPA can't do easily. First, scaling to zero. When there are no messages, KEDA scales the worker to zero replicas, and when a message arrives, it activates the deployment again. That's great for background workers that are idle most of the day. Second, scaling on the real backlog instead of CPU. A queue worker might be mostly waiting on I/O, so CPU stays low even when thousands of messages are waiting. Scaling on queue length per replica, like one pod per 100 messages, matches the actual work.
KEDA also has ScaledJobs, which start a Kubernetes Job per batch of events, good for long-running tasks.

Things to watch: scale-to-zero adds a cold start delay, the target value needs tuning, and consumers must handle being stopped in the middle of work, so graceful shutdown and idempotent processing still matter.

p17-495.q: There are three different things you can scale in Kubernetes, and each tool handles one.
p17-495.k: cluster autoscaler, karpenter, vertical pod autoscaler, node autoscaling, vpa, pending pods scale nodes
x: There are three different things you can scale in Kubernetes, and each tool handles one.
The HPA scales the number of pods. But if new pods don't fit on any node, they stay Pending, so you also need node scaling.

Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes. It watches for pods that can't be scheduled because of insufficient resources, and adds nodes to a node group, like an AWS Auto Scaling group or an AKS node pool. It also removes underused nodes when their pods can be moved elsewhere. It works with predefined node groups, so you decide the instance types up front.

Karpenter, which started at AWS and is now used more widely, is a more flexible node provisioner. Instead of fixed node groups, it looks at the pending pods' requirements, like CPU, memory, architecture, zone and spot or on-demand, and launches the best-fitting instance directly, often within a minute. It also consolidates, replacing several half-empty nodes with fewer, cheaper ones. On EKS it's become the common choice, and EKS Auto Mode uses it under the hood.

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts a pod's requests and limits based on observed usage. It's useful for recommendations, running in recommendation-only mode to right-size requests. Applying changes historically required restarting pods, though in-place resizing is arriving. VPA and HPA shouldn't both act on CPU for the same workload.

p17-496.q: A PodDisruptionBudget protects an application's availability during voluntary disruptions. Voluntary disruptions are planned actions, like draining a node for an upgrade, the cluster autoscaler or Karpenter removing a node, or someone running kubectl drain. Involuntary ones, like a node crashing, aren't covered.
p17-496.k: pod disruption budget, pdb, voluntary disruption, node drain, minavailable maxunavailable, cluster upgrade downtime
x: A PodDisruptionBudget protects an application's availability during voluntary disruptions. Voluntary disruptions are planned actions, like draining a node for an upgrade, the cluster autoscaler or Karpenter removing a node, or someone running kubectl drain. Involuntary ones, like a node crashing, aren't covered.

A PDB selects pods by label and says either minAvailable, like at least two pods must stay running, or maxUnavailable, like at most one pod may be down at a time. When a drain tries to evict pods, the eviction API checks the budget and refuses evictions that would break it. The drain then waits and retries, so pods move one at a time and the service stays up.

Without a PDB, a node drain can evict all replicas of a service at once if they happen to sit on the same node, or a rolling node upgrade can take down too many replicas together, causing an outage during routine maintenance.

Some practical rules. A PDB only helps if you have more than one replica, so production services run at least two or three, spread across nodes and zones. Don't set minAvailable equal to the replica count, or maxUnavailable to zero, because then the node can never be drained and upgrades get stuck. And remember that pods failing their readiness checks count as unavailable, so an unhealthy deployment can also block drains.
I add a PDB to every production Deployment as part of the Helm chart.

p17-497.q: Both expose HTTP services from inside the cluster to the outside, but they're different generations.
p17-497.k: ingress vs gateway api, ingress controller, httproute, gatewayclass, ingress nginx retirement, kubernetes routing
x: Both expose HTTP services from inside the cluster to the outside, but they're different generations.

Ingress is the original API. An Ingress resource lists host and path rules, like api.example.com/shipments going to the shipments service, plus TLS settings. It needs an ingress controller to actually do the work, like ingress-nginx, Traefik, or a cloud load balancer controller. Its weakness is that the API is small, so anything advanced, like rewrites, timeouts, canary weights or header-based routing, goes into controller-specific annotations, which aren't portable and are easy to get wrong. The community ingress-nginx controller has also been announced for retirement in 2026, so many teams are planning migrations.

Gateway API is the newer, official successor, now generally available. It splits responsibilities into roles. A GatewayClass is defined by the infrastructure provider. A Gateway, owned by the platform team, describes the listeners, ports and certificates. HTTPRoutes, owned by application teams, attach to a Gateway and describe routing: path and header matching, traffic splitting by weight for canaries, redirects, rewrites and timeouts, all as first-class fields rather than annotations. There are also GRPCRoute and TLSRoute types, and support for cross-namespace references with explicit permission.

For a new cluster, I'd start with Gateway API, because it's more expressive, portable across implementations and where the ecosystem is heading. For existing Ingress setups, I'd migrate gradually, since both can run side by side.

p17-498.q: A Deployment is for stateless pods. All replicas are interchangeable, they get random names, they can be created and killed in any order, and if they use storage, they usually share it or don't need it. Web APIs and workers are Deployments.
p17-498.k: statefulset vs deployment, stateful workloads kubernetes, stable network identity, persistent volume claim template, headless service
x: A Deployment is for stateless pods. All replicas are interchangeable, they get random names, they can be created and killed in any order, and if they use storage, they usually share it or don't need it. Web APIs and workers are Deployments.

A StatefulSet is for workloads where each replica has its own identity and data. It gives three guarantees. Stable names: pods are named app-0, app-1, app-2, and keep those names when rescheduled. Stable network identity: combined with a headless service, each pod gets its own DNS name, like app-0.app.namespace.svc, so peers can find each other. Stable storage: volumeClaimTemplates create a separate persistent volume for each pod, and that volume follows the pod when it moves to another node. It also starts, scales and updates pods in order, one at a time, by default.

That's what clustered systems need: databases like PostgreSQL with replicas, Kafka brokers, RabbitMQ clusters, Elasticsearch, Redis with persistence, or ZooKeeper, where each member must know who it is and keep its own data.

In practice, I'd think twice before running databases on Kubernetes at all. Managed services like RDS, Azure SQL or a managed message broker remove a lot of operational work. If we do run stateful systems in the cluster, I'd use a mature operator, like CloudNativePG or the RabbitMQ cluster operator, which handles failover, backups and upgrades on top of StatefulSets.

p17-499.q: Besides Deployments, Kubernetes has workload types for other patterns.
p17-499.k: daemonset, kubernetes job, cronjob, run task once kubernetes, scheduled job kubernetes, node agent
x: Besides Deployments, Kubernetes has workload types for other patterns.

A DaemonSet runs one copy of a pod on every node, or on a selected set of nodes. When a node joins the cluster, the pod is added automatically. It's for node-level agents: log collectors like Fluent Bit, monitoring agents like the node exporter or the OpenTelemetry collector in agent mode, network plugins, storage drivers and security agents.

A Job runs pods until a task completes successfully, rather than keeping them running forever. It has settings for completions, parallelism, a backoffLimit for retries, an activeDeadlineSeconds timeout, and a ttlSecondsAfterFinished to clean up. It's for one-off work, like a database migration before a release, a data backfill, or a report generation.

A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule using cron syntax, with a time zone field. Useful settings: concurrencyPolicy set to Forbid, so a new run doesn't start while the previous one is still running; startingDeadlineSeconds, so missed runs after downtime don't pile up; and history limits for successful and failed jobs.

A few lessons. Jobs and CronJobs must be idempotent, because a pod can be retried or, rarely, run twice. The container must exit with a non-zero code on failure, or Kubernetes thinks it succeeded. And for business schedules, the logic is similar to our Quartz jobs on-premise: the schedule triggers the job, but the job itself must be safe to rerun.

p17-500.q: A pod can have more than one container, and two patterns are common.
p17-500.k: init container, sidecar container, native sidecar, restartpolicy always init, multi container pod
x: A pod can have more than one container, and two patterns are common.

Init containers run before the main containers start, one after another, and each must finish successfully. If one fails, the pod restarts it until it succeeds. They're for setup tasks: waiting for a dependency to be reachable, downloading configuration or certificates, running a schema check, or setting file permissions on a shared volume. Because they're separate images, they can contain tools you don't want in the main application image.

Sidecar containers run alongside the main container for the pod's whole life, adding a capability without changing the application. Examples: a log shipper reading log files from a shared volume, a service mesh proxy like Envoy, an OpenTelemetry collector, or a proxy that refreshes credentials.

Historically, sidecars were just extra regular containers, which caused problems: there was no guarantee they started before the app, and in Jobs, the sidecar kept running after the main container finished, so the Job never completed. Kubernetes now has native sidecars, which became stable in version 1.33: you declare them as init containers with restartPolicy Always. They start before the main containers, keep running, are restarted if they crash, and are shut down after the main containers stop, which fixes both problems.
I keep the number of containers per pod small, because every container adds resource requests and complexity.

p17-501.q: By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod, in any namespace. That's convenient, but it means a compromised pod can reach everything, including databases and internal admin services.
p17-501.k: network policy kubernetes, default deny, pod to pod traffic, namespace isolation, calico cilium, zero trust kubernetes
x: By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod, in any namespace. That's convenient, but it means a compromised pod can reach everything, including databases and internal admin services.

A NetworkPolicy restricts traffic to and from selected pods. It selects pods by label and lists allowed ingress sources and egress destinations, by pod labels, namespace labels or IP blocks, plus ports. Once any policy selects a pod for a direction, everything not explicitly allowed in that direction is denied.
Policies need a network plugin that enforces them, like Calico, Cilium, or the cloud provider's implementation. Without one, the objects are accepted but do nothing, which is a dangerous surprise.

My usual approach per namespace: start with a default deny for ingress, and often egress, for all pods. Then add explicit allows: the ingress controller can reach the API pods on port 8080; the API can reach the database or Redis on their ports; the worker can reach the message broker. Egress rules must also allow DNS to the cluster DNS service, or nothing works, which is the most common mistake.
I roll it out carefully, in audit or logging mode first where the plugin supports it, and test traffic paths in staging, because a wrong policy shows up as mysterious timeouts.
For richer rules, like by DNS name or HTTP path, Cilium and service meshes offer extended policies.

p17-502.q: Kubernetes RBAC controls who can do what with the Kubernetes API.
p17-502.k: kubernetes rbac, role vs clusterrole, rolebinding, service account permissions, least privilege kubernetes, kubectl auth can-i
x: Kubernetes RBAC controls who can do what with the Kubernetes API.

There are four objects. A Role lists permissions within one namespace: which API groups, which resources, like pods, deployments or secrets, and which verbs, like get, list, watch, create, update or delete. A ClusterRole is the same but cluster-wide, or reusable across namespaces. A RoleBinding grants a Role or ClusterRole to subjects within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.

Subjects are users, groups or service accounts. Kubernetes doesn't store users itself; humans come from the identity provider, like Entra ID on AKS or IAM on EKS through access entries, mapped to groups. Workloads use service accounts.

How I apply least privilege. Developers get read access in their team's namespaces, with no access to secrets in production. Deployment pipelines get a service account that can update deployments in specific namespaces only. Application pods get their own service account with no API permissions at all, unless they genuinely need them, and automountServiceAccountToken set to false otherwise. Cluster-admin is reserved for a small platform group, ideally with just-in-time access.
Things to watch: permission to read secrets, create pods or exec into pods is very powerful, because it can lead to reading any secret in the namespace, so I treat those verbs as sensitive.
kubectl auth can-i, with the as flag, is the quick way to check what a subject can do.

p17-503.q: Namespaces are the basic unit of sharing a cluster. Each team or application gets its own namespaces, often one per environment, and namespaces give separate names, RBAC boundaries, policies and quotas.
p17-503.k: namespaces multi tenancy, resourcequota, limitrange, team isolation kubernetes, namespace per team
x: Namespaces are the basic unit of sharing a cluster. Each team or application gets its own namespaces, often one per environment, and namespaces give separate names, RBAC boundaries, policies and quotas.

ResourceQuotas cap the total resources a namespace can consume: total CPU and memory requests and limits, number of pods, services, load balancers, persistent volume claims and storage. It stops one team's runaway deployment or a bad HPA setting from eating the whole cluster. Once a quota covers CPU or memory, every pod in that namespace must declare requests and limits, or it's rejected.

LimitRanges set per-container rules within a namespace: default requests and limits applied when a container doesn't specify them, plus minimum and maximum values. That makes the quota work smoothly and catches containers that ask for absurd amounts.

Together with RBAC per namespace, NetworkPolicies with default deny, and Pod Security admission labels, this gives soft multi-tenancy, which is fine for teams within one company who trust each other reasonably.

It isn't strong isolation, though. All namespaces share the same nodes, kernel and control plane. For hostile or strongly regulated tenants, I'd use separate node pools with taints, separate clusters, or virtual clusters.
I also label namespaces with owner and cost centre, so cost tools can show each team its share of the cluster.

p17-504.q: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. Instead of maintaining many raw YAML files per environment, you write a chart once and install it with different values.
p17-504.k: helm chart, helm values, helm release, helm upgrade rollback, helm template, kubernetes package manager
x: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. Instead of maintaining many raw YAML files per environment, you write a chart once and install it with different values.

A chart is a folder with a Chart.yaml for metadata and version, a values.yaml with default settings, and a templates folder with Kubernetes manifests written as Go templates, like a Deployment whose replica count, image tag, resources and environment variables come from values. Charts can depend on other charts, and helpers in a _helpers file avoid repetition, like standard labels.

Installing a chart creates a release, a named instance in a namespace. helm upgrade --install applies a new version with new values, and Helm keeps a history of release revisions, stored as secrets in the cluster, so helm rollback can return to a previous revision quickly. Flags like --atomic roll back automatically if the upgrade fails, and --wait waits for resources to become ready.

Per environment, I keep small values files, like values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml, that only override what differs: replica counts, resource sizes, hostnames and feature flags. Secrets don't go in values files; they come from a secrets manager.

Good habits: run helm lint and helm template in CI to render and validate manifests before deploying; version charts properly; publish charts to an OCI registry; and keep templates simple, because heavy template logic becomes hard to read and debug.

p17-505.q: Both solve the same problem, managing Kubernetes manifests across environments, but in different ways.
p17-505.k: helm vs kustomize, kustomize overlays, kubernetes configuration management, templating vs patching
x: Both solve the same problem, managing Kubernetes manifests across environments, but in different ways.

Helm uses templating. Manifests contain placeholders and logic, and values fill them in. It's a full package manager: charts are versioned, published to registries, have dependencies, and installations are tracked as releases with history and rollback. It's the standard way to distribute software for others to install, like ingress controllers, cert-manager or monitoring stacks. The downside is that templates can become hard to read, with lots of conditionals and indentation functions.

Kustomize uses patching, with no templates. You write plain, valid Kubernetes YAML as a base, then overlays per environment that patch it: change replicas, add a resource limit, set an image tag, add labels or generate ConfigMaps. It's built into kubectl with kubectl apply -k. It's simple, transparent and easy to review, because what you see is real YAML. But it has no packaging, versioning or release history, and complex variations become many patch files.

How I choose. For third-party software, I use the vendor's Helm chart. For our own services, either works. A team with many similar microservices benefits from one shared Helm chart with per-service values. A team that prefers plain YAML and GitOps may like Kustomize. They also combine well: Kustomize can render a Helm chart and then patch it, and Argo CD supports both.

p17-506.q: GitOps means Git is the single source of truth for what should run in the cluster. Instead of a pipeline pushing changes into the cluster with kubectl or helm commands, an agent running inside the cluster pulls the desired state from a Git repository and continuously makes the cluster match it.
p17-506.k: gitops, argo cd, flux, pull based deployment, desired state git, drift detection kubernetes
x: GitOps means Git is the single source of truth for what should run in the cluster. Instead of a pipeline pushing changes into the cluster with kubectl or helm commands, an agent running inside the cluster pulls the desired state from a Git repository and continuously makes the cluster match it.

Argo CD and Flux are the two main tools. In Argo CD, you define an Application that points to a repo path, a Helm chart or Kustomize folder, and a target cluster and namespace. Argo CD compares the rendered manifests with what's actually running, shows the difference in a UI, and syncs, automatically or after approval. Flux works similarly with Kustomization and HelmRelease objects, and is more CLI and controller oriented.

The benefits. Every change is a commit, reviewed in a pull request, so you have an audit trail and easy rollback by reverting. Drift detection: if someone changes something by hand in the cluster, the tool shows it as out of sync and can revert it. Security: CI doesn't need cluster admin credentials, because the cluster pulls changes. And disaster recovery is simpler, since the whole state can be reapplied to a new cluster.

A typical flow: CI builds and tests the image, pushes it, then updates the image tag in the config repo, often through a pull request. Argo CD sees the change and deploys it. Promotion between environments becomes a pull request too, which suits audited environments well.

p17-507.q: The latest tag is just a default name; it doesn't mean newest, and it moves every time someone pushes. If deployments use latest, you can't tell which code is running, two nodes can pull different images for the same deployment, a pod restart can silently upgrade the application, and rolling back is guesswork. With imagePullPolicy defaults, Kubernetes may also not pull the new image at all.
p17-507.k: image tagging strategy, latest tag problem, image digest, immutable tags, semantic version image, git sha tag
x: The latest tag is just a default name; it doesn't mean newest, and it moves every time someone pushes. If deployments use latest, you can't tell which code is running, two nodes can pull different images for the same deployment, a pod restart can silently upgrade the application, and rolling back is guesswork. With imagePullPolicy defaults, Kubernetes may also not pull the new image at all.

What I do instead. Tag every build with something unique and traceable, usually the Git commit SHA, and for releases also the semantic version, like 1.8.3. Both tags point to the same image. The deployment manifest references the exact tag, so every deployment is a recorded change and rollback means deploying the previous tag.
Make tags immutable in the registry. ECR, ACR and Artifact Registry all support this, so a tag can't be overwritten with different content.
For the strongest guarantee, deploy by digest, the sha256 of the image manifest, which is content-addressed and can never change. Tools can resolve a tag to a digest at deploy time and record both.

Build once and promote the same image through dev, test and production, rather than rebuilding per environment. In regulated work, that matters a lot, because what was tested is byte-for-byte what goes live.
Add OCI labels to the image, like source repo, commit and build time, so anyone can trace a running container back to its source.

p17-508.q: Distroless images contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, with no package manager, no shell and no extra operating system tools. Google popularised them, and Microsoft provides the .NET equivalent as Ubuntu chiseled images, like mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-noble-chiseled.
p17-508.k: distroless image, chiseled ubuntu, dotnet chiseled image, minimal container image, no shell container, attack surface
x: Distroless images contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, with no package manager, no shell and no extra operating system tools. Google popularised them, and Microsoft provides the .NET equivalent as Ubuntu chiseled images, like mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-noble-chiseled.

The benefits are real. They're much smaller, a chiseled ASP.NET Core image is around a quarter of the size of the full Debian one, so pulls and startup are faster. They have far fewer packages, so vulnerability scanners report far fewer CVEs, which cuts down patching noise. Attackers who get code execution find no shell or tools to work with. And chiseled images run as a non-root user by default.

There are trade-offs. You can't exec into the container and poke around with bash or curl, so debugging needs other approaches, like kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that has tools, or good logging and metrics. Some apps need native libraries, like ICU for globalisation or time zone data, and Microsoft offers extra variants that include them. Health checks can't use curl inside the container, so they must come from the orchestrator over HTTP.

My approach for .NET services: build in the SDK image in a multi-stage Dockerfile, publish, and copy the output into a chiseled runtime image, or use a self-contained or Native AOT build on the runtime-deps chiseled image for the smallest result.

p17-509.q: Slow image builds usually come from not using the cache well. BuildKit, the default builder in modern Docker, offers several tools.
p17-509.k: buildkit cache, docker build cache, cache mount nuget, layer cache ci, docker build slow, registry cache
x: Slow image builds usually come from not using the cache well. BuildKit, the default builder in modern Docker, offers several tools.

Layer order first. Docker reuses a layer only if the instruction and everything before it is unchanged. So for .NET, I copy the solution and project files first, run dotnet restore, and only then copy the rest of the source and run publish. Code changes then don't invalidate the restore layer. For Node, the same with package.json and the lock file before npm ci.
A good .dockerignore keeps bin, obj, node_modules, .git and test results out of the build context, which speeds up the upload and stops cache misses caused by irrelevant files.
Cache mounts keep package caches between builds without putting them in the image, for example RUN with --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.nuget/packages before dotnet restore, or the npm cache folder.

In CI, every build may run on a fresh agent with an empty cache. BuildKit can export and import cache: --cache-to and --cache-from with a registry, local or GitHub Actions cache backend, so the next pipeline run reuses layers.
Multi-stage builds also let BuildKit run independent stages in parallel, like building the API and running tests at the same time.
Secrets needed during build, like a private feed token, go in with --mount=type=secret, never as build args, which end up in the image history.

p17-510.q: By default, many images run as root inside the container. If an attacker breaks out of the application, root inside the container makes escaping to the host and causing damage much easier. So I harden containers at two levels.
p17-510.k: non root container, securitycontext, readonlyrootfilesystem, drop capabilities, runasnonroot, container hardening
x: By default, many images run as root inside the container. If an attacker breaks out of the application, root inside the container makes escaping to the host and causing damage much easier. So I harden containers at two levels.

In the image: create or use a non-root user and set USER in the Dockerfile. The official .NET images include an app user, and since .NET 8 they listen on port 8080, so no root is needed to bind to a low port.

In Kubernetes, the pod and container securityContext: runAsNonRoot true, so Kubernetes refuses to start a container that would run as root; runAsUser and runAsGroup with fixed non-zero ids; allowPrivilegeEscalation false; readOnlyRootFilesystem true, so the app can't modify its own files, with an emptyDir volume mounted only where it really needs to write, like /tmp; capabilities drop ALL, adding back only what's essential, which for a web API is usually nothing; and a seccompProfile of RuntimeDefault.

At cluster level, Pod Security admission with the restricted profile on application namespaces enforces these settings, so a manifest that forgets them is rejected rather than silently running as root.

Common issues when tightening: apps that write logs or temp files to their own folder, which I fix by writing to stdout and mounted temp volumes, and file permissions on mounted volumes, fixed with fsGroup.

p17-511.q: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable the container runs; CMD provides default arguments, or the default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT. Arguments passed to docker run, or args in Kubernetes, replace CMD, while command in Kubernetes replaces ENTRYPOINT. For a .NET app, a typical line is ENTRYPOINT in exec form, with "dotnet" and the API dll name as the array items.
p17-511.k: entrypoint vs cmd, pid 1 container, sigterm container, exec form vs shell form, graceful shutdown docker, tini
x: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable the container runs; CMD provides default arguments, or the default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT. Arguments passed to docker run, or args in Kubernetes, replace CMD, while command in Kubernetes replaces ENTRYPOINT. For a .NET app, a typical line is ENTRYPOINT in exec form, with "dotnet" and the API dll name as the array items.

The form matters. The exec form, with a JSON array, runs the process directly as PID 1. The shell form, written as plain text, runs it through /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and the app is its child.

Why that matters: when Kubernetes or Docker stops a container, it sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits for the grace period, 30 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL. A shell as PID 1 usually doesn't forward SIGTERM to the app, so the app never hears it, can't finish in-flight requests or close connections, and gets killed hard after 30 seconds. Deployments become slow and requests fail.
Also, PID 1 has special signal handling and is responsible for reaping zombie child processes. If the app starts child processes, a tiny init like tini, or docker run --init, handles that.

For .NET, the host listens for SIGTERM and triggers graceful shutdown: hosted services get StopAsync and Kestrel drains requests, within HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, which must be shorter than the Kubernetes grace period.

p17-512.q: Modern .NET is container-aware. It reads the cgroup limits instead of the host machine's resources, which matters a lot.
p17-512.k: dotnet container memory limit, server gc container, gcheaphardlimit, dotnet processor count, dotnet docker performance
x: Modern .NET is container-aware. It reads the cgroup limits instead of the host machine's resources, which matters a lot.

Memory: the GC sets its heap hard limit to 75 percent of the container memory limit by default, leaving room for native memory, thread stacks and other overhead. It can be tuned with GCHeapHardLimit or GCHeapHardLimitPercent. If you set no memory limit at all, the runtime sees the whole node's memory and may grow far more than you expect.

GC mode: ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, which creates a heap per logical CPU and favours throughput, but uses more memory. In a small container with a tight memory limit, workstation GC, or server GC with fewer heaps through GCHeapCount, can be a better fit. Since .NET 8 and 9, DATAS, dynamic adaptation to application sizes, is available and on by default in .NET 9 for server GC, which shrinks and grows the heap count with load and makes server GC much friendlier for containers.

CPU: Environment.ProcessorCount reflects the CPU limit, rounded up, and the thread pool and GC size themselves from it. DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT can override it when the limit is fractional or you want different behaviour.
Practically, I set a memory limit, watch GC heap size and working set through dotnet-counters or OpenTelemetry runtime metrics, and test under load with the real limits before going live.

p17-513.q: For local development, developers need the service's dependencies, like SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ and Keycloak, without installing them all by hand.
p17-513.k: local dev environment docker compose, dotnet aspire, compose healthcheck depends_on, run dependencies locally, aspire dashboard
x: For local development, developers need the service's dependencies, like SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ and Keycloak, without installing them all by hand.

Docker Compose is the classic answer. One compose file defines each dependency with an image, ports, volumes and environment variables. Health checks plus depends_on with condition service_healthy make the API wait until SQL Server is actually ready, not just started. Named volumes keep data between restarts, and seed scripts or a migration container load test data. Profiles let developers start only what they need, and an override file keeps personal tweaks out of the shared file. The same file is handy for integration tests in CI.

.NET Aspire is a newer, .NET-native option. An AppHost project describes the application in C#: add a SQL Server resource, a Redis resource, a RabbitMQ resource, and the API and worker projects that reference them. Running the AppHost starts the containers and projects, injects connection strings automatically through configuration, and opens a dashboard with logs, traces and metrics from every service, via OpenTelemetry. Service defaults add health checks, resilience and telemetry consistently. It can also generate deployment manifests.

My choice: Compose works for any stack and is well understood. For a .NET-heavy microservice solution, Aspire gives a much better inner loop and observability out of the box. For our on-premise platform, I'd only use either for local development and tests, since production deployment there is to IIS and servers.

p17-514.q: Pending means the pod has been accepted but not scheduled onto a node, or it's waiting for something before it can start. The answer is almost always in kubectl describe pod, in the Events section, under FailedScheduling.
p17-514.k: pod pending, unschedulable pod, insufficient cpu, failedscheduling, pvc pending, taint not tolerated
x: Pending means the pod has been accepted but not scheduled onto a node, or it's waiting for something before it can start. The answer is almost always in kubectl describe pod, in the Events section, under FailedScheduling.
Common causes and what the message looks like.

Insufficient CPU or memory: the requests don't fit on any node. Either requests are too large, the cluster is full, or the node autoscaler hasn't added capacity yet or has hit its max. Fix by right-sizing requests or adding capacity.

Node selectors, affinity or taints: a message like "didn't match node affinity" or "had untolerated taint". The pod wants a node type that doesn't exist or lacks the toleration for a dedicated node pool.

Volumes: the PersistentVolumeClaim is itself Pending, because there's no matching StorageClass, the provisioner failed, or the volume exists in a different availability zone than the available nodes. kubectl describe pvc shows why.
Quota: in a namespace with a ResourceQuota, the pod may be rejected at creation, so it shows up as a ReplicaSet event rather than a Pending pod; describe the ReplicaSet to see it.
Pod topology spread or anti-affinity rules that can't be satisfied, for example requiring one pod per zone with more replicas than zones.
I also check kubectl get events sorted by time and the autoscaler's logs, because they explain why no node was added.

p17-515.q: ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet tried to pull the container image, failed, and is backing off before retrying. kubectl describe pod shows the exact error in the events, and that tells me which of a few causes it is.
p17-515.k: imagepullbackoff, errimagepull, image pull error kubernetes, registry authentication, image not found, pull secret
x: ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet tried to pull the container image, failed, and is backing off before retrying. kubectl describe pod shows the exact error in the events, and that tells me which of a few causes it is.

Image doesn't exist: a typo in the repository name, or a tag that was never pushed, maybe because the build failed or the pipeline pushed a different tag than the manifest references. I check the registry for the exact tag.

Authentication: "unauthorized" or "access denied". The cluster needs permission to pull from a private registry. On EKS, the node role needs ECR read access; on AKS, the kubelet identity needs AcrPull on the registry; elsewhere, an imagePullSecret must exist in the same namespace as the pod and be referenced by the pod or its service account. Expired tokens or a secret created in the wrong namespace are common.
Network: the nodes can't reach the registry, because of a firewall, missing NAT, missing private endpoints or VPC endpoints for ECR, or DNS problems. The error is usually a timeout.
Rate limits: pulling from Docker Hub anonymously can hit "toomanyrequests". The fix is mirroring base images into our own registry or authenticating.
Platform mismatch: an image built only for arm64 on amd64 nodes gives "no matching manifest", so I build multi-arch images.
Once fixed, the pod retries on its own, or I delete it to retry immediately.

p17-516.q: When traffic through a Service or Ingress fails with 503 or connection refused, I follow the path from the outside in, checking each hop.
p17-516.k: service no endpoints, 503 ingress kubernetes, selector mismatch, service not routing, endpointslice empty, targetport wrong
x: When traffic through a Service or Ingress fails with 503 or connection refused, I follow the path from the outside in, checking each hop.

First, does the Service have endpoints? kubectl get endpointslices for that service, or kubectl describe service. If the endpoints list is empty, the Service isn't selecting any ready pods. The two usual reasons: the Service selector doesn't match the pod labels, maybe a typo, or a label changed in the Deployment but not in the Service; or the pods exist but aren't ready, because their readiness probe is failing, and Kubernetes removes unready pods from endpoints on purpose.

Second, ports. The Service's targetPort must match the port the container actually listens on. A classic .NET example: since .NET 8, the container images listen on 8080 by default, but the Service still points to 80, so everything is refused.
Third, the app itself. I port-forward directly to a pod, kubectl port-forward pod/name 8080, and call it. If that works, the problem is in the Service or Ingress; if not, it's the app.

Fourth, the Ingress or Gateway: the backend service name and port in the rule, the host and path matching, TLS secrets, and the ingress controller's logs, which usually say clearly that there's no healthy upstream.
Finally, NetworkPolicies that block traffic from the ingress controller's namespace to the app's namespace.

p17-517.q: NotReady means the control plane hasn't received healthy status from the node's kubelet for a while, about 40 seconds by default. After a few minutes, pods on that node are marked for eviction and rescheduled elsewhere, provided there's capacity and the workloads have more than one replica.
p17-517.k: node notready, kubelet not ready, node pressure, node troubleshooting kubernetes, disk pressure memory pressure
x: NotReady means the control plane hasn't received healthy status from the node's kubelet for a while, about 40 seconds by default. After a few minutes, pods on that node are marked for eviction and rescheduled elsewhere, provided there's capacity and the workloads have more than one replica.

My first step is kubectl describe node, looking at Conditions and recent events. The conditions say a lot: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure or PIDPressure being true points to resource exhaustion; NetworkUnavailable points to the network plugin; and if the kubelet has simply stopped posting status, the Ready condition shows Unknown.

Common causes. The kubelet or container runtime crashed or is stuck, often visible in the node's system logs with journalctl. The disk filled up with images, logs or emptyDir data, which triggers disk pressure and image garbage collection. Memory exhaustion where system processes got OOM-killed because pods had no limits. Network problems between the node and the control plane, like security group or firewall changes, or expired node certificates. On cloud providers, the underlying VM may be impaired or being retired.
For immediate impact, I cordon the node so nothing new lands there, and drain it if it's partly working, so pods move cleanly.

On managed node groups, often the quickest fix is to replace the node, letting the autoscaler or node group create a fresh one, and then investigate the root cause from logs rather than nursing the broken node.

p17-518.q: An evicted pod was stopped by the kubelet or the API, not because the app crashed. kubectl describe pod shows the reason, and it's usually one of these.
p17-518.k: pod evicted, eviction kubernetes, ephemeral storage eviction, node pressure eviction, priority class, evicted pods cleanup
x: An evicted pod was stopped by the kubelet or the API, not because the app crashed. kubectl describe pod shows the reason, and it's usually one of these.

Node pressure eviction. When a node runs low on memory, disk or process ids, the kubelet evicts pods to protect the node. It chooses by quality of service and usage: BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods using more than their requests, and Guaranteed pods last. Fix: set realistic requests, so heavy pods count properly at scheduling time, set memory limits, and right-size nodes.

Ephemeral storage. A container writing too much to its writable layer or an emptyDir volume, like large temp files or logs written to files instead of stdout, exceeds its ephemeral storage limit or fills the node's disk. Fix: set ephemeral-storage requests and limits, write logs to stdout, clean up temp files, and use a persistent volume for big data.

Preemption. A higher-priority pod needed room, so the scheduler evicted lower-priority pods. That's by design if PriorityClasses are used; critical services should have higher priority than batch jobs.
API-initiated eviction, during node drains for upgrades or autoscaler scale-down, which PodDisruptionBudgets control.
Evicted pods stay listed with status Failed until garbage collected, which is just noise, but a steady stream of evictions is a signal that capacity or limits need attention.

p17-519.q: With distroless or chiseled images, kubectl exec with bash fails, because there's no shell. That's good for security, but I still need ways to debug.
p17-519.k: kubectl debug, ephemeral container, debug distroless, kubectl exec no shell, node debugging kubernetes
x: With distroless or chiseled images, kubectl exec with bash fails, because there's no shell. That's good for security, but I still need ways to debug.

kubectl debug is the main tool. With an ephemeral container, kubectl debug -it pod-name --image=busybox --target=app-container adds a temporary container into the running pod. Sharing the process namespace with the target container, I can see its processes, look at its files through /proc/1/root, and use network tools in the same network namespace, like curl, nslookup or netstat, to test DNS and connectivity exactly as the app sees them. The ephemeral container goes away when the pod is deleted, and the pod itself isn't restarted.

kubectl debug can also create a copy of the pod with changes, like a different image with tools, or a changed command so a crashing container stays alive for inspection, without touching the real pod.
For node-level problems, kubectl debug node/name starts a privileged pod on that node with the host filesystem mounted, which replaces SSH in many cases.

For .NET specifically, the diagnostics tools, like dotnet-counters, dotnet-trace and dotnet-dump, can run from a sidecar or debug container sharing the process namespace and the /tmp folder, because they talk to the runtime over a diagnostics socket.
Of course, the first tools are still logs, metrics and traces; interactive debugging in production is a last resort, and access to it should be restricted and audited.

p17-520.q: These features control which pods run on which nodes, from two directions.
p17-520.k: taints and tolerations, node affinity, node selector, dedicated node pool, gpu nodes kubernetes, schedule on specific nodes
x: These features control which pods run on which nodes, from two directions.

Taints are on nodes and repel pods. A taint like dedicated=batch:NoSchedule means no pod is scheduled there unless it tolerates that taint. NoExecute also evicts running pods that don't tolerate it, and PreferNoSchedule is a soft version. Kubernetes uses taints itself, for example on nodes that are not ready or under pressure.
Tolerations are on pods and allow them onto tainted nodes. But a toleration only permits; it doesn't attract the pod to that node.

Node affinity is on pods and attracts them to nodes with certain labels, like a particular instance type, zone, or a GPU label. requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is a hard rule; preferredDuringScheduling is a weighted preference. nodeSelector is the simple, older form of a hard rule.
So, to dedicate nodes to a workload, you combine both: taint the node pool so other pods stay away, and give the workload a toleration plus node affinity so it goes there and only there.

Typical uses: GPU nodes for machine learning jobs, nodes with lots of memory for a cache, spot nodes for interruptible batch work with a toleration, separate system node pools for cluster add-ons, and Windows nodes for Windows containers, where Windows pods need a nodeSelector for the OS.

p17-521.q: Running three replicas doesn't help much if all three land on the same node or in the same availability zone. One node failure or zone outage takes the service down. So I tell the scheduler to spread them.
p17-521.k: topology spread constraints, pod anti affinity, spread across zones, high availability kubernetes, zone failure
x: Running three replicas doesn't help much if all three land on the same node or in the same availability zone. One node failure or zone outage takes the service down. So I tell the scheduler to spread them.

Pod anti-affinity is the older way. A rule says don't schedule this pod on a node, or in a zone, that already runs a pod with the same label. The required form is strict, which can leave pods Pending if there are more replicas than nodes; the preferred form is a soft preference. It also gets expensive to compute in large clusters.

Topology spread constraints are the better, more flexible tool. A constraint says spread pods matching a label across a topology key, like topology.kubernetes.io/zone or kubernetes.io/hostname, with a maxSkew, the maximum allowed difference in pod count between domains. whenUnsatisfiable set to DoNotSchedule makes it strict; ScheduleAnyway makes it best-effort. I usually add two constraints: across zones, and across nodes.

Some details matter. Spread only applies at scheduling time, so after a zone recovers, pods don't automatically rebalance; the descheduler can help with that. The autoscaler must be able to create nodes in each zone. And PodDisruptionBudgets keep the spread safe during maintenance.
Zone spreading can add cross-zone data transfer costs, which is usually worth it for production APIs.

p17-522.q: A frequent surprise: you update a ConfigMap, and the application keeps using old values. It depends on how the configuration is consumed.
p17-522.k: configmap change not reflected, reload config kubernetes, configmap hot reload, reloader, rollout restart config
x: A frequent surprise: you update a ConfigMap, and the application keeps using old values. It depends on how the configuration is consumed.
Environment variables are read only when the container starts. Changing the ConfigMap does nothing to running pods; they need a restart.

Mounted volumes are updated by the kubelet eventually, typically within a minute or so, because files are refreshed through a symlink swap. An application that watches the file can reload. In .NET, adding a JSON file with reloadOnChange and reading settings through IOptionsMonitor works, though file watching on these symlinked volumes can be unreliable, so polling may be needed. Volumes mounted with subPath are never updated.

Common approaches. Rollout restart: kubectl rollout restart deployment after the change, which recreates pods gradually. A checksum annotation in the Helm chart: the pod template includes a hash of the ConfigMap contents, so any config change changes the pod template, which triggers a normal rolling update automatically. That's my preferred method, because the change goes through the same safe rollout as a code change. A controller like Stakater Reloader watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and restarts deployments that reference them.
Immutable ConfigMaps with versioned names, like app-config-v12, are another pattern: each change creates a new ConfigMap, and the deployment references the new name, which also makes rollback clean.
Real feature flags that must change instantly are better served by a feature flag service than by ConfigMaps.

p17-523.q: Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default. Anyone who can read them through the API, or read etcd backups, can see the values. So I treat native Secrets carefully and usually source them from a real secrets manager.
p17-523.k: kubernetes secrets base64, external secrets operator, sealed secrets, secrets store csi driver, encrypt secrets etcd
x: Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default. Anyone who can read them through the API, or read etcd backups, can see the values. So I treat native Secrets carefully and usually source them from a real secrets manager.

Baseline protections: enable encryption at rest for secrets in etcd, which managed clusters support with a KMS key; restrict RBAC so few people and service accounts can get or list secrets; and never commit secret manifests to Git in plain form.
Then choose how secrets get into the cluster.

External Secrets Operator: an ExternalSecret resource says which keys to fetch from AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault or others, and the operator creates and refreshes a normal Kubernetes Secret. Apps stay unchanged, and rotation in the source flows through.
Secrets Store CSI Driver: mounts secrets from the external store directly as files in the pod, optionally syncing to a Kubernetes Secret.
Sealed Secrets: encrypt secrets with the cluster's public key so the encrypted version can be safely committed to Git, which suits GitOps; only the controller in the cluster can decrypt them.

Even better, avoid secrets where possible: use workload identity, like IRSA or Pod Identity on EKS and Workload ID on AKS, so pods authenticate to cloud databases and services without any stored credentials.

p17-524.q: Kubernetes releases a minor version roughly every four months, and each is supported for about a year upstream, longer on some managed services with paid extended support. So upgrades are routine, and I treat them as a process, not an event.
p17-524.k: kubernetes upgrade, eks upgrade, aks upgrade, deprecated api removal, node pool upgrade, version skew
x: Kubernetes releases a minor version roughly every four months, and each is supported for about a year upstream, longer on some managed services with paid extended support. So upgrades are routine, and I treat them as a process, not an event.

Before upgrading: read the release notes for removed or deprecated APIs. Tools like Pluto or kubent scan manifests and Helm releases for API versions that will stop working. Check that add-ons, like the ingress controller, CNI, CSI drivers, cert-manager and monitoring agents, support the new version, and upgrade them first if needed. Upgrade one minor version at a time; you can't skip versions on the control plane.

The order: upgrade a non-production cluster first and run the test suites. Then the control plane, which managed services do for you without downtime. Then the node pools, which must stay within the supported version skew of the control plane. For nodes, I prefer creating a new node pool on the new version and draining the old one, or using surge upgrades that add new nodes before removing old ones. PodDisruptionBudgets, multiple replicas, and graceful shutdown keep services up as pods move.
After: watch error rates and events, then upgrade remaining add-ons.
Teams that keep clusters disposable and fully defined in code sometimes do blue-green clusters instead: build a new cluster on the new version, shift traffic, and retire the old one.

p17-525.q: Admission control is the step where the Kubernetes API checks or modifies objects before saving them. It's where you enforce security rules on every workload, rather than trusting each manifest.
p17-525.k: pod security standards, pod security admission, restricted baseline privileged, kyverno, opa gatekeeper, validating admission policy
x: Admission control is the step where the Kubernetes API checks or modifies objects before saving them. It's where you enforce security rules on every workload, rather than trusting each manifest.

Pod Security Standards define three profiles. Privileged has no restrictions, for system components. Baseline blocks known privilege escalations, like privileged containers, host networking and host paths. Restricted enforces hardening best practices: non-root users, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, and a seccomp profile.

Pod Security Admission is built into Kubernetes and applies these profiles per namespace, using labels. Each profile can be set to enforce, which rejects violating pods; audit, which logs them; or warn, which returns a warning to the user. I usually start with warn and audit on restricted, fix the workloads, then enforce.

For rules beyond pod security, policy engines help. Kyverno writes policies as Kubernetes YAML: require labels like owner and cost centre, require resource limits, allow images only from our registry, require signed images, or add default settings automatically. OPA Gatekeeper uses the Rego language for the same purposes. Kubernetes also now has built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy using CEL expressions, which covers many simple rules without installing anything.
I keep policies in Git, test them in CI against our manifests, and roll them out in audit mode first, so nobody's deployment breaks without warning.

p17-526.q: Walking through it shows how the pieces fit together.
p17-526.k: kubectl apply flow, kubernetes control plane components, api server etcd scheduler, controller manager, kubelet, how kubernetes works
x: Walking through it shows how the pieces fit together.

kubectl reads the manifest and sends it to the API server over HTTPS, authenticating with my credentials. kubectl apply uses server-side or client-side apply to work out what changed compared to the last applied configuration.

The API server authenticates me, checks RBAC authorisation, then runs admission controllers: mutating ones, which may add defaults or sidecars, then validating ones, like Pod Security or policy engines. If everything passes, it stores the Deployment object in etcd, the cluster's key-value database. Nothing has run yet; we've only recorded desired state.

Controllers watch the API server for changes. The Deployment controller, in the controller manager, sees the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet controller sees that it needs three pods and creates three Pod objects, with no node assigned.
The scheduler watches for unassigned pods. For each, it filters nodes that fit the requests, taints, affinity and spread rules, scores them, and binds the pod to the best node.

The kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to it, asks the container runtime, like containerd, to pull the image and start the containers, sets up networking through the CNI plugin and volumes through CSI, runs probes, and reports status back.
Meanwhile, the EndpointSlice controller adds ready pods to the Service, and kube-proxy or the CNI updates routing so traffic can reach them.

p17-527.q: Containers are ephemeral, so anything written inside them disappears on restart. Persistent storage in Kubernetes has three layers.
p17-527.k: persistent volume, persistent volume claim, storage class, dynamic provisioning, access modes rwo rwx, reclaim policy
x: Containers are ephemeral, so anything written inside them disappears on restart. Persistent storage in Kubernetes has three layers.
A PersistentVolume is a piece of storage in the cluster, like an EBS volume, an Azure Disk, or a network file share, with a size, access modes and a reclaim policy.

A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request for storage by a workload: I need 20 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, of this class. The pod mounts the claim, not the volume directly, so application manifests don't depend on the storage details.

A StorageClass describes a type of storage and its provisioner, like gp3 EBS volumes, premium Azure disks, or EFS. With dynamic provisioning, creating a claim makes the provisioner create a matching volume automatically. volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer delays creation until the pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in the same availability zone as the pod.

Access modes matter. ReadWriteOnce means one node can mount it, typical for block disks. ReadWriteMany means many nodes, which needs a network file system, like EFS or Azure Files. ReadWriteOncePod restricts it to a single pod.

The reclaim policy decides what happens when the claim is deleted: Delete removes the underlying disk, Retain keeps it for manual recovery. For important data, I use Retain plus regular snapshots with the CSI snapshot feature.
For most stateless services, I avoid volumes entirely and use object storage or managed databases.

p17-528.q: Kubernetes talks to container runtimes through the Container Runtime Interface. Docker Engine never implemented CRI, so Kubernetes had an adapter called dockershim to talk to it. That adapter was removed in Kubernetes 1.24.
p17-528.k: containerd vs docker, dockershim removal, container runtime interface, cri-o, oci image, docker images still work kubernetes
x: Kubernetes talks to container runtimes through the Container Runtime Interface. Docker Engine never implemented CRI, so Kubernetes had an adapter called dockershim to talk to it. That adapter was removed in Kubernetes 1.24.

What that meant in practice: clusters switched to CRI-compatible runtimes, mainly containerd, which was actually the component Docker itself used under the hood, or CRI-O. Managed services like EKS, AKS and GKE moved to containerd.

What didn't change: images built with Docker still work everywhere, because they follow the OCI image standard, and containerd runs OCI images. Developers keep using Docker Desktop or Docker Engine to build and run containers locally; only the runtime on cluster nodes changed.

Things that did break: anything that relied on the Docker socket on nodes, like CI jobs building images inside pods by mounting /var/run/docker.sock, or monitoring agents reading Docker's API. Those moved to alternatives, like BuildKit, Kaniko or buildah for in-cluster builds, and runtime-agnostic agents. Debugging on nodes uses crictl instead of the docker command.

So in an interview, the key points are: Docker is a developer tool and image format ecosystem; containerd is the runtime; OCI standards make images portable between them; and Kubernetes only needs a CRI runtime on nodes.

p17-529.q: Yes, but only as Windows containers, because .NET Framework needs Windows. Microsoft provides images like the ASP.NET image based on Windows Server Core, with IIS and .NET Framework 4.8 included, so a classic MVC or Web API app can be published and copied into the image.
p17-529.k: windows containers, dotnet framework docker, windows server core image, iis container, legacy app containerize, windows nodes kubernetes
x: Yes, but only as Windows containers, because .NET Framework needs Windows. Microsoft provides images like the ASP.NET image based on Windows Server Core, with IIS and .NET Framework 4.8 included, so a classic MVC or Web API app can be published and copied into the image.

There are real constraints. The images are large, several gigabytes, so pulls are slow. The container's Windows version must be compatible with the host's Windows version, especially with process isolation, so you match image tags like ltsc2022 to the host. They need Windows nodes: AKS and EKS both support Windows node pools, alongside Linux nodes for system components, with nodeSelectors to keep Windows pods on Windows nodes. Some things behave differently, like file permissions, Active Directory integration, which needs group managed service accounts, and some features available on Linux nodes.

When it's worth it: as a step in modernising a big legacy application, to get consistent builds, repeatable deployments and the ability to run it alongside new services on one platform, without rewriting it all at once.

For our platform, the core .NET Framework 4.8 applications run on IIS on Windows servers today, and the newer services are .NET 8 and later. If we containerised, I'd prioritise the newer .NET services on Linux containers, and treat Windows containers for the legacy core only as an [option to evaluate], since migrating parts to modern .NET often brings more benefit.

p17-530.q: Running migrations from the application at startup, like calling Database.Migrate in Program.cs, is risky in Kubernetes. With several replicas starting at once, they race to apply the same migration, startup gets slow, and the app needs DDL permissions it shouldn't have at runtime.
p17-530.k: database migration kubernetes, ef core migrations kubernetes, migration job helm hook, init container migration, schema change deployment
x: Running migrations from the application at startup, like calling Database.Migrate in Program.cs, is risky in Kubernetes. With several replicas starting at once, they race to apply the same migration, startup gets slow, and the app needs DDL permissions it shouldn't have at runtime.
Better options.

A Kubernetes Job before the rollout. The pipeline runs a migration Job, using the same image or a dedicated migrator image, waits for it to complete successfully, and only then updates the Deployment. In Helm, this is often a pre-upgrade hook, so the release fails if the migration fails. The Job uses a separate database identity with schema-change rights.

A migration step in the pipeline itself, outside the cluster, applying an idempotent script or an EF Core migration bundle generated at build time. This makes the migration a visible, auditable release step.
Init containers can work for simple cases, but every pod would try to run them, so they need locking, and I don't usually prefer them.

Whatever the mechanism, the schema changes themselves must be backward compatible, because during a rolling update old and new versions run side by side. I use the expand and contract pattern: add new columns or tables first, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only drop old columns in a later release. That also keeps rollback of the application safe without rolling back the database.

p17-531.q: A plain Deployment does a rolling update: it replaces pods gradually, but it only checks readiness, not whether the new version is actually healthy for users. Progressive delivery tools add real canary and blue-green releases with automated analysis.
p17-531.k: argo rollouts, flagger, progressive delivery, canary analysis kubernetes, automated rollback metrics, analysis template
x: A plain Deployment does a rolling update: it replaces pods gradually, but it only checks readiness, not whether the new version is actually healthy for users. Progressive delivery tools add real canary and blue-green releases with automated analysis.

Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment with a Rollout resource. A canary strategy lists steps, like send 10 percent of traffic, pause five minutes, run analysis, go to 30 percent, analyse again, then 100 percent. Traffic splitting can be by replica count, or precise using an ingress controller, the Gateway API, or a service mesh. Analysis templates query a metrics provider, like Prometheus, Datadog or CloudWatch, with success conditions, like error rate below one percent and p95 latency below 400 milliseconds. If analysis fails, the rollout aborts and traffic returns to the stable version automatically. Blue-green is also supported, with preview services and promotion.

Flagger does the same with a different model: you keep your Deployment, and Flagger creates the canary and primary objects and drives traffic shifting with a mesh or ingress, using metric checks and webhooks for load tests or approvals.

What makes this work in practice: good metrics per version, labelled so you can compare canary with stable; enough traffic for statistics to mean something; and backward-compatible database changes, since both versions run together.
It's essentially the automatic rollback answer for Kubernetes: health is judged by real user signals, not by humans watching dashboards.

p17-532.q: Trunk-based development means everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily, through short-lived branches that live a day or two, instead of long-running feature or develop branches that merge weeks later with painful conflicts.
p17-532.k: trunk based development, short lived branches, main branch always releasable, trunk based vs gitflow, continuous integration practice
x: Trunk-based development means everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily, through short-lived branches that live a day or two, instead of long-running feature or develop branches that merge weeks later with painful conflicts.
Making it work needs a few supporting habits.
Small changes. A big feature is split into small, safe pull requests that each keep main working, like adding the database column first, then the API, then the UI.
Feature flags. Unfinished work merges behind a flag that's off in production, so code can be integrated before the feature is ready. Release becomes a flag switch, not a merge.
Fast, reliable CI. Every pull request runs build, unit tests and static checks in about ten minutes. Branch policies require a passing build and a review before merging.
