Keep main releasable. If main breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority, and reverting is a normal, blame-free action.
Release branches only when needed, cut from main for a release that needs stabilisation or hotfixes, and fixes go to main first, then are cherry-picked.

The payoff is fewer merge conflicts, earlier feedback and a codebase that's always close to shippable. In a regulated environment, the validated release is still a specific, tagged build from main, so traceability is kept.

p17-533.q: Feature flags let you change behaviour at runtime without deploying, but they turn into technical debt if unmanaged. I think about them by type.
p17-533.k: feature flags, feature toggles, release toggle, flag cleanup, feature management dotnet, kill switch
x: Feature flags let you change behaviour at runtime without deploying, but they turn into technical debt if unmanaged. I think about them by type.

Release flags hide unfinished or new features until they're ready. They should be short-lived: removed within a few weeks of full rollout. Ops flags or kill switches let you switch off an expensive or risky path during an incident, like disabling a heavy export; these can live longer. Experiment flags drive A/B tests. Permission flags enable features for specific customers or plans, which is really configuration and belongs in the product's settings model.

Implementation in .NET: Microsoft.FeatureManagement gives IFeatureManager and attributes for controllers, with filters for percentage rollout, user or group targeting, and time windows. Flags can come from configuration, Azure App Configuration, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash, and OpenFeature provides a vendor-neutral API.

Rules that keep it clean: every flag has an owner and an expiry date, recorded when it's created; check the flag at one place, near the edge, rather than scattering checks across the code; test both states; default to the safe value if the flag service is unreachable; and add a ticket to remove the flag and the dead code once rollout is done.
In a regulated product, a flag that changes validated behaviour is itself a configuration change, so its state per environment must be controlled and recorded.

p17-534.q: Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels, like 2.1.0-beta.3, mark builds that aren't final. For libraries and packages, this is essential, because consumers rely on it to know whether an upgrade is safe.
p17-534.k: semantic versioning, semver, gitversion, conventional commits, automatic version number, build number strategy
x: Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels, like 2.1.0-beta.3, mark builds that aren't final. For libraries and packages, this is essential, because consumers rely on it to know whether an upgrade is safe.
Manually editing version numbers doesn't scale, so I automate it.

GitVersion calculates the version from Git history: tags, branch names and commit messages. A tag v1.4.0 on main marks the release; builds after it become 1.4.1-something or 1.5.0 depending on configuration; feature branches get pre-release labels.

Conventional commits put intent in commit messages, like feat: for a feature, fix: for a fix, and feat! or BREAKING CHANGE for breaking changes. Tools like semantic-release or release-please read them, bump the version, create the tag and generate a changelog. That works well for npm packages.

The build then stamps the version everywhere: assembly versions in .NET through the Version property, package versions, container image tags, and the build name in the pipeline, so the running app can show its version on a health or about endpoint.
For deployable services, I also include the commit SHA in the build metadata, like 1.4.2+abc1234, so any running instance traces back to its exact source.

p17-535.q: When many services have similar pipelines, copying YAML into each repo leads to drift and painful updates. Azure Pipelines templates fix that.
p17-535.k: azure pipelines templates, yaml templates, extends template, template parameters, reusable pipeline, pipeline standardization
x: When many services have similar pipelines, copying YAML into each repo leads to drift and painful updates. Azure Pipelines templates fix that.

There are a few kinds. Step templates hold a sequence of steps, like restore, build, test and publish coverage for a .NET project. Job and stage templates hold whole jobs or stages, like a standard deploy stage with approvals and smoke tests. Variable templates hold shared variables. Templates take typed parameters, like the project path, .NET version, or environment name, with defaults and allowed values, and can use template expressions with each loops and conditions, evaluated at compile time.

Templates usually live in a central repository, referenced with a resources repositories block and pinned to a tag or branch, so a change to the shared template is versioned and teams can adopt it deliberately.

Extends templates go further: the pipeline in each repo just extends a central template and passes parameters, and the template controls the overall structure. Combined with a required template check on protected resources, like production environments or service connections, this enforces that every pipeline deploying to production runs the mandatory security scans and approvals, which is a strong governance tool.
I keep templates simple and well documented, avoid deep nesting, and test template changes on a sample pipeline before releasing a new version.

p17-536.q: An Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline has a clear hierarchy.
p17-536.k: azure pipelines stages jobs steps, deployment job, environments azure devops, pipeline structure, run once rolling canary strategy
x: An Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline has a clear hierarchy.

Stages are the big phases, like Build, Deploy to Dev, Deploy to QA and Deploy to Production. They run sequentially by default, can depend on each other with dependsOn, and can have conditions, like only deploying from main. Approvals and checks are attached at the environment level, so a stage waits until they pass.
Jobs run inside stages. Each job runs on one agent, from a pool, and jobs in a stage can run in parallel. A job can be a normal job or a deployment job.
Steps are the individual tasks or scripts inside a job, like checking out code, running dotnet build, publishing artifacts, or running a PowerShell script.

Deployment jobs are special jobs for releases. They target an environment, which records deployment history: which build went to which environment and when. They support strategies: runOnce, rolling across virtual machines in the environment, and canary with increments. Each strategy has lifecycle hooks, like preDeploy, deploy, routeTraffic, postRouteTraffic, and on failure or success, so you can run smoke tests after routing traffic and roll back on failure.
Artifacts are published in the build stage and downloaded automatically in deployment jobs, so the exact same build output moves through every stage.
On our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, the older classic release pipelines are still used for some apps, but YAML pipelines with environments give us code review and history for pipeline changes.

p17-537.q: Build once, deploy many means the pipeline compiles and packages the application one time, and that exact artifact, the same zip, package or container image, is deployed to dev, test, UAT and production. Only configuration differs per environment.
p17-537.k: build once deploy many, artifact promotion, immutable artifact, rebuild per environment problem, environment specific config
x: Build once, deploy many means the pipeline compiles and packages the application one time, and that exact artifact, the same zip, package or container image, is deployed to dev, test, UAT and production. Only configuration differs per environment.

Why it matters. If you rebuild for each environment, you're not deploying what you tested. A different build agent, an updated base image, a newer dependency resolved by a floating version, or a different commit can sneak in. Then a bug appears in production that never existed in test, and you can't easily tell why.

With a single artifact, testing in each environment adds confidence to the same binary. It's faster, because builds happen once. And it's traceable: the artifact has a version and a hash, linked to a commit and a build, and each deployment records which artifact went where.

To make it work, configuration must be outside the artifact: environment variables, appsettings per environment loaded at runtime, a configuration service, or secrets managers, not build-time constants or per-environment build flags. Front ends need the same idea, loading a runtime config file rather than baking API URLs into the bundle.

In a validated GxP environment, this is close to mandatory, because the validated package must be provably identical to what goes into production. We keep the build artifact, its version and its approvals linked in Azure DevOps for that reason.

p17-538.q: Both are mature CI/CD systems with YAML pipelines, hosted and self-hosted runners, and support for any language. The differences are mostly in ecosystem and enterprise features.
p17-538.k: github actions vs azure pipelines, github actions vs azure devops, ci cd tool comparison, workflows vs pipelines
x: Both are mature CI/CD systems with YAML pipelines, hosted and self-hosted runners, and support for any language. The differences are mostly in ecosystem and enterprise features.

GitHub Actions is built into GitHub. Workflows trigger on almost any repository event: pushes, pull requests, issues, releases, schedules or manual dispatch. Its marketplace has a huge number of actions. Reusable workflows and composite actions share logic. Environments have protection rules and secrets, and OIDC federation to AWS, Azure and GCP is straightforward. It integrates naturally with GitHub's security features, like Dependabot, code scanning and secret scanning. It's the default for open source and many new projects.

Azure Pipelines is part of Azure DevOps, alongside Boards, Repos, Test Plans and Artifacts. It works with GitHub repos too. It's strong for enterprises with complex release processes: multi-stage pipelines, environments with approvals, checks like business hours, required templates and exclusive locks, deep traceability from work items to commits to builds to deployments, classic release pipelines for older setups, and an on-premise version, Azure DevOps Server, which matters for organisations that can't use cloud services.

The choice usually follows where the code and work tracking live. In our case, the on-premise platform uses Azure DevOps Server, so Azure Pipelines is natural there, while newer cloud-based work can use either. The concepts, like stages, jobs, runners, environments and secrets, transfer easily between them.

p17-539.q: Storing an AWS access key and secret as a pipeline secret is common but risky. The keys are long-lived, often over-privileged, hard to rotate, and if leaked, work from anywhere. The better way is OpenID Connect federation.
p17-539.k: oidc github actions aws, assume role with web identity, pipeline aws credentials, no access keys ci, aws federation ci
x: Storing an AWS access key and secret as a pipeline secret is common but risky. The keys are long-lived, often over-privileged, hard to rotate, and if leaked, work from anywhere. The better way is OpenID Connect federation.

How it works with GitHub Actions: in the AWS account, I create an IAM OIDC identity provider for GitHub's token issuer, and an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, with conditions on the token's claims: the audience must be sts.amazonaws.com, and the subject must match a specific repository and branch or environment, like repo:org/shipments-api:environment:production. In the workflow, I grant the id-token write permission and use the configure-aws-credentials action with the role ARN. Each run gets temporary credentials, valid for about an hour, and nothing is stored.
Azure Pipelines and GitLab support the same pattern, as does Azure with federated credentials.

Good practices: separate roles per environment and per purpose, like a deploy role that can update ECS services and push to ECR, and a read-only plan role for Terraform pull requests; least-privilege policies; tight subject conditions, never a wildcard on the whole organisation; and CloudTrail monitoring of role usage.

For our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, federation depends on network and version support, so the same least-privilege idea applies with whatever mechanism is available, with credentials stored only in a protected library and rotated.

p17-540.q: Supply chain attacks target the path from source code to production rather than the application itself, like a compromised dependency, a tampered build agent, or a malicious package with the same name as an internal one. So I protect each step.
p17-540.k: software supply chain security, sbom, slsa, sign artifacts, pipeline security, dependency confusion
x: Supply chain attacks target the path from source code to production rather than the application itself, like a compromised dependency, a tampered build agent, or a malicious package with the same name as an internal one. So I protect each step.
Source: branch protection with required reviews, signed commits where practical, and secret scanning to stop credentials getting committed.

Dependencies: lock files and pinned versions, so builds are reproducible; package source mapping in NuGet and scoped registries in npm, so internal package names can only come from the internal feed, which prevents dependency confusion; vulnerability scanning with dotnet list package --vulnerable, npm audit, Dependabot or a commercial scanner; and a review process for adding new dependencies.

Build: pipelines defined as code and reviewed; minimal permissions for the pipeline's token; pinned versions of actions or tasks, ideally by commit SHA; ephemeral, clean build agents; and no secrets available to builds from untrusted pull requests.

Artifacts: generate a software bill of materials, an SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format, so we know exactly what's inside each release and can quickly answer "are we affected?" when a new vulnerability is announced. Sign artifacts and images, with tools like Sigstore Cosign or Notation, and produce provenance attestations following SLSA. Verify signatures at deployment time.
Deployment: only signed, scanned artifacts from the trusted pipeline can reach production.

p17-541.q: Outdated dependencies pile up security vulnerabilities and make future upgrades painful, because jumping several major versions at once is much harder than small, regular steps. Automating update pull requests keeps it manageable.
p17-541.k: dependabot, renovate, dependency updates, outdated packages, automated dependency pull requests, nuget updates
x: Outdated dependencies pile up security vulnerabilities and make future upgrades painful, because jumping several major versions at once is much harder than small, regular steps. Automating update pull requests keeps it manageable.

Dependabot, built into GitHub, and Renovate, which works with GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab and others, scan manifests, like csproj files, Directory.Packages.props, package.json, Dockerfiles and pipeline files, and open pull requests to update versions. Security updates are raised as soon as a vulnerable version is known.
To make it workable rather than noisy:
Group related updates, like all Microsoft.Extensions packages or all testing packages, into one pull request, and schedule non-security updates weekly.
Automerge low-risk updates, like patch versions of dev dependencies, when the pipeline passes. This depends on a good test suite, which is the real safety net.
Treat major versions separately, with release notes read and changes planned, since they're often breaking.
Use central package management in .NET, so versions are defined in one place across a solution.
Keep base images current too, because the operating system packages in images are a big source of vulnerabilities.

The team also needs a habit: someone reviews update pull requests every week, so they don't become ignored noise. In a regulated product, dependency updates still go through the normal validated release process, but small regular updates make that process far lighter.

p17-542.q: The situation: production is on version 3.4, main already has weeks of changes for 3.5 that aren't ready, and a critical bug must be fixed in production today.
p17-542.k: hotfix process, hotfix branch, cherry pick hotfix, emergency fix production, patch release, release branch hotfix
x: The situation: production is on version 3.4, main already has weeks of changes for 3.5 that aren't ready, and a critical bug must be fixed in production today.
The process I follow.
Branch from what's in production, not from main. That's the release branch or the tag for 3.4, like release/3.4. Create a hotfix branch from it.
Make the smallest possible fix, with a test that reproduces the bug first. Keep it focused; no refactoring or extra changes.

Run it through the pipeline like any release: build, automated tests, review and approvals. Even in an emergency, I don't skip the review or the regression tests that matter. In a regulated environment, there's often an expedited change process, but it still records the risk assessment, testing evidence and approvals.
Release as 3.4.1, a new patch version, and deploy using the normal deployment pipeline, so the deployment itself is a known, tested process.

Bring the fix back to main: merge or cherry-pick it into main, and into any other active release branches, so 3.5 doesn't reintroduce the bug. Ideally, the fix is developed on main first and cherry-picked to the release branch, so it's never forgotten, but in urgent cases the order can be reversed.
Afterwards, a short review: why did the bug escape, and what test or check would have caught it.

p17-543.q: A slow pipeline costs focus and encourages people to batch changes, which is the opposite of what we want. My target for pull request validation is around ten minutes. First I measure where the time goes, using the pipeline's step timings over several runs, then work on the biggest items.
p17-543.k: slow ci pipeline, speed up build, pipeline caching, parallel tests, ci performance, incremental build
x: A slow pipeline costs focus and encourages people to batch changes, which is the opposite of what we want. My target for pull request validation is around ten minutes. First I measure where the time goes, using the pipeline's step timings over several runs, then work on the biggest items.

Caching: restore NuGet and npm packages from a pipeline cache keyed on the lock file hash, instead of downloading everything each time. For Docker, reuse layer caches through BuildKit and a registry cache.
Parallelism: split independent work into parallel jobs, like backend build and tests, front-end build and tests, and static analysis. Split large test suites across agents.

Do less work: path filters, so changes in the front end don't trigger the backend pipeline in a monorepo; only build affected projects with tools like Nx for front ends; and move slow, broad tests, like full end-to-end suites or long performance tests, to a nightly or post-merge pipeline, keeping a fast smoke set on pull requests.

Faster tests: find the slowest tests; replace sleeps with proper waits; share expensive fixtures like Testcontainers databases across a test class or collection; and run tests in parallel where they're isolated.
Better agents: more CPU, or self-hosted agents with warm caches, if the hosted agents are the bottleneck.
Then track the pipeline duration as a metric, so it doesn't slowly creep back up.

p17-544.q: Both work; the choice changes how builds, versioning and ownership are handled.
p17-544.k: monorepo vs polyrepo, monorepo ci, path filters pipeline, nx affected, repository strategy microservices
x: Both work; the choice changes how builds, versioning and ownership are handled.

In a monorepo, many services and packages live in one repository. Benefits: atomic changes across services and shared libraries in a single pull request, one place to search, consistent tooling and standards, and easy refactoring. Challenges for CI/CD: you don't want every commit to build and deploy everything, so pipelines need path filters or affected-project detection, like Nx affected for JavaScript, or a build graph tool. Ownership must be explicit, with CODEOWNERS files per folder. Versioning is either one version for all, or independent versions per package with tooling. And the repo can get big, needing shallow clones and sparse checkouts.

In multiple repositories, each service or package has its own repo, pipeline and version. Benefits: clear ownership and permissions, independent release cycles, smaller and faster pipelines. Challenges: changes across several repos need coordinated pull requests and releases; shared code becomes versioned packages, which brings dependency update work; and standards drift unless pipeline templates are shared.

What I've seen work: polyrepo for independently deployed services, with shared pipeline templates and packages published to an internal feed. Our React shell with npm feature packages is a good example: each feature package is versioned and published to the Azure DevOps feed, and the shell consumes specific versions. A monorepo makes sense for tightly coupled front-end packages where changes usually span several of them.

p17-545.q: Protecting main is the simplest, highest-value control in the whole delivery process. The rules I usually set:
p17-545.k: branch policies, branch protection rules, required reviewers, pull request validation build, code owners, protect main branch
x: Protecting main is the simplest, highest-value control in the whole delivery process. The rules I usually set:
No direct pushes to main; all changes go through pull requests.

A required build validation: the pull request pipeline must pass, compiling the code, running unit tests and static analysis, before merging. In Azure Repos, that's a build validation policy; in GitHub, a required status check. The build should run against the merged result, not just the branch.

Required reviewers: at least one or two approvals, with code owners automatically added for the areas they own, like the database schema or the security code. Approvals reset when new changes are pushed, so reviewers don't approve one version and merge another.
Linked work items, so every change traces to a requirement or bug, which matters a lot in a regulated environment.
All comments resolved before merging.
A merge strategy: squash merges for a clean history on main, or merge commits if detailed history matters.
Quality gates: a SonarQube or similar gate on new code, like no new critical issues and coverage on new code above a threshold, plus secret scanning and dependency checks.
Exceptions: administrators can bypass in emergencies, but bypasses are logged and reviewed.
These rules are only as good as the checks behind them, so I keep the pull request pipeline fast and reliable, otherwise people look for ways around it.

p17-546.q: DORA metrics come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program and measure software delivery performance with four key numbers.
p17-546.k: dora metrics, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, mean time to restore, delivery performance
x: DORA metrics come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program and measure software delivery performance with four key numbers.

Deployment frequency: how often you deploy to production. Lead time for changes: how long from a commit to that commit running in production. Change failure rate: the percentage of deployments that cause a failure needing a fix, rollback or hotfix. Time to restore service: how long it takes to recover from a failure in production. DORA has since added deployment rework rate and refined the model, but these four are the core.

The research shows the first two, throughput, and the last two, stability, improve together in high-performing teams. Going faster with small changes doesn't have to mean more failures; usually it means fewer, because each change is smaller and easier to understand.

How I'd use them: measure from data the tools already have, like pipeline runs, deployment records, and incident tickets, rather than manual reporting. Look at trends for a team over time, not comparisons between teams. Use them to find bottlenecks, like a long lead time caused by waiting days for a manual test environment, or a high failure rate pointing at weak tests.
What to avoid: turning them into targets for individuals, which leads to gaming, like splitting deployments artificially.
In a regulated release process, lead time includes validation and approval steps, so measuring it shows where automation of evidence collection would help most.

p17-547.q: In our front-end architecture, the React shell consumes feature packages, each built and versioned independently and published to a private npm feed on Azure DevOps. The pipeline for each package looks like this.
p17-547.k: publish npm package azure artifacts, private npm feed, versioning feature packages, npm package pipeline, shell app packages
x: In our front-end architecture, the React shell consumes feature packages, each built and versioned independently and published to a private npm feed on Azure DevOps. The pipeline for each package looks like this.

On pull request: install with npm ci using the lock file, run lint, type checks with tsc, unit tests with coverage, and a build with Vite in library mode, producing ES module output and type declarations. The package.json lists React, MUI and Redux Toolkit as peer dependencies, so the shell provides a single copy of each, instead of every package bundling its own.

On merge to main: calculate the version, using conventional commits or a manual version bump reviewed in the pull request, then publish to the feed with an npmrc that authenticates through the pipeline's identity, never a personal token committed to the repo. Pre-release versions, like 2.3.0-beta.1, can be published from feature branches for testing in the shell without affecting stable consumers.
Feed views help promote versions: a package goes to the Prerelease view first, and once validated, is promoted to Release, so consumers only see approved versions.

In the shell, versions are pinned exactly, and upgrading a feature package is a reviewed change with its own release notes. That gives traceability: for any shell release, we know exactly which version of each feature it contained.
Changelogs per package make it clear what each version changes.

p17-548.q: SSDT database projects keep the database schema as code: tables, views, stored procedures and functions as .sql files in a project, compiled into a dacpac, which is a package describing the desired schema.
p17-548.k: ssdt dacpac deployment, sqlpackage publish, database project pipeline, schema drift sql server, dacpac pipeline
x: SSDT database projects keep the database schema as code: tables, views, stored procedures and functions as .sql files in a project, compiled into a dacpac, which is a package describing the desired schema.

In the build stage, the pipeline builds the database project, which validates references and syntax, and publishes the dacpac as an artifact, alongside the application artifacts, with the same version.

In the deployment stage, SqlPackage compares the dacpac with the target database and generates a change script to bring it to the desired state. My practice is to generate the script first, with the Script action, publish it as an artifact and review it for production, especially in a regulated environment, rather than blindly applying it. Then apply with Publish or by running the reviewed script.

Publish profiles control dangerous behaviour: BlockOnPossibleDataLoss stays true, so a change that would drop a column with data fails instead of losing data; DropObjectsNotInSource is used carefully. Pre- and post-deployment scripts handle data changes, like seeding reference data, written to be idempotent.

Since our platform has a database per study plus a master database, the same dacpac is applied to many databases, so the deployment loops over the target list, records each result, and stops or continues according to a clear rule when one database fails.
Drift reports detect changes made directly in production outside the process, which should then be either reverted or brought into source control.

p17-549.q: For applications hosted on IIS, which is how our on-premise platform runs, deployments typically use Azure DevOps deployment groups or environments with VM resources, where an agent on each server runs the deployment steps.
p17-549.k: deploy to iis pipeline, web deploy, app_offline, iis deployment azure devops, zero downtime iis, deployment group iis
x: For applications hosted on IIS, which is how our on-premise platform runs, deployments typically use Azure DevOps deployment groups or environments with VM resources, where an agent on each server runs the deployment steps.

The basic steps: download the build artifact; stop the site or put app_offline.htm in place, which tells the ASP.NET Core Module or ASP.NET to stop the app and serve a maintenance page, releasing file locks; copy the new files with Web Deploy, msdeploy, or a robocopy-style file copy; apply configuration transforms or environment-specific settings; start the app pool or remove app_offline; then warm the site with a request and run smoke tests.

To get close to zero downtime with multiple servers behind a load balancer, I deploy one server or a batch at a time: take it out of the load balancer pool, or let health checks drain it, deploy, warm up, verify, and put it back, then move to the next. The rolling strategy in deployment jobs supports this with a maximum number of targets in parallel.
For a single server, a blue-green style setup with two IIS sites or folders and a switch in the binding or reverse proxy, like ARR or URL Rewrite, allows switching instantly and switching back.

Important details: the Application Initialization module to preload the app; consistent versions across all nodes, verified after deployment; and keeping the previous version's folder for quick rollback.

p17-550.q: The goal is one build artifact and different configuration per environment, applied at deployment or runtime, never by rebuilding.
p17-550.k: web.config transformation, appsettings environment, configuration per environment, parameters.xml, environment variables dotnet config
x: The goal is one build artifact and different configuration per environment, applied at deployment or runtime, never by rebuilding.

For .NET Framework apps, configuration lives in web.config. Traditionally, build configurations had transforms, like Web.Release.config, applied at build time, which ties configuration to the build. Better options for build once, deploy many: apply transforms at deployment time, which Azure DevOps IIS deployment tasks support with environment-named transform files; use token replacement, where the web.config contains placeholders like #{DbServer}# replaced from pipeline variables or variable groups during deployment; or Web Deploy parameters.xml, which declares parameters that get values per environment. Since .NET Framework 4.7.1, configuration builders can also pull values from environment variables or a secrets store at runtime.

For modern .NET, configuration is layered at runtime: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then environment variables, then sources like Key Vault, App Configuration or Parameter Store, with later sources overriding earlier ones. The ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable selects the environment. Nested keys map to environment variables with double underscores, like ConnectionStrings__Default.
Secrets never go in config files in the repo; they come from pipeline secret variables or secrets managers.
I also make the app validate its configuration at startup, with options validation, so a missing or wrong setting fails the deployment immediately instead of failing later on the first request.

p17-551.q: Front-end frameworks encourage build-time configuration: Vite injects import.meta.env values, Create React App had process.env, and Angular has environment files selected by build configuration. The values are baked into the JavaScript bundle. That means a separate build per environment, which breaks build once, deploy many, and in a regulated setting means the tested bundle isn't the one that goes to production.
p17-551.k: spa runtime configuration, react environment variables build time, angular environment per deployment, config.json spa, build once spa
x: Front-end frameworks encourage build-time configuration: Vite injects import.meta.env values, Create React App had process.env, and Angular has environment files selected by build configuration. The values are baked into the JavaScript bundle. That means a separate build per environment, which breaks build once, deploy many, and in a regulated setting means the tested bundle isn't the one that goes to production.

The usual solution is runtime configuration. The app ships with a small config file, like /config.json or env-config.js, that's not part of the bundle. At deployment, the pipeline writes the environment's values into that file, like the API base URL, the identity provider authority and client id, feature flags and the telemetry key. At startup, the app fetches the file before rendering, or the index.html loads env-config.js, which sets a global object.

In Angular, an APP_INITIALIZER, or provideAppInitializer in newer versions, can load the config before the app bootstraps, and a config service exposes it. In React, the root component waits for the config before rendering the router.
For containers, the entrypoint can generate the file from environment variables at startup.

Important points: the config file must not be cached aggressively, or users get stale values after a change, so it gets no-cache headers; it must contain no secrets, since everything in a browser is public; and the app should fail clearly if the config is missing.

p17-552.q: With a database per study, a schema change isn't one deployment; it's hundreds. Doing it reliably needs orchestration.
p17-552.k: deploy to many databases, multi tenant database migration, database per tenant deployment, schema rollout many databases, migration orchestration
x: With a database per study, a schema change isn't one deployment; it's hundreds. Doing it reliably needs orchestration.

First, the change itself must be backward compatible, because databases are updated over minutes or hours, and the application must work with both old and new schemas during that time. Expand and contract again: add new structures first, and remove old ones only in a later release once every database is updated.

Then the rollout process. Keep a registry of all target databases, from the master database, with each one's current schema version, recorded in a version table inside each database. Run the migration in waves: first internal test databases, then a small canary group of production databases, then the rest in batches with limited parallelism, so the database server isn't overloaded. Each run is idempotent and records success or failure per database, with the script version and timestamps, which also gives the audit evidence a regulated environment needs.

Failure handling: a failure in one database must not leave it half-migrated, so each database's change runs in a transaction where possible, or in carefully ordered idempotent steps. Failed databases are reported and retried after investigation, without blocking the others, unless the failure suggests a systemic problem, which halts the rollout.
Long-running changes, like adding an index to a huge table, are scheduled for quiet periods per region, and online index operations are used where available.
A dashboard showing the version of every database makes it obvious when something is behind.

p17-553.q: When a release causes problems, the decision is about restoring service fastest with the least risk, not about pride.
p17-553.k: rollback vs roll forward, fix forward, release went wrong decision, revert deployment, incident release decision
x: When a release causes problems, the decision is about restoring service fastest with the least risk, not about pride.

I lean towards rolling back when the previous version is known good and rollback is cheap and safe: stateless services, an artifact still available, no irreversible database changes, and the impact is serious. Rolling back is usually a pipeline run or a traffic switch, and it restores the known state while we investigate calmly. Feature flags are an even faster form: switch off the new feature without redeploying.

I lean towards rolling forward, deploying a quick fix, when rollback isn't safe or possible: the release included database changes the old version can't work with, data has already been written in the new format, external partners have already integrated with a new API, or the fix is tiny, well understood and can go through the pipeline quickly. Rolling forward under pressure carries risk, so the fix still goes through tests and review.

Preparation makes this easier. Backward-compatible database changes keep rollback possible. Every release has a documented rollback plan before it goes out. Deployments are automated, so rolling back isn't a manual scramble. And monitoring with clear signals, like error rate and key business events, tells you quickly whether the action worked.
In a regulated environment, either action is a controlled change, so the decision, approvals and verification are recorded in the incident and change records.

p17-554.q: In regulated companies, production changes often need approval from a change advisory board, a CAB. A heavyweight CAB meeting for every change slows delivery, encourages big risky batches, and research shows external approval boards don't actually reduce failure rates. So the goal is to keep the control but make it lighter and smarter.
p17-554.k: change advisory board, cab approval, change management itil, standard change, regulated release approvals, change request
x: In regulated companies, production changes often need approval from a change advisory board, a CAB. A heavyweight CAB meeting for every change slows delivery, encourages big risky batches, and research shows external approval boards don't actually reduce failure rates. So the goal is to keep the control but make it lighter and smarter.
Things that help.

Classify changes. Standard changes are pre-approved because they're low-risk and follow a proven, automated process, like a routine deployment through the validated pipeline. Normal changes get a review. Emergency changes have an expedited path with review afterwards. Getting our routine pipeline deployments classified as standard changes was a big win.

Bring evidence automatically. The pipeline produces what the CAB wants to see: the linked work items, test results, code review approvals, security scan results, the deployment plan and the rollback plan. The change record is created and updated by the pipeline, not typed by hand.
Shift approvals left. Peer review in pull requests and automated checks provide most of the assurance; the CAB focuses on genuinely risky changes, like data migrations or infrastructure changes.
Make releases smaller and more frequent, so each change is easier to assess.
Show the data, like change failure rate, to build trust that the process works.
In our GxP context, validation evidence and approvals are mandatory, but automating their collection kept releases moving without cutting corners.

p17-555.q: An ephemeral preview environment is a short-lived copy of the application created automatically for a pull request, with its own URL, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. Reviewers, testers and product owners can try the change for real before it merges, instead of reading code or waiting for a shared test environment.
p17-555.k: preview environments, ephemeral environments, pull request environment, review apps, environment per branch
x: An ephemeral preview environment is a short-lived copy of the application created automatically for a pull request, with its own URL, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. Reviewers, testers and product owners can try the change for real before it merges, instead of reading code or waiting for a shared test environment.

How it's typically built. For front ends, it's easy: services like Azure Static Web Apps, Vercel or Netlify, or a pipeline that uploads to a bucket under a pull-request path, create a preview site per pull request automatically.

For back-end services on Kubernetes, the pipeline deploys the pull request's image into a new namespace named after the pull request, using the same Helm chart with a small values override, and a dynamic host name like pr-123.dev.example.com. Dependencies are either shared, like a common dev database with test data, or created per environment, like a small database container seeded with test data, depending on cost and isolation needs. A cleanup job deletes the namespace when the pull request closes, plus a nightly sweep for anything left behind.
On Azure Container Apps or AWS, infrastructure as code can create and destroy a small stack per pull request.
Watch-outs: cost, so environments are small and auto-expire; secrets, which shouldn't be exposed to pull requests from forks; and data, which must be synthetic, never copies of production data.

p17-556.q: GitHub Actions has two main ways to reuse logic, at different levels.
p17-556.k: reusable workflows, composite actions, github actions reuse, workflow_call, github actions templates
x: GitHub Actions has two main ways to reuse logic, at different levels.

Composite actions bundle several steps into one action, defined in an action.yml with inputs and outputs. For example, a setup-dotnet-build action that installs the SDK, restores with caching, builds and runs tests with coverage. Any job can use it as a single step. They're good for sharing step sequences, and they run inside the caller's job, on the caller's runner.

Reusable workflows are whole workflows triggered with workflow_call, with defined inputs, secrets and outputs. A caller job uses them with uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v2. They can contain multiple jobs, use their own runners, environments and protection rules, and are good for standardising entire processes, like build-and-push-image or deploy-to-environment with approvals.

Good practices: keep shared workflows in a central repository, version them with tags, and have consumers pin a tag or, for third-party actions, a full commit SHA, so an upstream change can't silently alter pipelines. Pass secrets explicitly rather than using secrets: inherit everywhere. Set minimal permissions for the GITHUB_TOKEN at the workflow level. Document inputs clearly.
Organisation-level rulesets can require certain workflows to run on all repositories, like a security scan, which gives similar governance to required templates in Azure Pipelines.
Changes to shared workflows are tested on a sample repository before a new version is tagged.

p17-557.q: Traceability means for any change running in production, I can answer: which requirement or bug it came from, who wrote and reviewed it, which tests verified it, which build produced it, and when and by whom it was deployed and approved. In a GxP environment, auditors expect exactly this.
p17-557.k: traceability requirement to deployment, work item linking, audit trail release, gxp traceability, commit to production
x: Traceability means for any change running in production, I can answer: which requirement or bug it came from, who wrote and reviewed it, which tests verified it, which build produced it, and when and by whom it was deployed and approved. In a GxP environment, auditors expect exactly this.
How the tooling provides it in Azure DevOps.
Work items: every requirement, user story and bug is a work item. Branch policies require pull requests to link work items, and commits mention them too.
Pull requests: record the reviewers, approvals, comments and the validation build.
Builds: link to the commits and work items included since the last build, and publish test results and coverage, which attach to the build. The build number carries the version.

Releases and environments: the deployment records which build artifact went to which environment, with timestamps, approvals and who approved. Release notes can be generated from the linked work items.
Test management: test cases link to requirements, and test runs, manual or automated, link to builds, so validation evidence connects requirement to verification.
Going the other way, from a requirement I can find all the code and every release that included it.

What makes it actually work is enforcement through policies rather than discipline alone, and keeping retention settings long enough, because pipeline runs and artifacts are deleted by default after some time, which would break the audit trail. We set retention to match our records requirements.

p17-558.q: Testcontainers is a library that starts real dependencies in Docker containers from inside the test code, and throws them away afterwards. There's a .NET version, with ready-made modules for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for AWS, Azurite for Azure Storage, and many more.
p17-558.k: testcontainers, testcontainers dotnet, real database in tests, docker integration tests, sql server container tests
x: Testcontainers is a library that starts real dependencies in Docker containers from inside the test code, and throws them away afterwards. There's a .NET version, with ready-made modules for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for AWS, Azurite for Azure Storage, and many more.

Why it's better than the alternatives. In-memory fakes, like the EF Core in-memory provider or SQLite standing in for SQL Server, behave differently from the real database: no real transactions, different SQL translation, no stored procedures or constraints. Tests pass and production fails. A shared test database is slow to reset, and tests interfere with each other. Testcontainers gives each test run a real, clean instance of the same engine and version used in production.

How I use it in .NET with xUnit: a fixture class implements IAsyncLifetime, builds a container with something like new MsSqlBuilder().Build(), starts it in InitializeAsync, applies migrations, and exposes the connection string. WebApplicationFactory then overrides the app's connection string to point at the container, so the API runs end to end against the real database. The fixture is shared across a test collection, because starting a container takes a few seconds, and Respawn or transactions reset data between tests.
It runs the same on a developer laptop and in CI, as long as Docker is available on the agent, which is the main setup requirement.

p17-559.q: Integration tests that call secured endpoints need an authenticated user, but they shouldn't depend on a real identity provider like Keycloak. There are two common approaches.
p17-559.k: test authentication handler, fake jwt integration tests, webapplicationfactory auth, authorize in tests, test user claims
x: Integration tests that call secured endpoints need an authenticated user, but they shouldn't depend on a real identity provider like Keycloak. There are two common approaches.

A test authentication handler. In WebApplicationFactory's ConfigureTestServices, I register a custom AuthenticationHandler under a test scheme and make it the default. Its HandleAuthenticateAsync builds a ClaimsPrincipal with the claims the test needs: user id, roles, site or study scopes, and returns success. Tests can control the claims per request, for example by reading a test header, so one test runs as a site user and another as an admin. Authorisation policies, role checks and resource-based handlers still run for real, which is exactly what I want to test.

Locally signed JWTs. Configure the JWT bearer options in tests to trust a signing key created in the test, then mint tokens with the claims needed. This exercises the real JWT bearer pipeline, including issuer, audience and expiry validation, which is good for testing token-related behaviour.

Whichever I use, I always include negative tests: no token gives 401, a valid user without permission gives 403, and a user from one site can't read another site's data. Those are the tests that catch real security bugs.
What I avoid is disabling authorisation in tests altogether, with AllowAnonymous filters, because then the most important rules are never tested.

p17-560.q: When a service calls an external HTTP API, like a partner's shipment API or an identity provider, tests shouldn't call the real thing. It's slow, flaky, may cost money, and you can't make it fail on demand.
p17-560.k: wiremock dotnet, stub http api, mock external service, fake http server tests, test third party api
x: When a service calls an external HTTP API, like a partner's shipment API or an identity provider, tests shouldn't call the real thing. It's slow, flaky, may cost money, and you can't make it fail on demand.

WireMock.Net starts a real HTTP server inside the test process on a random port. I configure the app's HttpClient base address to point at it, then set up stubs: when a GET arrives at /shipments/123 with a certain header, return 200 with this JSON body; when a POST arrives, return 201. It records all requests, so tests can verify exactly what was sent: URL, headers and body.

Its real value is testing failure behaviour, which is hard with the real API. I can stub a 500, a 429 with a Retry-After header, a slow response that exceeds the timeout, malformed JSON, or a connection reset. Then I check that retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks behave as designed, like the Polly pipeline retrying twice and then the service returning a clear error.
Scenarios let stubs change state across calls, like failing on the first call and succeeding on the second.
Compared with mocking HttpMessageHandler in unit tests, WireMock exercises the real HTTP stack, serialisation and handler pipeline.
The stubs should match the real API's contract; if the partner provides an OpenAPI spec or a sandbox, I check stubs against it, or use contract tests, so the fake doesn't drift from reality.

p17-561.q: In microservices, an API change can break a consumer without anyone noticing until integration or production. End-to-end tests catch this, but they're slow and fragile. Contract testing catches it earlier and cheaper.
p17-561.k: pact contract testing, consumer driven contracts, contract test microservices, pact broker, provider verification
x: In microservices, an API change can break a consumer without anyone noticing until integration or production. End-to-end tests catch this, but they're slow and fragile. Contract testing catches it earlier and cheaper.

With Pact, the consumer team writes tests describing the interactions they rely on: when I call GET /shipments/123, I expect 200 with a body containing id, status and site. During the consumer's test run, Pact acts as a mock provider and records these expectations into a contract file, the pact. The pact is published to a Pact Broker.

The provider then runs verification in its own pipeline: Pact replays each interaction from every consumer's pact against the real provider service, using provider states to set up data, like a shipment with id 123 exists, and checks the responses match. If the provider renamed a field a consumer uses, verification fails in the provider's pipeline, before release.
The broker tracks which versions of consumers and providers are compatible, and the can-i-deploy check answers whether a specific version can safely go to an environment.
The benefits: each consumer only specifies what it actually uses, so providers can change everything else freely; teams find breaking changes early; and fewer slow end-to-end tests are needed.

It works for messages too, like event payloads on RabbitMQ or Kafka. The investment is mainly setting up the broker and provider states, so it pays off most with several teams and many service interactions.

p17-562.q: Mock Service Worker intercepts network requests at the network level. In the browser, it uses a service worker; in Node, for Jest or Vitest, it hooks into the request layer. The application code keeps using fetch or axios normally; it doesn't know requests are mocked.
p17-562.k: msw, mock service worker, mock api react tests, network level mocking, msw handlers, storybook msw
x: Mock Service Worker intercepts network requests at the network level. In the browser, it uses a service worker; in Node, for Jest or Vitest, it hooks into the request layer. The application code keeps using fetch or axios normally; it doesn't know requests are mocked.

I define handlers with the http helpers, like http.get('/api/shipments', ...) returning a JSON response. Tests use the real data-fetching code, like RTK Query, TanStack Query or a service, so I'm testing what users experience: the component renders, fetches, shows a loading state, then shows data or an error.

Why it's better than mocking fetch or the API module. Mocks at the module level tie tests to implementation details; refactoring how data is fetched breaks tests even when behaviour hasn't changed. MSW tests survive refactors.
Per-test overrides make error cases easy: server.use with a handler returning 500 or a delayed response, then assert that the error message and retry button appear. After each test, handlers reset.
The same handlers are reused in Storybook, so components show realistic data in isolation, and in local development, so front-end work can continue before the back-end endpoint exists.
To keep mocks honest, I generate handlers or types from the OpenAPI spec where possible, so if the API changes, TypeScript flags the mismatch.
Configuration tip: fail tests on unhandled requests, so a missing handler is caught instead of silently hitting nothing.

p17-563.q: Code coverage tells you which lines ran during tests, not whether the tests would notice if those lines were wrong. A test that calls a method and asserts nothing gives full coverage and catches nothing.
p17-563.k: mutation testing, stryker dotnet, stryker mutator, test quality, mutation score, coverage is not enough
x: Code coverage tells you which lines ran during tests, not whether the tests would notice if those lines were wrong. A test that calls a method and asserts nothing gives full coverage and catches nothing.

Mutation testing measures test quality directly. A tool makes small changes to the code, called mutants: changing greater than to greater than or equal, flipping a boolean, replacing a plus with a minus, removing a method call, or returning a default value. Then it runs the tests against each mutant. If a test fails, the mutant is killed, which is good. If all tests still pass, the mutant survived, meaning nothing in the test suite would notice that bug. The mutation score is the percentage killed.

For .NET, Stryker.NET does this, and Stryker exists for JavaScript and TypeScript too. It produces an HTML report showing each surviving mutant in the code, which points directly to missing assertions or untested edge cases, like boundary conditions in a date or quantity check.

It's slow, because it runs the tests many times, so I don't run it on every build. I run it on critical modules, like calculation, validation or allocation logic, periodically or in a nightly pipeline, and use the --since option to mutate only changed code in pull requests.
I don't chase 100 percent; some mutants are equivalent and can't be killed. The value is finding important gaps that coverage hides.

p17-564.q: Normal example-based tests check specific inputs: given 10 kits and 3 requested, 7 remain. Property-based testing instead states a rule that must hold for all valid inputs, and the framework generates hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.
p17-564.k: property based testing, fscheck, cscheck, hypothesis python, generative testing, invariants testing
x: Normal example-based tests check specific inputs: given 10 kits and 3 requested, 7 remain. Property-based testing instead states a rule that must hold for all valid inputs, and the framework generates hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.

Examples of properties: serialising and then deserialising any object gives back the same object; sorting is idempotent and preserves the items; for any sequence of reservations and releases, available stock never goes negative and reserved plus available always equals the total; or a parsing function never throws for any string, it either succeeds or returns a validation error.
When a property fails, the framework shrinks the input to the smallest failing example, like an empty list or a value of exactly zero, which makes the bug easy to understand.
Tools: FsCheck and CsCheck for .NET, which integrate with xUnit; Hypothesis for Python; fast-check for TypeScript.

Where it pays off: algorithms with clear invariants, like allocation, scheduling, calculations, encoders and parsers; code with many edge cases; and stateful systems, where the framework generates random sequences of operations and compares the system against a simple model.

It doesn't replace example tests, which document specific business cases clearly. And properties need some thought to write well; a property that just reimplements the code proves nothing. I use it for the most logic-heavy parts, where it often finds bugs no one thought of.

p17-565.q: Snapshot or approval testing checks a complex output against a previously approved version stored in a file, instead of writing many individual assertions.
p17-565.k: snapshot testing, approval testing, verify dotnet, verify tests, snapshot test api response, received approved files
x: Snapshot or approval testing checks a complex output against a previously approved version stored in a file, instead of writing many individual assertions.

With the Verify library in .NET, a test ends with await Verify(result). The first time, Verify serialises the result, like an object graph, an API response, a generated document, or even HTTP calls made, into a received file, and the test fails. A developer reviews it, and if it's correct, accepts it as the verified file, which is committed to the repository. On later runs, the new output is compared with the verified file; any difference fails the test and shows a diff.

It's great for: API response shapes, so an accidental field rename or format change is caught; generated output like reports, emails, CSV or XML exports, PDFs and images; complex mapping results; and characterising legacy code before refactoring, capturing its current behaviour.
Verify handles noise: it scrubs values that change every run, like GUIDs and dates, replacing them with stable placeholders, and lets you ignore specific members.

The risks: if reviewers just accept every changed snapshot without reading, tests catch nothing. Snapshots should be small and focused enough to review. And for simple values, plain assertions are clearer.
Jest has the same idea for JavaScript, with toMatchSnapshot, often used for serialisable outputs rather than whole component trees.

p17-566.q: Load testing checks how a system behaves under realistic and peak traffic, before users find out.
p17-566.k: load testing, k6, nbomber, performance testing api, load test script, thresholds k6
x: Load testing checks how a system behaves under realistic and peak traffic, before users find out.

k6 is a popular open-source tool where tests are JavaScript scripts. A script defines what a virtual user does: log in, list shipments, open one, create an allocation, with realistic think times and data. Scenarios define the load shape, like ramping to 200 virtual users over five minutes, or a constant arrival rate of 50 requests per second, which is better for APIs because it doesn't slow down when the system slows down. Thresholds define pass or fail: p95 latency below 500 milliseconds and error rate below one percent. That makes load tests usable as pipeline gates. Results can stream to Grafana or other backends.
NBomber is a .NET alternative, writing scenarios in C#, which suits teams that want to reuse existing .NET clients and models, and it's handy for testing non-HTTP things too, like message consumers.

Getting meaningful results. Test in an environment sized like production, with production-like data volumes, because a query that's fast on 1,000 rows may crawl on 10 million. Generate load from outside the system under test, with enough load-generator capacity. Watch the server side during the test, with CPU, memory, database waits, thread pool queue length, GC and dependency latency, so you know where the bottleneck is, not just that there is one. Run a baseline before changes, then compare.

p17-567.q: Different performance tests answer different questions, so I pick based on the risk.
p17-567.k: load test vs stress test, soak test, spike test, endurance test, capacity test, performance testing types
x: Different performance tests answer different questions, so I pick based on the risk.

A load test runs the expected normal and peak traffic, like the busiest hour of a typical day, for a period. It checks that response times and error rates meet the targets under the load we actually expect.

A stress test increases load beyond expectations until the system breaks, to find the breaking point and, importantly, how it fails. Does it slow down gracefully, shed load with 429 or 503 responses, and recover when load drops? Or does it fall over and stay down?

A spike test applies a sudden jump, like ten times normal traffic within seconds, which tests autoscaling speed, connection pools, caches warming and queues absorbing bursts. Think of a study going live at many sites at once, or a batch import triggering many events.

A soak or endurance test runs a moderate load for many hours or days. It finds problems that only appear over time: memory leaks, connection leaks, growing queues, log disks filling up, slow degradation from fragmentation, and scheduled jobs interfering with traffic.
A capacity test finds how much load a given configuration can handle while meeting targets, which feeds sizing and cost decisions.
Breakpoint and scalability tests check whether adding instances actually increases throughput, or whether a shared resource, like the database, caps it.
All of them need clear targets defined beforehand, and monitoring on the server side to explain the results.

p17-568.q: Tests become hard to read when the arrange section is 30 lines of object construction, and fragile when a new required property means updating hundreds of tests. Good test data tools fix both.
p17-568.k: test data builder, autofixture, bogus fake data, object mother, test data setup, arrange section too long
x: Tests become hard to read when the arrange section is 30 lines of object construction, and fragile when a new required property means updating hundreds of tests. Good test data tools fix both.

The test data builder pattern: a ShipmentBuilder class with sensible defaults for every property and fluent methods to change only what matters for this test, like new ShipmentBuilder().WithStatus(Delivered).ForSite(site).Build(). The test shows only the relevant details, and when the model changes, only the builder changes. Builders can create valid object graphs, respecting domain rules, which is important when constructors enforce invariants.

AutoFixture creates anonymous test data automatically, filling every property with generated values, and can be customised for specific types. Combined with xUnit's AutoData attributes, it removes boilerplate for tests where the values don't matter, and AutoMoq integration creates mocks for dependencies automatically.

Bogus generates realistic fake data: names, addresses, dates, numbers in realistic ranges, with a seed for reproducibility. It's great for seeding development databases, demo environments and load tests, and for UI work where realistic data reveals layout problems.

My guidelines: values that matter to the test's outcome should be visible in the test, not hidden in defaults; generated data should be valid by default; seeds make random data reproducible when a test fails; and never use real production or patient data in tests, which in a clinical domain is especially important.

p17-569.q: Code that calls DateTime.Now or DateTime.UtcNow directly is hard to test. A rule like "a kit expires after 30 days" or "send a reminder if a visit is overdue by two days" depends on the clock, and tests either become flaky or need to wait.
p17-569.k: testing datetime, timeprovider, faketimeprovider, mock datetime now, time dependent tests, clock abstraction
x: Code that calls DateTime.Now or DateTime.UtcNow directly is hard to test. A rule like "a kit expires after 30 days" or "send a reminder if a visit is overdue by two days" depends on the clock, and tests either become flaky or need to wait.

The fix is to inject the clock. Since .NET 8, there's a built-in abstraction, TimeProvider. Code depends on TimeProvider, registered as TimeProvider.System in production, and calls GetUtcNow(), GetLocalNow(), or CreateTimer and Task.Delay overloads that accept a TimeProvider.

In tests, FakeTimeProvider, from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing, lets me set the current time to an exact value and advance it with Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31)). Timers and delays scheduled through the fake provider fire when time is advanced, so tests of timeouts, expiry, retries with delays or periodic background work run instantly and deterministically.
Before .NET 8, teams wrote their own IClock or ISystemClock interface, which works the same way.

Things worth testing explicitly with a controllable clock: boundaries, like exactly at the expiry moment versus one second before; time zones, especially for sites in different countries and daylight saving transitions, where a visit window can be 23 or 25 hours; and month ends and leap years.
For front-end code, Jest and Vitest have fake timers and can set the system time, which serves the same purpose.

p17-570.q: A BackgroundService runs a loop in ExecuteAsync, often reading from a queue or polling on a timer. Testing it directly is awkward because of the infinite loop, timing and cancellation, so I separate concerns.
p17-570.k: test backgroundservice, test hosted service, test worker service, executeasync test, test queue consumer dotnet
x: A BackgroundService runs a loop in ExecuteAsync, often reading from a queue or polling on a timer. Testing it directly is awkward because of the infinite loop, timing and cancellation, so I separate concerns.

Keep the loop thin. The hosted service only handles the mechanics: wait for the next item or tick, create a DI scope, call a handler, and handle errors and cancellation. The real work lives in a separate class, like ProcessShipmentEventHandler, which is a normal class with injected dependencies and is unit-tested like anything else. That's where most tests go.

Test the loop's mechanics separately, with a small number of focused tests: start the service with a cancellation token, feed it an item through a fake queue or a Channel, wait until the handler is called, using a TaskCompletionSource rather than sleeps, then cancel and check it stops cleanly. Check that an exception in one item doesn't kill the loop, and that a scope is created per item. With TimeProvider and FakeTimeProvider, periodic services can be tested without real waiting.

Integration tests run the whole host with WebApplicationFactory or a test host, and a real broker through Testcontainers, publishing a message and asserting the expected database change appears, with a timeout and polling.
I also test graceful shutdown: stopping the host while an item is being processed should either finish it or leave it safely to be redelivered, never half-done.

p17-571.q: Retry, timeout and circuit breaker logic is easy to get wrong and rarely exercised until an outage, so it deserves deliberate tests.
p17-571.k: test polly retry, test circuit breaker, test resilience pipeline, simulate transient failures, chaos testing httpclient
x: Retry, timeout and circuit breaker logic is easy to get wrong and rarely exercised until an outage, so it deserves deliberate tests.

At the unit level, I test the policy configuration itself. With Polly v8, I can build the resilience pipeline and execute a delegate that fails a set number of times, like throwing HttpRequestException twice and then succeeding, and assert that it was called three times. For circuit breakers, I fail enough calls to open the circuit and assert that the next call fails fast with BrokenCircuitException, then advance a fake TimeProvider past the break duration and check that a trial call is allowed. Injecting the TimeProvider means no real waiting for backoff delays.

At the integration level, I put a fake server, like WireMock.Net, behind the real typed HttpClient with its real resilience handler, configured from the real settings. Then stub sequences: 503 then 200, 429 with Retry-After, a delay longer than the attempt timeout. I assert what the caller experiences and how many requests reached the server.

Important cases: non-idempotent requests, like POSTs, should not be retried unless they carry an idempotency key; the total timeout should cap the whole sequence; and retries shouldn't happen for 400-type errors.
Polly also has chaos strategies, to inject faults, latency or fake results in a test environment, which validates the whole system's behaviour under failure.

p17-572.q: Migrations change production data structures, often irreversibly, so they need testing beyond "it ran on my machine".
p17-572.k: test ef core migrations, migration testing, test schema changes, migration rollback test, migration ci check
x: Migrations change production data structures, often irreversibly, so they need testing beyond "it ran on my machine".
Checks I put in the pipeline.

Model and migrations are in sync: for EF Core, a test or a pipeline step fails if there are pending model changes without a migration, which .NET 8 and later can check with dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes.
Apply from scratch: create an empty database in a container with Testcontainers and apply all migrations from the beginning. That catches broken or order-dependent migrations.

Apply to a realistic existing state: restore a copy of the schema, or an anonymised dataset, at the current production version, then apply the new migrations. Many failures only happen with real data, like adding a NOT NULL column without a default, a unique index on a column that has duplicates, or a data conversion that fails on unexpected values.

Measure duration on production-sized data: a migration that takes two seconds on test data might lock a large table for 20 minutes. If it's slow, it needs to be redesigned as an online change or batched.
Compatibility: run the previous application version's tests against the new schema, since during a rolling deployment the old version runs against the migrated database.
Rollback: if down migrations are supported, test them too; otherwise, document the forward-fix plan.
For SSDT projects, the same applies to the generated deployment script, reviewed and run against a production-like copy.

p17-573.q: When important business logic lives in stored procedures, which is common in older systems like ours, it deserves tests just like C# code.
p17-573.k: test stored procedures, tsql unit testing, tsqlt, database unit tests, sql logic testing
x: When important business logic lives in stored procedures, which is common in older systems like ours, it deserves tests just like C# code.

tSQLt is a unit testing framework that runs inside SQL Server. Tests are themselves stored procedures, grouped in test classes, and each test runs in a transaction that's rolled back, so tests don't leave data behind. Its key feature is faking: FakeTable replaces a table with an empty copy without constraints, so a test inserts only the rows it needs; SpyProcedure replaces a called procedure with a spy that records calls; and assertions like AssertEqualsTable compare expected and actual result sets. That isolates the logic of one procedure from the rest of the schema.

An alternative is testing procedures from .NET integration tests: spin up a real SQL Server with Testcontainers, deploy the schema from the SSDT project or migrations, insert test data, call the procedure through Dapper or ADO.NET, and assert results. This tests the procedure and the calling code's mapping together, and fits the existing .NET test tooling and CI.

What I focus on: boundary conditions, null handling, transactions and error handling with THROW, concurrency-related logic, like whether two calls can allocate the same item, and performance with realistic data volumes, checking execution plans for scans.
Whatever the tool, the database schema should be in source control, so tests run in CI against the exact schema being released.

p17-574.q: Integration tests that share a database can interfere: one test's data changes another test's results, tests pass alone but fail together, and order matters. There are several strategies to keep them isolated.
p17-574.k: test database isolation, respawn, reset database between tests, transaction rollback tests, parallel integration tests
x: Integration tests that share a database can interfere: one test's data changes another test's results, tests pass alone but fail together, and order matters. There are several strategies to keep them isolated.

Reset between tests. Respawn is a .NET library that deletes data from all tables quickly, in the right order respecting foreign keys, while keeping reference tables you list. Calling it before each test gives a clean database in milliseconds, much faster than recreating the database.

Wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back at the end. It's fast and clean, but doesn't work if the code under test manages its own transactions, uses multiple connections, or if you're testing through HTTP where the request runs on a different connection.

Unique data per test. Each test creates its own data with unique ids or names and only asserts on that data. That allows parallel tests on one database, but queries like "count all shipments" become unreliable.

Database per test class or collection. With Testcontainers, each test collection can get its own database inside a shared container, created from a template or snapshot, which allows parallel collections.

My typical setup: one container per test run, one database per test collection, Respawn before each test, and tests that create their own data. In xUnit, collections run in parallel and tests within a collection run sequentially, which fits this model nicely.

p17-575.q: Concurrency bugs, like two requests reserving the same last kit, or a duplicate message being processed twice at the same time, rarely show up in normal tests because tests run one call at a time.
p17-575.k: test concurrency, race condition test, concurrent requests test, double booking test, optimistic concurrency test
x: Concurrency bugs, like two requests reserving the same last kit, or a duplicate message being processed twice at the same time, rarely show up in normal tests because tests run one call at a time.
I test them deliberately.

Fire concurrent requests in integration tests: start, say, 20 tasks that call the same endpoint at once, released together with a barrier or a SemaphoreSlim, against a real database. Then assert the invariant: exactly one reservation succeeded, the others got a conflict, and the stock count is correct. Run it multiple times, because a race may not show every run.

Test the concurrency control itself: for optimistic concurrency, load an entity in two DbContexts, save one, then assert the second save throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, and that the application turns it into a 409 or a retry. For unique constraints, assert the database rejects duplicates and the code handles the error.
Test idempotency under concurrency: deliver the same message twice in parallel to the consumer and assert the effect happened once.

Use deterministic tools where possible: for code using locks or channels, control the interleaving by pausing one operation at a specific point with hooks, so the test hits the dangerous window every time rather than by luck.
Load tests at higher concurrency also surface deadlocks and lock contention.
The key mindset: identify the invariant that must hold, then try hard to break it.

p17-576.q: Security testing works best as several layers, from code to running system, mostly automated in the pipeline.
p17-576.k: security testing, sast dast, owasp zap, penetration testing, dependency scanning, security tests pipeline
x: Security testing works best as several layers, from code to running system, mostly automated in the pipeline.

Static analysis, SAST: tools like SonarQube security rules, Roslyn analyzers, Semgrep or GitHub CodeQL scan source code for injection risks, unsafe deserialisation, weak cryptography, hardcoded secrets and similar patterns, on every pull request.
Dependency scanning, SCA: checks NuGet and npm packages and container images for known vulnerabilities, and licences, failing builds on critical issues.
Secret scanning: blocks credentials from being committed.

Dynamic analysis, DAST: tools like OWASP ZAP run against a deployed test environment, crawling and attacking the running application, finding issues like missing security headers, cookie flags, reflected XSS and some injection problems. The baseline scan is quick enough for a nightly pipeline; full scans run less often.

Security unit and integration tests: these are the ones teams often skip, and they're the most valuable for business logic. Tests that a user from site A can't read site B's data, that a role without permission gets 403, that IDs from other tenants are rejected, that input validation rejects malicious values, and that sensitive fields don't appear in responses or logs.
Infrastructure scanning: Checkov or similar for Terraform and Kubernetes manifests.
Penetration testing by specialists, periodically and before major releases, finds what automated tools miss, especially logic flaws.
Findings are tracked like bugs with severity-based fix deadlines.

p17-577.q: Accessibility matters for users with disabilities and is often a legal or contractual requirement, typically meeting WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA. Testing it combines automation with manual checks, because tools catch only part of the issues.
