Multiple instances: a scheduled job, like a daily reminder, running on every server instead of one, often introduced when scaling out from one server to two.
Duplicate events: the publishing side emitted the event twice, maybe from two code paths or a replay of the dead-letter queue.

Fixes. Make sending idempotent: record each notification with a unique key, like event id plus recipient plus template, in a table with a unique constraint, and skip if it already exists, before or atomically with sending. Use the email provider's idempotency key, if supported. Ensure scheduled jobs run once using clustering or a distributed lock. Make consumers deduplicate by message id.
I also clean up user impact, explaining and apologising if needed, and add a metric for notifications per event so duplicates are visible.

p17-622.q: If the code is truly identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare systematically rather than guessing.
p17-622.k: works on one server not another, config drift, environment difference, server inconsistency, same build different behavior
x: If the code is truly identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare systematically rather than guessing.

Verify it's really the same version: file versions and hashes of the deployed binaries, the build number shown by a version endpoint, and the deployment logs for that server. Partial deployments, where some files didn't copy because they were locked, are surprisingly common.

Compare configuration: web.config or appsettings files, environment variables, IIS settings like app pool identity, .NET CLR version, 32-bit mode and pipeline mode, and machine-level config. A diff tool on exported config shows differences quickly.

Compare the runtime and OS: installed .NET runtime and framework versions, Windows updates and patches, TLS settings and cipher suites in the registry, installed certificates and their private key permissions, regional settings and time zone, which affect date and number parsing.
Compare dependencies and network: connection strings pointing to different databases, firewall rules, DNS resolution, proxy settings, and access to file shares.
Compare permissions: the app pool identity's rights on folders, certificates and databases.

Once found, I fix the immediate difference, but the real fix is preventing drift: infrastructure and configuration defined as code, servers built from the same scripts, configuration applied by the deployment pipeline rather than by hand, and periodic drift detection that compares servers against the expected configuration.

p17-623.q: This is usually caching combined with code splitting.
p17-623.k: blank page after deployment, chunkloaderror, old version after release, spa cache issue, failed to fetch dynamically imported module
x: This is usually caching combined with code splitting.
Single-page apps load index.html, which references bundles with hashed names, like main.a1b2c3.js, and lazy-loaded chunks. Two things go wrong after a release.

Stale index.html: if index.html is cached by the browser, a proxy or the CDN, users keep loading the old version, which may call APIs that changed. Fix: serve index.html with Cache-Control no-cache, so the browser revalidates every time, while hashed assets get long cache times.

Missing old chunks: a user has the old app open, navigates to a lazy route, and the old chunk file it references no longer exists on the server because the deployment replaced all files. The browser throws ChunkLoadError or "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module", and the route shows a blank screen. Fixes: keep previous versions' assets for a while after deploying, rather than deleting them; and in the app, catch chunk load errors and reload the page once, which picks up the new index.html.
Service workers can also keep serving an old version until all tabs close. Fix: a proper update flow that detects a new version and prompts the user to refresh.

Other causes of a blank page: a JavaScript error early in startup on certain browsers, missing runtime config, or a wrong base href on a sub-path. The browser console and front-end error tracking show which one, so I check those first.

p17-624.q: In a single-page app with HTML5 routing, URLs like /shipments/123 are handled by the router in the browser. Navigating within the app works because no request goes to the server. But refreshing the page, or opening a bookmarked link, sends a request for /shipments/123 to IIS, which looks for that file, doesn't find it, and returns 404.
p17-624.k: spa refresh 404 iis, angular deep link 404, react router 404 refresh, url rewrite spa, history api fallback iis
x: In a single-page app with HTML5 routing, URLs like /shipments/123 are handled by the router in the browser. Navigating within the app works because no request goes to the server. But refreshing the page, or opening a bookmarked link, sends a request for /shipments/123 to IIS, which looks for that file, doesn't find it, and returns 404.
The fix is a fallback rule: any request that isn't for a real file, a real folder, or an API route should return index.html, and the router then shows the right screen.

On IIS, I install the URL Rewrite module and add a rule to web.config: match all URLs, with conditions that the request isn't a file, isn't a directory, and doesn't start with /api, and rewrite, not redirect, to /index.html or the app's base path. If the app lives under a virtual directory, like /study-admin/, the base href in index.html and the rewrite target must both use that path, otherwise assets fail to load.

Other hosts have equivalents: try_files in nginx, custom error responses or a function in CloudFront, navigationFallback in Azure Static Web Apps, and MapFallbackToFile in ASP.NET Core when it serves the SPA.

One detail: API calls that hit a non-existent route should still get a real 404, not index.html, which is why the API exclusion matters; otherwise, clients get HTML where they expect JSON and fail with confusing parse errors.

p17-625.q: CORS errors after a deployment mean the browser's preflight or response check failed, so first I find out why, from the browser's network tab, not just the console message.
p17-625.k: cors error after deployment, no access-control-allow-origin, preflight failed, cors production issue, options request failing
x: CORS errors after a deployment mean the browser's preflight or response check failed, so first I find out why, from the browser's network tab, not just the console message.

Look at the actual request: is it the OPTIONS preflight that failed, or the real request? What status did it get? A CORS error often hides a different problem: if the API returned 500, 404 or 401 without CORS headers, the browser reports it as a CORS error. So a broken API, a wrong route after the deployment, or an authentication failure can all look like CORS.
Then check what changed in the deployment.
The allowed origins configuration: the new environment's front-end URL isn't in the list, a trailing slash or http versus https mismatch, or a port difference. Origins must match exactly.
Middleware order in ASP.NET Core: UseCors must come after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization, and before anything that might short-circuit, otherwise preflights get rejected by auth.
Infrastructure: a new proxy, gateway or IIS setting stripping headers, or IIS handling OPTIONS itself with a WebDAV module or the OPTIONSVerbHandler before the app sees it.
Credentials: if the front end sends cookies or credentials, AllowAnyOrigin can't be combined with AllowCredentials; the origin must be listed explicitly.
Custom headers: a new header the front end sends, like a correlation id, must be in the allowed headers.
The longer-term fix: environment-specific origin lists in configuration, and an automated smoke test that runs a cross-origin call after each deployment.

p17-626.q: When everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everyone, not individual credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate response header often includes it too, so I start there.
p17-626.k: all requests 401, jwt validation failed, signing key rotation 401, issuer mismatch, audience mismatch, 401 after keycloak change
x: When everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everyone, not individual credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate response header often includes it too, so I start there.
The usual causes.

Signing key rotation: the identity provider, like Keycloak, rotated its signing keys, and the API is validating with old keys, maybe because keys were configured statically instead of read from the JWKS endpoint, or a long cache. The error mentions the signature key wasn't found, with a kid. Fix: always use the metadata and JWKS endpoints, which the handler refreshes automatically, and make sure the API can reach them through firewalls and proxies.
Issuer mismatch: the realm name, hostname or URL scheme changed, so the iss claim no longer matches the configured authority. Behind proxies, the issuer can differ between internal and external URLs.
Audience mismatch: the client configuration changed, so tokens no longer include the API's audience.
Clock skew: a server's clock drifted, so tokens look expired or not yet valid. Check NTP.
Network: the API can't download metadata at all, so every validation fails.
Front-end side: the app's client id or scopes changed, so it gets tokens for something else, or the interceptor stopped attaching tokens.
I decode a failing token at a safe local tool and compare its iss, aud, kid and expiry against the API's configuration, which usually reveals the mismatch in a minute.

p17-627.q: Usually the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed.
p17-627.k: role change not applied, stale claims, permissions not updated, token claims stale, user still has access after removal
x: Usually the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed.

Access tokens are self-contained: when the identity provider issues a JWT, the roles inside it are fixed until it expires. If an admin adds a role, the user's existing token doesn't have it, so they get 403 until they get a new token. Worse, when a role is removed, the user keeps access until the token expires. Cookie sessions that store claims behave the same way until the session is refreshed.

Other places permissions get stuck: the application caches user permissions in memory or Redis, the front end caches the user's profile and hides or shows menus based on old data, or the role was changed in one system, like the identity provider, but the application maps it from its own database, which wasn't updated.

How I handle it. Keep access tokens short-lived, like five to fifteen minutes, so changes apply quickly through normal refresh. For removal of access, which is security-sensitive, don't wait: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens in the identity provider, and for very sensitive applications, check permissions from a server-side source per request, or use a revocation list or a security stamp checked on each request. Clear or invalidate permission caches on role changes, through events. On the front end, refresh the user profile after changes, and never rely on the front end for enforcement.
And explain to support teams the expected delay, so they don't raise bugs for normal behaviour.

p17-628.q: A 429 means we're exceeding the partner's rate limit. Hammering them with retries makes it worse and can get us blocked, so I handle it on our side.
p17-628.k: third party api 429, rate limited by partner, too many requests external api, throttled by vendor, retry-after handling
x: A 429 means we're exceeding the partner's rate limit. Hammering them with retries makes it worse and can get us blocked, so I handle it on our side.

Immediate actions. Respect Retry-After: if the response says wait 30 seconds, wait. Make sure our retry policy isn't amplifying the problem, like three retries from each of ten instances turning one failure into many calls. Slow down: reduce concurrency for that client, pause non-urgent work like background syncs, and prioritise the calls that matter to users.

Understand why: did our traffic grow, did a new feature or bug cause a burst, like an N+1 pattern calling the API per item, or did the partner lower the limit? Check our metrics for calls per minute to that API, and the partner's documentation or dashboard for our quota.

Longer-term fixes. Client-side rate limiting: a shared rate limiter for all instances, like a token bucket in Redis, or route calls through a single queue-based worker that sends at a controlled pace. Caching responses that don't change often. Batch endpoints, if the partner offers them, instead of one call per item. Spreading scheduled jobs over time instead of all at the top of the hour. Asking the partner for a higher limit if our usage is legitimate.
And monitoring: track 429 rates and remaining quota headers, if provided, with an alert before we hit the limit.

p17-629.q: First, stop the damage, then fix, then protect against the next time.
p17-629.k: partner api changed, breaking change external api, integration broke, deserialization error partner, vendor api contract change
x: First, stop the damage, then fix, then protect against the next time.

Contain: identify the failing integration from errors, like deserialisation failures or missing fields. If messages or files are failing, make sure they're kept, in a dead-letter queue or an error folder, not lost, so they can be reprocessed later. If the integration writes bad data instead of failing, which is worse, pause it.

Understand the change: capture actual responses, compare them with what we expect, and contact the partner, both to confirm the change and to ask whether it's intended or a mistake on their side. Sometimes they roll back.
Fix: update our mapping to handle the new format, ideally accepting both old and new for a transition period. Then reprocess the stored failures and verify the data.
Protect for the future.
Tolerant reader: our deserialisation should ignore unknown fields and not break when optional fields are missing, only failing on what we truly need.
Validation at the boundary: validate incoming data against our expectations, and fail loudly with clear errors, instead of writing nulls into the database.
Contract tests or scheduled checks against the partner's sandbox, so a change is detected before production traffic.
An anti-corruption layer, so the partner's format is translated in one place, not throughout our code.
Monitoring of integration health, like success rates and records processed, with alerts.
And agree with the partner on a change notification process and versioning in the contract.

p17-630.q: When slowness affects only some users, the cause is something that differs between them, usually data size, permissions, configuration or location.
p17-630.k: slow for some users, slow for one customer, data skew performance, tenant specific slowness, site slow only
x: When slowness affects only some users, the cause is something that differs between them, usually data size, permissions, configuration or location.

Narrow it down. From traces or logs, group latency by user, site, tenant, region or browser. Is it one site, all users of one role, or one region? Reproduce it if possible by calling the same endpoint with the same parameters, in a safe way.
Typical causes.

Data volume: the slow site has far more data, like 50,000 kits versus 500. A query that scans or returns everything for a site is fine for small sites and terrible for big ones. Paging, filters and indexes that match the large case fix it.
Parameter sniffing: SQL Server built a plan optimised for small sites, which is slow for large ones, or the reverse. Query Store shows this.
Permissions logic: an admin or multi-site user has access to many sites, so the permission filter builds a huge IN list or runs a check per site, which is slow only for them.
Configuration: a feature or setting only that tenant has enabled, triggering extra work.
Network: users in a distant region or behind a corporate proxy have high latency, or a CDN node is misbehaving; real-user monitoring by geography shows this.
Client side: older devices or browsers struggling with a large page.
The fix depends on the cause, but I always add the dimension, like site, to the latency metrics, so this kind of problem shows up directly next time.

p17-631.q: Test and production differ in many ways, and the most common one is data.
p17-631.k: slow in production fast in test, works in test slow in prod, production performance difference, test data too small
x: Test and production differ in many ways, and the most common one is data.

Data volume and distribution. Test databases have thousands of rows; production has millions, with skew, like one huge customer. Queries without proper indexes, or that load everything into memory, look fast in test. Checking the actual execution plan in production, or in a performance environment loaded with production-sized, anonymised data, usually reveals a scan or a bad join.
Concurrency. Test has one or two users; production has hundreds at once. Lock contention, connection pool limits, thread pool starvation and cache stampedes only appear under real load.

Configuration differences. Debug logging enabled, different cache settings, a feature flag on, smaller instance sizes, or database settings differing, like compatibility level or read committed snapshot.
Network and integration. Production calls real external services with real latency, through proxies, firewalls and gateways, while test may use stubs or services in the same network.
Background workload. In production, scheduled jobs, reports and integrations run at the same time and compete for the database.
Front-end factors. Production users have more data on the page, older devices, slower networks, or extensions.

My approach is to measure in production first, using traces to see where time is actually spent, rather than guessing from test. Then reproduce the specific condition in a performance environment, fix it, and make that environment closer to production in data size so it catches the next one.

p17-632.q: First, figure out whether it's legitimate, like a study going live at many sites, a batch import, or a partner integration resending data, or something bad, like a bot, a misbehaving client in a retry loop, or an attack. The response differs.
p17-632.k: sudden traffic spike, 10x traffic, traffic surge, handle load spike, scale under sudden load, load shedding
x: First, figure out whether it's legitimate, like a study going live at many sites, a batch import, or a partner integration resending data, or something bad, like a bot, a misbehaving client in a retry loop, or an attack. The response differs.

For abusive or accidental traffic: identify the source from logs, like IP, API key, client id or user agent, and block or rate-limit it at the gateway or WAF. A client stuck in a retry loop can be throttled while we contact its owner.
For legitimate traffic, keep the system up in order of speed.
Scale out the stateless tiers: increase instance counts or autoscaling limits. This helps only if the bottleneck isn't shared.
Protect the shared bottleneck, usually the database: serve more from cache, defer non-essential work like reports and exports, and disable expensive optional features with feature flags.

Shed load gracefully: rate limits per client, returning 429 with Retry-After, so the system keeps serving most users well rather than failing everyone. Queue-based workloads absorb bursts naturally, as long as consumers don't overwhelm the database.
Communicate: tell stakeholders what's happening and what users might see.

Afterwards: load test for that level of traffic, add autoscaling based on the right signals, and plan with the business for known events, like scaling up before a large study launch, because the cheapest spike is the one you prepared for.

p17-633.q: A job that overruns its window starts competing with users for the database, causing locks and slowness, so it needs attention before it becomes an outage.
p17-633.k: batch job running long, nightly job overrun, job takes too long, batch window exceeded, long running job business hours
x: A job that overruns its window starts competing with users for the database, causing locks and slowness, so it needs attention before it becomes an outage.
Short term: if it's affecting users right now, decide whether it's safe to pause or stop it, which depends on whether it's restartable and what happens if it doesn't finish. Communicate the impact.
Then find out why it's slower.

Data growth: the job processes everything every night, and the data has grown. Jobs that scale with total data instead of changed data eventually break. Fix: process incrementally, only records changed since the last run, using a watermark like a last-modified timestamp or change tracking.
Inefficient processing: row-by-row work with a query per row, which can often be replaced with set-based SQL or batched operations. Missing indexes for the job's queries.
Contention: something new runs at the same time, like a backup, index maintenance or another job, and they block each other. Check the job schedule and wait stats.
External dependency: a slow partner API or file transfer.

Improvements: break the job into chunks with commits per batch, so it doesn't hold long locks and can resume after failure; parallelise independent parts carefully; run heavy reads on a readable replica if available; and spread jobs across the night.
Monitoring: record duration and records processed per run, and alert when duration trends upward, so we see it long before it hits business hours.

p17-634.q: Jobs run twice for a few reasons, and each has its own fix.
p17-634.k: job ran twice, duplicate job execution, scheduled job multiple servers, distributed lock job, quartz clustering
x: Jobs run twice for a few reasons, and each has its own fix.

Multiple instances: the most common. The app was scaled from one server to two, or deployed to several nodes, and every instance has the same scheduler, so each runs the job. Fixes: use a clustered scheduler, like Quartz with a shared database job store and clustering enabled, which ensures only one node fires each trigger; or a distributed lock, like a Redis lock or a SQL application lock with sp_getapplock, acquired at the start of the job; or move scheduling to a single external trigger, like a cron job in Kubernetes, EventBridge Scheduler or an Azure Functions timer, which has singleton behaviour.

Overlapping runs: the previous run hadn't finished when the next one started. Quartz's DisallowConcurrentExecution attribute, or a lock, prevents this; Kubernetes CronJobs have concurrencyPolicy Forbid.
Misfire handling: after downtime, the scheduler fires missed runs on startup. Configure misfire instructions deliberately.
Manual reruns or retries after a partial failure.

Because some duplication is always possible, the job itself must be idempotent. Track what's been processed, with a run id or per-record processed flag, use unique constraints for outputs, like invoices or notifications, and design steps so rerunning them doesn't double the effect.
Then fix the data from the double run carefully, using the job's own records to identify what was duplicated.

p17-635.q: A poison message is one that can never be processed successfully, like malformed data, an unexpected null, or a reference to something that doesn't exist. If the consumer crashes or rejects it with requeue, the broker delivers it again, it fails again, and the consumer is stuck in a loop, blocking everything behind it.
p17-635.k: poison message, consumer crash loop, message causes exception, bad message queue, dead letter poison message
x: A poison message is one that can never be processed successfully, like malformed data, an unexpected null, or a reference to something that doesn't exist. If the consumer crashes or rejects it with requeue, the broker delivers it again, it fails again, and the consumer is stuck in a loop, blocking everything behind it.

Immediate fix: get the message out of the way without losing it. With a proper setup, after a few failed attempts it goes to the dead-letter queue automatically. If not, I move it manually with the broker's tooling to a parking queue, so processing of other messages resumes. Never just purge the queue, especially with business events.
Then investigate: inspect the message, its headers and the consumer's error logs. Is the message invalid, sent by a buggy producer, or is our consumer failing to handle a valid edge case?
Fix the cause: either fix the producer, or fix the consumer to handle the case, and then replay the parked message, or correct it if it's truly invalid.
Prevention.
Retry limits with backoff and a dead-letter queue for every consumer, with retry counts tracked in headers.
Distinguish error types: transient errors, like timeouts, get retried; permanent errors, like validation failures, go straight to the dead-letter queue without retries.
Catch exceptions per message, so one bad message never crashes the whole consumer process.
Validate messages at the start of processing.
Alert on dead-letter queue arrivals, with tooling to inspect and replay.

p17-636.q: A sudden jump in log volume is both a symptom and a problem: it may signal something broken, and it can fill disks, slow the application and create a huge bill.
p17-636.k: log volume spike, logs increased suddenly, logging flood, log cost spike, disk filling with logs, noisy logs
x: A sudden jump in log volume is both a symptom and a problem: it may signal something broken, and it can fill disks, slow the application and create a huge bill.
Find the source: group log counts by service, logger category, level and message template in the logging tool. Usually one or two messages account for most of the increase.
Then understand why.

An error loop: something is failing repeatedly, like a consumer retrying a poison message, a client in a retry loop, or a background job failing every second. The logs are the symptom; fix the failing thing.
A config change: debug or trace logging turned on in production and forgotten, or a library's log level lowered.
A code change: a new log statement inside a hot loop, or logging full request bodies.
A traffic change: legitimate traffic increased, so logs grew proportionally, which may need sampling.

Mitigate quickly: raise the log level for the noisy category through runtime configuration, if supported, or filter it in the collector, without a redeploy. If disks are at risk, ensure rotation is working.

Prevent: alerts on log volume per service, rate-limited or deduplicated logging for repetitive errors, like logging one summary per minute instead of every occurrence, code review attention to logging in loops, and budgets per team so the cost is visible.
Also check that sensitive data didn't start appearing in the new logs, which would need a separate clean-up.

p17-637.q: If one instance fails while others are fine, the code is probably fine, and something about that instance is different.
p17-637.k: one instance errors, bad node, single server failing, one pod failing, instance specific errors
x: If one instance fails while others are fine, the code is probably fine, and something about that instance is different.

Contain first: take it out of the load balancer or let health checks remove it, so users stop hitting it, but keep it running if possible to investigate. In Kubernetes, I can remove the pod from the service by changing a label, which keeps it alive but out of rotation.
Then compare it with a healthy instance.
Version: did a deployment only partially succeed, so it runs an old or mixed version?
Configuration: a different setting, environment variable or config file, maybe edited manually.

Local state: a corrupted local cache, a full disk, a stuck background thread, exhausted connections or memory, or a resource leak that's built up since that instance started earlier than the others. Restart time is a clue: if the failing one has been up longest, a leak is likely.
Host problems: the underlying server or node has hardware, network or noisy neighbour issues, or a different patch level.
Network path: that instance can't reach a dependency due to a firewall rule, DNS or routing, which applies only to its subnet or availability zone.
Capture evidence, like logs, metrics and a memory dump if relevant, then replace or restart the instance to restore capacity.

Prevent: health checks that test real dependencies so bad instances are removed automatically, immutable deployments instead of manual changes, and dashboards that show metrics per instance, so outliers stand out.

p17-638.q: These come from the load balancer or proxy, not directly from the app, so the app's logs may show nothing. A 502 means the proxy got an invalid response or the connection failed; a 504 means it waited too long.
p17-638.k: intermittent 502, 504 gateway timeout, load balancer 502, bad gateway intermittent, alb 502 troubleshooting
x: These come from the load balancer or proxy, not directly from the app, so the app's logs may show nothing. A 502 means the proxy got an invalid response or the connection failed; a 504 means it waited too long.

For 504s: some requests take longer than the proxy's timeout. Find which endpoints, from the load balancer access logs, which record target response time. Fix the slow operations, or make long operations asynchronous; raise timeouts only if the long duration is legitimate.
For 502s, the common causes.

Keep-alive mismatch: the app server closes idle connections before the load balancer does. The load balancer reuses a connection the server just closed, and the request fails. The rule: the app's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout. For Kestrel, KeepAliveTimeout; for Node, server.keepAliveTimeout; for IIS, connection timeout settings.
Deployments: instances shutting down while still receiving requests, without connection draining or graceful shutdown. If 502s cluster around deployment times, that's the cause.
App crashes or restarts: the process dies mid-request, from out-of-memory kills or unhandled exceptions.
Response problems: invalid headers, oversized headers, or the app resetting connections.
Health and capacity: all targets unhealthy briefly, or the app's connection or thread limits reached, so new connections are refused.
The investigation is mostly correlation: load balancer logs with timestamps and target, against app logs, restarts and deployments. The pattern, random versus clustered, quickly narrows it down.

p17-639.q: If an app takes longer to become ready than the health check allows, the orchestrator kills or replaces it before it's ready, the deployment fails or loops, and old instances may be removed too early.
p17-639.k: slow startup health check failure, startup probe, warmup dotnet, deployment fails slow start, health check grace period
x: If an app takes longer to become ready than the health check allows, the orchestrator kills or replaces it before it's ready, the deployment fails or loops, and old instances may be removed too early.

First, find out why startup is slow. Measure the startup phases with logs or a trace: loading configuration from remote stores, running database migrations at startup, warming caches by loading large reference data, connecting to many dependencies, JIT compiling a large application, or waiting on a slow dependency that's timing out.
Then fix both sides.

Make startup faster: move migrations out of startup into a pipeline step; load caches lazily or in the background, with the app serving requests from the database while the cache warms; parallelise independent initialisation; use ReadyToRun compilation to reduce JIT time in .NET; and set timeouts on dependencies so a missing one doesn't hang startup.

Make health checks reflect startup properly: use a startup probe in Kubernetes with enough time allowed, separate from liveness, so slow starts aren't treated as deadlocks; in ECS, set the health check grace period; on IIS, Application Initialization warms the app before taking traffic. Readiness should become true only once the app can actually serve requests.
Deployment strategy: ensure the rollout waits for new instances to be ready before removing old ones, so a slow start doesn't reduce capacity.
And keep a startup duration metric, so regressions are noticed when a change adds seconds to startup.

p17-640.q: Error 9002 means the transaction log is full and SQL Server can't write new transactions, so all writes to that database fail. It's urgent.
p17-640.k: transaction log full, log file full sql server, error 9002, log_reuse_wait_desc, log backup, database log growth
x: Error 9002 means the transaction log is full and SQL Server can't write new transactions, so all writes to that database fail. It's urgent.
First, find out why the log can't be reused: query sys.databases for log_reuse_wait_desc for that database. The value tells me the cause.

LOG_BACKUP: the database is in full recovery model, but log backups haven't run, maybe the backup job failed. Fix: take a log backup immediately, which allows the log space to be reused, then fix the backup job and alert on its failures.

ACTIVE_TRANSACTION: a long-running or forgotten open transaction is holding the log. Find it with DBCC OPENTRAN or sys.dm_tran_active_transactions, and decide with the owner whether to wait or kill it, remembering that killing triggers a rollback that also takes time.
REPLICATION or AVAILABILITY_REPLICA: a replica or replication process isn't keeping up, so the log must be kept for it.
Other causes: a huge single operation, like an index rebuild or a delete of millions of rows in one transaction.

To get running quickly, if the disk has space, I can grow the log file or add a log file on another drive. What I don't do is switch to simple recovery and shrink everything in a panic, because that breaks the backup chain and point-in-time recovery, which matters a lot for regulated data.
Prevention: monitored, working log backups, alerts on log usage percentage, and batching large data operations into smaller transactions.

p17-641.q: tempdb is shared by everything on the server, so when it fills up, queries across all databases start failing. I find out which kind of usage is growing.
p17-641.k: tempdb full, tempdb growth, tempdb contention, version store growth, sort spill tempdb, tempdb space usage
x: tempdb is shared by everything on the server, so when it fills up, queries across all databases start failing. I find out which kind of usage is growing.
sys.dm_db_file_space_usage shows tempdb space split into user objects, internal objects and the version store.

User objects: temporary tables and table variables created by queries or procedures. sys.dm_db_session_space_usage and sys.dm_db_task_space_usage identify the sessions using the most, which leads to the query or job. A procedure loading millions of rows into a temp table, or temp tables not dropped in long-lived connections, are typical.

Internal objects: work tables and spills from sorts, hashes and spools, when a query's memory grant is too small, or a query sorts or hashes a huge result. Execution plans with spill warnings show this. Fix: better indexes to avoid big sorts, fixing bad cardinality estimates, or rewriting the query.

Version store: with read committed snapshot or snapshot isolation enabled, row versions are kept in tempdb as long as the oldest open transaction needs them. One long-running transaction, even an idle open one, prevents cleanup, so the version store grows and grows. Find the oldest active snapshot transaction and deal with it.
Immediate relief: kill the offending session if appropriate, after checking impact, or add space. Restarting SQL Server resets tempdb, but that's a last resort with full downtime.
Prevention: size tempdb properly with multiple equal data files, monitor its usage, and alert on long-running transactions.

p17-642.q: When the identity provider is down, nobody can start a new session, so it's a full outage for new users even if every application is healthy.
p17-642.k: login down, keycloak down, identity provider outage, sso outage, users cannot login, auth server slow
x: When the identity provider is down, nobody can start a new session, so it's a full outage for new users even if every application is healthy.

Confirm scope: are logins failing for everyone, or only some apps or realms? Are users with existing sessions still working? Access tokens already issued keep working until they expire, so existing sessions often survive for a while, and refresh failures start later.

Check the identity provider itself: for Keycloak, the server's health and logs, its database, which is a common bottleneck, memory and garbage collection, and the cluster's cache state if running multiple nodes. Check what's in front of it: load balancer, certificates, DNS. And check for unusual load, like a credential-stuffing attack or a misbehaving client hammering the token endpoint in a loop, which can take an identity provider down.
Mitigate: scale or restart nodes, block abusive traffic at the WAF or gateway, and fix the database issue. Communicate clearly, because users will flood support.

What applications can do: they shouldn't validate every request against the identity provider; local JWT validation with cached signing keys means APIs keep working with existing tokens. Front ends should show a clear message rather than looping on redirects.

Afterwards: run the identity provider in a highly available setup with health monitoring and synthetic login checks, rate-limit the token and login endpoints, and include it in capacity planning, since it's a dependency of everything.

p17-643.q: Large uploads usually hit a size limit or a timeout somewhere in the chain, and production has more layers than local development, each with its own limit.
p17-643.k: large file upload fails, 413 request entity too large, upload size limit, maxallowedcontentlength, request body too large, upload timeout
x: Large uploads usually hit a size limit or a timeout somewhere in the chain, and production has more layers than local development, each with its own limit.

Find where it fails: the status code and response tell a lot. A 413 Request Entity Too Large comes from a component rejecting the size; a 404.13 on IIS means request filtering's maxAllowedContentLength; a 502 or 504 suggests a timeout at a proxy; a connection reset suggests a component closing the connection.
Check each layer.
The CDN, WAF or API gateway: many have body size limits, like WAF inspection limits, or API Gateway's 10 MB payload limit.
The load balancer or reverse proxy: nginx's client_max_body_size defaults to 1 MB, a common surprise in Kubernetes ingress setups.
IIS: requestLimits maxAllowedContentLength, default about 30 MB, and maxRequestLength for classic ASP.NET.
Kestrel and ASP.NET Core: MaxRequestBodySize, default about 30 MB, and form options for multipart limits, adjustable per endpoint.
Timeouts: slow uploads over corporate networks can exceed proxy and server timeouts.

The better design for large files: don't send them through the API at all. The client asks the API for a pre-signed upload URL, uploads directly to S3 or Blob Storage, possibly in chunks with multipart upload so it can resume, and then the API processes the file asynchronously after an upload event. That avoids all these limits, keeps the API light, and handles unreliable networks.

p17-644.q: A synchronous export that builds the whole file inside an HTTP request works for small data and fails for large data, hitting request timeouts, memory limits or locking the database for a long time.
p17-644.k: export timeout, large report timeout, csv export slow, excel export large data, async export, export job
x: A synchronous export that builds the whole file inside an HTTP request works for small data and fails for large data, hitting request timeouts, memory limits or locking the database for a long time.

Quick improvements, if the export only slightly exceeds limits: stream the output directly to the response instead of building the whole file in memory, write rows as they're read with a forward-only reader, use AsNoTracking and select only needed columns, and fix slow queries. Streaming a CSV can handle very large data with low memory.
But for truly large exports, I change the design to asynchronous.

The user requests an export; the API validates the request and creates an export job, returning 202 Accepted with a job id. A background worker processes the job: it queries the data in pages, writes the file to blob storage, records progress, and marks the job complete. The user sees progress in the UI and gets a notification, or the page polls, and downloads the file through a short-lived signed URL. Files expire after a while.
Benefits: no HTTP timeouts, retry if the worker fails, controlled concurrency so ten simultaneous big exports don't overload the database, and the option to run heavy queries against a read replica.
Also consider whether the export is really the need. Sometimes users export everything to filter it in Excel, and better filters or a report in the app serve them better.
In a regulated context, exports of sensitive data are logged with who exported what.

p17-645.q: Mixing heavy reporting queries with transactional work on the same database is a classic problem: reports scan large amounts of data, use lots of CPU, memory and I/O, and can hold locks that block users' writes.
p17-645.k: reports slow down system, reporting load oltp, heavy queries blocking users, separate reporting database, read replica reporting
x: Mixing heavy reporting queries with transactional work on the same database is a classic problem: reports scan large amounts of data, use lots of CPU, memory and I/O, and can hold locks that block users' writes.

Short-term relief: identify the heaviest reports from Query Store or query stats; tune the worst queries with indexes or rewriting; schedule heavy reports outside peak hours; limit how many run at once, with a queue; and if read committed snapshot is enabled, readers don't block writers, which removes much of the lock contention. I avoid sprinkling NOLOCK, because it gives incorrect results.
The structural fix is separating the workloads.
Read replicas: in SQL Server, Always On readable secondaries, or read replicas in managed databases. Reports run there, with slightly delayed data, which is fine for most reports.

A reporting database or data warehouse: data copied, through change tracking, change data capture, or ETL, into a schema designed for reporting, with denormalised tables and columnstore indexes, which make aggregations over millions of rows dramatically faster. Tools like Power BI or SSRS read from there.
Pre-aggregation: for dashboards that show the same summary repeatedly, compute aggregates on a schedule or incrementally, and serve them from a summary table or cache.
With a database per study, a central reporting store that aggregates across studies also makes cross-study reporting possible without querying hundreds of databases live.

p17-646.q: Stay calm, stop the damage, then recover precisely.
p17-646.k: accidental delete production, restore deleted data, recover deleted rows, point in time restore, data loss incident
x: Stay calm, stop the damage, then recover precisely.
Stop the damage: find out what was deleted, when, by what, a person, a script, a bug or a job, and make sure it can't continue. Disable the job or feature if needed.
Assess: which tables, which rows, how many, and what happened after the deletion? New writes since then complicate recovery, because I can't just roll the whole database back without losing them.
Recover, choosing the least disruptive option.
Soft-deleted data, if the system uses soft delete, can simply be restored by flipping the flag.
Audit or history tables, like temporal tables or audit logs, can provide the old values.

Point-in-time restore: restore a copy of the database, never over production, to a moment just before the deletion, using full and log backups or the cloud's point-in-time restore. Then copy just the missing rows back into production with a careful, reviewed script that handles keys, foreign key order and identity values.
Verify with the business that the data is correct, and check dependent systems that may have reacted to the deletion, like sent notifications or synced partners.
Document everything; in a regulated system, the incident, the correction script, approvals and verification are part of the record.

Prevention: restricted production access, reviewed scripts with WHERE clauses checked and run in a transaction with row count verification, soft deletes for important entities, tested backups, and least privilege so applications can't delete what they shouldn't.

p17-647.q: The key point: once a secret is pushed, assume it's compromised. Removing it from the code isn't enough, because it's in the history, in clones, possibly in CI logs, and if the repo is public, bots scan for secrets within minutes.
p17-647.k: secret committed to git, leaked credentials, password in repo, api key leaked github, rotate leaked secret
x: The key point: once a secret is pushed, assume it's compromised. Removing it from the code isn't enough, because it's in the history, in clones, possibly in CI logs, and if the repo is public, bots scan for secrets within minutes.
Immediate steps, in order.

Revoke or rotate the secret first: create a new credential, update the applications using it through the proper secrets store, and disable the old one. This is the most important step, and it should happen before cleaning the history.
Check for misuse: look at the access logs of whatever the secret protected, like cloud audit logs, database logins or API usage, for activity from unknown locations or times since the commit.
Remove it from the code, and load it from a secrets manager or environment instead.

Clean the history if needed, with git filter-repo or BFG, and force-push, coordinating with the team because everyone must re-clone. For hosted platforms, contact support to purge cached views. This matters less once the secret is rotated, but it reduces noise and exposure.
Report it according to the security incident process, which may require notifying the security team or, depending on what was exposed, others.

Prevention: pre-commit hooks with secret scanners like gitleaks, push protection on the platform, secret scanning in CI, a .gitignore for local settings files, and making the right way easy, with user secrets for local development and a secrets manager everywhere else.

p17-648.q: A spike of failed logins from many IP addresses usually means credential stuffing: attackers trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping users reused passwords. It's a security incident, so I involve the security team early.
p17-648.k: credential stuffing, brute force login attack, failed logins spike, login attack, account takeover attempt, bot login attack
x: A spike of failed logins from many IP addresses usually means credential stuffing: attackers trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping users reused passwords. It's a security incident, so I involve the security team early.
Immediate defence.
Rate limit and block at the edge: WAF rules limiting login attempts per IP and per account, bot detection, and blocking obviously malicious sources or regions if the business allows.

Protect accounts: temporary lockout or progressive delays after repeated failures per account, careful not to let attackers lock out every real user; and require additional verification, like MFA or a CAPTCHA, when risk signals are high.
Check for successful logins from the same sources, because those accounts may be compromised. Force password resets and revoke sessions for affected accounts, and notify those users.

Investigate: logs from the identity provider and WAF, patterns in the targeted accounts, and whether attackers are enumerating usernames, which the login page shouldn't reveal through different error messages.

Longer term: MFA for all users, especially privileged ones, which defeats most credential stuffing; checks against known breached passwords at registration and password change; consistent error messages; monitoring and alerts on failed login rates; and identity provider features like brute force detection, which Keycloak has built in.
Afterwards, a review of what was accessed, and any required notifications under the company's policies.

p17-649.q: Browser-specific bugs usually come from a feature or behaviour that differs between engines: Chrome and Edge use Blink, Safari uses WebKit, and Firefox uses Gecko.
p17-649.k: works in chrome not safari, browser compatibility bug, safari bug, cross browser issue, ios safari issue
x: Browser-specific bugs usually come from a feature or behaviour that differs between engines: Chrome and Edge use Blink, Safari uses WebKit, and Firefox uses Gecko.

Reproduce it in the actual browser: Safari on a Mac, or a real iPhone, because iOS browsers all use WebKit. Cloud device services help if no device is available. Then open the developer tools, with Safari's Web Inspector, connected to the phone if needed, and check the console for errors and the network tab for failed requests.
Common culprits.
Date parsing: new Date with non-standard strings, like 2024-03-10 10:00 with a space, works in Chrome and returns Invalid Date in Safari. Use ISO formats or a date library.

Newer JavaScript or CSS features not supported in the user's Safari version, like some regex features, newer array methods, or CSS properties, which compile settings or polyfills should handle. Checking browserslist and caniuse helps.

Third-party cookies and storage: Safari's tracking prevention blocks third-party cookies and limits storage, breaking silent token renewal through hidden iframes, or embedded apps. Fix: same-site deployments, or authorisation code flow with refresh token rotation.
Autoplay, file input and date input differences, and iOS-specific viewport and keyboard behaviour.
Caching differences, like more aggressive back-forward cache.
After fixing, I add the browser to the test matrix, like running Playwright tests in WebKit in CI, so it doesn't regress.

p17-650.q: If an app gets slower over hours, something accumulates, usually memory, listeners or DOM nodes, so each interaction does more work than before.
p17-650.k: angular app slow over time, spa memory leak, browser tab memory grows, angular subscription leak, detached dom nodes
x: If an app gets slower over hours, something accumulates, usually memory, listeners or DOM nodes, so each interaction does more work than before.

Confirm with the browser's tools: Chrome DevTools Performance monitor shows JS heap size, DOM node count and event listeners over time. Perform a repeated action, like opening and closing a dialog or navigating between two screens 20 times, and see if the numbers keep climbing. Then take heap snapshots before and after, and compare them to see which objects are growing; detached DOM trees are a strong clue.
Common causes in Angular.

Subscriptions not unsubscribed: a component subscribes to a long-lived observable, like a store selector, a router event or an interval, and never unsubscribes, so destroyed components stay in memory and keep reacting to events. Fix: the async pipe, takeUntilDestroyed, or toSignal.
Event listeners added to window or document manually without removing them in ngOnDestroy.
Third-party libraries, like charts or grids, not destroyed properly.
Caches in services that grow without limits, like storing every loaded record.
Timers and intervals still running after navigation.
Growing change detection work: large lists without trackBy, or many components with default change detection.

The fix is targeted at whatever the heap comparison shows. Then I add a check to our testing: a scripted navigation loop that verifies memory returns to a baseline, which catches regressions in shared components.

p17-651.q: I treat a cost spike like an incident: find what changed, stop the bleeding, prevent it from recurring.
p17-651.k: aws bill spike, unexpected aws cost, cost anomaly, cloud cost increase, find aws cost driver
x: I treat a cost spike like an incident: find what changed, stop the bleeding, prevent it from recurring.

Find the driver: Cost Explorer, grouped by service, then by usage type, region, account and tags, comparing daily costs before and after the spike. It usually points to one or two line items. Cost Anomaly Detection may have already flagged it.
Typical causes.

Data transfer: NAT gateway processing charges, when services in private subnets pull large amounts through NAT instead of VPC endpoints, like container images from ECR or data from S3; or cross-AZ and cross-region traffic.
Runaway compute: autoscaling that scaled up and never came down, a Lambda function in a loop, like an S3-triggered function writing to the same bucket, or a retry storm.
Logging and monitoring: a debug log level left on, multiplying CloudWatch Logs ingestion, or high-cardinality custom metrics.
Forgotten resources: test environments, large instances, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers.
Storage: a lifecycle rule missing, so logs or backups accumulate in expensive tiers.
Database: DynamoDB on-demand absorbing a huge spike in traffic, or provisioned IOPS increased.
Then stop it: fix the loop, scale down, delete what's unused, add endpoints.
Prevent: budgets and anomaly alerts per account and team, required cost tags, regular cost reviews, and guardrails like Lambda concurrency limits and maximum autoscaling sizes.

p17-652.q: When tasks get marked unhealthy only under load, the health check endpoint is usually suffering from the same resource exhaustion as the rest of the app, and killing tasks under load makes things worse, because the remaining tasks take even more traffic. It becomes a death spiral.
p17-652.k: ecs health check fails under load, tasks killed under load, health check timeout load, unhealthy targets during peak
x: When tasks get marked unhealthy only under load, the health check endpoint is usually suffering from the same resource exhaustion as the rest of the app, and killing tasks under load makes things worse, because the remaining tasks take even more traffic. It becomes a death spiral.
What I check.

Is the health endpoint cheap? If it checks the database and other dependencies deeply, under load those checks time out, and every task looks unhealthy at once, even though the problem is a shared dependency. A liveness-style check should only confirm the process can respond; dependency checks belong in readiness logic or monitoring, not in a check that triggers replacement.

Is it getting starved? With thread pool starvation or a saturated request queue, the health request waits behind user requests and times out. ALB health check timeouts are short by default. Thread pool metrics, request queue length and CPU tell me.
Is the container CPU or memory limit too tight, causing throttling or out-of-memory kills, visible in ECS stopped task reasons and Container Insights?
Are the thresholds too aggressive? A couple of slow responses shouldn't remove a task; increase the unhealthy threshold and timeout sensibly.
Then fix the real bottleneck, scale out earlier with autoscaling on request count rather than CPU, and load test with health checks running, so we see this behaviour before production does.

p17-653.q: Growing lag means consumers process messages more slowly than they're produced. I find out which side changed and where the time goes.
p17-653.k: kafka consumer lag growing, kafka lag, consumer cannot keep up, kafka backlog, slow kafka consumer
x: Growing lag means consumers process messages more slowly than they're produced. I find out which side changed and where the time goes.

Look at lag per partition, not just total. If lag is high on all partitions, consumers are generally too slow or producers sped up. If it's concentrated on one or two partitions, it's a hot partition, where a popular key sends most messages to one partition, or one consumer instance is stuck.

Check consumer health: are all consumers in the group active, or did some crash, leaving fewer consumers than partitions? Are there frequent rebalances, visible in logs, which pause consumption each time? Rebalance storms happen when processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker thinks the consumer died.
Check processing time: what does each message wait on? Usually a database write or an external API call. Traces and timing metrics per message show it.
Fixes.
Scale out consumers, up to the number of partitions; beyond that, extra consumers sit idle, so more partitions may be needed for future growth.
Speed up processing: batch database writes, process messages concurrently within a partition where ordering per key allows, and cache lookups.
Fix hot keys by choosing a better partition key.
Tune polling: smaller batches or a longer max poll interval if processing is slow, to stop rebalances, and cooperative rebalancing to reduce pauses.
Then alert on lag and its growth rate, since lag translates directly into how stale downstream data is.

p17-654.q: A batch import writes much faster than normal traffic, so it hits either the table's capacity or a hot partition, and normal user traffic gets throttled too.
p17-654.k: dynamodb batch import throttling, bulk load dynamodb, batchwriteitem throttled, dynamodb import s3, unprocessed items
x: A batch import writes much faster than normal traffic, so it hits either the table's capacity or a hot partition, and normal user traffic gets throttled too.

Immediate fixes: slow the import down. Throttle the writer to a rate the table can take, with retries and exponential backoff with jitter. BatchWriteItem returns UnprocessedItems when throttled; the code must retry those, otherwise data is silently lost, which is a classic bug.

Look at key distribution: if the import data is sorted by partition key, like all items for one customer together, writes hit one partition at a time. Shuffling the order spreads the load across partitions.

Capacity: for a one-off import into a provisioned table, temporarily raise write capacity or switch to on-demand for the import, then switch back. Keep in mind that on-demand also has a ramp-up behaviour for brand new peaks.

Better approaches for large loads: DynamoDB's import from S3 feature loads CSV, JSON or Ion files into a new table without consuming write capacity, which is ideal for initial loads. For ongoing large imports, put the data on a queue and have consumers write at a controlled rate, which also protects user traffic.
Also check secondary indexes: each write to the table also writes to its GSIs, and if a GSI is under-provisioned, it throttles the base table writes too.
Afterwards, monitor throttled requests and consumed capacity per table and index.

p17-655.q: S3 access is decided by several policies at once, so I check each layer, guided by what changed.
p17-655.k: s3 access denied, s3 403 forbidden, bucket policy denied, kms access denied s3, iam permission s3 error
x: S3 access is decided by several policies at once, so I check each layer, guided by what changed.

Get the details: the exact action, like s3:GetObject or s3:PutObject, the resource ARN, and the identity making the call. CloudTrail shows the failing call, and newer error messages often say which kind of policy denied it.
Then check the layers.

Identity policy: does the role the app uses, like the ECS task role, allow the action on that bucket and prefix? A common mistake: allowing the bucket ARN but not bucket/*, or the reverse; ListBucket needs the bucket ARN, while GetObject needs the object path.

Bucket policy: an explicit deny overrides everything. Policies requiring encryption headers, specific VPC endpoints, TLS, or a specific organisation can deny calls that don't meet their conditions; after a network change, requests may no longer come through the expected VPC endpoint.
KMS: if objects are encrypted with a customer managed key, the role also needs kms:Decrypt or GenerateDataKey, and the key policy must allow it. This is one of the most common causes.
Object ownership: objects uploaded by another account may not be accessible, unless bucket owner enforced ownership is set.
Organisation guardrails: a new Service Control Policy or Resource Control Policy can deny the action.
Block Public Access, if the app expected public reads.
The IAM policy simulator and Access Analyzer help confirm the fix, which I make through infrastructure as code, not by hand.

p17-656.q: Stop and don't apply. A destroy-and-recreate of a production database means data loss and an outage, so I find out why Terraform thinks replacement is needed.
p17-656.k: terraform plan destroy database, forces replacement, terraform recreate resource, prevent destroy terraform, terraform replace production
x: Stop and don't apply. A destroy-and-recreate of a production database means data loss and an outage, so I find out why Terraform thinks replacement is needed.
The plan marks the attribute causing it with "forces replacement". Common reasons.

A changed immutable attribute: some properties can't be updated in place, like the database identifier, engine type, availability zone, encryption settings or certain subnet group changes. Someone may have changed one intentionally without realising the effect.

A renamed or moved resource: the resource address changed, from a rename or moving it into a module, so Terraform sees an old resource to delete and a new one to create. Fix: a moved block, which updates state without touching the resource.
Provider or module upgrades: a new provider version or module version changed defaults or how an attribute is represented.
Drift: someone changed the resource outside Terraform, and the configuration now disagrees with reality.

The fix depends on the cause: add a moved block; revert the attribute change; align the configuration with reality; use lifecycle ignore_changes for attributes that are managed elsewhere; or, if the change is truly needed, plan a proper migration, like snapshot, create new, migrate, switch over, rather than letting Terraform do it.

Prevention: lifecycle prevent_destroy on critical resources, deletion protection enabled on the database itself, plan review in pull requests with automated checks that fail on destroys of protected resource types, and applies only from the pipeline.

p17-657.q: This is exactly why we run smoke tests, so it's caught early. Now the decision is fast: fix quickly or roll back.
p17-657.k: smoke test failed production, release failed production, passed uat failed prod, post deployment failure, release night issue
x: This is exactly why we run smoke tests, so it's caught early. Now the decision is fast: fix quickly or roll back.

First, assess impact: are real users affected, or only the tested path? How severe is it? If a critical flow is broken and the cause isn't obvious within minutes, I prefer rolling back, if it's safe with the database changes, and investigating calmly. In a release window, there's usually a defined time limit for this decision.
Then find what's different between UAT and production, since the code is the same build.
Configuration: a missing or different setting, connection string, feature flag or secret in production. This is the most common cause.
Infrastructure: firewall rules, certificates, DNS, permissions of the production service account, or a dependency endpoint that exists in UAT but not in production.
Data: production data has cases UAT didn't, like old records, larger volumes, or study configurations that UAT doesn't have.
Integrations: real partner endpoints behave differently from test endpoints.
Deployment issues: a step failed silently on one server, a migration didn't run, or a cache wasn't cleared.
The logs and the smoke test's exact failure usually point to one of these quickly.

After resolving, a short review: add the missing check to the pre-production checklist or pipeline, like validating configuration at startup, or a connectivity check against production dependencies before switching traffic.

p17-658.q: "I saved it, but the screen still shows the old value" usually comes from a cache that wasn't invalidated, or from reading from somewhere that hasn't caught up.
p17-658.k: stale data after update, cache invalidation bug, users see old data, cache not updated, read after write inconsistency
x: "I saved it, but the screen still shows the old value" usually comes from a cache that wasn't invalidated, or from reading from somewhere that hasn't caught up.

Find which layer is stale. Check the database: is the new value there? If yes, step outward: the API's in-memory or Redis cache, an HTTP or CDN cache, the front-end's client cache, like RTK Query or TanStack Query, or a read replica with replication lag.
Common causes and fixes.

Cache-aside without invalidation: the update path writes to the database but doesn't remove the cached entry, so readers see the old value until TTL expiry. Fix: invalidate or update the cache entry in the same code path as the write, after the commit.

Multiple instances with local in-memory caches: one instance invalidates its own cache, others still have the old value. Fix: a distributed cache, or invalidation messages broadcast to all instances, like Redis pub-sub, or short TTLs for local caches. HybridCache in .NET 9 helps with tags and a shared second level.
HTTP caching: responses with Cache-Control headers that allow caching of data that changes; API responses for user data should usually be no-store or use ETags.
Front-end caches: after a mutation, the client must invalidate the related queries, with RTK Query tags or TanStack Query's invalidateQueries.
Read replicas: reading immediately after writing from a lagging replica. Fix: read-your-writes by reading from the primary for that user shortly after a write.

p17-659.q: This is a serious security and privacy incident, so it gets top priority, and I involve security and management immediately, following the incident process.
p17-659.k: user sees another users data, data leak between users, cross tenant data leak, wrong user data shown, singleton state bug
x: This is a serious security and privacy incident, so it gets top priority, and I involve security and management immediately, following the incident process.
Contain first: if it's reproducible or ongoing, disable the affected feature or take the endpoint offline. Preserve logs and evidence.
Investigate the cause. The usual suspects in web applications.

Shared state in a singleton: a service registered as a singleton holding per-request data, like the current user or tenant in a field, so concurrent requests overwrite each other's values. Static fields used for request data have the same effect.

Caching with wrong keys: a cached response or object keyed without the user or tenant, so the first user's data is served to everyone, including HTTP caching of personalised responses by a CDN or proxy because of missing Cache-Control: private or no-store.
Authorisation gaps: an endpoint that takes an id and doesn't check the record belongs to the user, an insecure direct object reference.
Async context mistakes, like AsyncLocal or thread-static values leaking between requests.
Front-end issues: state persisted in local storage not cleared on logout, so the next user on the same device sees it.
Assess impact: which users and data were exposed, during what period, using access logs. That's needed for notifications, which may be legally required for personal or clinical data.
Fix, test with concurrent users, and add tests for isolation, then a thorough review, because such bugs often have siblings.

p17-660.q: Email problems split into "we didn't send it" and "we sent it but it didn't arrive".
p17-660.k: emails not delivered, email going to spam, smtp failure, spf dkim dmarc, notification email missing
x: Email problems split into "we didn't send it" and "we sent it but it didn't arrive".

Did we send it? Check application logs for the send attempt and the response from the SMTP server or email API. Errors like authentication failure, relay denied, connection timeouts or rate limits mean it never left. Check any queue or outbox between the app and the sender, and whether a background worker is processing it.

Did the provider accept and deliver it? Email services like SES, SendGrid or the corporate mail relay keep delivery logs: delivered, bounced, deferred or dropped. Bounces explain themselves, like invalid address or mailbox full. Suppression lists silently drop emails to addresses that previously bounced or complained.

Was it delivered to spam or quarantined? Corporate recipients often have strict filters. Check authentication of our domain: SPF must authorise the sending servers, DKIM must sign messages, and DMARC must align them. A new sending service added without updating SPF and DKIM is a classic cause. Content issues, like links to unusual domains, can also trigger filters. Recipients' IT teams can check their quarantine.

For important emails, I also design for failure: track send status per message, retry transient failures, show users important information in the app rather than only by email, and monitor bounce and complaint rates.
In clinical systems, sites may depend on emails for important notifications, so delivery issues get treated as functional failures, not cosmetic ones.

p17-661.q: Duplicate files can cause a partner to process orders or shipments twice, so I treat it seriously and coordinate with the partner.
p17-661.k: file sent twice, duplicate file transfer, integration duplicate, sftp duplicate file, idempotent file transfer
x: Duplicate files can cause a partner to process orders or shipments twice, so I treat it seriously and coordinate with the partner.
Contain: if more duplicates are coming, pause the job or flow, and tell the partner which file is the duplicate so they can avoid processing it, or reverse it if already processed.
Find out why it was sent twice.
Retries after an uncertain failure: the upload succeeded, but the connection dropped before confirmation, so the job retried and uploaded again.
The job ran twice: on two servers without clustering, overlapping runs, or a manual rerun.
The source selection logic picked the same data again, because the "already sent" marker wasn't saved, maybe the job crashed after sending but before updating the status.

Fix and prevent: make sending idempotent. Use deterministic file names, like including a batch id and date, so a resend overwrites or is detected rather than creating a second file, and agree with the partner that they deduplicate by file name or batch id. Record each transfer in a table with a unique constraint on the batch, with states like prepared, sent and confirmed, and before sending, check whether this batch was already sent. For uncertain outcomes, check the remote side, like listing the target folder, before retrying. And ensure the job runs once, with clustering or a lock.
Monitoring: a dashboard of files per partner per day, with alerts on unexpected counts, catches duplicates or missing files quickly.

p17-662.q: JWTs have time-based claims: issued at, not before and expiry. If a server's clock is ahead or behind the identity provider's clock, it may think a fresh token is expired or not yet valid. When it happens only on some servers, clock drift on those machines is the prime suspect.
p17-662.k: clock skew jwt, token not yet valid, server time wrong, ntp time sync, intermittent token expired
x: JWTs have time-based claims: issued at, not before and expiry. If a server's clock is ahead or behind the identity provider's clock, it may think a fresh token is expired or not yet valid. When it happens only on some servers, clock drift on those machines is the prime suspect.

Confirm: the error messages say the lifetime validation failed, with the token's times and the server's current time. Compare the clock on the affected servers with a reliable time source; a few minutes' difference is enough.

Fix: correct time synchronisation. Windows servers should sync with the domain's time hierarchy or an NTP source through w32time; Linux uses chrony or systemd-timesyncd. Virtual machines sometimes drift after being suspended or migrated, or if the host's time sync and guest NTP conflict. Containers use the host's clock, so the fix is on the node.

The JWT handler in .NET has a ClockSkew setting, five minutes by default, which tolerates small differences. Some teams set it to zero for strictness, which then exposes any drift. A small tolerance, like 30 seconds to two minutes, is a reasonable balance; increasing it a lot to hide a broken clock is the wrong fix.

Time affects much more than tokens: TOTP codes, certificate validity, log correlation across servers, scheduled jobs and audit trail timestamps, which in a regulated system must be accurate. So I add monitoring of clock offset on all servers, with alerts.

p17-663.q: Frequent recycles drop in-memory state, sessions and caches, and cause slow first requests, so users feel it.
p17-663.k: iis app pool recycling, app pool restart frequent, w3wp restart, rapid fail protection, iis recycle causes
x: Frequent recycles drop in-memory state, sessions and caches, and cause slow first requests, so users feel it.

First, find out why each recycle happened. With recycle event logging enabled in the app pool's advanced settings, Windows Event Viewer's System log records the reason, from WAS events. Typical reasons.

Memory limits: private or virtual memory limits configured on the app pool were exceeded, so IIS recycles. That points to high memory use or a leak in the app, which needs investigation with memory dumps.

Configuration changes: any change to web.config, or files in the bin folder, triggers a recycle. Something writing to those, like an app writing logs or temp files into its own folder, or antivirus touching files, can cause it.
Scheduled or periodic recycling: the default regular time interval of 1,740 minutes, which recycles at a different time each day, sometimes during peak hours. Better to set a specific off-peak time.

Crashes: an unhandled exception on a background thread, a stack overflow or an access violation kills the worker process, and rapid-fail protection may then stop the app pool entirely after several crashes. The Application event log shows .NET runtime errors and Windows Error Reporting entries.
Idle timeout: the pool shuts down after inactivity, which is a different symptom: slow first request.
For crashes, I configure ProcDump or DebugDiag to capture a crash dump, then analyse it to find the exception and stack trace, fix the bug, and verify the recycle events stop.

p17-664.q: When a process dies without logging anything, it's usually a crash the app couldn't catch: a stack overflow, an out-of-memory kill from outside, a native crash, or an unhandled exception on a background thread before logs were flushed.
p17-664.k: process crash no logs, stackoverflow crash dotnet, unhandled exception crash, app dies silently, crash dump analysis
x: When a process dies without logging anything, it's usually a crash the app couldn't catch: a stack overflow, an out-of-memory kill from outside, a native crash, or an unhandled exception on a background thread before logs were flushed.

Find external evidence first. On Windows, the Application event log usually has a .NET Runtime error with the exception type and stack, or an Application Error entry with the faulting module. On Linux or containers, the exit code tells a lot: 137 means killed by SIGKILL, often out-of-memory; 139 is a segmentation fault; 134 is an abort. The orchestrator shows the reason, like OOMKilled, and the kernel log shows OOM killer messages.

Capture a crash dump next time: on Windows, ProcDump with the -e flag or Windows Error Reporting LocalDumps; for .NET on Linux, the DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump environment variables to write a dump on crash. Then analyse with dotnet-dump analyze, WinDbg or Visual Studio, looking at the exception and the thread stacks.
Common findings.
Stack overflow: infinite recursion, often from a property calling itself, or a deep recursive algorithm on unexpected data. It can't be caught in .NET, and kills the process instantly.
Unhandled exceptions in async void methods or background threads.
Native library crashes, from interop with unmanaged code.
Logs lost because they were buffered: configure logging sinks to flush on shutdown, and log to stdout for containers.
Add an AppDomain UnhandledException handler that logs synchronously, as a last resort.

p17-665.q: High latency with low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. In older ASP.NET apps on .NET Framework, two causes are very common.
p17-665.k: aspnet hangs low cpu, sync over async deadlock, result wait deadlock, requests stuck legacy aspnet, thread pool blocked
x: High latency with low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. In older ASP.NET apps on .NET Framework, two causes are very common.

Sync over async: code calls .Result or .Wait() on a Task, for example to call an async HttpClient method from a synchronous controller. In classic ASP.NET, there's a synchronisation context that allows only one thread at a time per request; the async method tries to continue on that context while the request thread is blocked waiting for it, so it deadlocks, and the request hangs forever. Under load, even without full deadlocks, blocking threads drains the thread pool, and new requests queue up.
Thread pool starvation: many requests block threads on slow I/O, like synchronous database calls or HTTP calls, and the thread pool grows slowly, adding threads gradually, so requests wait in queues.

How to confirm: take a memory dump during the hang and look at thread stacks with DebugDiag or WinDbg. Many threads waiting in Task.Wait, Result, or Monitor.Enter, or in synchronous network calls, show the pattern. Performance counters show requests queued rising while CPU stays low.

Fixes: make the call chain async all the way, from the controller down, instead of blocking. If that's not immediately possible, ConfigureAwait(false) in library code avoids the context deadlock, but still blocks threads. Add timeouts to every outbound call. Raising minimum threads is a temporary relief only.

p17-666.q: Errors like "Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted" or connection failures under load, with thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT state, typically mean the app is creating a new HttpClient for every request.
p17-666.k: socket exhaustion, httpclient per request, too many sockets time_wait, only one usage of each socket address, httpclientfactory fix
x: Errors like "Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted" or connection failures under load, with thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT state, typically mean the app is creating a new HttpClient for every request.
