Why it happens: each HttpClient instance has its own connection pool. Disposing it closes its connections, but the operating system keeps each closed socket in TIME_WAIT for a while, up to minutes. Under load, the app opens new sockets faster than old ones are released, and runs out of ephemeral ports. The using statement around HttpClient looks like good practice, but it's the cause here.
How to confirm: netstat shows many connections in TIME_WAIT to the same destination, and the code creates HttpClient per call.

Fixes: reuse connections. In ASP.NET Core, use IHttpClientFactory with typed or named clients, which pools and recycles the underlying handlers properly. Or use a single long-lived HttpClient, a static or singleton instance, with SocketsHttpHandler and PooledConnectionLifetime set, like two minutes, so connections are recycled periodically and DNS changes are picked up, which a plain static client would miss.
For .NET Framework, a shared static HttpClient plus ServicePointManager settings, like ConnectionLeaseTimeout, give similar behaviour.
Also check connection limits per server, and that responses are disposed or fully read, because unread response bodies can keep connections busy.

p17-667.q: Disconnections usually come from something between the client and the server closing idle or long-lived connections, or from scaling issues.
p17-667.k: signalr disconnects, websocket disconnect, signalr reconnecting, websocket proxy timeout, real time connection drops
x: Disconnections usually come from something between the client and the server closing idle or long-lived connections, or from scaling issues.

Check the pattern: do disconnects happen after a fixed idle time, like 60 seconds? That points to a proxy or load balancer idle timeout. Do they happen when servers are deployed or scaled? Do they affect only users behind certain corporate networks?
Common causes.

Proxy and load balancer timeouts: idle connection timeouts on the load balancer, IIS, nginx or a corporate proxy. SignalR's keep-alive pings, every 15 seconds by default, should keep connections alive, as long as the keep-alive interval is shorter than every timeout along the path. Some proxies don't support WebSockets properly, so SignalR falls back to Server-Sent Events or long polling, which may behave differently.
WebSockets not enabled: on IIS, the WebSocket Protocol feature must be installed; on load balancers, WebSocket upgrade must be allowed.

Multiple servers without sticky sessions: SignalR's negotiation and connection requests must reach the same server unless using Azure SignalR Service or WebSockets only with skip negotiation. Without that, connections fail randomly once there are two instances. A backplane, like Redis, is also needed so messages reach users connected to other servers.
Deployments and restarts: connections drop when the server restarts; clients must reconnect with withAutomaticReconnect, and the app should resync state after reconnecting.
Client-side: browsers throttle background tabs, and mobile networks switch.
Logging on both client and server, with transport and close reasons, quickly shows which case it is.

p17-668.q: Rate limiting by IP address assumes one IP is one user. Large organisations, like a hospital or a sponsor's office, often route everyone through a few NAT or proxy IPs, so hundreds of real users look like one very busy client, and they all get 429s.
p17-668.k: rate limiter blocking users, rate limit by ip problem, corporate nat rate limit, false positive rate limiting, 429 legitimate users
x: Rate limiting by IP address assumes one IP is one user. Large organisations, like a hospital or a sponsor's office, often route everyone through a few NAT or proxy IPs, so hundreds of real users look like one very busy client, and they all get 429s.
Immediate relief: identify the affected IP ranges from logs and raise their limits or temporarily allowlist them, while understanding the rest of the traffic so we don't open a hole for attackers.
Better fix: rate limit by a more meaningful key.

For authenticated endpoints, partition by user id or client id from the token, so each user gets their own budget. ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware supports partitioned limiters with a custom key.
For API clients, partition by API key or client application.
Keep IP-based limits only for unauthenticated endpoints, like login, and set them higher, combined with per-account limits, which is where brute-force protection matters.

Also check that the app sees the real client IP: behind a load balancer, without forwarded headers configured, every request appears to come from the load balancer's IP, so everyone shares one bucket. ForwardedHeaders middleware with known proxies fixes that.

Tune limits with real data: look at the distribution of request rates per user, set limits well above legitimate peaks, return Retry-After headers, and monitor 429 counts per client so false positives show up quickly.

p17-669.q: When the client says slow and our server says fast, the time is being spent somewhere our server metrics don't measure. I get specifics first: which endpoints, what times, request ids or timestamps, and the latency they measure.
p17-669.k: partner says api slow, client reports slowness, server metrics fine client slow, latency discrepancy, network latency partner
x: When the client says slow and our server says fast, the time is being spent somewhere our server metrics don't measure. I get specifics first: which endpoints, what times, request ids or timestamps, and the latency they measure.
Then compare what we measure with what they experience.

Our server metrics usually measure from when the request reaches the app to when the response leaves it. They miss time spent before: TLS handshakes, load balancers, WAF inspection, API gateway processing, and queueing in the web server before the app sees the request, like IIS queues or Kestrel connection limits. Load balancer and gateway logs, which record total time, help here.
Network: the partner may be far away, behind a slow proxy, or have packet loss. Large response bodies make this worse. Compression and smaller payloads help.

Connection handling: if their client opens a new connection for every request, each call pays DNS, TCP and TLS setup, which can add hundreds of milliseconds across continents. Keep-alive and connection reuse on their side fix this.
Their own processing: their latency measurement may include their own retries, serialisation or queueing.
Averages hide tails: our average might be fine while the p99 is bad, and they may be hitting those slow cases. I check percentiles for their specific client id.
A joint test with timestamps on both sides, or a synthetic check from their region, usually settles where the time goes.

p17-670.q: When dashboards say healthy and users say broken, the monitoring is checking the wrong things. First I help the users, then fix the blind spot.
p17-670.k: health checks green users errors, monitoring blind spot, false healthy, health check misleading, users report errors dashboards green
x: When dashboards say healthy and users say broken, the monitoring is checking the wrong things. First I help the users, then fix the blind spot.

Find the user problem directly: get specific examples, like the screen, the action, the time and the user, and trace those requests in logs. Often the errors are in a specific flow, a specific browser, or a specific tenant.
Typical blind spots.

Health checks that only test that the process responds, not that it can do real work. The app returns 200 on /health while the database, a queue or an external dependency is failing for actual requests.

Errors that aren't errors to the server: the API returns 200 with an error message in the body, or business failures, like "no kits available", that are logged as information. Front-end failures, like JavaScript errors, failed chunk loads or CORS failures, never reach server metrics.
Averages hiding problems: overall error rate at 0.5 percent looks fine, but it's 100 percent for one feature or one site.
Asynchronous failures: the API accepted the request, but the background processing failed later.

Fixes: synthetic monitoring of real user journeys; real-user monitoring and front-end error tracking; SLIs per important flow, not just overall; business metrics, like successful randomisations per hour; consistent use of correct HTTP status codes; and alerts on dead-letter queues and async processing failures. Each incident like this should add the missing signal.

p17-671.q: When many alerts fire together, they usually share one root cause, and the job is to find it quickly rather than chase each alert.
p17-671.k: alert storm, many alerts at once, incident triage, on call triage, alert flood, where to start incident
x: When many alerts fire together, they usually share one root cause, and the job is to find it quickly rather than chase each alert.

First, assess user impact: are key user journeys failing? Check the top-level SLO or service overview dashboard and synthetic checks. That sets the urgency and whether to declare an incident and bring in others.

Then look for the common factor. Group the alerts by time: which fired first? The earliest alert is often closest to the cause, and the rest are downstream effects. Group by dependency: if every service alerts on database latency or timeouts to the same component, that component is the suspect. Check for recent changes: deployments, configuration changes, infrastructure maintenance, certificate expiry, or a scheduled job that started at 2 AM.
Check shared infrastructure: database, message broker, identity provider, DNS, network, storage, and the cloud provider's status page.
Act on the likely cause, like rolling back the change, failing over, or restarting the stuck component, and watch whether alerts clear.
Communicate early and regularly, even "we're investigating", to stakeholders and support.

Afterwards, improve the alerting itself: dependency-aware alerting, so a database outage produces one alert rather than fifty; grouping in the alert manager; and runbooks linking symptoms to likely causes. An alert storm is a sign that alerts describe symptoms everywhere rather than the problem once.

p17-672.q: As incident commander, my job is coordination, not debugging. I make sure the right people work on the right things, decisions get made, and everyone is informed.
p17-672.k: incident commander, major incident management, run an incident, incident roles, incident communication, severity 1 outage
x: As incident commander, my job is coordination, not debugging. I make sure the right people work on the right things, decisions get made, and everyone is informed.

Set up: declare the incident with a severity, open a dedicated channel or bridge, and assign roles: a technical lead or operations lead who drives investigation, a communications lead for stakeholders and customers, and a scribe who records the timeline. In a small team, one person may hold two roles, but the commander shouldn't also be deep in the logs.

Run it in short cycles: what do we know, what are we trying now, who's doing it, and when do we check back, every 15 to 30 minutes. Keep focus on restoring service first, like rollback, failover or disabling a feature, rather than finding the root cause. Make decisions explicitly, accepting imperfect information, and record them with the time.
Manage people: bring in specialists when needed, stop too many people from making changes at once, and keep side discussions out of the main channel. Rotate people on long incidents to avoid fatigue.

Communicate: regular updates to stakeholders with impact, current status, and the next update time, even if there's no news. For customer-facing systems, consistent messaging through support and status pages.
Close: confirm recovery with monitoring and users, stand down, and schedule a blameless review.
In a regulated environment, the incident record also captures data impact and any deviations, for quality follow-up.

p17-673.q: First, fix the problem, then fix the process, and treat the person with respect throughout.
p17-673.k: colleague broke production, config change outage, teammate mistake production, blameless incident, human error production
x: First, fix the problem, then fix the process, and treat the person with respect throughout.

Restore service: revert the configuration change, which is usually faster and safer than a forward fix, and verify recovery. If the teammate is around, I involve them, because they know exactly what they changed and why, and it helps them feel part of the solution rather than blamed.
Talk to the person privately and supportively. Mistakes happen to everyone, and if the reaction is blame, people stop admitting mistakes, which makes future incidents worse and slower to resolve.
Then focus on the system: why could a single configuration change break production without being caught?

Questions in the review. Was the change reviewed? Configuration changes deserve the same review as code. Was it tested in a lower environment first? Did the app validate the configuration at startup, or did it fail only on certain requests? Was the change applied by hand on a server, outside the pipeline? Was there a way to see the change quickly, like change logs and alerts linked to deployments? Could we roll it back in one step?

Typical improvements: configuration in source control and deployed through the pipeline, configuration validation at startup with clear failures, staged rollout of config changes like code, and audit logging of changes.
The best outcome is when the teammate presents the review themselves and leads one of the improvements.

p17-674.q: When a background job updates many rows in one big transaction, it holds locks for its whole duration, and users trying to read or update those rows wait, time out, or deadlock.
p17-674.k: background job blocking users, long running batch locks, batch update blocking, job causes timeouts, chunked batch processing
x: When a background job updates many rows in one big transaction, it holds locks for its whole duration, and users trying to read or update those rows wait, time out, or deadlock.
Confirm: during the problem, sys.dm_exec_requests and blocking queries show the job's session as the head blocker, holding many locks, maybe escalated to a table lock.
Fixes.

Process in small batches: update or delete, say, 1,000 to 5,000 rows per transaction, commit, and continue. Each transaction is short, so locks are released quickly, and lock escalation, which happens around 5,000 locks, is avoided. The job also becomes restartable, tracking progress, and uses less transaction log.
Make sure batch queries use indexes, so each batch touches only its rows rather than scanning the table, which takes more locks.
Use read committed snapshot isolation, so readers aren't blocked by the job's writes, which removes most user-facing blocking for read-heavy screens.
Schedule it away from peak hours, and throttle between batches with a short delay if needed.
Avoid unnecessary work: only update rows whose values actually change, and do calculations before the transaction rather than inside it.
For very large changes, consider building the new data in a separate table and switching over, instead of updating in place.
Then monitor blocking and job duration, so regressions show up before users notice.

p17-675.q: Index maintenance is meant to help performance, but done carelessly it can take locks, fill the transaction log and saturate I/O.
p17-675.k: index rebuild outage, index maintenance blocking, rebuild index locks, online index rebuild, maintenance window issue
x: Index maintenance is meant to help performance, but done carelessly it can take locks, fill the transaction log and saturate I/O.
What usually goes wrong.

Offline rebuilds: on editions or settings without online operations, ALTER INDEX REBUILD takes a schema modification lock, blocking all access to the table for the duration. On a large table, that's minutes or hours of outage.

Log growth: rebuilding a big index generates a lot of transaction log, which can fill the log disk, especially if log backups don't run during the job, and in availability groups it can overwhelm replicas.
Running at the wrong time: overlapping with business hours in another region, or with batch jobs and backups.
Doing too much: rebuilding every index every night regardless of need, burning resources for little benefit.
Fixes.
Use online rebuilds, with WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY so the rebuild yields to user queries, and resumable index operations, which can be paused and resumed.

Be selective: rebuild only fragmented indexes that matter, reorganise moderately fragmented ones, or skip; on modern SSD storage, fragmentation matters less than statistics. Updating statistics is often the more valuable part.
Use a proven maintenance solution, like Ola Hallengren's scripts, with thresholds and time limits.
Schedule it in a quiet window for every region, ensure log backups run frequently during maintenance, and monitor blocking and log usage while it runs.

p17-676.q: Major .NET upgrades include breaking changes and behaviour changes that compile fine but act differently at runtime.
p17-676.k: dotnet upgrade broke, behaviour change after upgrade, breaking change dotnet version, migration issue net 8, upgrade regression
x: Major .NET upgrades include breaking changes and behaviour changes that compile fine but act differently at runtime.
Contain: if the issue is serious, roll back to the previous build, which still targets the old version, while investigating.

Investigate with the breaking changes documentation: Microsoft publishes a breaking changes list for each version, by area, like ASP.NET Core, serialisation, globalisation, networking and containers. Matching the symptom to an area usually finds it.
Examples I've seen or watch out for.
Container images: since .NET 8, the default port changed from 80 to 8080 and images run as non-root, which breaks services and health checks expecting port 80.
Globalisation: different ICU behaviour on Linux versus NLS on Windows changes string comparisons, culture formatting or sorting.
Serialisation: System.Text.Json behaviour differences, like stricter handling, case sensitivity or new defaults, when moving from Newtonsoft.Json or between versions.
EF Core: query translation changes between major versions, like how collections or Contains are translated, affecting results or performance.
Security defaults: TLS versions, cipher suites or cookie settings becoming stricter.
Fix, then add a test that captures the behaviour.

Prevention: upgrade non-production first, run full regression and performance tests, read the breaking change list before upgrading, and upgrade regularly, version by version, rather than leaping several versions at once.

p17-677.q: Changing or upgrading a JSON serialiser can silently change the shape of API responses, and front ends, which depend on exact property names and formats, break.
p17-677.k: json serialization change, camelcase pascalcase json, newtonsoft to system text json, enum serialization changed, date format json changed
x: Changing or upgrading a JSON serialiser can silently change the shape of API responses, and front ends, which depend on exact property names and formats, break.
Typical differences, especially moving from Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json.
Property naming: camelCase versus PascalCase, depending on configuration. If the front end expects shipmentId and now gets ShipmentId, everything is undefined.
Enums: serialised as numbers by default, unless a JsonStringEnumConverter is configured; the front end expected "Delivered" and now gets 3.
Dates: formats and time zone handling differ, like DateTime with Kind Unspecified, or offsets included or not.
Nulls and defaults: whether null properties are included or omitted.
Reference loops and polymorphism: Newtonsoft handled some cases with settings that System.Text.Json handles differently or requires attributes for.
Case-insensitive deserialisation: Newtonsoft was case-insensitive by default; System.Text.Json is case-sensitive unless configured, although ASP.NET Core's web defaults are case-insensitive.
Fixing: configure the serialiser explicitly to match the previous contract, like naming policy, enum converter and date handling, rather than relying on defaults; then verify with the front end.

Prevention: treat the API's JSON as a contract. Snapshot tests of responses, with Verify, catch accidental shape changes; contract tests with consumers, or OpenAPI-based checks in CI comparing the schema against the previous version, flag breaking changes before release.

p17-678.q: Off-by-a-cent errors almost always come from using floating point types for money, or from inconsistent rounding.
p17-678.k: rounding error money, floating point currency, decimal vs double money, off by one cent, rounding mode, precision loss json
x: Off-by-a-cent errors almost always come from using floating point types for money, or from inconsistent rounding.

Floating point: double and float in C#, and number in JavaScript, are binary floating point, which can't represent many decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3. Summing many values accumulates tiny errors that eventually show up as a cent difference. Fix: use decimal in C#, and DECIMAL or NUMERIC with fixed scale in SQL, never FLOAT or REAL for money.

Rounding rules: .NET's Math.Round uses banker's rounding by default, rounding 2.5 to 2, while business users and other systems may expect away-from-zero rounding, 2.5 to 3. Use MidpointRounding explicitly, and agree on the rule with the business.

When to round: rounding each line and then summing gives a different total than summing and then rounding. The business rules must define which one, like rounding per line item for invoices, and the code must do it consistently everywhere, including reports and exports.

Front end: JavaScript numbers can lose precision on very large values, and calculations in the browser can disagree with the server. Do authoritative calculations on the server, send money as strings or with known scale if precision matters, and only format on the client.
Currency: different currencies have different numbers of decimal places, so the scale comes from the currency.
Then add tests with known tricky values and compare totals across the system.

p17-679.q: A half-finished migration leaves data in a mixed state, so the first job is to understand exactly what state it's in, before doing anything else.
p17-679.k: data migration failed halfway, partial migration recovery, resume migration, batch migration failure, migration rollback data
x: A half-finished migration leaves data in a mixed state, so the first job is to understand exactly what state it's in, before doing anything else.

Stop and assess: make sure the migration isn't still running or retrying. Find out which batches or rows were migrated and which weren't, and whether any batch was partially applied. Good migrations make this easy, because they log progress per batch.

Decide: resume, or roll back. If the migration is designed to be resumable and idempotent, I fix the cause of the failure, like bad data in one batch, a timeout, or a constraint violation, and resume from the last completed batch. If it's not resumable, or the data is suspect, I restore the affected tables from a backup taken just before, or reverse the migrated batches with a tested script.
Validate: row counts, checksums, and business-level checks between source and target, like totals per study or site, and samples reviewed with business users.
How I design migrations to avoid this.
Batch processing with a progress table, recording each completed batch, so it can resume.
Idempotent operations: running a batch twice gives the same result, like upserts with stable keys.
Keep the source data unchanged until the migration is verified; write to new tables or columns, then switch over.
Dry runs on a production copy, measuring duration and catching data surprises.
Validation queries prepared in advance.
In a regulated system, the migration plan, results and verification are documented and approved as part of the change.

p17-680.q: This is the situation where availability directly affects patients and trials, so it's planned for in advance, not improvised.
p17-680.k: irt down randomization, system outage clinical site, business continuity irt, randomization during outage, irt downtime procedure
x: This is the situation where availability directly affects patients and trials, so it's planned for in advance, not improvised.
From the system side: the incident is handled as top severity, with the focus on restoring service as fast as possible, and clear communication to the support teams who talk to sites.

From the business side, IRT providers have business continuity procedures defined with the sponsor for each study. Typically the site contacts the support helpdesk, which is available around the clock, and the procedure defines what can be done manually and who can authorise it. [For example, the protocol may allow a short delay of the randomisation visit, or a documented manual process.] Any manual action must be recorded with full details, so that when the system is back, the transactions are entered or reconciled, the audit trail is complete, and the randomisation list and drug supply records stay consistent. Because blinding and allocation integrity matter so much, manual steps are tightly controlled.

What engineering does to make this rare and short: high availability infrastructure, tested failover and backups, careful releases with rollback plans, and monitoring that detects problems before sites do.
After recovery, we verify that no transactions were lost or duplicated, especially those in flight when the outage started, and support any reconciliation.
In an interview I'd emphasise that we design with this patient-facing impact in mind.

p17-681.q: This is urgent, because a patient visit may be blocked. I look for why the system wouldn't allocate kits it appears to have.
p17-681.k: site no kits available, inventory mismatch, stock discrepancy, kits not allocatable, drug supply discrepancy
x: This is urgent, because a patient visit may be blocked. I look for why the system wouldn't allocate kits it appears to have.
Clarify the symptom: what exactly did the site see, a "no kits available" message during dispensing, or a missing physical shipment? Which patient, visit, treatment arm and kit type?
Then check the reasons a kit can exist but not be dispensable.
Status: the kits may be in a status that excludes them, like quarantined after a temperature excursion, damaged, lost, expired, or not yet received at the site.
Expiry and use-by rules: kits may be within stock but too close to expiry to cover the dosing period, based on the study's configured buffer days.
Treatment arm and blinding: the site has kits, but not of the type needed for this patient's arm. The site view, being blinded, may just show total stock, so it looks like there's stock.
Configuration: a recent study configuration change, like a new kit type or dosing rule, that the existing stock doesn't match.
Data issues: shipment receipt not recorded properly, or a stuck transaction.
Immediate action: work with support and the supply team on an emergency shipment or a documented manual process if the protocol allows.

Root cause: if it's a supply shortfall, resupply settings, like trigger and resupply levels per site, may need tuning; if it's a defect, it's fixed and assessed for other sites. The investigation steps, data checks and any data correction go through the controlled process.

p17-682.q: A day before go-live, the question is how serious the bug is and whether it can be fixed safely in time, without compromising validation.
p17-682.k: study go live bug, config issue before go live, last minute defect, release decision go live, study launch issue
x: A day before go-live, the question is how serious the bug is and whether it can be fixed safely in time, without compromising validation.

Assess the impact quickly with the study team: which functionality, which visits or sites, and what's the patient and data risk if we go live with it? Is it in day-one functionality, like screening and randomisation, or something used weeks later, like a later visit or resupply rule?
Options.

Fix and retest: if the fix is a small configuration change, apply it in the study build, rerun the affected test scripts and the relevant parts of user acceptance testing, and get approvals. Configuration changes still need validation evidence.

Go live with a workaround: if the affected functionality isn't needed immediately, go live on schedule with a documented plan to fix it before it's needed, agreed and signed off by the sponsor and quality.

Delay: if day-one functionality affecting patients or randomisation is wrong and can't be fixed and tested safely, a short delay is the right call. Going live with a randomisation or dosing error is far worse than a delay.
Whatever the decision, it's made with the sponsor, study team and quality, documented, and communicated to everyone involved, including sites.
Afterwards, review why the bug wasn't caught earlier, like a missing test scenario in the study specification review or simulation, and improve the configuration checks and test templates.

p17-683.q: Audit trail gaps are a serious data integrity finding in a GxP system, so the response is thorough and documented.
p17-683.k: audit trail gaps, missing audit records, audit finding, part 11 audit trail, data integrity finding
x: Audit trail gaps are a serious data integrity finding in a GxP system, so the response is thorough and documented.

Understand the scope precisely: which records, which fields, which time period, which actions are missing audit entries? Is it all changes of a certain type, changes made through a particular path, like a back-end process, a data correction script, or an integration, or something intermittent?
Find the cause. Common ones.
A code path that bypasses the audit layer: for example, a bulk operation or a direct SQL update that doesn't go through the normal service, or a new feature that wasn't wired into audit logging.
Audit writes failing silently: if audit entries are written separately from the main change and errors are swallowed, a failure leaves a change without an audit record.
Data corrections done outside the controlled process.
Retention or archiving processes removing records too early.

Respond: assess the impact with quality, determine whether the missing information can be reconstructed from other sources, like database logs, application logs or backups, and document what can and can't be recovered.

Fix: make the audit record part of the same transaction as the change, so neither can exist without the other; or use database-level mechanisms, like triggers or temporal tables, for completeness. Add tests that verify every write path creates audit records, and monitoring for audit write failures.
Then the formal CAPA process tracks corrective and preventive actions to closure.

p17-684.q: With a database per study, all databases share the same schema and code, so differences come from data, configuration, or the database's own state.
p17-684.k: one database slow, study database slow, tenant database performance, per tenant db slow, database per tenant performance
x: With a database per study, all databases share the same schema and code, so differences come from data, configuration, or the database's own state.
Compare the slow database with a typical one.

Data volume and shape: a large, long-running study may have far more subjects, kits, visits and audit records, so queries that are fine elsewhere hit large tables here. Specific tables may have grown unusually, like audit or log tables without archiving.

Statistics and plans: statistics may be stale because large data changes happened, so plans are poor. Query Store on that database shows the top queries and any plan changes. Parameter sniffing can affect one database differently because its data distribution is different.

Index health: missing or fragmented indexes, or an index that exists in the standard schema but is missing here because a deployment failed for this database. Schema drift between study databases is worth checking against the expected version.
Study configuration: features enabled only for this study, like complex randomisation, more strata, or particular integrations, which drive heavier queries.
Placement: the database may be on a busier server, sharing resources with other heavy databases, or its files on slower storage.
Maintenance: did index and statistics maintenance run successfully for this database?

The fix follows the cause: updating statistics, adding indexes, archiving old data, tuning specific queries, or moving the database to a less busy server. Then I check whether other large studies are heading for the same problem.

p17-685.q: Gradual slowdown with growth is predictable, so I treat it as capacity planning, not a surprise.
p17-685.k: database growing slow, data growth performance, archiving old data, partitioning large tables, long term database performance
x: Gradual slowdown with growth is predictable, so I treat it as capacity planning, not a surprise.
Measure: track table sizes, row counts, query durations and resource usage over time, so I know which tables and queries are growing and at what rate, and can predict when they'll hurt.
Typical fixes, roughly in order of effort.

Indexes and queries: queries written when tables were small often scan; with millions of rows, they need proper indexes, and queries should filter on indexed columns and return only needed data, with paging.

Archiving: move old, rarely accessed data, like closed records, old audit entries or historical logs, to archive tables or a separate archive database, while keeping it accessible for reporting or regulatory needs. Retention requirements decide what can move and what must stay.

Partitioning: for very large tables, like audit or transaction history, table partitioning by date makes maintenance and archiving efficient, with partition switching to move old data almost instantly. It helps queries only when they filter by the partition key.
Columnstore indexes for reporting over large historical data.
Separating workloads: move reporting and analytics to a replica or warehouse.
Hardware and configuration: more memory to keep the working set cached, faster storage, and database settings.
For a regulated system, archiving has to keep data complete, retrievable and auditable for the full retention period, so it's designed with quality and compliance input.

p17-686.q: In a database-per-study design, the master database often holds shared data, like users, permissions, study registry and global configuration, and every request across all studies may touch it. As the number of studies and users grows, it becomes a hotspot.
p17-686.k: master database bottleneck, shared database bottleneck, central database contention, multi tenant shared db hot, scaling shared database
x: In a database-per-study design, the master database often holds shared data, like users, permissions, study registry and global configuration, and every request across all studies may touch it. As the number of studies and users grows, it becomes a hotspot.
First, find out what load it carries: the top queries by frequency and cost from Query Store, and which applications and features issue them. Often a few lookups, executed on every request, dominate.
Fixes.

Caching: data like study configuration, user permissions and reference data changes rarely but is read constantly. Caching it in memory or Redis, with invalidation when it changes, can remove most of the load. This is usually the biggest win.
Query efficiency: fix the expensive queries with indexes and better access patterns, and avoid chatty patterns, like one query per study in a loop.
Read scaling: route read-only queries to a readable replica.
Reducing coupling: move data that's really study-specific out of the master into the study databases, and avoid cross-database queries from study databases to master in hot paths.
Splitting responsibilities: separate the master's different roles, like identity, configuration and job scheduling, into separate stores or services, so they scale independently.
Connection management: ensure applications use pooled connections and don't hold them open.
I'd also check the master's availability setup, because if everything depends on it, its outage is everyone's outage.

p17-687.q: When two systems disagree, like our system and a partner's warehouse showing different shipment or stock counts, the goal is to find which records differ and why, then fix both the data and the cause.
p17-687.k: data mismatch between systems, reconciliation, inconsistent data two systems, data sync issue, integration discrepancy
x: When two systems disagree, like our system and a partner's warehouse showing different shipment or stock counts, the goal is to find which records differ and why, then fix both the data and the cause.

Define the comparison precisely: the same entity, the same time cut-off, and the same definition. Many "mismatches" are actually different definitions, like counting shipped versus received, or different time zones for the cut-off.

Compare at record level, not just totals: export keys and key attributes from both sides for the period and match them. The result falls into three groups: records only in system A, only in B, and in both but with different values. Each group points to a different cause.
Only in one system: messages or files that failed, were never sent, were dead-lettered, or were rejected by the other side's validation. Check integration logs and dead-letter queues.
Different values: updates that didn't propagate, out-of-order processing where an older update overwrote a newer one, or mapping and conversion differences, like units or status codes.
Fix the data through the controlled process: reprocess failed messages, resend corrected records, or apply documented corrections.
Fix the cause: idempotent, ordered processing with version checks; better error handling and alerts for integration failures.
Prevent: an automated daily reconciliation job that compares counts or checksums and alerts on differences, so mismatches are found in a day, not at month end.

p17-688.q: Urgency changes the speed, not the safety requirements. A configuration change in a validated study can affect patients, so it still follows a controlled process, just expedited.
p17-688.k: urgent configuration change, study amendment urgent, emergency config change, change production configuration safely, protocol amendment change
x: Urgency changes the speed, not the safety requirements. A configuration change in a validated study can affect patients, so it still follows a controlled process, just expedited.

Clarify the need: what exactly must change, why it's urgent, like a protocol amendment taking effect, a safety issue, or a supply problem, and what happens if we wait. That defines how fast we must go.

Assess impact: which parts of the study the change affects, like visit schedules, dosing, randomisation, supply settings or eligibility, and what happens to subjects already enrolled. Amendments can apply differently to existing subjects and new ones.

Make the change in the study build environment, never directly in production: configure, then test with focused test scripts on the affected areas plus a regression check on core flows like randomisation and dispensing, ideally using simulation.
Get approvals through the expedited path: sponsor sign-off on the change, quality review of the testing evidence. The documentation can be lighter in format but not missing.
Deploy using the standard study promotion process from UAT to production, so it's the same mechanism we trust, and verify in production after deployment.
Communicate to sites and support teams about what changed and when.

Afterwards, review why it became urgent, like late notice of an amendment, and whether the process could be faster for this type of change, such as pre-approved test templates for common configuration changes.

p17-689.q: After a partner upgrades their SFTP server, connection failures are often about security algorithms, keys or network changes, so I check the connection log details carefully.
p17-689.k: sftp connection refused after upgrade, ssh key algorithm not supported, sftp negotiation failed, host key changed, cipher mismatch sftp
x: After a partner upgrades their SFTP server, connection failures are often about security algorithms, keys or network changes, so I check the connection log details carefully.
Enable verbose logging in the SFTP client: the handshake log shows exactly where it fails, like key exchange, host key verification, authentication or channel opening.
Common causes.

Algorithm mismatch: newer servers disable old algorithms, like ssh-rsa with SHA-1 signatures, older key exchange methods, or CBC ciphers. If our client library or configuration only offers those, negotiation fails with "no matching algorithm". Fix: update the client library and enable modern algorithms, like rsa-sha2-256 or ed25519 keys and curve25519 key exchange.

Host key changed: the upgrade generated a new host key, so our client, which pins the old fingerprint, refuses to connect, correctly, because it could be a man-in-the-middle attack. Fix: get the new fingerprint from the partner through a trusted channel, verify, and update our configuration.
Authentication: our public key wasn't migrated, or the server now requires a different key type, or password authentication was disabled.
Network: a new IP address or port, or their firewall only allows our old IP, or our egress IP changed.
Permissions: the folders or paths changed.

Because our SFTP component supports multiple client libraries behind one interface, if one library can't support the new algorithms, switching provider through configuration is an option, tested first.
Afterwards, agree with partners on advance notice of upgrades and a test endpoint.

p17-690.q: An actively exploited vulnerability changes the balance: the risk of not patching is now higher than the usual risk of change. But a careless rollout can still cause an outage, so I move fast with structure.
p17-690.k: emergency patch, urgent security patching, zero day patch servers, patch rollout plan, critical vulnerability servers
x: An actively exploited vulnerability changes the balance: the risk of not patching is now higher than the usual risk of change. But a careless rollout can still cause an outage, so I move fast with structure.

Assess exposure: which servers and components are affected, which are internet-facing or hold sensitive data. Prioritise those. Check whether there are temporary mitigations, like a WAF rule, disabling a feature or blocking a port, that reduce risk immediately while patching proceeds.
Get approval through the emergency change process, with the risk assessment written down, which in a regulated environment is required anyway.
Test quickly: apply the patch to a non-production environment and run smoke and key regression tests, focusing on the components the patch touches.

Roll out in waves: one production server or a small group first, out of the load balancer, patch, reboot, verify health and functionality, then return it and continue with the next group. This keeps capacity and lets us stop if something breaks. For clusters, drain nodes one at a time.
Have a rollback plan: snapshots or the ability to uninstall the patch.
Verify: confirm the patch is installed everywhere with an inventory or scanning tool, and that no server was missed, which is common with forgotten or rarely used machines.
Communicate status throughout, then close the change with evidence.
Afterwards, review how long patching took and how to make the routine process faster for next time.

p17-691.q: A recurring weekly pattern points to something that builds up over the weekend, or to load that peaks at that time.
p17-691.k: slow monday morning, slow after weekend, cold start monday, cache cold after weekend, weekly peak performance
x: A recurring weekly pattern points to something that builds up over the weekend, or to load that peaks at that time.

Load pattern: Monday morning is often the busiest period, with everyone logging in, catching up on work from the weekend, and processing backlogs. Combined with a different time zone's Monday overlapping, peak load may simply exceed capacity. Metrics comparing Monday with other days confirm it. Fix: scale up ahead of the known peak with scheduled scaling, and fix the queries that are most expensive at peak.

Cold caches and idle shutdown: if app pools idle out, containers scale to zero, or caches expire over a quiet weekend, the first users on Monday pay for warming everything: JIT compilation, loading configuration, filling caches. Fix: Always On or Application Initialization, warm-up jobs before business hours, and minimum instance counts.

Weekend jobs: maintenance jobs, like index rebuilds, statistics updates or large batch imports, running over the weekend and still running Monday morning, or leaving statistics stale. Fix: check job schedules and durations, and ensure they finish well before business hours.

Backlogs: messages or files accumulated over the weekend being processed Monday morning, competing with user traffic. Fix: process them continuously, or throttle background processing during peak hours.
Authentication: many users' tokens and sessions expired over the weekend, so the identity provider gets a login surge.
I'd look at Monday's metrics hour by hour to see which of these lines up.

p17-692.q: When the release is blocked by tooling, I fix the tooling rather than bypassing it, because bypassing the pipeline undermines everything the release process guarantees, especially in a regulated environment.
p17-692.k: build agent offline, pipeline broken before release, cannot deploy release, self hosted agent down, release blocked pipeline
x: When the release is blocked by tooling, I fix the tooling rather than bypassing it, because bypassing the pipeline undermines everything the release process guarantees, especially in a regulated environment.

Diagnose the agent: is the agent service stopped, the machine down, out of disk space, lost network access to the Azure DevOps Server, or has its access token expired? The agent pool page shows its status and last contact, and the agent's diagnostic logs on the machine show errors. Disk full with old build folders and caches is a very common cause; cleaning the work folder often brings it back.

Alternatives: if another agent in the pool has the same capabilities, the job can run there. If the agent machine is truly broken, a new agent can be set up quickly, if agents are built from a documented script or image, which is why we keep that script.
Communicate: tell the release coordinator the expected delay, so stakeholders can decide whether to keep the release window or move it.

What I don't do: build on a laptop and copy files manually to servers. That artifact wouldn't be traceable, tested or approved through the normal flow. If the release truly can't wait, it goes through the emergency change process, with documented justification.
Afterwards: monitor agent health and disk space, keep more than one agent capable of each critical job, and automate agent provisioning, so one machine isn't a single point of failure for releases.

p17-693.q: If a request takes minutes, like generating a large report, running a simulation, or importing a big file, keeping the HTTP request open causes timeouts at proxies and browsers, holds server resources, and fails badly if the connection drops.
p17-693.k: long running request, request takes minutes, move to background processing, async request reply, 202 accepted pattern
x: If a request takes minutes, like generating a large report, running a simulation, or importing a big file, keeping the HTTP request open causes timeouts at proxies and browsers, holds server resources, and fails badly if the connection drops.
The redesign is the asynchronous request-reply pattern.
The API validates the request quickly, creates a job record with a status like Pending, puts a message on a queue, and returns 202 Accepted with a job id and a status URL.

A background worker, a hosted service, a separate worker service or a function, picks up the message and does the work, updating the job's progress and status, and storing the result somewhere, like blob storage or a results table.
The client checks the status URL periodically, or receives a push notification through SignalR or email when it's done, then fetches the result.

Benefits: no request timeouts; work survives server restarts because it's queued; retries happen on failure; concurrency is controlled, so ten big jobs don't overload the database; and the UI can show progress and let users keep working.

Details to get right: idempotency, so a retried submission doesn't create duplicate jobs, using an idempotency key; authorisation on the status and result endpoints, so users only see their own jobs; cancellation support; cleanup of old results; and clear error states.
For moderately long operations, under a minute, simply optimising the work may be enough; for anything longer, this pattern is the reliable answer.

p17-694.q: A mystery value in production configuration is risky both ways: changing it might break something, and leaving it might be hiding a problem. So I investigate before touching it.
p17-694.k: unknown config value, mystery configuration, undocumented setting, config archaeology, configuration ownership
x: A mystery value in production configuration is risky both ways: changing it might break something, and leaving it might be hiding a problem. So I investigate before touching it.

Find its history: source control history for config files and pipeline variables, deployment logs, change tickets, and the configuration store's audit history. Often a commit message or ticket explains why it was set, like a timeout increased during an incident years ago.
Find its usage: search the code for the key, including libraries and scripts, to see what reads it and what effect it has. Sometimes nothing reads it anymore, and it's a leftover.
Ask people: the team, previous owners, operations and the vendor documentation, if it's a framework setting.
Test the effect in a lower environment: change it there and observe, ideally with load or integration tests that exercise the related path.
Then decide: keep it and document why, change it through a normal change with monitoring, or remove it if unused, again through a normal change, not quietly.

Prevent future mysteries: keep all configuration in source control with meaningful commit messages, document non-obvious settings next to the value or in a configuration reference, use strongly typed options classes with validation and comments, and remove unused settings regularly.
In a regulated system, configuration values that affect validated behaviour need to be controlled anyway, so this kind of documentation is part of the expected evidence.

p17-695.q: I can't always fix the legacy system, but I can stop its slowness from becoming my users' problem.
p17-695.k: slow legacy dependency, protect from slow dependency, legacy system bottleneck, wrap slow service, cache legacy data
x: I can't always fix the legacy system, but I can stop its slowness from becoming my users' problem.
Measure first: which calls are slow, how slow, and how often my service calls it per user action. Sometimes the biggest issue is my side calling it too often.
Then apply protections.

Timeouts on every call, so a slow response fails fast instead of holding threads and connections. Paired with a circuit breaker, so when the legacy system is struggling, we stop hammering it and fail fast or degrade.
Caching: if the data changes rarely, like reference data or configuration, cache it with a sensible TTL, so most requests never touch the legacy system.
Asynchronous integration: for writes or long operations, put requests on a queue and process them in the background at a pace the legacy system can handle, giving users an immediate acknowledgement.

Replicated read model: for frequently read data, keep a local copy synchronised through change data capture, events or scheduled sync, and serve reads from it. Users get fast responses, accepting a small delay in freshness.
Bulkheads: isolate calls to the legacy system in their own limited pool, so its slowness doesn't consume all of my service's resources.
Graceful degradation: show what's available, and clearly mark what couldn't be loaded, rather than failing the whole page.
Longer term, these protections often become the first step of a strangler fig migration, replacing the legacy system piece by piece.

p17-696.q: If errors spike every time we deploy, something in the release process interrupts in-flight work or sends traffic to instances that aren't ready.
p17-696.k: errors during deployment, downtime during release, zero downtime deployment, deploy causes errors, graceful shutdown deploy
x: If errors spike every time we deploy, something in the release process interrupts in-flight work or sends traffic to instances that aren't ready.
Check each phase.

Instances starting: are new instances receiving traffic before they're ready, before caches warm, JIT completes or connections are established? Fix: readiness checks that only pass when the app can serve, warm-up requests, and Application Initialization on IIS.

Instances stopping: are old instances killed while handling requests? Fix: remove them from the load balancer first, let connections drain with a deregistration delay, and implement graceful shutdown, so the app stops accepting new requests, finishes in-flight ones and closes consumers cleanly on SIGTERM, within the timeout.
Capacity during rollout: if half the instances are replaced at once, the rest may be overloaded. Fix: rolling updates with extra capacity, like surge, so capacity never drops.

Incompatibility between versions: during a rolling update, old and new versions run together, and clients or other services may hit both. API changes must be backward compatible, database schema changes must use expand and contract, and message formats must be readable by both versions.
Sessions and state: in-memory sessions lost when an instance stops. Fix: stateless services with external session storage.
Background workers: messages in progress during shutdown should be completed or returned to the queue, not lost.
I measure errors per deployment as a metric, so improvements are visible and regressions get caught.

p17-697.q: A full region or data centre outage is what disaster recovery plans are for, and the response follows the plan rather than improvisation.
p17-697.k: region outage, data centre outage, cloud outage response, failover to dr, disaster recovery activation
x: A full region or data centre outage is what disaster recovery plans are for, and the response follows the plan rather than improvisation.

Confirm and assess: check the provider's status page and our own monitoring from outside the affected region. Determine which systems are affected and the expected duration, if the provider has an estimate.

Decide whether to fail over: failing over has its own risks and costs, especially if data replication is asynchronous, where some recent data may be lost, up to the recovery point objective. If the provider expects recovery soon, waiting may be better. The decision criteria and who makes it are defined in the DR plan in advance, typically based on the expected outage duration versus our recovery time objective.

Fail over, if decided: promote the replicated databases in the secondary region, switch DNS or global load balancing to the secondary, start or scale up compute there, from infrastructure as code, and verify the critical journeys. Communicate to users and stakeholders.
During the outage, track what data may have been lost or is in an uncertain state, like transactions in flight.
Fail back: once the primary is healthy, resynchronise data and switch back in a planned window, which is often harder than the failover itself.

Afterwards: review against the plan, measure actual recovery time and data loss, and fix gaps. The most important preparation is regular DR testing, because an untested DR plan usually fails when it's needed.

p17-698.q: Full-text search, faceting and fuzzy matching are much better in a search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, than in SQL. But then the same data lives in two places, and the challenge is keeping the index in sync reliably.
p17-698.k: elasticsearch sync sql, opensearch sync, search index synchronization, change data capture search, reindex search
x: Full-text search, faceting and fuzzy matching are much better in a search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, than in SQL. But then the same data lives in two places, and the challenge is keeping the index in sync reliably.
Options, from simple to robust.

Dual writes from the application: after saving to SQL, also update the index. Simple, but if the index call fails after the database commit, they diverge, and there's no easy way to know. I avoid this as the only mechanism.

Events through an outbox: the service writes the change and an outbox record in the same transaction; a relay publishes the event; an indexer consumer updates the search index. Reliable, with retries, and the index catches up even after failures.

Change data capture: read the database's change stream, like SQL Server CDC or Debezium on the transaction log, and feed changes to the indexer. No application changes, and every change is captured, including ones made by scripts or other apps.
Periodic sync: an incremental job using a last-modified watermark, simpler but with more delay.

Whichever path, I design for drift: index documents carry a version or timestamp, so older updates don't overwrite newer ones; there's a full reindex capability, building a new index alongside and switching an alias atomically, for mapping changes or recovery; and a reconciliation check comparing counts or checksums.
Security trimming matters too: index the fields needed for permission filtering, like site or tenant, and always filter by them.

p17-699.q: The core problem is concurrency: two requests see one item left, and both take it. The design must make the check and the update atomic.
p17-699.k: inventory reservation design, prevent overselling, stock reservation, concurrent allocation, kit allocation design, reserve and confirm
x: The core problem is concurrency: two requests see one item left, and both take it. The design must make the check and the update atomic.
Data model: stock per location and item type with available and reserved quantities, or individual items, like kits with unique ids and statuses, which is the case in clinical supply.
Atomic reservation, with a few options.

Conditional update in the database: UPDATE stock SET available = available - 1 WHERE id = @id AND available >= 1, then check the affected row count. If zero, there was no stock. One statement, no race.
For individual items: select and lock one available item with UPDLOCK and READPAST hints, so concurrent requests skip each other's locked rows, then mark it reserved in the same transaction.
Optimistic concurrency with a row version, retrying on conflict.

Reserve, then confirm: a reservation has an expiry. If the process completes, like a dispensing confirmed, the reservation becomes final; if it's abandoned, a background job releases expired reservations, so stock isn't locked forever.
Idempotency: each request carries an idempotency key, so retries don't reserve twice.
Rules applied during selection: expiry dates, first-expiry-first-out, blinding constraints and the right item type for the patient's arm.
Scaling: partition by location, so contention is only between requests for the same site's stock, and keep transactions short.
And reconciliation jobs compare reservations with confirmed transactions, flagging anything stuck.

p17-700.q: Requirement: send reminders at the right time, like three days before a patient's visit window opens, reliably, once, and adapting when schedules change.
p17-700.k: design reminder service, scheduled notifications design, visit reminder system, delayed jobs design, scheduler service design
x: Requirement: send reminders at the right time, like three days before a patient's visit window opens, reliably, once, and adapting when schedules change.

Data model: a scheduled_notifications table with the target, like subject and visit, the type, the due time in UTC, the status and a version. Reminders are created or updated whenever the visit schedule changes, like after a randomisation or a visit being recorded.

Triggering: a scheduler process polls for due items, using an index on due time and status, in small batches. Each item is claimed atomically, with an update that sets status to Processing where status is Pending, or SELECT with UPDLOCK and READPAST, so multiple scheduler instances can run without double sending. Alternatives include delayed messages, like Service Bus scheduled messages, SQS delay up to 15 minutes plus a store, or EventBridge Scheduler for individual schedules, but a table gives easy querying, cancellation and auditing.
Sending: the claimed item becomes a message on a queue to the notification service, which renders the template and sends via email or SMS, with retries and idempotency by notification id.
Changes and cancellations: if the visit is rescheduled, update the due time; if the subject withdraws, cancel pending reminders. A version check prevents sending a stale reminder.
Time zones: compute due times from the site's time zone, handling daylight saving changes.
Monitoring: overdue pending items are alerted, so a stuck scheduler is noticed quickly, which is the same kind of check our AlertWatchDog jobs perform.

p17-701.q: Reports and documents, like PDFs, Excel files or regulatory exports, are often slow, resource-heavy and occasionally fail, so they belong in a separate, asynchronous service.
p17-701.k: report generation service design, pdf generation service, document generation microservice, async report design, template rendering service
x: Reports and documents, like PDFs, Excel files or regulatory exports, are often slow, resource-heavy and occasionally fail, so they belong in a separate, asynchronous service.

Flow: the client requests a report with parameters. The API validates input and permissions, stores a job record, and returns 202 with a job id. A worker picks the job from a queue, gathers data through APIs or a read replica, renders the output with a template engine, like a Razor or HTML template converted to PDF, or a library for Excel, stores the file in blob storage, and marks the job complete. The client is notified or polls, then downloads through a short-lived signed URL.
Design points.
Templates are versioned separately from code, so report layouts can change through a controlled process, which matters for regulated documents.
Determinism: the same inputs and template version should produce the same document; record the template version, parameters and data timestamp in the job, for traceability.
Scaling: rendering is CPU and memory heavy, so workers scale independently on queue depth, with limits per user or tenant so one big request doesn't starve others.
Resilience: retries with idempotency, timeouts for very large reports, and clear error messages.
Security: authorisation checked again when the file is downloaded, files encrypted at rest, expiry and deletion of old files, and an audit record of who generated and downloaded what.
Caching: identical requests within a short time can reuse the previous result.

p17-702.q: Outgoing webhooks push events to subscribers' URLs, and the main challenges are unreliable receivers, retries, ordering and security.
p17-702.k: webhook delivery design, outgoing webhooks, webhook retries, webhook dispatcher, deliver events to customers
x: Outgoing webhooks push events to subscribers' URLs, and the main challenges are unreliable receivers, retries, ordering and security.

Flow: when an event happens, the service records it through an outbox. A dispatcher finds subscriptions matching the event type and creates a delivery record per subscriber, then queues the deliveries.

Delivery workers send HTTP POSTs with the event payload, an event id, a timestamp and an HMAC signature header, so receivers can verify authenticity and reject replays. Short timeouts, like ten seconds, so slow receivers don't tie up workers.

Retries: on failure or non-2xx response, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, over hours or days, like at 1 minute, 5, 30, 2 hours, and so on. After the final attempt, mark it failed and notify the subscriber. Receivers must deduplicate by event id, because retries mean at-least-once delivery.

Isolation: one subscriber being down mustn't delay others, so queues or concurrency limits are per subscriber. A circuit breaker per endpoint pauses deliveries to a dead endpoint and disables subscriptions that fail consistently.
Ordering: if order matters, deliver sequentially per subscriber and entity, or include a sequence number so receivers can order or ignore stale events.
Visibility: a delivery log per subscriber, with request, response code and timing, a replay function, and a test endpoint feature for subscribers.
Security: validate subscriber URLs against SSRF, require HTTPS, and support secret rotation with two valid signatures during rotation.

p17-703.q: Id choice affects database performance, security and how distributed systems create records.
p17-703.k: guid vs int id, sequential guid, snowflake id, distributed id generation, uuid v7, primary key choice
x: Id choice affects database performance, security and how distributed systems create records.

Auto-increment integers: small, fast, naturally ordered, great for clustered indexes. But the database generates them, so you only know the id after insert, merging data from several databases causes collisions, and exposing them in URLs reveals counts and makes guessing other records easy.

Random GUIDs, version 4: generated anywhere without coordination, globally unique, unguessable. But they're 16 bytes, and their randomness fragments clustered indexes in SQL Server, because inserts land all over the index, causing page splits and slower writes.

Sequential GUIDs: NEWSEQUENTIALID in SQL Server, or UUID version 7, which .NET 9 supports with Guid.CreateVersion7(). They embed a timestamp at the start, so values are roughly ordered, which keeps index inserts at the end like integers, while remaining globally unique and generated in the application. That's a good default for distributed systems now.
Snowflake-style ids: 64-bit integers combining a timestamp, a machine id and a sequence. Ordered, compact and generated without coordination, but they need machine ids assigned uniquely.

My approach: internal clustered keys can be integers or UUID v7; public identifiers in URLs should not be guessable, so either UUIDs or a separate public id; and authorisation checks never rely on ids being secret.
For business identifiers, like kit numbers or subject numbers, those follow their own business formats separately from technical keys.

p17-704.q: Two-phase commit is a protocol for making a transaction atomic across several resources, like two databases, or a database and a message broker. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare, meaning to promise they can commit; if all say yes, it tells everyone to commit; if anyone says no, everyone rolls back. In the .NET Framework world, MSDTC did this, often transparently with TransactionScope across connections.
p17-704.k: two phase commit, 2pc, distributed transaction, xa transaction, msdtc, why not distributed transactions
x: Two-phase commit is a protocol for making a transaction atomic across several resources, like two databases, or a database and a message broker. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare, meaning to promise they can commit; if all say yes, it tells everyone to commit; if anyone says no, everyone rolls back. In the .NET Framework world, MSDTC did this, often transparently with TransactionScope across connections.
Why microservices avoid it.

Availability: all participants must be up and responsive for the transaction to complete. If one service or database is slow or down, the whole operation waits or fails. Locks are held during the prepare phase, so a stuck coordinator can leave resources locked.

Coupling: services would need to share transaction infrastructure, which defeats independent deployment and technology choices. Many modern components, like HTTP APIs, Kafka or cloud services, don't support it at all.
Scalability: coordination round trips and held locks limit throughput.

Instead, microservices accept eventual consistency with patterns that give reliability without global locks: the outbox pattern, so a local database change and an event are recorded atomically; idempotent consumers; and sagas, a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a later step fails.
Where strong consistency really is required, the better answer is often to keep that data in one service and one database, so a normal local transaction does the job.

p17-705.q: Both solve coordination problems when several instances of a service run at once.
p17-705.k: leader election, consistent hashing, distributed coordination, single leader pattern, partition assignment, hash ring
x: Both solve coordination problems when several instances of a service run at once.

Leader election: sometimes exactly one instance must do a task, like run a scheduler, process a singleton queue, or coordinate others. Instances compete for a leadership lease; one wins and does the work, renewing the lease periodically; if it dies or stops renewing, another takes over after the lease expires. Implementations: a Kubernetes Lease object, which client libraries support; a distributed lock with expiry in Redis, a database row with an expiry timestamp, or sp_getapplock in SQL Server; or coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd. Watch-outs: a paused leader, like during a long GC pause, may think it's still leader after its lease expired, so work should carry a fencing token, an increasing number that downstream systems check, to reject stale leaders.

Consistent hashing: distributes keys across a changing set of nodes. Nodes are placed on a hash ring, and each key goes to the next node clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys near it move, instead of almost all keys, as happens with simple hash modulo N. Virtual nodes smooth the distribution. It's used in distributed caches, like Redis Cluster's slot model, which is a related idea, partitioned databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB, and load balancers with session affinity.
In application design, I usually use these through infrastructure rather than building them, but understanding them helps reason about failover and rebalancing.

p17-706.q: Events outlive code: consumers may be deployed at different times, and stored events may be replayed months later. So event schemas need careful evolution.
p17-706.k: event schema evolution, event versioning, schema registry, backward compatible events, breaking event change
x: Events outlive code: consumers may be deployed at different times, and stored events may be replayed months later. So event schemas need careful evolution.
Rules for compatible changes.
Adding optional fields is safe, provided consumers ignore unknown fields, which I make a standard: tolerant readers.

Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings is breaking. Instead, add a new field alongside the old one, populate both for a transition period, migrate consumers, and then remove the old one only when nobody uses it.
Never change the meaning of an existing field silently, like changing an amount from units to cents.

Versioning: include an event type and version in the envelope, like ShipmentDelivered v2. For a truly breaking change, publish a new version as a new event type, possibly both versions in parallel for a while, and let consumers migrate at their own pace.

Schema registry: with Kafka, a schema registry, using Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, enforces compatibility rules at publish time, like backward or full compatibility, so an incompatible schema is rejected before it reaches consumers.
Contracts and tests: consumer-driven contract tests for messages catch breaking changes in the producer's pipeline.
Upcasting: for event-sourced systems, old event versions are converted to the current shape when read, so business logic handles only the latest version.
Documentation of events in a catalogue, like AsyncAPI, makes ownership and versions visible.

p17-707.q: Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, puts the application's core logic in the middle, with no dependencies on technology, and connects everything else through ports and adapters.
p17-707.k: hexagonal architecture, ports and adapters, onion architecture, clean architecture vs hexagonal, domain isolation
x: Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, puts the application's core logic in the middle, with no dependencies on technology, and connects everything else through ports and adapters.

Ports are interfaces defined by the core: incoming ports describe what the application can do, like an IAllocateKit use case; outgoing ports describe what it needs from the outside, like IKitRepository, IClock, or INotificationSender.

Adapters implement those ports for specific technologies. Driving adapters call into the application, like an ASP.NET Core controller, a message consumer, or a CLI command. Driven adapters are called by the application, like an EF Core repository, a RabbitMQ publisher or an SMTP sender.
The dependency rule: adapters depend on the core, never the other way round. The core doesn't know about HTTP, SQL or message brokers.

Benefits: business logic is testable with simple in-memory fakes for the outgoing ports; technology can change, like swapping a message broker, by writing a new adapter; and the same use case can be triggered from different entry points, an API, a queue or a scheduled job, without duplication.
Onion architecture and clean architecture are close relatives with the same core idea, differing mostly in how they name layers.
The risk is over-engineering: lots of interfaces and mapping for simple CRUD services. I apply it where there's meaningful business logic, and keep simple services simple.
Our newer APIs follow clean architecture, which is this idea in practice.

p17-708.q: When a legacy system writes directly to a database and can't be modified to publish events, change data capture lets other services react to its changes anyway.
p17-708.k: change data capture events, debezium, cdc to kafka, publish events from database, legacy database events
x: When a legacy system writes directly to a database and can't be modified to publish events, change data capture lets other services react to its changes anyway.

How it works: CDC reads the database's transaction log, which records every committed insert, update and delete, and turns each change into an event. SQL Server has built-in CDC, which writes changes to change tables; Debezium is a popular open-source tool that reads logs from SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others, and publishes change events to Kafka, usually through Kafka Connect. Cloud services offer similar features.

Benefits: no changes to the legacy application; every change is captured, including those from scripts and other applications; ordering per row is preserved; and nothing is lost, because it reads committed data from the log.
Challenges.

Raw change events reflect table structure, not business meaning. An "UPDATE on table X" isn't a "ShipmentDelivered" event. So a translation step, sometimes called an event transformer, should turn low-level changes into meaningful domain events, otherwise consumers become coupled to the legacy schema.
Schema changes in the legacy database affect the event stream.
Initial snapshots of existing data and catching up after outages need care.
Operational overhead: running Kafka Connect, monitoring lag, and the impact on the database's log retention.
It's an excellent tool for strangler fig migrations, syncing data into new services while the legacy system remains the source of truth.

p17-709.q: The database is usually the hardest part of breaking up a monolith, because many modules read and write the same tables, often with joins, triggers and stored procedures crossing boundaries.
p17-709.k: split shared database, database decomposition, extract data from monolith database, shared tables migration, data ownership migration
x: The database is usually the hardest part of breaking up a monolith, because many modules read and write the same tables, often with joins, triggers and stored procedures crossing boundaries.
The approach I'd follow, gradually.
Map data ownership: for each table, which module writes it and which read it. The goal is a single owner per table, with others getting the data through the owner's API or events.

Separate within the same database first: move the new service's tables into their own schema, give the service its own database user with access only to its schema, and replace cross-boundary joins and foreign keys with API calls or local copies. This reveals hidden dependencies cheaply, while the data is still in one place.
Handle shared reads: other modules that need the data get it through an API, or keep a read-only copy updated by events or change data capture.
Handle shared writes: route all writes for that data through the owning service. Where the monolith still writes directly, synchronise temporarily with CDC, while code is moved over.
Move to a separate database once the service no longer depends on cross-schema access, with a data migration and a cutover, possibly using dual writes with verification for a while.
Throughout: reconciliation checks between old and new, feature flags for switching paths, and the ability to roll back each step.
It's slow, but each step reduces coupling while keeping the system working.

p17-710.q: Batch processing handles data in large chunks at intervals, like a nightly job processing all of yesterday's transactions. Stream processing handles each event continuously as it arrives, within seconds.
p17-710.k: batch vs stream processing, real time vs batch, etl vs streaming, kappa lambda architecture, when to use streaming
x: Batch processing handles data in large chunks at intervals, like a nightly job processing all of yesterday's transactions. Stream processing handles each event continuously as it arrives, within seconds.
