Batch suits: reports and analytics where hourly or daily freshness is fine; heavy computations over complete datasets, like month-end reconciliation, billing or full recalculation of forecasts; data loads into warehouses; and simplicity, since batch jobs are easier to reason about, rerun and test, and can use cheap resources during quiet hours.

Streaming suits: things that need fast reactions, like alerts, fraud or anomaly detection, notifications and live dashboards; keeping derived data up to date, like search indexes or caches; and spreading load evenly instead of a big nightly spike.

Trade-offs of streaming: more complex, with ordering, late-arriving events, exactly-once concerns, state management for aggregations over windows, and more infrastructure, like Kafka, Kinesis, or stream processors like Flink or Kafka Streams.

Many systems combine them: a stream handles real-time needs, while batch jobs do periodic full recomputation and reconciliation to correct any drift. Modern tools blur the line, as micro-batching gives near-real-time results with batch simplicity.

My rule: start with the business's freshness requirement. If daily is genuinely fine, batch is simpler and cheaper. If people act on the data within minutes, it needs streaming or at least frequent incremental processing.
In supply management, for example, resupply checks can be frequent incremental jobs, while temperature excursion alerts need near-real-time handling.

p17-711.q: Contract-first means designing the API's contract, usually an OpenAPI document, before writing the implementation, and treating that document as the source of truth.
p17-711.k: contract first api, api first design, openapi design first, swagger contract, generate client from openapi
x: Contract-first means designing the API's contract, usually an OpenAPI document, before writing the implementation, and treating that document as the source of truth.

The process: the team writes or edits the OpenAPI spec, with paths, operations, request and response schemas, error formats, and examples. It's reviewed in a pull request with the consumers, like front-end developers, partner teams, or other services, who can comment on naming, shapes and error handling before any code exists. Mock servers generated from the spec, with tools like Prism, let consumers start building against realistic responses immediately, in parallel with the backend work.

Then code generation helps keep everything aligned: server stubs or interfaces from the spec, and typed clients for consumers, like TypeScript clients for the React front end or C# clients for other services, using tools like NSwag, Kiota or openapi-typescript. In CI, the implementation is validated against the spec, and a diff against the previous version flags breaking changes.
Benefits: better API design through early review, consistency across teams with shared style guides and linting with Spectral, parallel development, and fewer integration surprises.
The alternative, code-first, generates the spec from code, which is convenient for internal APIs with a single consumer. ASP.NET Core's built-in OpenAPI support in .NET 9 makes that easy too.
For public or partner APIs, I prefer contract-first, because the contract is the product.

p17-712.q: A golden path, or paved road, is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run a service in an organisation. Instead of every team deciding how to set up logging, health checks, pipelines, containers and monitoring, a platform team provides a ready-made path that already does it right.
p17-712.k: golden path, service template, platform engineering, internal developer platform, backstage, paved road
x: A golden path, or paved road, is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run a service in an organisation. Instead of every team deciding how to set up logging, health checks, pipelines, containers and monitoring, a platform team provides a ready-made path that already does it right.

What it typically includes: a service template, like a dotnet new template or a repository template, with the project structure, OpenTelemetry, structured logging, health checks, configuration and secrets handling, authentication, error handling, a Dockerfile, and a test project already set up. Pipeline templates for build, test, security scanning and deployment. Infrastructure modules for the standard resources, like a database, a queue or a cache, with security defaults. Dashboards and alerts generated for each service. And documentation.

An internal developer portal, like Backstage, often hosts this: a software catalogue listing all services with owners and documentation, and scaffolding where a developer fills in a form and gets a new repository, pipeline and environment in minutes.

Benefits: new services start production-ready, standards are consistent, security and compliance are built in, and engineers focus on business logic. It's especially valuable in regulated environments, where consistency simplifies validation and audits.
The key is that it's a path, not a cage: teams can deviate when they have good reasons, but the easy way is the right way.

p17-713.q: When personal data must be deleted, for example under GDPR's right to erasure, the challenge in microservices is that the data is spread across many services, databases, caches, search indexes, logs, backups and event streams.
p17-713.k: right to erasure microservices, gdpr delete across services, delete personal data distributed, data retention vs deletion, crypto shredding
x: When personal data must be deleted, for example under GDPR's right to erasure, the challenge in microservices is that the data is spread across many services, databases, caches, search indexes, logs, backups and event streams.
Approach.
Know where personal data lives: a data inventory listing which services store which personal data, maintained as part of service design.

Orchestrate deletion: a deletion request creates a workflow, often a saga, that publishes a "delete data for person X" command or event. Each service owning personal data handles it: deleting or anonymising the records, and confirming back. The workflow tracks confirmations and retries, and produces an audit record that the deletion was completed, without keeping the deleted data itself.
Derived stores: search indexes and caches must also be cleared, and analytics data anonymised.

Event streams and backups: immutable logs and backups make physical deletion hard. Crypto-shredding helps: encrypt each person's data with a personal key, and delete the key, making the data unreadable everywhere. Backups that can't be edited are kept for limited periods, with deleted data not restored into live systems.

Conflicting obligations: in clinical trials, regulations require keeping trial data for many years, which can override deletion requests, and clinical data is usually pseudonymised, with identities held by the sites, not in the IRT. The legal and privacy teams define what can be deleted versus retained, and the system implements those rules.

p17-714.q: In active-active, both regions accept writes, and data replicates asynchronously between them. If the same record is changed in both regions before replication catches up, there's a conflict, and the system must decide what the final value is.
p17-714.k: active active conflicts, multi region writes, last writer wins, conflict resolution, crdt, multi master replication
x: In active-active, both regions accept writes, and data replicates asynchronously between them. If the same record is changed in both regions before replication catches up, there's a conflict, and the system must decide what the final value is.
Strategies.

Avoid conflicts by design: route all writes for a given entity to one home region, like by tenant or customer, so each record has a single writer at a time, while reads happen anywhere. This gives most of the availability benefits with few conflicts, and is often the most practical choice.

Last writer wins: the update with the latest timestamp wins. Simple, and built into databases like DynamoDB global tables and Cosmos DB by default, but it silently loses the other update, and depends on clock accuracy. Acceptable for data where losing a concurrent change doesn't matter, like a user's preferences.
Merge logic: application-specific resolution, like merging non-overlapping field changes, or a custom resolver in Cosmos DB.

CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types: data structures like counters, sets and maps designed so concurrent changes always merge to a consistent result, used for things like collaborative editing or distributed counters.
Record and escalate: keep both versions and flag the conflict for human resolution, appropriate for important business data.
For critical operations with strict invariants, like allocating a limited item, active-active writes are risky; a single primary region for those writes, with fast failover, is often safer.

p17-715.q: Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so it can keep serving the rest well. Without it, an overloaded service tries to handle everything, queues grow, every request becomes slow, timeouts cause client retries, and the system collapses for everyone.
p17-715.k: load shedding, admission control, shed load under overload, priority requests, graceful degradation overload
x: Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so it can keep serving the rest well. Without it, an overloaded service tries to handle everything, queues grow, every request becomes slow, timeouts cause client retries, and the system collapses for everyone.
How to implement it.

Concurrency limits: cap the number of requests processed at once, with a short queue; beyond that, return 503 or 429 immediately with Retry-After. ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware has a concurrency limiter for this, and Kestrel and IIS have connection and queue limits.
Queue time limits: if a request has waited too long to start, drop it, because the client has probably given up already. Processing it wastes capacity.

Prioritisation: not all requests are equal. Keep capacity for critical operations, like a patient randomisation or dispensing, and shed lower-priority work first, like reports, exports, bulk syncs and background refreshes. This can be done with separate limiters per endpoint class, or separate deployments for critical and non-critical traffic.
Adaptive limits: adjust the concurrency limit based on observed latency, growing when the system is healthy and shrinking when latency rises.
Client cooperation: clients should back off on 429 and 503, with exponential backoff and jitter, and not retry immediately.
Degradation: serve cached or simplified responses instead of full ones.
Load tests should show the system shedding load gracefully, not falling over.

p17-716.q: In distributed systems, a request often fans out to several backends, and the slowest one decides the total latency. Even if each backend is usually fast, occasional slow responses, from GC pauses, noisy neighbours or network hiccups, make the p99 latency much worse than the median. That's tail latency.
p17-716.k: hedged requests, tail latency, p99 latency reduction, speculative retry, backup requests
x: In distributed systems, a request often fans out to several backends, and the slowest one decides the total latency. Even if each backend is usually fast, occasional slow responses, from GC pauses, noisy neighbours or network hiccups, make the p99 latency much worse than the median. That's tail latency.

A hedged request sends the same request to a second replica if the first hasn't responded within a short delay, like the p95 latency of that call, and uses whichever response arrives first, cancelling the other. Because the delay is set at a high percentile, only a few percent of requests get hedged, so extra load is small, but the slow outliers are cut off.
Polly v8 has a hedging strategy, and the .NET resilience packages provide AddStandardHedgingHandler for HttpClient, which can also route the hedged request to a different endpoint.

When it's appropriate: read operations, or idempotent ones, because the request may execute twice. Never for non-idempotent writes without idempotency keys. And when the backend has multiple independent replicas, so the second attempt is likely to land somewhere healthier.
Risks: under overload, hedging adds load exactly when the system is struggling, so limit the number of hedged attempts and combine it with circuit breakers.
Other tail latency techniques: timeouts with fast fallbacks, reducing fan-out, caching, and fixing the cause of slow outliers, like GC pauses.

p17-717.q: At a visit, the system must assign the right kit to the patient: correct treatment, available at the site, not expired before the next visit, while keeping the blind and never double-assigning.
p17-717.k: design allocation service, kit allocation design, drug dispensing design, clinical supply allocation, assign kit to patient design
x: At a visit, the system must assign the right kit to the patient: correct treatment, available at the site, not expired before the next visit, while keeping the blind and never double-assigning.
Inputs: the subject, their treatment arm from randomisation, the visit and its dosing requirements from the study configuration, and the site's inventory.

Selection logic: filter the site's kits to those of the required kit type for the arm, in an available status, not quarantined or damaged, and with an expiry date beyond the next visit plus a configured buffer. Then choose by a rule, typically first-expiry-first-out to reduce waste. Several kits may be needed per visit.

Concurrency: two dispensing requests at the same site must not pick the same kit. Selection and status update happen atomically in one transaction, using row-level locking with UPDLOCK and READPAST, or a conditional update checking the status hasn't changed. An idempotency key per dispensing request prevents double allocation on retries.
Blinding: the response to the site shows only the kit number, never the treatment; kit numbering itself must not reveal the treatment.

Low stock: if no suitable kit exists, return a clear error to the site and alert supply management; separately, allocations feed resupply calculations, which trigger shipments when inventory drops below thresholds.
Audit: every allocation is recorded with who, when, which kit and why, including manual overrides with reasons and approvals.
Testing: simulation with many concurrent visits and edge cases around expiry, as part of validation.

p17-718.q: A hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows, that's fine. But as workflows grow longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, the custom state machine code becomes complex and fragile.
p17-718.k: workflow engine, temporal io, durable execution, orchestration engine vs custom saga, durable functions vs saga
x: A hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows, that's fine. But as workflows grow longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, the custom state machine code becomes complex and fragile.

Durable execution engines, like Temporal, Azure Durable Functions, AWS Step Functions, or newer .NET options, take over the hard parts. You write the workflow as ordinary code, or a definition for Step Functions: call activity A, wait for an approval signal for up to three days, then call B, and on failure run compensation. The engine persists every step's result, so if the process crashes, the workflow resumes exactly where it was. Retries with backoff, timeouts, timers lasting days or months, and visibility into each running workflow come built in.

When it's worth it: long-running business processes spanning hours to weeks; workflows with many steps, waits and human interaction; complex compensation logic; and when visibility into each instance's state is valuable for support and audit.

Trade-offs: a new platform to run or pay for, a learning curve, constraints like deterministic workflow code that can't call random or the current time directly, and versioning running workflows when the code changes.
For a two-step flow, a simple outbox and consumer is enough. For something like a multi-day approval and transfer process, an engine saves a lot of code and bugs.

p17-719.q: When a user calls API A, and API A must call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions, simply forwarding the user's token is a problem: the token's audience is API A, so B should reject it, and forwarding broad tokens everywhere increases the damage if one service is compromised.
p17-719.k: on behalf of flow, token exchange, obo flow, downstream api user context, delegated token microservices
x: When a user calls API A, and API A must call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions, simply forwarding the user's token is a problem: the token's audience is API A, so B should reject it, and forwarding broad tokens everywhere increases the damage if one service is compromised.

The on-behalf-of flow, in Entra ID, and the standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange, RFC 8693, supported by Keycloak and others, solve this. API A sends the incoming user token to the identity provider's token endpoint, authenticating as itself, and asks for a new token for API B. The identity provider checks that A is allowed to call B on behalf of users and issues a token with audience B, containing the user's identity, and often A's identity as the actor. A calls B with that token, and B validates it normally.

Benefits: each token is scoped to exactly one audience, so tokens can't be replayed against other services; downstream services see the real user and enforce their own authorisation; and the identity provider controls which services may delegate to which.

Alternatives: if B doesn't need the user's identity for authorisation, A can call B with its own client credentials token and pass the user id as context, with B trusting A. That's simpler but means B trusts A to have checked permissions.
I'd use token exchange when downstream authorisation depends on the user, and client credentials otherwise.

p17-720.q: In normal TLS, only the server presents a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, at the transport level, before any HTTP request is processed.
p17-720.k: mutual tls, mtls, client certificate authentication, certificate based auth api, two way ssl
x: In normal TLS, only the server presents a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, at the transport level, before any HTTP request is processed.

How it works: the server is configured to request client certificates and trusts a specific certificate authority. During the handshake, the client proves it holds the private key for its certificate. The server validates the certificate chain, expiry and revocation status, then maps the certificate, by thumbprint or subject, to a client identity. In ASP.NET Core, Kestrel's ClientCertificateMode and the certificate authentication handler do this; behind a load balancer or gateway that terminates TLS, the gateway validates the certificate and forwards details in a header, which the app must only trust from that gateway.
When I'd use it.
Service-to-service communication in a zero trust network, often automated through a service mesh, which issues and rotates certificates.
Partner and B2B integrations, where a partner system connects to our API: certificates are harder to steal and replay than API keys, and some industries require them.
Device authentication, like IoT devices or machines.
OAuth can also bind tokens to the client certificate, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.
The operational cost is certificate management: issuing, distributing, rotating before expiry, and revoking, so automation is essential.

p17-721.q: Both authenticate a system rather than a user, but they differ a lot in security properties.
p17-721.k: api keys vs oauth, partner api authentication, client credentials flow, api key security, machine to machine auth
x: Both authenticate a system rather than a user, but they differ a lot in security properties.

API keys are simple static secrets sent with each request, usually in a header. They're easy for partners to use, which is why they're popular. But they're long-lived, sent on every call, so any leak, in logs, proxies or code, gives access until someone notices and rotates them; they carry no scopes or expiry by themselves, unless the server implements that; and rotation needs coordination.

OAuth 2.0 client credentials: the partner authenticates to the token endpoint with its client id and a secret, or better, a private key JWT or certificate, and receives a short-lived access token with specific scopes, which it sends to the API. The long-lived credential is only sent to the identity provider, not to every API; access tokens expire in minutes; scopes limit what the partner can do; and the identity provider centralises management, rotation and revocation.

My choice: for anything sensitive, like clinical or personal data, or write operations, OAuth client credentials, ideally with private key JWT or mTLS for client authentication. API keys are acceptable for low-risk, read-only or public-ish APIs, or as an additional identifier for rate limiting and analytics alongside OAuth.
If API keys are used, I store only hashes, support multiple active keys for rotation, scope them, log usage per key, and allow fast revocation.

p17-722.q: An open redirect happens when an application takes a URL from user input, like a returnUrl parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links using our trusted domain: our-site.com/login?returnUrl=https://evil-site.com. The user sees our domain, logs in, and is sent to a fake page that might ask them to "log in again" and steal their credentials. In OAuth flows, open redirects can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.
p17-722.k: open redirect, returnurl validation, unvalidated redirect, redirect after login security, localredirect aspnet core
x: An open redirect happens when an application takes a URL from user input, like a returnUrl parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links using our trusted domain: our-site.com/login?returnUrl=https://evil-site.com. The user sees our domain, logs in, and is sent to a fake page that might ask them to "log in again" and steal their credentials. In OAuth flows, open redirects can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.
Prevention.

Only allow local redirects: in ASP.NET Core, Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl) checks that a URL is relative to our site, and LocalRedirect() throws if it isn't, which is what the default login templates use. Be careful with tricky inputs like //evil.com or /\evil.com, which some naive checks treat as local; the built-in helpers handle these.
Allowlists: if redirects to other domains are needed, like between our own applications, compare against an explicit list of allowed hosts, not a substring match.
Indirect references: instead of passing a URL, pass an identifier, like a page key, that the server maps to a URL.
For OAuth and OpenID Connect: register exact redirect URIs in the identity provider, with no wildcards, so codes can only go to our own applications.
Front-end code too: SPAs that read a redirect parameter from the URL and assign window.location need the same validation.
It's a small fix with big phishing protection value.

p17-723.q: Insecure deserialisation happens when an application turns untrusted data into objects using a serialiser that lets the data choose which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, leading to remote code execution.
p17-723.k: insecure deserialization, binaryformatter, typenamehandling, deserialization attack, json deserialization security
x: Insecure deserialisation happens when an application turns untrusted data into objects using a serialiser that lets the data choose which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, leading to remote code execution.
In .NET, the classic dangers.

BinaryFormatter: fundamentally unsafe with untrusted data, and Microsoft has removed it from .NET 9. Same for NetDataContractSerializer, SoapFormatter, LosFormatter and ObjectStateFormatter used without protection. Legacy .NET Framework apps may still use them, for example in caches, session state, or ViewState with MAC validation disabled.

Newtonsoft.Json with TypeNameHandling set to Auto, Objects or All: the JSON includes a $type property, and the serialiser creates whatever type it names. That's exploitable. Keep TypeNameHandling at None, or if polymorphism is really needed, use a strict SerializationBinder that only allows specific known types.

How I avoid it: use System.Text.Json, which doesn't instantiate arbitrary types; for polymorphic JSON, use its explicit JsonDerivedType attributes, which only allow declared types. Deserialise into specific DTOs, never object or dynamic. Treat any data from outside, including cookies, message queues and caches shared with other systems, as untrusted. Sign or encrypt serialised data that round-trips through clients, using Data Protection.
Scanning tools and analyzers flag dangerous serialiser use, which helps find it in large legacy codebases.

p17-724.q: Path traversal happens when user input is used to build a file path, and the attacker includes sequences like ../ to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint like /files?name=report.pdf becomes /files?name=../../web.config, and the server returns its own configuration, with connection strings. On upload, attackers might write files into executable locations.
p17-724.k: path traversal, directory traversal, dot dot slash attack, file download vulnerability, safe file paths
x: Path traversal happens when user input is used to build a file path, and the attacker includes sequences like ../ to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint like /files?name=report.pdf becomes /files?name=../../web.config, and the server returns its own configuration, with connection strings. On upload, attackers might write files into executable locations.
Prevention.

Don't use user input as a path at all, where possible: store files with server-generated names, like a GUID, and keep the original name only as metadata in the database. The user requests a file by id, the server checks authorisation and looks up the stored path.

If names must be used, validate strictly: take only the file name part with Path.GetFileName, reject names with path separators, .., drive letters or invalid characters, and use an allowlist of characters and extensions.

Canonicalise and check containment: combine the base folder with the name, get the full path with Path.GetFullPath, and verify it still starts with the base folder's full path, with a trailing separator, before accessing the file. That catches encoded tricks and different separator styles.
Least privilege: the application's identity should only have access to the folders it needs, read-only where possible, so a traversal can't reach sensitive files.
Better still, store files in object storage, like S3 or Blob Storage, with keys generated by the server, which removes the file system from the equation.
Archives need care too: extracting zip files with entries named ../something, called Zip Slip, is the same bug.

p17-725.q: Command injection happens when user input is included in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like ; rm -rf or && net user, which the shell executes. In .NET, it typically appears when code builds a command string for Process.Start with cmd.exe or bash, for example to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
p17-725.k: command injection, os command injection, process start security, shell injection, run external process safely
x: Command injection happens when user input is included in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like ; rm -rf or && net user, which the shell executes. In .NET, it typically appears when code builds a command string for Process.Start with cmd.exe or bash, for example to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
Prevention, in order of preference.
Avoid shelling out: use a library or API to do the job in-process, like an image library instead of calling a command-line tool.

If an external program is needed, don't use a shell. Start the executable directly with ProcessStartInfo, UseShellExecute false, and pass arguments through the ArgumentList collection, which passes each argument separately and handles quoting, so input can't break out into new commands. Never concatenate input into a single command string passed to cmd /c or bash -c.
Validate input strictly with an allowlist: if a parameter should be a file id or a known option, check it matches exactly, and map user choices to fixed values rather than passing raw input.
Watch for argument injection: even without a shell, input starting with a dash can be interpreted as an option by the target program; use -- to end options where supported, or validate.
Run the process with least privilege, a restricted account, a timeout, and in a sandbox or container where possible.
The same thinking applies to PowerShell scripts run from pipelines or automation: parameters, not string-built commands.

p17-726.q: XML External Entity attacks exploit XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. An attacker sends XML with an entity that refers to an external resource, like file:///c:/windows/win.ini or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content ends up in the parsed document, which may be returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests to internal systems, which is server-side request forgery. A related attack, the billion laughs or XML bomb, uses nested entities to expand a tiny document into gigabytes, exhausting memory.
p17-726.k: xxe, xml external entity, xml parsing security, dtd processing, xmlreader secure settings, xml bomb
x: XML External Entity attacks exploit XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. An attacker sends XML with an entity that refers to an external resource, like file:///c:/windows/win.ini or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content ends up in the parsed document, which may be returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests to internal systems, which is server-side request forgery. A related attack, the billion laughs or XML bomb, uses nested entities to expand a tiny document into gigabytes, exhausting memory.

In .NET: modern .NET, and .NET Framework 4.5.2 and later, have safe defaults for most XML APIs: XmlReader prohibits DTD processing by default, and XmlDocument doesn't resolve external resources by default in newer framework versions. But older code, and explicit settings, can reintroduce risk: setting DtdProcessing to Parse, using an XmlUrlResolver, or old XmlTextReader usage on .NET Framework versions before 4.5.2.

What I do: parse untrusted XML with XmlReader.Create and settings with DtdProcessing.Prohibit and XmlResolver null, which also stops entity expansion; set limits like MaxCharactersFromEntities and MaxCharactersInDocument; and validate against an expected schema where relevant.

This matters in integrations that receive XML files from partners, like older clinical data exchanges or SOAP services, which are common in legacy systems. Security scanners and analyzers flag unsafe XML settings, so I fix any findings in legacy code.

p17-727.q: SQL Server has several encryption options that protect against different threats.
p17-727.k: tde vs always encrypted, sql server encryption at rest, column level encryption, always encrypted, encrypt pii database
x: SQL Server has several encryption options that protect against different threats.

Transparent Data Encryption, TDE, encrypts the database files, logs and backups at rest. It's transparent to applications and protects against someone stealing the disks or backup files. But anyone who can query the database, including DBAs and the application, sees plain data. It's a baseline, and usually on by default in cloud databases.

Always Encrypted encrypts specific columns in the client driver, so data is encrypted before it leaves the application and stays encrypted in the database, in memory on the server and in backups. The keys are held by the client, in Key Vault or a certificate store, not by SQL Server. So DBAs and anyone with database access can't read those columns. The trade-off is that the server can't operate on encrypted data: deterministic encryption allows equality lookups, randomised encryption allows nothing. Secure enclaves extend this to some range comparisons and pattern matching. It needs driver support and careful key management.
Cell-level encryption with ENCRYPTBYKEY uses keys inside SQL Server, which gives control but means the server and its administrators can decrypt.
Application-level encryption: the app encrypts fields itself, with envelope encryption using a key management service. Flexible and database-independent.

My choice: TDE everywhere, plus TLS in transit; Always Encrypted or application-level encryption for a few highly sensitive columns, like personal identifiers, where restricting access even from administrators is required.

p17-728.q: Prevention isn't enough; we also need to notice attacks and misuse. That starts with the application logging the right security events.
p17-728.k: security monitoring, siem, security logging, detect attacks application, security events logging, audit security events
x: Prevention isn't enough; we also need to notice attacks and misuse. That starts with the application logging the right security events.

What I log, in structured form with user, source IP, time and correlation id: authentication successes and failures, MFA events, password and permission changes, access denied events, like 401s and 403s, especially repeated ones, input validation failures that look like attacks, admin actions, exports of sensitive data, configuration changes, and use of emergency or privileged functions. Never passwords, tokens or sensitive data in the logs themselves.

Where they go: a central log platform and, for security analysis, a SIEM, like Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk Enterprise Security or Elastic Security, which also collects identity provider logs, WAF logs, cloud audit logs, endpoint and network data.

Detection rules: many failed logins for one account or from one IP, logins from unusual countries or impossible travel, a user suddenly accessing many records or exporting lots of data, privilege escalation, access outside normal hours for admin functions, and patterns like SQL injection attempts in WAF logs. Alerts go to the security operations team with runbooks.
Integrity: security logs must be protected from tampering, sent off the server quickly, with restricted access, and retained according to policy.
Testing: during penetration tests or simulated attacks, check that the expected alerts fired, because detection that's never tested often doesn't work.

p17-729.q: Automated tools catch common patterns, but many real vulnerabilities are logic flaws that only a human reviewer sees. In a security-focused review, I go through a mental checklist.
p17-729.k: security code review, secure code review checklist, review for vulnerabilities, security review pull request
x: Automated tools catch common patterns, but many real vulnerabilities are logic flaws that only a human reviewer sees. In a security-focused review, I go through a mental checklist.

Authorisation: does every new endpoint have the right authorisation attribute or policy? Does it check that the user can access this specific record, not just that they're logged in? Are tenant or site filters applied consistently?

Input handling: is all external input validated, with types, lengths and allowed values? Any SQL built with string concatenation, raw HTML rendering, file paths, redirects or commands built from input?
Data exposure: do responses return only what's needed, or whole entities with internal fields? Are sensitive values excluded from logs and error messages?
Secrets and configuration: any hardcoded credentials, keys or connection strings? Are new settings secure by default?
Authentication and sessions: token handling, expiry, cookie flags, and changes to the auth pipeline.
Cryptography: standard libraries, no home-made crypto, no weak algorithms, randomness from secure generators.
Error handling: no stack traces to users, and failures fail closed, denying access rather than allowing it.
Dependencies: new packages, their trustworthiness and versions.
Concurrency and business logic: can actions be repeated, raced or done out of order to gain an advantage, like double-submitting or skipping a step?
For high-risk changes, like authentication or payment-like flows, I ask for a second reviewer with security experience, and threat-model the feature.

p17-730.q: A penetration test report usually contains findings rated by severity, like critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well is about triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.
p17-730.k: penetration test findings, pen test remediation, vulnerability remediation process, security findings triage, pentest report
x: A penetration test report usually contains findings rated by severity, like critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well is about triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.

Triage: for each finding, confirm it's valid in our context, understand the real risk, considering exploitability, data exposure and existing controls, and agree on the severity with the security team. Sometimes the tester's rating is adjusted, with justification, but I'm careful not to downplay findings just to avoid work.

Plan: each finding becomes a tracked work item with an owner and a deadline based on severity, like critical within days, high within a few weeks, per the security policy. Critical findings may need immediate mitigation, like a WAF rule or disabling a feature, before the code fix.

Fix the root cause, not just the instance: if the tester found an IDOR on one endpoint, review all endpoints for the same pattern; if they found missing output encoding in one place, find all similar places. Often a central fix, like a shared authorisation filter or a security header middleware, solves a whole class.
Add tests: an automated test that reproduces each finding, so it doesn't come back.
Verify: ask the testers to retest, or verify internally with evidence, and record the closure.
Learn: look at patterns across findings, and feed them into coding guidelines, review checklists, training and automated scans.
Accepted risks, if any, are documented and approved by the right people, with review dates.

p17-731.q: Zero trust means no implicit trust based on network location. The old model assumed everything inside the corporate network or VPN was trusted; once an attacker got in, they could move freely. Zero trust says: verify explicitly every time, use least privilege, and assume a breach has already happened.
p17-731.k: zero trust, zero trust architecture, never trust always verify, zero trust network, beyondcorp
x: Zero trust means no implicit trust based on network location. The old model assumed everything inside the corporate network or VPN was trusted; once an attacker got in, they could move freely. Zero trust says: verify explicitly every time, use least privilege, and assume a breach has already happened.
What it means in practice for applications.

Every request is authenticated and authorised, including internal service-to-service calls. Services verify tokens or mutual TLS identities, rather than trusting calls because they come from the internal network.
Strong identity for users and workloads: MFA and conditional access for users, managed or workload identities for services, and short-lived credentials everywhere.
Least privilege and just-in-time access: services get only the permissions they need; administrators get elevated access temporarily, with approval.

Micro-segmentation: network policies and security groups restrict which services can talk to which, so a compromised service can't reach everything, even though network controls are no longer the main defence.
Encryption in transit everywhere, including internal traffic.
Device and context awareness: access decisions consider device health, location and risk.
Continuous monitoring: log and analyse access, and detect anomalies.

For legacy systems that rely on network trust, like intranet apps with Windows authentication, zero trust is applied gradually: putting them behind an identity-aware proxy, adding MFA, and tightening network paths.

p17-732.q: Admin tools are high-value targets: they can change configuration, data and permissions for everyone. Yet they're often less protected, because they're "internal". I treat them as the most sensitive applications.
p17-732.k: secure admin tools, internal tools security, back office app security, admin panel security, privileged application
x: Admin tools are high-value targets: they can change configuration, data and permissions for everyone. Yet they're often less protected, because they're "internal". I treat them as the most sensitive applications.

Access: strong authentication through the company identity provider, with MFA, and conditional access, like requiring a managed device. No local accounts or shared logins. Access granted by role, with least privilege, and reviewed periodically. Privileged functions can require just-in-time elevation with approval.
Network: not exposed to the internet, or only through an identity-aware proxy or VPN, with IP restrictions. But not relying on the network alone.

Authorisation in depth: every action checked on the server, with fine-grained permissions for dangerous operations, like bulk changes or deleting data, possibly requiring a second person's approval, the four-eyes principle.
Safety: confirmation steps showing the impact before applying changes, like "this will affect 3 studies and 120 sites", dry-run modes, and the ability to undo.
Audit: every action logged with who, what, when, old and new values, and a reason where appropriate, stored where admins can't alter it.
Secure development: the same code review, scanning and testing as customer-facing apps, because internal tools are often built quickly and skip these.
Our admin console, used to configure studies, follows this thinking: role-based access, controlled promotion from build to UAT to production, and full audit of configuration changes.

p17-733.q: A break-glass account is an emergency account used only when normal access methods fail, like when the identity provider is down, MFA is broken, conditional access policies lock everyone out, or the usual administrators are unavailable during a critical incident.
p17-733.k: break glass account, emergency access account, emergency admin access, break glass procedure, privileged emergency access
x: A break-glass account is an emergency account used only when normal access methods fail, like when the identity provider is down, MFA is broken, conditional access policies lock everyone out, or the usual administrators are unavailable during a critical incident.
Because it's powerful and bypasses some normal controls, it needs strict management.

Setup: at least two emergency accounts, cloud-only so they don't depend on on-premise directory sync, excluded from conditional access policies that could lock them out, but protected with strong authentication, like FIDO2 security keys stored securely, or very long passwords split between people and stored in a safe.
Storage and access: credentials sealed in a physical safe or a secure vault, with access requiring more than one person, and documented procedures for when use is allowed.

Monitoring: any sign-in with a break-glass account triggers an immediate high-priority alert to the security team, because legitimate use is rare. Every use is followed by a review: why it was used, what was done, and then the credentials are rotated.
Testing: periodically verify the accounts still work, for example every few months, as a controlled exercise, otherwise you discover they're broken in the emergency.

The same principle applies to applications and databases: a documented, audited emergency access path for production data fixes during incidents, with approval and full logging, instead of developers keeping permanent production access "just in case".

p17-734.q: ReDoS is a denial of service caused by a regular expression that takes exponential time on certain inputs. Patterns with nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, like (a+)+$ or (\w+\s?)*$, can make the regex engine backtrack through an enormous number of combinations when the input almost matches but fails at the end. A short malicious string, a few dozen characters, can keep a CPU core busy for seconds or minutes. A handful of such requests can take down an API.
p17-734.k: redos, regex denial of service, catastrophic backtracking, regex timeout dotnet, nonbacktracking regex
x: ReDoS is a denial of service caused by a regular expression that takes exponential time on certain inputs. Patterns with nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, like (a+)+$ or (\w+\s?)*$, can make the regex engine backtrack through an enormous number of combinations when the input almost matches but fails at the end. A short malicious string, a few dozen characters, can keep a CPU core busy for seconds or minutes. A handful of such requests can take down an API.
Where it appears: validation of emails, URLs or names with home-made patterns, parsing log lines, and search features that accept user patterns.
Prevention in .NET.

Set timeouts: pass a TimeSpan to the Regex constructor, or set a default with the REGEX_DEFAULT_MATCH_TIMEOUT AppContext setting, so a pathological match throws RegexMatchTimeoutException instead of running forever.

Use RegexOptions.NonBacktracking, available since .NET 7, which uses an automata-based engine with linear-time guarantees, for patterns that don't need backtracking features like lookarounds and backreferences.
Write safer patterns: avoid nested quantifiers on overlapping groups, anchor patterns, and limit input length before matching.
Never run user-supplied patterns without these protections.
Use the source-generated regexes with GeneratedRegex for performance, combined with the above.
Static analysis tools and analyzers can flag risky patterns, and fuzz tests with long near-matching inputs catch them in testing.

p17-735.q: Files often contain the most sensitive data, like reports, exports and documents, and a common mistake is protecting the page that lists them but not the files themselves.
p17-735.k: secure file download, download authorization, signed url download, direct object reference files, protect documents access
x: Files often contain the most sensitive data, like reports, exports and documents, and a common mistake is protecting the page that lists them but not the files themselves.

Problems I look for: files stored in a public web folder or public bucket, reachable by anyone who knows or guesses the URL; predictable names, like report_1001.pdf, so changing the number reveals other users' files; and download endpoints that take an id without checking ownership.
Secure design.
Store files privately: outside the web root, or in object storage with no public access.

Serve through an authorised endpoint: GET /documents/{id} checks that the current user may access that document, based on its owner, site, study or tenant, then streams the file. Resource-based authorisation makes this check consistent.

Or issue short-lived signed URLs after the authorisation check: S3 pre-signed URLs or Azure SAS tokens valid for a few minutes, for one specific file, read-only. That offloads the transfer from the API while keeping control.
Use unguessable ids, like GUIDs, as an extra layer, though never as the only protection.
Set the right headers: Content-Disposition attachment for downloads to prevent rendering active content in the browser, correct Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options nosniff.
Audit downloads of sensitive documents: who downloaded what and when.
Expire and clean up temporary files, like generated exports, after a period.

p17-736.q: Password reset is a favourite attack path because it bypasses the password entirely. A secure flow looks like this.
p17-736.k: password reset security, forgot password flow, reset token security, account recovery, password reset best practices
x: Password reset is a favourite attack path because it bypasses the password entirely. A secure flow looks like this.

Request: the user enters their email. The response is always the same, like "if an account exists, we've sent a link", whether or not the account exists, so attackers can't use it to discover registered emails. Rate-limit requests per account and per IP.

Token: generate a long, random, single-use token from a cryptographically secure generator, store only its hash, linked to the user, with a short expiry, like 15 to 60 minutes. ASP.NET Core Identity's token providers handle this, and tokens become invalid if the user's security stamp changes.

Link: sent to the registered email address only, never to an address provided in the request; using HTTPS, and avoiding leaking the token through referrer headers by not loading third-party resources on the reset page.

Reset: verify the token, require a strong new password, checked against breached password lists, then invalidate the token, invalidate all existing sessions and refresh tokens, and notify the user by email that their password changed.
MFA: if the account has MFA, the reset shouldn't silently bypass it; require the second factor during reset or after.
Logging and monitoring: record reset requests and completions, and alert on unusual volumes.
In enterprise setups with SSO, like Keycloak or Entra ID, the identity provider owns this flow, and the application just links to it, which is better than building our own.

p17-737.q: Account enumeration means an attacker can find out which usernames or emails are registered, by watching how the application responds. With a list of valid accounts, credential stuffing and targeted phishing become much more effective.
p17-737.k: username enumeration, account enumeration, user enumeration login, login error messages security, registration enumeration
x: Account enumeration means an attacker can find out which usernames or emails are registered, by watching how the application responds. With a list of valid accounts, credential stuffing and targeted phishing become much more effective.
Where it leaks.
Login: "user not found" versus "wrong password" messages. Fix: one generic message, like "invalid username or password".
Password reset: "no account with that email" versus "email sent". Fix: always respond the same way.

Registration: "this email is already registered". Harder to avoid; options include sending an email to the address instead, saying "you already have an account", while the screen shows a neutral confirmation.

Timing: even with identical messages, the response may be faster for unknown users, because no password hash is computed. Fix: perform equivalent work, like hashing against a dummy hash, so timing is similar.
Other signals: different HTTP status codes, response sizes, or account lockout messages that only appear for real accounts.
APIs: endpoints like /users/{email}/exists, or profile lookups, that confirm existence to unauthenticated callers.
Complementary defences: rate limiting and bot detection on these endpoints, CAPTCHA after repeated attempts, and monitoring for enumeration patterns, like many different usernames from one source.
There's a usability trade-off, so for internal enterprise apps using SSO, the identity provider handles most of this; for public-facing apps, I follow these practices fully.

p17-738.q: Keycloak puts roles into access tokens in its own structure: realm roles under realm_access.roles, and client roles under resource_access, keyed by client id, then roles. ASP.NET Core's role checks, like the Authorize attribute with Roles, or User.IsInRole, look for role claims with a specific claim type, so out of the box they don't see Keycloak's nested roles.
p17-738.k: keycloak roles aspnet core, realm roles client roles, map keycloak claims, keycloak jwt roles, resource_access roles
x: Keycloak puts roles into access tokens in its own structure: realm roles under realm_access.roles, and client roles under resource_access, keyed by client id, then roles. ASP.NET Core's role checks, like the Authorize attribute with Roles, or User.IsInRole, look for role claims with a specific claim type, so out of the box they don't see Keycloak's nested roles.
How I connect them.

Claims transformation: implement IClaimsTransformation, which runs after authentication. It reads the realm_access and resource_access JSON from the token, extracts roles for our client, and adds them as role claims to the ClaimsPrincipal. Then normal role checks and policies work.

Alternatively, configure a protocol mapper in Keycloak to put roles in a flat claim, like roles, and set RoleClaimType in the JWT bearer options to that claim name. That moves the mapping into Keycloak configuration, which keeps application code simple.

Policies on top: rather than checking raw role names everywhere, define authorisation policies, like CanManageShipments, which map to one or more roles, and use those in controllers. Roles can then change in Keycloak without code changes.

Fine-grained data permissions, like which sites or studies a user can access, often come from the application's own database rather than the token, because they change frequently and can be large. A claims transformation or authorisation handler can load them with caching.
I also make sure role names and the mapping are tested, with test tokens containing Keycloak's structure, so a configuration change doesn't silently remove access.

p17-739.q: Windows authentication lets users on domain-joined machines sign in to intranet apps automatically with their Windows login, no password prompt. IIS, or ASP.NET Core with the Negotiate handler, supports it.
p17-739.k: windows authentication, kerberos vs ntlm, intranet authentication iis, negotiate authentication, integrated windows auth
x: Windows authentication lets users on domain-joined machines sign in to intranet apps automatically with their Windows login, no password prompt. IIS, or ASP.NET Core with the Negotiate handler, supports it.

It uses two protocols. Kerberos is the preferred one: the browser gets a service ticket from the domain controller for the web application's service principal name, and presents it to the server, which validates it without contacting the domain controller each time. It supports delegation, so the app can call another service, like SQL Server, as the user, if constrained delegation is configured. It requires correct SPNs registered for the service account, and the client must reach the domain controller.

NTLM is the fallback, used when Kerberos isn't possible, like when accessing by IP address or when SPNs are missing. It's a challenge-response protocol, weaker, doesn't support delegation, and is being deprecated by Microsoft.

Limits: it only works well for domain-joined devices inside the corporate network; external users, mobile devices and other platforms struggle. It doesn't fit cloud and SaaS scenarios, it ties the app to Active Directory, and it's hard to combine with modern MFA and conditional access. Proxies and load balancers can break NTLM because it's connection-based.

For modern applications, I'd use OpenID Connect against an identity provider, like Entra ID or Keycloak, which can itself use Kerberos for seamless sign-in on the corporate network, while supporting MFA, external access and token-based APIs.

p17-740.q: Reflection lets code inspect and use types at runtime: list a type's properties, methods and attributes, read or set property values by name, call methods dynamically, and create instances with Activator.CreateInstance. A lot of framework magic is built on it: ASP.NET Core model binding and controller discovery, dependency injection containers, serialisers, ORMs like EF Core and Dapper mapping columns to properties, and test frameworks finding test methods.
p17-740.k: reflection c#, system reflection, gettype getproperties, reflection performance, activator createinstance
x: Reflection lets code inspect and use types at runtime: list a type's properties, methods and attributes, read or set property values by name, call methods dynamically, and create instances with Activator.CreateInstance. A lot of framework magic is built on it: ASP.NET Core model binding and controller discovery, dependency injection containers, serialisers, ORMs like EF Core and Dapper mapping columns to properties, and test frameworks finding test methods.
The costs.

Performance: reflective calls are much slower than direct calls, because of lookups, security checks, boxing of arguments and lack of inlining. Doing GetProperties and PropertyInfo.GetValue in a hot loop, for every row or request, can be a real bottleneck.
Type safety: errors that the compiler would catch, like a renamed property, only appear at runtime.
Trimming and Native AOT: the trimmer can't see what reflection will use, so it may remove needed code, and AOT doesn't support some dynamic features at all.

How I reduce the cost: cache reflection results, like PropertyInfo arrays, per type in a static dictionary; compile expression trees or create delegates once with Delegate.CreateDelegate, then call those fast delegates; and, best of all, use source generators to produce the code at compile time, which is what System.Text.Json, the logging generator and regex generator do.

In our projects, I'd use reflection for startup-time work, like scanning assemblies to register handlers or plugins, and avoid it in per-request paths, where a generated or cached approach is much faster.

p17-741.q: These all run work in parallel, but they suit different kinds of work.
p17-741.k: parallel foreach, parallel foreachasync, plinq, asparallel, cpu bound vs io bound parallelism
x: These all run work in parallel, but they suit different kinds of work.

Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach are for CPU-bound work on in-memory data, like processing thousands of records with calculations. They split the work across thread pool threads and block the calling thread until done. MaxDegreeOfParallelism controls how many run at once, usually around the number of cores.

PLINQ, with AsParallel(), does the same for LINQ queries: filtering, projecting and aggregating large in-memory collections across cores. Order isn't preserved unless you add AsOrdered. Good for data-parallel queries, but overhead makes it slower for small collections or cheap operations.

Task.WhenAll is for I/O-bound async work, like calling several APIs or databases at once. You start the tasks and await them together; no threads are blocked while waiting. But starting thousands of tasks at once can overwhelm the downstream service or exhaust connections.

Parallel.ForEachAsync, since .NET 6, combines both: it runs an async delegate for each item with a limit on concurrency, like processing 500 files with at most 8 uploads at a time. That's my default for "many I/O operations with throttling", instead of hand-writing SemaphoreSlim logic.

Rules of thumb: CPU-bound use Parallel or PLINQ; I/O-bound use async with WhenAll or ForEachAsync; never use Parallel.ForEach with async lambdas, because it treats them as async void and doesn't wait for them; and in ASP.NET Core request handling, avoid heavy CPU parallelism, because requests already share the thread pool.

p17-742.q: The Mediator pattern reduces direct dependencies between objects by having them communicate through a mediator. In .NET APIs, it's usually applied through a library like MediatR: a controller doesn't call a service directly; it sends a request object, like CreateShipmentCommand, and the mediator finds the one handler for that request type and calls it.
p17-742.k: mediator pattern, mediatr, pipeline behavior, ipipelinebehavior, request handler pattern
x: The Mediator pattern reduces direct dependencies between objects by having them communicate through a mediator. In .NET APIs, it's usually applied through a library like MediatR: a controller doesn't call a service directly; it sends a request object, like CreateShipmentCommand, and the mediator finds the one handler for that request type and calls it.
Benefits: controllers become thin, each use case is a separate handler class with its own dependencies, which fits vertical slices and CQRS, and handlers are easy to test.

Pipeline behaviours are the most useful part. They wrap every request, like middleware for use cases. A behaviour receives the request and a next delegate, can run code before and after, and can short-circuit. Typical behaviours: validation, running FluentValidation validators and returning errors before the handler runs; logging and timing each request; transactions, wrapping commands in a database transaction; caching for queries; authorisation checks; and retry or idempotency for commands. They're registered once and apply to all handlers, or to specific request types through generic constraints.

Trade-offs: an extra layer of indirection makes navigation harder, since you can't just jump from controller to service; it adds some overhead; and for small apps it can be over-engineering. Also, recent MediatR versions moved to a commercial licence, so some teams use alternatives or a small hand-written dispatcher.
I like the pattern for medium to large APIs with many use cases and cross-cutting concerns, and I keep it simple: one request, one handler, behaviours for cross-cutting work.

p17-743.q: C# lets a type define how operators like +, -, == and < work with it, through static operator methods. For example, a Money type can define operator + to add two amounts, checking they have the same currency, or a Vector type can define arithmetic. When you overload ==, you must also overload !=, and override Equals and GetHashCode consistently; comparison operators come in pairs too.
p17-743.k: operator overloading c#, implicit operator, explicit operator, user defined conversion, value object operators
x: C# lets a type define how operators like +, -, == and < work with it, through static operator methods. For example, a Money type can define operator + to add two amounts, checking they have the same currency, or a Vector type can define arithmetic. When you overload ==, you must also overload !=, and override Equals and GetHashCode consistently; comparison operators come in pairs too.

Conversion operators define how a type converts to or from another type. An implicit conversion happens automatically, like assigning a ShipmentId to a Guid variable, and should only be used when it can never fail and loses no information. An explicit conversion requires a cast, like (Celsius)fahrenheitValue, and is for conversions that might fail, lose precision or surprise the reader.

Where I find them useful: value objects and strongly typed ids, like ShipmentId wrapping a Guid, where an explicit conversion from Guid prevents accidentally mixing up different ids, while an implicit conversion to Guid makes it easy to pass to data access code. Also mathematical or measurement types.

Cautions: don't overload operators with meanings that surprise people, like using + for something that isn't addition; avoid implicit conversions that hide expensive work or possible exceptions; and remember that operators are static and resolved at compile time, so they don't behave polymorphically through base types or interfaces, except with static abstract interface members and generic math in newer C#.
Records give you == and != for value equality automatically.

p17-744.q: I try to use newer language features where they make code clearer, not just because they're new. The ones I use regularly:
p17-744.k: new c# features, c# 12 features, collection expressions, raw string literals, list patterns, c# 11 features
x: I try to use newer language features where they make code clearer, not just because they're new. The ones I use regularly:

Collection expressions, C# 12: square-bracket syntax to create arrays and lists with values, an empty list with just empty brackets, and the spread operator with two dots to combine collections. One syntax for arrays, lists, spans and immutable collections, and the compiler picks an efficient implementation.
Raw string literals, C# 11: triple quotes let me write JSON, SQL or XML snippets in tests and templates without escaping quotes, and with interpolation using $$ when the content has braces.

Pattern matching improvements: switch expressions, property patterns like order is { Status: "Shipped", Total: > 1000 }, relational and logical patterns like >= 0 and < 100, and list patterns, C# 11, which match on the first and last elements or on a single-element list, and are handy for parsing arguments or messages.
Records and with-expressions for DTOs and immutable values; required members and init setters for safe object construction; primary constructors, C# 12, for simple classes and DI.
File-scoped namespaces and global usings, which reduce noise; nullable reference types enabled for all new projects.
Smaller ones: target-typed new, the null-coalescing assignment ??=, and the field keyword in C# 14 for properties with simple backing logic.

Because our legacy projects are on .NET Framework 4.8 with older C# versions, these features are available mainly in our newer .NET 8 services, which is one of the small productivity wins we point to when making the case for migration.

p17-745.q: .NET has a garbage collector, but leaks still happen whenever objects stay reachable when they shouldn't. The GC can't collect anything that something still references.
p17-745.k: memory leak dotnet, managed memory leak, event handler leak, find memory leak, dotnet-gcdump
x: .NET has a garbage collector, but leaks still happen whenever objects stay reachable when they shouldn't. The GC can't collect anything that something still references.
Common causes.

Event handlers: subscribing to a long-lived object's event, like a static event or a singleton service, from a short-lived object, and never unsubscribing. The publisher holds a reference to the subscriber forever.
Static collections and caches without limits: a static dictionary that only grows, or an in-memory cache with no size limit or expiration.
Captive dependencies: a singleton holding scoped or transient objects, which then live forever.
Timers and background tasks referencing objects they never release.
Unmanaged resources not disposed, like streams, database connections or native handles, which also leak memory outside the managed heap.
Closures and lambdas capturing large objects unintentionally, and held by long-lived delegates.
HttpClient created per request, leaking sockets rather than memory.

Finding them: watch the trend, with dotnet-counters or metrics showing GC heap size growing after each full GC, rather than levelling off. Take two memory snapshots some time apart, with dotnet-gcdump or a full dump with dotnet-dump, and compare them in Visual Studio, PerfView or another memory profiler: which types increased in count, and what's the retention path, meaning the chain of references keeping them alive. That path usually points straight to the event subscription or static collection responsible.
Fixes follow the cause: unsubscribe or use weak events, bound caches, fix lifetimes, and dispose properly.

p17-746.q: Most code only needs List, Dictionary and HashSet, but knowing the others helps choose the right tool.
p17-746.k: priorityqueue c#, sorteddictionary, sortedset, linkedlist c#, queue and stack c#, specialised collections
x: Most code only needs List, Dictionary and HashSet, but knowing the others helps choose the right tool.
Queue<T> and Stack<T>: first-in-first-out and last-in-first-out, with O(1) enqueue and dequeue or push and pop. Queues for processing work in order, stacks for undo or depth-first traversal.

PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>, since .NET 6: a min-heap where Dequeue always returns the item with the lowest priority value, in O(log n). Useful for scheduling, like processing the most urgent jobs first, merging sorted streams, or algorithms like Dijkstra's shortest path. It's not thread-safe and doesn't support updating priorities directly.

SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> keeps keys sorted, using a red-black tree, with O(log n) operations; good when you insert and remove frequently and need ordered iteration. SortedList is similar but array-based, using less memory and faster for lookups but slower for inserts. SortedSet gives a sorted unique set with range queries, like GetViewBetween.

LinkedList<T>: a doubly linked list with O(1) insertion and removal when you already have the node, used for LRU caches combined with a dictionary. In general it's slower than List because of poor memory locality, so I rarely use it otherwise.
Concurrent collections for multi-threading: ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentBag, BlockingCollection, and Channels for async producer-consumer.
Immutable and frozen collections for shared read-only data.
Choosing correctly turns O(n) scans into O(log n) or O(1) operations, which matters at scale.

p17-747.q: Attributes add metadata to code: classes, methods, properties, parameters. They don't do anything by themselves; some other code reads them and acts on them. Frameworks use them everywhere: Authorize, HttpGet, Required, JsonPropertyName, and test attributes like Fact.
p17-747.k: custom attributes c#, create attribute, read attributes reflection, attribute usage, metadata attributes
x: Attributes add metadata to code: classes, methods, properties, parameters. They don't do anything by themselves; some other code reads them and acts on them. Frameworks use them everywhere: Authorize, HttpGet, Required, JsonPropertyName, and test attributes like Fact.

Creating one: a class that inherits from Attribute, named with the Attribute suffix by convention, like AuditedAttribute, with an AttributeUsage attribute saying where it can be applied, like methods or classes, whether it can appear multiple times, and whether it's inherited. Constructor parameters and public properties become the attribute's arguments, and they must be compile-time constants, like strings, numbers, enums or types.

Reading it: through reflection, with GetCustomAttribute<AuditedAttribute>() on a type, method or property. In ASP.NET Core, endpoint metadata makes this easy: a middleware or filter can check context.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<AuditedAttribute>() and act, for example writing an audit record only for endpoints marked with the Audited attribute, or applying a specific rate-limit policy.

Examples I've used: marking endpoints that need audit logging, marking properties that contain sensitive data so logging and serialisation can mask them, and marking handler classes for automatic registration.

Considerations: reading attributes through reflection has a cost, so cache results; for performance-critical or AOT scenarios, source generators can read attributes at compile time and generate code instead. And I don't hide important business logic in attributes, because it makes behaviour less obvious to readers.

p17-748.q: An immutable object can't change after it's created. Any "change" produces a new object. This makes code easier to reason about, because nothing can modify an object behind your back, it's naturally thread-safe, and it's safe to use as a dictionary key or share in caches.
p17-748.k: immutable types c#, immutability c#, immutable class, readonly properties, record with expression
x: An immutable object can't change after it's created. Any "change" produces a new object. This makes code easier to reason about, because nothing can modify an object behind your back, it's naturally thread-safe, and it's safe to use as a dictionary key or share in caches.
How I build them in C#.

Records are the simplest: positional records, like record Address(string Street, string City), have init-only properties, value equality, and with-expressions to create modified copies, like address with { City = "Pune" }.

For classes: properties with get only or init, set through the constructor or object initialisers, and required members to ensure they're set; fields marked readonly; no methods that modify state; methods that return new instances instead, like Money.Add returning a new Money.

Watch out for shallow immutability: a record with a List<string> property is not truly immutable, because the list can still be changed. Use IReadOnlyList with a copy, ImmutableArray or ImmutableList, or FrozenSet for collection properties, and copy incoming collections in the constructor.
readonly struct for small value types guarantees all fields are read-only.

Where I use immutability: value objects in the domain, like Money, DateRange or strongly typed ids; DTOs and messages, which shouldn't change after creation; configuration snapshots; and state in front-end code, like Redux, where the same idea applies.
The cost is more allocations when changing objects frequently, which is rarely an issue in business code, but matters in tight loops.

p17-749.q: .NET has several timers, which causes confusion.
p17-749.k: periodictimer, system threading timer, system timers timer, timers in dotnet, run code every n seconds
x: .NET has several timers, which causes confusion.

System.Threading.Timer: a lightweight timer that calls a callback on a thread pool thread at intervals. Callbacks can overlap if one takes longer than the interval, exceptions in callbacks are unhandled and can crash the process, and you must keep a reference so it isn't garbage collected.
System.Timers.Timer: a wrapper with an Elapsed event and AutoReset property; it swallows exceptions from handlers, which hides errors, and also allows overlapping callbacks. Mostly legacy.
UI timers, like the Windows Forms and WPF dispatcher timers, run on the UI thread, for desktop apps only.

PeriodicTimer, since .NET 6, is designed for async code: you write a loop, while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken)) { await DoWorkAsync(); }. Ticks never overlap, because the next wait only starts after the work finishes; exceptions are handled in normal async code; and cancellation is built in. This is my default inside a BackgroundService for periodic jobs, like polling an outbox table or refreshing a cache.
For testability, TimeProvider in .NET 8 can create timers, so tests can control time.

For schedules more complex than fixed intervals, like "every weekday at 2 AM", or jobs that must survive restarts and run once across multiple instances, I use a scheduler like Quartz.NET or Hangfire instead of a raw timer, which is how our alert watchdog runs scheduled checks.

p17-750.q: Compilers, the JIT and CPUs are allowed to reorder memory reads and writes, and to cache values in registers, as long as single-threaded behaviour is unchanged. In multi-threaded code, this means one thread may not see another thread's writes when expected, or may see them in a different order.
p17-750.k: volatile keyword c#, memory model dotnet, memory barrier, instruction reordering, volatile read write
x: Compilers, the JIT and CPUs are allowed to reorder memory reads and writes, and to cache values in registers, as long as single-threaded behaviour is unchanged. In multi-threaded code, this means one thread may not see another thread's writes when expected, or may see them in a different order.

The .NET memory model defines what's guaranteed. volatile on a field makes reads have acquire semantics and writes have release semantics: a volatile read always reads the current value from memory, and operations after it can't be moved before it; a volatile write makes all earlier writes visible before it. A classic use is a stop flag: private volatile bool _stopRequested; one thread sets it, and a worker loop checks it, without the JIT hoisting the read out of the loop and spinning forever.

What volatile doesn't do: it doesn't make compound operations atomic. count++ on a volatile field is still a read-modify-write race; Interlocked.Increment is needed for that. It also doesn't give full ordering between a write followed by a read.

In practice, I rarely use volatile directly. Higher-level tools are clearer and safer: lock, which includes full memory barriers; Interlocked for atomic updates; Volatile.Read and Volatile.Write methods for explicit cases; CancellationToken for stop signals instead of a volatile bool; and concurrent collections, Lazy<T> and Channels for coordination.
Knowing the memory model mainly helps me recognise subtle bugs in lock-free code, and avoid writing it unless really necessary.

p17-751.q: TaskCompletionSource<T> lets you create a Task that you complete manually. You give the Task property to callers, who await it, and later your code calls SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled, or the Try versions, to complete it.
