x: TaskCompletionSource<T> lets you create a Task that you complete manually. You give the Task property to callers, who await it, and later your code calls SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled, or the Try versions, to complete it.
Where it's useful.

Wrapping callback or event-based APIs into async ones: an older library raises a Completed event; you subscribe, and in the handler you call tcs.SetResult(value). The method returns tcs.Task, so callers can just await it.

Request-response over messaging: when sending a request over a message queue or WebSocket and waiting for a reply with a matching correlation id, store a TaskCompletionSource in a dictionary keyed by the id; when the response arrives, find it and complete it. Combine with a timeout and cancellation, and remove the entry afterwards.
Signals between components: one part waits until another part reaches a state, like "service is ready".
Testing: controlling exactly when a fake async dependency completes.

Important detail: create it with TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously. Otherwise, when you call SetResult, the awaiting code's continuation can run synchronously on your thread, inside your lock or event handler, which can cause deadlocks or unexpected re-entrancy.
Also make sure every path completes it, including errors and cancellation, by registering a cancellation callback that calls TrySetCanceled; otherwise awaiting code waits forever.

p17-752.q: The .NET garbage collector has modes tuned for different kinds of applications.
p17-752.k: server gc vs workstation gc, gc modes dotnet, concurrent gc, background gc, dotnet gc settings
x: The .NET garbage collector has modes tuned for different kinds of applications.

Workstation GC is designed for desktop and client apps. It uses a single heap and collects on the thread that triggered the collection, with lower memory usage, so it's friendly to machines running many processes.

Server GC is designed for high-throughput server apps. It creates a separate heap and a dedicated GC thread per CPU core, so allocations scale across cores and collections run in parallel, finishing faster. It uses more memory, because each heap has its own budget. ASP.NET Core apps use Server GC by default.
Both can run with concurrent, or background, GC enabled, which is the default: full, generation 2 collections mostly run in the background while application threads continue, reducing pauses.
Why it matters in practice.

Containers: with Server GC on a machine with many cores but a small memory limit, heap counts and memory usage can surprise you. .NET respects container CPU and memory limits, and you can tune with settings like GCHeapCount, GCHeapHardLimit, or the newer DATAS mode, dynamic adaptation to application sizes, on by default in .NET 9 for Server GC, which adjusts heap count to load and reduces memory for small apps.
Many small services on one host: Workstation GC, or DATAS, may be better to save memory.
Latency-sensitive work: GC latency modes, like SustainedLowLatency, can reduce blocking collections during critical periods.
I don't change GC settings by guess; I measure with dotnet-counters, looking at GC pause time, heap size and allocation rate, and then adjust.

In hot paths, like per-message processing in a busy consumer, this adds allocations and CPU.

LoggerMessage solves it. The modern way is the source generator: you declare a static partial method, like LogProcessed(ILogger logger, int count, string studyId), with the LoggerMessage attribute, giving an event id, a level like Information, and the message template "Processed {Count} items for {StudyId}". The generator writes an optimised implementation at compile time: it checks whether the level is enabled before doing any work, avoids boxing with strongly typed parameters, and pre-parses the template.

Benefits beyond speed: strongly typed log methods give consistent event ids and messages across the codebase, which makes searching and alerting in Splunk or Grafana easier; parameter names are checked at compile time; and log calls in business code read cleanly, like _logger.LogProcessed(count, studyId), when written as extension methods.
When I use it: libraries, high-volume paths like message handlers, middleware and data processing loops. For rare log statements, like startup messages, regular calls are fine.
I also avoid string interpolation in log calls, because it builds the string even when the level is off, and loses structured properties.

p17-754.q: There are a few ways to sort objects in C#, and the differences matter.
p17-754.k: icomparable, icomparer, sort custom objects c#, orderby thenby, stable sort c#
x: There are a few ways to sort objects in C#, and the differences matter.

IComparable<T> defines a type's natural order: the type implements CompareTo, returning negative, zero or positive. For example, a Version or Money type that has an obvious order. Then List.Sort() and SortedSet use it automatically.

IComparer<T> defines an order outside the type, so you can have several: by name, by date, by priority. You pass it to Sort, OrderBy, or sorted collections. Comparer<T>.Create(lambda) builds one quickly, and StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase is a built-in comparer for strings.

LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy: the most readable for most business code, like shipments.OrderBy(s => s.Priority).ThenByDescending(s => s.CreatedAt). It returns a new sequence, and it's a stable sort, meaning items with equal keys keep their original order.

List.Sort and Array.Sort sort in place and are faster with less allocation, but they're unstable: equal items can be reordered. If stability matters, like sorting a table by one column while keeping a previous order, use OrderBy or add a tie-breaker key, like an id.

Common mistakes: inconsistent comparers that don't follow the rules, like returning random results or not handling nulls, which can cause exceptions or wrong results; subtracting integers in CompareTo, which can overflow, instead of using CompareTo on the values; and culture-sensitive string sorting where ordinal is intended.
For data from a database, I sort in the SQL query, with a deterministic tie-breaker, especially for pagination.

p17-755.q: var and dynamic look similar but are completely different. var is static typing: the compiler infers the type at compile time, and you get full type checking and IntelliSense. object is also static: you need casts to use its members.
p17-755.k: dynamic keyword c#, dynamic vs var vs object, dlr, dynamic language runtime, expandoobject
x: var and dynamic look similar but are completely different. var is static typing: the compiler infers the type at compile time, and you get full type checking and IntelliSense. object is also static: you need casts to use its members.

dynamic switches off compile-time type checking for that variable. Member access, method calls and operators are resolved at runtime by the Dynamic Language Runtime. If the member doesn't exist, you get a RuntimeBinderException at runtime instead of a compile error.
Where it's appropriate.
COM interop, like automating Office, where APIs are loosely typed; dynamic made this much simpler.
Interop with dynamic languages, like IronPython.
Working with truly dynamic data structures, like ExpandoObject, or dynamic JSON in some scenarios, though System.Text.Json's JsonNode or JsonDocument are usually better choices.
Some reflection-heavy scenarios, where dynamic is shorter than reflection code, like calling a generic method with a runtime type, which uses dynamic dispatch to pick the right overload.

Why I avoid it in normal code: no compile-time safety, so typos and refactoring mistakes become runtime errors; slower than static calls, though the DLR caches call sites; no IntelliSense; and it's not compatible with trimming and Native AOT.

In business applications and APIs, I prefer strong types, DTOs and generics. If I see dynamic in a code review outside interop scenarios, I usually ask whether a proper type or JsonNode would be clearer.

p17-756.q: Access modifiers control which code can use a type or member.
p17-756.k: access modifiers c#, protected internal, private protected, internal vs public, file access modifier
x: Access modifiers control which code can use a type or member.
public: accessible from anywhere.
private: only within the same class or struct. The default for members.
protected: within the class and derived classes, even in other assemblies.
internal: anywhere within the same assembly, but not from other assemblies. The default for top-level types.
protected internal: accessible from the same assembly, or from derived classes in any assembly. It's an OR of protected and internal.
private protected, since C# 7.2: accessible only from derived classes that are in the same assembly. It's an AND of protected and internal.
file, since C# 11: a type visible only within the same source file, mainly useful for source generators and helper types.
How I use them in practice.

Default to the most restrictive access, and open up only when needed. In a library or shared NuGet package, everything not intended as public API is internal, which lets us change implementations without breaking consumers.
InternalsVisibleTo lets a test project see internal types, so I don't have to make things public only for tests, though I prefer testing through public behaviour.
In clean architecture solutions, keeping infrastructure implementations internal and exposing only interfaces and a registration extension method enforces boundaries.
sealed alongside access modifiers prevents unintended inheritance.
Interviewers often ask the difference between protected internal and private protected; I remember them as OR versus AND.

p17-757.q: A shallow copy creates a new object, but copies references for reference-type fields, so the copy and the original share nested objects. Changing a nested list in the copy also changes it in the original. A deep copy duplicates the nested objects too, so the copies are fully independent.

MemberwiseClone: a protected method on object that creates a shallow copy. You can call it from a Clone method in your class.
Records with with-expressions: also shallow. order with { Status = "Shipped" } copies the top-level values, but a List property is shared.
ICloneable: an old interface that doesn't specify shallow or deep, so it's not recommended for public APIs.
For deep copies:

Manual copy methods or copy constructors: the most explicit and fastest; each class copies its own nested objects, like new Order(other) creating new item objects. Safe, but must be maintained when properties are added.

Serialisation round-trip: serialise to JSON with System.Text.Json and deserialise into a new object. Simple and generic, but slower, and it only copies serialisable data, losing private state, references and cycles unless configured.
Mapping libraries or source-generated mappers can also produce copies.

Often the best answer is to avoid needing deep copies: make objects immutable, so they can be shared safely, and use immutable collections. Then "changing" means creating a new version, and there's no risk of accidental shared mutation.

p17-758.q: The Proxy pattern puts a stand-in object in front of a real object, implementing the same interface, to control access to it. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a proxy. The proxy can add behaviour before or after forwarding the call.

x: The Proxy pattern puts a stand-in object in front of a real object, implementing the same interface, to control access to it. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a proxy. The proxy can add behaviour before or after forwarding the call.

Common kinds: a virtual proxy delays creating an expensive object until it's needed, like lazy loading; a protection proxy checks permissions before calling; a remote proxy represents an object in another process, like a generated gRPC or WCF client; and a caching or logging proxy adds those concerns.
It looks similar to the Decorator pattern. The difference is intent: decorators add behaviour and are often stacked; proxies control access to the object. In code they can look identical.

Dynamic proxies generate proxy classes at runtime, so you don't write one per interface. In .NET: DispatchProxy, built in, lets you create a proxy for any interface and handle all calls in one Invoke method; Castle DynamicProxy is a popular library that supports interfaces and virtual class members, used by Moq and NSubstitute to create mocks, and by some frameworks for interceptors, like adding logging, timing or retries to every method of a service.

Where it appears in our stack: EF Core lazy-loading proxies, which override navigation properties to load data on access; mocking libraries in unit tests; and HTTP client libraries like Refit, which generate implementations of an interface that make API calls.
Because runtime proxies use reflection, source generators are increasingly used to produce the same thing at compile time.

p17-759.q: In .NET, the most common GraphQL server library is Hot Chocolate. You define a schema from C# types: a Query class with resolver methods, like GetShipments, object types for Shipment and Site, and mutations for changes. Clients send one query describing exactly the fields they want, including nested data, like shipments with their site name and items, and get back exactly that shape.
p17-759.k: graphql dotnet, hot chocolate, graphql n+1, dataloader, graphql asp.net core
x: In .NET, the most common GraphQL server library is Hot Chocolate. You define a schema from C# types: a Query class with resolver methods, like GetShipments, object types for Shipment and Site, and mutations for changes. Clients send one query describing exactly the fields they want, including nested data, like shipments with their site name and items, and get back exactly that shape.

The N+1 problem is GraphQL's classic trap. If a query asks for 50 shipments and each shipment's site, a naive site resolver runs one database query per shipment: 1 query for shipments plus 50 for sites.

DataLoader solves it. Instead of loading the site immediately, each resolver asks a DataLoader for site id X. The DataLoader collects all requested ids during that execution step, then makes one batched call, like WHERE Id IN (...), and hands each resolver its result. It also caches within the request, so the same site isn't loaded twice. Hot Chocolate has built-in DataLoader support, and integrates with EF Core projections so only requested columns are queried.

Other things I'd set up: query depth and complexity limits, so a client can't send a huge nested query that overloads the server; persisted or allow-listed queries for public APIs; authorisation on fields and types, not just the endpoint; and pagination with cursor-based connections.
When I'd choose GraphQL: many different front ends needing different shapes of related data. For simple CRUD or service-to-service calls, REST or gRPC is simpler to operate, cache and monitor.

p17-761.q: Mapping between entities and DTOs is repetitive, so libraries exist to automate it. Each approach has trade-offs.
p17-761.k: automapper vs manual mapping, mapster, mapperly, object mapping dotnet, dto mapping
x: Mapping between entities and DTOs is repetitive, so libraries exist to automate it. Each approach has trade-offs.

AutoMapper uses conventions and reflection-based configuration: properties with matching names are mapped automatically, and profiles define exceptions. It saves typing, and ProjectTo can turn mappings into EF Core query projections. Downsides: mistakes appear at runtime, not compile time; mapping logic is hidden, making debugging and "find references" harder; complex configurations become a puzzle; and recent versions moved to a commercial licence.
Mapster is similar in style but faster, with optional code generation.

Mapperly is a source generator: you declare a partial mapper class with method signatures, and it generates plain mapping code at compile time. You get compile-time warnings for unmapped properties, no reflection, good performance, and generated code you can read and debug.

Manual mapping: writing the assignments yourself, often as extension methods like ToDto(), or constructors. It's explicit, fast, easy to debug and refactor-safe. The cost is typing, but with modern IDEs and AI assistants that's small.

My preference: manual mapping or Mapperly for most code, because mappings often contain small business decisions, like formatting, combining fields or hiding data, which are clearer in code. For EF Core queries, I write Select projections directly, so only needed columns are fetched. I'd keep AutoMapper in existing codebases that use it consistently, but always with configuration validation tests, AssertConfigurationIsValid, to catch mistakes early.

p17-762.q: In ASP.NET Core, each request runs on a thread pool thread. If an action calls a database or another API synchronously, that thread sits blocked, doing nothing, until the response comes back. Under load, all threads can end up blocked waiting on I/O. The thread pool then grows slowly, requests queue up, and latency spikes, even though the CPU is mostly idle. That's thread pool starvation.
p17-762.k: async controller actions, async await scalability, why async in web api, thread pool web requests, async io scalability
x: In ASP.NET Core, each request runs on a thread pool thread. If an action calls a database or another API synchronously, that thread sits blocked, doing nothing, until the response comes back. Under load, all threads can end up blocked waiting on I/O. The thread pool then grows slowly, requests queue up, and latency spikes, even though the CPU is mostly idle. That's thread pool starvation.

With async actions, when the code awaits an I/O operation, like await db.Shipments.ToListAsync() or await httpClient.GetAsync(), the thread is released back to the pool while the operating system waits for the I/O. When the result arrives, a pool thread continues the method. So a small number of threads can serve many concurrent requests that are mostly waiting.
Important points.
Async improves scalability and throughput under concurrency, not the speed of a single request; a single request may even be slightly slower due to overhead.
It only helps for I/O-bound work. CPU-bound work still needs a thread; wrapping it in Task.Run inside a request just moves it to another pool thread and adds overhead.
It must be async all the way: calling .Result or .Wait() on async methods blocks a thread again and can cause starvation.
Pass the request's CancellationToken to async calls, so work stops when the client disconnects.
In our legacy ASP.NET MVC applications, moving data access to async was one of the changes that helped the application handle peak usage better without more servers.

p17-763.q: In ASP.NET Core controllers, there are three common return styles.
p17-763.k: iactionresult vs actionresult, actionresult t, return types web api, controller return type, typed results controllers
x: In ASP.NET Core controllers, there are three common return styles.

Returning the DTO directly, like public ShipmentDto Get(int id): simple, and the framework serialises it with a 200 status. But you can't return other status codes, like 404, without throwing exceptions or using workarounds.

IActionResult: you can return any result, like Ok(dto), NotFound(), BadRequest(problem) or CreatedAtAction(...). Flexible, but the return type says nothing about the response body, so tools like OpenAPI generators can't infer the schema; you need ProducesResponseType attributes with the DTO type and status code.

ActionResult<T>: combines both. You can return a ShipmentDto directly, which is implicitly converted to a 200 result, or return NotFound() or other results. The T tells OpenAPI and readers the success body type. This is my default for controllers: public async Task<ActionResult<ShipmentDto>> Get(int id). I still add ProducesResponseType for the error status codes, so documentation is complete.
For minimal APIs, the equivalent is TypedResults with Results<Ok<ShipmentDto>, NotFound>, which gives compile-time checked status codes and automatic OpenAPI metadata.
One caveat: ActionResult<T> doesn't work with interfaces as T, because implicit conversions aren't allowed from interfaces, so I return concrete DTO types, which I'd do anyway.
Consistency matters more than the choice: the team agrees on one style for new code, along with ProblemDetails for errors.

p17-764.q: Some teams wrap every response in an envelope, with properties like success, data, errors and message. Others return the resource directly, using HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails for errors. Both exist in real systems, and I've seen the trade-offs.

x: Some teams wrap every response in an envelope, with properties like success, data, errors and message. Others return the resource directly, using HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails for errors. Both exist in real systems, and I've seen the trade-offs.

Arguments for an envelope: one consistent shape for front-end code to handle; a place for metadata like pagination info, warnings or request ids; and it was common practice in older systems where clients couldn't easily read status codes.

Arguments against: it duplicates what HTTP already provides, success: false with a 200 status confuses monitoring, caches, gateways and retry logic, which all rely on status codes; it adds nesting to every client call; and standard tools, like OpenAPI generators, HTTP clients and API gateways, work more naturally with plain resources and standard errors.

My preference: return resources directly with correct status codes; use ProblemDetails, RFC 9457, for all errors, with extensions like an error code and validation errors; put pagination in a consistent wrapper only for list endpoints, with items, nextCursor and totalCount; and use headers for cross-cutting metadata, like correlation ids.

If an existing API already uses an envelope, I keep it consistent rather than mixing styles, but I make sure the HTTP status still reflects the outcome, so failures aren't hidden behind 200 responses. In our legacy APIs consumed by Angular sub-apps, consistency for the front end was the priority, so new endpoints follow the same contract.

Steps I follow.
Announce early: publish a deprecation notice with the reason, the replacement, a migration guide, and a sunset date, giving consumers enough time, often months for external partners.

Signal in the API itself: add the Deprecation header and the Sunset header, RFC 8594, with the retirement date to responses from the old version, plus a Link header pointing to documentation. Mark operations as deprecated in the OpenAPI document, so generated clients show warnings. Asp.Versioning supports reporting deprecated versions in api-deprecated-versions headers.
Measure usage: log and dashboard calls to deprecated endpoints by client id. This tells us who still needs to migrate, so we can contact them directly instead of guessing.
Help consumers migrate: examples, side-by-side comparison of old and new contracts, and a test environment where both work.
Brownouts before removal: temporarily disable the old version for short planned windows, returning a clear error, so remaining consumers notice before the final shutdown.
Retire: after the sunset date, return 410 Gone with a helpful message for a period, then remove the code.

Internally, for APIs only used by our own front ends, the process is shorter, since we can coordinate releases, but I still check usage logs before removing anything, because there's often a forgotten report or integration still calling it.

p17-771.q: Model binding decides where each action parameter comes from. Binding source attributes make that explicit.

x: Model binding decides where each action parameter comes from. Binding source attributes make that explicit.
FromRoute: from the URL path template, like id in /shipments/{id}.
FromQuery: from the query string, like ?status=Shipped&page=2. Complex types can bind from multiple query parameters, which is handy for filter objects.
FromBody: from the request body, deserialised by the input formatter, usually JSON. Only one parameter can bind from the body, because the body stream is read once.
FromForm: from form fields and multipart data, including IFormFile for uploads.
FromHeader: from a request header, like X-Correlation-Id, using its Name property.
FromServices: injects a service from DI into that action only, useful when only one action needs a dependency.

With ApiController, inference rules apply: complex types are assumed to be FromBody, simple types that match route parameters come from the route, other simple types from the query, and registered services are inferred as FromServices in newer versions. Minimal APIs have similar inference, plus AsParameters to group parameters into one object.

Common problems: a complex type for filters wrongly inferred as body for a GET request, so it needs FromQuery; content type mismatches, like sending form data to a FromBody parameter, which gives 415 Unsupported Media Type; and JSON property names not matching.
I'm explicit with attributes when there's any ambiguity, because it documents the API and avoids surprises.

For public partner APIs, a published developer portal is better than exposing Swagger UI on the live service. If it must be in production, protect it with authentication and don't expose internal or admin endpoints in the document.

For TypeScript: openapi-typescript generates types only, which pair nicely with a small fetch wrapper like openapi-fetch; orval and openapi-generator can generate full clients and even React Query or Angular service code.

How I set it up: the API produces its OpenAPI document at build time, for example with the build-time document generation in .NET 9; the client is generated in CI or as a build step, not edited manually; and the generated code is versioned, either committed or published as a package, like an internal npm package on our Azure DevOps feed, so front ends depend on a specific API version.
Benefits: compile-time errors when the contract changes, no typos in URLs or property names, and less boilerplate.

Watch-outs: the OpenAPI document must be accurate, with correct nullability, enums and response types, otherwise generated code is wrong; generated clients can be large; and breaking changes in the API show up as compile errors, which is good, but need coordination.
Combined with contract tests, this catches integration mistakes very early.

p17-774.q: Sometimes an app isn't at the root of a domain, but under a path like company.com/portal, either as an IIS sub-application, or behind a reverse proxy that routes /portal to the app.

The challenge: the app must generate correct links, redirects, cookie paths and static file URLs including /portal, and routing must ignore that prefix.
On IIS with the ASP.NET Core Module, sub-applications are handled automatically: IIS passes the path base, and HttpContext.Request.PathBase is set, so Url helpers and redirects include it.

Behind a reverse proxy that forwards the full path, use app.UsePathBase("/portal") early in the pipeline: it moves /portal from Path to PathBase, so routes like /api/shipments still match. If the proxy strips the prefix, it should send it in X-Forwarded-Prefix, and the forwarded headers middleware can apply it to PathBase.
Things to check.
Cookie paths, so authentication cookies are scoped correctly, especially when several apps share a domain.
OpenID Connect redirect URIs registered with the full path.
Swagger and OpenAPI server URLs.
SPA front ends: the base href in Angular, or the base option in Vite for React, must match, otherwise scripts and assets load from the wrong place.
Absolute URLs hardcoded in code or configuration.

This is a common setup with on-premise IIS, where several applications share one site, like our MVC host with Angular sub-apps and APIs under different paths, so getting path base handling right avoids broken links and login loops.

AddControllers registers what's needed for API controllers: controller discovery, model binding, validation, formatters, filters, authorisation and CORS integration. No views, Razor or tag helpers. It's the right choice for Web APIs.

AddControllersWithViews adds view support on top: Razor view engine, tag helpers, view components, antiforgery for forms, and temp data. Used for traditional MVC web applications that return HTML views.
AddRazorPages registers Razor Pages, the page-based model, and can be combined with the others.
AddMvc registers everything: controllers, views and Razor Pages. It exists mainly for compatibility with older apps migrated from ASP.NET Core 2.x, where it was the standard call.

Matching endpoint mapping is also needed: app.MapControllers() for attribute-routed API controllers, app.MapDefaultControllerRoute() or MapControllerRoute for conventional MVC routes, and app.MapRazorPages() for pages.

Why it matters: registering unnecessary services increases startup time and memory slightly, and enables features that aren't needed, like view-related behaviour in a pure API. Also, AddControllers doesn't include antiforgery validation for views, so if a migrated app uses forms, you need the views version.
In a migration from ASP.NET MVC 4.8, a hybrid app with both views and APIs would use AddControllersWithViews and map both route styles, while new pure API services use AddControllers or minimal APIs.

p17-776.q: Sometimes clients need only a few fields of a large resource, like a mobile app that needs shipment id, status and date, not the full object with items and addresses. Sending everything wastes bandwidth and database work.

Options.

A fields query parameter: GET /shipments?fields=id,status,shippedAt. The API returns only those fields. Implementation: validate requested fields against an allowlist, then either build a dynamic projection, like a Select expression built from the field list, so the database only fetches those columns, or fetch a standard DTO and shape the output by serialising selected properties into a dictionary or JsonObject. JSON:API standardises this with a fields parameter per resource type.

Predefined views: instead of arbitrary fields, offer a few named shapes, like ?view=summary or ?view=detail, or separate endpoints, like /shipments/summary. Simpler to optimise, cache and document, and usually enough.
Expansion the other way: return a lean resource by default, and let clients request related data with ?expand=items,site.
GraphQL, if many clients need many different shapes; it's built for exactly this.

Trade-offs: arbitrary field selection makes caching harder, since each combination is a different response, complicates OpenAPI documentation, and needs careful security so clients can't select fields they shouldn't see.

My usual approach is predefined summary and detail shapes, because they cover most needs and are predictable for performance. I'd add field selection only if there's a clear, measured need, such as large payloads hurting a mobile or partner client.

Override CanWriteType to say which types it handles, for example IEnumerable of a DTO type. Override WriteResponseBodyAsync to write the data: write a header row, then each item's values, escaping commas, quotes and newlines correctly, and write to the response body asynchronously. Register it with AddControllers(o => o.OutputFormatters.Add(new CsvOutputFormatter())), and optionally add a format mapping so ?format=csv or a .csv extension works, using FormatFilter.
