Use a proper CSV library, like CsvHelper, for escaping and culture-safe formatting of numbers and dates, rather than string concatenation.
Large data: stream rows instead of building everything in memory, ideally from an IAsyncEnumerable, so big exports don't consume lots of memory.
Security: CSV injection, where values starting with =, +, - or @ are interpreted as formulas when opened in Excel; prefix or escape them for user-provided data.
Set Content-Disposition with a file name, so browsers download it.
For very large or slow exports, I'd generate the file in a background job and return a download link, instead of formatting it in the request.

p17-778.q: Every HTTP request has a Host header saying which host name the client wants. Applications often use it to build absolute URLs, like links in password reset emails, redirect URLs, or callback URLs. If the app trusts any Host header, an attacker can send a request with Host: evil.com, and the app may generate links pointing to the attacker's site, like a password reset email whose link sends the token to the attacker, or poison caches with wrong URLs.
p17-778.k: allowedhosts, host filtering middleware, host header attack, host header injection, allowed hosts configuration
x: Every HTTP request has a Host header saying which host name the client wants. Applications often use it to build absolute URLs, like links in password reset emails, redirect URLs, or callback URLs. If the app trusts any Host header, an attacker can send a request with Host: evil.com, and the app may generate links pointing to the attacker's site, like a password reset email whose link sends the token to the attacker, or poison caches with wrong URLs.

ASP.NET Core's host filtering middleware checks the Host header against the AllowedHosts setting. The default template sets AllowedHosts to *, which allows any host, convenient for development but not ideal in production. Setting it to specific names, like "app.example.com;api.example.com", makes the app reject requests with other hosts with 400 Bad Request.

When the app is behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, the forwarded headers middleware may replace the host with X-Forwarded-Host, so configure KnownProxies, KnownNetworks and AllowedHosts on ForwardedHeadersOptions too, so spoofed forwarded headers aren't trusted.
Even better: don't build security-sensitive URLs from the incoming request at all; use a configured public base URL for emails and callbacks.
Kestrel doesn't validate host headers by itself, and IIS bindings only partly protect if a site binding accepts all hosts.
It's a small configuration change that closes a real class of attacks, so I include it in production readiness checks.

p17-779.q: The first requests after a deployment or app pool recycle are often slow: the JIT compiles code on first use, DI builds services, EF Core builds its model and compiles queries, connection pools are empty, caches are cold, and HttpClient connections and TLS handshakes are new. Users hitting the app first see seconds of delay.
p17-779.k: slow first request, warm up aspnet core, application initialization iis, cold start dotnet, startup warmup
x: The first requests after a deployment or app pool recycle are often slow: the JIT compiles code on first use, DI builds services, EF Core builds its model and compiles queries, connection pools are empty, caches are cold, and HttpClient connections and TLS handshakes are new. Users hitting the app first see seconds of delay.
How I reduce it.

Warm up before taking traffic: in rolling or slot deployments, call key endpoints or run a warm-up routine before the instance is marked ready. An IHostedService can run warm-up work at startup, like touching the DbContext, loading reference data into cache, and opening connections, and a readiness health check only passes after warm-up completes.

IIS specifics: enable the Application Initialization module with preloadEnabled and startMode AlwaysRunning, and configure initialisation pages, so IIS starts the app and calls warm-up URLs after a recycle, before users arrive. Also avoid unnecessary recycles, like the default idle timeout that shuts down quiet apps.

Reduce startup cost itself: ReadyToRun compilation to pre-compile code, EF Core compiled models for large models, which matters with hundreds of tables, avoiding heavy reflection scanning at startup, and lazy initialisation only for rarely used parts.
Measure: track the latency of the first requests after deployments, and the startup duration, so regressions are visible.
For serverless, like Lambda or Azure Functions, the same idea applies as cold starts, with provisioned concurrency or premium plans as additional options.

p17-780.q: Both are reusable database code, but they have different rules and uses.
p17-780.k: stored procedure vs function, sql function vs procedure, udf vs stored procedure, table valued function
x: Both are reusable database code, but they have different rules and uses.

Stored procedures are executed with EXEC. They can contain almost any T-SQL: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, transactions, TRY/CATCH, temp tables, dynamic SQL, and calls to other procedures. They can return multiple result sets, output parameters and a return code. They can't be used inside a SELECT statement. They're used for business operations, data changes and batch processes.

Functions return a value and can be used inside queries, like in SELECT, WHERE or JOIN. They're not allowed to change database state: no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on real tables, no transactions, no dynamic SQL, and limited error handling.

Types of functions: scalar functions return a single value; inline table-valued functions are a single SELECT statement and behave like a parameterised view, which the optimiser expands into the main query, so they perform well; multi-statement table-valued functions build a table variable in several steps, and historically had poor cardinality estimates, so they often performed badly.

Performance notes: scalar functions used per row in large queries were notoriously slow, though SQL Server 2019 can inline many of them automatically. Inline table-valued functions are usually the best choice when you need reusable query logic.

My rule of thumb: procedures for operations and data changes; inline table-valued functions for reusable filters or calculations inside queries; avoid scalar and multi-statement functions in hot queries. From .NET, procedures are easy to call with EF Core or Dapper, and functions can be mapped too.

p17-781.q: PIVOT turns rows into columns. For example, a table has rows of site, month and shipment count, and the report wants one row per site with a column for each month. PIVOT aggregates the value, like SUM(ShipmentCount), for each listed column value, like Jan, Feb and Mar.
p17-781.k: pivot sql server, unpivot, rows to columns sql, crosstab query, conditional aggregation
x: PIVOT turns rows into columns. For example, a table has rows of site, month and shipment count, and the report wants one row per site with a column for each month. PIVOT aggregates the value, like SUM(ShipmentCount), for each listed column value, like Jan, Feb and Mar.
The syntax: select from a source subquery of site, month and count, then PIVOT with SUM of ShipmentCount FOR Month IN the list of month columns, each written as a quoted identifier.

The limitation: the column list must be known when writing the query. If columns depend on data, like a variable list of studies or visit types, you need dynamic SQL to build the column list, and that must be done safely, with QUOTENAME for column names.

Conditional aggregation is an alternative I often prefer: SELECT Site, SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN ShipmentCount END) AS Jan, ... GROUP BY Site. It's more flexible, works across databases, can mix different aggregations, and is easier to read for many developers.

UNPIVOT does the opposite: columns into rows, like turning Jan, Feb and Mar columns into rows of month and value. CROSS APPLY with a VALUES list is a more flexible alternative, and it handles NULLs the way you choose, while UNPIVOT drops them.

In practice, I'm careful about doing pivoting in SQL for reports at all: often it's simpler to return normalised rows and let the reporting tool or front end pivot them, which keeps queries stable when new columns appear.

p17-782.q: APPLY lets you run a table expression for each row of the outer table, where the inner expression can reference columns from the outer row. It's similar to a lateral join in other databases.
p17-782.k: cross apply, outer apply, apply operator sql server, lateral join, top n per row
x: APPLY lets you run a table expression for each row of the outer table, where the inner expression can reference columns from the outer row. It's similar to a lateral join in other databases.

CROSS APPLY returns only outer rows for which the inner expression returns rows, like an inner join. OUTER APPLY returns all outer rows, with NULLs when the inner expression returns nothing, like a left join.
Common uses.

Top N per row: for each site, get its latest 3 shipments: SELECT s.Name, x.* FROM Sites s CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 3 * FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id ORDER BY ShippedAt DESC) x. With a good index on SiteId and ShippedAt, this is very efficient.
Calling table-valued functions per row, passing columns from the outer row as parameters.
Splitting or parsing values: CROSS APPLY STRING_SPLIT(row.Tags, ',') to expand a delimited column into rows, or OPENJSON to shred JSON stored in a column.
Computing reusable expressions: CROSS APPLY (SELECT Total = Qty * Price) calc, then using calc.Total in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY without repeating the expression.
Unpivoting columns into rows with CROSS APPLY (VALUES ...).

Performance: APPLY with a correlated subquery runs effectively per row, so it's great when the outer set is small and the inner query uses an index seek; for large outer sets, a window function approach, like ROW_NUMBER partitioned by site, may be better. I check the execution plan to decide.

p17-783.q: LAG and LEAD are window functions that read a value from a previous or following row in a defined order, without a self-join.
p17-783.k: lag lead sql, running total sql, cumulative sum, window function over, previous row value sql
x: LAG and LEAD are window functions that read a value from a previous or following row in a defined order, without a self-join.

LAG(Quantity, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShippedAt) gives the previous shipment's quantity for the same site, or 0 if there's none. LEAD does the same for the next row. Uses: comparing each value to the previous one, like stock change since last count; finding time between events, like days between visits; and detecting status changes.

Running totals use an aggregate with an OVER clause: SUM(Quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShippedAt ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) gives a cumulative quantity per site over time.

Important detail: always specify ROWS for running totals. Without a frame, the default with ORDER BY is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, which treats rows with the same order value as peers, giving surprising totals when there are ties, and it's slower because it may use an on-disk worktable. ROWS is precise and faster.
Moving averages work the same way with a limited frame, like ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-day average.
Other useful window functions: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE, NTILE for buckets, and PERCENT_RANK.

Performance: an index matching the PARTITION BY and ORDER BY columns lets SQL Server compute these without sorting. These functions replaced many old cursor-based or self-join solutions for reports, and they're usually much faster.

p17-784.q: Hierarchical data, like an organisation chart, a folder tree, a bill of materials, or regions containing countries containing sites, is often stored as a parent-child table, where each row has a ParentId.
p17-784.k: recursive cte, hierarchical query sql, parent child query, org chart sql, tree query sql server
x: Hierarchical data, like an organisation chart, a folder tree, a bill of materials, or regions containing countries containing sites, is often stored as a parent-child table, where each row has a ParentId.

A recursive CTE walks the tree. It has two parts joined with UNION ALL: the anchor member selects the starting rows, like the root node, or a specific node; the recursive member joins the table to the CTE itself, to find children of the rows found so far. SQL Server repeats the recursive part until no new rows are found.

Example: WITH Tree AS (SELECT Id, ParentId, Name, 0 AS Level FROM Locations WHERE Id = @rootId UNION ALL SELECT l.Id, l.ParentId, l.Name, t.Level + 1 FROM Locations l JOIN Tree t ON l.ParentId = t.Id) SELECT * FROM Tree.
You can also build a path string to sort and display the tree, and walk upwards from a node to find all its ancestors.

Safety: MAXRECURSION defaults to 100 levels; if the data has a cycle by mistake, the query errors out rather than looping forever. Adjust with OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) if needed, and detect cycles by checking whether an id already appears in the path.

Performance: index ParentId. For large, frequently queried trees, alternatives include the hierarchyid data type, closure tables that store all ancestor-descendant pairs, or a materialised path column, which make subtree queries fast at the cost of more work on updates.
In EF Core, recursive CTEs are written as raw SQL or a view, since LINQ doesn't express recursion directly.

p17-785.q: Gaps and islands is a classic SQL pattern. Islands are runs of consecutive values, like consecutive days a temperature sensor was out of range, or continuous periods a site was active. Gaps are the missing ranges, like missing ids in a sequence or days with no data.
p17-785.k: gaps and islands, consecutive rows sql, find gaps in sequence, group consecutive dates, streaks sql
x: Gaps and islands is a classic SQL pattern. Islands are runs of consecutive values, like consecutive days a temperature sensor was out of range, or continuous periods a site was active. Gaps are the missing ranges, like missing ids in a sequence or days with no data.
Finding gaps: use LEAD to compare each value with the next one. SELECT Id + 1 AS GapStart, NextId - 1 AS GapEnd FROM (SELECT Id, LEAD(Id) OVER (ORDER BY Id) AS NextId FROM T) x WHERE NextId - Id > 1.

Finding islands: the trick is the difference between the value and a row number. For dates, compute DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SensorId ORDER BY ReadingDate), ReadingDate). For consecutive dates, this difference stays the same; when there's a gap, it changes. Then GROUP BY sensor and that group key, and take MIN and MAX dates to get each island's start and end, and COUNT for its length.

For status changes, like periods when a depot was in each state, compare each row's status with the previous one using LAG, mark a change with 1, take a running SUM of those flags to create a group number, and aggregate by group.

Real uses: temperature excursion periods for shipments, continuous enrolment periods, consecutive missed visits, finding missing sequence numbers in imported files, and outage windows from monitoring data.
These set-based solutions replace cursor loops and are much faster on large data, especially with an index on the partition and order columns.

p17-786.q: On-premise SQL Server doesn't look after itself; a few regular jobs keep it healthy, usually scheduled with SQL Server Agent, often using a well-known maintenance script solution rather than basic maintenance plans.
p17-786.k: sql server maintenance, maintenance plan, dbcc checkdb, update statistics job, backup and index maintenance
x: On-premise SQL Server doesn't look after itself; a few regular jobs keep it healthy, usually scheduled with SQL Server Agent, often using a well-known maintenance script solution rather than basic maintenance plans.

Backups: full backups, for example weekly or daily; differential backups in between; and transaction log backups every few minutes in the full recovery model, which also keep the log from growing endlessly. Backups go to separate storage, are checked with RESTORE VERIFYONLY or CHECKSUM, and, most importantly, restores are tested regularly.
Integrity checks: DBCC CHECKDB regularly, to detect corruption early, while good backups still exist. For large databases, run it on a restored copy or split it across days.
Statistics: update statistics regularly, especially on tables with large data changes, because auto-update thresholds can be too slow for big tables, leading to poor plans.

Index maintenance: reorganise or rebuild only indexes that are actually fragmented and large enough to matter, with sensible thresholds, online where the edition allows, and scheduled outside business hours. Many teams now focus more on statistics than fragmentation, since modern storage reduces fragmentation's impact.
Cleanup: purge old backup history, job history and maintenance logs; manage tempdb and log file sizes.
Monitoring: alerts for failed jobs, low disk space, long-running jobs, blocking, and high severity errors.
With many databases, like one per study, the jobs must loop through all databases, scale well, and be staggered so they don't all run at the same time and overload storage.

p17-787.q: Sometimes a table is used as a work queue, like an outbox table or a list of jobs, with several workers taking items. The challenge is letting multiple workers dequeue concurrently without processing the same item twice and without blocking each other.
p17-787.k: queue table sql server, readpast updlock, database as queue, dequeue sql, outbox processing locking
x: Sometimes a table is used as a work queue, like an outbox table or a list of jobs, with several workers taking items. The challenge is letting multiple workers dequeue concurrently without processing the same item twice and without blocking each other.

The standard pattern uses locking hints: WITH (ROWLOCK, UPDLOCK, READPAST). UPDLOCK takes an update lock on rows being read, so two workers can't grab the same row; READPAST skips rows already locked by other workers, instead of waiting for them; ROWLOCK keeps locks fine-grained.

A dequeue in one statement: WITH next AS (SELECT TOP (10) * FROM WorkQueue WITH (ROWLOCK, UPDLOCK, READPAST) WHERE Status = 'Pending' ORDER BY Id) UPDATE next SET Status = 'Processing', LockedBy = @worker, LockedAt = SYSUTCDATETIME() OUTPUT inserted.*. Or delete the rows with OUTPUT if processing is idempotent and failures are handled elsewhere.

Other essentials: an index on Status and Id, or a filtered index for pending rows, so the query doesn't scan; a timeout for stuck items, where items in Processing for too long are reset to Pending, because a worker might crash; an attempt counter, moving items to a failed state after several attempts, like a dead-letter queue; and handlers that are idempotent, because an item may be processed again after a timeout.

When not to use it: very high throughput or many consumers, where a real message broker like RabbitMQ is better. But for outbox tables and moderate job volumes, a queue table keeps work transactional with business data, which is a big advantage.

p17-788.q: SQL is written in one order but logically processed in another, and knowing that order explains many common errors.
p17-788.k: logical query processing order, sql order of execution, why can't use alias in where, select execution order
x: SQL is written in one order but logically processed in another, and knowing that order explains many common errors.

The logical order is: FROM, including JOINs and APPLY; then WHERE; then GROUP BY; then HAVING; then SELECT, where expressions and aliases are computed, along with window functions; then DISTINCT; then ORDER BY; then TOP, or OFFSET and FETCH.
What this explains.
You can't use a column alias from SELECT in WHERE, because WHERE is processed before SELECT. You can use it in ORDER BY, which comes after SELECT.
You can't use aggregates in WHERE; filtering on aggregates belongs in HAVING, after grouping.
Window functions like ROW_NUMBER can't appear in WHERE, because they're computed in the SELECT phase; you wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter outside.

With an outer join, a filter in the ON clause behaves differently from the same filter in WHERE: in ON, it decides which rows match, keeping unmatched outer rows; in WHERE, it removes rows after the join, which can effectively turn a left join into an inner join.
TOP without ORDER BY gives arbitrary rows, since ordering is only guaranteed by ORDER BY.

This is the logical order, not the physical execution order. The optimiser can reorder operations, like pushing filters down or choosing join orders, as long as the result is the same. But for reasoning about what a query means, the logical order is the right model.

p17-789.q: SQL Server has several date and time types, and the choice affects precision, storage and time zone handling.
p17-789.k: datetime vs datetime2, datetimeoffset sql, sql server date types, store dates utc sql, date column type
x: SQL Server has several date and time types, and the choice affects precision, storage and time zone handling.
datetime: the old type, range from 1753, precision about 3 milliseconds, rounded to .000, .003 or .007, using 8 bytes. Its rounding can cause surprising comparisons. I don't use it for new columns.

datetime2: range from year 1, configurable precision up to 100 nanoseconds, and 6 to 8 bytes. It's the recommended type for date and time without an offset. EF Core maps DateTime to datetime2 by default.
datetimeoffset: datetime2 plus a time zone offset, like +05:30, using 10 bytes. It records the moment and the offset it was captured in. It maps to DateTimeOffset in .NET.
date: just the date, 3 bytes, for things like date of birth or a visit date with no time. Maps to DateOnly in newer .NET.
time: just the time of day.
How I choose.

Timestamps for events, like created, updated or shipped times: either datetime2 holding UTC, with a clear naming convention like CreatedAtUtc, or datetimeoffset if the original local offset matters, like when and where a user performed an action.
Business dates without time: date, to avoid off-by-one-day issues caused by time zone conversions.
Comparisons: be consistent, because mixing types causes implicit conversions that can prevent index use.
Also avoid GETDATE(), which returns server local time; use SYSUTCDATETIME() or SYSDATETIMEOFFSET() so values don't depend on the server's time zone setting.

p17-790.q: A computed column is defined by an expression based on other columns in the same row, like FullName AS FirstName + ' ' + LastName, or LineTotal AS Quantity * UnitPrice, or extracting a value from JSON, like JSON_VALUE(Payload, '$.status').
p17-790.k: computed column sql server, persisted computed column, index computed column, derived column sql
x: A computed column is defined by an expression based on other columns in the same row, like FullName AS FirstName + ' ' + LastName, or LineTotal AS Quantity * UnitPrice, or extracting a value from JSON, like JSON_VALUE(Payload, '$.status').
By default, it's virtual: not stored, calculated whenever it's read. That keeps storage small but costs CPU on each read.

PERSISTED stores the computed value physically, updated automatically when the source columns change. Reads are faster, writes slightly slower. The expression must be deterministic, meaning it always returns the same result for the same inputs; functions like GETDATE() aren't allowed.

Indexing: you can create an index on a computed column, persisted or not, if it's deterministic and precise. This is very useful for making queries SARGable: if queries filter on an expression, like WHERE YEAR(ShippedAt) = 2025, or a JSON property, a computed column with an index lets the optimiser seek instead of scanning. SQL Server can even match the expression in the query to the indexed computed column automatically.

Uses I find practical: indexing JSON properties stored in a JSON column; normalised search keys, like upper-cased or trimmed codes; derived values used in filters or sorting; and keeping calculated values consistent without application code.

Cautions: certain SET options must be correct for indexes on computed columns, which can affect older applications or connections; and complex expressions with scalar user-defined functions can hurt performance and prevent parallelism.
In EF Core, HasComputedColumnSql maps them, and the values are read back after saves.

p17-791.q: Constraints make the database itself reject invalid data, no matter which application, script or person writes it. Application validation is important, but it can be bypassed by bugs, other services or manual fixes.
p17-791.k: check constraint, default constraint, data integrity constraints, not null unique foreign key, database constraints vs application validation
x: Constraints make the database itself reject invalid data, no matter which application, script or person writes it. Application validation is important, but it can be bypassed by bugs, other services or manual fixes.
The main constraints.
NOT NULL: required columns. Simple and very effective.
Primary key: uniquely identifies each row.
Unique constraints or unique indexes: business uniqueness, like one kit number per study, or one active record per patient, using a filtered unique index.

Foreign keys: relationships must point to existing rows, so you can't have shipments for a site that doesn't exist. They also document the data model. Options like ON DELETE CASCADE should be used carefully.
Check constraints: rules on values, like Quantity >= 0, Status IN ('Pending', 'Shipped', 'Received'), or EndDate >= StartDate. Can reference multiple columns in the same row.
Default constraints: values when none is provided, like CreatedAtUtc defaulting to SYSUTCDATETIME().

Why I like them: they catch bugs early, protect against bad data from imports and manual scripts, help the optimiser, since trusted foreign keys and check constraints let it skip unnecessary work, and serve as documentation.

Things to watch: constraints added WITH NOCHECK, or disabled during loads, become untrusted, and the optimiser ignores them, so re-enable them WITH CHECK. Name constraints explicitly, so deployments and error messages are predictable; SSDT manages them well. And translate constraint violations into friendly API errors, rather than showing raw SQL errors.

p17-792.q: For on-premise SQL Server, there are a few main options, often combined.
p17-792.k: always on availability groups, failover cluster instance, log shipping, sql server high availability, sql server disaster recovery
x: For on-premise SQL Server, there are a few main options, often combined.

Always On availability groups: a group of databases is replicated from a primary replica to secondary replicas on other servers. Synchronous commit replicas, usually in the same data centre, give zero data loss and automatic failover; asynchronous replicas, often in another data centre, give disaster recovery with a small potential data loss. Secondaries can be readable, used for reports and backups. Applications connect through a listener name, so failover is transparent apart from a brief interruption. Note that only databases are replicated; logins, jobs and linked servers must be synchronised separately.

Failover cluster instances: the whole SQL Server instance fails over to another node, using shared storage. Protects against server failure, including instance-level objects, but the shared storage is a single point of failure, so it's often combined with something else for DR.
Log shipping: transaction log backups are copied and restored on a standby server on a schedule. Simple and reliable for DR, with data loss equal to the shipping interval and manual failover.
Backups to offsite storage: always needed, because replication also replicates mistakes, like accidental deletes.
Choosing depends on RPO and RTO targets, budget and licensing.

Application side: use the listener, set MultiSubnetFailover=True in connection strings, add retry logic for transient errors during failover, and practise failovers regularly. With many databases, like one per study, availability groups need planning for the number of databases per group and the synchronisation load.

p17-793.q: When you have a class hierarchy, like a base Notification with EmailNotification and SmsNotification, EF Core can map it to tables in three ways.
p17-793.k: ef core inheritance, tph vs tpt vs tpc, table per hierarchy, table per type, discriminator column
x: When you have a class hierarchy, like a base Notification with EmailNotification and SmsNotification, EF Core can map it to tables in three ways.

TPH, table per hierarchy, is the default: one table holds all types, with a discriminator column saying which type each row is, and columns for all properties of all types, which are nullable for types that don't use them. Queries are fast, with no joins, and polymorphic queries are simple. Downsides: many nullable columns, you can't enforce NOT NULL for subtype-specific columns at database level, and a wide table if there are many subtypes.

TPT, table per type: a table for the base type, and a table for each derived type with its specific columns, linked by the primary key. The schema is clean and normalised, but every query for derived types needs joins, and polymorphic queries join all tables, which gets slow with many types.

TPC, table per concrete type, since EF Core 7: each concrete type has its own complete table with all properties, including inherited ones, and no base table. Queries for one specific type are fast with no joins; polymorphic queries use UNION ALL across tables. Keys must be unique across all tables, so you need sequences or GUIDs instead of identity columns per table.
My default is TPH for small hierarchies with few differing properties, because it performs best. TPC fits when you mostly query specific types. I'd avoid TPT for performance-sensitive paths.
Often, the best option is to avoid inheritance in the data model and use composition or a type column with a JSON column for type-specific details.

p17-794.q: Before EF Core 7, updating or deleting many rows meant loading entities into memory, changing them, and calling SaveChanges, which sends one statement per row and uses lots of memory, or writing raw SQL.
p17-794.k: executeupdate, executedelete, ef core bulk update, set based update ef core, update without loading entities
x: Before EF Core 7, updating or deleting many rows meant loading entities into memory, changing them, and calling SaveChanges, which sends one statement per row and uses lots of memory, or writing raw SQL.

ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, with their async versions, run set-based statements directly in the database from a LINQ query, without loading entities. For example: await db.Shipments.Where(s => s.Status == "Pending" && s.CreatedAt < cutoff).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(x => x.Status, "Expired").SetProperty(x => x.UpdatedAt, now)); becomes a single UPDATE ... WHERE statement. Similarly, ExecuteDeleteAsync becomes a single DELETE. Both return the number of affected rows.
Benefits: much faster for bulk changes, minimal memory, and still type-safe LINQ instead of raw SQL strings.
Important caveats.
They bypass the change tracker: entities already loaded in the DbContext aren't updated, so they may be stale.

They don't run SaveChanges logic: interceptors and overrides that set audit fields, raise domain events or write audit trails won't run. In regulated systems where every change needs an audit record, that's a serious issue. You must handle auditing explicitly, for example with database triggers or temporal tables, or avoid these methods for audited data.
They run immediately, outside SaveChanges, so wrap them with other changes in an explicit transaction if consistency matters.
Concurrency tokens aren't checked automatically.
For huge operations, batch them, like deleting in chunks, to avoid long locks and big log growth.
I use them for maintenance, cleanup and non-audited bulk updates, and keep normal SaveChanges for business operations needing auditing.

p17-795.q: Sometimes you need query results that don't match a normal entity: results of a reporting query, a view, a stored procedure, or a projection from raw SQL.
p17-795.k: keyless entity ef core, sqlquery unmapped types, hasnokey, query view ef core, raw sql dto ef core
x: Sometimes you need query results that don't match a normal entity: results of a reporting query, a view, a stored procedure, or a projection from raw SQL.

Keyless entity types: configure a class with HasNoKey(), and map it to a view with ToView("vw_SiteSummary") or to a SQL query with ToSqlQuery. You can query it with LINQ, including filtering and sorting on top. They're read-only: EF Core never tracks or saves them, because there's no key to identify rows. Good for views and reporting projections that you use often.

SqlQuery for unmapped types, since EF Core 8: db.Database.SqlQuery<SiteSummaryDto>($"SELECT SiteId, COUNT(*) AS Shipments FROM ... WHERE StudyId = {studyId}") maps results directly into any class, without registering it in the model. The interpolated string is turned into parameters, so it's safe from injection. You can even compose LINQ on top, like adding Where or OrderBy, when the SQL can be used as a subquery. It also works with scalar types, like SqlQuery<int>.
FromSql on a DbSet: for raw SQL returning a mapped entity type.

When I use them: complex reporting queries that LINQ can't express well, like window functions, recursive CTEs or hints; existing views or stored procedures in a legacy database; and read models in a CQRS-style design.
Alternatives: Dapper for heavy read queries, which some teams use alongside EF Core.
Either way, I keep the SQL in one place, test it against a real database, and watch for column name mismatches, which surface only at runtime.

p17-796.q: SQL Server doesn't create indexes on foreign key columns automatically, unlike primary keys. Whether you need one depends on how the column is used, but most of the time the answer is yes.
p17-796.k: index foreign key, foreign key index sql server, missing index on foreign key, fk index performance, delete slow foreign key
x: SQL Server doesn't create indexes on foreign key columns automatically, unlike primary keys. Whether you need one depends on how the column is used, but most of the time the answer is yes.
Why foreign key indexes matter.
Joins: queries usually join on foreign keys, like Shipments to Sites on SiteId. Without an index, finding shipments for a site requires scanning the shipments table.
Filtering: "all shipments for this site" or "all items for this order" are among the most common queries.

Deletes and updates of parent rows: when you delete a site, or update its key, SQL Server must check the child table for referencing rows. Without an index on the child's foreign key, it scans the whole child table for each parent row, holding locks, which can make deletes extremely slow and cause blocking or deadlocks. This is a classic hidden problem in cleanup jobs.
Cascading deletes need to find child rows the same way.

When it might be skippable: very small tables, or a foreign key that's never used for lookups and whose parent rows are never deleted, like a lookup to a static reference table with few rows. Even then, I'd check the access patterns.
Often, the best index has the foreign key as the leading column plus other columns used together, like (SiteId, ShippedAt), which serves both the foreign key and common queries.

EF Core creates indexes on foreign keys by default in migrations, which is a good default. In databases built by hand or with SSDT, I check for missing ones, with a query against the system views listing foreign keys without a matching index.

p17-797.q: A heap is a table without a clustered index. Rows are stored in no particular order, on whatever pages have space, and nonclustered indexes point to rows using a physical row identifier, the RID, made of file, page and slot.
p17-797.k: heap table sql server, table without clustered index, forwarded records, rid lookup, when to use heap
x: A heap is a table without a clustered index. Rows are stored in no particular order, on whatever pages have space, and nonclustered indexes point to rows using a physical row identifier, the RID, made of file, page and slot.
Problems with heaps.

Forwarded records: when a row is updated and grows, like a varchar column getting longer, and no longer fits on its page, SQL Server moves it to another page and leaves a forwarding pointer behind. Reads then follow extra pointers, causing more I/O. Over time, heavy updates make heaps slower.
Space isn't reclaimed well after deletes, unless the table is rebuilt or deletes take table locks, so heaps can grow with empty pages.
Lookups from nonclustered indexes use RID lookups, and range queries on any order require sorts or scans.

Why clustered indexes are the default: rows are stored in key order, range scans on the key are efficient, there are no forwarded records, and space management is better. A narrow, unique, ever-increasing key, like an identity or sequential value, makes a good clustered key.
When a heap can be fine: staging tables used for fast bulk loads that are read once and truncated, where insert speed matters and data is read fully anyway; or temporary tables.

How I find heaps: query sys.indexes for index_id 0, and check sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats for forwarded record counts. In older databases, finding large, frequently updated heaps and adding a clustered index can give a noticeable performance improvement.

p17-798.q: These two functions handle converting between rows and delimited strings, which used to need awkward tricks.
p17-798.k: string_agg, string_split, concatenate rows sql, comma separated values sql, split string sql server
x: These two functions handle converting between rows and delimited strings, which used to need awkward tricks.

STRING_AGG, since SQL Server 2017, concatenates values from multiple rows into one string with a separator. For example, SELECT SiteId, STRING_AGG(KitNumber, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY KitNumber) AS Kits FROM Kits GROUP BY SiteId gives one row per site with a comma-separated list of kits. WITHIN GROUP controls the order. Before this, people used FOR XML PATH with STUFF, which was hard to read and had escaping issues. Watch out for result length: cast the input to nvarchar(max) if the result can exceed 8000 bytes, otherwise it errors.

STRING_SPLIT, since SQL Server 2016, splits a delimited string into rows, with a column named value. Used as SELECT value FROM STRING_SPLIT(@ids, ','), or with CROSS APPLY to split a column for each row. Limitations: in older versions, the output order isn't guaranteed; SQL Server 2022 adds an enable_ordinal argument that returns the position. It only supports a single-character separator.

Where they help: building display strings for reports or exports; accepting a list of ids as a parameter in legacy code, though from .NET I prefer table-valued parameters or JSON with OPENJSON, which are typed and handle larger lists better; and parsing simple imported data.

One design caution: storing comma-separated values in a column is usually a normalisation problem. These functions make it easier to work with such data, but for new designs, a proper child table or a JSON column is better.

p17-799.q: In SQL Server, you can query another database on the same instance with three-part names, like OtherDb.dbo.Table, and another server with linked servers and four-part names, or OPENQUERY. It's convenient, and common in older systems, like a setup with a database per study plus a master database [and some cross-database queries]. But it has real risks.
p17-799.k: cross database query, linked server sql server, three part names, four part names, distributed query risks
x: In SQL Server, you can query another database on the same instance with three-part names, like OtherDb.dbo.Table, and another server with linked servers and four-part names, or OPENQUERY. It's convenient, and common in older systems, like a setup with a database per study plus a master database [and some cross-database queries]. But it has real risks.

Coupling: queries depend on another database's schema and name. Renaming, moving or splitting databases breaks code in places that are hard to find, and database names often differ between environments, so code needs synonyms or dynamic names.
Deployment and tooling: SSDT projects need database references to validate cross-database objects; migrations must be coordinated across databases.

High availability: databases in different availability groups may fail over separately, so cross-database queries may suddenly point at a different server or fail. Cross-database transactions in availability groups need special support.

Performance with linked servers: the optimiser often has poor information about remote data, so it may pull whole remote tables across the network and filter locally. Distributed transactions need MSDTC, adding latency and failure points.
Security: linked servers are often configured with a fixed, highly privileged login, which is a common security gap. Permissions and ownership chaining across databases need care.

Better approaches: use synonyms to isolate names in one place; keep cross-database access in a small number of views or procedures; move shared reference data access behind an API or cache; and replicate needed data into the local database with ETL or change data capture, rather than querying remotely in real time.

p17-800.q: Schema changes on large, busy tables can lock the table for a long time, blocking users. The trick is knowing which operations are cheap and splitting risky ones into safe steps.
p17-800.k: add column large table, online schema change sql server, alter table without downtime, add not null column big table, schema migration downtime
x: Schema changes on large, busy tables can lock the table for a long time, blocking users. The trick is knowing which operations are cheap and splitting risky ones into safe steps.
Adding a nullable column: metadata-only in SQL Server, instant regardless of table size.

Adding a NOT NULL column with a default: since SQL Server 2012 Enterprise Edition, this is also metadata-only for runtime constant defaults; older or lower editions may rewrite every row, which is slow and locks the table.

Changing a column's type, or making a column NOT NULL: may scan or rewrite the table. Safer approach: add a new column, backfill it in small batches during quiet times, switch the application to use it, then drop the old column later.
Creating indexes: use ONLINE = ON where the edition allows, and RESUMABLE in newer versions, so it can be paused and continued; otherwise schedule during maintenance windows.
Adding foreign keys or check constraints: WITH NOCHECK first to avoid a long validation, then validate later at a quiet time, so they become trusted.
Use a low lock timeout, like SET LOCK_TIMEOUT, or WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY for online operations, so a schema change waiting for a lock doesn't block everyone queued behind it.
Expand and contract: deploy the schema change first in a backward-compatible way, release code that works with both shapes, then remove the old structure in a later release.
Test on a production-sized copy, measuring duration and lock behaviour, because something instant on a small test database can take an hour in production.

p17-801.q: The Angular CDK, Component Dev Kit, is a set of behaviour primitives from the Angular Material team, without Material's visual design. It's useful when building your own design system or custom components, because it solves the hard interaction problems.
p17-801.k: angular cdk, component dev kit, cdk overlay, cdk drag drop, cdk virtual scroll
x: The Angular CDK, Component Dev Kit, is a set of behaviour primitives from the Angular Material team, without Material's visual design. It's useful when building your own design system or custom components, because it solves the hard interaction problems.
The parts I use most.

Overlay: creates floating panels, like dropdowns, tooltips, popovers and dialogs, positioned relative to an element or the screen, with automatic repositioning when there isn't space, scroll handling and backdrop clicks. Writing that from scratch is surprisingly hard.
Portal: renders a component or template into a different place in the DOM, which overlays and dialogs use.
Drag and drop: reorderable lists, moving items between lists, and drag handles, with animations and accessibility support. Useful for things like ordering steps in a configuration screen.
Scrolling: virtual scroll for long lists, rendering only visible rows.

Accessibility: FocusTrap to keep focus inside dialogs, LiveAnnouncer for screen reader announcements, ListKeyManager for keyboard navigation in menus and lists, and FocusMonitor to know whether focus came from keyboard or mouse.
Layout: BreakpointObserver to react to screen size changes in code.
Others: table, stepper, tree, clipboard and text-field auto-resize.

Why it matters: it lets a team build components that match their own styling, while getting tested, accessible behaviour. In our Angular 17 study builder, CDK features like drag and drop and overlays are the kind of building blocks that save weeks compared to writing custom implementations, and they're maintained alongside Angular versions.

p17-802.q: Angular Material components are styled through a theming system built on Sass, and since Angular Material 17 and 18, on Material 3 design tokens.
p17-802.k: angular material theming, custom theme angular material, material 3 angular, override material styles, design tokens angular
x: Angular Material components are styled through a theming system built on Sass, and since Angular Material 17 and 18, on Material 3 design tokens.

Creating a theme: in the global styles, use the mat.theme mixin, or in older versions define palettes with mat.define-palette and mat.define-light-theme, choosing primary, tertiary or accent colours, typography and density. Applying it to html generates CSS variables that all components use. Dark mode is a second theme applied under a class or a prefers-color-scheme media query.
Customising components the right way.

Use design tokens and the component override mixins, like mat.button-overrides, in newer versions, to change specific properties, like a button's container colour or shape, without fighting internal CSS.
Use CSS variables exposed by the theme for your own components, so custom parts match Material colours and respond to theme switches.

Avoid ::ng-deep and deep selectors targeting internal class names like .mat-mdc-..., because they break when Material updates its internals, which happened in the MDC migration around Angular 15, causing big upgrade work for many teams.
Density settings reduce spacing for data-heavy business screens, which is often needed in enterprise apps.

For a company design system shared with React, the brand colours, spacing and typography should come from one set of design tokens, generating both the Angular Material theme and the MUI theme, so both front ends look consistent, which matters while Angular and React live side by side.

p17-803.q: Accessibility means everyone, including keyboard and screen reader users, can use the app. In Angular, most rules are standard web accessibility, plus some framework-specific tools.
p17-803.k: angular accessibility, a11y angular, aria angular, cdk a11y, screen reader angular
x: Accessibility means everyone, including keyboard and screen reader users, can use the app. In Angular, most rules are standard web accessibility, plus some framework-specific tools.

Semantic HTML first: real buttons for actions, anchors for navigation, labels linked to inputs, headings in order, and tables for tabular data. Angular components should render semantic elements rather than clickable divs. For custom components, use host bindings to add roles and ARIA attributes, like role and aria-expanded.
Forms: every control has a label, error messages are linked with aria-describedby, and invalid fields set aria-invalid. Reactive forms make it easy to show errors consistently.

Focus management: in single-page apps, route changes don't move focus like a page load does. After navigation, move focus to the main heading or content, and announce the new page title. In dialogs, trap focus inside, and return it to the trigger when closing; CDK FocusTrap and Material dialogs do this.
Dynamic updates: use LiveAnnouncer from the CDK to announce things like "3 results found" or "saved successfully" to screen readers.
Keyboard support: all interactions work with the keyboard, focus is visible, and custom widgets like menus follow standard keyboard patterns; CDK key managers help.
Angular Material components come with good accessibility built in, which is a reason to use them over custom widgets.
Testing: the Angular ESLint accessibility rules, automated checks with axe in component or end-to-end tests, and manual checks with a keyboard and a screen reader for key flows.

p17-804.q: Users need feedback when the app is waiting, but a spinner per component gets messy. I use two global mechanisms, plus local indicators where they make more sense.
p17-804.k: global loading spinner angular, loading indicator interceptor, router events loading, progress bar angular, busy indicator
x: Users need feedback when the app is waiting, but a spinner per component gets messy. I use two global mechanisms, plus local indicators where they make more sense.

HTTP loading: an HTTP interceptor increments a counter in a LoadingService when a request starts, and decrements it in finalize when the request completes, errors or is cancelled. The service exposes a signal or observable, isLoading, which is true when the counter is above zero. A progress bar at the top of the shell binds to it. Using a counter, not a boolean, handles parallel requests correctly.

Exclusions: some requests shouldn't show the global indicator, like background polling or typeahead searches. I use an HttpContextToken, like SKIP_LOADING, which callers set on specific requests, and the interceptor checks it.

Route changes: subscribe to router events: show loading on NavigationStart, hide on NavigationEnd, NavigationCancel or NavigationError. This covers lazy-loaded chunks and resolvers, which can take noticeable time.
Avoid flicker: only show the indicator if loading takes longer than about 200 milliseconds, using a delay, and keep it visible for a minimum time once shown.

Local indicators: for parts of the page, like a grid reloading, a skeleton or a small spinner in that component is better than blocking the whole screen. With signals and the resource API, components get isLoading states easily.
Accessibility: announce loading and completion for screen readers with aria-busy on the region or a live announcer, and don't block keyboard focus unnecessarily.

p17-805.q: Since Angular 15, standalone components are stable, and since Angular 19 they're the default. Migrating an existing NgModule-based app reduces boilerplate and makes lazy loading and dependencies clearer.
p17-805.k: migrate to standalone angular, standalone migration schematic, remove ngmodules, bootstrapapplication, standalone components migration
x: Since Angular 15, standalone components are stable, and since Angular 19 they're the default. Migrating an existing NgModule-based app reduces boilerplate and makes lazy loading and dependencies clearer.
Angular provides a schematic: ng generate @angular/core:standalone. It runs in three steps, and I run them one at a time, committing and testing after each.
Step 1: convert all components, directives and pipes to standalone, adding the imports each one actually needs, based on their templates.
Step 2: remove NgModules that are no longer needed, those that only declared and exported things.

Step 3: switch bootstrapping from bootstrapModule(AppModule) to bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig), moving providers into an app.config.ts with provider functions like provideRouter, provideHttpClient with interceptors, and provideAnimations.
Then manual clean-up.
Routing: change lazy loading from loadChildren with modules to loadComponent for single components, or loadChildren returning a routes array.
Providers from modules, like StoreModule.forRoot or third-party modules, switch to their provide functions, or importProvidersFrom as a bridge for libraries that don't have them yet.
Shared modules that exported many common components: replace them with direct imports, or a constant array of commonly used imports.
Tests: TestBed configurations need updating, importing standalone components instead of declaring them.

Web workers run JavaScript on a separate background thread. Angular supports them directly: ng generate web-worker my-worker creates a worker file and configures the build. In the component or service, you create the worker with new Worker(new URL('./my.worker', import.meta.url)), send data with postMessage, and receive results with onmessage. Inside the worker, you listen for messages, do the work, and post the result back.

Deployment: the service worker serves the old version until it updates, so make sure version checks work, and ngsw.json must not be cached by the server or CDN.
Debugging: service workers can make problems like "users see the old version" confusing, so teams need to know how to clear them.

A clean RxJS approach: timer(0, 3000).pipe(switchMap(() => this.api.getJobStatus(jobId)), takeWhile(status => status.state === 'Running', true), takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef)).

How it works: timer emits immediately and then every 3 seconds; switchMap calls the API each time, cancelling a previous call if it's still running; takeWhile keeps going while the job is running, and the true argument also emits the final status, like Completed or Failed, so the UI can show it; takeUntilDestroyed stops polling if the user leaves the page.
Improvements.

Avoid overlapping calls: if responses can be slow, use exhaustMap instead of switchMap, so a new call isn't made while one is in flight, or poll with a delay after each response, using repeat({ delay: 3000 }) on the request observable.
Backoff: increase the interval over time, like 2, 4 then 8 seconds, for long jobs.
Errors: use retry with a count and delay for transient failures, and a timeout to give up eventually with a clear message.
Visibility: pause polling when the browser tab is hidden, using the visibilitychange event, to save server load.

Alternatives: for many users or frequent updates, server push with SignalR or Server-Sent Events is more efficient than polling. But for occasional long-running jobs, polling is simple, reliable and works through all proxies.

p17-818.q: These operators all limit how often values pass through, but they pick different values at different times.
p17-818.k: debouncetime vs throttletime, audittime, sampletime, rate limiting rxjs operators, rxjs throttle
x: These operators all limit how often values pass through, but they pick different values at different times.

debounceTime(300): waits until the source has been quiet for 300 milliseconds, then emits the last value. If values keep coming, it keeps waiting. Perfect for search boxes: only search after the user stops typing. The downside: during continuous activity, nothing is emitted.

throttleTime(300): emits the first value immediately, then ignores values for 300 milliseconds, then lets the next one through. Good for things like button clicks, to prevent double submits, or for scroll events where you want an immediate reaction and then regular updates. With the config { leading: true, trailing: true }, it also emits the last value at the end of the window.

auditTime(300): when a value arrives, waits 300 milliseconds, then emits the most recent value. So during continuous activity it emits regularly, with the latest value, not the first. Good for things like window resize or drag positions, where you want the latest state at a steady rate.

sampleTime(300): emits the most recent value every 300 milliseconds on a fixed timer, regardless of when values arrived, and only if there was a new value. Good for periodically sampling a fast-changing stream, like progress or sensor readings, for display.
A simple way to remember: debounce waits for silence; throttle takes the first and ignores the rest for a while; audit takes the last after a delay; sample checks on a clock.
Choosing the right one makes the UI feel responsive without flooding the server or the rendering.

How it works: in createApi, declare tagTypes, like Shipment. Query endpoints say what data they provide: getShipments provides a Shipment tag with id LIST plus one Shipment tag per returned id, and getShipment provides the Shipment tag for its id. Mutation endpoints say what they invalidate: addShipment invalidates the Shipment LIST tag, so lists refetch; updateShipment invalidates the Shipment tag for that id, so that shipment's detail and any list containing it refetch.
When a mutation succeeds, RTK Query finds active queries with matching tags and refetches them. Components subscribed through hooks re-render with fresh data, with no manual dispatching.
Fine-tuning.
Optimistic updates with onQueryStarted and updateQueryData, to update the cache immediately and undo it if the mutation fails.
Pessimistic updates: write the mutation's response directly into the cache instead of refetching, to save a request.
keepUnusedDataFor controls how long unused cache entries stay; refetchOnFocus and refetchOnReconnect refresh data when users return.
Common mistakes: providing only a generic tag, so every mutation refetches everything; or forgetting the LIST tag, so new items don't appear in lists.
In the React shell with Redux Toolkit, RTK Query keeps API state consistent without hand-written loading flags and thunks, which removes a lot of boilerplate compared to our older patterns.

p17-822.q: These two settings confuse many people because both relate to caching, but they control different things.

x: These two settings confuse many people because both relate to caching, but they control different things.

staleTime: how long fetched data is considered fresh. While fresh, TanStack Query serves it from cache without refetching, even when a new component mounts with the same query key. The default is 0, meaning data is stale immediately, so it refetches in the background on events like mount, window focus or reconnect. Setting staleTime to, say, 5 minutes for reference data, like a list of countries or sites, avoids unnecessary requests.

gcTime, called cacheTime before version 5: how long unused data stays in the cache after no component is using it. The default is 5 minutes. After that, it's garbage collected. If a component mounts again before then, cached data shows instantly, possibly with a background refetch if stale.
So: staleTime decides when to refetch; gcTime decides when to forget.

Query keys matter as much: a key array of 'shipments' plus an object with siteId and page includes all parameters, so different filters are cached separately, and invalidateQueries with just the 'shipments' prefix after a mutation refetches all shipment queries.

Typical settings I use: frequently changing data, like statuses, keep staleTime low; reference data gets a long staleTime; refetchOnWindowFocus can be turned off for heavy queries if it causes too many requests.

p17-823.q: Both build React apps, but they solve different problems.

x: Both build React apps, but they solve different problems.

A Vite single-page app is a client-side React app: the server sends a small HTML file and JavaScript bundle, and everything renders in the browser. Routing, data fetching and state are handled with libraries like React Router and TanStack Query. It's simple to deploy as static files on any web server or CDN, behind IIS, or inside an existing application, and it works well with a separate API backend, like ASP.NET Core.

Next.js is a full-stack React framework: server-side rendering, static generation, React Server Components, file-based routing, API routes and server actions, image optimisation and more. Pages can render on the server, so users see content quickly and search engines can index it.

When I'd choose Next.js: public websites where SEO and first-load speed matter, like marketing sites, e-commerce or content; when the team wants server-side React with a Node runtime; and when using React Server Components to reduce client JavaScript.

When I'd choose a Vite SPA: internal business applications behind login, where SEO doesn't matter; when there's already a separate backend, like .NET APIs; when the app must be embedded in or hosted by another platform, like our MVC host on IIS; and when the team wants simple static hosting without running Node servers in production.

For our React 17 shell with Vite, MUI and Redux Toolkit, a SPA is the right fit: it's an authenticated enterprise app on-premise, with .NET APIs. Next.js would add a Node server layer without real benefit there.

p17-824.q: State colocation means keeping state as close as possible to where it's used. If only one component needs a value, like whether a dropdown is open, it lives in that component's useState, not in Redux or a parent.
p17-824.k: state colocation, lift state up react, where to put state react, local vs global state, keep state close
x: State colocation means keeping state as close as possible to where it's used. If only one component needs a value, like whether a dropdown is open, it lives in that component's useState, not in Redux or a parent.

Why it matters: when state lives high up, every change re-renders a large part of the tree, and the code becomes harder to follow, because you have to trace where state is set and passed. Colocated state is easier to understand, delete and refactor, and performs better.

Lifting state up is the opposite move, done when needed: if two sibling components need the same state, like a filter panel and a results table, move the state to their closest common parent, and pass it down as props, with callbacks to change it.
A practical order of choices.
Local component state for UI-only state.
Lift to the nearest common parent when siblings share it.
Use the URL for state that should survive refresh or be shareable, like filters, sorting and pagination.
Use a server-state library, like TanStack Query or RTK Query, for data from APIs, rather than copying it into global state.
Use Context for rarely changing app-wide values, like theme, current user or locale.
Use a global store, like Redux Toolkit or Zustand, for complex client state shared widely, like a multi-step workflow or cross-feature selections.
A common anti-pattern I've cleaned up is putting everything into Redux, including form inputs and modal flags, which made simple components depend on the global store and re-render unnecessarily.

p17-825.q: Custom hooks contain logic, like data fetching, debouncing or form handling, and they should be tested too. But hooks can only run inside components, so you need a test harness.
p17-825.k: renderhook, test custom hooks, testing library react hooks, act testing hooks, test usefetch hook
x: Custom hooks contain logic, like data fetching, debouncing or form handling, and they should be tested too. But hooks can only run inside components, so you need a test harness.

renderHook from React Testing Library does this: const { result, rerender, unmount } = renderHook(() => useCounter(5)). result.current holds the hook's latest return value. You call functions it returns inside act, like act(() => result.current.increment()), then assert expect(result.current.count).toBe(6).
Changing props: renderHook(({ delay }) => useDebounce(value, delay), { initialProps: { delay: 300 } }), then rerender({ delay: 500 }).
Async behaviour: use waitFor(() => expect(result.current.data).toBeDefined()) for hooks that fetch data, and fake timers, like vi.useFakeTimers(), to control debounce or polling without real waiting.
Context and providers: pass a wrapper option that renders required providers, like a QueryClientProvider with a fresh client per test, a Redux Provider with a test store, or a router.
Mocking network calls: use Mock Service Worker to return fake API responses, so the hook runs its real fetch code.
Cleanup: unmount() to check that effects clean up, like cancelling subscriptions or timers.

When I don't use renderHook: if the hook is simple and only used by one component, testing the component's behaviour covers it. renderHook is most valuable for shared hooks in a library, where the hook is the public API, like hooks in our npm feature packages.

p17-826.q: Without a plan, error handling ends up scattered: some components show alerts, some log to the console, some do nothing. I set up layers.
p17-826.k: global error handling react, api error handling react, error toast react, axios interceptor errors, handle 401 react
x: Without a plan, error handling ends up scattered: some components show alerts, some log to the console, some do nothing. I set up layers.

A central API client: one fetch or axios wrapper used by all features. It converts error responses into a consistent error object, reading ProblemDetails from the .NET API, like status, title, error code and validation errors, and adds the correlation id from response headers, which helps support teams find the logs.
Global handling for cross-cutting cases.
401 Unauthorized: try a token refresh, and if that fails, redirect to login.
403 Forbidden: show a "you don't have access" message or page.
Network errors and 5xx: show a toast like "Something went wrong, please try again", with the reference id.
These can live in an axios interceptor, a TanStack Query QueryCache onError callback, or RTK Query middleware with isRejectedWithValue, so every query and mutation gets the same behaviour.

Local handling for business errors: validation errors, 400 or 422, are shown next to form fields, using React Hook Form's setError. Conflict errors, 409, show a specific message, like "this record was changed by someone else".
Rendering errors: error boundaries catch exceptions during rendering, showing a fallback per section instead of a white screen.
Logging: send unexpected errors to a front-end monitoring tool with user context and the correlation id, so we can link front-end and back-end errors.
Avoid duplicate toasts: if a component handles an error locally, mark it so the global handler skips it.

p17-827.q: For a React single-page app, login uses OpenID Connect with the authorisation code flow and PKCE, against an identity provider like Keycloak, Entra ID or Cognito.

Libraries: oidc-client-ts with react-oidc-context works with any standard provider; MSAL React for Entra ID; and keycloak-js with a React wrapper for Keycloak. They handle the redirect to the login page, the code exchange, token storage, silent renewal and logout.

A protected route component checks useAuth().isAuthenticated, and calls signinRedirect if not, saving the original URL so the user returns there after login. Calling APIs: the API client gets the access token from the auth context and adds the Authorization header, only for our API's base URL. Before tokens expire, the library renews them silently, or the API client retries once after a refresh if it gets a 401.

Security choices: keep tokens in memory or session storage rather than localStorage where possible; use short access token lifetimes; and consider the BFF pattern, where a backend handles tokens and the browser only gets a secure, HttpOnly cookie, which is the most secure option for SPAs.
Roles and permissions: read them from the token or a user profile endpoint to show or hide features, but the API always enforces authorisation.
With Keycloak providing SSO across our legacy MVC app, Angular sub-apps and the React shell, a user signs in once and moves between them without logging in again.

Libraries.

TanStack Virtual: headless, giving you the virtual items and positions while you render the markup, so it fits any design system, including MUI. Supports variable heights by measuring rows, horizontal lists and grids.
react-window: simple components like FixedSizeList and VariableSizeList, small and fast; react-virtuoso handles variable heights and grouping with little setup.
Grid components like MUI X Data Grid and AG Grid include virtualisation for rows and columns built in.

Things to get right: give the scroll container a fixed height; use stable keys based on item ids; memoise row components so scrolling doesn't re-render everything; and for variable heights, use measuring support rather than guessing.

Alternatives: often the better first step is server-side pagination or filtering, so users don't load thousands of rows at all. Infinite scrolling loads more as you scroll, and can be combined with virtualisation for very long feeds.
In our data-heavy screens, like inventory or shipment lists, virtualisation or a grid with built-in virtualisation keeps the UI smooth.

p17-829.q: Large JavaScript bundles slow down the first load, especially on slower machines and networks. I treat bundle size as something to measure regularly, not guess.
p17-829.k: react bundle size, vite bundle analyzer, rollup visualizer, reduce javascript bundle, tree shaking react
x: Large JavaScript bundles slow down the first load, especially on slower machines and networks. I treat bundle size as something to measure regularly, not guess.

Analyse: add rollup-plugin-visualizer to the Vite build to get a treemap of what's in each chunk. Look for large libraries, duplicated packages with different versions, and code that shouldn't be in the initial bundle. Also check the network tab and Lighthouse for real load behaviour.
Common fixes.
Route-based code splitting: lazy-load pages with React.lazy and dynamic imports, so users only download what they visit.
Lazy-load heavy components: charts, rich text editors, PDF viewers and export libraries load when needed.

Replace or trim heavy libraries: moment.js with date-fns or dayjs; import only what you use from lodash, like lodash-es with named imports; check that icon libraries are imported per icon, like @mui/icons-material per-file imports, rather than whole packages.
Tree shaking: prefer ES module packages and avoid side-effect imports, so unused code is removed.
Deduplicate: make sure shared libraries like React, MUI and Redux are peer dependencies in internal packages, so the app has one copy, and use npm ls or the visualiser to spot duplicates.
Vendor chunking: configure manualChunks for rarely changing libraries, so they're cached by browsers across releases.
Compression: serve Brotli or gzip from the server or IIS, with long cache headers for hashed files.
Guard it in CI: set a size budget with a tool like size-limit, so a pull request that adds a large dependency fails or gets flagged.

p17-830.q: A generic component works with any data type while keeping full type safety. Typical examples: a Table that renders rows of any type, a Select whose options are any objects, or a List with a custom item renderer.
p17-830.k: generic react component, typescript generic props, generic table component, generic select react, react typescript generics
x: A generic component works with any data type while keeping full type safety. Typical examples: a Table that renders rows of any type, a Select whose options are any objects, or a List with a custom item renderer.

How: declare a type parameter on the component function. For example, TableProps<T> has rows, an array of T; columns, each with a key of type keyof T, a header and an optional render function taking a T; a getRowId function; and an optional onRowClick callback. Then function Table<T>(props: TableProps<T>).

When used as <Table rows={shipments} columns={...} getRowId={s => s.id} />, TypeScript infers T as Shipment, so column keys must be real Shipment properties, and callbacks receive typed rows. Typos in keys become compile errors.
Tips.
In .tsx files, arrow functions with generics need a trailing comma or constraint, like <T,>() => or <T extends object>, so the parser doesn't confuse them with JSX.
Constraints: <T extends { id: string }> when the component needs certain fields.
Wrapping with memo or forwardRef loses generics, so you may need a type assertion to keep the generic signature; React 19's ref-as-prop makes this easier.
Avoid over-engineering: if a component is only used with one type, generics add complexity for nothing.

Generic components are especially valuable in shared design system packages used across features, like our npm feature packages, where many teams render different data with the same grid or picker, and type safety prevents integration mistakes.

The non-null assertion operator, a postfix exclamation mark, like user!.name or document.getElementById('root')!, tells the compiler: trust me, this isn't null or undefined. It removes those types without any runtime check.

The problem: if you're wrong, you get a runtime error, like "cannot read properties of undefined", exactly the error that strict null checks were meant to prevent. It silences the compiler instead of handling the case. Over time, code with many exclamation marks gives a false sense of safety.
Better alternatives.
Narrowing with checks: if (!user) return null; then TypeScript knows user is defined below.
Optional chaining and nullish coalescing: user?.name ?? 'Unknown'.
Assertion functions that check at runtime and throw a clear error: function assertDefined<T>(v: T): asserts v is NonNullable<T>.
Better types: if a value is always present after loading, model the loading state with a discriminated union, so the component handles loading and loaded states explicitly.

Definite assignment for class fields initialised outside the constructor, like in Angular with ViewChild, uses a similar exclamation mark, field!: Type, with the same risks; signal-based queries reduce the need for it.
Where it's acceptable: places where the guarantee is obvious and local, like the root element in main.tsx that always exists, or in tests.
I enable the ESLint rule no-non-null-assertion as a warning, so each use is a conscious decision visible in code review.

Bundled types: many libraries ship their own .d.ts files, referenced by the types field in package.json.
DefinitelyTyped: community-maintained types published as @types packages, like @types/lodash, installed as dev dependencies.

Publishing a TypeScript library: generate .d.ts files with declaration: true in tsconfig, so consumers get types automatically. Our internal npm packages ship declarations, so apps get type checking and IntelliSense for shared components.
I make sure custom declaration files are included in tsconfig and kept near the code they describe, and replace them when libraries add official types.

p17-833.q: React has many styling options, and each has trade-offs.
p17-833.k: css modules vs styled components, tailwind vs mui, css in js, react styling approaches, emotion styling
x: React has many styling options, and each has trade-offs.

CSS Modules: regular CSS files where class names are scoped automatically per component, so there are no global conflicts. No runtime cost, works with any build tool including Vite, and familiar to anyone who knows CSS. Dynamic styling uses conditional class names.

CSS-in-JS, like styled-components and Emotion: styles written in JavaScript, colocated with components, with props-based dynamic styles and theming. MUI uses Emotion internally. The downside is runtime cost, since styles are generated in the browser, and less compatibility with React Server Components. Newer zero-runtime options, like Pigment CSS or vanilla-extract, address that.

Tailwind CSS: utility classes directly in markup, like className="flex gap-2 p-4". Very fast to build with, consistent spacing and colours from a design system, small production CSS. Some find markup cluttered, and it's a different way of thinking.

MUI's sx prop and styled: if the app uses MUI, these integrate with the theme, so colours and spacing come from theme tokens. sx is convenient for one-off adjustments; styled is better for reusable styled components.

How I choose: consistency with the component library matters most. In a React shell built on MUI 5, I'd use the theme, sx for small tweaks, and styled for reusable pieces, rather than mixing in Tailwind or another system. For a new project without a component library, CSS Modules or Tailwind are good, low-runtime choices.
Whatever the choice, design tokens should be the single source of truth for colours, spacing and typography.

Parse and validate: URL values are strings and can be edited by users, so parse them into typed values with defaults, for example with a small Zod schema, and ignore invalid values.

p17-836.q: Redux reducers must be pure, so side effects, like API calls, timers or navigation, live elsewhere. Redux Toolkit offers two built-in options.
p17-836.k: listener middleware redux, createlistenermiddleware, redux side effects, thunks vs listener, redux saga alternative
x: Redux reducers must be pure, so side effects, like API calls, timers or navigation, live elsewhere. Redux Toolkit offers two built-in options.

Thunks, with createAsyncThunk, are functions you dispatch directly from a component, like dispatch(fetchShipments(siteId)). They run the async work and dispatch pending, fulfilled and rejected actions automatically. Good for request-response flows triggered by a user action. For server data, RTK Query usually replaces hand-written thunks.

The listener middleware, with createListenerMiddleware, reacts to actions or state changes after they happen. You register a listener with a matcher, like startListening({ actionCreator: siteSelected, effect: async (action, listenerApi) => { ... } }). The effect can read state, dispatch actions, wait for other actions with take or condition, delay, and cancel previous runs with cancelActiveListeners, which gives debounce-like or takeLatest behaviour.
When I use listeners.
Cross-feature reactions: when a user changes the selected study, clear caches in several slices and load new reference data, without the component knowing about all of them.
Persisting state: save certain slices to local storage when they change.
Analytics and logging of specific actions.
Workflows: wait for one action, then another, with timeouts.
It's a lightweight alternative to Redux-Saga or Redux-Observable, without generators or RxJS, and it's part of Redux Toolkit already.
Caution: listeners make behaviour less obvious, because effects happen away from where actions are dispatched. I keep them in clearly named files per feature, and document what triggers them.

Client setup: install @microsoft/signalr.
