Updating the UI: on a message, update the relevant cache, like queryClient.setQueryData or invalidateQueries in TanStack Query, or dispatch a Redux action, so components re-render through normal state, rather than each component holding its own copy.

Reconnection: withAutomaticReconnect retries with backoff. On reconnect, refetch data that may have changed while disconnected, because messages sent during the gap are lost. Show a small "reconnecting" indicator.
Groups: the server adds connections to groups, like per study or site, so users only get relevant messages.
Scale: with multiple servers, the backend needs a backplane like Redis, or Azure SignalR Service, which the server side handles.
Testing: mock the hub connection in component tests.

p17-838.q: React has two main rules for hooks.
p17-838.k: rules of hooks, hooks rules react, conditional hooks, eslint plugin react hooks, why hooks order matters
x: React has two main rules for hooks.
First, only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook: not inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or after an early return.
Second, only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks, not from regular JavaScript functions or class components.

Why: React doesn't identify hooks by name. It tracks them by the order they're called during each render. The first useState call gets the first state slot, the second gets the second, and so on. If a hook is inside a condition, it may run in one render and not the next, so the order shifts, and React gives one hook's state to another. That causes confusing bugs, and React throws errors like "Rendered fewer hooks than expected".

How to handle conditional logic: put the condition inside the hook, not around it. For example, an effect that returns early when enabled is false, with enabled in its dependency array, or for data fetching, TanStack Query's enabled option. If a component needs very different hooks in different cases, split it into separate components and render one or the other.
Custom hooks must start with "use", so React and linting tools know to apply the rules.
The eslint-plugin-react-hooks package enforces both rules, and its exhaustive-deps rule checks dependency arrays. I keep both as errors in CI, because they catch real bugs.
React 19's use function is an exception: it can be called conditionally, because it doesn't rely on call order in the same way.

p17-839.q: The function you return from a useEffect callback is the cleanup function. React runs it to undo whatever the effect set up.
p17-839.k: useeffect cleanup, cleanup function react, unsubscribe in useeffect, clear interval react, effect cleanup timing
x: The function you return from a useEffect callback is the cleanup function. React runs it to undo whatever the effect set up.

When it runs: before the effect runs again because its dependencies changed, with the old values, and when the component unmounts. In development with StrictMode, React also runs an extra setup, cleanup, setup cycle on mount, to reveal effects that don't clean up properly.
What needs cleanup.
Subscriptions: event listeners on window or document, WebSocket or SignalR handlers, observable subscriptions, store subscriptions. Remove them in cleanup.
Timers: clearInterval or clearTimeout.
Network requests: abort with an AbortController, so a slow response for old parameters doesn't update state after the parameters changed or the component unmounted.
Third-party widgets: destroy chart or map instances created in the effect.
Example: an effect that calls setInterval(refresh, 5000) and returns a cleanup that calls clearInterval with that id, with refresh as its dependency.

Common bugs without cleanup: memory leaks, duplicated event handlers firing several times, intervals multiplying each time dependencies change, and race conditions where old responses overwrite newer data.
Good practice: every effect that starts something should stop it, so a quick mental check during code review is "what does this effect start, and where is it stopped?"

Many effects can be avoided altogether: data fetching through TanStack Query or RTK Query handles cancellation and caching, and derived values can be computed during render, so fewer effects means fewer cleanup bugs.

p17-840.q: A good upload experience shows progress, allows cancellation, validates early and handles errors clearly.
p17-840.k: file upload react, upload progress react, cancel upload, axios onuploadprogress, drag and drop upload react

Selecting files: an input of type file, or a drag-and-drop area with a library like react-dropzone. Validate on the client first: file type, size and count, with clear messages. The server must validate again, since client checks can be bypassed.

Uploading: send FormData with the file and metadata. The fetch API doesn't report upload progress, so I use XMLHttpRequest directly, or axios with onUploadProgress, which gives loaded and total bytes to calculate a percentage for a progress bar.
Cancellation: axios supports an AbortController signal; on cancel, abort the request and update the state to cancelled. Abort on unmount too.
Multiple files: upload with limited concurrency, like two or three at a time, each with its own progress and status, and allow retrying failed files individually.

Large files: chunked or resumable uploads, splitting the file into parts, so a network failure doesn't restart from zero. Or upload directly to object storage with pre-signed URLs, so files don't pass through the API servers.
After upload: show processing status if the server scans or parses the file, like virus scanning or validating an import file, possibly with polling or SignalR updates.
Accessibility: the drop zone must be keyboard accessible, with a normal file input fallback, and progress announced to screen readers.
On the server side, the ASP.NET Core API enforces size limits, streams large files rather than buffering, and checks content type and file signatures.

p17-841.q: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, but it isn't single-threaded underneath. libuv, the C library behind Node's event loop, handles I/O in two ways. Network I/O, like sockets and HTTP, uses the operating system's non-blocking mechanisms, epoll, kqueue or IOCP, so it needs no extra threads. Other work that has no good non-blocking API runs on a small libuv thread pool: most file system operations, DNS lookups with dns.lookup, some crypto functions like pbkdf2, scrypt and randomBytes, and zlib compression.
p17-841.k: libuv thread pool, uv_threadpool_size, node thread pool, node fs crypto thread pool, libuv
x: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, but it isn't single-threaded underneath. libuv, the C library behind Node's event loop, handles I/O in two ways. Network I/O, like sockets and HTTP, uses the operating system's non-blocking mechanisms, epoll, kqueue or IOCP, so it needs no extra threads. Other work that has no good non-blocking API runs on a small libuv thread pool: most file system operations, DNS lookups with dns.lookup, some crypto functions like pbkdf2, scrypt and randomBytes, and zlib compression.

The default pool size is 4 threads. If an app does lots of these operations at once, like hashing passwords for many logins, compressing responses, or reading many files, requests queue for the pool, and latency rises even though CPU and the event loop look fine. A classic surprise is slow outbound HTTP calls caused by dns.lookup waiting behind file or crypto work.

What I do: increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, set as an environment variable before the process starts, up to 1024, sized to the workload and cores; use the async versions of crypto and fs functions, never the Sync versions on request paths; cache DNS results or use connection keep-alive so lookups are rare; and move heavy CPU work, like large compression or image processing, to worker threads or separate services.
To diagnose, I look at event loop delay and pool queueing in profiles or traces; if latency rises while CPU and event loop lag stay low, thread pool saturation is a likely cause.

p17-842.q: NestJS handles authentication and authorisation with guards, which run before a route handler and decide whether the request may continue.
p17-842.k: nestjs jwt auth, nestjs guards, passport jwt nestjs, nestjs authguard, nestjs roles guard
x: NestJS handles authentication and authorisation with guards, which run before a route handler and decide whether the request may continue.

A typical setup for an API that receives tokens from an identity provider like Keycloak or Cognito: install @nestjs/passport and passport-jwt, and create a JwtStrategy. It reads the bearer token, validates the signature using the provider's JWKS endpoint with a library like jwks-rsa, and checks issuer, audience and expiry. Its validate method returns the user object, which Nest attaches to the request.

Then apply AuthGuard('jwt'). I prefer registering it globally with APP_GUARD, so every route is protected by default, and marking the few public routes with a custom @Public() decorator that the guard checks with the Reflector. Secure by default is safer than remembering to add guards.

Authorisation: a RolesGuard reads required roles from a @Roles('admin') decorator via metadata and compares them with roles in the user object, mapped from the token claims. For record-level checks, like "can this user see this site's data", I do the check in the service, with the user passed in, because guards don't know the specific record.

Other pieces: a custom @CurrentUser() parameter decorator to get the user in handlers cleanly; tests that override the guard or generate test tokens signed with a test key; and consistent 401 versus 403 responses through an exception filter.
The same ideas, validate tokens properly, deny by default and check resource ownership, are what I apply in ASP.NET Core too.

p17-843.q: NestJS has several building blocks that wrap route handlers, each with a specific job, and they run in a defined order.
p17-843.k: nestjs guards interceptors pipes filters, nestjs request lifecycle, nestjs middleware vs interceptor, nestjs pipes validation
x: NestJS has several building blocks that wrap route handlers, each with a specific job, and they run in a defined order.
Middleware runs first, like Express middleware, with access to the raw request and response. Good for things like request logging or correlation ids that don't need to know which handler will run.

Guards decide whether the request may proceed, returning true or false, or throwing. Used for authentication and authorisation. They know the execution context, so they can read metadata like required roles from decorators.

Interceptors wrap the handler call, before and after, using RxJS. Used for logging timings, transforming responses into a standard shape, caching, adding timeouts, or mapping errors. They're similar to action filters in ASP.NET Core.

Pipes transform and validate input parameters before the handler gets them. The ValidationPipe with class-validator DTOs validates request bodies, and ParseIntPipe converts route parameters. Validation failures become 400 responses automatically. Zod-based pipes are a popular alternative.
Exception filters catch exceptions thrown anywhere and turn them into HTTP responses, so you can return a consistent error format, like ProblemDetails, and log unexpected errors.
The order: middleware, then guards, then interceptors before the handler, then pipes, then the handler, then interceptors after, with exception filters catching errors from any stage.

Each can be applied globally, per controller or per route. For a .NET developer, the mapping is easy: middleware is middleware, guards are authorisation filters, interceptors are action filters, pipes are model binding and validation, and exception filters are exception handlers.

p17-844.q: For caching in Node, I use Redis through a client like ioredis or the official node-redis package, created once at startup and shared, since clients maintain their own connections and pipelining.
p17-844.k: redis cache node, ioredis, node caching, cache aside node js, redis client node
x: For caching in Node, I use Redis through a client like ioredis or the official node-redis package, created once at startup and shared, since clients maintain their own connections and pipelining.

The usual pattern is cache-aside: on a read, try the cache with a key like site:123:summary; on a hit, parse and return it; on a miss, load from the database, store it with an expiry using SET with EX, and return it. On updates, delete or overwrite the related keys.
Details that matter.
Key design: include versions or tenant and study identifiers, like v2:study:42:site:7, so changing the data shape or isolating data is easy.
Serialisation: JSON is simple; for large values, consider compression or storing only what's needed.
Expiry with jitter: add randomness to TTLs so many keys don't expire at the same moment.
Stampede protection: when a hot key expires, many requests may hit the database at once. Use an in-process promise map so concurrent requests for the same key share one load, or a short Redis lock.
Failure handling: Redis being slow or down shouldn't take the service down. Set command timeouts, catch errors and fall back to the database, and add a circuit breaker if needed.
In-process cache as a first layer: a small LRU cache, like lru-cache, for very hot, rarely changing data, in front of Redis.
Monitoring: hit ratio, latency and memory, plus Redis eviction counts.
On AWS this would be ElastiCache; the code stays the same, with TLS and authentication configured.

p17-845.q: The principles are the same as in .NET; the libraries differ.
p17-845.k: node rabbitmq consumer, amqplib, kafkajs consumer, node message consumer, reliable consumer node
x: The principles are the same as in .NET; the libraries differ.
For RabbitMQ, I use amqplib or a wrapper like amqp-connection-manager, which handles reconnection. For Kafka, kafkajs or the Confluent JavaScript client.
Key practices.

Acknowledge after processing: in RabbitMQ, use manual acks and only ack after the work and database writes succeed. On failure, nack without requeue so the message goes to a retry or dead-letter exchange, instead of looping forever. In Kafka, commit offsets after processing, not before.

Limit concurrency: set the RabbitMQ prefetch count, like 10, so one consumer doesn't grab thousands of messages. In Kafka, control partitions per consumer and process a batch with limited parallelism, keeping order per key where it matters.
Idempotency: messages can be delivered more than once, so record processed message ids, or make operations naturally idempotent with upserts.
Retries with backoff: use delayed retry queues, or a retry topic in Kafka, with a maximum attempt count, then dead-letter with error details.
Validate messages: parse with a schema, like Zod, and dead-letter invalid ones immediately instead of retrying.
Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop consuming, finish in-flight messages, then close the channel and connection.
Observability: log with message id and correlation id, propagate trace context from message headers, and monitor queue depth, consumer lag, processing time and dead-letter counts.
Don't block the event loop: CPU-heavy processing in a consumer stalls heartbeats and can cause the broker to think the consumer died.

p17-846.q: Unit tests check functions; integration tests check that routes, middleware, validation, serialisation and data access work together. For Node APIs, I use Supertest with Jest or Vitest.
p17-846.k: supertest, integration test express, nestjs e2e test, test node api, api testing node
x: Unit tests check functions; integration tests check that routes, middleware, validation, serialisation and data access work together. For Node APIs, I use Supertest with Jest or Vitest.

Express: export the app without calling listen, then in tests call request(app).post('/shipments').send(body).set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + testToken), and assert the status and body. Supertest starts the app on an ephemeral port automatically.

NestJS: create a testing module with Test.createTestingModule, import the AppModule, override providers that talk to external systems with overrideProvider, then create the Nest application, call init, and use Supertest against app.getHttpServer(). This exercises guards, pipes and filters just like production.
Dependencies.
Database: a real database in a container with Testcontainers, migrated before tests and cleaned between them, gives much more confidence than mocks, especially with ORMs.
External HTTP APIs: mock at the network level with nock or Mock Service Worker for Node, so the real HTTP client code runs.
Auth: sign test tokens with a test key and configure the app to trust it in tests, or override the guard.
Message brokers: an in-memory fake, or a containerised broker for a few key tests.

Good habits: each test arranges its own data, tests are independent so they can run in parallel, and cases cover error paths, like validation failures, 404s and unauthorised access, not just the happy path.
These run in CI on every pull request, the same way I run WebApplicationFactory tests for .NET APIs.

p17-847.q: Since Node 18, and stable since Node 20, Node has a built-in test runner in the node:test module. You import test and describe from node:test and assertions from node:assert, write tests, and run them with node --test, which finds test files automatically.
p17-847.k: node test runner, node:test, node --test, built in test runner node, jest vs node test
x: Since Node 18, and stable since Node 20, Node has a built-in test runner in the node:test module. You import test and describe from node:test and assertions from node:assert, write tests, and run them with node --test, which finds test files automatically.

What it offers: describe and it style, subtests, before and after hooks, skipping and only, mocking of functions, timers and modules, watch mode, code coverage with a flag, and reporters including TAP, spec and JUnit for CI. It runs test files in separate processes for isolation, in parallel.

Advantages: no dependencies to install, which reduces supply chain risk and setup; fast startup; and it's maintained with Node itself, so it works with the latest Node features, like ES modules and native TypeScript type stripping, without extra configuration.

Where Jest or Vitest are still better: rich ecosystem and integrations, like Testing Library for React; snapshot testing; mature mocking of modules; better watch mode experience; and many teams already know them. For front-end code, Vitest with Vite is the natural choice.

My choice: for small backend libraries, CLI tools or scripts, the built-in runner is great, and keeps the project lean. For larger backend services, either works, and I'd follow the team's existing tool. For a repo with both front end and back end, using Vitest everywhere gives one consistent experience.
Whatever the runner, the important things are the same: fast, independent tests, meaningful assertions, and running them in CI on every change.

p17-848.q: OpenTelemetry gives Node services the same traces, metrics and log correlation that I use in .NET, so a request can be followed across both stacks.
p17-848.k: opentelemetry node, otel nodejs, node auto instrumentation, node tracing, otel sdk node
x: OpenTelemetry gives Node services the same traces, metrics and log correlation that I use in .NET, so a request can be followed across both stacks.

Setup: install @opentelemetry/sdk-node and @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node, plus an OTLP exporter. Create the NodeSDK with a resource describing the service name, version and environment, the exporters and the instrumentations, and start it before the rest of the app loads, usually with the --import or --require flag pointing to an instrumentation file. Loading order matters, because instrumentation works by patching modules like http, express, pg and ioredis when they're first required.

Auto-instrumentation then creates spans for incoming HTTP requests, outgoing calls, database queries, Redis commands and messaging clients, and propagates trace context through W3C traceparent headers, so traces connect with .NET and Python services.
Custom spans: use the tracer API around important business operations, adding attributes like study or site ids, while avoiding personal data.
Metrics: use the meter API for counters and histograms, like messages processed or job duration, and the instrumentations emit HTTP metrics.
Logs: configure the logger, like Pino, to include trace and span ids, so logs and traces link together.
Export: send everything to an OpenTelemetry Collector, which forwards to Datadog, Grafana, CloudWatch or another backend, keeping vendor choice out of the code.
Practical tips: set sampling to control cost, check the instrumentation overhead in load tests, and flush telemetry on graceful shutdown so the last spans aren't lost.

p17-849.q: Node has a predictable release schedule: a new major version every six months, and even-numbered versions become LTS, long-term support, maintained for about 30 months. Odd-numbered versions are short-lived and not for production.
p17-849.k: node lts, node version upgrade, nvmrc, node release schedule, upgrade node version
x: Node has a predictable release schedule: a new major version every six months, and even-numbered versions become LTS, long-term support, maintained for about 30 months. Odd-numbered versions are short-lived and not for production.
My policy: production services run on an active LTS version, and we upgrade before the version reaches end of life, so we keep getting security fixes.

Keeping versions consistent: an .nvmrc or the engines field in package.json documents the expected version; developers use nvm, fnm or Volta to switch automatically; the Docker base image pins the same major version, like node:22-slim or a digest; and CI uses the same version, so there are no "works on my machine" differences.
Upgrade process.
Read the release notes and breaking changes, like removed APIs, changed defaults or OpenSSL updates.

Update in a branch: Docker image, CI and local tools, then run the full test suite. Pay special attention to native modules, like bcrypt or database drivers, which need versions built for the new Node.
Check deprecation warnings when running tests and the app, since they show what will break next.
Roll out gradually: deploy to test environments, run load tests if performance matters, then production, with monitoring for memory and latency changes.
Automate the reminder: Renovate or Dependabot can propose base image and version updates.
Benefits of staying current: security fixes, performance improvements, and newer features like native fetch, the built-in test runner, and type stripping for TypeScript, which simplify the toolchain.

p17-850.q: PM2 is a process manager for Node: it keeps the app running, restarts it on crashes, runs multiple instances in cluster mode to use all CPU cores, handles log files, supports zero-downtime reloads, and offers basic monitoring. It's popular for deploying Node directly on virtual machines.
p17-850.k: pm2, pm2 vs docker, node process manager, pm2 cluster mode, run node production
x: PM2 is a process manager for Node: it keeps the app running, restarts it on crashes, runs multiple instances in cluster mode to use all CPU cores, handles log files, supports zero-downtime reloads, and offers basic monitoring. It's popular for deploying Node directly on virtual machines.

Containers with an orchestrator, like ECS, Kubernetes or Azure Container Apps, provide most of the same features at the platform level: restarts on failure, health checks, scaling by running more containers, rolling deployments, and central logging from stdout.
My view: on VMs without containers, PM2 is a solid choice. Use its ecosystem file for configuration, cluster mode for multiple cores, startup scripts so it survives reboots, and log rotation.

With containers, don't use PM2 inside the container in most cases. Run one Node process per container, with node as the command directly or through a small init like tini so signals are handled correctly. Scale by adding containers, not processes inside one container. Running PM2 inside containers hides crashes from the orchestrator, because PM2 restarts the process itself, makes health and resource limits less accurate, and complicates logging.
Exceptions: pm2-runtime is designed for containers if a team really wants PM2 features, and on a large VM-based host, cluster mode is the simplest way to use all cores.
Either way, the app should handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, log to stdout in a structured format, and expose a health endpoint, so whichever runner is used can manage it properly.

p17-851.q: File uploads arrive as multipart/form-data, which Express doesn't parse by default.
p17-851.k: file upload node, multer, busboy, stream upload to s3 node, multipart node express
x: File uploads arrive as multipart/form-data, which Express doesn't parse by default.
Options.

Multer: Express middleware that parses multipart requests, with memory storage, keeping files as buffers, or disk storage. Simple, but memory storage is dangerous for large files, since everything is held in RAM.
Busboy, which Multer is built on, or Fastify's multipart plugin: give you a stream for each file, so you can pipe it directly to its destination without buffering the whole file.

For larger files, I stream: pipe the upload stream to S3 with the AWS SDK's Upload helper from lib-storage, which does a multipart upload and handles backpressure. Memory stays low no matter how big the file is.

Even better for large files: pre-signed URLs. The API checks authorisation and returns a pre-signed S3 URL, and the browser uploads directly to S3. The API never handles the bytes; an S3 event then triggers processing.
Security and limits.
Limit file size, number of files and field sizes in the parser, and at the reverse proxy.
Check the content type and the file's actual signature, not just the extension.
Generate storage names on the server; never use the client's file name as a path.
Scan for malware before making files available, for example with an asynchronous scanning step.
Store files privately and serve them through authorised endpoints or short-lived signed URLs.
Error handling: clean up partial uploads on failure or client disconnect, and return clear errors for oversized or rejected files.

p17-852.q: For real-time features in Node, there are two main choices.
p17-852.k: websockets node, socket.io vs ws, node real time, socket io scaling redis adapter, websocket server node
x: For real-time features in Node, there are two main choices.

ws is a fast, minimal WebSocket library implementing the standard protocol. Clients can be any WebSocket client, including the browser's native WebSocket. You handle reconnection, heartbeats, rooms and message formats yourself.

Socket.IO is a higher-level framework on top of WebSockets, with fallbacks to HTTP long polling, automatic reconnection, acknowledgements, rooms and namespaces, and broadcasting. Clients must use the Socket.IO client library, because it has its own protocol.
How I'd decide: for internal apps where I want features quickly, Socket.IO saves time. For interoperability with standard clients or maximum performance, ws.
Important concerns either way.
Authentication: validate a token during the connection handshake, and close connections whose tokens expire or are revoked. Don't trust data sent later without checking permissions per action.

Scaling: with several instances behind a load balancer, a message published on one instance must reach clients connected to others. Socket.IO's Redis adapter, or a pub/sub layer like Redis or a broker for ws, solves this. Load balancers need WebSocket support and suitable idle timeouts, and sticky sessions for Socket.IO's polling fallback.
Heartbeats: ping and pong to detect dead connections, since proxies may drop idle connections silently.
Backpressure: don't send faster than a slow client can receive; check buffered amounts and drop or coalesce updates.
Managed options, like API Gateway WebSocket APIs on AWS or Azure Web PubSub, remove the scaling work, which I'd consider for large numbers of connections.

p17-853.q: Node is one of the best runtimes for Lambda because it starts quickly. A few practices make functions faster and cheaper.
p17-853.k: node lambda, lambda nodejs best practices, lambda cold start node, aws sdk v3 lambda, lambda handler node
x: Node is one of the best runtimes for Lambda because it starts quickly. A few practices make functions faster and cheaper.

Initialise outside the handler: create SDK clients, database connections and configuration at module level, so they're reused across invocations on a warm execution environment. Only per-request work goes inside the handler.

Keep the bundle small: use AWS SDK v3 modular clients, importing only what's needed, and bundle with esbuild, which tree-shakes code into one small file. Smaller packages load faster on cold starts. Avoid heavy frameworks inside functions unless needed.
Use async handlers properly: return a promise, or use async functions, and don't leave work running after returning, because the environment freezes and that work may never finish.
Connections: reuse HTTP connections with keep-alive, which SDK v3 enables by default. For relational databases, use RDS Proxy to avoid exhausting connections when many functions scale out.
Memory setting: CPU scales with memory, so increasing memory often makes functions faster and sometimes cheaper overall. Tools like Lambda Power Tuning find the best setting.
Timeouts: set timeouts close to what's needed, and shorter than upstream timeouts like API Gateway's.
Error handling: for SQS triggers, report partial batch failures so only failed messages are retried; use dead-letter queues or destinations for async invocations.
Observability: structured JSON logs, Powertools for AWS Lambda for logging, metrics and tracing, and X-Ray or OpenTelemetry.
For predictable latency-sensitive endpoints, provisioned concurrency removes cold starts, at extra cost.

p17-854.q: Opening a database connection is expensive: TCP, TLS and authentication. A pool keeps a set of open connections and lends them to queries, returning them afterwards.
p17-854.k: node connection pool, pg pool, node postgres pool, mysql2 pool, connection pool size node
x: Opening a database connection is expensive: TCP, TLS and authentication. A pool keeps a set of open connections and lends them to queries, returning them afterwards.

In Node, with Postgres for example, you create one Pool from the pg library at startup with settings like max connections, idle timeout and connection timeout, and run queries with pool.query, which takes a connection, runs the query and releases it. For transactions, you check out a client with pool.connect, run BEGIN, the queries and COMMIT, and always release it in a finally block, otherwise the pool leaks connections and eventually every request waits forever. ORMs like Prisma, TypeORM and Knex manage a pool internally.

Sizing: because Node handles many concurrent requests on one process, it's easy to send more queries than the database can handle. The pool's max limits concurrency per process. Total connections are max multiplied by the number of processes and containers, which must stay under the database's limit. A smaller pool often gives better throughput than a large one, because databases do best with limited concurrent queries.
Common problems.
Pool exhaustion: slow queries or leaked clients mean requests wait for a connection. Monitor waiting counts and acquisition times.
Serverless: each Lambda instance has its own pool, so scaling out can open thousands of connections; use RDS Proxy or a pooler like PgBouncer, and keep the per-instance pool small.
Connection timeouts: set them so requests fail fast rather than hanging.
On shutdown, call pool.end to close connections cleanly.

p17-855.q: Long-running or deferred work, like sending emails, generating reports or calling slow third-party APIs, shouldn't run inside HTTP requests. In Node, BullMQ is a popular job queue built on Redis.
p17-855.k: bullmq, node background jobs, node job queue, redis queue node, repeatable jobs node
x: Long-running or deferred work, like sending emails, generating reports or calling slow third-party APIs, shouldn't run inside HTTP requests. In Node, BullMQ is a popular job queue built on Redis.

How it works: the API adds a job to a named Queue with data and options, and returns immediately. Separate Worker processes take jobs from the queue and run a processor function. Jobs move through states like waiting, active, completed, failed and delayed, stored in Redis.
Useful features.
Retries with backoff: set attempts and an exponential backoff, so transient failures are retried automatically.
Delayed jobs: run at a later time, like a reminder in two hours.
Repeatable jobs: cron-style schedules, with BullMQ making sure only one instance runs each scheduled job even with several workers, which solves the "job ran twice" problem.
Concurrency per worker and rate limiting, to protect downstream APIs.
Priorities, job dependencies with flows, progress reporting, and events for completed or failed jobs.

Good practices: keep job data small, like ids rather than whole objects; make processors idempotent, since a job may run again after a crash; set removeOnComplete and removeOnFail limits so Redis doesn't fill up; run workers as separate deployments from the API, so they scale independently; handle graceful shutdown with worker.close so active jobs finish; and monitor queue length, failure rates and job duration, with a dashboard like Bull Board.
If guaranteed durability or cross-language consumers matter more, a message broker like RabbitMQ or SQS may be a better fit than a Redis-based queue.

p17-856.q: Locally: start Node with the --inspect flag, or --inspect-brk to pause on the first line, and attach Chrome DevTools via chrome://inspect, or the VS Code debugger, which can also launch the app directly from a launch configuration. Then set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables and the call stack, and use conditional breakpoints and logpoints, which print values without changing code. For TypeScript, source maps make breakpoints work on the original .ts files. In tests, Vitest and Jest can also be run under the debugger.
p17-856.k: debug node, node inspect, chrome devtools node, vscode debug node, node production debugging
x: Locally: start Node with the --inspect flag, or --inspect-brk to pause on the first line, and attach Chrome DevTools via chrome://inspect, or the VS Code debugger, which can also launch the app directly from a launch configuration. Then set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables and the call stack, and use conditional breakpoints and logpoints, which print values without changing code. For TypeScript, source maps make breakpoints work on the original .ts files. In tests, Vitest and Jest can also be run under the debugger.
In containers: expose the inspector port only to localhost and use port forwarding, like kubectl port-forward, never exposing it publicly, because the inspector allows running arbitrary code.
In production, attaching a debugger to a live service is risky and rarely allowed, so I rely on other tools.
Structured logs with correlation ids, and log levels that can be raised temporarily through configuration.
Distributed traces to see where time goes across calls.
Metrics like event loop delay, heap usage and garbage collection.

Heap snapshots and CPU profiles: Node can write a heap snapshot on a signal or when memory is near the limit, with flags like --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit, and CPU profiles with --cpu-prof, which you analyse in DevTools afterwards.
Diagnostic reports: process.report or --report-on-fatalerror writes a JSON report with stack, heap and system information when the process crashes.
Reproducing locally with production-like data and configuration, once the evidence narrows the problem down.

p17-857.q: Deno and Bun are newer JavaScript runtimes competing with Node.
p17-857.k: deno vs node, bun vs node, javascript runtimes, bun runtime, deno runtime
x: Deno and Bun are newer JavaScript runtimes competing with Node.

Deno, from Node's original creator, focuses on security and modern defaults: permissions are off by default, so a script can't access the network, files or environment unless allowed; TypeScript runs out of the box; it includes a formatter, linter and test runner; and it now supports npm packages and Node APIs for compatibility.

Bun focuses on speed and an all-in-one toolkit: a very fast runtime built on JavaScriptCore, a package manager that installs much faster than npm, a bundler, a test runner and native TypeScript support. It aims for high Node compatibility, so many Node apps run unchanged.

Would I use them in production? It depends on risk tolerance. Node has the largest ecosystem, long-term support releases, mature tooling for observability and profiling, and support from every cloud and platform. Its gaps have narrowed too: native fetch, a test runner, watch mode, and running TypeScript with type stripping.
For core business services in a regulated enterprise, I'd stay on Node LTS, because stability, support and compatibility with monitoring, security scanning and hosting matter more than raw speed.

Where the others make sense: Bun as a fast package manager or test runner in development, or for internal tools and scripts; Deno for scripts where its permission model adds safety, or edge platforms built around it.
I'd evaluate them on a real service with benchmarks and compatibility tests before committing, rather than choosing based on headline performance numbers.

p17-858.q: Passwords must never be stored in plain text or with fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256, because attackers with a leaked database can try billions of guesses per second. Password hashing algorithms are deliberately slow and use a unique salt per password.
p17-858.k: password hashing node, bcrypt vs argon2, scrypt node, hash passwords nodejs, password storage
x: Passwords must never be stored in plain text or with fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256, because attackers with a leaked database can try billions of guesses per second. Password hashing algorithms are deliberately slow and use a unique salt per password.
Options in Node.

Argon2id, through the argon2 package: the current recommendation from OWASP, memory-hard, which makes GPU and specialised hardware attacks expensive. Configure memory, iterations and parallelism to take a reasonable time on your servers.
bcrypt, through bcrypt or bcryptjs: widely used and still acceptable, with a cost factor of at least 10 to 12. It has a 72-byte input limit, so very long passwords are truncated.
scrypt, built into Node's crypto module: memory-hard and needs no native dependencies.

Usage: hash on registration, and verify with the library's verify function, which uses constant-time comparison. Store the full encoded hash, which includes the algorithm, parameters and salt, so you can upgrade parameters later: when a user logs in successfully with an old-parameter hash, rehash with the new parameters.

Performance: hashing is intentionally CPU-heavy. Use the async versions, which run on the libuv thread pool, never the sync versions on request paths, and consider increasing the thread pool size, otherwise a burst of logins blocks other work. Rate-limit login attempts too.
Other practices: check new passwords against breached password lists, and require MFA for sensitive systems.
Best of all, for most business apps, delegate authentication to an identity provider like Keycloak, Cognito or Entra ID, so the application never handles passwords.

p17-859.q: tRPC lets a TypeScript backend expose procedures that a TypeScript front end calls with full type safety, without writing an API schema or generating code. You define a router on the server with queries and mutations, each with an input validator, usually Zod, and a resolver. The client imports only the router's type, and calls procedures like functions, such as trpc.shipments.byId.query({ id }). If the server changes an input or output type, the front end gets a compile error immediately.
p17-859.k: trpc, type safe api typescript, trpc vs rest, trpc vs graphql, end to end type safety
x: tRPC lets a TypeScript backend expose procedures that a TypeScript front end calls with full type safety, without writing an API schema or generating code. You define a router on the server with queries and mutations, each with an input validator, usually Zod, and a resolver. The client imports only the router's type, and calls procedures like functions, such as trpc.shipments.byId.query({ id }). If the server changes an input or output type, the front end gets a compile error immediately.
Benefits: end-to-end type safety with almost no boilerplate, great developer experience with autocomplete, and integration with TanStack Query for caching and loading states in React.
Limits.
TypeScript on both ends: it only works when the client and server are both TypeScript, ideally in the same monorepo. It doesn't suit public APIs or other languages, like a .NET or mobile client.
Coupling: the front end and back end are tightly linked, which is fine for one product team but not for APIs shared across teams.
Tooling: REST with OpenAPI has better support for documentation, gateways, caching and monitoring.
When I'd use it: a full-stack TypeScript app, like Next.js with a Node backend, owned by one team, where speed of development matters.

When I wouldn't: our architecture, where the backends are .NET and the API is consumed by multiple front ends and partners. There, OpenAPI with generated TypeScript clients gives similar type safety across languages, which is what I'd recommend instead.

p17-860.q: gRPC works well across languages, because the contract is a .proto file shared by all services. A .NET service can expose a gRPC API, and a Node service can call it, or the other way around.
p17-860.k: grpc node, grpc-js, node grpc client, protobuf node, cross language grpc
x: gRPC works well across languages, because the contract is a .proto file shared by all services. A .NET service can expose a gRPC API, and a Node service can call it, or the other way around.

In Node, the official library is @grpc/grpc-js, which is pure JavaScript. There are two ways to use the .proto file: load it at runtime with @grpc/proto-loader, which is quick to start but gives no types; or generate TypeScript code with tools like ts-proto or protobuf-es with Connect, which gives typed clients and messages, my preference for TypeScript services.

Creating a client: point it at the service address with TLS credentials, and call methods. Unary calls return a single response; server streaming returns a stream you read with async iteration; client and bidirectional streaming are also supported.
Important settings.
Deadlines on every call, so a slow service doesn't hang the caller; they propagate across hops.
Retries and keep-alive configuration through the service config, with care for idempotency.
Metadata for auth tokens and correlation ids.
Error handling with gRPC status codes, mapped to meaningful errors, like NOT_FOUND to 404 if the Node service exposes REST.

Contract management: keep .proto files in a shared repository or package, version them, and follow protobuf compatibility rules: never reuse field numbers, and add new fields instead of changing existing ones.
For browser clients, gRPC needs gRPC-Web or Connect, so I'd normally keep REST at the edge and gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where performance or streaming matters.

p17-861.q: Express 5 was finally released as stable after many years of Express 4. The changes are mostly about modernising and removing old behaviour.
p17-861.k: express 5, express 5 changes, express v5 migration, express async errors, upgrade express 4 to 5
x: Express 5 was finally released as stable after many years of Express 4. The changes are mostly about modernising and removing old behaviour.
Key changes.

Async error handling: if an async route handler or middleware returns a rejected promise, Express 5 passes the error to the error-handling middleware automatically. In Express 4, an unhandled rejection in an async handler could hang the request or crash the process, unless you wrapped handlers or used a helper package. This alone is a strong reason to upgrade.

Path matching: the route path syntax moved to a newer path-to-regexp version. Some patterns changed, like wildcards needing names and optional parameters having new syntax, and regular-expression characters in strings are no longer supported. Routes need review during upgrade.
Removed deprecated APIs: things like app.del, res.send with a status number, and several older method signatures were removed, and req.query is now read-only by default with a simpler parser.
Node version: requires a modern Node version, dropping very old ones.
Body parsing changes: the built-in urlencoded parser defaults changed, and some behaviour is stricter.

Should you upgrade? For active services, yes, planned like any major upgrade: read the migration guide, run the codemods where available, update route patterns, run the full integration test suite, and check middleware packages for compatibility.

For new projects, I'd also consider Fastify or NestJS, which offer built-in validation, better performance or structure. But if the team knows Express well, Express 5 is a reasonable, simpler choice than before.

p17-862.q: These are Python's four core built-in collections, and choosing well affects correctness and performance.
p17-862.k: python list vs tuple, list tuple set dict, python data structures, when to use tuple, python collections basics
x: These are Python's four core built-in collections, and choosing well affects correctness and performance.

A list is ordered and mutable, allows duplicates, and is indexed by position. Appending is fast, and membership checks with in are O(n), because Python scans the list. Use it for ordered sequences you'll change, like rows read from a file.

A tuple is ordered and immutable. Because it can't change, it's hashable if its contents are, so it can be a dictionary key or a set member, like a key of site id and date. Tuples signal "this is a fixed record", like coordinates or a function returning several values, and they're slightly lighter than lists.

A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items, with O(1) average membership checks, and operations like union, intersection and difference. Use it for de-duplication, or checking membership in large collections, like "have I already processed this id?". frozenset is the immutable version.
A dict maps unique, hashable keys to values with O(1) average lookups, and since Python 3.7, it preserves insertion order. Use it for lookups by key, counting, grouping, and JSON-like data.
A common performance bug I've seen in scripts is checking if item in some_list inside a loop over thousands of items, which makes the work quadratic; converting the list to a set first fixes it.
The collections module adds specialised versions: defaultdict for grouping, Counter for counting, deque for fast appends and pops at both ends, and namedtuple for readable records.

p17-863.q: They let a function accept a variable number of arguments.
p17-863.k: args kwargs python, star args, double star kwargs, variable arguments python, keyword only arguments
x: They let a function accept a variable number of arguments.
*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. def log(message, *args) can be called as log("x", 1, 2, 3), and args is the tuple 1, 2, 3.
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. def create(**kwargs) called as create(name="kit", qty=5) gives kwargs as a dict with name and qty.
The names args and kwargs are just conventions; the star and double star are what matter.

The same symbols unpack at call time: func(*my_list) passes list items as separate positional arguments, and func(**my_dict) passes dict items as keyword arguments. They also merge dicts, like combined = {**defaults, **overrides}, and unpack lists inside list literals.
Related parameter features.
Keyword-only parameters: anything after a bare star, like def send(to, *, retries=3), must be passed by name, which makes calls clearer and safer.
Positional-only parameters: anything before a slash must be passed by position.

Where they're useful: decorators and wrappers that pass any arguments through to the wrapped function, like def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return func(*args, **kwargs); functions that forward options to another library; and flexible logging or formatting helpers.

The downside: overusing kwargs hides what a function actually accepts, hurting readability, type checking and autocomplete. For business code, I prefer explicit parameters, and for typed wrappers, ParamSpec in type hints preserves the wrapped function's signature.

p17-864.q: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression: squares equals x times x for x in numbers if x is positive, written inside square brackets. It's concise, readable for simple transformations, and usually faster than an equivalent loop with append, because the loop runs in optimised C code. Python also has dict comprehensions, like {s.id: s for s in sites}, and set comprehensions.
p17-864.k: list comprehension, generator expression, python comprehension, dict comprehension, comprehension vs for loop
x: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression: squares equals x times x for x in numbers if x is positive, written inside square brackets. It's concise, readable for simple transformations, and usually faster than an equivalent loop with append, because the loop runs in optimised C code. Python also has dict comprehensions, like {s.id: s for s in sites}, and set comprehensions.

A generator expression looks the same but with parentheses: total = sum(x * x for x in numbers). It doesn't build a list; it produces items one at a time, lazily. That uses almost no memory, which matters for large data, like processing millions of lines from a file, and it can stop early, for example with any() or next().
How I choose.
If I need the result as a collection to reuse, index or iterate more than once, a list or dict comprehension.
If I'm feeding the values into a function that consumes them once, like sum, max, any, join or writing to a file, a generator expression.

If the logic has multiple steps, side effects, nested conditions or error handling, a normal for loop. Comprehensions with several nested loops and conditions become hard to read, and readability matters more than saving lines.

Watch out: a generator can only be consumed once; iterating it again gives nothing, which surprises people. And comprehensions shouldn't be used just for side effects, like calling print, because they build a useless list.
These map nicely to C#: list comprehensions are like LINQ with ToList, and generator expressions are like deferred LINQ queries.

p17-865.q: Dunder, or double-underscore, methods are special methods Python calls to implement built-in behaviour. Defining them lets your classes work naturally with the language.
p17-865.k: dunder methods python, magic methods, __init__ vs __new__, __repr__ vs __str__, python special methods
x: Dunder, or double-underscore, methods are special methods Python calls to implement built-in behaviour. Defining them lets your classes work naturally with the language.

Common ones: __init__ initialises a new object; __repr__ gives an unambiguous developer representation, used in debugging and logs, while __str__ gives a user-friendly string for print; __eq__ and __hash__ define equality and hashing, which must be consistent, like Equals and GetHashCode in C#; __lt__ and friends define ordering; __len__, __getitem__ and __iter__ make objects behave like collections; __enter__ and __exit__ make context managers; __call__ makes an instance callable like a function; and arithmetic methods like __add__ allow operator overloading.

__new__ vs __init__: __new__ is a static-like method that actually creates and returns the new instance; __init__ then initialises that instance, setting attributes. You rarely override __new__. It's needed for immutable types, like subclassing tuple or str, where values must be set at creation, or for patterns like singletons or caching instances.

Practical advice: always define __repr__ for domain classes, because good logs and debugging output save time; if you define __eq__, Python sets __hash__ to None unless you define it, making objects unhashable, which surprises people.

Dataclasses generate __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you, and with order=True or frozen=True, comparison and hashing too, which is why I usually use dataclasses or Pydantic models for data-holding classes instead of writing dunder methods by hand.

p17-866.q: These decorators change how methods in a class behave.
p17-866.k: python property decorator, classmethod vs staticmethod, python getter setter, alternative constructor python, python class methods
x: These decorators change how methods in a class behave.

@property turns a method into an attribute-like accessor. order.total looks like an attribute, but runs a method computing it. You can add a setter with @total.setter for validation when assigning. This lets you start with a plain attribute and later add logic without changing callers, so Python doesn't need Java-style getters and setters. For expensive computed values that don't change, functools.cached_property computes once and caches it.

@classmethod receives the class itself, cls, as its first argument instead of an instance. The main use is alternative constructors, like Shipment.from_dict(data) or Config.from_env(), which return cls(...), so they also work correctly for subclasses. They can also access class-level state.

@staticmethod receives neither the instance nor the class; it's a plain function placed inside the class for organisation, like a helper to validate a kit code format. It can't access instance or class data.
Regular methods receive the instance as self, and are used for behaviour that depends on an object's state.

How I decide: if it needs instance data, a regular method or property; if it creates instances or needs the class, a classmethod; if it needs neither, I ask whether it should just be a module-level function, which is often more Pythonic than a staticmethod.
Comparing to C#: properties are like C# properties, classmethods used as factories are like static factory methods, and staticmethods are like static helper methods.

p17-867.q: Python's abc module lets you define abstract base classes: a class inheriting from ABC with methods marked @abstractmethod. You can't create an instance of the base class, or of any subclass that hasn't implemented all abstract methods; Python raises a TypeError at instantiation.
p17-867.k: abc python, abstract base class, abstractmethod, python interface, abc module
x: Python's abc module lets you define abstract base classes: a class inheriting from ABC with methods marked @abstractmethod. You can't create an instance of the base class, or of any subclass that hasn't implemented all abstract methods; Python raises a TypeError at instantiation.

Example: a Notifier base class with an abstract send method, and EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier subclasses implementing it. Code depends on Notifier, and the implementation is chosen through configuration or dependency injection, like in FastAPI with Depends.

Why use them: they document and enforce a contract, so forgetting to implement a method is caught early when objects are created, rather than later when the method is called. They can also provide shared implementation in non-abstract methods, like a template method pattern.
Alternatives.

Protocols, from typing, define interfaces structurally: any class with matching methods satisfies the protocol, without inheriting from it. Checked by type checkers like mypy, not at runtime unless marked runtime_checkable. Good for decoupling, especially from third-party classes you can't change.
Duck typing: Python's traditional approach, just call the method and trust the object has it.

How I choose: ABCs when I own the hierarchy and want runtime enforcement and shared code; Protocols when I want lightweight interfaces for type checking and testing, which fits a dependency-injection style; duck typing for small scripts.
Coming from C#, ABCs feel like abstract classes, and Protocols are the closest thing to interfaces, with the difference that implementing them is implicit.

p17-868.q: CPython, the standard Python implementation, manages memory mainly with reference counting. Every object keeps a count of references to it. When a variable is reassigned, goes out of scope, or a container drops the object, the count decreases, and when it hits zero, the object is freed immediately. That makes memory release predictable, unlike .NET's generational GC, where objects are collected later.
p17-868.k: python memory management, reference counting python, python garbage collector, gc module, python memory leak
x: CPython, the standard Python implementation, manages memory mainly with reference counting. Every object keeps a count of references to it. When a variable is reassigned, goes out of scope, or a container drops the object, the count decreases, and when it hits zero, the object is freed immediately. That makes memory release predictable, unlike .NET's generational GC, where objects are collected later.

Reference counting can't handle cycles, like two objects referring to each other, or an object referring to itself. So Python also has a cyclic garbage collector, in the gc module, which periodically looks for groups of objects only reachable from each other and frees them. It uses generations, like .NET, checking young objects more often.

Memory allocation: small objects use pymalloc, a specialised allocator with pools, so freed memory is often reused by Python rather than returned to the operating system. That's why a Python process's memory may not shrink after a big job, even when objects are freed.

Common memory problems: holding references longer than needed, like global caches, lists that keep growing, or closures capturing large objects; loading whole files or query results into memory instead of streaming them; and C extensions that leak.
Tools: tracemalloc to see where memory is allocated and compare snapshots, memory profilers like memray, and objgraph to find what's keeping objects alive.
For long-running workers with memory growth, I fix the cause where possible, and as a safety net use worker recycling, like Gunicorn's max_requests or Celery's max tasks per child.

p17-869.q: FastAPI is built on Starlette, so it has middleware and exception handlers similar to ASP.NET Core.
p17-869.k: fastapi middleware, fastapi exception handler, fastapi global error handling, starlette middleware, fastapi correlation id
x: FastAPI is built on Starlette, so it has middleware and exception handlers similar to ASP.NET Core.

Middleware wraps every request. The simple way is a function decorated with @app.middleware("http"), which receives the request and a call_next function: code before call_next runs on the way in, and code after it runs on the way out. Typical uses: a correlation id, read from a header or generated, stored in a context variable for logging and added to the response; request timing; and security headers. For performance and access to the raw ASGI flow, you can write pure ASGI middleware classes. Built-in middleware includes CORSMiddleware, GZipMiddleware and TrustedHostMiddleware. Order matters: middleware added later wraps earlier ones.

Exception handlers turn exceptions into HTTP responses. Register them with @app.exception_handler(SomeError). For example, map a custom NotFoundError to a 404 JSON response, a business rule error to 409 or 422, and a catch-all for unexpected Exception to a 500 with a generic message and the correlation id, while logging the full details server-side. You can also override the handler for RequestValidationError to change the shape of validation errors, and HTTPException for consistency.

I aim for one error format across services, like ProblemDetails with type, title, status, detail and an error code, so front ends and other services handle errors the same way whether they come from .NET or Python.
Dependencies with yield are another place for per-request setup and cleanup, like database sessions and transactions.

p17-870.q: In FastAPI, the request side is defined by function parameters, and the response side by response models.
p17-870.k: fastapi response model, fastapi status code, fastapi 422 validation error, pydantic response schema, fastapi output filtering
x: In FastAPI, the request side is defined by function parameters, and the response side by response models.

Response models: declare the return type annotation, like -> ShipmentOut, or response_model=ShipmentOut in the decorator. FastAPI then validates and serialises the returned data through that Pydantic model, and filters out any fields not in it. That's important for security: if you return an ORM object with internal fields, like a password hash or internal notes, only the fields declared in ShipmentOut are sent. It also documents the response in the OpenAPI schema automatically.

Separate models for input and output: ShipmentCreate for requests, without id and server-set fields; ShipmentOut for responses; and maybe ShipmentUpdate with optional fields for patches. It's the same idea as DTOs in .NET.

Status codes: set the default with status_code=201 for creation endpoints, use HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=...) for errors, or return a Response object to control headers and status fully. Document other responses with the responses parameter, so OpenAPI shows them.

Validation errors: when request data doesn't match the parameter types or Pydantic models, FastAPI returns 422 Unprocessable Entity automatically, with details of each failing field. Many teams keep that, though some override the handler to return 400 and their own error format.
Options like response_model_exclude_none remove null fields from output.
Because the OpenAPI document is generated from these models, front ends can generate typed TypeScript clients, just as with .NET APIs.

p17-871.q: FastAPI makes API testing straightforward with pytest.
p17-871.k: test fastapi, fastapi testclient, httpx asyncclient, dependency overrides fastapi, pytest fastapi
x: FastAPI makes API testing straightforward with pytest.

TestClient: from fastapi.testclient, wraps the app so tests call client.post("/shipments", json=payload) and get a response, without starting a server. It runs the full stack: routing, validation, dependencies, middleware and exception handlers. For async tests, httpx.AsyncClient with ASGITransport does the same, which is useful when tests need to await other async things, like database setup.

Dependency overrides: the most useful feature. setting app.dependency_overrides for get_current_user to a lambda returning a fake admin user lets tests act as any user without real tokens; overriding get_db can point to a test database session; and external API clients can be replaced with fakes. Clear overrides after each test, usually in a fixture.

Database: for meaningful tests, use a real database, like Postgres in a container with Testcontainers, apply Alembic migrations once per session, and wrap each test in a transaction that's rolled back, so tests are isolated and fast.
External HTTP calls: mock with respx for httpx, or responses for requests, so the real client code runs against fake responses.
Fixtures: pytest fixtures for the app, client, database session and test data builders keep tests short; factories like factory_boy or polyfactory create valid objects.
What I cover: happy paths, validation failures with 422, authorisation with 401 and 403, not found cases, and business rule errors, plus the response shape against the response model.
In CI, tests run on every pull request with coverage reports, like any other service.

p17-872.q: Pydantic validates data based on type hints, and custom validators add business rules.
p17-872.k: pydantic validators, field_validator, model_validator, pydantic v2 validation, custom validation pydantic
x: Pydantic validates data based on type hints, and custom validators add business rules.

Built-in constraints first: Field(gt=0, max_length=50, pattern=...), constrained types, Literal for allowed values, EmailStr, and Annotated types let you express many rules declaratively, without custom code.

field_validator: a classmethod decorated with @field_validator("kit_code") that receives the value and returns it, possibly transformed, or raises ValueError with a message. mode="before" runs before type conversion, useful for cleaning input like stripping spaces or parsing unusual formats; the default "after" mode runs on the already-typed value.

model_validator: validates the whole model, for rules across fields, like end_date must be after start_date, or either email or phone must be provided. mode="after" receives the constructed model instance; mode="before" receives the raw input data.
Errors: all validation failures are collected into a ValidationError with the location and message of each, which FastAPI turns into a 422 response automatically.

Other v2 features: computed_field for derived values in output; field_serializer for custom output formats; model_config with settings like extra="forbid" to reject unknown fields, and frozen=True for immutability; and much better performance, since the core is written in Rust.
Migrating from v1: validator becomes field_validator, root_validator becomes model_validator, Config becomes model_config, and dict() becomes model_dump().
I keep validators focused on data shape and simple rules; checks that need the database, like uniqueness, belong in the service layer.

p17-873.q: Consistent formatting and linting make Python codebases easier to review and maintain, especially with several developers.
p17-873.k: ruff python, black formatter, python linting, flake8 vs ruff, python code quality tools
x: Consistent formatting and linting make Python codebases easier to review and maintain, especially with several developers.

Ruff has become the standard tool for both. It's written in Rust, very fast, and replaces many older tools: it implements rules from flake8, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, flake8-bugbear, bandit's security rules and more, plus a formatter compatible with Black. One tool, one configuration in pyproject.toml.

How I set it up: choose rule sets under the lint select setting, like E and F for errors, I for import sorting, B for bugbear's common bug patterns, UP for modernising syntax, S for security checks, and others gradually. Run ruff check --fix to apply safe fixes automatically, and ruff format to format code.
Type checking is separate: mypy or Pyright checks type hints, which catches a different class of bugs.
Workflow.
Editor integration, so issues show while typing and formatting happens on save.
Pre-commit hooks running Ruff, so badly formatted code never gets committed.
CI checks that fail the build on lint errors or unformatted code, so the main branch stays clean.
For an existing codebase with many issues, start with formatting in one commit, then enable rule sets gradually, using per-file ignores or a baseline for legacy areas, so the team isn't overwhelmed.

This is the Python equivalent of what we do in .NET with analyzers, .editorconfig and dotnet format, and in front-end projects with ESLint and Prettier: automate style so code reviews focus on logic and design.

p17-874.q: In async Python, like FastAPI with async def endpoints, all requests on a worker share one event loop thread. If any code blocks that thread, every other request on that worker waits. It's the same problem as blocking the event loop in Node.
p17-874.k: blocking event loop python, asyncio blocking call, run_in_executor, asyncio.to_thread, async fastapi blocking
x: In async Python, like FastAPI with async def endpoints, all requests on a worker share one event loop thread. If any code blocks that thread, every other request on that worker waits. It's the same problem as blocking the event loop in Node.

Common blocking calls: requests.get instead of an async HTTP client; synchronous database drivers, like psycopg2 or pyodbc, inside async endpoints; time.sleep instead of asyncio.sleep; reading large files synchronously; and CPU-heavy work like parsing big files, image processing or heavy calculations.
Fixes.
Use async libraries: httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp for HTTP, asyncpg or SQLAlchemy's async engine for databases, aiofiles for files, and asyncio.sleep.

If a library is only synchronous, run it in a thread: await asyncio.to_thread(func, args), or loop.run_in_executor. In FastAPI, simply declaring the endpoint with def instead of async def makes FastAPI run it in a thread pool automatically, which is the easiest fix for sync code.
For CPU-heavy work, threads don't help much because of the GIL; use a ProcessPoolExecutor, or better, a background task queue like Celery, so the API stays responsive.
Detecting it: enable asyncio debug mode, which logs callbacks taking longer than a threshold; watch for latency rising across all endpoints when one slow operation runs; and profile with py-spy.

Mixing rules I follow: async def endpoints only call async I/O; anything sync goes through to_thread or a sync endpoint. Mixing them carelessly is the most common cause of mysterious slowness in FastAPI services.

p17-875.q: To run several async operations at the same time, like calling three APIs in parallel, Python offers a few tools.
p17-875.k: asyncio gather, taskgroup python, asyncio concurrency, asyncio timeout, structured concurrency python
x: To run several async operations at the same time, like calling three APIs in parallel, Python offers a few tools.

asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()) runs the coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order. By default, if one raises an exception, gather raises it, but the other tasks keep running in the background, which can leave work orphaned. With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are returned as results instead, so you can inspect each.

TaskGroup, since Python 3.11, is structured concurrency: async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: t1 = tg.create_task(a()); t2 = tg.create_task(b()). When the block exits, all tasks have finished. If any task fails, the others are cancelled, and the errors are raised together as an ExceptionGroup, handled with except*. No orphaned tasks, which makes it my default for new code, much like Task.WhenAll in C# but with automatic cancellation.
Timeouts: asyncio.timeout(5), since 3.11, as an async context manager, or asyncio.wait_for for a single awaitable. Every external call should have a timeout.

Limiting concurrency: when processing hundreds of items, don't start them all at once; use an asyncio.Semaphore inside each task, or process in batches, to protect downstream services and connection pools.
asyncio.as_completed processes results as they finish, useful for showing progress.

Common mistakes: calling a coroutine without awaiting it, which never runs it; creating tasks with create_task and not keeping a reference, so they may be garbage collected; and mixing blocking calls into async code, which serialises everything.

p17-876.q: Both are DataFrame libraries for tabular data, used for analysis, ETL, reports and data preparation for things like RAG ingestion or exports.
p17-876.k: pandas vs polars, polars python, dataframe performance, python etl, pandas performance tips
x: Both are DataFrame libraries for tabular data, used for analysis, ETL, reports and data preparation for things like RAG ingestion or exports.

pandas is the long-established standard: huge ecosystem, integrations everywhere, and most data people know it. But it's mostly single-threaded and eager, it can use a lot of memory, and some APIs are inconsistent.

Polars is newer, written in Rust, and designed for performance: it uses all CPU cores, has a lazy API that builds a query plan and optimises it, like pushing filters down and reading only needed columns, and uses Apache Arrow memory, which is efficient. It's often much faster than pandas, with lower memory, and its expression API is consistent.

How I choose: for new data processing pipelines, especially with large files, Polars is a strong choice. For existing code, or when a library expects pandas, stay with pandas; conversion between them is easy through Arrow.
Performance tips that apply to both.
Vectorise: use column operations instead of Python loops or apply with lambdas row by row, which are very slow.
Read only what you need: select columns and filter early, use efficient formats like Parquet instead of CSV for intermediate data, and specify data types, like categories for repeated strings.
Process in chunks or with lazy streaming for data bigger than memory.
Push heavy filtering and aggregation to the database with SQL when the data lives there, instead of loading everything into a DataFrame.
For very large or distributed workloads, tools like DuckDB, which runs SQL on files directly, or Spark come into play.

p17-877.q: For RabbitMQ in Python, the main libraries are pika, which is synchronous, and aio-pika, which is asyncio-based and fits services built with FastAPI or other async code. For Kafka, confluent-kafka, a wrapper around the fast librdkafka C library, or aiokafka for asyncio.
p17-877.k: python rabbitmq consumer, aio-pika, pika, confluent kafka python, python message consumer
x: For RabbitMQ in Python, the main libraries are pika, which is synchronous, and aio-pika, which is asyncio-based and fits services built with FastAPI or other async code. For Kafka, confluent-kafka, a wrapper around the fast librdkafka C library, or aiokafka for asyncio.
The reliability rules are the same as in .NET and Node.

Manual acknowledgement after processing: with aio-pika, use the message.process() context manager, which acks on success and rejects on exception, or ack explicitly. In Kafka, disable auto-commit and commit offsets after processing.
Prefetch: set_qos with a prefetch count to limit in-flight messages per consumer.
Retries and dead-lettering: reject without requeue to send failures to a dead-letter exchange, with retry queues using TTLs for delayed retries, and a maximum attempt count tracked in headers.
Idempotency: store processed message ids, because redelivery happens.
Validation: parse message bodies with Pydantic models, and dead-letter invalid messages immediately.
Connection resilience: aio-pika's connect_robust reconnects and restores channels automatically after network blips.
Concurrency: in asyncio, process messages concurrently up to the prefetch limit; for CPU-heavy processing, use separate processes, since the GIL limits threads.
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM, stop consuming, finish in-flight messages, then close the connection.
Observability: structured logs with message and correlation ids, OpenTelemetry context propagated through message headers, and metrics for processing time and failures.
Celery is another option for task-style work over RabbitMQ or Redis, but for consuming domain events from other services, a plain consumer gives more control.

p17-878.q: Python's standard library saves a lot of code if you know it. The modules I use most often:
p17-878.k: python standard library, itertools, collections module, functools, pathlib python
x: Python's standard library saves a lot of code if you know it. The modules I use most often:

collections: defaultdict for grouping without checking keys, like grouping shipments by site; Counter for counting and most_common; deque for queues and sliding windows; and namedtuple for lightweight records, though I often use dataclasses now.

itertools: chain to iterate several sequences as one; islice to take part of an iterator; groupby for consecutive grouping, after sorting; product and combinations for combinations; and batched, since 3.12, to split an iterable into chunks, very handy for batching database inserts or API calls.

functools: lru_cache and cache to memoise pure functions; partial to pre-fill arguments; wraps for writing decorators that keep the wrapped function's name and docstring; reduce occasionally; and cached_property.
pathlib: object-oriented file paths, like Path("data") / "file.csv", reading and writing text, and globbing, cleaner and safer than string paths with os.path.
datetime and zoneinfo: timezone-aware dates, with zoneinfo providing IANA time zones since 3.9.
json, csv, and logging for everyday I/O and logs.
dataclasses and enum for clear data and constants.
contextlib: contextmanager to write context managers with a generator, and suppress to ignore specific exceptions.
concurrent.futures for thread and process pools, and subprocess for running commands safely with argument lists.
secrets for secure random tokens, and hashlib for hashing.
Knowing these avoids extra dependencies, which also reduces supply chain risk.

p17-879.q: Python has caching options at different levels.
p17-879.k: python caching, lru_cache, functools cache, redis python cache, cachetools ttl
x: Python has caching options at different levels.

In-process with functools: @lru_cache(maxsize=1024) on a function memoises results based on arguments, evicting the least recently used entries. @cache is the unbounded version. Good for pure functions with hashable arguments, like parsing configuration, expensive calculations or loading reference data that never changes. Limitations: no expiry, arguments must be hashable, it's per process, so each worker has its own copy, and on methods it can keep instances alive. It doesn't work on async functions directly, since it would cache the coroutine object; libraries like async-lru handle that.
With expiry: cachetools provides TTLCache and LRUCache classes with time-based expiry, for data that changes occasionally.

Shared cache with Redis: when several processes or instances need the same cache, or the data should survive restarts, use Redis with the redis-py client, which has an asyncio interface too. The usual cache-aside pattern: try Redis, on a miss load from the source, then set with an expiry. Serialise with JSON or orjson. Pydantic models can be dumped to JSON and validated on the way back.

Good practices: include versions and identifiers in keys; add jitter to expiries; protect against stampedes with a short lock or request coalescing; set Redis timeouts and fall back to the source if Redis is unavailable; and measure hit ratios.
In our RAG service, caching embeddings for repeated queries and caching document metadata are typical places where this saves time and model cost.

p17-880.q: When several Python services share code, like logging setup, auth helpers or API clients, an internal package avoids copying code between repositories.
p17-880.k: private python package, internal pypi, azure artifacts python, publish python package, pyproject build twine
