x: When several Python services share code, like logging setup, auth helpers or API clients, an internal package avoids copying code between repositories.

Packaging: define the package in pyproject.toml with a name, version, dependencies and a build backend, like hatchling or setuptools. Use a src layout, so tests run against the installed package rather than local files by accident. Build with python -m build or uv build, which produces a wheel and a source distribution.
Versioning: semantic versioning, with the version set from Git tags in CI, using a tool like hatch-vcs or setuptools-scm, so versions are never edited by hand.

Publishing to a private feed: Azure Artifacts supports Python feeds, as do AWS CodeArtifact, GitHub Packages and JFrog. In the pipeline, authenticate with the platform's mechanism, like the Twine authenticate task in Azure Pipelines or a short-lived CodeArtifact token, and upload with twine or uv publish. No personal credentials in scripts.

Consuming: configure pip or uv with the feed as an index URL, using a keyring or environment-based credentials in CI and developer machines. Be careful with mixing public and private indexes, because of dependency confusion attacks: use a feed that proxies PyPI with upstream sources, and give internal packages a unique name prefix, so a public package with the same name can't be installed by mistake.
Quality: the package has its own tests, type hints with a py.typed marker so consumers get type checking, a changelog, and declared dependency ranges that aren't too strict.
It's the same discipline we use for npm feature packages and NuGet packages on our Azure DevOps feed.

p17-881.q: Recent Python releases have focused heavily on performance and developer experience.
p17-881.k: python 3.13 features, python 3.12 features, free threading python, no gil python, python jit
x: Recent Python releases have focused heavily on performance and developer experience.
Faster CPython: since 3.11, the interpreter has become much faster, often 10 to 60 percent compared with 3.10, through specialising adaptive interpretation. Upgrading alone gives noticeable speedups.

Free-threaded Python: 3.13 introduced an experimental build without the GIL, and 3.14 made it officially supported, though still optional. Threads can run Python code truly in parallel on multiple cores, which helps CPU-bound multi-threaded work. Trade-offs: single-threaded code can be a bit slower, and C extensions must be updated to be thread-safe, so ecosystem support is still maturing.
Experimental JIT compiler: 3.13 added a copy-and-patch JIT, disabled by default, laying groundwork for future speedups.
Better error messages: clearer suggestions, like "did you mean", and precise locations in tracebacks.

Language features: exception groups and except* in 3.11; the type statement and new generic syntax in 3.12, where a function can declare its type parameter T right after its name; f-string improvements in 3.12; template strings in 3.14; and deferred evaluation of annotations.
Standard library: tomllib for reading TOML in 3.11, asyncio TaskGroup and timeout, itertools.batched in 3.12, and a new improved interactive shell in 3.13.

Practical approach: run services on a recent supported version, upgrade yearly after checking dependencies support it, and test performance-sensitive services on the new version, since the speed gains often come for free.

p17-882.q: Python is a natural fit for Lambda, with fast cold starts and a simple handler model: def handler(event, context), returning a response.
p17-882.k: python lambda, aws lambda python, lambda powertools python, package python lambda dependencies, lambda layers python
x: Python is a natural fit for Lambda, with fast cold starts and a simple handler model: def handler(event, context), returning a response.

Structure: initialise clients, like boto3 clients and configuration, at module level so they're reused across warm invocations. Keep the handler thin: parse the event, call business logic in separate functions or modules, and return the result. That keeps logic testable without Lambda.

Packaging dependencies: for pure-Python packages, a zip file with dependencies installed into the package folder is enough. For packages with compiled parts, like pydantic-core, cryptography or numpy, they must be built for Amazon Linux and the right architecture, x86 or arm64, so build in a matching container or use the right platform flags with pip. Large dependencies can go in layers, shared across functions, or use a container image, up to 10 GB, when packages are big, like data or ML libraries.

Tools: AWS SAM or CDK to define and deploy functions, with sam build handling dependency packaging; Powertools for AWS Lambda for structured logging, metrics, tracing, event parsing with Pydantic, idempotency, and batch processing helpers for partial SQS failures.
Performance: increase memory to get more CPU; choose arm64 Graviton for better price-performance; avoid importing heavy libraries you don't need; and use SnapStart for Python if cold starts matter.
Testing: unit-test business logic directly, test handlers with sample events, and use moto to mock AWS services, or LocalStack for integration-style tests.
Security: least-privilege execution roles, secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not environment variables in plain text.

p17-883.q: Python's datetime objects are either naive, with no time zone information, or aware, with a tzinfo attached. Mixing them causes errors, like being unable to compare naive and aware datetimes, and naive values cause silent bugs when code assumes a time zone that isn't there.
p17-883.k: python timezone, naive vs aware datetime, zoneinfo python, utc python datetime, datetime pitfalls python
x: Python's datetime objects are either naive, with no time zone information, or aware, with a tzinfo attached. Mixing them causes errors, like being unable to compare naive and aware datetimes, and naive values cause silent bugs when code assumes a time zone that isn't there.
My rules.
Use aware datetimes in UTC internally: datetime.now(timezone.utc), not datetime.utcnow(), which returns a naive value and is deprecated, and not datetime.now(), which returns local server time.
Store UTC in databases, in timestamp with time zone columns in Postgres, or as UTC with a clear naming convention in SQL Server.

Convert to the user's or site's local time only for display or for business rules that depend on local time, using zoneinfo with IANA names, like ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata"), which handles daylight saving correctly. Never use fixed offsets for regions that change for daylight saving.
Use date, not datetime, for business dates without a time, like a visit date or date of birth, to avoid off-by-one-day bugs when converting between zones.
Parse and format with ISO 8601: datetime.fromisoformat handles most ISO strings since 3.11, and APIs should exchange ISO strings with offsets or a trailing Z. Pydantic parses these automatically.
Arithmetic across daylight saving changes: adding 24 hours isn't always "the same time tomorrow" in local time, so for schedules, compute in local time and convert.
Testing: use freezegun or time-machine to control the current time in tests, and test around midnight and daylight saving changes.
These are the same principles I follow in .NET with DateTimeOffset and DateOnly.

p17-884.q: When a consumer calls ReceiveMessage, SQS can respond in two ways.
p17-884.k: sqs long polling, receive message wait time, sqs short polling, sqs message size limit, sqs extended client
x: When a consumer calls ReceiveMessage, SQS can respond in two ways.

Short polling returns immediately, checking only a subset of SQS servers, so it may return nothing even when messages exist, and an idle consumer makes constant empty calls, which costs money because SQS bills per request.

Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for messages to arrive before responding, and checks all servers. Set WaitTimeSeconds on the receive call, or ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds on the queue, to 20. It reduces empty responses, cost and latency for message pickup. I use it by default for every consumer; Lambda's SQS integration already uses long polling.
Batching: receive up to 10 messages per call with MaxNumberOfMessages, and delete them in batches too, which cuts request count further.

Message size: SQS messages are limited to 256 KB, recently raised to 1 MB. For bigger payloads, the claim-check pattern applies: store the payload in S3 and send a message with a reference to it. The SQS Extended Client Library does this automatically for Java and Python, and there are equivalents for .NET. Consumers fetch the object from S3, and a lifecycle rule cleans old payloads.
Even under the limit, I keep messages small, with ids and essential data, because smaller messages are cheaper, faster, and avoid putting sensitive data into queues unnecessarily.

Other settings to pair with this: a visibility timeout longer than processing time, a dead-letter queue with a sensible maxReceiveCount, and monitoring of ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage to catch consumers falling behind.

p17-885.q: Multipart upload splits a large object into parts, uploaded independently and in parallel, then combined by S3. Benefits: faster uploads through parallelism, retrying only failed parts instead of the whole file, and the ability to upload objects up to 5 TB. AWS recommends it for objects over 100 MB, and it's required above 5 GB for a single PUT. The AWS SDKs do this automatically with the TransferUtility in .NET or the Upload helper in JavaScript.
p17-885.k: s3 multipart upload, s3 performance, s3 transfer acceleration, s3 request rate, s3 large file upload
x: Multipart upload splits a large object into parts, uploaded independently and in parallel, then combined by S3. Benefits: faster uploads through parallelism, retrying only failed parts instead of the whole file, and the ability to upload objects up to 5 TB. AWS recommends it for objects over 100 MB, and it's required above 5 GB for a single PUT. The AWS SDKs do this automatically with the TransferUtility in .NET or the Upload helper in JavaScript.
Hidden cost: incomplete multipart uploads keep their parts stored, and billed, forever, unless cleaned up. I always add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days.
Browser uploads: the backend can create a multipart upload and return pre-signed URLs per part, so large files go directly from the browser to S3 in parallel.
Performance tips.
Request rates: S3 supports at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix, and scales automatically, so spreading keys across prefixes allows more throughput for very heavy workloads.
Parallelism for downloads too: byte-range fetches download parts of a large object in parallel.
Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations for faster long-distance uploads, for example from users in other continents, at extra cost.

Same region: keep compute and buckets in the same region to avoid latency and data transfer charges, and use a VPC gateway endpoint for S3 so traffic doesn't go through NAT gateways, which saves money.
CloudFront in front of S3 for frequently read content.

p17-886.q: Access to S3 is decided by several layers, and an action is allowed only if something allows it and nothing denies it.
p17-886.k: s3 bucket policy, s3 block public access, s3 acl, s3 permissions, bucket policy vs iam policy
x: Access to S3 is decided by several layers, and an action is allowed only if something allows it and nothing denies it.
IAM policies are attached to users and roles, saying what that identity can do, like s3:GetObject on a bucket's objects. This is the normal way to give your own applications access.

Bucket policies are resource-based policies attached to the bucket, saying who can do what on it. They're needed for cross-account access, for granting access to AWS services like CloudFront through origin access control, and for enforcing rules on everyone, like denying requests that don't use TLS, requiring encryption, or allowing access only from a specific VPC endpoint.
ACLs are the old mechanism. AWS now recommends disabling them by setting Object Ownership to bucket owner enforced, which is the default for new buckets.

Block Public Access is a safety net at the account and bucket level. When enabled, it overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public. I keep it on at the account level, and only turn it off for buckets that genuinely must be public, which is rare, since CloudFront with origin access control serves public content without a public bucket.
Encryption: if objects use SSE-KMS, the caller also needs permission on the KMS key, a common cause of AccessDenied surprises.

Good practices: least privilege with specific actions and prefixes, deny insecure transport, enable server access logging or CloudTrail data events for sensitive buckets, and use IAM Access Analyzer to detect buckets shared outside the account.

p17-887.q: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations. What's cached, for how long, and under which key is controlled by cache behaviours and policies.
p17-887.k: cloudfront cache policy, cloudfront invalidation, cache key cloudfront, cloudfront ttl, cdn caching aws
x: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations. What's cached, for how long, and under which key is controlled by cache behaviours and policies.
Cache behaviours match path patterns, like /assets/* or /api/*, each with its own origin and policies, so static files and API calls can be treated differently.

Cache policy defines the cache key, which headers, cookies and query strings make a response unique, plus minimum, default and maximum TTLs. A smaller cache key means more cache hits. Include only what changes the response; for example, don't include all cookies for static assets.
Origin request policy defines what's forwarded to the origin without being part of the cache key, like a header the origin needs but which doesn't change the response.
TTL interplay: the origin's Cache-Control headers set the time, bounded by the policy's minimum and maximum.

Invalidation removes objects from edge caches before they expire, using paths like /index.html or /*. The first 1,000 paths per month are free, then they're charged, and they take a little time to complete.

My approach for SPAs avoids frequent invalidation: hashed file names for JavaScript and CSS, like main.3f9a1c.js, cached for a year, because a new build produces new names; and index.html with no-cache or a very short TTL, so users get the new version immediately after a deployment. Then one small invalidation of index.html, or none, is enough.
For APIs: usually caching disabled with the managed CachingDisabled policy, or short caching only for public, non-personalised GET responses.

p17-888.q: Amazon Cognito has two parts that are often confused.
p17-888.k: cognito user pool vs identity pool, amazon cognito, cognito federated identities, cognito jwt, cognito hosted ui
x: Amazon Cognito has two parts that are often confused.

User pools are a user directory and OpenID Connect identity provider. They handle sign-up, sign-in, password policies, MFA, account recovery, and federation with external identity providers like Entra ID, Google or SAML providers. After login, users get JWTs: an ID token, an access token and a refresh token. APIs validate these tokens, for example with a JWT authorizer in API Gateway, or JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core using the user pool's issuer and JWKS. Cognito provides a hosted login UI, now called managed login, or you can build your own UI with the SDK.

Identity pools, or federated identities, exchange a token from a user pool or another identity provider for temporary AWS credentials, through IAM roles. That lets a client app, like a mobile app, call AWS services directly, like uploading to S3 or reading DynamoDB, with permissions scoped per user, without a backend in between. They can also give limited guest access.
So: user pools answer "who is this user?" and issue app tokens; identity pools answer "which AWS permissions does this user get?"
Most web apps with their own backend only need a user pool. Identity pools are useful when the front end talks directly to AWS services.

Considerations: Cognito's customisation and some features are more limited than full identity products like Keycloak or Entra ID, and migrating users out later can be hard because password hashes can't be exported, so the choice deserves thought for large systems.

p17-889.q: In ECS, tasks start and stop with changing IP addresses, so services need a way to find each other without hard-coded addresses.
p17-889.k: ecs service connect, aws cloud map, ecs service discovery, service to service ecs, ecs internal dns
x: In ECS, tasks start and stop with changing IP addresses, so services need a way to find each other without hard-coded addresses.
Options.

Internal load balancer: put an internal ALB in front of each service and call it by DNS name. Simple and gives health checks and load balancing, but adds cost per load balancer and an extra network hop.

Cloud Map service discovery: ECS registers each task's IP address in AWS Cloud Map, which creates DNS records, like orders.internal.local, in a private hosted zone. Callers resolve the name and get task IPs. No load balancer, but clients must handle DNS caching and choose healthy instances, and there's no built-in retry or metrics.

ECS Service Connect: the newer, recommended approach. ECS injects a managed Envoy proxy sidecar into each task. Services get simple names, like http://orders:8080, the proxy does load balancing across healthy tasks, retries and outlier detection, and publishes traffic metrics, like request counts, latency and errors, to CloudWatch for each service, without code changes. It's built on Cloud Map namespaces.

How I'd choose: Service Connect for service-to-service calls within ECS; an ALB for traffic coming from outside or from other platforms; and for complex cross-platform meshes, a full service mesh, though that adds operational complexity.

Whatever the discovery method, the calling code still needs timeouts, retries with backoff for idempotent calls and circuit breakers, and propagates correlation and trace context, so requests can be followed across services in IQVIA's newer AWS services.

p17-890.q: Sometimes you need to look inside a running container, like checking files, environment, DNS resolution or connectivity to a database, especially on Fargate, where there's no host to SSH into. ECS Exec provides this.
p17-890.k: ecs exec, execute command ecs, shell into fargate container, debug ecs task, ssm ecs exec
x: Sometimes you need to look inside a running container, like checking files, environment, DNS resolution or connectivity to a database, especially on Fargate, where there's no host to SSH into. ECS Exec provides this.

How it works: it uses Systems Manager Session Manager. When enabled on the service or task, ECS adds an SSM agent to the task. You run aws ecs execute-command with the cluster, task, container and command, like /bin/sh, with the interactive flag, and get a shell or run a single command. No inbound ports, no SSH keys, no bastion host.

Requirements: enable execute command on the service, give the task role permissions for SSM messages, make sure the task can reach the SSM endpoints, through a NAT gateway or VPC interface endpoints, and have the Session Manager plugin installed locally. If the image has no shell, like distroless or chiseled images, you can only run binaries that exist in the image, so debugging needs other approaches.

Security and audit: access is controlled by IAM, so only specific roles can execute commands, ideally only in non-production or through a break-glass process in production. Sessions can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and are recorded in CloudTrail, which matters in regulated environments.

Good practice: use it for investigation, not for fixing things by hand. Changes made inside a container are lost on restart and create drift. Once I find the problem, the fix goes through code or configuration and a normal deployment.
It's the AWS equivalent of kubectl exec in Kubernetes.

p17-891.q: There are two main ways to send custom metrics, like orders processed or job duration, to CloudWatch.
p17-891.k: cloudwatch embedded metric format, emf, cloudwatch custom metrics, putmetricdata, metrics from logs aws
x: There are two main ways to send custom metrics, like orders processed or job duration, to CloudWatch.
PutMetricData API: the application calls CloudWatch directly. It works, but each call is a network request with latency and cost, and it needs batching and error handling, which is awkward in Lambda.

Embedded Metric Format, EMF: the application writes a structured JSON log line with a special _aws section describing which fields are metrics, their units and dimensions. CloudWatch Logs automatically extracts the metrics from these log events asynchronously. No extra API calls, no latency added to the request, and the same log line also carries high-cardinality context, like request id or study id, which you can query in Logs Insights without making them metric dimensions.

How to use it: Powertools for AWS Lambda, for .NET, Python and TypeScript, has a Metrics utility that writes EMF; the aws-embedded-metrics libraries do it for other workloads; on ECS, logs go to CloudWatch through the awslogs driver or the CloudWatch agent, which processes EMF too.

Dimensions and cost: each unique combination of metric name and dimension values is a separate custom metric, billed monthly. Keep dimensions low-cardinality, like service, environment and operation, never user ids or request ids.

Alternatives: if the organisation uses OpenTelemetry and a vendor like Datadog, metrics go through the OpenTelemetry SDK and collector instead, which keeps the code vendor-neutral. EMF is the simplest choice when CloudWatch is the main monitoring tool.

p17-892.q: AWS describes four disaster recovery strategies, trading cost against recovery time, RTO, and data loss, RPO.
p17-892.k: aws disaster recovery strategies, pilot light, warm standby, multi site active active, rto rpo aws
x: AWS describes four disaster recovery strategies, trading cost against recovery time, RTO, and data loss, RPO.

Backup and restore: regularly back up data, with AWS Backup, snapshots and S3 cross-region replication, and keep infrastructure as code. In a disaster, recreate infrastructure in another region and restore data. Cheapest, but RTO is hours and RPO depends on backup frequency.

Pilot light: core data is continuously replicated to the recovery region, like an Aurora global database or cross-region read replica, while compute is off or minimal. In a disaster, scale up compute from templates and switch traffic. RTO in tens of minutes.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy runs in the recovery region, with data replicated. It can serve traffic immediately after scaling up. RTO in minutes, higher cost.

Multi-site active-active: full capacity in two or more regions, both serving traffic, with Route 53 or Global Accelerator routing users. Near-zero RTO, but the highest cost and complexity, especially for data conflicts between regions.

How to choose: start from business requirements: how long can the system be down, and how much data can be lost? Clinical systems that sites use to randomise patients need short RTO and near-zero RPO for transactional data, while reporting systems may tolerate more.

What makes any strategy work: everything as code, so environments can be rebuilt; automated, tested runbooks; regular DR drills, including failing back; monitoring of replication lag; and remembering dependencies like DNS, certificates, secrets and third-party allow-lists in the recovery region.

p17-893.q: An Auto Scaling group manages a fleet of EC2 instances: it keeps the desired number running, replaces unhealthy instances, spreads them across Availability Zones, and scales in and out.
p17-893.k: auto scaling group, launch template, ec2 auto scaling, scaling policies ec2, instance refresh
x: An Auto Scaling group manages a fleet of EC2 instances: it keeps the desired number running, replaces unhealthy instances, spreads them across Availability Zones, and scales in and out.

A launch template defines how to create each instance: AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM instance profile, user data script for bootstrapping, storage and tags. Templates are versioned, so you can roll out changes and roll back.
Scaling policies.
Target tracking: keep a metric at a target, like average CPU at 50 percent or ALB requests per target at 1,000. The simplest and usually best choice.
Step scaling: add or remove instances in steps based on alarm thresholds.
Scheduled scaling: known patterns, like scaling up before business hours.
Predictive scaling: uses history to scale ahead of expected load.
Health checks: use ELB health checks, not just EC2 status checks, so instances that are running but whose app is broken get replaced.
Deployments: instance refresh replaces instances gradually with a new launch template version, respecting a minimum healthy percentage, with checkpoints and automatic rollback on failure.

Other useful features: lifecycle hooks to run actions when instances launch or terminate, like draining work or copying logs; warm pools of pre-initialised instances for faster scaling; and mixed instance policies combining On-Demand and Spot across several instance types to reduce cost.
For a Windows and IIS-based application moved to AWS as-is, an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with a golden AMI is a reasonable first step, before containerising.

p17-894.q: Amazon SES is AWS's email sending service, used for transactional email like notifications, password resets and reports.
p17-894.k: amazon ses, send email aws, ses dkim spf, ses bounce handling, ses sandbox
x: Amazon SES is AWS's email sending service, used for transactional email like notifications, password resets and reports.
Setup.

Verify the sending domain, and configure DKIM, with records SES provides, SPF, and DMARC in DNS. These prove emails are really from your domain, which is critical for deliverability and avoiding spam folders. A custom MAIL FROM domain aligns SPF properly.
Leave the sandbox: new accounts can only send to verified addresses with low limits; request production access, explaining your use case and how you handle bounces and complaints.

Sending: from .NET, use the AWS SDK's SES v2 client with the application's IAM role, or the SMTP interface for existing code that uses SMTP. Use templates for consistent content, and configuration sets to group sending and track events.

Bounces and complaints: subscribe to bounce, complaint and delivery events through SNS or EventBridge, process them, and stop sending to addresses that hard bounce or complain. Account-level suppression lists help. High bounce or complaint rates can get the account paused.
Reliability: send email asynchronously through a queue, so a slow or failing email call doesn't fail the business transaction, with retries and idempotency to avoid duplicate emails.

Security and compliance: avoid sensitive data in email bodies, send links to the secure application instead, and use dedicated IPs or separate configuration sets for different kinds of email if volumes justify it.
Monitoring: delivery, bounce and complaint rates on a dashboard, with alarms.

p17-895.q: AWS AppConfig, part of Systems Manager, manages application configuration and feature flags that change at runtime without redeploying code.
p17-895.k: aws appconfig, appconfig feature flags, dynamic configuration aws, appconfig deployment strategy, appconfig agent
x: AWS AppConfig, part of Systems Manager, manages application configuration and feature flags that change at runtime without redeploying code.
What it adds over storing configuration in Parameter Store or files.
Validation: configurations can have JSON schema or Lambda validators, so an invalid change is rejected before it's deployed.
Controlled deployments: changes roll out gradually using deployment strategies, like 10 percent of targets every few minutes, with a bake time.

Automatic rollback: linked to CloudWatch alarms, so if error rates rise during a configuration rollout, AppConfig rolls the change back automatically. That's valuable because bad configuration changes cause many outages.
Feature flags: a dedicated feature flag type with on and off flags, attributes, and multi-variant flags for targeting.

How applications read it: the AppConfig Agent, as a Lambda extension, ECS sidecar or local process, polls for changes and caches the configuration, and the app reads it from a local HTTP endpoint, which is fast and cheap. Or use the SDK's configuration data API with session tokens. Applications should cache values and refresh periodically, not call AppConfig on every request.
In .NET, a configuration provider can load AppConfig data into IConfiguration, and IOptionsMonitor picks up changes.

Compared with Azure: it's similar to Azure App Configuration with its feature manager. Compared with dedicated tools like LaunchDarkly, AppConfig is simpler and cheaper but has less user targeting and analytics.
I'd use it for kill switches, gradual feature rollouts, and operational settings, like rate limits or batch sizes, that need changing quickly but safely.

p17-896.q: In a multi-account AWS setup, a workload or person in one account often needs access to resources in another, like a deployment pipeline in a tools account deploying to production, or a service reading a shared S3 bucket.
p17-896.k: cross account access aws, assumerole, sts assume role, trust policy, external id
x: In a multi-account AWS setup, a workload or person in one account often needs access to resources in another, like a deployment pipeline in a tools account deploying to production, or a service reading a shared S3 bucket.
The mechanism is role assumption with AWS STS.

In the target account, create an IAM role with two policies: a trust policy saying which principals may assume it, like a specific role in the tools account, and a permissions policy saying what the role can do in the target account.
In the source account, the calling identity needs permission for sts:AssumeRole on that role.

The caller calls AssumeRole, getting temporary credentials, valid from 15 minutes to a few hours, and uses them to call services in the target account. The SDKs and CLI profiles can do this automatically.
Security details.
Trust specific roles, not the whole account root, unless intentional, and add conditions, like requiring MFA for humans, or source identity and session tags for auditing.
External ID: when allowing a third party to assume a role, require an external ID they must provide, which protects against the confused deputy problem.
Session duration: keep it short.
CloudTrail logs AssumeRole calls and the actions taken with the session, so every action is traceable to the original identity.
For people, IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on into multiple accounts with permission sets, which creates and manages these roles for you, so nobody needs long-term IAM users.
For pipelines, combine this with OIDC federation, so no access keys exist anywhere.

p17-897.q: Athena is a serverless query service that runs SQL directly on files in S3. You pay per amount of data scanned, with no servers to manage.
p17-897.k: amazon athena, query s3 with sql, athena glue catalog, athena partitions, analyze logs s3
x: Athena is a serverless query service that runs SQL directly on files in S3. You pay per amount of data scanned, with no servers to manage.

How it works: a table definition in the AWS Glue Data Catalog describes where the data lives in S3, its format and its columns. You can create tables with DDL statements, or use Glue crawlers to infer schemas. Then you query with standard SQL, joining and aggregating.

Common uses: analysing ALB, CloudFront, VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail logs stored in S3, for example finding which IPs caused a spike of 5xx errors, or which role made a configuration change; querying data lake exports for reporting; and ad hoc analysis of exported application data.
Making it fast and cheap.
Columnar formats: convert data to Parquet or ORC, compressed. Queries read only needed columns, often reducing scanned data by 90 percent or more compared to CSV or JSON.

Partitioning: organise S3 paths by date or other keys, like year, month and day, and filter on partition columns, so Athena skips irrelevant files. Partition projection avoids managing partitions manually.
Avoid many tiny files; combine them into larger files.
Select only needed columns, never SELECT star on big tables.
Governance: workgroups with per-query data scan limits and separate result locations control costs; Lake Formation can manage fine-grained permissions.
It's very useful during incident investigations, when logs in S3 are too large for quick searches in other tools, and it complements CloudWatch Logs Insights for recent logs.

p17-898.q: A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a single function, created with one setting. Requests go straight to the function, with no API Gateway in between.
p17-898.k: lambda function url, function url vs api gateway, lambda http endpoint, lambda url auth
x: A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a single function, created with one setting. Requests go straight to the function, with no API Gateway in between.

What function URLs offer: HTTPS endpoint with no extra service, no added cost beyond Lambda, longer timeouts up to the function's 15 minutes, compared to API Gateway's integration timeout, response streaming for sending large or progressive responses, CORS configuration, and authentication either with IAM, requiring SigV4-signed requests, or none, meaning public.

What API Gateway adds: custom authorizers, including JWT validation against Cognito or another OpenID Connect provider; request validation; throttling and usage plans with API keys; caching in REST APIs; request and response transformations; routing many paths to different backends; custom domains with base path mappings; WAF integration directly; and better API lifecycle features like stages.

When a function URL is enough: internal webhooks with signature verification in the function; service-to-service calls using IAM auth; simple single-function backends; or endpoints needing streaming or long processing time. CloudFront can sit in front of a function URL for a custom domain, caching and WAF, with origin access control so only CloudFront can call it.
When I'd use API Gateway: public APIs with several routes, central authentication with JWTs, per-client throttling, or when the API is a product with documentation and keys.
For an ASP.NET Core API hosted on Lambda, either can work; I'd still choose API Gateway or an ALB for production APIs with multiple consumers, to get centralised auth and throttling.

p17-899.q: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service running Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ. AWS handles provisioning, patching, high availability across Availability Zones, and backups, while applications use the standard broker protocols, like AMQP 0-9-1 for RabbitMQ, MQTT, STOMP or JMS for ActiveMQ.
p17-899.k: amazon mq, rabbitmq on aws, managed rabbitmq, amazon mq vs sqs, activemq aws
x: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service running Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ. AWS handles provisioning, patching, high availability across Availability Zones, and backups, while applications use the standard broker protocols, like AMQP 0-9-1 for RabbitMQ, MQTT, STOMP or JMS for ActiveMQ.

Why it exists: many existing applications are built on RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, with exchanges, routing keys, topic patterns, priority queues and existing client libraries. Rewriting them for SQS and SNS takes effort and changes behaviour. Amazon MQ lets you move them to AWS with minimal code changes, just a new connection string and TLS settings.
When I'd use it.
Lift and shift of applications using RabbitMQ, like an on-premise system with RabbitMQ workers, retry queues and dead-letter exchanges, where keeping the same messaging model reduces migration risk.
When you need protocol-level features SQS doesn't offer, like complex routing, message priorities, or standard protocols for interoperability with other systems.

When I'd prefer SQS and SNS, or EventBridge: new cloud-native services, because they're serverless, scale without capacity planning, cost nothing when idle, and integrate directly with Lambda and other services. Amazon MQ runs on broker instances you size and pay for continuously, and has throughput limits per broker.

Migration thought: a reasonable path for a RabbitMQ-based system is to move to Amazon MQ first, keeping everything working, and then gradually move new or simpler flows to SQS, SNS or EventBridge where it makes sense, rather than doing both changes at once.

p17-900.q: I'd start by choosing the target, then the migration method.
p17-900.k: migrate sql server to aws, aws dms, rds for sql server, sql server to aurora, database migration aws
x: I'd start by choosing the target, then the migration method.
Target options.

RDS for SQL Server: managed SQL Server, with backups, patching and Multi-AZ handled by AWS. The least change for applications. Limits: no full sysadmin access, some features restricted, and SQL Server licensing included in the price, which is expensive.
SQL Server on EC2: full control and every feature, for databases that need things RDS doesn't support, but you manage everything.
Aurora PostgreSQL or Babelfish: a bigger change to save licensing costs, requiring code and schema conversion, which is a project in itself.
Migration methods.

Native backup and restore: take a full backup on-premise, upload to S3, and restore into RDS with the native restore procedure. Simple and reliable; for minimal downtime, follow with differential and log backups, then a short cutover.

AWS DMS, Database Migration Service: copies data and keeps replicating changes with change data capture, so the target stays in sync until cutover. Useful for heterogeneous migrations with the Schema Conversion Tool, or to minimise downtime.
Distributed availability groups or log shipping to EC2 for near-zero downtime.

Planning: inventory features in use, like SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, CLR, cross-database queries and SSIS packages, since some don't work the same on RDS; size the instance from current metrics; test performance with production-like load; rehearse the cutover; and plan rollback.
For a setup with many databases, like one per study, automation and wave planning are essential: migrate a few low-risk databases first, learn, then scale up.

p17-901.q: Choosing where to run scheduled and batch work depends on duration, resources and complexity.
p17-901.k: scheduled jobs aws, ecs scheduled task, aws batch, cron jobs aws, batch processing aws
x: Choosing where to run scheduled and batch work depends on duration, resources and complexity.
Lambda with EventBridge Scheduler: for short jobs, under 15 minutes, like nightly cleanups, sending reminders or calling an API. Cheap and simple, with retries and dead-letter queues on the schedule.

ECS scheduled tasks: EventBridge Scheduler starts a Fargate or EC2 task on a cron schedule. Good for longer jobs, jobs needing more memory or CPU, or jobs that already exist as containers, like a .NET console app. No time limit, and you pay only while the task runs.

AWS Batch: for large-scale batch processing with many jobs, queues and priorities, job dependencies and array jobs, like processing thousands of files or heavy computations. Batch manages compute environments, including Spot instances, and schedules jobs efficiently.
Step Functions: to orchestrate multi-step jobs, with retries, branching, parallel steps and error handling, calling Lambda, ECS tasks or Batch jobs, triggered by a schedule.
Design rules for any of them.
Idempotent and restartable: a job that fails halfway must be safe to rerun, with checkpoints for long jobs.
No overlapping runs: ensure only one instance runs at a time if that matters, using locks or Step Functions.
Monitoring: alarms on failures, and on jobs that didn't run, using a heartbeat pattern, because silent non-execution is a common problem.
Timeouts and resource limits so stuck jobs don't run forever.
This is the AWS equivalent of what we do on-premise with Quartz jobs, and what our AlertWatchDog-style checks would look like if they ran in IQVIA's newer AWS services.

p17-902.q: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for OpenSearch, the open-source fork of Elasticsearch. It's used for two main things.
p17-902.k: amazon opensearch, opensearch service, elasticsearch aws, full text search aws, opensearch dashboards
x: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for OpenSearch, the open-source fork of Elasticsearch. It's used for two main things.

Search: full-text search with relevance ranking, fuzzy matching, autocomplete, filtering and faceting, for searching products, documents or records much better than SQL LIKE queries. Data is indexed from the main database, often through change events or a sync process, with the database remaining the source of truth.

Log and observability analytics: ingesting application logs, metrics and traces, then searching and visualising them with OpenSearch Dashboards, the Kibana equivalent. It's an alternative to CloudWatch Logs or commercial tools for teams wanting more powerful search over large log volumes.
It also supports vector search with k-nearest-neighbour indexes, used for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, combining keyword and vector search in one query.
Operational points.
Sizing: choose instance types and counts, storage, and dedicated master nodes for stability; plan shard counts carefully, since too many small shards wastes resources.
OpenSearch Serverless removes cluster management, scaling automatically, with a different cost model.
High availability: multiple Availability Zones and replicas.
Security: VPC access, fine-grained access control, and encryption.
Index lifecycle: rollover and delete or move older log indexes to cheaper UltraWarm and cold storage tiers, otherwise log clusters grow expensive quickly.

When I wouldn't use it: if search needs are simple, database full-text search may be enough; and if logs are already handled well by CloudWatch, Splunk or Datadog, adding another log platform increases cost and complexity.

p17-903.q: AWS Systems Manager is a set of tools for managing EC2 instances and on-premise servers at scale, through the SSM agent installed on each machine.
p17-903.k: systems manager patch manager, ssm run command, aws patching, ssm state manager, fleet management aws
x: AWS Systems Manager is a set of tools for managing EC2 instances and on-premise servers at scale, through the SSM agent installed on each machine.
The parts I'd use for operations.

Patch Manager: defines patch baselines, which patches to approve, like security updates automatically after seven days, and patch groups by tags, like web servers or database servers. Patches are applied in maintenance windows, with compliance reports showing which servers are missing patches.

Maintenance Windows: schedule patching and other tasks during agreed times, with controlled concurrency and error thresholds, like patching 10 percent of servers at a time and stopping if more than one fails.
Run Command: run scripts or commands across many servers at once, by tag, with output logged, instead of logging in to each one. For example, collecting diagnostics or restarting a service.
State Manager: keep servers in a defined state, like ensuring an agent is installed or a configuration is applied, and reapplying if it drifts.
Session Manager: shell access without SSH keys or open ports, fully audited.
Inventory: collects installed software, updates and configuration from all servers.
Hybrid: the agent can also run on on-premise servers, so the same tools manage both cloud and data centre machines, which helps during a long migration.
For safe patching: patch lower environments first, take snapshots or AMIs before patching critical servers, drain servers from load balancers during patching, and check health afterwards.
In a containerised world, patching moves to rebuilding images with updated base images, but for VM-based and Windows workloads, Systems Manager is the main tool.

p17-904.q: Azure Functions for .NET historically had two hosting models.
p17-904.k: azure functions isolated worker, in process vs isolated, dotnet isolated functions, functions worker model, migrate to isolated worker
x: Azure Functions for .NET historically had two hosting models.

In-process: the function code ran inside the Functions host process, sharing its .NET version and assemblies. It was fast to start and supported some bindings directly, but your app was tied to the host's .NET version, and dependency conflicts with the host's assemblies were common. Microsoft has ended support for the in-process model with .NET 8 as its last version, with support ending in November 2026.

Isolated worker: the function app runs in its own .NET process, separate from the host, communicating over gRPC. Benefits: you choose the .NET version, including newer ones as soon as they're supported; no assembly conflicts; full control over startup with the normal Program.cs, dependency injection and configuration, just like any .NET app; and middleware support, so cross-cutting concerns like logging, correlation and exception handling work like in ASP.NET Core. It's now the only supported model going forward.

Migration steps: change the project to the isolated worker packages, Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker and extension packages instead of WebJobs extensions; add a Program.cs with the host builder; update function signatures, since bindings and types differ, like HttpRequestData or ASP.NET Core integration for HTTP functions; replace ILogger injection patterns; update settings, like FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME to dotnet-isolated; and test each trigger carefully, especially Durable Functions, which have their own isolated package.

If I were moving our AlertWatchDog-style scheduled checks to Azure Functions, I'd write them on the isolated model from the start, with timer triggers and dependency injection shared with our other .NET code.

p17-905.q: The concepts map reasonably well, but not one to one, so I'd plan the mapping first.
p17-905.k: rabbitmq to service bus, migrate rabbitmq azure, service bus vs rabbitmq, exchanges to topics, messaging migration azure
x: The concepts map reasonably well, but not one to one, so I'd plan the mapping first.

Mapping: a RabbitMQ queue with a single consumer group maps to a Service Bus queue. A fanout or topic exchange with several queues bound to it maps to a Service Bus topic with subscriptions; routing keys and binding patterns map to subscription filters, SQL or correlation filters. Dead-letter exchanges map to the built-in dead-letter sub-queue on every queue and subscription. Retry queues with TTLs, which we build manually in RabbitMQ, can be replaced with Service Bus's delivery count and max delivery count, plus scheduled messages for delayed retries. Consumer acks map to peek-lock with Complete, Abandon or DeadLetter. Message ordering per key maps to sessions.

Differences to handle: Service Bus has message size limits per tier, 256 KB on Standard and up to 100 MB on Premium; lock durations need renewing for long processing; and duplicate detection is built in, based on message id.
Migration approach.
Abstract messaging behind an interface, or use a library like MassTransit, which supports both brokers, so switching transport is mostly configuration.
Run both in parallel: bridge messages from RabbitMQ to Service Bus for a period, or move one flow at a time, starting with low-risk ones.
Make consumers idempotent, since a migration increases the chance of duplicates.
Monitor dead-letter counts and queue lengths on both sides during cutover.

Connectivity matters for on-premise apps: they need reliable outbound access to Azure, ideally through private endpoints over ExpressRoute or VPN, and managed identity is only available to Azure-hosted workloads.

p17-906.q: Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, is an open-source project that runs as a sidecar next to each service and provides common microservice capabilities through simple HTTP or gRPC APIs, so application code doesn't depend on specific infrastructure SDKs.
p17-906.k: dapr, distributed application runtime, dapr sidecar, dapr pub sub, dapr building blocks
x: Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, is an open-source project that runs as a sidecar next to each service and provides common microservice capabilities through simple HTTP or gRPC APIs, so application code doesn't depend on specific infrastructure SDKs.
Building blocks.
Service invocation: call another service by its app id, with service discovery, retries, mTLS and tracing handled by the sidecars.
Pub/sub: publish and subscribe to events, with the broker, like Service Bus, RabbitMQ, Kafka or Redis, chosen through configuration components.
State management: key-value state with pluggable stores, like Redis or Cosmos DB, with concurrency control.
Bindings: input and output connectors to external systems, like queues, storage or cron schedules.
Secrets and configuration: read from Key Vault or other stores through one API.
Workflows and actors for stateful patterns.
Resiliency policies: timeouts, retries and circuit breakers defined in configuration.

Why teams use it: services in different languages, like .NET, Node and Python, get the same capabilities consistently; switching infrastructure, like from RabbitMQ in one environment to Service Bus in another, is a configuration change; and observability is built in.
Azure Container Apps has Dapr integration built in, enabled per app with a setting, which makes it easy to try. On Kubernetes, it's installed in the cluster.

Trade-offs: an extra sidecar per service adds latency, resource use and another moving part to operate and upgrade; abstractions hide broker-specific features; and teams must learn its concepts. For a small number of .NET-only services, native SDKs with a library like MassTransit may be simpler.

p17-907.q: Many organisations run Azure DevOps Server, formerly TFS, on-premise, like our setup, and consider moving to the cloud service. There are two main approaches.
p17-907.k: azure devops server migration, tfs to azure devops services, data migration tool azure devops, on premise azure devops to cloud, tfs migration
x: Many organisations run Azure DevOps Server, formerly TFS, on-premise, like our setup, and consider moving to the cloud service. There are two main approaches.

High-fidelity migration with Microsoft's data migration tool: it imports a whole collection, including work item history, Git and TFVC repositories, pipelines, test plans and artifacts, into Azure DevOps Services. It requires the server to be on a recent supported version, identities to be synchronised with Entra ID, and a validation step that reports issues to fix first. There's a dry run, then a production run with downtime for the collection.

Selective migration: create new projects in the cloud and move only what's needed: Git repositories with full history, which is easy; recent work items with tools or scripts; and pipelines rebuilt as YAML. Simpler and a chance to clean up, but loses some history and links.
Things to plan for.
TFVC repositories: still supported in the cloud, but it's a good time to migrate to Git.
Classic release pipelines: work in the cloud, but YAML multi-stage pipelines are the modern direction.
Build agents: on-premise deployments still need self-hosted agents inside the network, since cloud-hosted agents can't reach internal servers. Agents connect outbound to the cloud service.
Secrets and service connections: recreate them, preferably using workload identity federation for Azure.
Compliance: regulated environments must confirm data residency, retention, audit logs and validation requirements.
Integrations: tools connected to the old server, like reporting or custom extensions.
This is part of why our MCP server talks to on-premise Azure DevOps: with work items and pipelines still on-premise, automation had to work there, not only in the cloud.

p17-908.q: Azure Arc extends Azure's management plane to resources outside Azure: on-premise servers, servers in other clouds, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances. Once connected, these resources appear in Azure as if they were Azure resources, with a resource id, tags and RBAC.
p17-908.k: azure arc, hybrid cloud azure, arc enabled servers, manage on premise servers azure, azure arc kubernetes
x: Azure Arc extends Azure's management plane to resources outside Azure: on-premise servers, servers in other clouds, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances. Once connected, these resources appear in Azure as if they were Azure resources, with a resource id, tags and RBAC.
What you can do with Arc-enabled servers.
Azure Policy and guest configuration: audit and enforce settings, like required security configurations, across on-premise machines.
Update Manager: assess and schedule operating system patching for on-premise Windows and Linux servers from Azure.
Azure Monitor: collect logs and metrics with the Azure Monitor agent into Log Analytics, so on-premise and cloud monitoring use the same queries and alerts.
Microsoft Defender for Cloud: security posture and threat protection for on-premise servers.

Managed identity for on-premise servers: apps on Arc-enabled servers can get Entra ID tokens to access Azure services, like Key Vault, without storing secrets, which is a big improvement for hybrid apps.
Arc-enabled SQL Server: inventory, best-practice assessments, and licensing management for on-premise SQL Server.
Arc-enabled Kubernetes: GitOps configuration and policy for clusters running anywhere.

Why it's relevant for a mostly on-premise system: it gives cloud-style governance, patching, monitoring and identity without moving the workloads, which can be a stepping stone for a future migration, and helps when some services already run in the cloud while the core stays in the data centre.
Requirements: the Connected Machine agent on each server, with outbound connectivity to Azure endpoints, possibly through a proxy or private link.

p17-909.q: Exposing RDP or SSH ports to the internet is one of the most common causes of compromised VMs, because attackers scan constantly for them. Azure Bastion provides secure access without public IPs on the VMs.
p17-909.k: azure bastion, rdp ssh without public ip, secure vm access azure, jump box azure, just in time vm access
x: Exposing RDP or SSH ports to the internet is one of the most common causes of compromised VMs, because attackers scan constantly for them. Azure Bastion provides secure access without public IPs on the VMs.

How it works: Bastion is a managed service deployed into a dedicated subnet, AzureBastionSubnet, in the virtual network. Users connect through the Azure portal over HTTPS, or with the native RDP or SSH client using the Azure CLI on the Standard tier, and Bastion opens the RDP or SSH session to the private IP of the VM. The VMs need no public IP, and their network security groups can allow RDP and SSH only from the Bastion subnet.

Benefits: no exposed management ports; authentication through Entra ID for portal access, so MFA and Conditional Access apply; session recording on the Premium tier for audit; and with peering, one Bastion can serve VMs across peered networks.
Complementary controls.
Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud opens management ports only when requested, for a limited time and specific source IP.
Entra ID login for VMs, so users sign in with their corporate identity rather than local accounts.
Run commands and automation, instead of interactive logins, for routine tasks.
Compared to AWS: the equivalent is Systems Manager Session Manager, which needs no network entry point at all, since it uses an agent connecting outbound.
My principle is the same in any environment: interactive server access should be rare, audited and time-limited, and routine work should go through automation and pipelines.

p17-910.q: Both provide queues on Azure, but they're aimed at different needs.
p17-910.k: storage queue vs service bus, azure storage queues, azure queue options, simple queue azure, service bus features
x: Both provide queues on Azure, but they're aimed at different needs.

Azure Storage queues are part of a storage account. They're simple and cheap, can hold very large numbers of messages, up to the storage account's capacity, and are accessed over HTTP. Messages are up to 64 KB. Features are basic: at-least-once delivery with a visibility timeout, a dequeue count, and that's mostly it. No ordering guarantee, no topics, no built-in dead-lettering; you implement poison message handling yourself, though Azure Functions moves messages to a poison queue after several failures.

Service Bus queues are an enterprise message broker: larger messages, up to 256 KB on Standard or 100 MB on Premium; FIFO ordering with sessions; built-in dead-letter queues; duplicate detection; scheduled and deferred messages; transactions across operations; topics and subscriptions with filters for publish-subscribe; and AMQP protocol support.
How I choose.

Storage queues: simple background work distribution, like resizing images or sending notifications, where order doesn't matter, high volume is expected and cost should be minimal, or when the app already uses a storage account.

Service Bus: business messaging between services, where losing, duplicating or misordering messages matters, like order processing or integration events; when you need publish-subscribe, dead-lettering, sessions or transactions.
Event Grid and Event Hubs are different again: event notification and high-throughput streaming, rather than command queues.
For business integration flows, like the ones we run on RabbitMQ with retries and dead-letter handling, Service Bus is the natural Azure equivalent.

p17-911.q: Azure Data Factory is Azure's managed data integration service for ETL and ELT: moving and transforming data between many sources and destinations on a schedule or trigger.
p17-911.k: azure data factory, adf pipelines, etl azure, data integration azure, self hosted integration runtime
x: Azure Data Factory is Azure's managed data integration service for ETL and ELT: moving and transforming data between many sources and destinations on a schedule or trigger.
Main concepts.
Pipelines contain activities, like Copy data, run a stored procedure, call a web endpoint, run a notebook, or control flow like loops and conditions.
Linked services hold connection information to sources and destinations, ideally using managed identity and Key Vault for secrets.
Datasets describe the data structure in those sources.

Integration runtimes provide the compute. The Azure integration runtime works for cloud sources; the self-hosted integration runtime is installed on a machine inside the corporate network, letting Data Factory reach on-premise databases, file shares and SFTP servers securely through outbound connections.
Mapping data flows offer visual, Spark-based transformations without writing code.
Triggers run pipelines on schedules, tumbling windows or storage events.

Where it fits: loading data from operational databases into a data warehouse or lake, moving files between systems, scheduled data exports to partners, and migrating data. It has many built-in connectors and monitoring of every run.

Where I'd be careful: complex business logic in visual pipelines becomes hard to test and review; for that, code in Functions or a service is better, with Data Factory orchestrating. Version control through Git integration and deployment through ARM templates or pipelines is essential. Microsoft is also moving many of these capabilities into Microsoft Fabric.
Compared to our integration world, it overlaps with what an integration platform like MuleSoft does for file and data transfers, but is aimed more at data movement than API-led integration.

p17-912.q: Key Vault holds the most sensitive items: secrets, keys and certificates. Protecting the vault itself matters as much as using it.
p17-912.k: key vault soft delete, purge protection, key vault rbac vs access policies, key vault security, key vault firewall
x: Key Vault holds the most sensitive items: secrets, keys and certificates. Protecting the vault itself matters as much as using it.
Soft delete: deleted vaults and objects are kept for a retention period, 7 to 90 days, and can be recovered. It's now enabled on all vaults by default and can't be turned off.

Purge protection: prevents anyone, even administrators, from permanently purging deleted items or vaults until the retention period ends. This protects against malicious or accidental permanent deletion, especially important for encryption keys, because losing a key means losing the data it encrypts. Once enabled, it can't be disabled. I enable it for production vaults, especially those holding keys used for encryption at rest.

Access control: Azure RBAC is now the recommended permission model, instead of vault access policies. RBAC gives fine-grained roles, like Key Vault Secrets User for reading secrets, can be scoped down to individual secrets, is managed in the same way as other Azure permissions, and works with Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time admin access. Access policies were vault-wide and harder to audit.
Network: disable public network access and use private endpoints, or at least the vault firewall with allowed networks.
Separate vaults per application and environment, so access and blast radius are limited.
Monitoring: diagnostic logs to Log Analytics, with alerts on unusual access patterns, failed access attempts, and deletions.
Rotation: set expiry dates on secrets and certificates, with Event Grid notifications before expiry, and automate rotation where possible.

p17-913.q: An Azure landing zone is a pre-configured, well-governed environment into which workloads are deployed. It's the foundation from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework, so every team doesn't have to design networking, security and governance from scratch.
p17-913.k: azure landing zone, cloud adoption framework, enterprise scale landing zone, azure governance setup, management groups subscriptions design
x: An Azure landing zone is a pre-configured, well-governed environment into which workloads are deployed. It's the foundation from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework, so every team doesn't have to design networking, security and governance from scratch.
What it typically includes.

Management group and subscription structure: a hierarchy like platform, landing zones for corporate and online workloads, sandbox and decommissioned, with subscriptions per application or environment, so policies and access can be applied at the right level.
Identity: Entra ID integration, role assignments with least privilege, and Privileged Identity Management for administrative access.
Networking: a hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN topology, with central firewall, DNS, connectivity to on-premise through ExpressRoute or VPN, and private endpoints for PaaS services.
Governance: Azure Policy assignments enforcing rules, like allowed regions, required tags, no public IPs, and diagnostic settings on all resources.
Security: Defender for Cloud enabled, centralised logging to Log Analytics, and Sentinel for security operations.
Management: monitoring, backup, update management and cost management with budgets.
Platform vs application landing zones: a central platform team owns the shared parts, and application teams get subscriptions with guardrails, where they can deploy freely within policy.
Implementation: Microsoft provides reference implementations through Bicep and Terraform modules, deployed and maintained as code.

The AWS equivalent is a multi-account setup with Organizations, Control Tower and Service Control Policies. For an organisation moving workloads into the cloud, establishing the landing zone first avoids a sprawl of inconsistent, insecure subscriptions later.

p17-914.q: Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of identical or mixed VMs that scale automatically, similar to Auto Scaling groups in AWS.
p17-914.k: vm scale sets, vmss, azure autoscale vms, scale set orchestration modes, azure vm autoscale
x: Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of identical or mixed VMs that scale automatically, similar to Auto Scaling groups in AWS.
Key features.
Autoscale: rules based on metrics, like CPU, memory or queue length, or schedules, add and remove instances automatically, with minimum and maximum counts.
High availability: instances spread across availability zones and fault domains.
Load balancing: integrates with Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway, with health probes so unhealthy instances stop receiving traffic, and automatic instance repairs to replace them.

Orchestration modes: Flexible orchestration, now the default, supports mixing VM sizes and Spot with regular VMs, and treats instances as normal VMs; Uniform mode uses identical instances from one model, mainly for older large-scale workloads.
Upgrades: when the model changes, like a new image, rolling upgrade policies update instances in batches, and automatic OS image upgrades keep the OS patched.
Images: build a golden image with Azure Image Builder or Packer, stored in an Azure Compute Gallery, so new instances start ready to serve, rather than installing software at boot.

Uses: stateless web tiers that can't be containerised yet, like Windows and IIS applications; build agents, since Azure DevOps supports scale set agent pools that scale with pipeline demand; and batch or compute workloads.

For new applications, I'd usually prefer PaaS options like App Service, Container Apps or AKS, which handle more for you. But for lifting existing VM-based apps, scale sets bring elasticity and automated recovery without rewriting.

p17-915.q: An elastic pool lets many Azure SQL databases share a set amount of resources, compute and storage, instead of each database having its own fixed size. Databases use what they need from the pool, within per-database minimum and maximum limits.
p17-915.k: azure sql elastic pool, elastic pool many databases, database per tenant azure, edtu vcore pool, saas database pool
x: An elastic pool lets many Azure SQL databases share a set amount of resources, compute and storage, instead of each database having its own fixed size. Databases use what they need from the pool, within per-database minimum and maximum limits.

Why it helps: in a database-per-tenant or database-per-customer model, most databases are idle or lightly used most of the time, and their peaks happen at different times. Sizing each database for its own peak wastes money. In a pool, the combined capacity can be much smaller than the sum of individual peaks, so costs drop significantly while each database still gets resources when busy.

This pattern is very similar to a system with one database per study plus a master database. Studies have different activity levels: a few are in busy enrolment phases while others are in maintenance or closing, which fits pooling well.
Considerations.
Sizing: monitor combined usage and set the pool size to handle the busiest concurrent load, with per-database caps so one busy database can't starve others, the noisy neighbour problem.
Very large or consistently busy databases may be better as single databases outside the pool.
Operations across many databases: Elastic Jobs run T-SQL across all databases in a pool for maintenance or schema changes, and deployment pipelines need to update all databases consistently.
Limits: there's a maximum number of databases per pool, so very large estates need several pools.
High availability and backups work per database, as usual, and failover groups can include pooled databases.
On-premise, the equivalent is consolidating databases on shared instances, but elastic pools add per-database limits and easier scaling.

p17-916.q: Both are excellent, but they're built for different access patterns.
p17-916.k: cosmos db vs azure sql, nosql vs sql azure, when to use cosmos db, document database vs relational, azure database choice
x: Both are excellent, but they're built for different access patterns.

Azure SQL is a relational database: strong schema, joins, complex queries and reporting, foreign keys, multi-row ACID transactions across any tables, and mature tooling. It fits most business systems, especially with complex relationships and reporting needs, like clinical supply data with studies, sites, kits and shipments all linked together.

Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database, with document, key-value and other APIs. It offers single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale, automatic horizontal scaling through partitioning, multi-region writes, tunable consistency levels, and a change feed. Transactions are limited to items within one logical partition, and queries across partitions are more expensive. You design the data model around access patterns, often denormalised, with the partition key as the most important decision.

When I'd choose Cosmos DB: very high scale with predictable access by key, like user profiles, device telemetry, session state, product catalogues or event data; globally distributed apps needing low latency in many regions; flexible schemas that change often; and event-driven architectures using the change feed.
When I'd choose Azure SQL: complex relationships and queries, ad hoc reporting, strong consistency across many entities, and teams with strong SQL skills. Most line-of-business systems fall here.
Cost: Cosmos DB charges by request units, so inefficient queries or poor partition keys get expensive quickly; Azure SQL charges by compute and storage.
Often the best architecture uses both: SQL for the core transactional system, and Cosmos DB for specific high-scale features.

p17-917.q: Operational tasks, like starting and stopping VMs, cleaning up resources, rotating something on a schedule, or running maintenance scripts on servers, can be automated in Azure in a few ways.
p17-917.k: azure automation, runbooks azure, powershell runbook, operations automation azure, azure update manager
x: Operational tasks, like starting and stopping VMs, cleaning up resources, rotating something on a schedule, or running maintenance scripts on servers, can be automated in Azure in a few ways.

Azure Automation: runs PowerShell or Python runbooks in the cloud or on machines through Hybrid Runbook Workers, which run on on-premise or other servers. Good for traditional IT automation written by operations teams in PowerShell, with schedules, webhooks, shared credentials and modules. Hybrid workers make it useful for on-premise tasks, like maintenance on servers in a data centre. Its older Update Management and change tracking features have moved to Azure Update Manager and Azure Monitor.

Azure Functions: event-driven code, in .NET, PowerShell, Python or others, triggered by timers, queues, HTTP or events. Better for developer-built automation with tests, dependency injection, source control and CI/CD, and for reacting to events, like processing a resource change from Event Grid.
Logic Apps: low-code workflows connecting services, like sending approvals or tickets when something happens.
Azure Update Manager: patching for Azure and Arc-enabled servers on schedules.

How I choose: PowerShell-heavy, admin-owned tasks, especially on servers, go to Automation; developer-owned, event-driven or complex logic goes to Functions; integrations with business tools and approvals go to Logic Apps.

Whichever I use: managed identity instead of stored credentials, code in source control with pipelines deploying it, logging and alerting on failures, and least-privilege permissions, because automation accounts often have broad rights and are attractive targets.

p17-918.q: Yes. Application Insights doesn't require the application to run in Azure; it only needs outbound connectivity to Azure Monitor endpoints, directly, through a proxy, or through Azure Monitor Private Link.
p17-918.k: application insights on premise, app insights iis, application insights .net framework, azure monitor agent on prem, hybrid monitoring azure
x: Yes. Application Insights doesn't require the application to run in Azure; it only needs outbound connectivity to Azure Monitor endpoints, directly, through a proxy, or through Azure Monitor Private Link.
Options for on-premise IIS apps.

SDK-based instrumentation: add the Application Insights SDK to the .NET Framework 4.8 or ASP.NET Core application, configured with a connection string. It collects requests, dependencies like SQL and HTTP calls, exceptions, performance counters and custom telemetry. This gives the most control and custom events.

OpenTelemetry: the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro for ASP.NET Core, or the OpenTelemetry SDK with the Azure Monitor exporter, which keeps instrumentation vendor-neutral, so the same code could also send data to Datadog or another backend later.
Agent-based, codeless instrumentation: the Application Insights Agent, a PowerShell module, can instrument IIS-hosted .NET apps on-premise without code changes, which is useful for legacy apps.
Server-level monitoring: the Azure Monitor agent, ideally on Arc-enabled servers, collects Windows event logs, IIS logs and performance counters into Log Analytics.

Considerations for regulated, on-premise systems: data leaves the data centre, so confirm what telemetry contains, avoiding personal or clinical data in logs and custom properties; check data residency and retention; use sampling to control cost; and ensure the security team approves the outbound connection.

In our case, monitoring goes to Splunk and Grafana for the on-premise platform, and OpenTelemetry with Datadog for the newest services, so Application Insights would be an option rather than the current choice, but it shows how cloud monitoring can cover on-premise apps.

p17-919.q: The Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus SDK provides ServiceBusProcessor, which handles receiving, concurrency and lock management, so I don't write receive loops by hand.
p17-919.k: servicebusprocessor, service bus consumer dotnet, azure service bus dotnet, peek lock dotnet, service bus retry
x: The Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus SDK provides ServiceBusProcessor, which handles receiving, concurrency and lock management, so I don't write receive loops by hand.

Setup: create one ServiceBusClient per application, registered as a singleton, using DefaultAzureCredential with managed identity rather than connection strings. Create a processor for a queue or topic subscription with options: MaxConcurrentCalls to control parallelism, PrefetchCount for throughput, AutoCompleteMessages set to false so I complete messages explicitly, and MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration so locks are renewed for long-running processing.

Handlers: ProcessMessageAsync receives each message. I deserialise and validate the body, process it idempotently, checking the message id against a processed-messages store or using upserts, then call CompleteMessageAsync. For invalid messages that will never succeed, DeadLetterMessageAsync with a reason and description. For transient failures, let the exception propagate or abandon the message, so it's retried, and after MaxDeliveryCount attempts, Service Bus dead-letters it automatically. ProcessErrorAsync logs errors from the processor itself, like connection issues.
Hosting: run the processor inside a BackgroundService, starting it in StartAsync and stopping it gracefully in StopAsync, so in-flight messages finish during deployments.
Ordering: for per-entity ordering, use sessions with ServiceBusSessionProcessor.
Delayed retries: schedule a copy of the message for later with an attempt count, and complete the original, for backoff beyond immediate redelivery.
Observability: the SDK supports distributed tracing, so traces connect producer and consumer; monitor active and dead-letter message counts with alerts.
These are the same reliability habits as our RabbitMQ consumers, translated to Service Bus.
